Taiwan tracks 12 Chinese military aircraft and 9 ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:46:53 UTC
13:46:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 12 Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and three official ships between 6 a.m. on Saturday and the same time Sunday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Five of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s southwestern air defense identification zone, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 63 times and ships 116 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Coalition defends migration cuts on economic grounds, rejects One Nation-style bans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:37:34 UTC
13:37:34 KST

In Brief
- Coalition says cutting migration to 100,000 would lift productivity by prioritising higher-skilled workers.
- Taylor rejected One Nation-style country bans, saying migrants should be judged on conduct and character.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has defended the Coalition's proposed migration overhaul as an economic reform designed to boost productivity, while rejecting the idea of banning migrants based on their country of origin.
The Coalition's plan would cut net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000, about a third of current levels, while increasing the share of "high-value" migrants entering Australia.
They have called it the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history".
However, Taylor's comments to ABC's Insiders on Sunday also appeared to mark a shift in tone from his last appearance on the show.
This time, he repeatedly framed the changes as an economic measure aimed at boosting productivity and competitiveness, rather than focusing on national security or cultural concerns.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Taylor highlights migration plan as economic reform
Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.
"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.
"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.
"It will raise productivity, it will raise competitiveness, it will raise the average income of the people coming into this city."
Taylor said the policy would increase the average skill level of migrants entering Australia while reducing overall numbers through changes to a range of visa programs, including student, graduate and bridging visas.
He repeatedly argued migration settings should be geared towards lifting productivity rather than simply increasing population growth.
"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone," he said.
Bringing in more highly skilled migrants would put downward pressure on inflation because it would raise productivity, Taylor argued, saying "this is pretty simple economics".
"When you bring someone to Australia, you are bringing demand and supply. If that person is low-skilled, you are bringing more demand than supply. If they are high-skilled, you are bringing the opposite, actually bringing more supply.
"One of the reasons why we've had a collapse in productivity in this country ... is that our immigration program has not been working to drive up our productivity and it should be."
He also defended the Coalition's proposal to halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places, saying "charity begins at home" and such measures were designed to "balance the budget".
Taylor distances Coalition from One Nation approach
While much of Taylor's defence of the policy focused on economics, he also sought to draw a distinction between the Coalition's approach and proposals advanced by One Nation.
The comments marked a different emphasis from Taylor's previous appearance on the same program in April, when he argued migrants from "bad countries" posed a higher risk to Australia.
Pressed at the time on which countries he considered "bad", Taylor pointed to Iran and referred to security concerns involving people arriving from Gaza.
Asked on Sunday why the Coalition had not gone as far as One Nation in proposing immigration restrictions based on nationality, Taylor rejected the comparison.
"I've always said we will discriminate not based on the country someone comes from or their race or their religion, but based on the person and whether that person is a suitable person to be a resident or citizen of this country," he said.
"That's what we should focus on, and we should judge people on their character and conduct, not the colour of their skin."
Taylor maintained that some countries could present higher risks for security agencies to assess.
"It is true that risks are higher where there is a bad regime — there is no question about that."
"That doesn't mean screen them all out. That means make sure you are assessing those risks appropriately."
One Nation has previously proposed measures targeting migration from specific countries, including pausing new migration from countries subject to a federal government 'do not travel' warning.
However, Taylor also linked the Coalition's migration policy to a broader focus on screening prospective visa holders.
"People who do not believe in our system of law, people who do not believe in our basic freedoms, they shouldn't be coming to this country," he said.
"If they've got here on a visa, they should be thrown out."
Later on Sunday, other Coalition figures reiterated those sentiments, following reports that the flydubai co-pilot accused of attempting to hijack a flight bound for Israel was allegedly radicalised while studying in Melbourne.
Opposition home affairs spokesperson Jonno Duniam said there was no place for "hate preachers who spread extremism, glorify terrorism or encourage violence".
"That is why the Coalition will tighten visa laws to keep those who preach hatred out of Australia and deport non-citizens who promote violent extremism," he said.
“At a federal level, we also need stronger visa screening, better intelligence sharing and properly resourced counter-terrorism agencies. That is why the Coalition has committed to establishing an Enhanced Screening Coordination Centre to bring together our intelligence, policing and border protection capabilities."
The economic debate over immigration levels
Taylor's argument rests on the idea that a smaller, more highly skilled migration intake would boost productivity while reducing pressure on housing and infrastructure.
However, the economic impacts of migration cuts remain heavily debated among economists, migration experts, business groups and policymakers.
Critics argue lower migration can reduce labour supply, tax and visa revenue, population growth, consumer spending and business activity, particularly in industries that rely heavily on migrant workers.
A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education.
The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.
Debate over migration's impact on housing has also intensified in recent years. While higher migration can increase demand for homes, some experts argue migrant workers are also needed to address labour shortages in the construction sector.
In September, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said migration cuts would inevitably come with economic trade-offs and warned no industry would be immune from their effects.
"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he told SBS News.
"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure — as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."
Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.
One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which they say will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.
— With additional reporting by Charis Chang and Nigel Gladstone.

One year after ceasefire, Gaza’s promised ‘day after’ has yet to arrive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:23:51 UTC
13:23:51 KST

One year after the ceasefire took effect in the Gaza Strip, all the Israeli captives have been returned, but much of what the agreement promised the Palestinians remains unrealized.
Israeli attacks have continued, the military withdrawal has stalled and partly reversed, governance arrangements remain incomplete, and large-scale reconstruction has yet to begin.
Most of Gaza’s roughly 2.1 million people remain displaced, many living in tents, damaged buildings, or amid rubble, as Palestinian authorities say the continuing attacks are an extension of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, launched on Oct. 8, 2023.
The ceasefire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, after mediation by Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the US providing for a phased Israeli withdrawal, expanded aid, new governance arrangements, and reconstruction.
Israeli captives returned
On Oct. 13, 2025, Hamas released the remaining 20 living Israeli captives as Israel freed 1,968 Palestinian detainees, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The transfer of remains continued until Jan. 26, 2026, when the Israeli army announced the recovery of the last body.
Israeli attacks continue
But the ceasefire did not bring an end to Israeli attacks in Gaza.
Over the past year, Israeli violations of the agreement have killed more than 1,470 Palestinians and wounded over 5,180, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye said in August that continued Israeli attacks violated the agreement and were obstructing implementation of its second phase.
Israeli withdrawal reversed
Before the ceasefire was declared, the Israeli army controlled about 75% of Gaza.
The agreement initially brought a partial withdrawal to the so-called “yellow line,” leaving around 53% of the enclave under Israeli military deployment, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
But the pullback stalled and later reversed.
By late June, OCHA said Israeli forces had expanded westward beyond the yellow line, leaving 64.9% of Gaza under direct Israeli control or tighter restrictions.
By August, the UN said nearly two-thirds of the enclave was inaccessible to Palestinians or subject to severe restrictions.
Second phase remains stalled
A 15-point roadmap linked restrictions on the weapons of Hamas and other Palestinian factions to additional Israeli withdrawals, deployment of an international force, transfer of governance, and reconstruction.
Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye said on Aug. 3 that Hamas and other Palestinian factions had accepted the roadmap, including its provision on weapons.
Later that month, eight countries, including Türkiye, Egypt, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, said Israel had rejected the roadmap, obstructing implementation of the broader plan.
Governance transition incomplete
A technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, headed by Ali Shaath, was formed in January to oversee civilian affairs during the transitional period.
But the transfer of governing responsibilities remains incomplete, while a planned international stabilization force has yet to be deployed.
Reconstruction still out of reach
Despite provisions to increase humanitarian aid, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said in September that Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing for goods after the Zikim crossing was closed in May.
Israeli restrictions also continued on materials needed for shelter and construction.
The UN, European Union, and World Bank estimate Gaza will need $71.4 billion over 10 years for recovery and reconstruction, including $26.3 billion in the first 18 months.
Their assessment found that 1.9 million Palestinians had been displaced and 371,888 housing units damaged or destroyed.
OCHA said in September that Israeli restrictions were still blocking urgently needed shelter supplies, including thousands of tents and construction materials.
One year after the ceasefire, the issue of the captives is closed. For Gaza’s displaced population, however, the promised transition from war to recovery has yet to arrive.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Israeli attacks on Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian figures.

Russia reports a major Yandex Cloud outage following an attack on a Yandex data center. The problems may have affected more than 80 services.
Russia is reporting a large-scale disruption to the Yandex Cloud platform, which is being linked to an attack by the Ukrainian Defense Forces on a third data center of the Yandex company. According to preliminary reports, the problems affected more than 80 services and infrastructure components, UNN writes.
Details
In particular, disruptions have been reported in the operation of the popular services Yandex Music, Yandex Home, and Telemost. There are also reports of disruptions to the cloud infrastructure used by companies and developers to host applications, store information, and process data.
The services reportedly affected by the disruption include Compute Cloud, Virtual Private Cloud, Managed Service for Kubernetes, Cloud Functions, as well as load-balancing and network-management tools.
The problems may have affected more than 80 services
The unavailability of certain data-storage systems and managed databases has also been reported, including Object Storage, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, MySQL, YDB, and OpenSearch.

At the same time, the extent of the damage to the data center, the duration of the disruptions, and the direct link between the attack and the technical problems require independent confirmation.

Hong Kong finance chief highlights 4 priorities ahead of Apec meeting this month
Meeting will focus on areas that play to city’s strengths, such as fiscal policies that support livelihoods, digital infrastructure and young talent
The Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong this month will focus on fiscal policies that support livelihoods, digital infrastructure financing, inclusive finance and young financial talent, underlining the city’s role as an international financial centre, the finance chief said.
“These four priorities are areas of strength for Hong Kong and fields in which we can make an active contribution,” Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday.
“Hosting the finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong highlights the central government’s strong support for the city and reflects the city’s status as an important international financial centre in the region.”
About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from Apec’s 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21 at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. It will be the first time Hong Kong is hosting the event.

US says fighter jet struck cargo ship trying to break Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:20:57 UTC
13:20:57 KST

The U.S. military said overnight Saturday that it had disabled a commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman after its crew ignored warnings and attempted to breach the naval blockade on Iran. 
"A U.S. fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision-guided munition," U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said. "The strike completely disabled the vessel's propulsion system without injuring any crew members." CENTCOM said the cargo ship had attempted to navigate regional waters after departing an Iranian port.
"US forces resumed the blockade on all vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports on July 14," CENTCOM said. "During three months of strict enforcement, four commercial vessels have been disabled and 135 ships have been forced to change course and turn back. In addition, U.S. forces destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' multibillion-dollar shadow shipping network during the same period."
CENTCOM urged all mariners to comply with blockade warnings issued by U.S. forces, continue monitoring official Notices to Mariners and contact U.S. naval forces when sailing in the Gulf of Oman and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) reported that a tanker had been struck by an unidentified missile in the Strait of Hormuz, sparking a fire on board. No crew members were injured.
The U.S. operation comes amid heightened regional tensions following a ballistic missile attack on the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. At least 12 people were killed, including an American citizen, and more than 300 were injured. Following the attack, President Donald Trump said the United States might join Saudi Arabia in strikes against the Houthis, but emphasized that he had not yet made a decision.
In recent days, Trump has declared that the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. He also said Washington and Tehran were holding "productive discussions" and claimed that oil was flowing through the Strait of Hormuz at record levels.
In a post on his Truth Social platform overnight Wednesday, Trump wrote: "We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everyone that while Iran is in very bad shape, both economically and militarily, and while the blockade will remain in full force, with oil flowing at a record number of barrels through the Strait of Hormuz (22 million barrels just last night, with not a single barrel coming from or going to Iran!), we will not attack Iran at any time before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon!"
Trump's remarks about "productive discussions" came just a day after he said he did not really want another agreement with Iran. Speaking at a campaign rally alongside Republican candidates in San Antonio, Texas, he said: "I don't think another deal is really something I want to do." Despite weeks of stalled negotiations, the president claimed that "Iran is ready to offer us anything." He added that his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, was working on an agreement and "doing very well."

SYDNEY, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Rescue efforts are underway for 73 passengers stranded aboard the MV Awka in the Solomon Islands after the vessel's engine failed, with aircraft and vessels mobilized to deliver essential supplies.
The vessel issued a distress signal at around 7 a.m. local time on Friday while traveling from Anuta to Vanikoro in Temotu Province. The 73 passengers do not include the crew, the Solomon Islands Broadcasting Corporation (SIBC) reported on Saturday.
MV Awka has been drifting at sea amid rough seas and swells, raising concerns about conditions on board, SIBC News reported.
France, Australia and New Zealand had received the distress signal and offered assistance, including food, drinking water and medical supplies, Temotu Province Premier Stanley Tehiahua told SIBC News. ■

At least 40 houses swept away in flash flood in Nepal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:12:26 CST
13:12:26 KST

KATHMANDU, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- At least 40 houses and two suspension bridges were swept away by a flash flood in the Kaligandaki River in Nepal's Gorkha district on Sunday morning, a local official said.
A landslide blocked the river in Chumanubri Rural Municipality, causing a flash flood when the blockage broke.
"At least 40 houses in five different settlements have been swept away in the flood," Laxmi Gurung, vice-chairperson of the rural municipality, told Xinhua.
No casualties have been reported so far. Residents living along the river corridor were asked to evacuate their homes early Sunday morning following warnings of a possible flood.
Authorities are still gathering details of the damage, Gurung said. Rescue teams, including personnel dispatched from Kathmandu, have reached the disaster site, while further assessments of the disaster are ongoing. ■

US Justice Department probes major TV networks for suspension of Trump pool coverage

The US Justice Department on Saturday launched an antitrust investigation into five major television networks after they temporarily refused to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, NBC News reported.
The probe targets NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN, and Fox News, which collectively make up the White House television press pool, and take turns covering the president’s public engagements and trips. They suspended pool participation last month after three major outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and website Politico – were all banned from the White House.
A Justice Department official confirmed that the five networks were issued “civil investigative demands” on Friday as part of the investigation.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” said department spokeswoman Emily Covington.
“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
In the pool, the network assigned to pool duty shares its reporting materials, including video and audio recordings, with other news organizations.
When contacted for comment on the investigation, the White House did not provide a response.
ABC News said it had yet to receive a formal notice from the Justice Department but anticipated receiving one. NBC, CBS, and CNN declined to comment, while Fox News did not respond to a request for comment.
The investigation comes amid growing tensions between the Trump administration and the White House press corps.
In September, Trump accused journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico of spreading “FAKE NEWS” and barred their outlets from the White House grounds. The three later filed a legal challenge to the ban which is still playing out in court.
Following CNN’s removal from the pool rotation, the remaining television networks temporarily withdrew from their coverage assignments.

Unsung turtle conservation heroes in Malaysia’s Sabah unite to fight poachers

Roziah Jelali has a tip or two on catching a turtle poacher: carrying a pair of binoculars and having patience in spades are key to doing the job well.
The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah tracking a man whom she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles. Once thriving off the azure seas of Omadal Island in the Malaysian state, many turtles had been hunted down, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts.
Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands.
“Every day after my patrol, I would sit near my house with my binoculars and watch him. He was initially operating on Bum Bum Island, then he came to Omadal,” Roziah told This Week in Asia.

Admission scores for physiotherapy degree programmes at three Hong Kong tertiary institutions fell by as much as 10 per cent this year compared with 2025, amid gloomy career prospects in the sector, the latest data shows.

‘I get really upset when I visit’: the harsh reality of life in a high-security hospital in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:00:16 UTC
13:00:16 KST

Rampton high-security hospital in Nottinghamshire was built in 1912. Everything about the bleak, remote facility for mentally ill people is forbidding, says Jan Neate. “I get really upset going there,” she says. “Even though I really want to see Jake, visiting is an ordeal.”
Jake, 45, is Neate’s son. He has been held at Rampton for eight years. In 2017, many years after being diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, he killed his partner, Suzanne Brown, and was deemed mentally unfit to stand trial.
When Neate visits him, her fingerprints and biometrics are taken before she is escorted in. Jake is searched when he is brought into the room and searched again when he leaves. Mother and son are permitted a hug, which is often distressing. “Both of us usually cry when we hug,” says Neate. “It reminds me of what our lives were like before and I think it reminds Jake of that, too.”
England has three high-security hospitals – Rampton, Ashworth in Merseyside and Broadmoor in Berkshire. According to the NHS trust that manages Rampton, secure hospitals are for people with severe mental health disorders who pose grave or immediate danger to themselves or to the public. They have accommodated some of the country’s most abhorred criminals, including Peter Sutcliffe, Ronnie Kray, Ian Brady, Ian Huntley and Beverley Allitt. Valdo Calocane, who was convicted of killing three people in 2023 and diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, has spent time in Rampton.
These high-security hospitals have been in the spotlight this year, after it was reported that Axel Rudakubana – who murdered three young girls at a dance class in Southport in 2024 – had been moved from Belmarsh, a category A high-security prison, to Broadmoor, which has security equivalent to a category B prison. Officials said the move was due to the deterioration of his mental health and the fact he could no longer be safely managed in prison. The plan is to return Rudakubana to Belmarsh after treatment.
Throughout its history, Broadmoor has had a reputation for being tough, even menacing, given the notoriety of various people housed within its walls. Nonetheless, some saw this move as the start of a “cushier” life for Rudakubana and an attempt by him to manipulate the system. Mark Fairhurst, the chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said the move would afford him freedoms not available in a high-security prison.
Relatives of those incarcerated in high-security hospitals are usually unwilling to speak out because of the understandable stigma attached to the violent acts committed by those inside. But while Jake did something terrible, Neate is keen for people to understand the reality of this form of incarceration.
What happens inside high-security hospitals raises important questions about how we treat people who have committed extreme violence but who are also vulnerable themselves. These are difficult, emotive questions about mental health, retribution and rehabilitation.
Jake is sometimes placed in a form of segregation known as seclusion; Neate knows of at least two periods of seclusion so far this year. In both cases, she believes the seclusion lasted several days. She is given very little information about what happens to him during these periods, which she says is terrifying: “I dread the phone ringing one day and staff telling me that something terrible has happened to him.”
If Jake refuses his medication, his doctors have permission to administer it via injection.
He has been having seizures and injuring himself. “On one occasion, he fell and injured his shoulder when he was having a seizure,” says Neate. “On another occasion, also when he was thought to be having a seizure, he fell and injured his head.”
Jake was taken to an ordinary hospital after receiving these injuries, but Neate wasn’t given any information about where he was. Whenever she calls Rampton, to see how Jake is, she gets the briefest of replies – confirmation that he is eating, drinking and sleeping, but nothing else. “Anyone who thinks Rampton is an easy option for someone like Jake really doesn’t understand how things are,” she says.
Inspections of Rampton carried out by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) between July 2019 and June 2023 identified a number of failings, including a shortage of staff. Some therapy staff were used on wards to plug the gaps, leading to a reduction in patients’ therapeutic programmes. Concerns were also raised about overnight lock-ups in patients’ rooms being extended due to staff shortages, along with periods of “confinement” during the day. Poor medicine management was identified and there were repeated issues with the safeguarding of patients.
A focused review of Rampton by the CQC in March 2024 said staffing levels had improved and the use of confinement had decreased, but there remained a “culture of relying on therapy and education staff to cover nursing gaps”. While medicine management had also improved, staff did not always follow the correct procedure, “which could constitute an assault and trespass against the person”. The review added: “While we observed staff providing person-centred care, we remain concerned that people in long-term segregation were not always treated with dignity, compassion and respect.”
In a May 2025 CQC report, the hospital had its rating upgraded from “inadequate” to “requires improvement”. It was found that the trust still had work to do to address staff shortages and to support staff.
As a boy, Jake was happy and playful, says Neate: “We went on loads of outings like swimming, football and visits to museums. He was a really nice boy.” When he was 17, he started to get ill. “He became paranoid and was admitted to hospital for two weeks as a voluntary patient. The doctors said if he stopped smoking skunk, he would recover.”
He went on to study geography at the University of Birmingham, but left when he was headhunted by a bank in Canary Wharf, London. Then, at 20, he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. He had to leave his job, but he built up a window-cleaning round where he lived in Essex and he was popular with his customers. To treat his schizophrenia, he was put on the drug clozapine and he gave up recreational drugs, living successfully in the community. At that point, says Neate, Jake had an illness, but he also had a life.
In 2007, Jake and Suzanne met at a disco in Harlow. “He was 26 and she was 23,” says Neate. Suzanne, who was known as Sue, worked as a nursery nurse. “Sue had such a sweet, kind nature. Whenever she came to my house, she would always bring a homemade cake with her. She really looked after Jake, made sure he took his medication and went to all his appointments with him. She was a very giving person. I miss her.”
At this stage, “Jake had dreams and ambitions and he loved Sue to pieces”, says Neate. “His schizophrenia then was nothing like it is now. He was never violent. I don’t think he and Sue even argued with each other.” When they bought their first flat together, in Braintree, they had a new kitchen fitted and were full of plans for the future.
Jake had received excellent care and support from the NHS mental health trust in Harlow, but their move meant Jake’s care was transferred to a new trust. For 10 years, clozapine had kept him stable. But in 2017, after he started to experience physical side-effects – severe constipation, urine retention and an inability to eat or sleep – the drug was stopped suddenly.
Withdrawal from clozapine is supposed to be closely monitored, but Jake, Sue and Neate were unaware of this. “None of us had any idea what could happen as a result of him being taken off clozapine,” says Neate. “Sue and Jake really trusted their clinical team. I thought that the worst that might happen would be that Jake might have a row with Sue. I had no concept of the gravity and severity of it all. It’s a heavy-duty drug and taking him off it should have been treated as a medical emergency.”
Jake began to experience psychosis and repeatedly tried to seek help, but little was forthcoming. Jake wrote to his doctors, listing the symptoms he was experiencing after being taken off clozapine, but he didn’t receive a response. Neate says she made dozens of phone calls and sent numerous emails during this period, trying to get help for Jake, but this didn’t result in any interventions. She believes that, had there been effective responses to the pleas she, Sue and Jake were making, the horror that followed could have been avoided.
In texts to his mother in this period, Jake said he had been researching private hospitals. “I feel a bit angry that no one told me of the implications of going on to this drug,” he wrote. “I would like to be an inpatient to deal with all the issues.”
His condition worsened. On 15 December 2017, a mental health worker visited the couple’s flat and said telephone support would be put in place and a home visit organised for the following week. That evening, Neate received a call from Sue, “screaming and hysterical”. She said Jake was hurting her. Neate told her to get out of the flat and immediately called the police.
Three hours after that call, police officers arrived at the flat. By then, it was far too late. Jake had stabbed Suzanne 173 times.
Neate says she didn’t understand the severity of what was happening until the police called her and said: “‘We’ve taken the dead woman from the flat.’ All I could say was: ‘Oh my God, what do you mean?’ … I am always asking myself if I could have prevented this happening if I had been close by.”
Jake was initially charged with murder, but was found to be unfit to stand trial. He said he had been hearing voices coming out of the TV urging him to kill Sue and was having terrible thoughts about God, the devil and the battle between good and evil.
When a person is deemed mentally unfit to stand trial, a trial of the facts takes place. Rather than deciding on a defendant’s criminal guilt or innocence, this determines whether the defendant carried out the alleged acts. The trial found that Jake had killed Sue. The jury heard that Sue was devoted to Jake and that she had looked after him when he was unwell with “the patience of a saint”.
“I miss Sue so much,” says Neate. “I miss her lovely sunny nature … We used to go on outings together, to spas and to the cinema. I feel so lonely. I don’t have Jake as he was and I don’t have Sue. Jake was a perpetrator, but I believe he was also a victim of the system.”
A report on mental health services after Sue’s killing identified eight failings and made seven recommendations for change. It found that an up-to-date risk assessment was not carried out after the sudden cessation of clozapine and that there was neither appropriate professional monitoring nor guidance for Jake and his family. It also found that clinical information was not communicated consistently within and between teams.
An investigation for the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) found that the police response was delayed because it was initially miscategorised by the call handler. The IOPC did not identify any misconduct, but found that two members of staff in the control room “had not met expected standards”.
When Jake was sent to Rampton, it was supposed to be temporary. Neate was told that when he was more stable he could be moved to a medium-security unit with a less restrictive regime. Jake is held at Rampton on what is known as a section 37 order; the Home Office has to give permission for the release of those held under this type of indefinite hospital order.
In a letter to Neate on 28 July 2026, Jake’s doctor at Rampton wrote: “In recent years we have seen several episodes of decline in his condition, but overall he is making progress.” He also described Jake as having a serious mental health disorder that is “very resistant to treatment”.
A spokesperson for Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS foundation trust said: “While we cannot comment on the care of individual patients, we fully understand that families want the very best for their loved ones and we recognise how difficult it can be when progress feels slow. We always welcome families raising concerns with us and are committed to working with them openly.
“Decisions about moving a patient to a lower level of security are made carefully, taking account of their recovery and wellbeing alongside wider safety considerations. For many patients at Rampton these decisions also involve the Ministry of Justice and the receiving service, which can mean the process takes time.”
Neate firmly believes Jake is deteriorating at Rampton. “Jake says he is fighting a battle between good and evil and says he has to rescue Sue,” she says. “He isn’t the same person he used to be … I don’t think he’s always treated as a human being, as a person. Everything is so clinical there. They talk about his presentation, as if he’s a thing, rather than a human with a heart.
“I feel like I’m banging my head against a wall trying to help him. All I want for Jake is a life that’s reasonable, with some hope in it. People who are mentally ill are entitled to a bit of care. But I don’t believe Jake’s getting that. It’s not at all cushy or luxurious for him in Rampton, very far from it.”

Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned.
Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”.
“Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said.
Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt.
Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East.
The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures.
But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs.
“What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said.
“We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.”
Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs.
De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9%. That is really, really high.”
He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring. “For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.”
His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs.
It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8% since 2019, and wider public spending by 2%.
Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.”
Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring.
Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.”
De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action.
“We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said.
He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields.
But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. And that coordinated policy for developing countries cannot just be, ‘you are at the end of the line and we’ll see what happens’.”
He declined to say what the specific response should be, but stressed that it should create “time and space” for developing countries to carry out much-needed changes.
During the Covid crisis, G20 nations implemented a temporary standstill on debt repayments for developing countries.
De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.

US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott for antitrust violation

US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott
October 11, 2026
The US Department of Justice announced on Saturday that it is investigating whether the White House press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month, violated the nation's anti trust law.
Group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law, spokesperson Emily Covington said.
"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said.
The networks under the scrutiny are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate.
"The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access," Zamora said on X. "The public's right to know depends on that access."
Why is Trump's press pool under investigation?
On September 21, a pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage after the Trump administration barred news networks CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying covering the president was a "privilege, not a right."
As a result, the five television networks suspended coverage in protest and refused to provide replacement program.
The news outlets also sued the administration, accusing it of violating free speech and free press rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and pursuing retaliation over their coverage.
On September 24, the White House reinstated their press credentials after a US district Judge ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.
The president has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and clashed with reporters during interviews.
The White House press pool is a roating group of news outlets which cover the president and accompany him on official duties.
CNN is one of the five news organizations, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBS, that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the cost of covering the president and take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
The White House press pool has now become a proxy for a fight over press freedom.

Tsai urges democratic cooperation, says Taiwan offers more than chips

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) called for greater international cooperation with Taiwan, saying the country can contribute to regional peace and democratic resilience beyond its semiconductor and technology industries.
Speaking at a forum titled “Taiwan Beyond the Headlines: How Taiwan Builds Resilience Through Democracy,” Tsai discussed political polarization, the value of restraint in leadership, and Taiwan’s role in strengthening international cooperation, per Liberty Times.
A day earlier, Tsai delivered an address at a VIP dinner for the Stanford DEFCON 2026 Technology & National Security Conference. Her talk covered Taiwan’s asymmetric defense, indigenous submarine program, semiconductor industry, and drone supply chains.
The Hoover forum focused more closely on democratic resilience and political cooperation. Former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Larry Diamond, scholars, researchers, and Stanford students attended the event.
Tsai began with a lighthearted reflection on her political career, noting that some people had described her as “boring” during her presidency. She argued that restraint can be valuable in an era when provocation often attracts more attention than measured leadership.
This approach, she said, was particularly important when balancing Taiwan’s security needs with the search for common ground necessary to sustain democratic progress.
When discussing Taiwan, people often ask why the country matters, Tsai said. An equally important question, she added, is what Taiwan can contribute to the broader democratic community.
“Taiwan can offer more than just semiconductors and technology,” she said, pointing to the country’s experience in protecting elections, maintaining public trust, and fostering cooperation between government and civil society.
Cooperation with Taiwan would not simply help the country but also strengthen a broader system of peace, trade, technological development, and democratic cooperation, she argued. “Taiwan is ready to participate in this joint effort,” she said.
Tsai said the international order was undergoing a profound transformation but stressed that external threats and coercion would not weaken Taiwan’s determination to engage with the world and contribute to the international community, per Liberty Times.
She also cautioned against defining Taiwan solely through the risks it faces, arguing that the country should be recognized for its democratic achievements and contributions to global cooperation.
Tsai concluded by emphasizing the need for leaders and societies to work through disagreements, exercise patience, and seek common ground. Although such an approach might appear boring, she said, the ability to show restraint and cooperate across differences is precisely what leadership requires in a polarized political environment.
After the forum, Tsai visited Startup Island Taiwan, a startup hub in Palo Alto, California, where she met with young entrepreneurs and discussed technology and innovation. She emphasized the human dimension of technological development and joked that she had not asked artificial intelligence for help while serving as president, drawing laughter from the audience.

Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:41:58 UTC
12:41:58 KST

Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
Medical services in Taiz risk shutting down as fuel, medicines, and supplies run alarmingly low under Houthi blockade.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”.
Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.
It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.
Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.
It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.
It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.
“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.
Renewed siege
The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.
Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.
The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.
The renewed siege took shape in early October.
The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.
Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.
He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.
Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).
“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.
The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.
“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast has been completely shut down following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said on Oct. 11, citing the company.
The reported strike marks the third near-consecutive day of attacks on Yandex data centers in Russia, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
Earlier on Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir.
"There are power interruptions in the ru-central1-a availability zone. The team is working to resolve the issue," the company said in a statement published on its official Telegram channel.
Yandex Go users across Russia reported being unable to order taxis on Oct. 11, with similar disruptions reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, according to Russian independent media outlet Ostorozhno Novosti..
The outlet also reported that Yandex Pro, an application used by taxi drivers and couriers, was unavailable, while employees experienced problems accessing internal support systems. Users also reported disruptions to Yandex's smart home services.
Russian independent media outlet ASTRA reported that Yandex Cloud experienced power disruptions at its Vladimir data center following warnings of a drone attack in the region. Ukrainian monitoring channels also circulated images purportedly showing a fire near the facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the images or the extent of damage at the facility or to any of the Yandex apps or services.
The latest incident follows two drone strikes that Yandex has publicly acknowledged.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing it to suspend operations completely. Yandex said it could not yet determine when the facility's equipment could be restored.
A second strike on Oct. 9 damaged the company's data center in Kaluga, disabling several modules and potentially disrupting services.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine was responding to Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. "We always respond in kind," he told journalists, adding that Russia "has been and still is striking our data centers."
In a statement on Oct. 9, Yandex described its data centers as critical infrastructure for its services and said employees were working around the clock to restore operations.
On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
The reported attacks come amid an expanding campaign of Ukrainian long-range strikes against infrastructure inside Russia.

Hurricane Simon strengthens into Category 4 storm as it takes aim at Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:28:31 UTC
12:28:31 KST

Hurricane Simon strengthens into Category 4 storm as it takes aim at Mexico's Pacific coast
Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrels toward Mexico's Pacific coast.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said Saturday that Simon's maximum sustained winds increased to 155 miles per hour.
The hurricane center said it expects Simon to approach Mexico's west-central coast on Sunday as a major hurricane, which is defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger, with winds of at least 111 mph.
Simon on Saturday night was just below a Category 5 classification, which requires maximum sustained winds of 157 mph. Forecasters said that Simon could weaken rapidly if its core moves fully onshore once it makes landfall.
The hurricane could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches.
"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the center warned in a bulletin that also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare as tropical storm conditions arrived Saturday afternoon.
According to the hurricane center, Simon was about 65 miles south-southwest of Manzanillo, Mexico, on Saturday and moving slowly northward at 5 mph.
"Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion in the hurricane warning area before conditions deteriorate later tonight," the hurricane center warned.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors were fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.
Convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows Saturday morning, when few were walking the streets under overcast skies.
"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."
The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge "along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall." The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Meanwhile, Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do Saturday. "I just don't know what to expect."
Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo, which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

Czech opposition retains Senate majority after elections

Unknown Publisher

12:26:50 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Czechia's opposition parties will retain their majority in the Senate after securing five seats outright in the first round of elections for the upper house of parliament, according to preliminary results released early Sunday.
The five winners include candidates from the Christian Democrats, the Mayors and Independents and other opposition parties.
Under the Czech electoral system, one-third of the 81-member Senate, or 27 seats, are contested every two years. Candidates must win more than 50 percent of the vote in their respective constituencies to secure a seat outright in the first round.
The three main opposition groups hold 37 of the 54 seats not up for election. With five more seats secured in the first round, the opposition has ensured a majority of at least 42 seats, leaving Prime Minister Andrej Babis' ruling coalition in the minority.
In the nationwide municipal elections also held on Friday and Saturday, independent candidates and local groups won the majority of local council seats, while Babis' ANO party led in several major regional cities. ■

Descendants of Doolittle Raid participants visit Shangrao, China's Jiangxi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:33 CST
12:26:33 KST

A descendant of a rescued Doolittle Raid participant (R) hugs a descendant of a Chinese villager who took part in the rescue in Shangrao, east China's Jiangxi Province, Oct. 10, 2026. The Doolittle Raid, planned and led by U.S. Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle on April 18, 1942, was an air raid on Japan as a retaliation for the attack on the U.S. Pearl Harbor.
After the raid, 15 planes heading for an airport in Quzhou ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China.
Chinese villagers risked their lives to rescue the parachuting airmen and helped them evacuate to safety. Of the 75 airmen aboard the planes, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people. However, many locals were suspected of sheltering the Americans, and some were tortured or even killed by Japanese soldiers.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
On Oct. 10, 6 representatives of descendants of the Doolittle Raid participants visited Shangrao to view a historical exhibition, revisit rescue sites and pay tribute to the Chinese people who rescued American airmen 84 years ago. (Xinhua/Zhou Mi)

Australia's Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility closes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:21 CST
12:26:21 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility closed on Sunday, with some residents asked to relocate about 100 km south of the Northern Territory capital.
The 400-bed YiSSA facility, which had been operating at capacity with a waiting list, provided temporary accommodation for people experiencing homelessness, residents from remote Aboriginal communities visiting Darwin for medical treatment and families escaping domestic violence, according to local media reports.
The Northern Territory government has established a smaller replacement facility in Batchelor, about 100 km south of Darwin, with capacity for around 150 people.
The closure has raised concerns over access to health, legal and other support services that are concentrated in Darwin.
Danila Dilba Health Service said about 250 of its clients had YiSSA registered as their address and warned that some could face difficulties continuing to access services after the closure.
The Northern Territory government has said medically vulnerable residents would not be relocated to Batchelor without arrangements for continued access to necessary care.
The government previously rejected a joint funding proposal from the federal government to keep the Darwin facility operating.
The government has said the Batchelor site will provide transitional accommodation as well as emergency evacuation capacity during extreme weather events. ■

China retains world junior badminton team title after dramatic final against Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11

CAIRO, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- China successfully defended its title at the Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Junior Team Championships on Saturday, defeating Malaysia 2-1 in a dramatic final that saw both teams battle through three closely contested sets.
The Chinese team won the opening set 55-46 before Malaysia fought back to take the second 55-53. China then regained control in the deciding set, winning 55-45 to lift the Suhandinata Cup.
The final was closely contested, with China recovering from 43-50 to level the second set at 52-52 before Malaysia held on to force a decider. China built an early lead in the third set through women's and men's singles and maintained its advantage despite Malaysia's late challenge.
China's coach Guo Zhendong credited the team's balanced strength across all five disciplines and praised the players' composure under pressure.
"In the deciding third game, we had a clear advantage in the singles events and managed to build a substantial lead. Although Malaysia narrowed the gap by several points during the women's doubles, our players managed to withstand the pressure and ultimately defend our title," Guo said, adding that the experience of handling pressure in closely contested matches would benefit their future development.
Feng Yilang, an 18-year-old Chinese player who competed in mixed doubles, acknowledged feeling nervous during the opening two sets but said he became more confident as the final progressed.
"In the third game, I was able to relax more and play with greater confidence. My performance was better than in the first two games," Feng said.
His teammate Wei Yueyue, also 18, who competed in women's doubles, identified "team unity" as the key to China's victory.
"Whenever we face difficulties, there is always someone who steps up. That's what makes our team so united," she said.
Malaysia's team manager Vincent Chin praised his players' determination despite the defeat, saying they fought until the final set.
"We are happy that we got a silver medal in the team event, but we are looking for the gold medal in the individual event," Chin told Xinhua, expressing optimism about the upcoming individual championships.
Thailand and Indonesia shared the bronze medals after losing their semifinals to China and Malaysia, respectively.
Looking ahead to the individual championships, which begin Monday in Cairo, Guo said the Chinese team would review its performances and allow the players time to recover before preparing for the different technical and tactical demands of the five disciplines.
"We will continue to give our best and strive for strong performances in the individual events," he said. ■

Shahar Nevo's double life as Bar-Ilan math professor accused of plotting massacre - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:17:20 UTC
12:17:20 KST

For more than two decades, Prof. Shahar Nevo built an extensive career in the world of mathematics: he graduated with honors, published dozens of studies, and taught generations of students at Bar-Ilan University.
Until this week, his name was known mainly in the hallways of the math department and among those who took his courses in calculus and analysis. His online presence consisted mainly of scientific articles, course pages, exams, and lecture summaries, with no interviews, public statements, or social media presence.
However, this academic career now exists under the shadow of a severe indictment: the 60-year-old professor is accused of preparing to execute an act of terrorism, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice. According to the indictment, he planned an attack for more than three years, with the aim of killing hundreds of Israeli Arabs.
Academic Background and Research Career
Nevo was born on October 12, 1966. He began his academic path at Tel Aviv University in 1984 and, three years later, completed a bachelor's degree in mathematics. In 1992, he moved to Bar-Ilan University, where he completed a master's degree in 1995 and a Ph.D. in 1999. He completed his master's studies summa cum laude, earning the Dean's Prize in 1996, and his doctoral dissertation was also praised. He wrote his research under the supervision of Prof. Lawrence Zalcman, an expert in complex analysis, and the two maintained a professional connection through the joint studies they published.
Upon completing his Ph.D. in 1999, Nevo joined the tenured academic faculty at Bar-Ilan. He started as a lecturer and, over the years, advanced through the ranks to Associate Professor in the Department of Mathematics.
According to his official profile, he specializes in complex analysis, operator theory, and matrices of rational functions.
Over the years, he accumulated 51 academic outputs, including 40 published papers. His research activity continued uninterrupted into recent years: in 2023, he co-authored a study with Zeev Shem-Tov published in the Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications, and in 2024, he published another study with Tomer Menaket.
Concurrently, he maintained long-standing international collaborations, including a series of publications with the German mathematician Jürgen Grahl from the University of Würzburg, alongside participation in conferences in Israel and abroad.
In 2012, he was among the organizers of an analysis session at the Israel Mathematical Union conference and even lectured there, and in 2017 he served as a visiting researcher at the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Sydney in Australia.
Teaching Activity and Personal Profile
Alongside his research, Nevo remained an integral part of the teaching framework at Bar-Ilan. Traces of the courses he taught have been scattered online for over a decade - from exercise sheets and exams to lecture summaries prepared by students; in 2023, for example, a document titled "Summary of Infi 4 Course based on lectures by Prof. Shahar Nevo" was uploaded to the Math-Wiki website.
In the last academic year, he continued to lecture as usual. In the university's schedule, he is registered as a lecturer in the courses "Mathematics for Chemists C" and "Infinitesimal Calculus 4," and even appears as an academic advisor to students on the department website. The most recent retake exam (Moed B) for the calculus course took place on September 1 of this year, just weeks before his arrest.
Outside of academia, almost no public information exists regarding Nevo's personal life. According to the details of the case revealed in prosecution documents, he lives alone in Petah Tikva and holds a firearm license.
An examination of his past highlights the near-total absence of any non-professional dimension: despite decades at the university, dozens of studies, and generations of students, his digital footprint consists almost entirely of pure mathematics.
Online, an old personal website remains on the Bar-Ilan University server, including a curriculum vitae, a list of publications, and contact details, alongside various academic and professional profiles. Meanwhile, no public social media accounts can be definitively attributed to him, nor are there any past interviews or opinion pieces.
Even on the "Dargo" website, where students typically review teaching staff, a page exists under his name, but it has no reviews. His official page on the Department of Mathematics website, last updated on June 9 of this year, displayed him as Prof. Shahar Nevo and detailed his research areas before it was removed from the internet.
At Bar-Ilan University, officials quickly disavowed the veteran faculty member. Following the filing of the indictment, the institution stated that they "condemn and is shocked by the acts attributed to the lecturer," clarifying that he would be suspended immediately pending the conclusion of proceedings. Concurrently, his name was removed from the university's lecturers page.
The Terror Plot Details
According to the indictment filed by the State Attorney's Office to the Central District Court in Lod, the 60-year-old lecturer, a resident of Petah Tikva, planned to execute an extreme plan - which he conceived over several years out of an ideological motive. The defendant named his plan after an acronym for "Am Ya'ase Transfer" ("The Nation Will Execute a Transfer").
The Central District Attorney's Office attributes to the defendant in the indictment the commission of security offenses of preparation to commit an act of terrorism under the Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice, and is requesting that the court detain him until the conclusion of legal proceedings against him.
From the indictment filed by attorneys Roy Reis and Tomer Steinberg of the Central District Attorney's Office, it emerged that against the backdrop of the "Operation Guardian of the Walls" riots and later, with greater intensity against the backdrop of the Swords of Iron war, the defendant decided to plan and carry out numerous terror acts simultaneously, and to cause the deaths of many hundreds of Arab Israeli citizens, including Bedouins, throughout the entire country, including Arabs residing in east Jerusalem and the West Bank.
The plot was intended to cause their flight and permanent deportation to the territories of Jordan, Lebanon, and the Gaza Strip.

Abbas delays elections until 2027, Palestinian democracy demands genuine reform - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:17:05 UTC
12:17:05 KST

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections on Saturday, replacing the November 28 vote with a promise of presidential and parliamentary elections on September 11, 2027.
His decree cited Israeli actions and deteriorating conditions across Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.
The difficulties facing election organizers are substantial. Gaza is devastated, Hamas remains armed, and movement restrictions complicate preparations. Those conditions require serious practical arrangements.
Abbas also owes Palestinians an explanation of how another postponement will produce a political system capable of holding its leaders accountable.
Palestinians last elected a president in 2005 and a legislature in 2006. Abbas’s presidential mandate expired in 2009. An entire generation has reached adulthood without choosing its national leadership.
Responsibility for that prolonged failure rests heavily with the Palestinian leaders who have retained power throughout it.
Palestinians need accountable leadership, Israel needs reliable security
Palestinians deserve the opportunity to replace their rulers peacefully. Israel also has an interest in credible Palestinian institutions that can maintain security, implement agreements, and exercise authority over armed factions.
Building such institutions requires sustained reform, enforceable rules, and leaders prepared to accept limits on their power.
Hamas’s victory in the 2006 legislative election and its subsequent violent takeover of Gaza must inform any discussion of another vote. The organization responsible for the October 7 massacre cannot acquire a legitimate claim to govern while retaining its terrorist infrastructure.
Its weapons threaten Israeli lives and the freedom of Palestinians to organize, campaign, and disagree.
Participation should therefore require renouncing terrorism, recognizing Israel, accepting existing agreements, and dismantling independent armed forces. These obligations must apply equally to every faction and be verified in practice.
Candidates running under alternative labels must face the same scrutiny when evidence establishes organizational ties to armed groups.
Eligibility rules should be published in advance and subject to independent review. Their enforcement must rest on documented conduct, with a fair appeal process protecting peaceful challengers from arbitrary exclusion by incumbents.
A credible election also requires an independent electoral commission, accessible voter registration, impartial courts, and protection for journalists and opposition candidates.
Voters must be able to criticize the Palestinian Authority without fear. Parties must commit to respecting the results and allowing future elections, including when their own hold on office is threatened.
Abbas must set clear reform deadlines ahead of September 2027 elections
Abbas should publish a timetable for those reforms, with deadlines that can be assessed before September 2027.
Preparations for polling and international monitoring should proceed alongside transparent public finances, scrutiny of security institutions, and action against incitement.
Public funds must be subject to safeguards preventing their use to reward or encourage terrorism.
These changes will face resistance from those whose influence depends on patronage, secrecy or coercion. International partners should make clear that another postponement carries political consequences.
Donors should condition support for governing institutions on measurable progress, with humanitarian assistance protected so ordinary Palestinians are spared the cost of their leaders’ failures.
Countries recognizing Palestine must demand accountable governance
Governments that have recognized a Palestinian state have a particular responsibility to insist on these standards. Their diplomatic commitments should be followed by scrutiny of how Palestinian institutions operate. Recognition creates no guarantee that a government respects its citizens, controls its territory, and intends to live peacefully alongside Israel.
Israel has responsibilities too. Its government should work toward practical arrangements for voting, election observers, and necessary movement, consistent with protecting Israeli citizens.
Specific restrictions should be justified by concrete security needs and reviewed when circumstances change. Facilitating credible Palestinian government can serve Israel’s long-term interests.
Jerusalem voting arrangements will require careful negotiation. Security concerns must be addressed through workable procedures, while Palestinian leaders must demonstrate that they are pursuing solutions in good faith. Progress on electoral independence, financial transparency, and political freedoms can begin immediately, even while difficult logistical questions remain unresolved.
The new election date should carry obligations that can be checked throughout the coming year. Abbas should face regular public scrutiny over what has changed, which commitments remain unmet, and who is responsible. Palestinian civil society deserves access to that information and space to challenge official explanations.
Palestinians need accountable leadership, and Israelis need reliable security.
Elections conducted within a reformed political system can advance both interests. The months ahead should be used to establish the freedoms, safeguards, and enforceable commitments that give a future vote meaning.

The United States had the highest number of expected demonstrations across the two-week period, followed by Spain, Britain and Australia.
In the UK on Saturday, thousands of demonstrators marched through London, wearing keffiyehs and waving Palestinian flags. The Palestine Solidarity Campaign claimed that more than 250,000 people took to the streets of London in support of Palestine, though the figure was not independently verified by JTA.
“Today we’re marching for Palestine in London to mark three years of Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people and demand our government go further to sanction Israel for its crimes. Britain must stop arming Israel now,” the group wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Footage posted by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign showed thousands of demonstrators marching through the British capital, waving Palestinian flags.
Police, counter-protestors present
Local police imposed restrictions on the march to “minimize the risk of serious disruption to communities.” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Carl Galvin was quoted in British media as saying that “Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”
He added that police would use their powers to require anyone deliberately concealing their identity with a face covering in the protest area to remove it.
British media also reported that a counter-protest organized by Stop the Hate was taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside the Metropolitan Police headquarters.
Across the Irish Sea, more than 10,000 demonstrators gathered in Dublin for a march in support of Palestine, according to RTÉ. The wave of demonstrations was organized by several pro-Palestinian groups under the slogan “The End of the Genocide.” Sky TG24 reported that Swedish activist Greta Thunberg was present at a demonstration in Naples.
'From the river to the sea' chanted throughout Italy, Europe
