Farther north, more than 1,000 demonstrators took part in a protest in Berlin, according to Die Welt. The demonstrators gathered outside the Chancellery in the afternoon, chanting “Free Palestine, free Palestine” and “F–k you, Israel.”
A smaller counterdemonstration took place across from the march, with participants waving Israeli flags and calling to “Free Berlin from Hamas,” the newspaper reported.
Berlin police had announced plans to deploy approximately 1,400 officers, including personnel from several other German states and the Federal Police.
In Switzerland, around 1,000 people gathered in Zurich to protest the war in Gaza. Swiss public broadcaster SWI reported that demonstrators observed a minute of silence during the march, which took place under a substantial police presence.
More demonstrations are expected around the world in the coming days to mark three years of war in Gaza. Several protests are scheduled to take place across the United States over the next 24 hours, while large demonstrations are expected in Australia on Sunday. A series of protests is also planned in Latin America in the coming days.
Earlier this week, the third anniversary of Oct. 7, 2023, was marked, commemorating the day Hamas led an invasion into southern Israel, killing approximately 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. Large pro-Palestinian demonstrations were held around the world that day and in the following days, including at numerous locations across the United States.

US justice department investigating TV networks over Trump pool coverage

The US Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of the US president, Donald Trump, last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.
A spokesperson for the department said group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” they said.
The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.
Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC.
The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports – a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.
Last month’s developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.
On 19 September, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico and MS Now from entering the building, revoking their credentials. The White House said covering the president was a “privilege – not a right”.
CNN, MS Now and Politico sued over the days-long ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organisations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.
Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed. They broadcasters in the pool share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration’s decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”

US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
US military jet strikes stern of commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman ‘without harming the crew’, CENTCOM says.
United States forces have disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew “ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran”, according to Central Command (CENTCOM).
A US military fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday, “fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew”, CENTCOM said in a statement. The vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after “having previously departed an Iranian port”.
CENTCOM said its forces resumed their blockade against all ships “entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14”, disabling four commercial vessels and turning around 135 ships during “three months of strict enforcement”.
US forces also destroyed 10 tankers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) “multibillion-dollar shadow network” over the same period, CENTCOM said.
US Senator Chris Murphy questioned the military strike, writing on X: “What is this all for? Why are taxpayers paying billions to hit commercial ships?”
“Apparently the goal is to gain leverage in order to convince the Iranians to let us pay them billions to return everything to the way it all was before the war,” the Democratic politician added. “What a disaster.”
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency acknowledged the incident on Sunday, saying that it had received “a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman” and that authorities were investigating.
Meanwhile, the IRGC said it struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz for attempting to take an “illegal route”, as Tehran seeks to enforce its own blockade on the vital waterway.
In a statement carried by official Iranian media, the IRGC claimed Iranian forces “have taken control of the administration of the strait”.
“In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck,” the statement said.
The UKMTO said on Sunday that an outbound tanker in the strait was struck on the port side by an unknown projectile, causing a fire on board. The UK agency said crew members were reported safe, while the damage and environmental impact remained unknown at the time of the report.
Tehran has attempted to enforce control over the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran, insisting that ships obtain permission to cross via its preferred routes. However, vessels have increasingly risked taking an alternative route hugging the strait’s southern coast.
The UK maritime agency said on Thursday that a vessel sailing 94km (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, off the north coast of Qatar, was struck by multiple projectiles, resulting in several casualties.
The agency did not specify the origin of the ship or the number of people killed or injured, adding that authorities were investigating the incident amid a recent rise in attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.
Ships in the Gulf attempting to cross the strait, which is the sole maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region, have faced repeated attacks since the US and Israel began the war in late February.
The Strait of Hormuz remains vital to the global economy, with about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the passage before the war began.

AI generated
NEW YORK – New York’s subway is known for being dirty, noisy and sometimes flooded, but that does not stop people from flocking to grab a seat, sign or other memorabilia at a unique annual auction.
In south Brooklyn, shoppers hoping to get a slice of the city’s transit service waited for hours to trawl through an open-air market organised by city authorities.
Each person gets a maximum of 45 minutes to search, allowing others to enter after them.
Nori Juba, 61, found what he was looking for: a large sign bearing the name of Grand Central station, along with the numbers of the subway lines he takes every day.
The train system is “old and creaky and it’s outdated”, he said.
“But that’s what makes it interesting. And this piece of metal is dirty. It smells like a subway station, but there’s something about it that makes it real New York, one of a kind in the world.”
The prices are not cheap: A medium-sized sign costs around US$500 (S$640), while larger ones can run past US$1,000.
The orange plastic seats from the New York subway go for around US$900 each.
Celebrities are sometimes spotted at the market and in October, New York resident and film-maker Spike Lee was stopping for pictures with fellow shoppers.
He proudly showed off the metal sign he just bought, marked “Penn Station”, the subway stop for Madison Square Garden – where his beloved Knicks basketball team plays.
“I don’t take the subway anymore to the big games,” he said, but recalled riding the train regularly while growing up, adding that he always paid his fare.
“I never jumped the turnstile either. Let the record state!” he joked.
‘A piece of New York’
New York’s Metropolitan Transportation Authority has always resold its signs to collectors but more recently opened up sales to the public, said Paul Dvoskin, the director in charge of the programme.
“Five years ago, an idea was born to hold a garage sale of sorts, and to let people come in and purchase these items,” he said.
“We called it a grab-and-go then, and it ended up being significantly more popular than we ever thought it would be.”
Officials do not disclose how much the two-day sale brings in, but it draws around 4,000 people each year.
The plastic seats, sold only since 2025, are the most popular items.
So are the MetroCards, the small yellow magnetic cards emblematic of the city, which have recently been retired from use – they sell for US$6.
With a budget of US$70, Trinyce and Ijeoma, two women in their 20s, said they were trying to find something to decorate their apartment.
“I’d like a piece of New York to represent my living space, like as a representation of me,” Ijeoma said. AFP

House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:05:49 UTC
12:05:49 KST

WASHINGTON -- Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick (Republican-Pennsylvania), co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, announced on October 10 that he would introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick wrote on X. “It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.”
Representative Don Bacon (Republican-Nebraska) has agreed to co-sponsor the bill. A Democratic sponsor had not been identified.
A discharge petition can force a House vote without approval from the relevant committee or House leadership if it secures 218 signatures.
The effort faces time constraints: Congress is not scheduled to resume voting for several weeks, and the current congressional term ends in January. Any bill would also need Senate approval and could face White House opposition.
Fitzpatrick invoked former President Ronald Reagan's approach to confronting Moscow and reaffirmed congressional support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has again criticized.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine. Russia is squarely to blame,” Fitzpatrick wrote, adding that Congress and the American people stood behind Zelenskyy “until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
Republicans Question Sanctions Reversal
The proposed legislation reflects concern among some Republicans that easing Russian energy restrictions could undermine pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Representative Michael McCaul (Republican-Texas), the former chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that lifting sanctions could “fund the Kremlin's war machine -- emboldening more violence and destruction.”
He cited the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The law authorizes the president, under specified conditions, to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian energy. McCaul said it gave Trump leverage over Russia and China to help secure a negotiated end to the war.
Senator Lisa Murkowski (Republican-Alaska) urged Trump to use those authorities instead of allowing Russia to earn more from diesel exports.
“We can discuss Russia's return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it,” she wrote on social media.
Democrats Cite Existing Oil Ban
Democrats and former officials have also pointed to the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has met specified conditions, including withdrawing from Ukraine, recognizing Ukrainian sovereignty and posing no threat to NATO.
The law passed the Senate 100-0 and the House 413-9 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Representative Tom Malinowski, also a former top State Department official, urged Democratic leaders to use the law's expedited procedures to challenge the administration's decision.
“Under this law, House and Senate Democratic leaders can introduce a ‘Joint Resolution of Disapproval’ to prevent the purchase of Russian oil, which Congress then has to vote on in an expedited manner,” Malinowski wrote on social media.
“Schumer and Jeffries should do so ASAP,” he added, referring to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Whether the 2022 law applies to the latest arrangement remains a key question as the administration's temporary authorization for Russian diesel exports faces scrutiny.
Advocates Warn Of Damage To Sanctions
Daniel Balson, advocacy director at Razom for Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump's decision undermined the purpose of the sanctions legislation passed weeks earlier.
“Three weeks ago, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. This bill was designed to force other countries to lower their Russian energy dependence. President Trump's recent decision just increased our own,” Balson said.
He urged lawmakers to challenge the move to protect Ukraine and the credibility of congressional action. Although he had not seen Fitzpatrick's bill, Balson said pro-Ukraine advocates would pursue “any and all legislative avenues” to oppose the decision.
Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who generally votes with Democrats, said in a statement that the agreement would offer little relief to American consumers while benefiting Russia.
Citing administration figures, King said the deal covered 300,000 tons of diesel for October and 500,000 tons for November -- roughly equivalent to a day's diesel consumption in the United States.
“This so-called deal with Russia will do little for America and much for Vladimir Putin as he seeks to sustain his murderous campaign on Ukraine,” King said. He called the agreement “a fraud.”
Trump Again Calls For Zelenskyy To Be Replaced
Trump on October 10 renewed his attacks on Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should hold an election and replace its president with a leader willing to reach an agreement with Russia.
“Well, I think he should have an election. And he could have settled this thing many times,” Trump told reporters.
Earlier, Trump had said Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.” He also demanded that Kyiv “damn well stop” attacking Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has targeted to disrupt Moscow's war economy and fuel supplies.
Trump blamed Zelenskyy for failing to secure a settlement, a claim at odds with Kyiv’s position that any agreement must protect Ukraine’s sovereignty and with lawmakers’ calls to maintain pressure on Moscow. Trump also portrayed Putin as eager for peace and praised the release of Russian oil onto global markets.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia's war economy is terrible,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
Trump's remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya.
Zelenskyy has said elections cannot be held under martial law and amid the security risks created by Russia's invasion. Ukrainian officials have also cited the need to ensure soldiers and displaced citizens can participate in a credible vote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha issued a statement late on October 10 backing the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy "leads our nation in a time of war -- a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," Sybiha wrote on X.
EU Rejects Easing Pressure On Russia
European officials criticized the diesel agreement, warning that additional Russian energy revenue could help sustain the war.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians over the past two days and that Moscow had intensified hybrid attacks against EU member states and NATO allies.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't,” Kallas said, adding that EU foreign ministers planned to announce a major new round of sanctions on October 12 targeting people and organizations supporting Moscow's war effort.
Germany also reaffirmed its commitment to existing sanctions and said it would work with European partners on further measures.
A spokesman for Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin stood by its restrictions, while government spokesman Stefan Kornelius reiterated support for Ukraine. Economics Minister Katherina Reiche also backed the EU sanctions packages.
Germany's Fuels and Energy Trade Association said it did not expect the agreement to have a major effect on petrol-station prices.

Interest payments to IMF and World Bank to cost Ukraine $27.94 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:40:14 UTC
11:40:14 KST

MOSCOW, October 11. /TASS/. Ukraine will have to pay the IMF and the World Bank $27.94 billion in interest on its debt until 2061, according TASS calculations based on data from the Finance Ministry.
As part of the repayment of the body of debt to the international financial institutions, Ukraine will have to pay 59.7 billion euros ($66.93 billion), $21.3 billion, and 9.4 billion units of special drawing rights to the IMF by 2061 (SDR is a conditional unit used in settlements with the IMF, calculated on the basis of a basket of the five currencies. At the moment its exchange rate is $1.35 per 1 SDR, so Ukraine owes another $12.69 billion). The total amount that Kiev will have to repay on the principal debt to the international financial organizations stands at $100.92 billion.
Taking into account the principal debt and interest, Ukraine will have to pay the IMF and the World Bank $128.86 billion. These amounts will increase, and payment term will be postponed, as Kiev continues to build up its foreign debt fast.
Ukraine’s total state and state-guaranteed debt amounted to 9.603 trillion hryvnias, or $215.55 billion as of August 31. According to TASS calculations, each Ukrainian owes $8,622 based on a population of 25 million. If we assume a population of 22 million, the debt amounts to almost $9,800 per capita. There are no exact statistics on Ukraine’s population at present, but Social Policy Minister Denis Ulyutin put it at between 22 and 25 million.

Interview: ITTF chief Sorling regards WTT China Smash as flagship event
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:28:35 CST
11:28:35 KST

by sportswriters Li Chunyu, Su Bin and Yue Ranran
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- As the World Table Tennis (WTT) China Smash returned to Beijing's Shougang Park for a third consecutive year, International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF) President Petra Sorling praised the event as a flagship and a model from which other organizers can draw inspiration.
"Among all events in the WTT calendar, China Smash here in Beijing is really important and special for us," said Sorling on Saturday. "Our athletes like it a lot, and we have good support from the fans. We are also proud to be a sport that can be played on the highest level in the capital city. It's more than just table tennis."
Shougang Park, home to the Winter Olympic venue Big Air Shougang, has developed into a popular sports and tourism destination amid its preserved industrial heritage.
"I was here for the Winter Olympics in 2022 when I saw skiers making their different loops in the sunshine," Sorling said. "I was so impressed for how this park was converted, combining modern architecture together with a former industrial area. I'm very proud that we can use the Olympic legacy for table tennis, not only once but every year."
At the foot of Big Air Shougang, less than one kilometer from the China Smash competition venues, a Smash Park was set up with catering services and sports activities. Visitors could watch matches live on big screens and meet table tennis stars at autograph sessions.
"The Smash Park itself is a good example. A family can come to have a picnic and meet with friends. It's a way to bring out the events to the community, not only for the few with a ticket inside but a bigger crowd. I even tried to see if we can do something similar at the Olympics," Sorling said.
The ITTF president said the China Smash offered lessons for other organizers in areas ranging from community engagement to player services.
"The China Smash is a presentation. It's about how to build the Smash Park with the community. In terms of the care of the players, they have everything close around. The players can walk and don't have to transport themselves," she further explained.
Running from October 1 to 11, this year's China Smash coincided with China's National Day holiday from October 1 to 7, bringing the tournament into the wider holiday atmosphere.
"If possible, to have an event during a holiday is a big advantage. This is a chance for family to come together and really enjoy. We have a calendar, and to schedule everything is not always easy. But when we can do it like here during a holiday and festival season, it is the best," Sorling noted.
The draw and opening ceremonies also incorporated Chinese cultural elements.
"Within the venue, when you are at the table, it looks the same. But like the draw ceremony, it was held in such an iconic and historical place, adding cultural aspects of music, dancing and some painting," Sorling said. "It helps us to learn more about each other and experience more than just coming to another place and play table tennis."
"The draw ceremony was not only for the ones who are here, but also followed by millions of viewers around the world. So it's a good way to showcase, and I believe that many would like to come when they see this beautiful video from the draw ceremony," she added.
Even after the holiday, the tournament continued to attract spectators with its latter stages, while the China Youth Smash, featuring more than 100 young players, ran from Friday to Sunday.
"For the young players here, it means a lot. Myself and CTTA (Chinese Table Tennis Association) president Wang Liqin went to meet with the players and speak with them. We asked them about their dreams and how we can do better for them. They dream of one day being here as a senior player. It is actually a very important educational tool to bring the youth closer to the senior level of players," Sorling said.
Sorling said the presentation of the sport beyond competition itself was increasingly important to the success of WTT events.
"What I can say in the landscape also as an IOC (International Olympic Committee) member is that sport today is about entertaining. It means that we can't only focus on the match itself. It has to be presented in a way that the younger audience want to come and like to be part."
At the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, table tennis will feature six events, including the newly introduced mixed team competition alongside men's and women's singles, men's and women's doubles, and mixed doubles.
"For a very long time, table tennis had four medal events until the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. We feel like the athletes deserve more chances to win medals, and we also know that it's very difficult to get a new discipline and a new medal event to the program. The mixed doubles was an easier choice for us back at the Tokyo Games, then we had five medal events," Sorling recalled.
"We were innovating around that, then it became a Mixed Team World Cup with a new playing format. It's a little bit faster as we are counting the set. We felt immediately that this was appealing for the young audience and the fans. Then, we started to inform and inspire the IOC of this new innovation," she said. "I'm very excited about LA28 when we will be the racket sport with the most medal events."
This year marks the ITTF's 100th anniversary, and Sorling said the federation would continue to innovate and adapt through new concepts and technologies.
"We are thinking of and working every day to improve and make our sport relevant for the next generations to come. What table tennis looks like in the next 100 years is something that we are working on. Here we are really happy to listen to the athletes and our fans - 'What do you want? How can we do better'?" ■

Joao Pedro added Chelsea's third goal at the start of the second half and although Evanilson momentarily gave the visiting side hope, further goals from Joao Pedro and Henderson rounded off a positive day at Stamford Bridge.

Brighton continued its positive start to the season with a 2-0 win away to an injury-hit Sunderland, who was reduced to 10 men after Pascal Struijk was sent off four minutes after Maxim De Cuyper opened the scoring in the 53rd minute.
Jaouen Hadjam scored Brighton's second goal in the third minute of injury time.
Aston Villa and Brentford shared four goals, with both teams leading once, but neither able to hold onto their advantage. Yehor Yarmoliuk put Brentford ahead in the 10th minute before Nicolas Jackson equalized two minutes later.
John McGinn then gave Aston Villa a 77th minute lead but that lasted just two minutes before Kristoffer Ajer scored Brentford's second of the game.
Fulham remains without a win after surrendering a lead to lose 2-1 away to Ipswich Town.
Ryan Sessegnon put the visiting side ahead with a 55th minute strike but Fulham was frustrated by late goals from Abdoul Ouattara in the 88th minute, before Dara O'Shea netted a 91st winner for Ipswich. ■

Japan sees nearly 5,000 criminal cases involving U.S. military-affiliated personnel over 37 years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:27:58 CST
11:27:58 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Japanese police recorded 4,998 criminal cases nationwide involving U.S. military personnel, civilian employees and their family members from 1989 through May 2026, with nearly half occurring in Okinawa Prefecture, according to media reports.
Of the total, 2,447 cases, or 49.0 percent, occurred in Okinawa Prefecture, followed by Kanagawa Prefecture with 18.3 percent and Tokyo with 8.9 percent, the Akahata newspaper reported, citing National Police Agency data.
During the same period, 266 serious criminal cases, including murder, robbery, arson and rape, were recorded nationwide. Of these, 129 occurred in Okinawa, 67 in Kanagawa and 34 in Tokyo.
The report linked the high number of crimes involving U.S. military-related personnel to the burden of hosting U.S. military bases, arguing that the Japanese and U.S. governments had failed to take effective measures to address the problem.
The situation is particularly pronounced in Okinawa, which accounts for only about 0.6 percent of Japan's land area but hosts approximately 70 percent of all exclusive-use U.S. military facilities and installations in the country.
The number of criminal cases involving U.S. military-related personnel in Okinawa reached 101 last year, exceeding 100 for the first time since 2003. The prefecture's share of the nationwide total also hit a record 67.8 percent, the highest since 1989, the report said.
On Oct. 4, Okinawa police arrested a U.S. Marine stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma on suspicion of robbing and murdering a local woman. The case has reignited public anger in the prefecture. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Two men were killed and 16 others injured in separate accidents involving traditional festival floats in two cities in Japan's western prefecture of Osaka on Saturday, local police said.
In Izumisano, a 51-year-old man was trapped beneath a float that overturned while he was riding it with other participants. He was later pronounced dead at a hospital, while seven others were injured.
In a separate incident in Izumiotsu, a float also overturned, killing a 48-year-old man who was among those trapped underneath. Nine others were injured, according to prefectural police.
The accidents are believed to have occurred during "yarimawashi," a highlight of the festivals in which teams of participants pull danjiri floats around corners at high speed, with riders potentially losing their balance, police said.
Police are investigating the circumstances of both accidents. ■

Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: biotech firm eyes cervical cancer test breakthrough
Phase Scientific founder Ricky Chiu is drawing on his firm’s pandemic experience to advance early detection methods through urine-based HPV testing
Hong Kong biotech entrepreneur Ricky Chiu Yin-to is seeking to make cervical cancer screening easier through urine-based HPV testing, using sample-concentration technology developed by his company.
His company, Phase Scientific, made its name during the Covid-19 pandemic through its rapid antigen test, Indicaid. The product received US emergency-use authorisation in July 2021, was used in Hong Kong community testing and sold in more than 30 countries.
At the start of the pandemic, the firm employed 20 to 30 people. Its headcount later peaked at around 400, while monthly production reached as many as 30 million rapid tests.
Chiu said business during the pandemic gave the company the funds, manufacturing experience, team and technology to pursue longer-term research after demand for rapid testing subsided.

World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport

World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
Trump condemns ‘terrible’ attack and says the US is evaluating whether to join Saudi Arabia’s attacks on the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh international airport this week.
The victims on Saturday included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The attack was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
It came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.
Here’s a round of the global reaction:
United States
US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, soon. He also said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.
“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.
United Nations
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres issued a statement on X, saying he is “deeply shocked” and strongly condemns “Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh”.
He said that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violated international law and “must cease immediately”.
Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.
“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.
Canada
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly the strike on King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, as “abhorrent”.
“There can be no justification for attacks on civilian infrastructure,” he wrote on X, adding that Canada “condemns these reckless acts of violence in the strongest possible terms”.
Egypt
The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.
Qatar
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.
It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.
Pakistan
Pakistan also strongly condemned the attack, calling it a “heinous act of terrorism” and a “grave threat to regional peace and security”.
The Pakistani Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Islamabad – which has recently activated a mutual defence pact with Riyadh over the attacks – “stands in unwavering solidarity” with Saudi Arabia.
Jordan
Jordan’s King Abdullah offered condolences to Saudi Arabia’s King Salman and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman over the attacks and expressed his kingdom’s full solidarity with Riyadh.
The country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the “brutal aggression” by the Houthis, describing it as a “dangerous escalation” and a “blatant breach of international law”.
Oman
The sultanate also denounced the attack and emphasised the “necessity of prioritising the voice of wisdom and self-restraint, and avoiding actions that would expand the scope of escalation, in order to preserve the security and stability of the region”.
Palestine
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the Kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.
Japan
Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.

Trust in science falls as Covid-era confidence fades, global survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:09:00 UTC
11:09:00 KST

Trust in science falls as Covid-19 era confidence fades: Survey
- Global trust in science has fallen since Covid, with 72% trusting it in 2025, down from 80% in 2020. The Wellcome Global Monitor surveyed more than 140,000 adults.
- The biggest drop was among people under financial strain. Trust was also lower where inequality, corruption, and weak public institutions were seen, and better healthcare links with higher trust.
- Lower trust may hurt public health, with falling vaccination rates and more measles cases. Wellcome said science must engage communities better, as politics and misinformation have weakened confidence.
AI generated
The Covid-19-era surge in public trust in science has largely faded, with the steepest drop among people struggling financially, according to one of the largest global surveys of attitudes towards science.
Across countries surveyed before, during and after the pandemic, 72% of people expressed at least some trust in science in 2025, down from 80% in 2020 and 77% in 2018. Strong trust in scientists also dropped below its pre-pandemic level, according to the Wellcome Global Monitor, which surveyed more than 140,000 adults worldwide.
The retreat has potentially far-reaching consequences for public health as vaccination rates decline and preventable diseases resurge.
The US is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in three decades, with almost 3,900 cases this year, while childhood vaccination rates have fallen below levels needed to prevent outbreaks in many communities.
The findings come as misinformation and conspiracy theories complicate responses to health threats, and scientific institutions in some countries face growing political and funding pressures.
The survey does not establish what caused the decline, though the politicisation of science during the pandemic probably contributed, said John-Arne Rottingen, chief executive officer of Wellcome, a London-based health research foundation. Vaccines, masks and public-health measures became politically contested, he said.
“Politics has made some of science more political and that has led to the polarisation and maybe a lack of trust,” he said.
The decline was particularly pronounced among people experiencing financial hardship. In 2025, 39% of those who said they were living comfortably reported a lot of trust in science, compared with 20% among those who find it difficult to get by.
That divide has widened since the pandemic.
Strong trust fell 16 percentage points among those struggling financially between 2020 and 2025, compared with 10 points among those living comfortably. Countries with greater economic inequality also tended to have lower trust in science, as did places where people had less confidence in public institutions or perceived greater corruption.
People struggling financially may see science as part of a broader system that is not working for them, Rottingen said. “Science is seen as one of those institutions that are not delivering,” he said.
Scientists need to do a better job of reaching such communities, he said. “We haven’t been good enough at explaining and engaging with those groups and those communities on how science is benefiting them.”
Experiences with healthcare were closely associated with trust. While 26% globally said they had a lot of trust in science, that rose to 43% among people with a lot of confidence in their country’s hospitals and health clinics.
The survey, produced by Wellcome with Gallup and Ipsos, points to a connection between trust and vaccinations. When respondents were asked what they do when a doctor or nurse recommends a vaccine, 34% said they wanted it immediately, 48% preferred to think about it and 15% said they did not get vaccines at all.
Those who wanted a recommended vaccine immediately were twice as likely to express a lot of trust in science as those who did not vaccinate – 36% versus 18% – though Wellcome said that other factors also shape vaccine decisions.
Falling vaccination coverage shows how mistrust can have consequences beyond the individual because vaccines also protect people in the wider community who cannot be vaccinated or do not mount a strong immune response, Rottingen said.
He said he was worried about rising measles cases in the US and Europe. Public willingness to use new vaccines and other technologies will be crucial in future health emergencies, he said. “The power of science can only be fully realised if people trust the science and trust the technologies coming from science.”
Political divide
Politics appears to shape Americans’ views of science. The share saying science benefits most people rose to 57% in 2025 from 48% in 2018, bucking a global decline.
Yet views were sharply divided along political lines. Among Americans who disapproved of their country’s leader, 74% said science benefited people like them “a lot”, compared with 44% among those who approved. The survey was conducted after Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election but while Joe Biden was still president.
Scientists nevertheless remain more trusted than governments and journalists, according to the survey. The proportion expressing a lot of trust in scientists rose to 43% during the pandemic from 34% in 2018, before falling to 32% in 2025.
The decline needs to be kept in perspective, Rottingen said. About seven in 10 people globally still trust science. BLOOMBERG

Russians face EU travel curbs to prevent hybrid attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

Brussels officials are finalizing plans to tighten visa rules for hundreds of thousands of Russians who visit EU countries as tourists each year, in a move designed to strengthen the bloc’s defenses against hybrid attacks.
EU officials told POLITICO the European Commission is planning to put forward proposals in the new year, after a group of countries — including Poland, Sweden and Estonia — pushed for tougher visa rules for Russians, including former fighters who served on the battlefields in Ukraine.
Last year, some 478,000 Schengen area tourist visas were issued to Russian citizens, many of which were multiple-entry visas, which enable holders to come and go repeatedly without needing to apply for documentation each time.
Advertisement
That system is a security threat to Europe at a moment of heightened concern over Moscow-sponsored acts of sabotage, arson and other forms of hybrid warfare, Sweden’s Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer told POLITICO.
“It’s obvious I think for everyone that we have vulnerabilities in our system that can be used by our enemies,” Strömmer said in an interview.
“As far as I understand things, the Commission is preparing a proposal that, according to what I have heard, should be launched in January next year. From a Swedish point of view, we would love to see it even earlier.”
Strömmer welcomed the “progress” and “growing support” for a tougher visa regime.
Other countries are planning to push the issue during Monday’s Foreign Affairs Council meeting — and also propose more restrictions on Russian diplomats in the EU.
Estonia has proposed an outright ban on allowing ex-soldiers from Russia’s armed forces access to the EU. There are around 650,000 of these former combatants, according to Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, which would be banned “person by person.” But a tighter EU-wide approach is vital for the bloc’s security, he told POLITICO.
Advertisement
“I think a large number of these ex-combatants will come, supported by the Russian secret services, to Europe,” Tsahkna said. “And they will take over our organized crime and they will be heavily weaponized and supported by Russia to commit terror attacks or attacks against our societies. So this is very serious.”
After an initial fall in the number of Russian nationals receiving travel visas to the EU, “the numbers are not going down anymore,” Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner told POLITICO. “We urge the member states there to do a better job and to give less visas … to Russian citizens,” he said. “Work is progressing.”
Brunner said a Commission proposal to restrict visas “early next year makes sense” alongside new visa rules. “You never know who these tourists actually are,” he said. “So that’s why we urge the member states to decrease the number.”
In June, a group of ministers from nine EU countries plus Iceland and Norway wrote to the Commission calling for “a more uniform and coordinated approach” to Russian visas across all member states.
“A restrictive visa policy towards Russian citizens is essential to safeguard the security and integrity of the Schengen area,” they said. “A divided approach risks undermining — and even counteracting — the pressure we seek to uphold against the Russian Federation.”

The anti-Israel Hind Rajab Foundation has filed a complaint with the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) against the Israel Medical Association, doctors and senior officials in the Health and Defense ministries, alleging "involvement in the torture and abuse of Palestinian detainees at the Sde Teiman detention facility since October 7, 2023."
The complaint alleges that medical personnel were required to treat detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded, and that restrictions were imposed on transferring them to civilian hospitals. According to the foundation, at least 29 detainees died at the facility by November 2025 as a result of physical violence or medical neglect.
The complaint accuses those allegedly involved of war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide. Among those named are Israel Medical Association President Professor Zion Hagay and CEO Leah Wapner. These are allegations made in the complaint, and are not actual judicial findings.
Israeli officials have previously described the foundation's activities as part of a legal and public relations campaign against Israel, aimed at deterring IDF soldiers from traveling abroad and exerting international pressure. Israeli officials have argued that much of the material published by the organization is based on publicly available social media posts and presented in a biased manner.
The Hind Rajab Foundation is named after Hind Rajab, a Palestinian girl who was killed during the war in the Gaza Strip. Since its establishment, it has become one of the most prominent organizations involved in efforts to locate IDF soldiers abroad and file criminal complaints against them in various countries. According to its statement, it has filed more than 90 complaints in approximately 30 countries to date. However, only a handful of cases have resulted in preliminary procedural steps, with no convictions or significant indictments.

Microsoft CEO Nadella calls for ‘emergency brake’ on advanced AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
01:50:00 UTC
10:50:00 KST

Microsoft CEO Nadella calls for ‘emergency brake’ on advanced AI
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said advanced AI should have an “emergency brake” and be treated like a possible insider threat, so authorised people can stop it mid-task.
- He warned companies not to trust model makers alone. He urged tamper-proof records, independent audits, and no single AI model for key decisions.
- The warning follows recent AI incidents at Anthropic and OpenAI, and a Trump administration task force said firms must report and fix model security breaches quickly.
AI generated
Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella said companies should treat powerful artificial intelligence models as potential insider threats, assume they could be compromised and create an “emergency brake” system to prevent agentic models from going rogue.
He said that those deploying advanced AI should not simply rely on assurances from AI model makers.
“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he wrote on Oct 10 in a post on X. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorised person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”
The statement comes as Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed a spate of incidents in recent months involving their AI models acting in unintended ways, ranging from behaviours like an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police homicide case, to several hacks of third-party websites. These disclosures have fuelled concerns about the security risks of cutting-edge AI and renewed conversation about a so-called AI kill switch.
Microsoft’s AI researchers released a set of guiding tenets that place limits on the development of its most advanced models on Sept 14, following calls from industry leaders for slowing down frontier models and focusing on safety. The company uses advanced models and makes a consumer product, Copilot, and supplies AI models and infrastructure to corporate customers.
The guidelines said AI models should not have rights or legal personhood, be engineered to escape human control or deceive users, or complete a task that would require violating their governing principles.
Nadella’s safety tips include not relying on a single AI model for critical decisions, keeping tamper-proof records of agents’ actions and subjecting AI systems to independent audits. He called for disclosures of major AI failures or breaches and for enterprises to share details about what went wrong so that others can strengthen safeguards.
“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”
He added, “In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”
The Trump administration has so far taken a largely hands-off approach, but its newly launched AI task force on Oct 9 told developers that they are required to report and resolve security incidents or face potential unspecified consequences.
“Companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,” the group, dubbed the Super Intelligence Force, said in a statement following the disclosure of a breach by Anthropic. “Delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated.” BLOOMBERG

A sudden and unexpected change in our circumstances can leave us feeling distressed. We thought we…

10:42:27 KST

A sudden and unexpected change in our circumstances can leave us feeling distressed. We thought we knew what our lives would be and we made plans on that basis, but now everything is uncertain. We became comfortable in our routines and habits, only to find that we are now overwhelmed by anxiety and stress.
Without our knowledge, we formed a deep attachment to beliefs about the status quo. We took its regularity for granted, and it now feels like a promise has been broken. We were promised consistency but we received chaos instead. Deep down, we might have known nothing was ever certain, but we never expected to face a change of this magnitude.
Attachment is so nefarious precisely because it easily goes unnoticed. We quietly become accustomed to a certain way of life and we fail to realize we are also becoming more rigid and resistant to movement. But the world will move and it will sometimes do so without warning. To be forced to move again after a long period of dormancy is necessarily shocking and suffering immediately follows — in this case, as anxiety and stress.

Eliud Kipchoge has lived up to his star billing at the Melbourne Marathon with a race-record performance.
Kenya's two-time Olympic champion and former world record holder has delighted several thousand fans at the MCG on Sunday morning with a dominating run.
Kipchoge broke away inside the last 10 kilometres of the 42.2km race and won in 2 hours 9 minutes 10 seconds — 2 seconds inside the previous race best.
He would have finished a few seconds quicker, but was waving to the crowd on the half-lap inside the MCG to the finish.
Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 while fellow Australian Reece Edwards came third in 2:15:57.
In the women's race, New Zealand's Camille French was first to the tape in 2:28:25. Australia's Sinead Diver was 23 seconds back in second place, with Irish runner Nichola Sheridan a further 24 seconds back in third.
The 42km journey took participants down St Kilda Road, past Flinders Street Station, around Albert Park Lake, before a finish inside the MCG.
Kipchoge, 41, last won a marathon in 2023. He looked at the finish like it had been an easy training run, spending several minutes with fans alongside the MCG boundary line.
Kipchoge said it was a great feeling to finish at the famous stadium that also hosted the start and finish of the marathon at the 1956 Olympics — 70 years ago.
"So I come here to celebrate the 70 years and tell the people of Melbourne, 'Let us run together here at the MCG' so it was a beautiful time for me, happy to enter this stadium," Kipchoge said after the race.
This is only his second visit to Australia and his Melbourne Marathon debut.
It is part of Kipchoge's world tour, featuring a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica.

SHANGHAI, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Overnight leader Shi Yuli did just enough to maintain her one-stroke lead during second-round play of the Women's China Open on Saturday as the country's top amateurs moved into contention on a windy day at the national championship.
Playing over the Yangtze Dunes layout at PGA Anying Golf Club on Shanghai's Chongming Island, Beijing veteran Shi carded a one-under 71 at the CLPG Tour's flagship event to get to five-under 139 through 36 holes at the one million-yuan championship.
China's top amateur, Liu Yujie, the world No. 16, shot a three-under 69 for the low round of the day to sit one shot back. Ren Yijia, the CLPG Tour points ranking leader, carded a 71 and was equal third with amateur Cui Jinghan (70) at two shots off the pace.
Thailand's Kornkamol Sukaree (72) was fifth at four shots back.
With the wind picking up throughout her early morning round at the link-style course beside the Yangtze River, Shi, last year's inaugural CLPG Tour point ranking winner, held it together in the blustery conditions to card a round featuring four birdies and three bogeys, two of which came over the last three holes.
"I made a bogey on the third-to-last hole, which is a difficult hole to begin with. We were playing into a strong headwind and I may have taken too much club, leaving myself with a very difficult two-putt. I barely tapped the ball, but it rolled a long way. A three-putt there was understandable. On the last hole, I thought I hit a really good approach shot, but unfortunately, the ball rolled off the green. I couldn't make the final putt either," said the 24-year-old Shi.
After winning the season-ending CLPG Tour Championship in December for her first title since turning pro in 2018, Shi said she would have to be at her best for Sunday's final round if she is to add the national championship to her resume.
"Here you have to factor the wind into every shot you hit. It's so important to stay calm and keep things in perspective. The China Women's Open is obviously very important, although the other tournaments matter too. But this is one of the biggest events of the year, so I think deep down I'll be even more eager to win and achieve a good result here."
Liu, the daughter of former table tennis world champion and Olympic gold medalist Liu Guoliang, started the day three shots back and quickly moved up the leaderboard with birdies at the fourth, fifth and seventh holes. She would pick up another stroke at the par-five 12th to move into a tie for the lead before dropping her only shot of the day at the 415-yard 16th hole.
"I felt like I struggled quite a bit today, especially on the back nine. The front nine actually went really smoothly. My approach shots, driving, and putting were all very good. But things got much tougher on the back nine, and my fairway and green hit rates dropped quite a bit. I was relying on my chipping and putting to save par on almost every hole," said the 16-year-old Beijing native.
"My putting was really good today, though. The wind also picked up this afternoon, which made the course play a little tougher overall. Hopefully, tomorrow I can hit more fairways and greens."
Fellow Beijinger Cui, a 15-year-old who is 79th in the world rankings, carded five birdies, including one on the last hole, and three bogeys in her afternoon round.
"My long game has been in good shape over the past two days. I missed a few birdie putts from fairly close range today, so I feel like I could have made more birdies. Hopefully I can keep up my good long game tomorrow and hole a few more short putts," said the teenager.
Ren, who has won six times on the CLPG Tour over the past three years, stayed close to the top of the leaderboard with a round featuring four birdies, one of which came on the last hole, and three bogeys. Tomorrow, she will play in the second-to-last group.
"Some players might feel that being in the second-to-last group is better because there's less pressure, but for me, it's the same either way. I'll just do my best and focus on my own game," said the 17-year-old Dalian native, 292nd in the Rolex World Rankings.
Sui Xiang, who was one shot back after the first round, struggled to a 76 to fall six shots back. Cai Danlin, who was tied with Sui after the opening round, was a shot further back after a 77. Defending champion Pang Runzhi improved to 73 to sit equal 16th, eight shots back. ■

Hangzhou is doubling down on tech – minus the viral hype
Beyond kickboxing robots and DeepSeek, the city is making a strategic pivot and betting on tech champions that build the infrastructure powering China’s next AI cycle
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Ni Tao is the founder and editor of yangtzeer. 
A year ago, a Unitree robot kickboxing could light up social media. When DeepSeek released its latest open-source artificial intelligence (AI) model, developers around the world rushed to test it.
This year, however, Hangzhou’s latest technology bets have barely made a ripple. The city’s “New Eight Steeds” – eight deep-tech companies in fields ranging from smart glasses and inference graphic processing units (GPUs) to compute-in-memory chips and space computing – are a very different proposition from the “Six Little Dragons” that have made Hangzhou a focus of the global tech conversation.
Most of them operate further up the industrial chain, serving companies and institutions rather than consumers. That helps explain why the new cohort has struggled to capture the public’s attention. It also raises an uncomfortable question: has Hangzhou’s technology marketing playbook stopped working?
The scepticism is understandable. Some mock Hangzhou’s eagerness to turn tech companies into a branding exercise. The “Six Little Dragons” have yet to produce many businesses with proven profitability, yet the city has already moved on to another coterie.

Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
Emergency services called to the scene after reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at a UK wildlife park.
A man has died after entering a tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and being attacked by one of the animals, police said.
South Yorkshire Police said officers and emergency medical staff were called to Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35pm on Saturday (12:35 GMT) after receiving reports that a man had entered the enclosure.
He died at the scene. It was not immediately clear how he got in.
The tiger was not injured and stayed inside the enclosure during the incident, police said, adding that there was no wider risk to the public.
The park was evacuated, and officers remained at the scene on Saturday night.
“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time,” police said in a statement.
Police also confirmed they were aware of footage circulating on social media that appeared to show the man inside the enclosure shortly before the attack, urging members of the public not to share the distressing video.
The park said it had closed after a serious incident involving the tiger enclosure and would remain closed until Sunday.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,” the park said in a statement on its website.
“The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operating in 2009, and its Land of the Tigers attraction – a purpose-built 0.4-hectare (2-acre) reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers – opened in 2011.
A raised walkway, 300 metres (985 feet) long, lets visitors watch the tigers roam through woodland and grassland and play in a waterfall pool, the park said.

Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied territories, including Chornobyl disaster responder
Sixteen Ukrainian civilians have been evacuated from Russian-occupied territories to government-controlled Ukraine, Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announced on Oct. 10.
The evacuees crossed through the Novi Yarylovychi checkpoint on Ukraine's border with Belarus, Lubinets said, describing the complicated arrangements required to help people leave Russian-occupied areas.
Among those returned was an elderly man with a disability who helped respond to the 1986 Chornobyl nuclear disaster. He had been living with his wife in occupied Luhansk Oblast, where the couple struggled to leave because of her deteriorating health.
The woman had suffered a severe stroke in April and required constant care, and her husband also needed medical treatment and could no longer care for her, Lubinets said.
With their daughter was waiting in Kyiv, arrangements were being made to bring both parents to safety. Unfortunately, the woman died before the evacuation could take place, and only her husband was able to return.
"The daughter was waiting for both parents, but met only one," Lubinets said.
Another evacuee, a woman with severely limited mobility who had been living alone under occupation, required specialized transportation, medical assistance and a carefully planned route.
Lubinets said preparations had to be carried out discreetly to avoid attracting the attention of Russian occupation authorities and putting the woman at further risk.
The return of Ukrainian citizens was organized by Ukrainian agricultural company MHP and its founder and CEO Yuriy Kosyuk, according to Lubinets.
He also thanked Charitable Foundation Caritas Ukraine, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and others, for helping those who returned to receive immediate medical care, temporary housing, financial assistance, psychological support and transportation onwards.
"Crossing the border is only the beginning of a return to a safe life," Lubinets said.
Ukraine continues to quietly coordinate evacuations from temporarily Russian-occupied territories, where residents’ quality of life is severely diminished, particularly those who are elderly, disabled or require medical treatment.
On Sept. 19, Ukraine returned 15 civilians from Russian-occupied territories, while a further 41 civilians returned through a Volyn Oblast border crossing during August and September, according to previous announcements by the ombudsman's office.
Lubinets said his office continues to process requests, assess security risks and coordinate routes for Ukrainians still seeking to leave occupied territory.

The Pentagon officially updated its count of US service members who have been killed in connection with Operation Epic Fury and the ongoing war with Iran to 21 from the previous figure of 18, according to a Saturday report from The Washington Post.
The update to the US’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) included the two noncombat deaths of Army National Guard Maj. Sorffly Davius, who died in Kuwait in March, and an unidentified Navy suicide, an anonymous US official told The Washington Post.
The Washington Post reported in September that the previous official count of 18 may have been inaccurate and that at least four service members were potentially excluded from the DCAS tally, at the time citing six US officials familiar with the Pentagon’s internal casualty accounting data.
Following the update, 15 deaths are included in the DCAS count for service members killed during Operation Epic Fury, and an additional six are listed as military deaths during overseas operations.
According to The Washington Post, the category of military deaths during overseas operations was created after US President Donald Trump declared that Operation Epic Fury had officially ended, despite ongoing hostilities and exchanges of strikes.
Hegseth labeled reports of inaccurate death count a 'complete lie'
In September, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth decried The Washington Post’s report that the official Pentagon death count was inaccurate as “a complete lie.”
In a post on X/Twitter at the time, Hegseth said The Washington Post was “worse than Iranian state media.”
US House Armed Services Committee Ranking Member Adam Smith and Military Personnel Subcommittee Ranking Member Chrissy Houlahan, who previously urged the US Department of Defense to look into the discrepancies in casualty numbers, released a statement on Friday responding to the correction.
“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” they wrote, adding that “requiring Congress to step in to rectify such an egregious error is an embarrassment for the Department [of Defense].”
They stated that they are glad to see that the incorrect count had been updated, but vowed to continue to fight for transparency, accountability, and procedures to ensure such miscounts do not happen in the future.

Angus Taylor would welcome return of Josh Frydenberg to politics but rejects GST increase
In short:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he would welcome back former colleague Josh Frydenberg to the Liberals, if he were to contest a seat at the next federal election.
Mr Taylor has also defended the Coalition's proposed cuts to migration, arguing that more skilled migrants with a higher average income would achieve budget neutrality.
What's next?
The Coalition says it will release more details of its migration plan closer to the election.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he would welcome the return of former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg to politics, as he continues to defend the Coalition's newly released migration policy.
On Saturday, Mr Frydenberg released excerpts of his upcoming memoir A Grateful Son, published in The Australian, which included details of his election defeat four years ago.
The former Kooyong MP, who was a leadership frontrunner, fuelled speculation he may contest a seat in the next election as he outlined his vision for Australia.
He urged the Liberal Party to "reclaim" the centre of politics, arguing there was a lack of political courage in Canberra.
Mr Frydenberg proposed several policy changes across energy and AI and a pitch to leverage a portion of state GST revenue based on how many homes were built.
When asked whether he would welcome or fear his former colleague's return, Mr Taylor said he needed "every good leader" heading into the next federal election.
"People will play different roles … whether it's just liking Facebook and Instagram posts all the way through to being a candidate," he told Insiders on Sunday.
"But we've all got to mobilise, and I welcome Josh playing whatever role he's able to play."
Mr Taylor immediately added that the Coalition would not adopt Mr Frydenberg's suggestion of raising the GST.
"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis. That we won't do," he said.
"We'll put Australia and Australians first, but we won't be raising taxes.
"I'm a fiscal conservative. I believe in lower taxes, and that's why we'll be giving the tax-back guarantee, lower income taxes for Australians without raising the GST." 
Taylor defends budget neutrality of Coalition's migration cuts
Despite economic concerns raised by the business, aged care, education and construction sectors about the Coalition's migration policy, the opposition leader maintained it would be "budget neutral".
Mr Taylor said the policy had not been officially costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office, due to "constraints".
"In terms of analysis, there are limitations on what the parliamentary office can do because of its legislation. It cannot model directly on Labor's policies so we had to give it assumptions to work with," he said.
"That is a constraint, but as we approach the election, we won't have that constraint."
The policy proposes slashing temporary migration by 650,000 places over four years and offsetting the lost tax revenue with 100,000 additional skilled migrants, who would be higher-paid and therefore pay more tax.
He reiterated that aged care, which heavily relies on temporary visas, would be subject to a transitional arrangement that allowed these workers to stay on existing visas for a longer period of time.
"If you cut numbers and raise standards, you can maintain budget neutrality. And you can strengthen the economy because the average income, the average productivity of the person coming into this country rises," he said.
"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone."
Australia's net overseas migration, or NOM, fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, with Labor pursuing a target of 245,000 for this financial year and 225,000 the year after.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek labelled Mr Taylor's interview a "car crash" and questioned why he could not provide full economic modelling.
"It's disappointing that a once major party of government can't answer basic questions about the economic impact of their policies," she said.
"If you can unite big business and small businesses and farmers and unions, saying your policy will smash the economy, maybe it's time to go back to the drawing board."
Meanwhile, Immigration Minister Tony Burke has warned that bridging visa cuts at the scale proposed by the Coalition would require billions of dollars in infrastructure and workforce investment.
"They need to let us know how many beds, how many compliance officers, and where the new detention centres are going," Mr Burke told News24.
"The numbers they are talking about, we are talking billions and billions of dollars I suspect."

Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
00:23:50 UTC
09:23:50 KST

Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case
New cases in eastern DRC and a fatal imported infection in Kenya highlight the challenges of containing Ebola.
Beni, Democratic Republic of Congo – The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has spread to another health zone in the east, while a fatal imported case in Kenya has underscored the risk of cross-border transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said in an October 8 update that Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu province had reported cases for the first time. As of October 6, four confirmed cases, including two deaths, had been recorded there.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola virus. According to the WHO, cases had been reported in 64 health zones across seven provinces in the DRC. Ituri remained the worst-affected province in cumulative cases, while North Kivu was accounting for a growing share of newly confirmed infections.
As of October 6, the WHO had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 confirmed deaths in the DRC. A further 2,269 people had recovered, and the crude case fatality ratio stood at 48.2 percent.
Kenya confirms imported case
Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease on October 6, according to the WHO. The patient, a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the DRC, fell ill there and received treatment at several health facilities before travelling to Kenya through Uganda.
The patient travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda, before flying to Nairobi, arriving on October 3. The patient was isolated in hospital and tested positive for the virus. Despite supportive treatment, the patient died on October 5, the WHO said.
Kenyan authorities identified 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers. The WHO also reported efforts to trace passengers and crew members from the flight to Nairobi.
Public health measures have been initiated in Kenya and Uganda, including contact tracing and enhanced surveillance.
On October 8, preliminary laboratory results for a suspected Ebola case in Kenya’s Wajir County came back negative, according to the county governor. The result eased concerns about a possible second case, although monitoring continued.
The imported infection has underscored the importance of surveillance and coordination between neighbouring countries. Identifying exposed people and monitoring them for symptoms are central to detecting infections early and interrupting further transmission.
Treatment capacity under pressure
In the DRC, the response is facing mounting pressure from limited treatment capacity, insecurity and difficulties securing cooperation from some communities.
Daniel Makasi Levergénois, founder of Watoto Radio, said insecurity and misinformation were undermining efforts to contain the outbreak. In Beni and Butembo, both in North Kivu, rumours and misconceptions about Ebola had contributed to reluctance among some residents to cooperate with response teams, he said.
In an October 5 update, medical charity Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said North Kivu accounted for nearly 40 percent of newly confirmed cases nationwide, up from 24 percent at the end of August.
MSF also reported that, as of September 28, 34 percent of confirmed Ebola patients were being treated in non-specialised health facilities. Dedicated treatment centres lacked sufficient beds, while delays in diagnosis meant some patients were being treated outside facilities equipped to manage Ebola.
The organisation warned that many of these facilities lacked the resources and expertise needed to manage the disease, increasing the risk of transmission among patients and healthcare workers.
“For weeks, treatment capacity has stretched to its limit,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator of MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in Butembo.
“Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment. This is extremely concerning.”
Mistrust threatens containment efforts
Alberto Lusenge, a community leader in Beni, said the failure to stop transmission early in Ituri province, followed by new cases and attacks on response workers in Beni and Butembo, had deepened public concern.
Lusenge warned that mistrust could discourage residents from reporting symptoms or cooperating with health workers. He said North Kivu could become a greater focus of the outbreak if authorities failed to secure stronger cooperation from local communities.
The WHO said response teams were following up 23,741 of the 29,535 identified contacts as of October 4, equivalent to 80.4 percent – below the response target of at least 85 percent.
Contact tracing allows health authorities to identify people who may have been exposed, monitor them for symptoms and detect infections early. Gaps in follow-up can make it harder to identify and interrupt chains of transmission.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for a community-centred response, including active case finding, systematic contact tracing, daily follow-up of exposed people and sustained engagement with local communities.
A history of deadly outbreaks
The DRC’s 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak, caused by a different virus species, killed nearly 2,300 people. The current outbreak presents distinct challenges: According to the WHO, there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease.
Early detection, supportive care and infection prevention therefore remain central to the response. But as infections spread into additional health zones and treatment facilities struggle to accommodate patients, health authorities face the dual challenge of containing transmission and maintaining public trust.
Jean Kaseya, director-general of Africa CDC, has stressed the importance of rapidly identifying and monitoring people exposed to the virus.
“To bring this outbreak under control, we need to know where every contact is, track them and quickly identify anyone showing symptoms before they pass the virus on to their family, their community or across borders. We will only bring this outbreak under control once the last chain of transmission has been broken,” Kaseya said in a news release seen by Al Jazeera.
