Rubio pledges US cooperation in Marine-linked murder case
A US Marine stationed on Okinawa has been arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman.
The United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has vowed to cooperate with Japanese authorities investigating allegations that a US Marine murdered a woman in Okinawa, a case that provoked protests and prompted a US military curfew and mandatory training in standards and discipline.
The top US diplomat spoke with Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu in a phone call, the US Department of State said in a statement on Saturday following the death of a local woman in a hotel that has renewed tensions over the US military presence.
“Rubio expressed sincere condolences over the death of a Japanese national in Okinawa, as well as the United States’ determination to communicate and fully cooperate with the Government of Japan and local authorities as they conduct an investigation,” the department said.
Devin Jacob Ballard, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on October 4 on suspicion of robbing and murdering Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in the capital Naha, according to local police.
Local media reported that she was choked to death and her wallet stolen.
Ballard has denied the allegations.
The killing triggered outrage in Japan, where crimes involving US forces have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies and have long inflamed criticism of US troops being stationed there. Japan hosts the largest overseas contingent of US forces globally, with most of the 18,000 Japan-based Marines stationed on Okinawa.
Following the killing, US military personnel stationed there have been given a monthlong curfew and banned from drinking alcohol while they undergo discipline training.
Rubio and Toshimitsu also discussed US sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the upcoming G20 Foreign Ministers meeting in Atlanta, scheduled to begin on October 30.

Isaias kills 4 in US, leaves 670,000 without power
The hurricane weakened to a post-tropical cyclone after making landfall, but hazardous conditions remain
Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services.
Two of the deaths resulted from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities.
Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said.
But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Centre said.

Netanyahu trial: former AG Mandelblit to testify as defense witness before election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:29:45 UTC
05:29:45 KST

Former attorney general Avichai Mandelblit, who approved criminal charges against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2019, is scheduled to testify Sunday in Netanyahu's corruption trial, just over two weeks before Israel's October 27 election. His appearance comes a decade after the initial examination of allegations against Netanyahu was announced.
Mandelblit was summoned as a defense witness at the request of Netanyahu's attorneys, Amit Hadad and Noa Milstein, who are expected to question him primarily about whether he authorized the investigations against the prime minister and whether police carried out investigative steps without his knowledge or approval.
The defense requested seven nonconsecutive days of testimony, although the judges may limit the questioning. Netanyahu's lawyers argue that certain investigative actions were conducted without the attorney general's authorization, as required by Israeli law. Prosecutors reject the allegation, maintaining that the investigations and investigative steps were conducted lawfully and with the necessary approvals.
A central point of contention concerns the way Mandelblit's authorization was documented. Rather than issuing separate formal written approvals, he gave permission orally during meetings with police officials, which were recorded in Justice Ministry minutes. The judges have previously criticized that procedure.
The defense is also expected to question Mandelblit about investigative tactics used against former Netanyahu aide and state witness Nir Hefetz, who testified that investigators subjected him to intense pressure. Hefetz nevertheless stated that a specific investigative maneuver involving people close to him did not influence his decision to become a state witness.
Mandelblit's testimony follows conflicting accounts from police investigators and prosecutors about the scope of his authorizations. The defense claims investigators exceeded their permitted authority, while prosecutors have presented internal records that they say demonstrate the investigations, including inquiries into gifts received by Netanyahu, were properly approved.

China’s Bid to Define the ‘Global South’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:29:00 UTC
05:29:00 KST

In the leadup to the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, President Xi Jinping attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and the BRICS summit in Delhi. He also visited the Middle East — all between August and September. What is notable is that in speeches delivered at both the SCO and BRICS summits, Xi made heavy use of the term “Global South.” This reflects China’s positioning of the SCO and BRICS as gatherings of the Global South, even though Russia and Turkey are among their members. How, precisely, does China understand and deploy this term “Global South” (全球南方, Quanqiu Nanfang)?
In academic usage, “Global South” originally carried the meaning that “South” issues exist within developed countries too, and that the North-South divide should not be understood in spatially separate terms; South issues are, rather, global in character. From around 2020, however, the term began to be used differently in international forums. In particular, following the war in Ukraine, a view spread — especially in Western countries — that sharply delineated the advanced democracies against China and Russia, drawing an axis of confrontation between the developed world and China, Russia (plus Iran and North Korea), and treating the remaining countries as the “Global South.” China responded to this by becoming very wary of the term, viewing “Global South” as a Western-originated concept designed to drive a wedge between China and the developing world. China’s self-identification has been as a developing country —indeed, as the representative of the developing world. For this reason, it was unwilling to accept a term that would separate China from developing countries.
Despite this, the term “Global South” became increasingly prevalent globally. In particular, when India hosted the “Voice of Global South Summit” online on January 12 and 13, 2023, and did not invite China, this appears to have come as a significant shock to Beijing. Yet even after the “Voice of Global South Summit,” Chinese criticism of the term continued. The shift came in the period following the enactment of the Foreign Relations Law on June 28, 2023. That law, in Article 4, calls for upholding the five principles [of peaceful coexistence], and also uses the term “developing country” (发展中国家) in two places, reaffirming China’s identity as a developing country.
From July 2023, Foreign Minister Wang Yi suddenly began using the term “Global South” at international conferences, albeit with quotation marks around it. At the Meeting of BRICS National Security Advisers and High Representatives on National Security held in Johannesburg on July 25, when Wang used “Global South” in quotation marks, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning then offered a definition of the term at a press conference: “The ‘Global South’ is the family of emerging markets and developing countries.” Wang Yi listed “independence,” “development,” and “justice” as the defining qualities of the Global South, and declared that “China is a natural member of the Global South and will always be part of the developing world.” This was a definition of the Global South that clearly differed from that used in developed countries.
China has offered no explanation for this shift in approach. The most plausible interpretation is that, as the term came to be widely used globally — particularly among leaders of developing countries — and as the term’s definition remained unsettled, China made a deliberate policy shift: to define the term itself, on its own terms, and thereby shape global discourse in its favor. This too can be counted as one instance of China’s pursuit of what it calls “discourse power.”
Subsequently, not only Wang but Xi himself began using the term with quotation marks. This signaled that the term had become domestically usable within China as well. By the end of 2024, quotation marks began to be dropped from “Global South” in Chinese documents, and in a piece by Wang published in Qiushi in 2025, the quotation marks were also absent. There remain, to be sure, some inconsistencies in usage (instances can still be found in 2025 where Chinese officials used “Global South” with quotation marks) but these have gradually become less common, and at the SCO and BRICS meetings in 2026 cited at the outset, Xi Jinping’s use of Global South carried no quotation marks.
Globally speaking, “Global South” remains a term without an agreed definition, with each actor investing it with its own meaning. China has positioned itself as a member of the Global South and has come to behave as its representative. China defines Global South as “the family of emerging markets and developing countries” — which amounts to the “non-West.” The contest over this term “Global South” throws into relief the differences in worldview between the developed world and China. The contest over this seemingly simple term, it turns out, is anything but.

Trehubov describes intensity of Russian airstrikes along front line

Trehubov describes intensity of Russian airstrikes along front line
Spokesperson for the Joint Forces Group Viktor Trehubov made the statement during a televised broadcast, responding to questions about the current activity of Russian aircraft and the extent to which Russian forces rely on guided aerial bombs, Ukrinform reports.
"Today, a guided aerial bomb is not very accurate, but it is still a fairly powerful weapon. Usually, several dozen of them hit along the entire line within our area of responsibility every day," he said.
Trehubov noted that Russian guided bombs have never been particularly accurate, adding that Ukrainian troops are taking certain technical measures to reduce their accuracy even further.
"So, on the one hand, one of these bombs will hit and explode with tremendous force, but there is no guarantee it will hit the target the Russians want. On the other hand, the fact that it hits and explodes at all does not exactly make the air any cleaner. So we are waiting for more effective means of combating Russian aircraft," the spokesperson said.
He suggested that a solution might be found next year.
In response to a question, Trehubov said Russian forces were undoubtedly trying to advance deeper into settlements near both Vovchansk and Lyptsi.
"Of course, they are trying both to bypass settlements and to advance directly into them. They are actively trying to push beyond Vovchansk to the south. Overall, along that entire line, they are simply trying to expand their zone of control southward," the spokesperson said.
Asked whether he had observed any changes in his area of responsibility following several phases of Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk region, whether the operation had disoriented Russian forces, or whether there had been any weakening of Russian positions along the front line, he said that this had occurred, if at all, only in the south, somewhere around Borova, from where some redeployments had taken place.
"But overall, I would say that this is more a matter of Russian forces becoming somewhat depleted at the beginning of autumn. They had many major objectives to achieve by the end of summer. They tried to accomplish some of them and became somewhat exhausted in the process, and the overall intensity of hostilities decreased in autumn," Trehubov said.
The spokesperson noted that the intensity of hostilities had increased somewhat recently, but remained moderate overall.
He also said that the area under his responsibility was currently fairly well equipped with engineering fortifications, including defensive and protective structures.
"In other words, there is reason to thank the engineers," Trehubov said.

Quick hits: AFL star in the sheds as Aussies go better than Bradman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:20:25 UTC
05:20:25 KST

Matt Renshaw and Nathan Lyon outdo Sir Donald Bradman while Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson watches on from the stands.
Here are the quick hits from day two of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Renshaw's drought-breaking century
It had been over nine years and nine months since Matt Renshaw's last and only Test century.
Opening the batting on January 3, 2017, a then 20-year-old Renshaw peeled off 184 against Pakistan in Sydney, a match in which he lined up alongside the likes of two-Test white-ball specialist Hilton Cartwright and New South Wales great Steve O'Keefe.
A few false dawns, a short-format reinvention and a red-ball renaissance later, and the Queenslander brought up his drought-breaking ton with an immaculately timed clip through mid-wicket for four.
Having lost overnight partner Pat Cummins and number nine Mitch Starc in quick succession after starting the day on 46, Renshaw was almost chanceless in reaching three figures.
It was a richly deserved milestone for a player, who, at 30, still has plenty of good years ahead of him.
And Renshaw just kept going.
And going.
He received much more than able support from Nathan Lyon as he passed 150, before kicking on with number 11 Josh Hazlewood to set a new Test best of 190, falling just short of a maiden double ton as he nicked off after tea.
2. Better than Bradman
The first innings appeared not long for this world when the best betters in the tail, Cummins and Starc, departed.
But Lyon picked up the mantle to knuckle under with Renshaw, albeit in slightly less expressive fashion. At least so it seemed.
After helping Renshaw to triple figures, there was no loss of application from the Aussie batters out in the middle and when Lyon clipped Anrich Nortje off his hip for four in the 108th over, they passed some pretty big names.
In the 124-year history of Tests against South Africa, no Australian ninth-wicket partnership had ever surpassed 78 runs until day two in Durban.
And the two pairings who had reached that mark included some all-time greats: Ian Meckiff and Ken McKay in Johannesburg in 1958, and Sir Donald Bradman with Bill O'Reilly in Adelaide Oval way back in 1932.
And the records kept tumbling as the runs kept coming, with the pair ticking past two Steve Waugh specials, the first a 130-run stand with Geoff Lawson in 1989, and the second a 133-run effort in tandem with Jason Gillespie in 2001.
By the time Lyon was eventually dismissed for a 92-ball 27 and the stand was over on 134, there was only one greater ninth-wicket partnership in the history of Australian cricket — and that had come in the 19th century.
3. Australia's best recovery in over a century
Given the shakiness of Australia's top order over the past decade or so, there have been plenty of opportunities for inspired rearguard actions.
Loading Twitter content
And we certainly have been treated to some remarkable recoveries — think Steve Smith's partnerships with Peter Siddle and Nathan Lyon that took Australia from 8-122 to 284 at Edgbaston in 2019, or Lyon and Cummins combining for a 55-run stand to guide Australia home during the 2023 Ashes.
But not for over 100 years have we seen an Australian comeback as dramatic as the one we were treated to on day two.
Per ABC Sport statistician Ric Finlay, Australia's recovery from 6-124 to 390 was the country's best rebuild since 1925, when an unbeaten double century to number seven Jack Ryder took Australia from 6-119 to 489.
4. Another selection shock for the Aussies?!
With the Australian rearguard action showing no signs of abating, the broadcast camera panned to the tourists' dugout, where it found an unexpected but familiar face for Aussie sports fan.
Dressed in full training kit and looking slightly surprised to be there himself, there he was, Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson.
Loading Instagram content
Anderson has travelled with the Australians to South Africa as part of a leadership fact-finding mission, according to Fox commentator Mark Howard.
As the cameras focused in on Anderson, a Sherrin suddenly appeared in the hands of Marnus Labuschagne, sitting alongside the Suns star.
5. Lyon walks off despite review
Nathan Lyon enjoyed a gutsy, record-breaking dig alongside Matt Renshaw, but when it was over it was pretty obvious.
Marco Jansen's return to the attack brought with it a short-pitched barrage that seemed to rattle the Aussies out of their methodical tactics of Renshaw seeing off the first four balls before giving Lyon a look.
After being twisted up by a bouncer, Renshaw scurried off strike and left Lyon with three balls to negotiate, but it only took Jansen one as he surprised the number 10 with a full one that smashed into his pads.
Jansen, the rest of South Africa's fielders and umpire Chris Gaffaney all knew it was out, and so did Lyon, despite deciding to review.
He made an immediate "T" sign before just as quickly walking off the field before the replays were finished.
By the time his dismissal was confirmed he was already halfway up the stairs.

Whither Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:16:00 UTC
05:16:00 KST

Debate over the three non-nuclear principles has resurfaced in Japan as the government of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae prepares a new National Security Strategy, due at the end of 2026. Even the status of the principles is contested. Some regard them as the country’s foundational principle (kokuze), while others describe them as a policy guideline, suggesting that the government is free to change it. Prime Minister Sato Eisaku first announced the principles in 1967, and the Diet has reaffirmed them on multiple occasions since then.
The principles state that Japan will neither possess nor produce nuclear weapons, nor permit their introduction into its territory. As long as Japan remains a party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), the only practical debate concerns the third principle: non-introduction. The commitments not to possess or produce nuclear weapons nevertheless sent an important message to the world when the principles were first articulated, before Japan ratified the NPT.
In March 2010, Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya revealed that a secret agreement (mitsuyaku), broadly defined, had existed between Washington and Tokyo over the introduction of nuclear weapons. Under the U.S. interpretation, “introduction” referred only to the permanent deployment of nuclear warheads in storage facilities ashore. The Japanese government, by contrast, regarded transit through Japan’s territorial waters or port calls by nuclear-armed vessels as introduction as well. Successive Japanese leaders maintained that, in the absence of a U.S. request for “prior consultation” under the arrangements associated with the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty of 1960, Tokyo assumed that visiting U.S. vessels were not carrying nuclear weapons. Yet such vessels could not simply leave their nuclear weapons elsewhere before entering Japan. It is now an open secret that, under the Japanese definition, the United States “introduced” nuclear weapons into Japan during the Cold War.
Since the revelation in March 2010, Tokyo has maintained that there is no need to be concerned about introduction because the United States does not deploy nuclear weapons on surface vessels and has no nuclear weapon system for the vessels that regularly visit Japan. At the same time, successive Japanese governments have upheld the position Okada first articulated in the Diet that month: in extreme circumstances in which Japan’s survival cannot be secured without allowing the introduction of nuclear weapons, the government of the day “shall make a decision by taking full responsibility.” This effectively leaves open the possibility of permitting introduction in a contingency. Some therefore argue there is no need to revise the three non-nuclear principles, since they have already become “two and a half” principles.
Okada’s formula, however, does not resolve all the problems surrounding the principles. First, it only addresses contingencies, leaving unanswered how Tokyo could handle the issue in peacetime. Second, the United States is developing a nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile (SLCM-N), with the aim of making it operational in the mid-2030s. While not officially confirmed yet, the missile is expected to be carried by attack submarines of the kind that regularly visit Japan. Third, Okada’s formula addresses introduction in the Japanese sense – transit and visiting – without addressing introduction in the U.S. sense: storage ashore.
Once U.S. attack submarines begin carrying SLCM-N – or, more precisely, once they become capable of carrying it – Tokyo will find it difficult to avoid allegations that the United States is introducing nuclear weapons into Japan, regardless of whether a particular visiting submarine actually carries them. Under its longstanding “neither confirm nor deny” (NCND) policy, Washington will not disclose whether visiting submarines carry nuclear weapons. Moreover, under the U.S. definition, neither transit nor port visits constitute introduction.
This will therefore be primarily a problem for Japan. Some, particularly critics of the U.S.-Japan alliance, will argue that Tokyo should ban visits by submarines that might be carrying nuclear weapons. Doing so, however, could undermine the alliance’s deterrence and damage relations with Washington.
If Tokyo rules out denying access to U.S. submarines, it has three options. First, it could drop or amend the non-introduction principle. Second, in the most far-reaching version of such a revision, it could explicitly permit the introduction of nuclear weapons, including storage ashore as well as transit and port visits, opening the way to possible future nuclear-sharing arrangements. Third, it could adopt a narrower, more technical change: revise its definition of introduction so that transit and port visits no longer fall within it, bringing Japan’s interpretation into line with that of the United States.
Whichever option Tokyo chooses, it will be highly contentious in political terms at home. Only strong political leadership could address this problem. Many politicians appear unprepared to tackle this issue now, believing that they still have time. But it is not too early to begin laying the groundwork for a decision.

In Croatia, a large-scale railway accident occurred on the morning of October 10 near the city of Rijeka. A freight train operated by the private carrier Transagent derailed, causing 11 cars to fall into a ravine. According to preliminary data, the train was carrying grain, likely of Ukrainian origin, Teklic.hr reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The accident occurred at approximately 9:25 a.m. at the entrance to Mejа railway station. According to local media reports, before the derailment, the driver told the dispatcher that the brakes had failed and that he was unable to stop the train. Despite the extensive damage, no one was injured in the incident.
The locomotive stopped just one meter from the home of Croatian Railways employee Vinko Boras, who has lived near the station for 28 years. The man said he immediately ran to the driver, who was not injured.
Railway service suspended, cause of accident under investigation
Because of the accident, train traffic on this section was completely suspended, and passengers are temporarily being transported by buses. Railway infrastructure sustained serious damage, particularly the rails and sleepers. The situation is complicated by the fact that the accident occurred on a section where the track branches in three directions.
Railway workers warn that restoration work may take a long time. First, specialists must partially repair the tracks to provide railway cranes with access to the accident site and begin lifting the cars from the ravine.
Croatia’s Minister of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure, Oleg Butkovich, said that preliminary data do not indicate the unsatisfactory condition of the railway infrastructure as the cause of the accident. A technical failure of the train or human error are among the main theories being considered.
Police and representatives of the Agency for the Investigation of Aviation, Maritime and Railway Accidents are working at the site. The exact cause of the train’s derailment will be established after the official investigation is completed.

Several ships near Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates were instructed by radio Saturday evening to leave their anchorages, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.
In an advisory, UKMTO said it received reports from several ship captains in the area that they had been directed via very high frequency (VHF) radio broadcast to move from their anchorages.
The agency classified the incident as "suspicious activity" and said authorities were investigating.
It urged vessels in the area to report any further suspicious activity.
UKMTO did not identify who issued the instructions or say whether any vessels complied. It also reported no attacks or damage to ships in connection with the incident.
The advisory comes amid heightened maritime tensions and a series of security incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf.
The strategic waterway has been a major point of contention in negotiations between Washington and Tehran, particularly over control and management of maritime traffic.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, prompting retaliatory Iranian attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire was reached in April.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation has stalled amid disagreements over maritime security.

Beyond Ideological Blocs: The ICDPP’s New Intercontinental Political Dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:01:00 UTC
05:01:00 KST

In September 2026, political leaders and party representatives from Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Europe gathered in Seoul to launch a new forum: the Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties (ICDPP). Your correspondent attended the inaugural meeting as part of the CDP delegation and spoke with Chung Eui-yong about how the ICDPP emerged and the principle behind it.
The inaugural meeting brought together 23 political parties from 23 countries, including 19 governing and four opposition parties. Participants included Chung Eui-yong, chair of the Standing Committee of the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP) and former South Korean foreign minister; Mushahid Hussain Sayed of the Pakistan Muslim League, a former information and broadcasting minister; Adem Farah Ibrahim, Ethiopia’s deputy prime minister and vice president of the ruling Prosperity Party; Milton Morrison of the Dominican Republic, vice president of the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL) and leader of the País Posible party; Zsolt Németh of Hungary, chair of the European Conservatives, Patriots and Affiliates group in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe; and Maiko Tajima, director of the International Department of Japan’s Constitutional Democratic Party.
The variety of political traditions represented in Seoul is central to understanding the ICDPP. This is not a forum limited to ideologically like-minded parties. Its purpose is to provide a forum in which parties with different political orientations – including governing and opposition parties – can remain in dialogue.
That principle was formally incorporated into the Seoul Declaration, unanimously adopted on September 7.
The declaration describes the ICDPP as a voluntary platform for consultation, cooperation, and confidence-building among political parties, open “irrespective of ideological orientation, governing status, or level of development.” It also stresses that the ICDPP is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing regional and international organizations.
The declaration addresses a broad range of challenges, including geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change, economic uncertainty, technological transformation, and inequality. Participants reaffirmed their commitment to the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights, the rule of law, sustainable development, and multilateral cooperation. They also agreed to continue ICDPP meetings and develop institutional arrangements and future work programs.
Its concluding phrase summarized the aspiration behind the new forum: “dialogue over dispute, cooperation over confrontation, and partnership over polarization.”
From ICAPP to ICDPP
The ICDPP did not emerge suddenly. It builds on more than two decades of political party dialogue developed through the ICAPP and its regional partners. The ICAPP was founded in 2000 at the initiative of former Philippine House Speaker Jose de Venecia Jr. Chung, who became involved after entering South Korean politics in 2004, later played an important role in its institutional development, including drafting the ICAPP Charter and helping establish its Standing Committee and regular meetings.
In addition to this institutional development, the ICAPP gradually expanded its dialogue beyond Asia. It established regular exchanges with the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL), developed the Asia-Europe Political Forum with European political groups, and promoted contacts with African political parties. The establishment in Ghana in 2025 of the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI) added a new institutional partner in Africa.
With ties established across the Americas, Europe, and Africa, Chung explained: “I thought it’s about time” to hold a meeting involving the four regions. He proposed the name “Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties,” and the idea received support from the regional partners.
The ICDPP can therefore be understood as the culmination of a gradual process: regional political party dialogue in Asia expanding into cross-regional dialogue and, eventually, an intercontinental framework.
Why Talk Across Ideological Divides?
The principle inherited from the ICAPP is as important as the network itself. The ICAPP developed as a forum open to political parties from different ideological traditions, rather than one organized around a single political family. Chung incorporated that principle into the ICAPP Charter when the organization was being institutionalized.
Asked why, Chung replied: “I tell you my conviction. Why should we be divided by ideological orientation? And why can’t we talk to each other?”
He explained that he had held the same view in domestic politics. When Chung entered politics in 2004, some in his own Democratic Party were skeptical of bipartisan diplomacy, while persuading the conservative opposition to cooperate was not easy. Today, however, South Korea’s major rival parties cooperate in ICAPP activities.
The same thinking is visible in the Seoul Declaration. It describes differences in political traditions and cultures not simply as obstacles, but as possible sources of “strength and mutual learning.” This does not mean that the ICDPP expects political disagreements to disappear. On the contrary, disagreement is built into the design of the forum.
At the welcome dinner on the eve of the inaugural meeting, Chung told delegates that they should not expect everyone around the table to think alike.
“Our political traditions, experiences, and perspectives are different,” he said. Those differences, he continued, should be acknowledged and respected. The aim was to create a space in which they could be discussed openly and constructively, while keeping channels of communication open – especially “when circumstances become difficult and dialogue is needed most.”
That may be the clearest expression of what distinguishes the ICDPP. Its purpose is not to create ideological unity, but to sustain political communication despite ideological difference.
From Dialogue to Action
The challenge now is whether that dialogue can produce results. A forum encompassing parties with widely different political traditions and geopolitical interests may find it relatively easy to meet, but much harder to reach common positions or act collectively.
Chung himself raised precisely this issue in his opening remarks. “The significance of this initiative,” he said, should not be measured simply by the number or diversity of participants around the table, but by the ability to “build sustained dialogue and turn our conversations into meaningful action.”
The Seoul Declaration provides the first steps: regular meetings, further discussions on rules and institutional arrangements, future work programs, and broader participation while retaining the voluntary and inclusive character of the forum.
Whether the ICDPP will develop into an effective mechanism for cooperation remains an open question. Its significance will ultimately depend not on the number of parties represented at future meetings, but on whether relationships built through repeated dialogue can survive periods of political tension – and whether those relationships can contribute to practical cooperation on common challenges.
At the welcome dinner in Seoul, Chung described what he hoped the gathering might eventually become: a community of political leaders who made a deliberate choice to continue talking, listening, and working together across continents, “even when our views are different.”

News from occupied Ukraine: Russia prepares Oleshky disinformation campaign, budgets for occupation for next three years
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Key news as of Oct. 10:
- Russia prepared series of Oleshky disinformation operations, SBU says
- Russia's new three-year federal budget maintains funding for occupied Ukraine
- Ukrainian troops struck Russian drone sites, command posts in occupied territories
- Residents in occupied Luhansk Oblast given less than two weeks to vacate apartments ahead of demolition
- Human rights activists document 64 elderly political prisoners from Crimea
- Ukraine evacuates teen detained by Russia over pro-Ukrainian views, alongside 25 other children from occupied territories
Russia prepares a disinformation campaign involving staged interviews with residents of the Russian-occupied front-line town of Oleshky, Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said on Oct. 7.
According to the SBU, Russian forces ordered one of their units to produce a series of videos featuring residents of the occupied city. The operation is planned for October and early November.
The interviews are intended to blame Ukrainian forces for air attacks and blockading Oleshky, discredit Ukraine's leadership, and portray Russian troops positively, the agency said.
"(Russia) is failing on the battlefield and is therefore attempting by any means possible to undermine the psychological and emotional well-being of Ukrainians and destabilize the situation within our country," the SBU said.
Oleshky in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town.
Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it almost impossible to evacuate safely.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
In September, only 12 people reached Ukraine-controlled territory from Oleshky, the local military administration head told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 6.
read also
Russia's new three-year federal budget maintains funding for occupied Ukraine
Russia plans to allocate more than 865 billion rubles ($10 billion) to a state program covering Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts over the next three years, according to the draft federal budget.
The Russian government submitted its proposed 2027-2029 budget to the State Duma on Sept. 30, Russian news agency Prime reported, citing the explanatory note accompanying the draft.
The proposed allocation totals 293.8 billion rubles ($3.4 billion) for 2027, 290.1 billion rubles ($3.4 billion) for 2028, and 281.7 billion rubles ($3.3 billion) for 2029. The figures were also published by the Russian-installed administration of occupied Kherson Oblast in its Oct. 6 report.
Moscow says the funding is intended to restore infrastructure and support socioeconomic development in the four occupied regions. The state program was established to oversee their reconstruction and development under Russian control.
"The relatively stable federal budget allocations... suggest that Russia continues to view investment in the occupation as a lucrative and necessary federal priority because it facilitates the forced integration of occupied territories into Russia," the Institute for the Study of War said on Oct. 8.

Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, called on Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara on Saturday to decide whether to indict Tzachi Braverman, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's former chief of staff, and others before the upcoming elections, following revelations that Braverman acknowledged changing the recorded time of a phone call on the morning of the October 7 massacre.
Eisenkot's appeal followed information that emerged about Braverman's acknowledgment during a police investigation that he had changed an official record documenting a conversation between Netanyahu and his military secretary on the morning of the October 7 attack. Eisenkot requested a response by October 16.
'Suspicions of serious offenses'
In his letter, titled "The Public's Right to Know," Eisenkot wrote that the information concerning Braverman's acknowledgment added to other incidents that, he claimed, pointed to a systematic pattern of falsifying and distorting official records, with the knowledge and at the direction of the prime minister and his senior advisers.
"These are suspicions of some of the most serious offenses in the criminal code, certainly if they involve the prime minister and those around him," he wrote.
The allegations concerning Netanyahu's involvement are Eisenkot's claims and have not been established as findings of the investigation.
Eisenkot added that "there is a clear public interest in reaching a decision on whether to file an indictment against Mr. Braverman and others before the elections."
He said that if there was suspicion that Netanyahu was involved in, directed, or was even aware of Braverman's actions, the investigation should be completed quickly and its findings made public.
Eisenkot is demanding a decision in the case, which has already been transferred to the State Attorney's Office, and the completion of any further investigation if there are grounds to suspect the prime minister's involvement.
He is not demanding that an indictment be filed regardless of the evidence, but rather that a decision on whether to indict be reached before the elections.
Braverman confirmed to authorities that he changed the recorded time
Braverman acknowledged changing recorded time, police sources say
Braverman was questioned under caution in November 2024 by the Israel Police's National Unit for the Investigation of Serious and International Crime.
Investigators collected testimony and seized documents and computer files, including, according to information released about the investigation, both the original record and the altered version.
According to information provided about the investigation, Braverman confirmed during questioning that he had changed the recorded time.
A senior police official said that investigators had established an evidentiary basis for indicting Braverman on a forgery charge in the case transferred to the State Attorney's Office.
The case has been awaiting a decision for more than a year.
Acknowledging a change to an official record does not necessarily constitute an admission of a criminal offense.
Braverman's attorney, Jacques Chen, previously argued that his client had acted within his authority to correct a recording error.
Prosecutors must determine whether the change was a lawful correction or an unauthorized alteration of an official document, taking into account the evidence concerning the circumstances in which it was made.
Former military secretary recounts request to alter call record
The appeal comes against the backdrop of the first public testimony by Maj.-Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who served as Netanyahu's military secretary on the morning of the October 7 massacre.
Gil said that in January 2024, a stenographer from the Prime Minister's Office approached him and told him she had been instructed to change the recorded time of a telephone conversation he had held with Netanyahu on the morning of October 7, from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m.
According to Gil, the instruction came from Braverman. Gil said that as early as late October 2023, he had received information about the unusual collection of official records and stenographic transcripts at the Prime Minister's Office, contrary to established procedures.
Following that information, he contacted the attorney-general and asked her to clarify the rules governing access to and copying of the records. After learning that the recorded time of the phone call had been changed, he updated Baharav-Miara again, but asked her not to take action at that stage, while the war was underway.
Gil recommended that a future commission of inquiry examine the original recordings rather than rely solely on written transcripts. The suspicions concern an 11-minute alteration to the record of a conversation that took place during the first hours of the Hamas attack.
The timing of the conversation could be significant in reconstructing the sequence of updates Netanyahu received on the morning of the massacre.
Changing the recorded time from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. places the conversation 11 minutes earlier in the official record, potentially affecting efforts to reconstruct the sequence of events and determine what information the prime minister possessed during those hours.
Gil emphasized that he did not know whether additional official records had been altered. Likud and police offer conflicting accounts of investigation
Following the publication of Gil's interview, Likud claimed that the affair had already been investigated and that investigators had recommended closing the case.
Police officials, however, said that investigators had established an evidentiary basis for prosecution and transferred the case to the State Attorney's Office for a decision. The accounts differ regarding the investigation's outcome.
The decision on whether the evidence justifies filing an indictment rests with prosecutors, and no indictment has been filed. Eisenkot is seeking to accelerate the decision in light of the approaching elections. According to information about the case's status, a decision is not expected for at least another month.
Eisenkot believes the public has a right to know, before casting its votes, whether an indictment will be filed in a case involving records of the prime minister's activities on the morning of October 7.
In his letter, he requested a response to his appeal no later than Friday, October 16.

Washington has put its sanctions on Russian diesel on hold. The US Treasury has authorized the sale, delivery, offloading, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel, effectively suspending sanctions on that trade until 7 April 2027, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said on its website on 9 October.
The waiver lets Russian diesel back onto world markets and, Ukraine argues, hands Moscow fresh revenue for its war, which has killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days. Until now, it was unclear whether Washington would roll back the sanctions it imposed on Russia in 2022.
OFAC has issued the measure as General License 135, signed by the office’s director, Bradley Smith, according to the report. It authorizes transactions in Russian-origin diesel that sanctions would otherwise block.
The license sets one limit. It does not permit any debits from accounts at US financial institutions held by Russia’s central bank, its National Wealth Fund, or its finance ministry, the document says.
Trump’s promise of cheaper fuel
On 9 October, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then 500,000 tons in November, and another million tons right after.
Moscow would later send the US up to 3 million more tons, depending on the state of Russia’s refineries, Trump added, framing the deal as a way to bring down energy prices.
Why the volumes fall short
Analysts say the amounts are too small to move prices much. Together, the first tranches would cover about a day and a half of US demand, while US diesel use alone runs near 16 million tons a month. Experts read the move as politics ahead of an election rather than a real shift in the market, pointing out that Trump cited volumes in tons, which look larger than the barrels traders track.
The deal drew fury in Kyiv, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a weak decision by strong partners. The EU is moving the other way, with ambassadors approving the bloc’s largest sanctions package against Russia’s war machine, due for final adoption on 12 October.

The password rules we've followed for years may be making us less secure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:44:31 UTC
04:44:31 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Passwords are supposed to keep us safe. Instead, they can leave us jumping through hoops just to end up less protected than where we started.
For years, we've been told a "strong" password needs a capital letter, a number, and a special character. But the rules designed to make passwords harder to crack were based on logic instead of evidence. It also made them harder to remember—pushing people to reuse the same passwords or make predictable changes.
That password paradox forced a rethink of one of the internet's most familiar security rituals almost ten years ago, and even one of the people who helped popularise the rules acknowledged they didn't work.
When William "Bill" Burr was a mid-level manager at the United States' National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), he was tasked with writing guidance on electronic authentication and password security.
That advice, published in 2004, helped cement the now-familiar idea that passwords should meet complexity requirements, including minimum length and a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 2017, Burr told The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) he regretted much of the guidance.
In the end, it was probably too complicated for a lot of folks to understand very well, and the truth is, it was barking up the wrong tree.
"It just drives people bananas," he said at the time.
When NIST updated its password guidance that same year, it moved away from some of those requirements, advising organisations against mandatory character-composition rules and routine password expiration.
Nearly a decade later, however, those rules remain common across websites and workplaces. So what does the evidence tell us about what actually makes a password secure?
The first computer passwords
The term password dates back to the late 1700s, and the idea of a secret phrase or access code to control entry goes back even further.
The first widely recognised computer password emerged in the early 1960s at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as researchers worked on a system that let multiple people share access to a single computer.
In 1961, computer scientist Fernando Corbató led a project that developed the Compatible Time-Sharing System, or CTSS.
Like a telephone exchange, the system let multiple users access a computer at the same time. But because they were sharing one machine, researchers needed a way to separate users and protect their individual files.
The password offered a simple solution: each user could have a secret string of characters controlling access to their files.
Corbató would later describe passwords as "kind of a nightmare" in a 2014 WSJ interview.
Why password complexity rules can backfire
Lorrie Cranor, a computer scientist and cybersecurity researcher at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania, tells SBS News passwords are "not a terrible idea" in a world where you have just one or two passwords.
But now we have the problem that we all have many passwords, because we have many accounts.
The premise behind password-composition rules was straightforward: if people were required to use a mix of letters, numbers and symbols, their passwords would be harder for attackers to guess.
But when those rules were first developed, evidence on how people would respond was limited.
NIST's initial guidelines also included a caveat: "Unfortunately, we do not have much data on the passwords users choose under particular rules."
It wasn't due to a lack of effort. In his 2017 interview, Burr said he even asked NIST's computer administrators to view actual passwords on their network, but they reportedly refused because of privacy concerns. The authors were therefore left to rely heavily on logic about how users might behave.
Since then, research has shown that the human response to password complexity is more complex.
A 2021 study from James Cook University found that increasing the number of password complexity rules did not necessarily produce stronger passwords and could increase user frustration.
It also found that users adopted strategies to make passwords easier to remember, including reusing passwords.
Why password reuse is a security problem
There are many ways to make a password weak, but reusing it across multiple services is one of the biggest risks.
Troy Hunt has seen many bad passwords. In 2013, he created Have I Been Pwned, a service that allows people to check whether their email address has appeared in a known data breach.
"As the internet came along, we already had these well-established principles that a password is memorable; it's something that you can type in," he tells SBS News.
"That came from an era where you needed things like physical presence in order to access services."
But the internet changed the scale of the problem. People now have passwords for email, banking, shopping, social media, work systems and countless other services.
Hunt says the path of least resistance for people trying to make memorable passwords is to make them reusable.
NIST's 2017 guidance recommended checking passwords against lists of previously compromised passwords, as well as common and predictable choices, rather than relying solely on composition rules.
Shortly after, Hunt expanded his site to include a password checker.
Reused passwords are risky because once a password is exposed in a data breach, it's not only that breached service that is at risk.
Chances are it's going to be the same password that they use to buy that T-shirt or something online as they use to log onto the corporate network.
"And maybe the only thing that'll be different is the number on the end, depending on how many times they've had to rotate it," Hunt says.
NIST's current guidance recommends that organisations block commonly used, expected or compromised passwords rather than relying solely on rules about the types of characters a password contains.
What makes a good password policy?
When Carnegie Mellon University updated its password policy to include more complexity requirements, Cranor was already studying privacy and security usability.
So when her colleagues came to her complaining about the difficulty of the new requirements, she saw an opportunity.
Cranor and her team started studying password policies, hoping to answer a simple question: what is the best password policy an organisation can have?
"We wrote 20 papers and finally came up with the answer," she says.
The answer wasn't to include more special characters or numbers. Instead, the research pointed towards giving users more freedom by using an add-on to assess password strength.
The team developed an evidence-based password strength meter that assesses a password as it is created, rather than simply checking whether it meets a predetermined mix of characters.
It can also check the potential password against a list of common or exposed passwords to limit reuse.
You can put this on the web browser so that people are creating the password on the browser and are not sending the password over the internet.
"Of course, I know no organisations that are actually doing this."
Why companies still use password complexity rules
Jose-Miguel Bello Villarino is a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney Law School. He says technical standards can have misleading names.
"Technical standards are agreements in the industry among the dominant players in the way technical goods or processes are developed in the future," he tells SBS News.
"The tricky bit is that if it's something that is not legally mandated as a technical standard that has to be implemented, the people developing the things need to see a value in changing the way they're doing things."
The exception is when the change in standards relates to a safety risk.
"When it's a safety-related issue, and the standard has been adapted to these kinds of new circumstances, and you do not use that new standard, what you're risking is liability, because you are not meeting the standard," he says.
Even then, if one standards body adopts new guidelines, several different standards bodies must also update theirs for organisations to be able to make changes while remaining compliant with the relevant industry body.
Cranor says security is about balancing risk with cost and benefit.
"There are a lot of security standards that companies follow and they're not all tied actually to the NIST guidelines," she says.
There's no perfect system, but if you're a security manager and you are appearing to be relaxing your requirements and then there's a breach, you're going to get the blame.
"Even if that's not true."
Hunt agrees. He says retaining the older rules often comes down to a "compliance officer with a checklist".
"A lot of security guidance has evolved, particularly in the last nine years since NIST put out their guidance. But a lot of computer systems and a lot of compliance regimes have taken a very long time to catch up as well."
So, what makes a strong password?
Cranor's main advice for making good passwords is not to make them yourself. Instead, she says to use a password manager to generate and store them.
You are not good at generating random passwords; your password manager is.
Hunt says the best passwords are the "ones you can't remember".
There is a small subset of passwords where this advice doesn't help, such as the password for your laptop or the one used to access your password manager.
Hunt describes this as distinguishing "what do you actually need to remember versus what do you need to be able to retrieve".
For the passwords you actually need to remember, contemporary advice generally favours length over arbitrary complexity.
One way to get that length is to use passphrases, but the key is to make the phrase hard to guess and ideally, random.
"Except the problem with random is that most of us are not very good at remembering things that actually are random," Cranor says.
"If you are, then do that. Roll a dice, pull from a hat, make something actually random."
To avoid this kind of predictability, Cranor recommends taking a memorable sentence that makes sense to you and using the first two letters of each word to create a new string, with some punctuation or a digit added somewhere in the middle.
And where its possible, Hunt suggests choosing non-password alternatives like passkeys. But their uptake has been slow, and he warns people will still have to deal with passwords for many years to come.
They will still be there because they will take a very, very long time to die.

South Melbourne make history, beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in Australia Cup final
In short:
South Melbourne have made history, becoming the first NPL side to win the Australia Cup, beating Melbourne Victory in the final.
South Melbourne and Victory were 0-0 after 90 minutes, then 1-1 after extra time.
Victory missed two of their penalties in the shootout, as South Melbourne clinched the Cup 4-3.
A-League aspirants South Melbourne have become the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup after beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotion-charged blockbuster final.
In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic soccer history, former NSL powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at AAMI Park.
South Melbourne, who have long craved an A-League licence, only strengthened their bid for that with a win that capped off an extraordinary evening.
Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.
In the penalty shootout, South goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.
Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line, but then saved the re-take too.
South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.
In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, Sinisa Cohadzic's South succeed where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.
With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.
The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.
South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.
A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of AAMI Park, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskas and John Margaritis.
The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.
On the field, South Melbourne attacking pair Juach and Yuki Uchida gave the Victory defence headaches all night.
Lopez made several great saves while Victory counterpart Jack Duncan was called into action on multiple occasions in regular time.
Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Guillermo May squared the ball to Santos but the Brazilian's poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.
But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.
Juach spurned a couple of great chances to equalise and the game appeared lost for South.
Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.
AAMI Park erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

Mass casualty attacks

The World Health Organization has said the cause of the pneumonia that killed a Russian laboratory worker at an anti-plague research centre in Siberia remains unknown, but it has found no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the case.
In a statement on Saturday, the WHO said no case of plague had been registered, and tests on the worker and her contacts were negative for the high-threat pathogens tested.
The 28-year-old researcher Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and fuelling public health fears on social media.
Her contacts remain symptom-free, and no further linked cases of severe pneumonia have been identified, the WHO said, citing information from Russia’s state regulator.
“Based on the information provided, WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said.
Russian authorities have said the worker was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body.
On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all her contacts and provided full information to the WHO in line with established procedures.
Global health officials have been particularly alert to fatal pneumonia cases of unknown cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of rapidly spreading respiratory illness in China.
However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases often remains undetermined.
Plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, is endemic to Siberian wildlife, though human transmission remains rare.
Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous airborne form and can be fatal within one to six days if untreated with antibiotics.

====================================================================================================

Money, networks and bias: Why women struggle to win seats in US politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:16:00 UTC
04:16:00 KST

US midterms: Women candidates could make history
October 10, 2026
Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.
There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."
Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.
Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."
The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa.
House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one
125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.
"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.
The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.
US Senate: Even higher bar for women
Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.
According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.
For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.
Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians.
First black woman state governor?
Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.
For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.
Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.
But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.

Cara Nachshon: The grandma with a red nose in her pocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:13:13 UTC
04:13:13 KST

Once a week, Cara Nachshon dresses in silly clothing and heads off to volunteer at Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem.
Four years ago, this British-born grandmother from Modi’in completed a six-month Simchat Lev course in which teacher Jeff Gordon taught her how to use performance arts, humor, and playful interaction to relieve fears and aid in the healing process.
“I think I’ve always been a clown. It’s always been inside me. But I finally did the course that entitled me to put on a red nose,” she said. “At 58, it was the right time in my life to do it.”
Using the nom de plume Miss Cara (read “Mascara” in Hebrew) and wearing red, black, and white – symbolic of life, as these are the colors a newborn differentiates first – she works with adult patients in the wards, emergency room, physiotherapy department, and surgical waiting rooms at Shaare Zedek Medical Center.
She has also volunteered at a school for children on the autism spectrum; at Keren Or – The Jerusalem Center for Blind Children; at ADI Jerusalem, a rehabilitative care facility for children and young adults with severe disabilities; and at sheltered housing.
And occasionally she clowns on the fly.
“I always have a [red] nose with me because I never know when I’ll be needed. One time I clowned in a mall when I came across a little girl screaming because they’d pierced her ear and she didn’t want the other one done. And then there are grandchildren who fall and get hurt and need to be calmed down. They know that Booba will end up doing a bit of shtick.”
Her shtick is informed by listening and observing to assess the situation before choosing which direction to take. She brings a range of accessories to capture attention and engage people through color, touch, sound, or movement. Sometimes the accessories are imaginary and she uses pantomime.
One time she fashioned a violin from balloons for a patient who was an orchestral violinist, and the two of them made pretend music together. Another time, Cara telephoned an artistic friend, who was dying of cancer, and guided her by voice in “painting” a picture on an imaginary canvas.
A tragic Shabbat in 1986
The notion that it is possible “to give a little bit of a lift, even momentarily, in very difficult situations of trauma and stress” germinated in Cara’s mind on a tragic Shabbat back in 1986. That morning, she discovered her second-born child, 10-week-old Catriel, lifeless in his crib.
For the remainder of the agonizing hours until sundown, when their son’s body could be removed for burial, Cara and her husband, Tony, were kept company by some close friends.
“It takes a lot of guts to walk into a house under those circumstances. But they sat in our living room and made us laugh. I don’t know how I laughed; I don’t remember what they said. Somehow, they made us laugh. What happened there made me think, many years later, that it doesn’t matter what the situation is; you can always find joy in pain, light in darkness – though sometimes it’s quite challenging,” Cara said.
She and Tony went on to have four more children. Their oldest, Avital, today is the mother of four. Sons Avinoam and Ze’ev also have four kids each. Daughter Tchiya is the mother of two. The youngest Nachshon child, Aderet (“She’s the cherry on the cake”), was born 12 years after Ze’ev.
'We couldn’t wait one more minute'
GROWING UP in England, Cara and Tony belonged to the Zionist youth movement Bnei Akiva. They made aliyah in 1983, a year after getting married. “Israel was crying out, ‘Come, come, come!’ and we couldn’t wait one more minute.”
They started out at Kibbutz Alumim, moved to the Gilo neighborhood of Jerusalem a year later, and went on to spend 38 years in Givat Ze’ev, about five kilometers northwest of Jerusalem.
“Our children grew up there, and it was a wonderful life. One by one, they left to embark on their own lives.
“Four years ago, our children said to us, ‘It’s time for you to move, Mom and Dad,’ so we downsized and moved to Modi’in when our youngest finished school, in August 2023. And we’ve been very happy there. Sometimes your children do know best,” said Cara, who returns to Givat Ze’ev once a week for pottery classes.
She believes that making changes at certain stages of life keeps things from getting stale. “That goes for marriage, parenthood, your profession, and where you live, too.”
The Hamas-led massacres of October 7 occurred just two months after the big move to the smaller home. On October 8, some of Avital’s family and a friend’s family arrived on their doorstep from Ashkelon. Without enough beds for all nine visitors, Cara reached out to her new community for help.
“A beautiful family I had never met gave us their home while they were in America. Avital’s family stayed there for five months, and the children were welcomed in school and kindergarten,” Cara said.
Cara emphasized that her “wonderful husband and children are a source of inspiration for me, together with their families.” Her granddaughter Odeya came clowning with her once a month for a year at ADI Jerusalem as a pre-bat mitzvah project. She learned a lot from her Booba.
“One of the things Jeff Gordon taught us was to always look for the ‘shakuf,’” the person in the room who feels invisible. “When you look at somebody who’s shakuf, it doesn’t matter what they look like on the outside; what’s going on inside is what needs to be noticed. And with God’s help, always with God’s help, I tend to pick up on it,” Cara said.
For a week after Oct. 7, Cara couldn’t bear to do her usual hospital volunteering. “But then I realized I had to. It was a need for me and for the patients. Of course, I was with [wounded] soldiers, and with soldiers who came to visit those soldiers, because they also needed clowning.
“Medical clowning is very rewarding – it’s the best profession in the world. I get much more than I give.” ■
Cara Nachshon, 64
From South End, England,
to Kibbutz Alumim, 1983;
to Jerusalem, 1984;
to Givat Ze’ev, 1985;
to Modi’in, 2023
