Sampling wizards The Avalanches mine magic from old ads and obsolete tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:52:47 UTC
03:52:47 KST

Sampling wizards The Avalanches weaponise old media nostalgia in No Bad Memories
A few familiar notes – the startup sound of an old computer, an antique advertising jingle – and suddenly you're teleported to the past.
The Avalanches know this power intimately. And their new album weaponises it.
"Everybody has a commercial they hear, a cereal or soft drink tune from 30 years ago, and it just transports them," Avalanches co-founder Robbie Chater tells Double J's Karen Leng.
"It's phenomenal how it sticks with you over so long. You think you've forgotten it and then it hits."
Nostalgia has been crucial to the Australian group since 2000's Since I Left You, their groundbreaking debut constructed from thousands of obscure analogue samples, made them unlikely stars.
It took 16 mythical years, and losing four members, to make a sequel: the warm, psychedelic Wildflower and its panoply of not just samples but rappers and singers.
We Will Always Love You in 2020 was a cosmic masterpiece inspired by the star-crossed romance of scientists Carl Sagan and Ann Druyan.
Now a trio – co-founders Chater, Tony Di Blasi and new member Andy Szekeres – they find inspiration in the past on new album No Bad Memories, mining sounds from outdated technology and advertising and their ability to trigger emotional impact.
"It's a special power," says Szekeres. "A sound that can instantly take millions of people back to this intense feeling of emotion that's separate from the product."
Even the album's title is sampled, from a 1980s ad for an obsolete medium most under 30 wouldn't recognise: floppy disks.
"It's spruiking the quality of their data storage," says Chater. "Really clever [and] funny. It was a working title [but] began to take on another meaning."
Talent and technology
Spanning 31 tracks, No Bad Memories has everything fans love about The Avalanches. A dense fantasia that's joyful, funky, soulful yet capable of tugging on the heartstrings and boasting another all-star cast of guests.
From returning collaborators Jamie xx, Karen O and Rivers Cuomo to in-demand producers Barry Can't Swim, Tunisia's Khadija Al Hanafi, Japanese music legend Haruomi Hosono and Ryoji Ikeda's sensory-testing experiments.
An overlooked bridge from Carly Simon's Make Me Feel Something becomes the sparkling centrepiece of One More Fantasy, an Avalanches specialty.
Lead single Together unites electronic acts Nikki Nair, Jessy Lanza and viral musician Prentiss with video game-y synths and a children's chorus liberated from a '70s TV adaptation of Enid Blyton's The Famous Five.
Its fizzy rhythm is threaded with mouse clicks, loading data, camera shutters and jingles for Nokia and Toshiba.
It's a kaleidoscopic album where legacy acts and emerging talent co-mingle with forgotten jingles and the physical clicking, whirring and static of antiquated devices.
"The sounds our generation knows," notes Chater, "also, when it goes wrong."
Szekeres adds: "I still have trauma … Like, a zip disk drive plugged into a sampler that stopped working. It's a very distinct sound."
The dreaded Windows error and malfunctioning hardware are among the record's numerous Easter eggs.
Where The Avalanches once dug through op-shop vinyl crates for inspiration, No Bad Memories sent them down YouTube rabbit holes.
"So much fun! We need to be excited to give us the energy to make a project because obviously it's lots of archival work; very time-consuming," says Chater.
The resulting tapestry thrives in whimsy, melancholy and imagination. A bittersweet soundtrack that both critiques and celebrates how consumer culture sells emotion, not just product.
"You're growing up and its capitalism coming at you. You don't have a choice of whether you absorb all this messaging or not," says Chater.
"But then also a lot of the ads are really beautiful – the photography, that saturated colour – and the jingles stick in your mind.
"I love how I'm not even sure how I feel about it. Because on one hand, we've been sold this impossible dream. And on the other hand, I remember it fondly."
The art of advertising
The three estimate they "probably made more [ads] than we sampled".
With visual artist Jonathan Zawada, they conjured Takumi Digital Archives, a fictional company behind walkmans, cameras, shampoo, magazines, you name it.
They built an interactive website, cast The Sixth Sense star Haley Joel Osment as a Takumi employee for promotional videos and made physical prototypes to market the album.
"You can really go off on a tangent. 'Maybe we're going to start actually making these products,'" Szekeres recalls. "Then you stop and go, 'actually, what are we doing here?'"
Stitching together commercials, real and imagined, was a challenge but a crucial "part of the record's DNA", says Chater.
"We had a lot of fun exploring the craft of advertising music."
A big influence was Suzanne Ciani, a 1970s electronic music pioneer known for pinball game sounds and brand audio idents.
"One of our heroes, [she] wrote amazing jingles for Coke and Atari on a modular synth," says Chater of Ciani, who features on the track Our Love Is Alive.
Another milestone was enlisting Mike Patton, the "phenomenal voice" out front of Faith No More and Mr Bungle.
A long-time fan, Patton narrates commercials for the "Superfun!" game system, emulating the '90s "console wars" between Sega and Nintendo.
"Always fighting with each other [through] very bro-y, frat-testosterone ads. Mike was perfect for that. Some of the stuff he sent through was just wild."
Deadlines and details
Initially, The Avalanches planned a swift follow-up to their last album.
"Eight to 10 songs, no concept. [Just] this great, feel-good party record," explains Chater. "We're like, 'We'll knock it out in six months!"
Those plans fell by the wayside as their tendency for painstaking detail emerged.
"It's difficult. I definitely know if something's not right and I'll be frustrated and push and push and push until it's working for me," says Chater. "We don't want to take too long making records.
"We love having a deadline now and trying to hit it. Even if we didn't hit it exactly.
"You certainly get better at letting go and relaxing a bit."
Chater says Di Blasi acts a welcome counterpoint.
"We can get a bit cerebral," he confesses.
"He's like, 'Sometimes guys, I don't want to have a f***ing instruction manual to understand the record. I just want to have a good time.'"
No Bad Memories manages to have its cake and eat it too.
Feel-good dance music and joyous pop rubs shoulders with experimental sound collage, like a house party featuring museum exhibits as breakout rooms.
You can switch off and enjoy the ride, or dig in and admire the artistic alchemy, flipping obsolete formats and overlooked sounds into collaborations subverting memory, loss and nostalgia.
No Bad Memories proves looking backward isn't just escapism; it's about reclaiming agency.
"That's been a big part of this whole project, thinking about that we're all participants in this crazy, late-stage capitalism system," Chater says.
"Our music's on Spotify, we're on Instagram that's owned by Meta, probably not the most ethical companies in the world.
"It's really important for each of us to think about how we participate in that system and where we're comfortable and what lines we want to draw."
No Bad Memories is out October 16. The Avalanches Australian tour kicks off in Perth on February 27.

Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended after the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) announced that it had opened disciplinary proceedings against the 41-year-old over his decision to walk out on the national team.
Ronaldo apologised to supporters earlier this week while criticising Portugal coach Jorge Jesus and said he would accept any punishment that was imposed.
"Disciplinary proceedings have been initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo," said the FPF in a statement, classifying the case as "urgent" and confirming Ronaldo is currently suspended pending a decision on the final punishment.
Ronaldo left Portugal's Nations League squad after first being made to warm up as a substitute against Norway on September 27 and not being brought on, and then finding out he would not start against Denmark in the match on October 1.
The former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker is the all-time top goalscorer and record appearance-maker in men's international football.
According to Portuguese media, under the federation's regulations, a player who misses a training session, a match, or a national team activity faces a suspension ranging from one to six months.
On Tuesday, Ronaldo accused Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time in Nations League matches but said he was not retiring from international duty and would be available to play once any potential punishment was served.
"I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team," Ronaldo said, while accepting his actions must be "punished" by the federation.
Pele, Maradona point
Ronaldo said Jesus had gone back on his word about bringing him on against Norway, and then, in a press conference before the Denmark match, had not said a series of points they had agreed upon during a conversation beforehand.
One of Ronaldo's pre-approved talking points was that Jesus had "made a mistake in asking someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona to warm up and then not sending him on in the match."
Jesus chose not to respond to Ronaldo's statement when asked about it.
"I read the statement, and now, like I do every day, I'm going to the federation headquarters to work, to think about the Portuguese national team," said the 72-year-old coach.
Jesus said last Sunday he would select Ronaldo for international duty if the forward was playing for his club and was interested in being called up.
Portugal won all four of their Nations League matches and qualified for the quarter-finals with two games to spare.
Portugal host Denmark on November 14 and then travel to face Wales on November 17 in their final two Nations League Group A4 matches.
Ronaldo returned to club action on Friday with Saudi Arabian side Al-Nassr and scored as they won 3-0 against Diriyah in a Saudi Pro League match. It was the striker's 980th career goal.

Oil tanker explodes after striking naval mine in Hormuz, IRGC claims - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:34:29 UTC
03:34:29 KST

US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced early on Sunday morning that it has disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to bypass the US naval blockade on Iranian ports along the Strait of Hormuz.
The vessel, a Panama-flagged merchant vessel named Ocean Molica, left an Iranian port and attempted to traverse into the Arabian Sea before being struck in the stern by a precision munition launched by a fighter jet, according to CENTCOM.
The confirmation came shortly after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it received a report that an outbound tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck on the port side by an unknown projectile, causing a fire on board.
The crew was reported safe, UKMTO said, adding that damage assessment and environmental impact were unknown at the time of the report.
The blockade, which began on April 13, 2026, was temporarily ended on June 18 following a US-Iran agreement, before being reinstated a month later on July 14.
According to CENTCOM, "four commercial vessels have been disabled, and 135 ships have been turned around during three months of strict enforcement." 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have been destroyed in that period of time.
Naval mine critically damages oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
Additionally, the IRGC said on Saturday that an oil tanker had exploded and caught fire after hitting a naval mine while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported.
The Guards did not specify the tanker's name or flag.
The IRGC Navy announced it was exercising control over the strait and would not allow "aggressor armies" in the area, saying it would counter attempts to disrupt management of the strait, according to the IRGC-linked Tasnim News Agency.
Tehran and Washington have been in diplomatic talks, exchanging and reviewing proposals under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen "within seven days."
Despite this, tankers are facing a higher risk of attacks and intimidation as they try to get critical shipments through the Strait of Hormuz after Iran issued new warnings that it would block routes that it has not authorized, sources said.
Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the key waterway since the Iran war began - cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Iran has warned regional countries that any attempt to open new oil export routes would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran told Reuters.
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major black eye for the Trump administration. Whether or not current US operational control there succeeds going forward, the US and the world economy have been shaken by Iran’s closure of the strait for much of 2026.
Yonah Jeremy Bob and Reuters contributed to this report.

Red Cross chief says she tried to arrange Gaza hostage visits through talks with Hamas's Haniyeh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:34:25 UTC
03:34:25 KST

International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) President Mirjana Spoljaric said that she met former Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in Qatar on two separate occasions with the goal of arranging a visit by the organization to Israeli hostages held in Gaza, making the comment as part of an interview on Saturday with New York Times reporter Lulu Garcia-Navarro.
"These were tough discussions, and trust me, we are very frank in these meetings," said Spoljaric, noting that she further met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the issue. "This is why these meetings have to always remain confidential."
When Garcia-Navarro asked the Swiss-Croatian diplomat whether the ICRC had any access to the hostages, Spoljaric shook her head.
She described the issue of visiting hostages as "much more complicated" than returning them home, saying that the ICRC can only "work with the tools that we have."
"In my opinion, they should have come back unconditionally as of day one," she said. "But that’s not the reality in which we operate."
In August 2025, the mothers of former hostages Evyatar David, Nimrod Cohen, Guy Gilboa-Dalal, and David and Ariel Cunio met with Spoljaric in Geneva, pushing for the organization to visit their loved ones in Gaza.
In addition, eight of the hostages released during the December 2025 temporary ceasefire wrote a letter to the ICRC asking them to visit the then-137 remaining hostages. No such visits ever took place.
Spoljaric: Nothing more 'complex,' 'brutal' than act of hostage-taking
Spoljaric, who has led the ICRC since 2022 and says she visited Gaza several times amid the war, told the NYT that there is "nothing more complex, and to a certain extent also more brutal, than hostage-taking."
"The objective always has to be to bring the hostages back," she explained. "And the longer it takes, the more complicated it becomes. I personally think that pressure should have come earlier in the negotiations. We could have saved more lives. And this was the subject of our conversations."
She cited the organization's "strict insistence on neutrality" as having been vital in the eventual return of many of the Gaza hostages to Israel.
"You’ve seen the pictures of our colleagues unarmed among thousands, if not tens of thousands, of armed men, surrounded by rubble from which there was no escape," she emphasized. "Nobody would have trusted us to be able to do this highly complex operation if we hadn’t defended our neutrality over 160 years. You tweak it once, you become political, and that’s it. I know it makes so many people angry, but that’s the essence of our mission."
Israel has 'moral,' 'legal' obligation to allow visits to detainees, Spoljaric says
Regarding ICRC visits to Israeli security detainees, which were halted following the October 7 massacre, Spoljaric claimed that Israel had both a "moral" and "legal" obligation to reinstate them.
"We need to inform the families about the whereabouts of or the fate of their relatives," she said. "You capture a soldier; this person is detained, but a soldier is not, per se, a criminal."
Responding to a question regarding the treatment of one's enemy, she noted the "dehumanization" of combatants who engage in torture and other illegal actions.
"If you tell your soldiers, 'Go and kill women and children, go rape them, looting is allowed, it’s our strategy,' these people dehumanize themselves. They will never be able to return to a normal life."
Jerusalem Post Staff and Reuters contributed to this report.

====================================================================================================

Understanding the tribe: Safeheart org. helps Nova survivors recover using psychedelic treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:34:16 UTC
03:34:16 KST

For thousands of people attending the Supernova music festival near Kibbutz Re’im, the joy of dancing at sunrise on Oct. 7 gave way to terror as Hamas rocket barrages streaked across the sky.
As festivalgoers tried to escape, gunmen attacked them along surrounding roads and at the festival site, killing hundreds.
For many, the trauma was compounded by being under the influence of mind-altering substances, leaving them uniquely vulnerable and in desperate need of specialized, trauma- and psychedelics-informed support.
In response to this crisis, a group of eight mental health professionals immediately came together.
Within hours, the eight – Guy Simon, Yair Grynbaum, Igal Tartakovsky, Tal Zagursky, Nir Tadmor, Karina Dessau, Prof. Roy Salomon, and Reut Plonsker – mobilized to help the survivors. By October 18, they had officially formed a nonprofit organization known as SafeHeart to provide specialized trauma care to survivors of the Oct. 7 music festival attacks.
Today, SafeHeart provides trauma treatment, counseling, support groups, crisis intervention, and long-term mental health care, free of charge, to survivors and their families.
Its team of 400 therapists has treated over 2,500 patients since Oct. 7.
The organization’s founders combine extensive experience in therapy, trauma care, and psychedelic harm reduction with close ties to the festival community.
Before the Oct. 7 attack, members were already working together to strengthen harm reduction in Israel through parliamentary advocacy and collaboration with leading organizations, including Safe-Zone, Hof Mivtachim, Impulse, and the University of Haifa.
Recently, the Magazine met with the SafeHeart founders in a wide-ranging interview to discuss its origins, the unique needs of the Nova survivors, how their psychological needs have changed since the first weeks after Oct. 7, and the difficulties they still face nearly three years later.
That terrible day three years ago
Dessau, a psychotherapist, leader of safe spaces, water-based emotional therapist, and one of SafeHeart’s founders, recalls the day’s events.
“I was at the sea that day and only understood what was happening at around 11:30 that morning. When I heard about the Nova festival, I messaged Nir [Tadmor] and Igal [Tartakovsky]. We were connected through Hof Mivtachim [Safe Harbor, an Israeli project specializing in psychedelic harm reduction and emotional crisis support], and I felt that we had to do something. We could not simply stay at home and absorb what had happened.
“They [the Nova survivors] were at the party at sunrise, at a moment of celebration and openness. Not everyone had taken drugs, but everyone had come to celebrate. That is a sensitive and exposed state in which to encounter such terror.”
SafeHeart co-founder Guy Simon, a clinical social worker and psychotherapist specializing in trauma and extreme states and co-founder of the Impulse Center for Integrative Therapy, shares, “My strongest memory from that period is sitting with my phone, which was already overheating in my hands. Hundreds of people were messaging me throughout the day, asking for help or to be connected with a therapist. My phone would crash and shut down. I would turn it back on, another flood of messages would pour in, and it would shut down again.
“I was overwhelmed by requests, harrowing personal stories, and so many pleas for help of one kind or another.
“Establishing the organization and creating a framework for care was exactly what we needed to do to respond to that endless stream of requests.”
As the scale of the attack became clear, the group began organizing support for survivors.
“When we began to understand what had happened at the festival,” explains Plonsker, a licensed clinical psychologist and SafeHeart’s vice president of clinical services, “we opened a WhatsApp group for therapists. It quickly became clear that many survivors would need help, and that understanding the context of their experience would be essential.
“We gathered colleagues with that knowledge and opened a shared Google document where people could leave their names and telephone numbers.
“Initially, we asked therapists to offer three sessions voluntarily. We acted because people needed us; we developed and improved the framework as we went.”
Tartakovsky, a mindfulness-based psychotherapist and co-founder of the Hof Mivtachim project, explains that the group had been providing support and psychological first aid at festivals, including earlier Nova events.
“We knew this community and understood the experiences people could have with psychedelics. Even before we understood the full scale of the attack, we recognized that some survivors would need therapists able to work with that part of their experience.”
Nova survivors’ singular trauma
Plonsker describes the unique trauma that the Nova survivors experienced.
“The attack happened in an open area. People had come to dance and celebrate; some were without their phones or shoes when they had to run. They described feeling hunted. This was very different from being inside a protected room at home.”
Approximately 70% of the Nova survivors whom they interviewed, she adds, reported taking psychedelics or other drugs during the event. That added another dimension to their memories, feelings, and thinking.
In addition, many of those in attendance came from outside the Gaza border area and were not used to dealing with rocket fire from across the border.
Prof. Salomon, head of the Laboratory for the Study of Consciousness and the Self at the University of Haifa, says that the fact that the attack began at sunrise, when celebrants were approaching the peak of the trance celebration, was significant.
“It was like falling from a great height into the depths. People had come to celebrate and let go, and suddenly they were facing terror. That contrast was an important part of the experience.”
One of his research questions is whether drug use helped some survivors survive the attack.
People who attended the festival reported using alcohol, cannabis, LSD, MDMA, cocaine, and other substances, sometimes in combination, and Salomon says that he is studying how those experiences interacted with the fear and trauma of the attack.
While the majority of those surveyed said that MDMA may have shielded them from the trauma and helped them survive and save others, the results are not conclusive at this point.
Salomon says the unprecedented scale of treating Nova survivors required changes in how care was delivered.
“Usually, you sit with a client for 50 minutes in a treatment room. Here, we needed to change. Some people wouldn’t leave their homes, and were spread out throughout the country.”
In addition, he continues, many times, relatives of the survivors were the ones who approached the therapists, asking them to help their children, or cousins, or siblings, who had been at the Nova.
“Some people went home from the Nova and stayed locked up in their houses, and sometimes the mother was the one who asked for our treatment for their child.
“How do you reach someone who is locked up in a room, and you want to help him and his mother wants it, and he didn’t ask for help?”
Salomon says that therapists had to adjust to a new reality. “There was a case where we told the mother to take the phone and put it under the door of her son’s room, so that we could try to talk to him.”
Silver lining: Seeing so many volunteers support survivors
Despite the difficulties, he says it was heartening to see so many therapists volunteer with SafeHeart to support Nova survivors.
“It was deeply moving that, in such a black period, people signed up to help. We had to reach everyone, and that is part of our ethos, to offer treatment to everyone.”
Salomon explains that the trance audience includes a wide range of the Israeli population, from soldiers to academics.
“It was important to reach everyone, and not everyone was easy to reach.”
Reaching those who needed assistance was only part of the solution. The background that the SafeHeart founders had in treating people who take psychedelics was invaluable.
“Many therapists are very judgmental about the use of psychedelics,” says Plonsker. “It was important to us to meet the survivors as equals, from a place of understanding their culture. A psychedelic experience can be a unique experience, and someone [a therapist] who can’t grasp it will have a hard time understanding what they [survivors] experienced in their trauma.”
Salomon relates that a person who came to SafeHeart for treatment told them that initially he had sought treatment through his kupat holim (health fund). When he told the kupah therapist that he had taken LSD, the therapist was unable to relate to his experience and treat him.
“When he entered treatment with us, he felt that we understood him and ‘saw’ him,” says Salomon.
Shiran Maor, chairman of the board of SafeHeart, adds that some survivors who had initially approached other organizations were judged by therapists and criticized for their drug use, which caused them pain.
He says that the therapists at SafeHeart are aware of the different substances and know how each one can affect trauma.
Tadmor, a psychotherapist, co-founder of the Hof Mivtachim project, and co-founder of the Impulse Center for Integrative Therapy, says that the fact that the group of founders built a reputation – even before Oct. 7 – over 10 years as therapists who can be relied on in sensitive situations for this group and community, has made a significant difference.
“We are people who are at these festivals in the safe spaces. They know us and can turn to us and rely on us.”
Tartakovsky says that if a person does not feel free to speak about his entire experience, the therapy will not be effective. “That’s why we made ourselves available, as a member of the ‘tribe’ of the trance community. We are with you and are part of the story, and we invite you to speak about it.”
Zagursky, SafeHeart’s head of therapeutic services, succinctly summarizes the approach:
“We are part of the trance community, and we came from this community. We want to bring to the front that we know that people do take these substances, and it is okay. We want to normalize it, so that they shouldn’t feel uneasy about undergoing treatment.”
Evolving treatment: From acute emergency response to long term rehabilitation
How has treatment for the survivors of the Nova changed since Oct. 7? Plonsker explains:
“At first, we were responding to an acute emergency. Today, much of our work concerns long-term trauma treatment and rehabilitation: getting up in the morning, returning to work, sustaining relationships, and living with persistent symptoms. Substance use and addiction can also become part of the clinical picture.”
Maor says one complicating factor in treatment is that rehabilitation began while the wider crisis was still unfolding. Some of the hostages were people from the festival, and survivors were living with the knowledge that friends were still being held.
“Sirens, further attacks, and continuing uncertainty kept producing new triggers,” he notes. “It is very hard to move forward while asking yourself how you can return to life when your friend is still captive.”
Some people who thought they had put the experience behind them, he says, later encountered its effects when they tried to return to work or study. Anger, difficulty functioning, and other symptoms could reappear. The need for support does not necessarily follow a straightforward timeline.
Looking back at the early days of SafeHeart, Grynbaum, who specializes at Magnus International Search & Rescue in rescuing people experiencing mental health crises, says that in the first weeks following Oct. 7, there were incredible initiatives. “So much adrenaline, so much motivation, and so many people stepping forward in extraordinary ways.
“Thank God, we brought together an exceptionally strong group of professionals, advisers, and others working in the field. It was very special. I think that period was marked by tremendously courageous action.”
Healing from trauma is a long-term process. For many, they say, recovery means living with trauma.
Says Efrat Atun, SafeHeart CEO: “After three years in which we have provided mental health care to more than 2,500 survivors through a network of 400 therapists specializing in trauma, it is important to emphasize that coping with trauma is a very long marathon – one that becomes even longer amid a security situation that offers no moment of stability.
“There is an expectation that survivors should have already ‘returned to normal life’ because three years have passed.
“And indeed, some survivors have made remarkable progress and feel much better today. That progress is real, moving, and a source of tremendous hope.”■
On November 11, the organization will hold its SafeHeart Conference at the Peres Center for Peace, in Jaffa, on the subject of trauma, psychedelics, and therapy, along with the power of community. The conference will serve as a central platform for therapists, researchers, and professionals to discuss the latest clinical and research insights at the meeting point of trauma, psychedelics, and healing.

Israel Election 2026: What does Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad stand for?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:34:12 UTC
03:34:12 KST

B’Yachad, formed through an alliance between former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in April 2026, is one of the parties vying for citizens’ votes in the elections for the 26th Knesset, which will be held on October 27.
Led by Bennett, with Lapid in second place, the party combines Bennett’s right-wing political background with Lapid’s centrist Yesh Atid party.
It is one of the major parties in the opposition bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The party offers a combination of a right-wing security stance while holding more liberal positions on issues of religion and state, and reforms aimed at lowering the cost of living and the country's education system.
Bennett and Netanyahu: From aide and coalition partner to rival
Bennett’s political career began close to the leader he is now seeking to replace. He served as Netanyahu’s chief of staff from 2006 to 2008, when Netanyahu was opposition leader, before building an independent political career on the religious-Zionist Right.
After winning the Bayit Yehudi leadership in 2012, Bennett and Netanyahu held a coalition agreement that neither would join without the other.
Following the 2015 election, Bennett joined another Netanyahu-led coalition and served as education minister alongside the haredi (ulta-Orthodox) parties. Netanyahu also appointed him defense minister in 2019.
In 2020, Bennett was outside Netanyahu’s government, and subsequently became the leader of the coalition that removed him from office, forming a rotation government with Lapid.
Lapid founded Yesh Atid in 2012 after a career in journalism and television. The party positioned itself as a secular, centrist, liberal-Zionist force, emphasizing the concerns of working Israelis, the economic burden on the middle class, and greater equality in military service.
It won 19 seats in its first election in 2013, becoming the Knesset’s second-largest party, and Lapid became finance minister in Netanyahu’s government.
In the current Knesset, Yesh Atid is also the second-largest party and holds 24 seats. Over time, Lapid became a leading opponent of the prime minister, and currently serves as opposition leader.
Lapid served as foreign minister and alternate prime minister in the government formed with Bennett.
The Ra’am coalition and Bennett’s changing red lines
A highly contentious move in the Bennett-Lapid government came in June 2021, when he formed a government with parties from the Right, Center, and Left, alongside Mansour Abbas’s Islamist Ra’am.
Ra’am became the first Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, and the partnership drew fierce criticism from Bennett’s former political camp, particularly because he had promised not to partner with an Arab party.
Bennett acknowledged the reversal in a recent interview with The Jerusalem Post, stating, “I did break a promise. That’s just a fact.” He defended forming the government as preferable to further elections.
Asked whether he could again join a coalition with Ra’am, he refused, saying, “October 7 changes a lot of things.”
Bennett has also campaigned against a coalition with the established haredi parties in the Knesset whose positions on military service conflict with his party's policies and plans to offer no exemptions to haredim who evade IDF service.
Where B’Yachad stands on the major issues
Bennett’s campaign has centered on rebuilding state institutions, drafting haredim, increasing economic competition, and improving Israel’s international standing.
In June, he presented his New Covenant plan, proposing changes to education, government administration, security, and the economy. The proposals included recruiting 20,000 additional soldiers, closing seven government ministries, and transferring more authority to local government.
Bennett also proposed restructuring the Education Ministry to direct more resources toward teachers and classrooms, alongside greater accountability for ministers and public officials.
The party’s approach to military service is among its clearest distinctions from Netanyahu’s current coalition.
In a March interview with the Post, Bennett said his next government would be based on a “covenant of those who serve.” He said haredi parties could not join unless they accepted his principles on education, universal service, and employment.
Bennett has called for mandatory haredi enlistment and an end to state funding for draft evasion and education without core subjects. He has argued that the shortage of soldiers places an unsustainable burden on those already serving and on reservists repeatedly called away from their families and jobs.
When presenting his plan in June, he described the state’s relationship with the haredi community as “a slow-motion suicide.” His proposals would instead offer military-service and employment pathways alongside state haredi schools.
Bennett’s economic platform focuses on reducing market concentration and increasing competition, particularly in the food sector.
His July plan called for breaking up monopolies, preventing exclusive importers from distributing additional major brands, and requiring Shufersal to sell stores in areas where its presence limits competition.
The plan set a target of bringing Israeli food prices into line with the OECD average, which the party said could save a family approximately NIS 8,000 annually. That figure is a campaign projection whose realization would depend on the reforms being implemented and producing lower prices.
These proposals sit alongside Bennett’s broader promise to streamline government ministries, appoint ministers with suitable backgrounds to each role, and oversee them to ensure they operate efficiently.
The Bennett-Lapid alliance has also committed to pushing for civil marriage to be preformed in the country, rather than through the Chief Rabbinate.
Lapid previously told the Post that B’Yachad would pursue civil marriage and equal rights for LGBTQ+ couples if it joined the next government. He said the party would seek legislation guaranteeing equal rights for every couple within the government’s first 100 days.
The party’s economic proposals also extend into religious services, with Bennett calling for greater competition in kosher certification.
Bennett has pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre on his government’s first day. He has called Netanyahu responsible for government failures that took place on that day, demanding that he take accountability.
Another law Bennett has stated that he seeks to pass is limiting a prime minister’s term to eight years.
Bennett has maintained his right-wing stance regarding security issues, arguing in favor of dismantling and disarming Hamas, and has expressed support for maintaining security zones in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.
However, he has also stated that military operations must be accompanied by diplomatic arrangements that prevent the organization from rebuilding, and with regard to Gaza, has favored a central role for Egypt, stating that rebuilding cooperation with Cairo could help contain and disarm Hamas.
What a vote for this party is likely to produce
Given the party’s alliance with the leaders of additional opposition parties - Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Golan’s Democrats, and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu - a vote for B’Yachad would strengthen the opposition’s bid to replace Netanyahu while bolstering Bennett’s effort to be the next prime minister.
The four parties have agreed to work to form a coalition. Eisenkot has called for the leader of the party with the most votes to receive backing for the premiership - though none of the opposition party leaders have outright committed to this - leaving the possibility for Bennett to once again become prime minister still on the table.
The party is currently polling at around 13 to 15 seats, making it currently the second largest party in the opposition bloc.
A vote for B’Yachad would support an alliance campaigning for broader military service, changes to funding for haredi institutions, civil marriage, and economic reforms aimed at lowering prices, alongside Bennett’s security policies.
However, the party’s recent lower standing in the polls behind Eisenkot does call into question its ability to implement those commitments.
Rejecting Arab parties in a coalition and opposing the current arrangements with the haredi parties also narrows the available routes to a majority.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
"I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Trump also accused Zelensky of ignoring US requests not to strike Russian diesel refineries because of the potential impact on global supplies.
"We said, you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don't hit the refineries because that's a world problem," Trump said.
He said he had told Zelensky directly: "There's plenty of targets. Don't hit refineries."
"And he went out, and he hit," Trump said, adding that Zelensky "better damn well stop."
Trump argued that strikes on Russian diesel facilities could affect American farmers and ranchers as well as energy markets worldwide.
*Trump again attacks Nobel Peace Prize decision*
Trump also renewed his criticism of the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay.
Asked about Pillay's criticism of sanctions against the court, Trump instead listed what he described as his own peace achievements.

Trump says there's 'something wrong in Norway' after not receiving the Nobel Prize

"We are not giving anyone a blank check. Anyone who wants our support is welcome to negotiate with us over the demands of our community."

"These are not ordinary elections. These are fateful elections for our future here, in our homeland, the only homeland we have," he said.

Eritrea urges UN deterrence measures against Ethiopia
October 10, 2026
In the ongoing struggle for control of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, both Ethiopia and Eritrea have appealed to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) for assistance.
On Friday, citing Article 51 of the UN Charter, Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said his country was making use of its right to exercise self-defense measures against Eritrea.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units in recent weeks and supporting, financing, arming and directing insurgent groups.
On Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, who rejected Ethiopia's accusations, responded in a letter, writing, "Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia's deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea... and take the requisite deterrent measures," asking the international body to invoke Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows measures from sanctions to military action.
Saleh said Ethiopia's actions could cause, "huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilize the region."
Ethiopian troops regaining ground lost to TPLF rebels
Last month, Tigrayan rebel groups announced they had joined forces to oust Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, swiftly launching major attacks on Ethiopian government forces and seizing regional airports.
Since then, Ethiopian troops have driven back Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) militants and taken control of large parts of the region, including the capital, Mekelle.
Recent fighting, which broke a 2022 peace agreement, and this weekend's exchange of accusations only deepen the growing rift between Ethiopia and Eritrea, who were allies in a bloody 2020-2022 border war that saw them team up against TPLF rebels.
The developments also come as Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed reiterates his landlocked country's need for access to the Red Sea — a demand he repeated on Monday — and which Eritrea regards as a direct threat to its sovereignty.

New Australian comedy horror asks if we can still laugh at Nazis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Australian killer gnome series rides the horror-comedy wave
After spending ten years developing her horror-comedy series Gnomes, co-writer Tegan Higginbotham had a concern plaguing her mind.
Can we still laugh at Nazis?
"We grew up on Mel Brook's comedies where Nazis are funny," she says.
Created by Joel Kohn (The Mirror), Higginbotham co-wrote the series with her husband Paul F Verhoeven, as well as pulling double duty as one half of a ditzy police duo, the other half being fellow comedian Matt Okine.
Gnomes might be set in a small Australian township but its set-up hinges on a deadly but petrified European gnome queen who was stolen by the Nazis in the final whiffs of WWII as Hitler's last-ditch attempt to regain power.
"We really enjoyed playing into genre and have the bad guy Nazis, and we wanted to evoke that straight from the get-go," Higginbotham says.
Hitler's bumbling Nazi guards fail to activate the gnome queen's power, inadvertently tipping the first domino that results in a plague of killer gnomes terrorising the tiny fictional town of Nompton.
"There is also, of course, that very known history that Hitler had that side where he's interested in the occult and would try to capture artefacts," Higginbotham says.
"And, you know what? I still want to exist in a world where Nazis are funny. It's really concerning me that we're back to a place where they're being taken seriously."
Screams of laughter
From Resident Evil's box office smash to Widow's Bay's near clean sweep of the Emmys, horror-comedy is having a moment in 2026.
It was the heady combination of genuine over-the-top, B-movie horror and smart, quippy comedy in Gnomes which secured its leading man, British actor Asa Butterfield.
"What attracted me to the project was the writing and comedy, and the sort of absurdity of it. There were great characters, some great gags, and some really funny references to some classic horror movies," Butterfield says.
The Sex Education star plays Senior Sergeant Arnold Kipps who is having one of the worst days in his career.
His ex-partner and former flame Ellie (Megan Smart) has long moved up in the police ranks but suddenly returns to Nompton's minuscule station to break the news that the town is just too darn boring to justify a full police staff.
The powers that be are closing up shop and Arnold and his sergeants are most likely getting the can.
As if this isn't enough to deal with, Arnold is stuck babysitting the aforementioned gnome queen, the star attraction at Nompton's Gnome-a-palooza festival.
An unfortunate accident involving Arnold reawakens the queen who animates all the garden gnomes in town to do her deadly bidding.
"It's been really fun to empower these gnomes with genuine fear and terror, but also knowing they are just garden gnomes," Butterfield says.
Creating the army of gnomes was a challenge for the production team, which brought the cursed creatures to life with a mix of puppetry and special effects.
"We had a great SFX team building hundreds of gnomes, some made of foam, some that could smash, some that can run," Butterfield says.
"Having natural puppets to react to really helps because you don't only have to imagine it. Like there's a vampire gnome there, it's stalking you on the top of a dresser. Or a wizard gnome shooting actual fire out its wand.
"It's the sort of a thing which, honestly, brings out the big kid inside me."
Higginbotham is still shocked that the movie star agreed to sign onto a tiny Australian show about killer gnomes.
"I can't believe he said yes. When they first mentioned that Asa was even considering the role and reading the script I was like, 'That's great. But this is never going to happen,'" she says.
"I've never quite worked with a performer like him. This is somebody who's been doing this since he's a kid. He's just a class above.
"The way he conducts himself on set, the love that he has for every single person on set and for their craft and what they individually do. I mean, I've never seen the man do a bad take.
"He's truly a remarkable actor and we've been so lucky to have him."
Quiet on set
While Butterfield might have been able to micro-dose a Melbourne lifestyle (read: get very into coffee) in his seven weeks filming the series, what impressed him most during his time in Australia was the quality of the local screen industry.
"We moved incredibly quickly, which is credit to the crew and the team to be able to pull off a show that's this ambitious. You couldn't do that back home or in the US, there's no way," he says.
"You would have thought that in doing that people would be more stressed. And yes, it's stressful. But everyone always has a smile on their face, which I really appreciate.
"Everyone says, 'Yeah, we can do that.' I wish our crews back home had a bit more of that energy."
It might have taken 10 years for Higginbotham to get anyone to jump on board with Gnomes, but for the writer the wait was worth it.
"I know 20-something-year-old me, who wanted it all to happen right away, wouldn't agree with me saying this, but I do believe that things happen when they're meant to," she says.
"It's the right time for this sort of entertainment. It was meant to be now. For whatever reason the universe wanted me to have that lesson, for all of us to have to be patient."
Gnomes is streaming on Stan now.

US Democrats call on FBI Director Kash Patel to cancel upcoming trip to Russia

Two top House Democrats are urging FBI Director Kash Patel to cancel a reported trip to Russia, warning in an Oct. 9 letter that the visit could pose security risks.
Politico first reported in July that Patel was planning a fall visit to Russia, where he will be hosted by Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). He is allegedly set to visit both Moscow and St. Petersburg during the trip, which is tentatively scheduled for Oct. 14.
In the letter, Rep. Jamie Raskin and Rep. Jim Himes urged the FBI director to cancel the trip, citing “urgent national security concerns,” including the FSB's history of conducting espionage operations against American officials.
Rep. Jamie Raskin is a Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee and Rep. Himes is a Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The Democrats refer to Russia as a "hostile foreign power" and question why the FBI Director would visit a country that "has been committing war crimes, conducting influence operations against U.S. elections, conducting malicious cyberattacks against our critical infrastructure, and helping our adversaries target and kill American soldiers?"
read also
The letter described the visit as part of the FBI’s expanded cooperation with Russian and Chinese law enforcement agencies, citing Reuters reports that Patel has forged new partnerships with agencies in both countries.
In their letter to Patel, officials also question the timing of the FBI director's visit, citing the sanctions bill signed by President Trump which targets Russia's economy over its war against Ukraine.
Yet, on the same day the letter was published, Trump announced that Russia would supply U.S. and global markets with millions of tons of Russian diesel.
"This is why I voted against the Russia sanctions bill," Rep. Himes wrote on social media on Oct. 9. "Trump was never going to sanction Russia. He's going to refill Putin’s coffers and get an oil deal done to enrich his cronies."
The FBI has not replied to the letter or confirmed Patel's travel plans.
Since taking over the bureau in February 2025, Patel has sought closer ties with Moscow. This has raised concerns within the FBI, given the Kremlin's history of aggressive intelligence operations against the United States, according to an Oct. 9 investigation by The Atlantic.
Patel has previously called on Congress to investigate how U.S. aid to Ukraine is being used, and has criticized the amount of aid being sent.
The Trump appointee has also taken money from pro-Kremlin operatives in the past, according to the Washington Post. Patel received $25,000 in 2024 from a film company run by pro-Kremlin filmmaker Igor Lopatonok, the WP reported in Feb. 2025.
While the role of FBI director has traditionally been considered independent from government influence, U.S. national security expert Evelyn Farkas has described Patel as one of Trump's "yes men."

Similar marches were held in Warsaw and Rome, where protesters denounced ongoing Israeli bombardment and their governments’ ties with Israel, echoing calls for an immediate and lasting ceasefire.
Israel’s genocide has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,200 Palestinians since October 2023.

Eisenkot vows to challenge Netanyahu for power after election, even without Knesset majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:22:11 UTC
03:22:11 KST

With less than three weeks until Israel's election, anxiety is growing among opposition parties as polls suggest neither political bloc is headed for a decisive victory. But Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff and leader of the Yashar party, remains confident that he will be Israel's next prime minister. Some in his own camp even describe that confidence as excessive. Eisenkot sees the same political deadlock as everyone else, but insists the opposition still has a path to power.
"I'm working to reach 61 Knesset members from the basic bloc of four parties: Yashar, Yisrael Beytenu, the Democrats and Beyachad," he says in an interview with Yedioth Ahronoth. "I look at what's happening on the ground and feel tremendous momentum." He claims to encounter dozens of Likud supporters every day, including party central committee members, and says his goal in the remaining campaign period is to attract moderate right-wing voters and members of the religious Zionist community.
The numbers, however, present a challenge. The opposition bloc had previously appeared to be approaching the 61-seat majority needed to control the Knesset, but Netanyahu's camp has narrowed the gap in recent surveys. Eisenkot rejects the suggestion that his strategy has failed. "On the contrary. I've been very successful in recent months," he says. "The four parties in our bloc have organized themselves with surplus-vote agreements, and we're completely coordinated."
He argues that the opposition is no longer threatened by small parties failing to cross the electoral threshold, as happened with Meretz in the 2022 election. Instead, he predicts that Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party and Yaron Zelekha's party will fail to enter the Knesset, leaving Netanyahu in the more difficult position. "When you take them out, that brings us to around 61," he says.
For Eisenkot, the election is about more than changing the prime minister. He wants to dismantle the traditional political division between left and right and build what he calls a broad, Zionist, national alliance. "My life's purpose in entering politics is to break the left-right divide and establish a national camp," he says. "That was the idea behind Blue and White, but it didn't succeed. I'm advancing it through Yashar. We need to throw away the curse of left versus right, which has gotten us nowhere."
He describes his preferred political coalition as an "alliance of those who serve," arguing that a broad national movement should lead Israel rather than parties representing ideological extremes. In his view, the current government is dominated by far-right politicians and ultra-Orthodox parties, with a liberal national minority caught between them.
‘I won't let Netanyahu win by not losing’
Eisenkot believes Netanyahu has a political interest in an inconclusive election. He argues that the prime minister understands that a large majority of Israelis support military or national service and the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre, making a clear electoral victory difficult.
"He understands politics extremely well," Eisenkot says. "He knows he can't win, so he's following the pattern he's used in recent years, which is winning by not losing." He accuses Netanyahu of delegitimizing Arab political parties and seeking to remain in office through political deadlock rather than a decisive victory.
Eisenkot says his goal is to defeat Netanyahu's bloc by 63 seats to 45. But even if the opposition falls short of 61, he insists he will not allow Netanyahu to remain prime minister indefinitely at the head of a caretaker government.
"If you think you're going to do to me what you did to others in the past, meaning that you'll remain in a caretaker government, that won't happen," he says. "If the worst-case scenario occurs and we don't reach 61, I'll put it to a vote on the strength of the Zionist majority."
Under that scenario, Eisenkot says he would call on all 120 Knesset members to vote according to their conscience. He would not seek support from ultra-Orthodox or Arab lawmakers, but believes he could still win a decisive majority.
He acknowledges that such a move would involve political risk, but maintains that Netanyahu's long-standing election strategy is vulnerable. According to Eisenkot, the prime minister repeatedly relies on three central arguments: that only the right can provide security, that his opponents would establish a Palestinian state, and that Arab political parties are disloyal to Israel.
Eisenkot points to the security failure of October 7 as a challenge to the first argument and accuses Netanyahu of repeatedly portraying Arab citizens as a threat. "This is the only prime minister in the world who attacks 21% of his own citizens," he says.
Yet Eisenkot himself rules out a governing partnership with Arab parties under their current positions. He says any coalition partner must accept four principles: Israel as a Jewish, democratic and liberal state; the values of the Declaration of Independence; compulsory IDF or national service; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be destroyed. "I don't know of any Arab party that accepts that," he says.
Nor does Eisenkot envision serving under Netanyahu again, even if the alternative is another election. "I don't see him continuing," he says. "It cannot be that after the failure of October 7 we continue seeing him in Israeli political life. I don't hate him, but I think that if we allow him to be appointed to another leadership position, we're crossing out the word 'accountability.'"
Fears of a government ‘surrounded by criminals’
Eisenkot stresses that his opposition to Netanyahu is not driven by personal animosity but by what he describes as deep concerns about the country's future. He warns that another term for the current coalition could lead to social, economic and diplomatic deterioration and leave Israel increasingly isolated internationally.
"It's not just Netanyahu, but his team and everyone who would surround him," he says, describing a hypothetical cabinet in which Itamar Ben-Gvir becomes defense minister, Bezalel Smotrich foreign minister, Tally Gotliv justice minister and Yaakov Bardugo communications minister. "I see this as a very serious threat to the State of Israel. That's why I'm sounding the alarm and saying this group will drag the country into an abyss that's difficult to imagine."
Asked about concerns raised by Avigdor Liberman and Yair Golan that Netanyahu might disrupt the election, potentially citing security circumstances, Eisenkot says he cannot rule out improper or illegal actions. "My concern stems from the fact that Netanyahu is surrounded by a criminal environment, so I don't rule out criminal acts," he says, citing Yonatan Urich, who is facing trial in the Bild affair, and Tzachi Braverman, who has been summoned to a hearing in connection with the so-called late-night meeting affair.
Eisenkot goes further, accusing Netanyahu of allowing political considerations to determine national security decisions. "Political motives guide him as prime minister, rather than considerations of national security," he says. Unlike many of Netanyahu's other critics, Eisenkot was a member of the emergency government and the small war cabinet from October 2023 until his resignation on June 13, 2024, giving him firsthand knowledge of the internal deliberations during the war.
He recalls a letter he sent Netanyahu and the chairman of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee less than two months before the October 7 massacre. In it, he urged the government to suspend its judicial overhaul legislation, warning that the internal crisis was damaging the IDF and endangering national security. "I wrote to them, listen carefully, the situation is extremely dangerous. The threats in the strategic environment have worsened. We could face an event like the Yom Kippur War."
‘Political considerations completely took over Netanyahu’
One of Eisenkot's most serious accusations concerns Netanyahu's handling of negotiations to release Israeli hostages from Gaza. He claims that the prime minister repeatedly put his coalition's survival ahead of opportunities to secure their release, leaving some hostages in Hamas captivity who might otherwise have returned alive.
He describes a cabinet meeting during the first hostage release deal in November 2023, when ministers discussed expanding the categories of hostages eligible for release. The initial agreement focused on women and children, but the proposed expansion would have included elderly and wounded captives, including Hersh Goldberg-Polin.
According to Eisenkot, Netanyahu retreated from the proposal because he feared National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who had issued an ultimatum shortly beforehand. Ben-Gvir threatened to bring down the government unless the military campaign resumed within 10 days. Eisenkot argues that Netanyahu chose political survival over the possibility of saving more hostages.
"I'm saying this unequivocally," he says. "Just this morning I heard Yoav Gallant being interviewed and saying that Nitzan Alon was right, that hostages did not return because of political considerations. Ultimately, that's why I left the government. I saw how political considerations completely took over Netanyahu. I lost trust in him."
Eisenkot recounts another episode from May 27, 2024, when Netanyahu unexpectedly presented the small war cabinet with a document titled "General Principles for an Agreement Between the Israeli Side and the Palestinian Side in Gaza Regarding the Exchange of Hostages and Prisoners and the Restoration of Sustainable Calm."
Netanyahu told the ministers that he wanted to approve a decision on releasing hostages. Eisenkot says he examined the proposal, which included a 42-day suspension of fighting and Israeli troop withdrawals from designated areas, before telling the prime minister that despite the difficult terms, he supported it.
"I read the paper, looked at Netanyahu and said to him, 'This is a very difficult document, but I support it and recommend that you accept it,'" Eisenkot recalls. According to his account, the proposal was put to a vote and approved by all the cabinet members present, including Eisenkot, Gallant, Benny Gantz, Ron Dermer, Aryeh Deri and Netanyahu himself.
Two days later, Eisenkot says, commentators associated with Netanyahu, including Bardugo, began criticizing the proposal. He initially dismissed the attacks. But after then-US President Joe Biden publicly outlined the Israeli ceasefire and hostage-release proposal on May 31, 2024, Netanyahu distanced himself from the initiative.
Eisenkot attributes the change to threats from Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to collapse the coalition if the agreement moved forward. "He passed a cabinet decision and then went back on it," Eisenkot says. "It's insane. It shows the state of vertigo he's in. Political considerations are present at every stage."
Eisenkot also rejects Netanyahu's assertion that he opposed an IDF operation in Rafah and wanted to end the war without dismantling Hamas rule. "Netanyahu is a pathological liar," he says, while pointing to Government Secretary Yossi Fuchs as someone whose account he trusts. Fuchs served under Eisenkot in the military, and the former chief of staff says the minutes of the May 2024 cabinet vote would establish that every minister, including himself, supported the Rafah operation.
He also cites a letter he sent Netanyahu on February 15, 2024, urging further military action. "Prime Minister, wake up," the letter said, according to Eisenkot. "The right thing to do is complete the operation in Khan Younis, intensify the operation in Rafah and maneuver." For Eisenkot, the document directly contradicts Netanyahu's account of his wartime position. "Credibility is not Netanyahu's strong suit," he says.
‘There is no total victory’
When the discussion turns to Netanyahu's repeated promises of "total victory," Eisenkot produces an old newspaper article that gives the phrase a deeply personal meaning.
The article, written by Yedioth Ahronoth military correspondent Alex Fishman and published on April 11, 2004, featured a young Brig. Gen. Gadi Eisenkot, then commanding IDF forces in the West Bank. Asked about the campaign against Palestinian terrorism, he offered a bleak assessment.
"Terrorism will continue for many years," Eisenkot said at the time. "The bitter truth is that there is no total victory in this struggle. Our job is to minimize Palestinian achievements. I expect that even my youngest son, who is now 5, will fight in the territories."
His youngest son was Gal Eisenkot, who was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023.
For Eisenkot, the passage underscores both the limitations of military power and the personal cost of the conflict. More than two decades after making that prediction, he remains convinced that promises of absolute victory misrepresent the nature of Israel's security challenges.
He is equally critical of Netanyahu's refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 failures. Eisenkot suspects that some of the records submitted concerning the period before the massacre may have been manipulated.
"I see something that carries potential criminal implications," he says. "In my assessment, reports were falsified. When I look at what was distributed to the state comptroller, and I know, as a cabinet member and member of the intelligence subcommittee, what material was there, I have a very deep suspicion of document falsification. In my opinion, this is a document somebody cooked up."
One document at the center of the dispute concerns possible operations against senior Hamas leaders. It was prepared by Netanyahu's military secretary on October 1, 2023, and placed on the prime minister's desk. The document referred to "advancing operational readiness for the recommended targeted killings, Hamas leaders, with an emphasis on emergency scenarios."
The document indicates that discussions about potential operations against Hamas leaders in Gaza did take place less than a week before the massacre, contrary to the account attributed to Netanyahu. A separate investigation by Yedioth Ahronoth journalists Ronen Bergman and Yuval Rubowitz examines the prime minister's account of the decisions and intelligence assessments that preceded October 7.
Eisenkot's allegations about falsified records remain allegations, but they form part of his broader argument that the government must face an independent examination of its conduct before and during the war.
Gantz, Winter and the battle for opposition votes
Returning to the election, Eisenkot faces challenges not only from Netanyahu's right-wing bloc but also from potential partners within the opposition. Despite his strong standing in the polls, other party leaders have been reluctant to declare him their candidate for prime minister.
Eisenkot recalls that when his party was polling at around six seats a year ago, he publicly argued that the leader of the largest party in the bloc should become its candidate for prime minister. He says that principle should still apply. "Under the circumstances that have developed, I'm the only candidate who knows how to defeat Netanyahu. I'm the only person in decades who has led him by a significant margin in polls asking who is best suited to be prime minister. I don't see this as an obsession with honor or power, but as a mission and a duty."
One unresolved issue is Benny Gantz, Eisenkot's former political partner in the National Unity party. The two were once close, but Eisenkot now believes Gantz should withdraw his Blue and White party from the race because polls indicate it will fail to cross the electoral threshold.
"I've met with him quite a few times, and we talk," Eisenkot says. "Gantz has made a major contribution to the country, but he's a political figure and he'll have to make a decision. Under the current circumstances, I'm convinced he'll decide to withdraw. I don't think he'll run all the way when the polls give him 1.5%. I'm certain he'll make a rational decision."
Gantz, however, declared Saturday evening that he intends to remain in the race until the end, despite the unfavorable polling. He argued that his campaign offers a path toward national unity rather than another government built around the traditional political blocs.
Eisenkot is more open to a partnership with Ofer Winter, the former IDF general who leads the Amcha Yisrael party, although his assessment of Winter's campaign is far from flattering. He says Winter accepts the four principles he has established for coalition partners but considers his party politically immature and unfocused.
"I see a party that isn't ready, that is very unfocused and confused about its own ideas," Eisenkot says. "I see pressure and panic, and they're firing in every direction. They're in favor of military service, but they go with Netanyahu, Goldknopf and draft evasion. Winter very much wants to uncover the truth, but he goes with Netanyahu, who doesn't want to establish a state commission of inquiry."
Winter recently told Yedioth Ahronoth that Eisenkot was not fit to become prime minister but could make an excellent culture minister. Eisenkot dismisses the criticism. "I don't judge him. He's under pressure."
Another issue facing Eisenkot is the composition of his own party list, which includes numerous political newcomers. Some within the opposition are concerned that inexperienced lawmakers could eventually defect or abandon the party, as happened with Idit Silman and Amichai Chikli during the previous political upheavals.
Eisenkot insists he has carefully examined the candidates he recruited, some of whom he has known for decades and others for only months. He says he has held meetings with prospective Knesset members to establish a shared understanding of political conduct, emphasizing that disagreements are legitimate but abandoning the party to join a rival political camp is not.
"I told them, look, I'm not going to ask you to sign anything, but I want there to be a covenant between us, a cultural understanding that we're practicing a different kind of politics," he says. "We argue and stand by our positions. If someone thinks something contradicts their values, I'll respect that very much, but I expect them to do what Matan Kahana and I did: resign and leave."
He expresses complete confidence that he can prevent defections of the kind that undermined previous governments. "I promise that there won't be a single Silman or Chikli in my party," Eisenkot says. A lawmaker might resign over a fundamental disagreement, he acknowledges, but he insists none would remain in the Knesset after switching allegiance to another party.
‘At this stage of my life, it's very hard to scare me’
The interview ends with a different concern: personal security. Eisenkot and Democrats leader Yair Golan have both raised questions about the level of official protection provided to them as senior opposition figures.
Eisenkot describes what he considers an unusual chain of decisions. According to his account, an advisory committee headed by Ronen Cohen recommended providing Golan with personal security. The recommendation reached Justice Minister Yariv Levin, who chaired the relevant ministerial committee, but Eisenkot says the meeting failed to proceed because the other members did not attend.
Levin then transferred responsibility to the Shin Bet, according to Eisenkot, who says the security agency eventually sent him a letter authorizing his privately hired guards to carry firearms.
Eisenkot suggests, without presenting evidence, that political considerations may have influenced the process. "I wouldn't be surprised if Netanyahu told the head of the Shin Bet that it would be preferable for Gadi Eisenkot not to have security, but that it shouldn't look like something that could help him in the campaign," he says.
He contrasts Netanyahu's concern for his own protection with his decision to waive the security arrangements available to him after leaving the IDF.
"As chief of staff, I was entitled to four years of security, but after six months I announced that I was taking responsibility for my own safety," Eisenkot says. "I asked to be released from the security detail, and from that point on, anything that happened to me in the future would be entirely my responsibility."
But his concerns are not merely theoretical. Eisenkot reveals that someone recently left a threatening message directed at him on the grave of his son Gal, who was killed in Gaza in December 2023.
"Someone made the effort to go to the cemetery and leave a threatening message aimed at me on Gal's grave," he says.
For a father who lost his son during the war, the choice of location adds a particularly painful dimension to the threat. Yet Eisenkot says he ultimately decided not to respond or take any action.
"I debated what to do about it, and in the end I decided to do nothing," he says. "At this stage of my life, it's very hard to scare me."

Polish police detain more teenagers over alleged school violence plans
Police in Poland have detained several teenagers following a wave of online threats against schools and students, amid heightened security fears over a series of recent mass stabbings in classrooms.
Law enforcement officials warned that perpetrators will face "serious consequences" as investigators look into whether the online posts are linked to a rumoured social media "challenge".
On Thursday, a 17-year-old boy was detained in Przasnysz county, north-central Poland, on suspicion of creating an AI-generated video threatening an attack on a local high school. According to the infoprzasnysz news portal, the artificial voice in the footage threatened a "slaughter" at the school, hinted at further attacks in other regions, and made death threats against a specific student named in the recording.
Ilona Cichocka of the local police command told PAP that an investigation is underway to verify if the detained youth was the actual creator of the footage.
Separately, early on Friday morning, a 16-year-old boy was arrested at his home in Szczytno. Police spokesperson Agata Stefaniak told PAP that the teenager is suspected of posting a video online threatening students and teachers at a local secondary school. The local newspaper Tygodnik Szczytno reported that the footage depicted a masked youth wielding a knife who announced an attack planned for Friday.
Also on Friday, officers in the Warsaw area apprehended two 15-year-olds from Pruszkow county and a 13-year-old from the capital's Bemowo district. The two 15-year-olds had reportedly published social media videos threatening to kill other people. Meanwhile, Warsaw Police confirmed on X that the 13-year-old had posted a photograph of a knife to a school class group chat alongside threats against a classmate. The youth reportedly told officers he did it "out of stupidity".
A short while later, Warsaw police reported on X that following a report from a student, a 14-year-old was detained in Jozefow near Warsaw on Thursday who allegedly planned to bring a knife into school and his behaviour could have threatened the safety of others.
Police officers from the town of Zyrardow south of Warsaw also reported the detention of a 15-year-old resident of Wiskitki county near the capital who allegedly issued online threats against other people. At the time of the apprehension, he carried a sharp tool.
In the capital, police officers detained a 14-year-old at a school in the Mokotow district who carried a knife and 11 firecrackers.
More arrests followed across the country, with police officers acting on reports by concerned Internet users or members of the public. A 13-year-old girl was apprehended in the central city of Plock, another girl aged 16 in the western Legnica and a 16-year-old boy in Zdunska Wola near Lodz in central Poland.
The detainees posted video clips or messages online allegedly containing threats of or suggesting school violence. According to police reports, some of them explained their behaviour as "silly jokes".
Three students in Dabrowa Bialostocka, northeastern Poland, have been detained by police after one of them brought a knife to school and took pictures with his friends while wearing balaclavas.
A total of six incidents involving potential threats at educational institutions, with students making jokes about possessing knives and explosives, were reported by police in the Podlaskie province in the northeastern part of the country.
Six students from the Malopolskie province, southern Poland, were investigated for making threats against schools and peers and for bringing knives to schools. Their cases are being reviewed by family courts.
Police detained a 16-year-old student from Kielce County, southern Poland, who had brought a small axe to school. In total, over a dozen interventions were recorded at schools in the Swietokrzyskie province, and dangerous items, such as knives and pocket knives, were seized.
The arrests come after two high-profile school attacks shook the country this week. On Thursday, a 15-year-old stabbed three people at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, killing one person. A regional court in Wyszkow, central Poland, decided to send the 15-year-old to a juvenile detention centre for three months, PAP was told by a court source.
A day earlier, a 19-year-old armed with a knife injured nine people - five students, two teachers, and two passers-by - at a vocational school in Ostroleka. The attacker also carried a backpack filled with homemade explosives.
In a separate incident on Wednesday, police in Sierpc detained another 17-year-old who told classmates he planned to "do something bad at school." Officers searching his belongings recovered two knives and found online search history related to mass attacks on his mobile phone.
After the fatal stabbing in Leszczydol-Nowiny, all primary and high schools as well as kindergartens in the county were to be closed on Friday.
Also other counties and municipalities in the central Mazowieckie province, including Pultusk, Wolomin and Ciechanow, were set to remain closed on that day. The same decision was made for schools and kindergartens in Piaseczno near Warsaw, and Gora Kalwaria called on parents to keep children at home on Friday.
Municipal authorities in Legionowo reported that two schools were closed due to unconfirmed reports that they had been listed as targets in the rumoured online school attack challenge. The matter is being investigated by the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime.
Following the incidents, police officers inspected 10,000 school facilities nationwide, the National Police Headquarters said on X on Friday. It further reported that ten individuals have been arrested over making criminal threats.
In a Friday announcement, Polish police also said that so far, any rumours of a social media "challenge" proved to be unsubstantiated. "Police officers across the country... are working on the case, reacting to all reports, and detecting any disturbing signals online," it said, appealing for restraint in spreading unverified information.
Deputy Interior Minister Wieslaw Szczepanski told Polish Radio 24 public broadcaster on Friday that starting from that day, police patrols around schools will be more frequent, with headmasters having the authority to let officers inside the buildings.

Attack on airport in Saudi capital, Riyadh, leaves several injured
