Saudi Arabia says 12 killed, 300 wounded in Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
Operations at King Khalid International airport suspended as authorities say victims include four Saudis and eight foreigners.
Twelve killed, more than 300 injured in Riyadh airport attack
Saudi Arabia has said at least 12 people were killed, and more than 300 were wounded in an attack by Yemen’s Houthis on the King Khalid International airport near its capital, Riyadh.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the attack on Saturday killed at least four Saudi citizens and two Bangladeshis.
The dead also included one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt.
At the latest count, at least 309 people were wounded, it said.
GACA added that some of the wounded were in critical condition and that all were receiving medical care in hospital.
The attack – which also caused property damage – marked the third assault by the Houthis on the international airport this week. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA.
Operations at the airport were temporarily suspended, with GACA saying officials were assessing the damage.
‘Decisive’ response
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen called the attack a “full-fledged war crime”. Spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Malki said the coalition would “respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law”.
Al-Malki also confirmed a separate incident, saying in a post on X that “a projectile fell in the vicinity of King Fahd International Airport in Dammam”.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said the Houthis had signalled that King Khalid International and other airports in Saudi Arabia would be among their main targets.
The attacks come as fighting intensified in Yemen, with forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government fighting the Iran-backed Houthis for control of the country.
Saudi Arabia has waged an air campaign in support of the Yemeni government’s ground war and claimed hundreds of strikes on Houthi-held territory, including the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after Saturday’s attack that the group had “shut down Riyadh international airport”.
The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.
It said any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target.
‘Direct threat’ to regional security
Qatar condemned the attack, saying in a statement that Doha considered it “a direct threat to the security of the region”. Egypt, Jordan and Oman also expressed sympathy and solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.
Separately, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in Saudi Arabia.
The US Mission said it was “aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh” and “strongly recommends” all US citizens avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
The UK and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”.
Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at King’s College London, said the Houthi strike on a civilian target in Saudi Arabia was an anticipated response.
“It’s a matter of expectation, considering what the Houthis are experiencing through the Saudi air strikes over the last 10 days, two weeks. It was expected that this is – in a way – the only way to retaliate,” he told Al Jazeera.
He condemned the attack on a “clearly civilian target”, saying the initial assessment appears to be that the Houthis used a ballistic missile in the attack. “That just gives you the nature of who and what Saudi Arabia and its allies are dealing with today,” he added.

'Misplaced, unwarranted': India slams OHCHR for raising concern over SIR protest

====================================================================================================

Screen time not consistently tied to children’s emotional or behavioral problems in a large Scottish study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:00:50 UTC
03:00:50 KST

An analysis of data from the Growing Up in Scotland study found that, after accounting for family circumstances, the amount of time children spent on screens was not linked to emotional, behavioral, or social difficulties at ages 5 and 10. At age 15, teens who spent 5 or more hours a day gaming were more likely to have elevated difficulties than those who gamed less than an hour a day, while those who spent at least an hour a day on social media and messaging were less likely to. The paper was published in JAMA Network Open.
Screen-based devices such as televisions, smartphones, computers, and tablets have become a routine part of childhood in many countries. In the United Kingdom, 85% of children aged 3 to 5 go online, a figure that reaches 100% by age 10, and 81% of children aged 10 to 12 use social media and messaging apps despite age limits of 13. This widespread exposure has prompted concern about whether large amounts of screen use might harm children’s emotional, social, and behavioral development.
However, research findings have been mixed, and there is still considerable debate about how large any harmful effects actually are. Some of the inconsistencies reflect differences in the type of screen activity, the amount of time spent using devices, and the age of the child.
Younger children may be especially sensitive if screen use replaces play, conversation, or interaction with parents and caregivers. Among adolescents, the picture is less clear because screen use takes place alongside major biological, social, and emotional changes. Many existing studies are also limited because they examine children at only one point in time and do not adequately account for other influences on development.
Study author Fiona McQuaid of the University of Edinburgh and her colleagues examined how screen use related to children’s psychosocial development, both at the same point in time and years later. A key aim was to account for family factors, such as the quality of the parent-child relationship, that earlier studies have often left out.
They analyzed data from the Growing Up in Scotland study, a government-funded study administered by the Scottish Centre for Social Research. Families with 10-month-old infants living in Scotland in 2005 and 2006 were identified from child benefit records, which cover more than 90% of Scottish children, and were followed up at regular intervals with interviews, questionnaires, cognitive tests, and physical measurements. In 2017, the study recruited 502 additional adolescents to make up for the loss of participants from the most deprived areas; they were included in the analyses at age 15 but not in the analyses that tracked children over time.
The analysis included 3,786 children at age 5, 3,126 at age 10, and 2,598 at age 15, with roughly equal numbers of boys and girls. Data were collected in 2009 and 2010, 2014 and 2015, and 2019 and 2020.
Out-of-school screen use was reported by the child’s main caregiver at ages 5 and 10 and by the adolescents themselves at 15. At ages 5 and 10, time spent watching television and using computers or playing games was combined into a daily total, while at 15, time spent on television and films, gaming, and social media and messaging was analyzed separately. The study captured only how much time was spent, not what children were watching or doing.
Parents completed the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire at each age, a widely used screening tool that covers emotional difficulties, conduct problems, hyperactivity, and problems with peers, along with prosocial behavior such as being kind and helpful. Children with a total difficulties score of 14 or more were classified as having above-average difficulties. The researchers adjusted for a wide range of factors, including household income, deprivation, parental education and health, children’s cognitive test scores, household chaos, and the warmth and conflict in the parent-child relationship.
About 11% of children had above-average difficulties at age 5, and about 12% did at ages 10 and 15. Daily screen use increased substantially with age. The share of children using screens for 3 or more hours a day rose from 25% at age 5 to 52% at age 10, and the share gaming for 3 or more hours a day rose from 1.7% at age 5 to about 21% at age 15. At 15, 28% of teens used social media and messaging apps for 3 or more hours a day.
After the researchers accounted for family and other factors, total screen time was not linked to above-average difficulties at ages 5 or 10. Associations seen before these adjustments largely weakened once they were taken into account.
At age 15, teens who gamed for 5 or more hours a day had 2.61 times the odds of above-average difficulties compared with those who gamed for less than an hour. By contrast, teens who used social media and messaging apps for at least an hour a day had about 40% lower odds of above-average difficulties than those who used them for less than an hour, though after the researchers corrected for running many comparisons at once, this held only for 1 to 2 hours a day.
The authors urged caution in interpreting the social media finding. Teens who use social media very little may differ from their peers in ways that affect their well-being, and those who are already doing well socially may simply be more inclined to use these apps.
Looking over time, children who used screens for 5 or more hours a day at age 5 had 2.68 times the odds of above-average difficulties at age 10 compared with those who used screens for less than an hour, but this association was no longer present at age 15. It also did not hold up in several alternative analyses, and only 119 children were in the highest-use group. Prosocial behavior showed no consistent links with screen use.
“In this cohort study, screen use was not consistently associated with poorer outcomes for children. These findings suggest that guidelines focusing solely on screen time may have limited impact on psychosocial outcomes,” study authors concluded.
The authors suggest that guidance should also consider the content of screen use, the context in which it happens, and parental involvement, rather than time limits alone. They note that screen use also carries known risks, including sedentary behavior, online bullying, and exposure to harmful content.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the relationship between screen use and children’s psychosocial development. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any definitive causal inferences to be derived from the results, and the links seen at age 15 could run in either direction. The study also measured only time spent on screens, not content, and screen use was reported by parents at younger ages but by adolescents at 15, while difficulties were rated by parents throughout.
Families from deprived areas, younger mothers, and single-parent households were more likely to drop out over time, and few participants were from ethnic minority backgrounds, which may limit how widely the findings apply. Most of the data were collected before the COVID-19 pandemic and before newer formats such as short-form video became widespread, so they may not fully reflect children’s current digital lives.
The paper, “Screen Use and Emotional, Behavioral, and Social Development in Children,” was authored by Fiona McQuaid, Valeria Skafida, Ruth McQuillan, and Bohee Lee.

Union says cruise ship crews still open to exploitation under legal loophole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Cruise ship crews still vulnerable to exploitation as government announces updated protections
In short:
A legal exemption for cruise ships from Australian labour law has been altered to allow some new protections for crew.
Critics say the legal loophole that left them vulnerable shouldn't have existed in the first place and allows for worker exploitation.
What's next?
The exemption was due to expire at the end of the year but has been extended to 2028.
The union that represents cruise ship workers has warned that the exploitation of staff will become "embedded" in the industry after the federal government extended a decades-old exemption that allowed cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour law.
The government has announced new protections for cruise workers following an ABC News investigation that revealed allegations of shocking conditions among the crew on some Carnival Cruise vessels.
It includes the ability to collectively bargain and make complaints to the maritime safety regulator.
But the government has decided to continue the practice of allowing cruise ships an exemption to labour laws, extending the long-standing exemption until 2028.
The ABC revealed in August that workers were accusing the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations.
Transport Minister Catherine King called the allegations "horrifying".
In response to the investigation Australia's anti-slavery commissioner said: "I think some change in this area is long overdue."
Exemption should never have existed: union
Maritime Union of Australia national secretary Jake Field said the exemption should never have existed in the first place and did so at the expense of Australian jobs.
Introduced in 1998, the exemption lets cruise ships avoid Australian labour law and instead follow the looser international Maritime Labour Convention.
The new obligations are the first time cruise operators have had conditions attached to their exemption.
Originally expiring at the end of this year, it was extended until 2028 with the new conditions that ship operators cannot restrict crews rights to collective bargaining, and complaints about working conditions must to be reported to the maritime regulator, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority.
"The exemption shouldn't exist at all. The government should do an investigation into the industry,"
Mr Field said.
Right to collective bargaining
Under the new conditions, cruise operators can no longer restrict crews' rights to collective bargaining.
The ABC has seen letters from Carnival that warned crew against the presence of Maritime Union of Australia representatives at ports and reminded staff that they were under no obligation to stop.
Transport Minister Catherine King said in a statement that the changes would protect workers while supporting Australia's maritime industry.
Carnival and Royal Caribbean Cruises did not comment when asked if they would begin bargaining with crews. Carnival said it was considering the details of the announcement.
Regulator to have more oversight of complaints
The changes also mean that all crew complaints regarding the Maritime Labor Convention must be reported to the Australian regulator.
It is intended to give the government a better understanding of the types of complaints being made about conditions and how they are managed.
Calls to protect foreign cruise ship workers
The government has said it will be the last time the exemption is renewed and it is considering a review of the laws, the findings of which are not yet public.
Carnival operates three ships full-time from Australia, with roughly 1,000 crew on each, mostly flown in from South-East Asian and African countries.
In a previous statement to the ABC, Carnival rejected the allegations made by crew and said the maritime authority had carried out "surprise inspections of our three ships in recent weeks and cleared Carnival on each occasion".
It said that the company followed international standards.
Critics say changes don't go far enough
The Maritime Union argued the changes do not go far enough.
Jake Field said the exemption should not exist in the first place and it would "further embed an industry built on exploitation at the expense of foreign seafarers".
"It's a thriving industry and it doesn't need to thrive on exploitation. It's a lie to say that it won't thrive on Australian wages."
Almost 1.5 million Australians went on cruises last year, according to the Cruise Lines International Association.
Ms King said that cruises were a vital economic driver for port towns across Australia and a draw for international tourists.
Mr Field said the union had been telling Carnival that their employees wanted to bargain with them, to no avail.
"They've responded to that by not allowing New South Wales [SafeWork] to access the vessel," he said.
"That's how serious they take the rights of workers."
Carnival previously said in a statement: "SafeWork NSW has no regulatory role covering international seafaring."

Trump argued that the Russia-Ukraine war could have been avoided. “If I were president, you wouldn't have ever had that war. That war would have never started,” he said.
The US president also accused Zelenskyy of missing multiple opportunities to end the conflict.
“Zelenskyy could have settled this war many times, many, many times, and he chooses not to,” Trump said, describing the situation as “very difficult.”
Criticising attacks on Russian refineries
Trump also criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, arguing that attacks on refineries could worsen global fuel shortages and affect American farmers and ranchers.
“We told them, do whatever you want, but don't hit the diesel fuel because there's a big problem. Big shortage,” he said.
Lashing out at Zelenskyy for strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to pre-election high diesel prices.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said.
Trump’s remarks came a day after he agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Moscow would supply diesel to the US and global markets to help lower fuel prices, prompting a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian fuel.
Zelenskyy condemned the agreement as a “weak decision” and “an investment in a war that must be ended.”

Inside the world of looksmaxxing where flaws can be fixed at a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:45:00 UTC
02:45:00 KST

Looksmaxxing: The business of telling young men they are not attractive enough
The seductive logic of looksmaxxing began with a promise to make young men better. Then it went too far.
At 20 years old, Cyrus's days are organised around numbers.
He estimates his body fat is close to 10 per cent and is trying to bulk to 100 kilograms. In the morning, Cyrus straps a cuff around his arm to establish a baseline blood-pressure reading, then pricks his finger to check his fasting blood glucose. He counts calories and tracks his sleep, wary that a bad night could crash his testosterone levels. His body is something to be measured, its changes carefully monitored.
One morning, the numbers give him pause.
"I'm not going to lie to you. It's 125 over 40 with a 72 resting heart rate," he says in a recent video documenting his bulking routine. "That's not good at all."
Cyrus's regimen extends beyond the gym. He takes an assortment of medications and supplements, tans because he says it makes his muscles look more defined, and dyes his hair and eyebrows to improve his colouring. About some of his other methods, he is more circumspect. But there are hints at the lengths involved: a recent echocardiogram detected "very slight changes" to his heart.
When Cyrus talks about his body, he treats it as something between a spreadsheet and a software system waiting to be calibrated. In his worldview, almost everything can be improved.
"I believe looksmaxxing is about more than just improving your physical appearance," Cyrus says. "It's also about your cognition and your mind … you're optimising your biology."
Still, he insists with a chuckle, it is "not a full-time occupation at all".
What Cyrus calls "looksmaxxing" is a sprawling online movement devoted to maximising physical attractiveness. Ordinary grooming, dieting and exercise sit at one end of the spectrum ("softmaxxing"); cosmetic procedures, experimental drugs and extreme attempts to alter the face and body — including "bonesmashing", the practice of striking facial bones — sit at the other ("hardmaxxing").
Looksmaxxers have developed an elaborate vocabulary for measuring their progress. Faces are dissected into jaw angles, eye shapes and proportions, then ranked according to "sexual market value". On the so-called PSL scale, using the initials of three online communities, the hierarchy stretches from "subhuman" at the bottom, through "normies" and "chadlites", to the almost cartoonishly masculine "Gigachad" at the top.
There is also "mewing", tongue exercises purported to develop the jaw; "mogging", the act of physically outclassing someone; and a "failo", a perceived flaw considered severe enough to diminish an otherwise attractive face. The ultimate goal is "ascension": through this imagined hierarchy of attractiveness.
Though its language borrows from meme culture and internet slang, looksmaxxing is not satire. What started on niche online forums has been popularised and redefined on mainstream platforms like TikTok and Instagram, and reaching a widening demographic
While there is no official count of the number of looksmaxxers in Australia, a 2025 report by the Movember Institute of Men's Health found almost two-thirds (63 per cent) of Australian men aged 16 to 25 engage with masculinity influencers.
Cyrus's introduction to this way of thinking came after a break-up, when he met one of Australia's biggest looksmaxxing influencers, Androgenic, in Brisbane's nightlife district. Androgenic offered advice on improving his appearance, and Cyrus later began helping behind the scenes with parts of his coaching business. What impressed him most was the way Androgenic commanded respect from those around him.
For millions of young men and boys encountering looksmaxxing on social media, this is its seductive promise. A better jawline or body is not presented as an aesthetic achievement, but as something capable of fixing social isolation, career barriers and romantic frustration.
Cyrus believes he has experienced those returns firsthand.
In high school he was picked on "a decent amount". The bullying became particularly noticeable after he buzzed his hair and, in his view, became "very unconventionally unattractive".
"I was treated far worse and a good percentage of that was due to my looks because the way I was treated improved after I changed my appearance," he says.
The transformation, Cyrus says, has "massively increased" his confidence and improved his quality of life. "There was a very positive feedback loop from going out and getting the 'halo effect', as people call it, where you just get treated better."
It is this core belief — changing the face can change the way the world responds to you — that gives looksmaxxing its power. Researchers say the same pursuit of control can lead young men somewhere else entirely: towards increasingly extreme interventions, communities steeped in fatalism and misogyny, and a marketplace that profits from ensuring there is always another flaw to fix.
What does it mean to be a man?
While women have faced pressures regarding beauty since time immemorial, looksmaxxing has emerged primarily as a male-centric subculture over the past decade. Researchers say it taps into a generation trying to answer a fundamental question: what does it mean to be a man when the traditional blueprint no longer fits?
Associate Professor Scott Griffiths, a psychologist at the University of Melbourne who studies male body image, says young men are more preoccupied with appearance than ever before. Social media intensifies the pressure, but is only part of the story. As gender roles shift and the expectation that men should be sole providers has waned, physical appearance has become another way of performing manhood.
"If you can't do it by becoming the breadwinner," Griffiths says, "you can build a body that others will perceive as masculine."
It is an ideal many young men have internalised: an Adonis-like figure whose "hunter eyes", strong brow ridge and sharply angled jaw promise something beyond beauty. Research suggests people with these traits are perceived as more masculine, reinforcing the belief that appearance can stand in for identity.
The impulse to read meaning into the face is hardly new. Across cultures and centuries, people have tried to infer character from the body's contours. The now-discredited practice of physiognomy treated facial features as clues to intelligence, morality and temperament. In the 19th century, "lion-like" features — a broad jaw, wide forehead and piercing gaze — were thought to signal nobility, courage and strength. A pointed, dog-like nose suggested an excitable nature, while a thick, rounded pig-like one signalled insensitivity.
We now know faces cannot reliably reveal the character within. But appearances do affect how people are perceived, with research showing it influences everything from hiring decisions to earnings. This phenomenon is sometimes called "pretty privilege" — the idea that some people move through the world with advantages conferred simply by being perceived as attractive.
Today, looksmaxxers take that premise further. If a face can shape how the world responds to you, perhaps changing the face can rewrite your fate.
On platforms like Instagram and TikTok, few Australians embody that promise more completely than Androgenic, who has a following of more than 1.3 million.
"I'm going to share the exact blueprint to ascend your looks using unconventional methods," Androgenic says in an online video, speaking in a deliberately affected vocal fry.
The 25-year-old has a chiselled jaw and the sculpted physique of a superhero. Over ten minutes, he recounts a familiar origin story: he was once "scrawny", "underdeveloped", "invisible" to girls and "bullied" by his peers. Then he discovered looksmaxxing.
Six years later, Androgenic says he has transformed himself. He claims to have grown three inches after puberty, reshaped his jaw, chin, cheekbones and brow ridge, gained 45 kilograms of muscle, changed his colouring, refined his skin, undergone cosmetic surgery and even "optimised" his brain.
The reward, he says, has been confidence, career success, commanding respect wherever he goes and attracting "more attention from women than I know what to do with". He calls it the "halo effect".
For $49 a month, Androgenic promises to remove the guesswork for others. His looksmaxxing program includes blood tests and hormone "protocols", facial analyses, surgery recommendations and even a "bonesmashing" guide.
"No cope," he says. "Just real methods that drive real change."
The deeper promise appears to be certainty: a blueprint for a body, and perhaps a life, that might otherwise feel governed by genetics, circumstance or chance.
Dr Krista Fisher, a research fellow at the Movember Institute of Men's Health, says that offer can be seductive when young people are confronting multiple sources of uncertainty. While housing feels unattainable, careers unpredictable and relationships harder to navigate, the body can be one of few things that can be controlled.
Young men around the world are experiencing high rates of anxiety and depression, Fisher says, alongside loneliness and social disconnection. Their online and offline lives have become intertwined, while the use of image — and performance-enhancing substances, including steroids and peptides, has grown.
For Cyrus, the appeal of Androgenic was that his philosophy did not stop at the face. He describes the influencer's approach as "holistic", applying it to the body, the mind and everything around them.
Borrowing the language of data science, Cyrus divides life into "vectors": appearance, money, the mind, status, relationships. Each can be invested in but, for now, appearance seems to him to offer the highest returns.
"I do believe the ROI [return on investment] from improving your appearance will benefit you in so many other vectors," he says. "It's just something that will benefit you in all the aspects of your life."
Once the body is understood as an investment, however, the question becomes how much a person is willing to put into it.
Entering the manosphere
Exercise and dieting are ordinary forms of self-care. But behind the language of "optimisation" lies an online ecosystem where pursuit of a better face can become entangled with extremist ideologies and self-harm.
Looksmaxxing forums, where young men post selfies and exchange tips on improving their appearance, overlap with the broader "manosphere" — a constellation of online communities offering answers about dating, masculinity, status and self-worth, while often trafficking in resentment towards women and rigid gender ideals.
"They are united in a certain grievance towards women," says Christopher David, a research associate in online extremism at Neu-Ulm University. "The belief is that feminism in primarily Western countries has wronged men and created a society where women have it easier than men."
David calls that grievance the manosphere's "common denominator". Online, it is expressed through the language of the "red pill", borrowed from the 1999 sci-fi film The Matrix. To take the red pill is to believe you have awakened to an uncomfortable truth about the world.
At the manosphere's extreme edge sit "incels", or involuntary celibates. "They have this veneration of violence, the glorification of past violent attacks, and this very strong emotional venting towards women," David says. "You don't find the same type of language in other communities."
Central to incel ideology is the "black pill" — a darker extension of the red pill. Its followers believe average or unattractive men are condemned by genetics to a predetermined fate in which they never find romantic or sexual partners. That worldview has been invoked by perpetrators of mass violence in north America.
But violence towards others is not the only concern.
David says research finds high levels of mental health problems in incel communities, and evidence some vulnerable men arrive in these spaces after seeking help elsewhere online. On Reddit, for example, it was found users who became active in incel communities had participated in suicide prevention or mental health forums
"So we can see a pathway there," David says.
Once inside, the language of optimisation can become brutally literal.
A 2025 Canadian study documented men rating one another's faces on the 1-10 PSL scale, with assessments devolving into abuse. One user told a poster he had been "f***ed big time by nature" and that his face looked "grotesque". Another was assigned a PSL score of 2.25 to 2.5, before the user declared that "burn victims look better". A third delivered a verdict in the language of the rating system itself: "Death tier mouth to nose ratio … death tier eyes. Just give up."
In the incel's black-pilled worldview, the face is evidence of a life already decided. Looksmaxxing offers a competing proposition: the verdict can be appealed — even if the appeal sometimes involves deliberately hurting yourself.
David says looksmaxxing was initially dismissed by many incels as "a cope" — an attempt to avoid accepting the supposed reality of the black pill.
Cyrus does not dispute the connection. Looksmaxxing emerged from incel culture "to a degree", he says, but has since fractured into distinct streams.
"There are a lot of incels on these forums who are just projecting hate all day," he says. "But I wouldn't even classify them as real looksmaxxers because they're just rotting on forums instead of improving their lives."
He points instead to Androgenic's paid community, which he describes as supportive.
"Everyone is giving advice and uplifting others," argues Cyrus, who features on Androgenic's social platforms. "I've never met someone who's truly ascended who is hateful towards women."
For some communities, researchers say, that distinction is genuine. But it does not eliminate the risk of what lies a few swipes away.
"It's often not the ideologies that draw young men in," Fisher says. "That is the cost of what they are exposed to by virtue of engaging with content about the way they look and the way they behave."
New research from the University of Melbourne found boys aged 13 to 17 are more likely to hold hostile attitudes towards women than their grandfathers' generation, with just over 30 per cent saying gender equality in Australia had "gone too far".
The study found these attitudes were associated with the online content young people were consuming online.
Fisher and her colleagues have developed a framework for the escalating "tiers" of content that they encounter. What begins with gym exercises, diet plans, grooming, sports and dating can gradually acquire messages about discipline, emotional restriction and male "worth". At the furthest extreme — less than 1 per cent of the videos they coded — the subtext becomes explicit: "misogyny and exclusivist ideologies, male supremacy, white supremacy, homophobia, [and] transphobia".
The behaviours being promoted become more extreme too.
"There are depictions of health risk-taking, so substance use, gambling, binge drinking, and physical augmentation like bone-smashing," Fisher says.
One of looksmaxxing's best-known creators, Clavicular, has turned that extremity into spectacle. In livestreams to more than 423,000 followers on Kick, he has repeatedly struck his face with a hammer in an attempt to change its shape.
During one broadcast in April, he appeared to lose consciousness while sitting with friends in a Miami restaurant. His body went limp on camera before the feed cut off.
Hours later, he posted a photograph of his scraped-up face to X.
"Just got home, that was brutal," he wrote. "All of the substances are just a cope trying to feel neurotypical while being in public, but obviously that isn't a real solution."
For Fisher, the extremity reflects a broader message embedded in some of the darkest material pushed towards boys and young men online.
"The undertone of this content is often that the world is broken, you are broken, and therefore the only way to make yourself feel better or to ascend as a man is these extreme health and social behaviours."
And that messaging can arrive quickly. Fisher says research has found self-harm, incel, misogynistic or suicide-related material can appear within 30 minutes of a 17-year-old boy creating a new TikTok account.
Another flaw to fix
For some, the promise that almost anything can be improved is empowering. But if looksmaxxing offers a solution to every flaw, its business model also depends on convincing young men there is always another flaw to fix.
"I do believe that it can become obsessive," Cyrus says. "It's easy to hyper-fixate on one feature or flaw that you have."
He says meditation and relationships can help keep that fixation in perspective, particularly when someone begins spiralling over a perceived flaw. "There's no benefit to rotting about it and letting it control your life."
But in a rare moment of vulnerability, Cyrus admits he has come close to doing exactly that. At one point, he says, it was "very easy" to go down a rabbit hole.
"I was impulsively considering using trenbolone to grow my bones, which is a very toxic and horrible compound for you," he says, with an embarrassed laugh. "But I'm very glad I didn't touch that at all because, for one, it is a cope."
Trenbolone, or "Tren", is a powerful anabolic steroid developed to increase muscle mass in livestock and is not approved for human use. Anabolic steroids are associated with serious cardiovascular, liver and hormonal complications, as well as infertility and psychiatric effects.
So where does ordinary self-improvement end and something more troubling begin?
For Griffiths, one useful dividing line is the "reversibility" of the actions young men take.
"If you are considering or are undertaking behaviours which have irreversible impacts on the body, for example, if you are taking anabolic steroids as a young man, you are risking irreversible changes to your fertility, to your cardiovascular health."
Going to the gym, dieting or taking greater care over one's appearance is not intrinsically harmful, he says. Those pursuits can provide direction and help establish healthy habits. The warning signs emerge when the routines begin to exert control in the other direction: when missing a workout produces intense anxiety, looking in the mirror triggers thoughts of being "fat and ugly" or "worthless", or the pursuit of an ideal begins to involve potentially irreversible changes to the body.
The 2025 Movember study, which surveyed young men in the UK and the US as well as in Australia, found 27 per cent of those who followed masculinity influencers experienced feelings of worthlessness, compared to 23 per cent of men who did not engage with their content.
At that point, Griffiths says, someone is likely "overinvested" in their appearance and entering "dangerous territory".
Looksmaxxing complicates that boundary because there is money to be made from moving it. An online economy has grown around male insecurities, offering everything from coaching and supplements to facial analyses, hormone protocols and cosmetic procedures. The more flaws that can be identified, the more solutions there are to sell.
And, increasingly, those perceived flaws are not even being identified by a person.
AI-powered looksmaxxing apps promise to analyse a photograph, score individual facial features and generate a personalised plan for improvement. David says generative AI has dramatically lowered the barrier to creating such tools; someone with little programming knowledge can build a rudimentary face-rating app in a matter of hours.
But it is the business model behind some of these apps that concerns him.
In his research, he examined discussions in which users shared screenshots and experiences of AI-generated assessments. A recurring pattern, he says, was an initially unflattering evaluation, often built around obscure measurements and relationships between facial features.
"First you get this relatively negative assessment because the app needs to give you enough room for improvement," he says. "Because it's a subscription, right? So they want to keep you subscribed."
The diagnosis is followed by an "ascension plan": a personalised list of interventions supposedly capable of raising the score. Some recommendations are mundane — exercise, for example — while others draw from looksmaxxing's more peculiar practices, such as "mewing".
The use of AI lends these prescriptions an appearance of precision and reliability. What might once have been the opinion of an anonymous stranger on a forum can now arrive as a personalised assessment, seemingly generated from the geometry of your own face.
"AI is used basically for this superficial assessment," David says, "and also for writing these ascension plans."
It produces a peculiar paradox: an app promising to make its users more attractive has little incentive to tell them they are attractive enough already. And in the world of looksmaxxing, "enough" may be the one measurement that cannot be optimised.
Is it game over?
"There are lot of grifters who want to rip off young men who are vulnerable," Cyrus says.
He points to influencers who promote "thumbpulling", a practice that involves pressing the thumbs against the roof of the mouth in the belief that it can widen the upper jaw or move the maxilla.
For Griffiths, helping young men avoid self-destructive behaviour means teaching them to distinguish between the small truths on which looksmaxxing is built and the sweeping conclusions the manosphere constructs around them.
"It concerns me that we could be walking into ever-more complex and irreversible and customisable ways of presenting our physical appearance that does nothing to build a stable and strong base of self-worth," Griffiths says.
The problem, he says, is that there is little online to help young men separate "granules of truth" from the black-and-white thinking that turns them into rules for living.
Take height, for example. Taller heterosexual men are, on average, perceived as more attractive by women. That is the granule of truth, Griffiths says. But a teenage boy worried about being short is unlikely to encounter it with those qualifications attached.
Instead, he might be served video after video of men approaching women on the street and asking how tall a prospective boyfriend needs to be: "6 foot 2, 6 foot 3, 6 foot 1, 6 foot 2."
"So instead of walking away with a grain of truth, and a reasonably sophisticated worldview that, on average, there are lots of different people out there with different interests and tastes, they walk away with [the assumption], if I'm not tall, if I'm just a short king, then it's game over for me."
That sophistication is difficult to impart on social media, which thrives on sound bites and quick clicks. Fisher argues some of the work therefore needs to happen away from screens, in sporting clubs, community groups and other places where boys already gather.
David says platforms could also do more to disrupt pathways towards blackpill material, including its constantly evolving euphemisms and abbreviations.
The coded language creates another problem. To an uninitiated parent glancing at a teenager's phone, a feed filled with jawlines, gym routines and hairstyle advice might look like little more than adolescent vanity.
"It might look very harmless," David says. "It is very camouflaged."
More difficult still is imparting the idea that a person can improve himself without treating their body as a problem to be solved.
For Cyrus, the promise remains that one day there will be an end point to his transformation. That somewhere beyond the next improvement lies a version of himself that he can finally stop optimising.
"I will definitely reach a point where I am much more content with my overall appearance," he says, before quickly qualifying the admission. "Like, I'm not brutally insecure."
Once he reaches that point, he says he can turn more fully towards the other "vectors" of his life: money, relationships, the mind. It is a revealing hierarchy: looks are not everything in Cyrus's worldview but improving them is imagined as a way of clearing the path towards everything else.
Perhaps that is what makes looksmaxxing so compelling, and so difficult to disentangle from ordinary self-improvement. It takes a common adolescent fear — "Am I attractive enough to be loved?" — and offers the certainty of a system.
The harder question is whether a person who has learned to see his face as a work in progress can ever recognise when the work is done.

Security guarantees for Ukraine must include readiness to fight alongside its forces, French expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:45:00 UTC
02:45:00 KST

Security guarantees for Ukraine must include readiness to fight alongside its forces, French expert says
Stéphane Audrand, an Associate Fellow at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI) Security Studies Center, said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the Ukraine–France Forum in Paris.
“Guaranteeing a country’s security means being prepared to fight for it if it is attacked. When we talk about ‘security guarantees,’ the term often sounds vague. But among allies, it has a concrete meaning,” Audrand said.
He cited Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty and Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union, which provide for assistance to a member state in the event of armed aggression. Since Ukraine is not yet a member of either organization, its security guarantees would require separate arrangements, with their terms depending on the circumstances under which hostilities end.
“If a ceasefire were simply declared tomorrow, that would be one of the worst possible scenarios. It would create an extremely difficult situation: ensuring compliance when the aggressor wants to continue its actions. In the age of drones, violating a ceasefire and denying responsibility is easier than ever,” he explained.
Audrand does not consider the deployment of a UN disengagement force or an OSCE mission an effective option for Ukraine. He also noted that establishing a demilitarized zone along the entire line of contact with Russia, similar to the border between North and South Korea, would be extremely difficult.
Therefore, foreign forces would need to be deployed in Ukraine from the very first day of a ceasefire. “They must enter with a clear commitment: if aggression resumes, we will fight alongside the Ukrainians.”
According to the expert, the presence of relatively small contingents of allied forces in the Baltic states serves precisely this deterrent purpose.
“The Coalition of the Willing must at least prepare us for such a scenario at the operational level. The question is whether we will be politically capable of making such a commitment,” he stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, Germany plans to host a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin this winter, together with France and the United Kingdom, to coordinate further assistance to Ukraine.

The Kyiv City State Administration called on Kyiv residents to stock up on water, food and lighting supplies in case of emergencies
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the intensification of shelling, the Kyiv City State Administration advises Kyiv residents to prepare supplies of water, food and lighting and to charge power banks for at least three days. They also recommend insulating homes and wearing reflective elements.
Kyiv city authorities urged residents of the capital to prepare individual supplies in case of emergencies. The Kyiv City State Administration reported this, according to UNN.
Details
The Kyiv City State Administration noted that the intensity of Russian shelling is increasing. Although energy workers are working around the clock to restore electricity to all consumers, and municipal utility services are working to restore standard water-supply parameters, residents of the capital are advised to:
-  stock up on drinking and utility water. One adult needs 3 liters of drinking water per day and 10–12 liters of utility water for hygiene and cooking. It is optimal to prepare supplies for at least 3 days; 
-  charge power banks and portable power stations; 
-  warm up your premises—seal window joints and check the external insulation of windows; place alufoam or another heat-insulating material between the wall and the radiator; 
-  prepare the necessary supply of flashlights, battery- or rechargeable-battery-powered lamps, candles, matches, batteries, and so on; 
-  ensure a supply of long-term storage food and food that does not require electricity to prepare; 
-  think about safe movement along the street during the hours of darkness. Wear reflective clothing or reflective strips on your sleeve, bag, or backpack. 
Reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that the situation with the capital’s energy supply had worsened due to damage to an energy facility in the Kyiv region as a result of a Russian strike.

Convicted murderer Christa Pike leaves hospital, returns to prison after botched execution
Christa Pike's lawyers on Saturday said that the 50-year-old convicted murderer has been discharged from the hospital and returned to prison. Pike was transported to the hospital in critical condition on September 30 after she survived Tennessee's botched effort to execute her for murdering a classmate when she was a teenager.
The convicted murderer who survived a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee last week has been discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers said Saturday.
Christa Pike, 50, was administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on September 30 that failed to kill her.
Read moreChrista Pike 'angry and confused' after surviving Tennessee execution attempt
She was transported to hospital in critical condition but later regained consciousness, with her lawyers saying this week that she was walking around but in a "foggy" mental state.
"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her lawyers said in a statement Saturday.
Pike was sentenced to death in Tennessee for murdering a classmate, a crime committed when she was a teenager.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the statement went on.
Pike "is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery", the lawyers said.
The attempted execution came after days of last-minute legal wrangling that ultimately reached the Supreme Court.
Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.
Since the botched execution, her lawyers have repeatedly called on Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.
Lee has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.

Pike's stunning survival renewed focus on the ethical debate surrounding capital punishment in the United States.
That debate has intensified following the Pentagon's announcement this week that it intends to livestream an execution by firing squad later this year.
The move has prompted outrage from a broad array of public figures in the United States, including many Republicans supportive of the death penalty.
Pope Leo, the first American pontiff, posted Saturday on X that "the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person".
"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," he said.
The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place.
The federal government instituted a moratorium under president Joe Biden, but President Donald Trump's administration lifted it when he returned to office in 2025.

Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution
Pope Leo XIV describes capital punishment as an ‘attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person’ in post on X.
Pope Leo XIV has declared that the death penalty is “inadmissible” while his home country, the United States, announces plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.
Marking World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, the pope reiterated the Catholic Church’s teaching on capital punishment, writing on X that it was “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person”.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” his post said.
“Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” added the leader of the Catholic Church.
The American Pope’s comments come days after US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan on December 3 will be livestreamed.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009.
Pope Leo did not specifically refer to the planned execution, or last month’s botched execution attempt on Christa Pike, who survived two doses of the lethal injection in Tennessee.
But his post came hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, told Vatican News that the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution was “unacceptable”.
It was Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, in 2018 who first amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances.
Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church did not exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.”
The planned livestream of Hasan’s execution has sparked outrage across the US political divide. Republican representative Austin Scott said he supported executing Hassan but that “livestreaming executions is what Jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice”, but that public executions are “the kind of thing that Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?”
On Thursday, a Pentagon official confirmed the plans, but on Friday, Vice President JD Vance, who is a practising Catholic, expressed doubt on whether the livestream would be going ahead, telling reporters that if it is, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

Man attacked by tiger in England after entering enclosure at wildlife park

Man attacked by tiger in England after entering enclosure at wildlife park
A man sustained serious injuries Saturday after entering the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England, police said.
The incident occurred at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35 p.m., South Yorkshire Police said in a statement. The tigers remained inside the enclosure and there was no danger to the wider public, the force said.
The Yorkshire Ambulance Service said it dispatched two ambulances, an air ambulance and a doctor to attend the scene. Authorities didn't immediately release information about the victim's injuries.
"We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,'' the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its "Land of the Tigers" attraction opening in 2011.
The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-meter raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or playing in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.
Visitors to several zoos and wildlife parks around the world have tried to enter tiger enclosures. A woman was caught in 2024 jumping over a fence and taunting a tiger at the Cohanzick Zoo in New Jersey. In 2016, a zookeeper was fatally attacked by a Malayan tiger at a Florida zoo when she entered the enclosure for the tigers' night house, a medical examiner's investigation found.
Several years earlier, in 2012, a man jumped from an area near the monorail in the Bronx Zoo over two fences, including an electrified one, in one bound to get into the tiger enclosure, police said. He was severely injured in what appeared to be a suicide attempt, police said.

"I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Trump has previously called for elections in Ukraine, amplifying Kremlin propaganda narratives about Zelensky's lack of legitimacy — often shortly after meetings with Russian delegates.
The tactic of blaming Zelensky has also allowed Trump to sidestep questions about Washington's warming relations with Russia amid mass attacks on Ukrainian cities.
read also
Trump's diesel deal with Putin came as a shock to Ukrainian officials, who felt they had been invited to diplomatic talks with U.S. officials in Miami on Oct. 9-10 as part of "a trap."
Officials involved in the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that they believed they would be discussing the terms of an energy ceasefire with Russia — one that would place equal demands on both sides.
Instead, the U.S. struck an economic deal with Moscow while pressuring Kyiv to halt refinery attacks, without any reciprocal demand for Russia to suspend strikes.
The deal seemed to be a way for Trump to dodge consequences — including skyrocketing gas prices and a steep drop in approval ratings — from his decision to wage war in Iran.
But Russian diesel may not provide relief at the pump or the polls, according to Seton Hall University Professor Margarita Balmaceda, an expert in the political economy of energy and associate at the Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute (HURI).
"As I see it, this deal has the potential to do much to help Russia — and to help Russia pursue its war against Ukraine — but not so much to help ease the diesel and gasoline crunch, the causes of which lie largely in the continued tensions around the Strait of Hormuz," Balmaceda said.
Zelensky has said repeatedly that Ukraine is ready to pause attacks against Russian energy infrastructure — as long as Russia agrees to the same terms. Thus far, Russia has shown no interest in de-escalating attacks.
Ukraine has long considered Russian oil refineries valid military targets, as Russian oil exports fund the Kremlin's war chest and refineries produce fuel for the armed forces. According to the Defense Ministry, Ukrainian attacks have disabled over 51% of Russia's total refining capacity.
When Trump announced the deal on Oct. 9, Zelensky said it was "a weak decision by our strong partners" that would allow Putin to prolong the war against Ukraine.
The next day, Kyiv was greeted by Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones in yet another daytime attack against the city's power grid. Residents were left without power and water.
"The consequences of allowing Russia to sell oil products were most clearly felt in Kyiv today, when, following numerous attacks with jet-powered Shahed drones against energy facilities, a ballistic missile attack began as well," Zelensky said in a message published on Telegram following the attack.
The money Russia earns from diesel exports will fund further destruction in Ukraine, the president warned.
"Every additional billion dollars Russia manages to earn from exports will be spent precisely on this: finding and importing critical components, equipment for weapons production, upgrading Shahed drones, manufacturing missiles, and recruiting additional mercenaries for the front," he said.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia targeted a residential building, killing 20 civilians, including three children.

Hurricane Simon strengthens to Category 4 off Mexico coast

- A hurricane warning covers areas south of Puerto Vallarta, including Manzanillo and the Islas Marias, as residents are told to rush preparations to protect life and property.
- Heavy rain, storm surge and large waves may cause deadly flooding and mudslides in Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, with damage and power cuts expected.
AI generated
MEXICO CITY - Hurricane Simon strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast on Oct 10, threatening destructive winds, storm surges and potentially deadly flooding as it approaches landfall.
The US National Hurricane Centre said Simon was located about 185km south-southwest of Manzanillo on the morning of Oct 10, packing maximum sustained winds of 240kmh as it moved northwards.
Simon is expected to approach the west-central coast of Mexico as a major hurricane late on Oct 10 or early on Oct 11, and some additional strengthening remains possible before landfall, the NHC said.
A hurricane warning was in effect for portions of Mexico’s Pacific coast south of the beach resort of Puerto Vallarta, including the area around Manzanillo, Mexico’s largest Pacific port. A tropical storm watch was in effect farther south toward Lazaro Cardenas.
The NHC urged residents in the warning area, which also includes the Islas Marias archipelago offshore, to rush preparations to protect life and property.
“Simon has strengthened incredibly quickly, and that’s what makes storms like this so dangerous,” said AccuWeather meteorologist Dan Pydynowski.
“Strong winds could damage homes and businesses, while flooding and mudslides could wash out roads and make it difficult for emergency crews to reach some communities. Even after the storm passes, power outages and damaged infrastructure could make recovery challenging.”
Mexican authorities warned that heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco.
The NHC said Simon was expected to produce 25cm to 51cm of rain across portions of southwestern Mexico through Oct 11, with isolated totals of up to 76cm possible in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The rainfall could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in mountainous areas.
A storm surge is expected along the coast near and to the east of where the centre makes landfall, accompanied by large and destructive waves, the NHC said. Swells generated by Simon are expected to affect portions of Mexico’s southwestern and west-central coast over the coming days, creating dangerous surf and rip current conditions.
Simon is forecast to be near or just inland of Mexico’s west-central Pacific coast on Oct 11.

Ukrinform presents ‘Commanders of Victory’ book at Donbas Media Forum 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:28:00 UTC

Ukrinform presents ‘Commanders of Victory’ book at Donbas Media Forum 2026
Ukrinform Director General Serhii Cherevatyi stressed the importance of telling the public about the efforts of Ukrainian service members to defend the country and shape its modern history in order to counter negative information trends.
“We began this project as a series of interviews. The first was with Pavlo Palisa, who at the time commanded the renowned 93rd Kholodnyi Yar Brigade and with whom I had the honor of serving in the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group of Forces. As we worked on all the materials, we realized that publishing the interviews on our website would not be enough. We needed a larger project to preserve the experience of Ukrainian commanders, document the contemporary history of the war and bring it to the public. That is how the idea for the book we are presenting today came about,” he said.
According to the agency’s head, Commanders of Victory is not merely a collection of interviews with leaders from various branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, including Kyrylo Budanov, Oleksandr Pivnenko and Oleh Ivashchenko, but also a historical document. He also noted that the project is available online.
Andrii Yusov, a representative of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, emphasized the importance of high-quality publications that can serve as gifts and research resources and be made available in libraries and government institutions.
“This is not just a book. It is an entire communications project, both multimedia and physical. Most importantly, it is about people. Ukraine has heroes. Ukrainian heroes are outstanding. We need to talk about them. This matters to service members who continue serving under difficult conditions, to veterans, to growing children and to Ukrainian citizens as a whole. And it matters for securing support for Ukraine around the world,” he said.
Yusov added that the world must be continually reminded of Russian aggression.
The book was created by the Ukrinform team, which independently handled every stage of production, from preparing and editing journalistic materials to design, layout and prepress work.
A distinctive feature of the publication is its clasp, which incorporates a cartridge case and a bullet at the end. These elements were specially created for the project by Olha Konoval, wife of Hero of Ukraine Serhii Konoval and Head of the Serhii Konoval Foundation.
She explained that the cartridge cases came from the Serebrianskyi Forest, allowing readers to literally touch an object connected to the war.
“Every cartridge case you hold in your hands has already done its job. It has been spent. I put this element together in a very interesting way. The cartridge case is from an M4A1, while the bullet is from a Kalashnikov rifle. In other words, we combined things that do not go together; this is not a live round,” she said.
The presentation also featured a panel discussion with people profiled in the book: Pavlo Kurylenko, Deputy Head of the Current Operations Directorate at the Headquarters of the Joint Forces Command; Oleksandr “Pryvyd” (“Ghost”), a sniper platoon commander with the Separate Presidential Brigade named after Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytskyi; and Dmytro Finashyn, an adviser to Ukraine’s Minister of Internal Affairs on veterans’ policy and a Hero of Ukraine.
The discussion focused, in particular, on the role of the media in documenting the war and preserving the voices of those directly leading Ukraine’s Defense Forces toward victory.
As reported, Ukrinform previously presented Commanders of Victory to cadets at the Kyiv Institute of the National Guard of Ukraine.

Russian Attack on Ukrainian City Kills 20, a Day After Trump Eases Diesel Sanctions on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:26:05 UTC
02:26:05 KST

Twenty people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after United States President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv.
"Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House.
Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.
A 6-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.
"Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," he said through tears.
Eighteen others were wounded in the attack on the industrial city, with a pre-war population of over 700,000 and whose outskirts lie less than 30 km (20 miles) from the front line.
Russia Escalating Attacks on Ukrainian Cities
It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.
Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, 80 miles east of Kyiv.
A senior official in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, said Russia had hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday.
Rescuers clambered through crumbled masonry to pull other residents of the building out alive. One man, whose leg was trapped in the rubble, screamed in pain as he was being freed.
"If (the Russians) have money, they’ll be able to carry on fighting us," said Nataliia Malysheva, a 49-year-old local resident whose parents died in hospital after being pulled from the rubble.
"How many lives have been lost here, how many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?"
Moscow Needs "Different Signals"
"Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed," Zelensky said.
A missile attack on Saturday afternoon also hit a restaurant, wounding seven people in Kyiv.
Russian drones flew over Kyiv throughout the day, part of a vast new wave of bombardment of the capital, the heaviest since the early days of the war.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday its drones had struck a data-processing centre in Kyiv and a cargo ship carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
Trump Lifts Diesel Sanctions
Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the U.S. conflict with Iran.
Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.
Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine's power grid.
On Saturday, parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro trains to a complete halt for the second time this week.
The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were underway, a move Zelensky said had caught Kyiv by surprise.
The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source.
Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said on Saturday.
Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

Finland to send F-16 ammunition to Ukraine within days
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:21:26 EEST
02:21:26 KST

Finland will supply ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets within the coming days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday, 10 October, following a telephone conversation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The delivery forms part of Finland's 35th military assistance package to Ukraine, valued at approximately €1 million, as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks across the country.
Zelenskyy disclosed the planned shipment in a Facebook post following his discussion with Stubb. He said the ammunition would help Ukrainian forces intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which Moscow has deployed in attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president did not specify the type or quantity of ammunition Finland would provide.
Stubb also confirmed the conversation in a post on X, stating that air defence was a central component of Finland's latest military assistance package.
The Finnish Ministry of Defence announced the package on Friday, 9 October, after the government accelerated its response to an urgent request from Kyiv.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Helsinki had brought forward its decision because of Ukraine's immediate defence requirements.
"We will not close our eyes to Ukrainians’ hour of need. Instead, we will stand with Ukraine and continue our materiel assistance deliveries," Häkkänen said in the ministry's statement.
The Finnish president formally approved the shipment on 9 October following a government proposal.
According to the Defence Ministry, the package consists of a single category of military equipment drawn from Finnish Defence Forces stocks.
The announcement brings the total value of Finland's military equipment assistance to Ukraine to approximately €3.6 billion since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Helsinki has also begun preparing another, more extensive assistance package, although officials have not announced its value or expected delivery date.
Ukraine has relied on Western-supplied F-16 aircraft to strengthen its air defences and counter Russian aerial attacks.
Denmark and the Netherlands supplied approximately 40 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine during 2024 and 2025. Ukrainian authorities have not disclosed how many remain operational.
During Saturday's conversation, Zelenskyy and Stubb also discussed the recent agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin concerning Russian diesel supplies to American and international markets.
Russian strikes across south-eastern Ukraine early on Saturday killed 15 people, including three children. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of responding to the US decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports by launching five glide bombs at residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy described the agreement as a new challenge and said Ukraine and Finland were coordinating further diplomatic discussions and responses.
Earlier in the week, Russian attacks reportedly killed nearly 80 civilians across Ukraine over two days.

US military has lost 81 aircraft in Iran war according to Congressional report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:21:01 UTC
02:21:01 KST

Eighty-one aircraft in the US military have been destroyed or damaged during the war with Iran, a congressional Research Service report released this week said.
Among the aircraft lost are some of the most advanced weapons in the US arsenal, including the F-35A fighter jet and the E-3 Sentry, which has four jet engines and a radar dome on its fuselage used to track targets and manage airspace during engagements.
MQ-9 Reaper drones accounted for more than half of the losses found in the report. Reaper drones are used in the Iran war for gathering intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
The total cost of the aircraft lost since February is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, according to the report, which cited figures from the congressional Budget Office.
US Central Command estimated that the ongoing war with Iran has cost the US roughly $44 billion total in September. However, that number does not include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the Middle East, according to reporting from the Washington Post.
CNN reported that some of the aircraft may have returned to service after being damaged, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets after they were damaged during an Iranian strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on the night of September 8.
The report examined statements and figures from the Department of Defense; its inspector general; CENTCOM; and external media reports reviewed by the CRS.
Senators accuse Pentagon of withholding information
Bipartisan criticism of the Pentagon has mounted over defense officials' unwillingness to be transparent with Congress about the cost of the Iran war and the Trump administration’s National Defense Strategy.
Following a meeting with Defense Undersecretary Elbridge Colby and the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senator Jacky Rose of Nevada said Colby “was not forthcoming” and “did not really address our concerns or issues.”
In a separate instance this week, US Senator Chris Murphy said on Tuesday that the US Defense Department denied him access to a key military base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East. He described it as part of a US government effort to conceal the impact of the Iran war.
"This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip.
Analysts cited by CNN said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and conflicts with Iran’s proxies, have taken a toll on the MQ-9 Reaper drones. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress that the MQ-9 was the “most valuable player” in the war with Iran
The US military is believed to have roughly 135 MQ-9 drones in its arsenal, the Air Force Times reported in May, 2026.
The military lost 45 of the drones in the Middle East this year alone, in what the Atlantic Council describes as losses at an “alarming rate.”
The US military has not experienced loss of aircraft at such a rate since Operation Desert Storm in 1991.
