Thousands march in London to mark three years of Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:03:26 UTC
02:03:26 KST

Breadcrumb
Thousands march in London to mark three years of Gaza genocide
Tens of thousands of pro-Palestine protesters marched through central London towards Westminster on Saturday to mark three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, demanding that Britain end arms sales to Israel and formally acknowledge the genocide.
Organisers said more than 250,000 people participated in the demonstration, which brought together Palestinian activists, Jewish groups, MPs and campaigners calling for stronger action from Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government.
Israel’s assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since October 2023, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Israeli attacks have continued despite the ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, with the ministry reporting more than 1,460 people killed since the agreement.
The march was organised by the Palestine Coalition, which includes the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC), Stop the War Coalition, Friends of Al Aqsa, Palestinian Forum in Britain, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament and the Muslim Association of Britain.
Gathering on the Embankment beside the Thames, protesters chanted "Free Free, Palestine", "Israel is a terrorist state" and "From the River to the Sea", before making their way towards a rally in Whitehall.
Marchers carried banners mourning Palestinian children killed in Gaza, demanding an arms embargo, and denouncing Israel’s genocide. Others held portraits of Hind Rajab, the five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli fire in January 2024 after pleading with rescue workers to save her from a car in Gaza City.
Placards also demanded the release of Palestinian prisoners, including Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital who was detained during an Israeli raid on the hospital in 2024, and Palestinian political leader Marwan Barghouti.
Hala Hanina, a Palestinian journalist who left Gaza days before the genocide began, leaving her husband behind, told The New Arab she had hoped to be in London celebrating the end of the genocide, Zionism and occupation.
Instead, she said, "unfortunately we’re still, for three years, marching for the same things".
Addressing the rally, Hanina said that although Israel might try to erase Palestinian bodies, it would "never erase out culture and our memory".
Jewish protesters reject antisemitism claims
Among those marching were boycott campaigners wearing avocado costumes in reference to Israeli agricultural exports, alongside Holocaust survivors, their families, and other Jewish demonstrators.
One group marched under a banner reading "Holocaust survivor descendants against Gaza genocide".
"We hoped after the end of the Holocaust that it would never be visited on any other country ever again because the lessons would be learned," Stephen Kapos, a child survivor of the Holocaust in Budapest, told The New Arab. "And now we discover with horror that another holocaust, a genocide, has been perpetrated on the Palestinian people".
Holding a sign reading "This Holocaust Survivor says stop the genocide in Gaza", Kapos said his presence challenged attempts to portray the pro-Palestine movement as inherently antisemitic.
He said he continued to advocate for Palestinians "to show that Jews are not a single homogeneous block all in favour of Israel. Quite the contrary – we are quite divided, and many are against what is going on, and our group is one of them".
"We’re here to prove that these marches are not antisemitic and not hate marches," Kapos said.
A few metres away, a small counter-protest of around two dozen people stood behind a police barrier, holding Israeli, American and English flags. Participants shouted that the march was antisemitic and said they felt victimised as Jews.
The Metropolitan Police said by mid-afternoon that several arrests had been made, including of two people carrying placards supporting the proscribed group Palestine Action. Others were arrested on suspicion of criminal damage after climbing onto the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.
Demands for action from Burnham government
Speakers at the Whitehall rally directed sharp criticism at Burnham’s government, demanding a comprehensive arms embargo, the expulsion of the Israeli ambassador and formal recognition that Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute genocide.
Burnham took office on 20 July, replacing Keir Starmer. His government has adopted tougher language towards Israel and imposed sanctions relating to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, but the prime minister has declined to recognise the genocide, saying Britain would take its lead from international courts.
Zarah Sultana, MP for Coventry South, said the government could not separate its human rights commitments from its decisions on arms exports.
"We need to be clear: this is not some distant tragedy beyond our control, the British government has choices to make, and Andy Burnham must be held to account because you cannot claim to stand for human rights while continuing to sell arms to a genocidal state".
She called for an end to arms sales, Israel’s occupation and apartheid.
John McDonnell, MP for Hayes and Harlington, called for measures that went beyond sanctions against individual Israeli officials. "We want to see Israel economically and politically isolated", he said, demanding that the Israeli ambassador be expelled from Britain.
Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn began his speech by describing Israel as "a rogue state of the first order".
Corbyn welcomed Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s recent acknowledgement of the protest movement, but said the government’s stated commitment to international law must translate into an end to arms sales to Israel.
Speaking at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool on 28 September, Miliband had addressed the millions outraged by Palestinians’ suffering, telling them: "We hear you. You were right". He said the government had reset its approach under Burnham, citing its condemnation of Israel’s occupation, evidence of war crimes in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.
Campaigners at Saturday’s march said that shift in language remained insufficient.
Dr Ismail Patel of Friends of Al Aqsa told The New Arab: "We see the change in language in Andy Burnham’s government, but at the moment this is just for politics. They’re trying to placate the movement by words rather than action."
Patel also questioned Miliband’s speech, saying "it was very telling" that while he was delivering it, "police were arresting pensioners for simply holding a placard", in reference to people arrested for allegedly expressing support Palestine Action.

Mohammad Sio

Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh temporarily suspended operations on Saturday after an attack left several people injured, the country's civil aviation authority said.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement that the airport was attacked Saturday afternoon, adding that authorities were still determining the number of people injured.
The authority said airport operations were temporarily suspended while officials assessed the damage and verified the safety of facilities in coordination with relevant agencies.
GACA said further updates would be announced later.
The statement did not specify the party responsible for the attack or the nature of the weapons used in it.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry called on citizens whose journeys were affected by suspended or delayed flights to King Khalid International Airport to contact Saudi diplomatic missions in the countries where they are currently located.
The ministry said the missions will provide assistance and necessary guidance to affected travelers.
A Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) issued for King Khalid International Airport said the airport will be unavailable from 1627 GMT to 2100 GMT Saturday due to “precautionary measures,” according to NOTAM Viewer website.
The US and UK embassies in Saudi Arabia also urged their citizens on Saturday to avoid King Khalid International Airport following attacks, warning of security risks and possible travel disruptions.
Earlier Saturday, King Khalid International Airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic.
The airport did not specify the cause of the disruptions in its initial advisory.
Kuwait Airways also announced Saturday that it had canceled flight KU775 from Kuwait to Riyadh and return flight KU776, citing the airport's closure due to the “security situation."
The airline urged passengers to monitor flight updates through its official channels, saying notifications would be sent to contact details registered with bookings.
Recent attacks on Saudi airports
The suspension came amid heightened aviation concerns following a series of Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports and other facilities.
Saudi authorities said Friday that three citizens were killed and others injured in two attacks Thursday targeting facilities at King Khalid International Airport and a Saudi Arabian Airlines aircraft.
Airport operations later resumed, and air traffic returned to normal, according to GACA.
The Houthis have claimed responsibility for several missile and drone attacks on King Khalid International Airport and other Saudi airports in recent days.
Yemen has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.
"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.
Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.
At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."
Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Coalition vows to respond
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively."
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack."
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable."
He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, confirming that an American citizen was killed in the strikes.
"These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately."
What do we know about the Riyadh attack?
A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.
The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."
Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."
What did the Houthis say?
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.
However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.
In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."
When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."
Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week
Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.
Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.
Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.
The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.
The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

From Athens to Anger

From Athens to Anger
Why Rubio's history lesson backfired in Iran
TEHRAN – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's October 7 speech at the Pnyx hill in Athens, in which he invoked ancient Greece to call for Western revival and labeled the Islamic Republic of Iran a "cult of death," has triggered a wave of angry reactions across Iran — from senior officials and former diplomats to academics, newspapers, and social media users.
While Rubio framed his address as a defense of Western civilization stretching from ancient Athens to the United States, Iranian respondents have described it almost unanimously as a selective, politicized reading of history aimed at providing an ideological cover for the ongoing US-Iran war.
 
Officials: Contradiction and distortion
The most detailed official response came from Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, who wrote on X that Rubio had reduced Western history "from ancient Greece to Trump's America" into a straight, unbroken line.
"This is precisely an instance of anachronism: distorting historical time by clumsily mixing concepts such as Greece, Rome, Christianity, Europe, America and finally America First," Baghaei wrote. "It is as if America has concluded that instead of naked bullying in cowboy language, it is better to justify its policy of intimidation and force under the beautiful neon lights of philosophy of history."
Baghaei added that Rubio had detached the Greek concept of thumos from its historical and philosophical context and redefined it as praise of power, competition and national will: "What he offers is not philosophy of history; but a manipulated and distorted version of history designed to justify the combative and warmongering policies of the US administration."
"The danger of this deviant narrative of history lies not merely in misreading past events, but in appropriating the past to legitimize naked force and sanctify it in the present," he said.
Ali Akbar Velayati, senior adviser to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, focused on the "cult of death" remark:
"There is a glaring contradiction in Rubio's recent speech: Standing firm 'to the last man' is praised in the context of ancient Greece, yet the steadfastness of the great Iranian nation is disparaged with the label of a 'death cult'."
"Mr. Rubio, your problem is not with the Islamic Revolution; it is with a strong and independent Iranian civilisation," Velayati added. "Glorifying resistance in the 'self' and despising it in the 'other' is not civilisation, but philosophy in service of domination."
Ebrahim Azizi, head of the Parliament's National Security Commission, wrote on X: "A country whose history began with the massacre of indigenous peoples and has never ceased from colonialism and bloodshed accuses the Achaemenids – who wrote the world's first declaration of human rights – of crimes! Your vile nature has a problem with Iran and Iranians."
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf both responded by recalling the capture of the Roman Emperor Valerian by Sassanid King Shapur I in 260 CE, warning: "Anyone who brings history into this must be prepared for its repetition."
Minister of Cultural Heritage Reza Salehi Amiri said: "Iran cannot be defined by one war, one king or one government. Iran's civilizational roots are deeper and more enduring than the lifespan of many of today's powers. Iran must be spoken to in the language of respect."
Former foreign ministers: Recycling Huntington
Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif reacted twice. In one post, sharing a photo of the IRDEXPO exhibition of rural and nomadic capabilities, he wrote that it offers "a glimpse of Iranian civilization; a country with a rich cultural and artistic heritage spanning several thousand years," and added that "Rubio is so ignorant and blinded by power that he cannot understand how Iran absorbed invaders into its rich culture."
In remarks on Rubio's objectives, Zarif said: "This is an attempt at narrative-building that presents the Western world's enmity with Iran as a civilizational enmity. In fact, they are recycling what Mr. Huntington put forward in the 1990s, but at a very vulgar and unscientific level. As I said, not only Mr. Rubio, even his speechwriter did not understand what he said."
Former Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Salehi said briefly: "Mr. Rubio! What do you think about Trump's threats? The land of Cyrus has no enmity with civilization."
Vali Nasr, professor at Johns Hopkins University, wrote on X that Rubio is presenting a second version of Huntington's "Clash of Civilizations" theory. "Instead of a confrontation between Islam and the West, he draws a civilizational confrontation between Iran and the West. In this way, the era of Islamophobia gives way to 'Iranophobia'."
Diplomatic mockery and social media anger
The Iranian Embassy in Bosnia joined the backlash on X, posting a photo of an ancient Iranian ewer and writing: "The Iranian ewer is 10 times older than your country."
On social media, reactions have been extensive, with Iranian users mocking and criticizing Rubio in different forms.
One user wrote about the speech: "Rubio recalls ancient Iranians as the enemy of the cradle of Western civilization, ancient Greece, and calls Xerxes, the Achaemenid king, an invader and aggressor. But the backward, regressive Iranian still thinks that by saying 'I am Persian, not Muslim' he can whitewash himself and pose as Western."
Another user wrote: "Rubio in Athens began his speech with Xerxes' and the Achaemenids' attack on Greece. 25 centuries have passed, but the US Secretary of State still uses Iran's war with ancient Greece to explain 'today's threats against the West'."
Front pages in Tehran
The controversy dominated Iran's Saturday press. Three national dailies — Jam-e Jam, Farhikhtegan and Vatan-e Emrooz — devoted their front pages to the speech, publishing reports and commentaries criticizing Rubio's remarks.
Vatan-e Emrooz ran a symbolic front page depicting Rubio in ancient Roman military dress with shield and sword, arguing he is trying to build a historical-ideological justification for America's war against Iran.

More than 50 Iranian army units deployed along borders, commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:49:12 UTC

More than 50 Iranian army units deployed along borders, commander says
TEHRAN — Iran has deployed more than 50 combat and support units of its Army Ground Force along the country’s borders, including mobile, rapid-reaction, armored and mechanized brigades, as well as artillery, engineering, missile and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) units, the force’s commander has said.
Brigadier General Ali Jahanshahi, commander of the Islamic Republic of Iran Army Ground Force, said the force had revised its operational plans, restructured elements of its combat organization and strengthened its readiness in response to lessons learned from previous conflicts, including the 12-day war and the conflict Iranian officials refer to as the Ramadan War.
In remarks reported by Mehr News Agency, Jahanshahi said the post-war reforms had prioritized the introduction of precision-strike, smart and network-enabled weapons systems, alongside expanded training programs to enhance personnel proficiency and operational effectiveness.
 
He added that measures to reduce personnel casualties, protect military assets and sustain operational readiness included the construction of extensive tunnel networks, trenches, firing positions and defensive fortifications at military installations.
Large-scale force deployment across Iran
Jahanshahi said that, following the outbreak of the Ramadan War, more than 50 combat and support units had been deployed to border areas across the country.
The deployments extended from Iran’s northwestern and western frontiers to the southwest, east and southeast, as well as the Makran coastline. According to the commander, the redeployment effort involved more than nine million kilometers of road movements, alongside the transport of substantial quantities of ammunition and military equipment by heavy vehicles.
He said the movements were conducted under the surveillance and potential threat of hostile drones and aircraft, with forces repositioned at night to reduce their exposure. Jahanshahi said the deployment had strengthened Iran’s deterrence posture and helped prevent enemy forces from crossing the country’s borders.
He added that Ground Force units remained deployed along the frontiers and maintained operational readiness despite temperatures exceeding 50 degrees Celsius, high humidity and limited logistical facilities.
ounter-infiltration measures and continued weapons production
Jahanshahi said military planners had identified locations that could potentially be used by hostile forces to enter Iranian territory, including disused airfields. Countermeasures had been planned for potential incursions, while intelligence operations had been conducted to improve situational awareness.
He also said domestic military production had continued throughout the conflict and remained ongoing.
According to Jahanshahi, the Army Ground Force, operating alongside other branches of Iran’s armed forces, launched thousands of Arash drones against US military bases in regional countries and targets associated with Israel during the war.
Passive defense measures limit personnel losses
The commander said several Ground Force installations had been struck during the conflict, with military buildings and personnel accommodation among the targets. At one base, he said, 10 barracks buildings were hit. Attacks also caused extensive damage to military infrastructure, destroying hundreds of thousands of square meters of buildings, according to his account.
Jahanshahi attributed the comparatively limited loss of life to the dispersal of personnel and the implementation of passive defense measures. Without those precautions, he said, the number of fatalities could have reached thousands.
Despite the damage, he added, personnel had maintained their positions and continued their missions.
Jahanshahi concluded that the Ground Force’s operational readiness and capabilities had improved significantly compared with the period before the conflict, with equipment production continuing and units maintaining their preparedness for potential threats.

French expert: Europe must prepare for ‘armed peace’ and strengthen Ukraine’s defense
Arnaud Valli, a representative of Comand AI, a company specializing in artificial intelligence software for military planning and operational management, said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the Ukraine–France Forum in Paris.
“Europe today is Ukraine’s strategic rear. We talk a lot about drone production, but a great deal of equipment is also serviced outside Ukraine,” Valli said. At the same time, he noted that power outages in Kyiv and other cities affect the capabilities of Ukrainian manufacturers, despite their exceptional flexibility and ability to rapidly adapt production.
Valli stressed that European companies should build cooperation based on the expertise of Ukrainian specialists.
“All the companies working in Ukraine today, including ours, understand that Ukrainians are the best at what they do. We can add our share to this – our engineers work in a country where there is no war, where electricity supplies are stable, and where there is time to think through solutions and engage in industrial cooperation,” he explained.
In the expert’s view, such synergy should continue after active hostilities end. European manufacturers fear that some Ukrainian defense companies could lose orders, while Ukraine could lose engineers, software developers and drone manufacturers whose expertise is in demand around the world.
“This is a shared concern, and the answer is cooperation. Today, the real question is not even what the French can give Ukraine, but what Ukraine can give us,” Valli stressed.
He expects Russia to continue expanding its military production. Therefore, future peace in Europe must be based on deterrence.
“The only way to ensure lasting peace with such a regime is an ‘armed peace’ – deterrence through sufficient weapons stockpiles. We have seen how important it is to have armies that are ready to act and capable of withstanding prolonged confrontation,” the expert added.
As reported by Ukrinform, participants in the fifth annual Ukraine–France Forum in Paris discussed diplomatic pathways to ending Russia’s war, Ukraine’s accession to the EU, relations with NATO and the conditions for lasting peace and postwar reconstruction.

MP warns any attack on Iran would trigger a much stronger response
TEHRAN — Abbas Goudarzi, a member of the Iranian Parliament’s Presiding Board, has described US President Donald Trump’s threats against Iran as part of Washington’s psychological warfare, warning that any attack on the country would be met with a response many times more forceful.
Speaking to Mehr News Agency, Goudarzi said the United States uses threats and public manipulation to undermine Iranian society’s resilience and influence the calculations of the country’s officials.
He said such pressure was not new, noting that Iran had faced threats and sanctions since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Nevertheless, he argued, the country had continued to withstand external pressure by relying on domestic capabilities, national self-confidence and public support.
Goudarzi described the confrontation between Iran and the United States as an existential struggle, arguing that despite the considerable costs Iran had incurred, Washington had failed to achieve its objectives. He said resistance to external pressure was not merely a political choice for Iran but a strategic necessity for safeguarding its independence, security and future development.
The lawmaker identified defensive deterrence as one of the principal factors in preventing aggression against Iran. He said any potential adversary must understand that an attack would carry serious consequences and could no longer be launched without the prospect of a forceful response.
Iran, Goudarzi added, should not only preserve its existing deterrent capabilities but also continue strengthening them. He argued that a combination of military advances and the capacity to respond decisively would discourage any attempt to threaten the country’s territory, resources or national interests.
He also linked defense capabilities to broader national development, saying security was essential to economic growth, scientific advancement and stronger domestic production. Without adequate security, he warned that other areas of national life would also face serious risks.
Addressing the differing and sometimes contradictory statements made by US officials about Iran, Goudarzi said the discrepancies could reflect divisions within the United States over how to pursue its Iran policy. They could also, he added, be part of an effort to complicate the calculations of Iranian decision-makers.
He argued that the failure of Washington’s anti-Iran policies to achieve their intended goals may have contributed to competing views within the United States about how best to deal with Tehran.
Goudarzi said Iran should remain alert to such developments without abandoning its principles or allowing uncertainty to undermine its resolve.
He concluded by stressing the importance of national unity and social cohesion, urging officials and the public to avoid division and remain focused on the country’s strategic priorities.

Reports state that Teva UK was set to exhibit and four college events as part of a £15,000 agreement.
Other organisations have also cut ties with Teva, including the Royal College of Nursing, noting that they would also be severing their sponsorship of its union and an event on headaches and migraines.
The British Nurses Union earlier this month said it would stop working with Teva as a supplier, due its links with the Israeli army and record of corporate misconduct.

The firm has been targeted with legal action multiple times, including a $225 million fine in 2023 for fixing the prices of three drugs, and $519 million in 2016 for bribing government officials in Mexico, Russia, and Ukraine.

Buoyed by the 14% won by his list in the 2024 European elections, Raphaël Glucksmann is facing several challengers in this primary, including Ségolène Royal, a prominent Socialist figure and former presidential candidate in 2007, Olivier Faure, the current Socialist Party (PS) leader, and MPs Jérôme Guedj and Emmanuel Maurel.
Before the cyberattack disrupted the ballot, the campaign had already been rocked by several controversies. Socialist MP Philippe Brun was excluded from the primary on September 16, following accusations of "violence" against a former staffer.
The debates have also been marked by heated exchanges, with Ségolène Royal going so far as to label Raphaël Glucksmann a "political intern".
The €15 fee charged to non-members of the PS and Place publique, reduced to €10 for those on lower incomes, has also drawn criticism. Critics argue the fee could favour Glucksmann's supporters, who are perceived as more affluent.
The result was initially expected on Saturday evening, but voting has been extended until Sunday at 6 p.m.

A Muslim prayer room at the Fugui Fishing Port Fishermen’s Rest Center in New Taipei City’s Shihmen District (石門) opened on Friday, as parts of the Fisheries Agency’s efforts in improving foreign fishing workers’ welfare.

Photo: Yu Chao-fu, Taipei Times

Caring for foreign fishery workers in Taiwan is a critical part of the nation’s Action Plan for Fisheries and Human Rights, it said.
A total of 45 restroom facilities and 18 lounges — including prayer rooms — have been set up at fishing ports nationwide for foreign fishery workers, the agency said.
The agency would continue to work with local governments and fishermen’s associations to provide proper spaces for foreign fishers’ religious and leisure activities onshore, it said.
The goal is to uphold fishery sustainability and human rights protection, building a friendly fishery environment that makes every foreign fisher in Taiwan feel respected.
Meanwhile, the Fisheries Agency has launched a basic safety training program for fishing vessel personnel.
The training program is aimed to enhance fishers’ safety awareness in their operations at sea, it said.
The training would focus on disaster prevention, emergency response and sea survival skills, the agency said.
Interested fishers can sign up for the program via the online registration system from Nov. 1 to Nov. 30, it said.
A random computer draw would be done on Dec. 1 to select the trainees, the agency said, adding that it would then notify trainees of relevant arrangements, such as accommodation and course rules.

====================================================================================================

Culture and industry clash in Alaska’s seas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

The net rose from the heaving Bering Sea swells, packed so tightly with Alaska pollock that their heads squeezed through the webbing.
As the catch spilled onto the deck, other marine life came with it: a skate, crabs, jellyfish and, among the most consequential, salmon — the fish at the center of a growing fight over industrial trawling in Alaska.
“This is a wild capture fishery, so you do run into your nontarget species, and a lot of people have a problem with that,” said Maverick Blake, the boat’s captain. “But this is what it takes to put seafood on the table.”
Photo: Bloomberg
Blake redirected the boat toward another fishing ground where he hoped to encounter fewer salmon.
Alaska pollock is the second-largest fishery on Earth. It is the fish inside McDonald’s Filet-O-Fish sandwiches and can be turned into fish sticks and imitation crab. The fishery uses methods that it — and McDonald’s — say are aimed at minimizing environmental impacts, but the nets that catch pollock catch other marine life, too.
Bycatch — marine life caught unintentionally while fishers target something else — makes up 2 percent of the pollock fishery’s total catch. At the scale of a fishery that harvests billions of pounds of pollock annually, that can mean hundreds of thousands of salmon. Over the last 10 years, Bering Sea pollock trawlers caught an average of about 18,000 Chinook and 288,000 other salmon a year, almost all of them chum.
Those catches have become especially contentious as salmon runs collapse across western Alaska, where dozens of Alaska Native communities have relied on salmon for generations. The backlash has spread to smaller commercial and charter fishers who say they, too, are bearing the costs of declining stocks. And trawling and bycatch have become prominent issues in Alaska’s midterm elections, with candidates for governor and in the state’s closely watched US Senate contest sparring over how aggressively to restrict the industry.
In 2024, Alaska and Canada instated a seven-year ban on Chinook fishing along the Yukon River — one full salmon life cycle — to give depleted populations a chance to rebuild. The Kuskokwim River has faced repeated Chinook and chum closures too, while other Yukon salmon fisheries have been restricted.
Scientists point to warming waters and changing ocean conditions, not trawl bycatch, as the primary causes of the declines. Warmer oceans can increase the risk of salmon bycatch by changing where salmon and pollock overlap, according to a study last year.
Critics say bycatch is one of the few sources of fish mortality managers can directly control, and even small losses matter when runs are depleted.
“Each fish is critical to communities along the Yukon River,” said Andrew Seitz, professor of fisheries at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. “The people who feel that they bear the brunt of the conservation measures are people along the river.”
AVOIDING SALMON
During the four days reporters spend aboard F/V Progress, the vessel caught 210 chum salmon. Blake, who has 13 years in the pollock industry, said avoiding salmon is a central part of his job. He said the search for waters with fewer salmon burned almost 3,000 gallons (11,360 liters) of fuel. Had he stayed put, he said, the boat could have filled its holds in half a day with far less.
“The subsistence users see this huge machine industry out here harvesting in the ocean and I can understand their frustration,” he said. “I would be upset if somebody told me that I wasn’t allowed to fish like my ancestors had done for thousands of years before.”
Blake and industry representatives call it one of the best managed fisheries in the world. Captains stay in contact with other vessels throughout each trip to share information about salmon concentrations, while the fleet follows weekly closure areas based on reports from the fishing grounds. Pollock vessels carry salmon excluders, devices which help salmon find a way out of the net.
Every salmon caught by the Bering Sea pollock fleet is counted. Trawlers are monitored by observers or cameras, as are deliveries at shoreside processing plants.
“The amount of science and management effort that goes into improving it is basically unprecedented anywhere,” said Matt Tinning, CEO of the At-Sea Processors Association, which represents five Alaska pollock companies. “The system is designed to really incentivize salmon avoidance every day, all the time.”
FLIP SIDE
At 9am on a July morning in Rampart, an Alaska Native village, about a dozen boats sat moored along the Yukon River. In years past, families would have been pulling nets and carrying salmon to their smokehouses.
The Yukon flows 2,010km across Alaska before emptying into the Bering Sea. Salmon born in its tributaries migrate to the ocean, spend years feeding at sea, then return to spawn, linking villages such as Rampart to the same waters where the pollock fleet fishes.
“We have this big void in our lives right now,” said Brooke Woods, a Koyukon Alaska Native, mother of six and commissioner for the Yukon River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission. “We’ve never had a generation that hasn’t had the opportunity to learn and be taught by elders and parents, and that has such a big impact on our youth.”
Woods’ family once spent long summer days checking nets, cutting fish and tending the smokehouse. This summer, her three-year-old son, Lewis, watched TV and played in the creek behind the house. He has never set a salmon net with his parents.
Restrictions on their own harvest are difficult to accept when pollock trawlers are fishing offshore.
“You really get angry. Why are we the only ones that have to take the burden?” said Brooke’s mother, Janet Woods.
Rampart has no grocery store, and reaching Fairbanks takes about five hours by boat and road. Families stock up when they travel and have long relied on fishing and hunting to fill their freezers.
Managers briefly opened chum fishing around Rampart this summer, but only with selective gear such as dip nets and beach seines. The Woods family did not have that equipment.
“You think back in history how they tried to destroy us,” Janet said. “Taking our language, our ceremonies, and now our culture, and it’s been forever a fight for us just to hang on to what very little we have.”
SOURCING FISH
Fish from across the North Pacific mix in the Bering Sea, so a salmon caught in a trawl net could have come from western Alaska, the Pacific Northwest or as far away as Russia or Japan.
NOAA has long used genetic testing to trace salmon bycatch. Since 2024, the Bristol Bay Science and Research Institute has produced weekly chum bycatch estimates from summer to fall to give the fleet faster information about where western Alaska salmon are showing up.
The results support one of the industry’s main arguments: Most chum caught by pollock trawlers are not from western Alaska. In the past few years, western Alaska fish made up an average of about 17 percent of chum and half of Chinook bycatch.
Even a small share means tens of thousands of salmon. In 2021, for example, 9 percent of chum bycatch came from western Alaska, or more than 51,000 salmon, according to NOAA.
In February, after hearing testimony from more than 170 people, the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, which sets many of the rules for the Bering Sea fleet, recommended a cap of 45,000 western Alaska chum bycatch. Critics said the limit was too high.
Pollock is big business in Alaska. More than 3 billion pounds (1.36 million tonnes) were landed from the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska in 2024, worth about US$432 million, according to NOAA. While the fishery supports thousands of Alaska jobs, critics said most of the economic benefit flows outside the state, with many of the largest vessels owned by Seattle-area companies.
“We’re trying to play this balancing game” between helping conserve western Alaska salmon for subsistence communities and maintaining “a very valuable economic fishery,” said Abby Duffy, who manages the Bristol Bay institute’s genetics lab in Dutch Harbor.
WIDESPREAD ISSUES
Small commercial halibut and crab fishers as well as charter operators have echoed the grievances heard along the Yukon. They too have faced shrinking catch limits and closures as stocks decline, while groundfish trawlers continue to catch both species as bycatch.
Last year alone, Alaska trawl fisheries discarded about 96 million pounds (43,500 tonnes) of bycatch, according to the North Pacific Fishery Management Council. That is about 100 fully loaded Boeing 747-8s.
“It’s extremely frustrating,” said Linda Behnken, a commercial fisher and executive director of the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association.
The larger concern is what trawling does to the seafloor, she said.
“The habitat damage is really insidious and long lasting,” she said.
Pollock vessels use pelagic, or midwater, trawls that are designed to fish in the water column rather than along the seafloor the way bottom trawls do. But pollock often swim close to the seafloor, so the nets make substantial bottom contact. That contact was evident during the trip aboard the F/V Progress, when Tanner crabs and basket stars — animals that live on the seafloor — came up with the net.
Meanwhile, some of the same areas that are closed to bottom trawling for the protection of coral, sponges, crab and other marine life are open to pelagic trawlers.
“So they’re dragging in the same areas, defeating the whole purpose of these habitat conservation areas,” said Ben Enticknap, fisheries campaign director at Oceana.
GROWING ANGER
Anti-trawl sentiment has attracted Democrats, Republicans, commercial and sport fishers, and Alaska Native communities — constituencies that do not often line up on the same side of resource debates.
At least half the original candidates in Alaska’s crowded governor’s race took positions critical of trawling or bycatch as contenders across the political spectrum called for tighter restrictions. The governor has significant influence over federal fisheries policy with the power to nominate five of the North Pacific council’s seven appointed voting seats. Several gubernatorial candidates campaigned specifically on using those appointments to shift the council away from trawl interests.
In the US Senate race, Democrat Mary Peltola has called for an end to large factory trawlers, while Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has introduced legislation aimed at reducing bycatch and keeping trawl gear off the seafloor.
Back in the Bering Sea, Blake kept fishing for pollock. Along the Yukon, the Woods family’s boat remained tied to the bank.
Blake hopes his son can one day fish beside him on the trawler. Brooke Woods hopes her son can one day set a salmon net with her.
“It’s frightening for me to not know if I’ll be able to pass on the same knowledge that my mother, grandmother and parents had,” Woods said. “I’ve heard elders say that if we lose our salmon, that assimilation has worked.”
Bankers in Hong Kong skipped the summer break as an artificial intelligence (AI)-fueled rush for capital sent share sales to a record, defying a bruising selloff in the city’s stocks. Initial public offerings (IPOs), placements and block trades raised US$47.5 billion in July to last month, the biggest haul ever for the period, data compiled by Bloomberg showed. That pushed fundraising this year above US$92 billion and within reach of the US$112.5 billion record set in 2021. Han warns Taiwan must not be a fake democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:42:09 UTC
01:42:09 KST

Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) yesterday warned that Taiwan’s democracy must not be seen as a “fake democracy.”
Taiwan’s democracy is showing signs of strain, Han said, speaking at the Double Ten National Day ceremony as chairman of the National Day Preparatory Committee.
He cited last year’s recall campaigns against opposition lawmakers, which he described as “political persecution,” and the executive branch’s refusal to countersign bills passed by the legislature.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
He warned that the standoff between the Executive Yuan and the Legislative Yuan could damage Taiwan’s international reputation as a democracy, saying: “Taiwan must not be seen by the world as a ‘fake democracy, real dictatorship.’”
Over the past year, he had accompanied lawmakers from different political parties on visits to countries around the world, where legislators had shown a keen interest in Taiwan and held highly favorable views of the nation, he said.
Such parliamentary diplomacy had enabled other people to hear the voice of the Republic of China (ROC), Han said, adding that through these exchanges, he had become convinced that Taiwanese could hold different political views, advocate different positions and engage in debate at home because this is democracy.
He made three wishes as the nation celebrated its 115th birthday: a secure Taiwan, prosperity for its people and a thriving democracy.
When it comes to national identity and ideology, Taiwanese should set aside their differences, consolidate strength and jointly defend the ROC, he said.
As party leaders, decisionmakers and supervisors of government affairs, officials must recognize that without security, everything else is lost, Han said.
“There will be no intact eggs in an overturned bird’s nest,” he said.
Taiwan’s security must always come first, Han said, outlining four goals.
First, Taiwan must do everything possible to defend and protect the ROC, he said.
Second, Taiwan must protect democracy and freedom, Han said.
Third, Taiwan must maintain good relations with the US, as its support is vital to the nation, he said.
Fourth, Taiwan must preserve peace across the Taiwan Strait, he added.
Taiwan’s democracy was built through generations of effort, and protecting it is a shared responsibility of the ruling and opposition parties, and the public, he said.
President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration had failed to resolve the confrontation between the executive and legislative branches, causing serious damage to his reputation, Han said.
He said he remained confident that Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) and the opposition parties could work together, expressing hope that Taiwan’s democracy would continue to advance.
In response, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said the Executive Yuan and Legislative Yuan were institutions that exercised their powers in accordance with the Constitution and should respect each other’s authority while jointly upholding constitutional order.
Neither side should exceed its constitutional boundaries or stigmatize constitutional mechanisms for political gain, she added.
Democratic Progressive Party caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) yesterday questioned whether Han had turned a national birthday celebration into a political denunciation rally.
People exercising their legal right to recall elected officials should not be branded as engaging in “political persecution,” and constitutional disputes between the executive and legislative branches should be resolved through institutional mechanisms and dialogue, he said.
If Han expected the ruling and opposition parties to put aside their differences, he should lead by example in his own remarks, Chuang said, adding that the legislative speaker should build bridges for communication rather than intensify political confrontation.

Indian police yesterday detained Abhijit Dipke, the political strategist who turned a “cockroach” jibe at unemployed young people into a nationwide protest movement that helped force the resignation of a federal minister.
Police met Dipke’s aircraft as it landed in the capital, New Delhi, ahead of a rally to demand the resignation of the head of elections over accusations of voter list manipulation that critics say dropped about 130 million voters from a draft roll.
“I have come to be arrested, arrest me... I am not afraid of you guys,” Dipke told police officers aboard the aircraft, in television images that showed one of them assuring him he was not being arrested, but rather that his cooperation was sought.
Photo: EPA
Dipke, 31, born in a Dalit family on the lower rungs of India’s caste system, shot to fame this year after his six-word response to Indian Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant’s remarks likening unemployed young people to “cockroaches” went viral online.
The post spawned the satirical Cockroach Janta Party, an online movement that rapidly evolved into a political force.
It mobilized mass street protests that culminated in the July resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as minister of education, a rare exit from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Cabinet, following sustained public pressure.
Photo: Reuters / Cockroach Janta Party via X / Handout
Dipke’s detention came after he called for a fresh protest yesterday seeking the resignation of election commission chief Gyanesh Kumar over the changes.
The election panel says the figure comprises entries flagged during draft revision and that voters wrongly removed can enroll again.
Bearded and usually wearing T-shirt and jeans, Dipke had led a protest in the southern tech hub of Bengaluru before traveling via Mumbai to the capital, where police detained him with two senior group leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.
Despite a police crackdown in Delhi and tight protest restrictions, Dipke urged supporters to demonstrate peacefully, citing the example of Mahatma Gandhi.
“I don’t know what will happen tomorrow, but one thing I am sure of is that I am not going to be afraid,” Dipke said in a video recorded before yesterday’s flight.
“Neither am I going to step back. We have to save our democracy,” he added.
Authorities called in thousands of security forces to fortify Delhi, with travel and telecom links suspended, in a lockdown designed to stop the protest.
“Why is the prime minister so scared of the country’s youth, the country’s people?” Dipke asked before his flight departed.
“What if all cockroaches come together?” was Dipke’s question in a May social media post that almost overnight turned the political communications professional into one of the most recognizable faces of India’s youth protest movement.
He returned to India after completing a master’s degree in public relations in the US, saying his viral success had given him “a chance to do actual, meaningful work,” despite threats he and his family received.
The Cockroach Janta Party amassed millions of followers online and helped drive protests over leaks of a medical entrance examination paper affecting about 2 million candidates.
The movement eventually focused its anger on Pradhan, who resigned on July 25.
Since then, Dipke and his supporters, who see the group as a political pressure movement rather than a party, have campaigned on issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs for young people.
It returned to the streets after a report last month in the Indian Express newspaper.
The paper said two of election chief Kumar’s deputies had repeatedly raised concerns about voter-roll revisions, registration procedures and the commission’s digital systems.

Like hundreds of thousands of Israelis, Amihai will be of voting age for the first time since Hamas carried out its attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
When he casts his ballot this month, he has one priority above all — security.
From a field overlooking the sprawling ruins of the northern Gaza Strip, the 18-year-old says he plans to vote for a far-right party at the ballot box, three years after the deadliest day in Israeli history.
Photo: AFP
“I’m voting based solely on security — not for whoever will help me buy an apartment in 10 years, but for whoever can guarantee that I’ll even still be alive here in 10 years,” he told reporters.
Amihai, from Shomria in southern Israel, was speaking less than 2km from Gaza, swathes of which have been flattened by Israeli bombardment since the war with Hamas erupted in 2023.
He was attending an event calling for Jewish settlement of the Palestinian territory and said that on Oct. 27 he would be casting a vote for the party of Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben Gvir.
“After October 7, [2023] I want death for the terrorists, I want the terrorists here to suffer in prison, I want there to be deterrence,” the teenager said, alluding to a recently passed death penalty law that applies to Palestinians.
Sporting a cap and T-shirt in support of the minister, Amihai said he also wanted “emigration from Gaza, that the people of Gaza will be dying to leave” — another policy advocated by government ministers in the past few months.
About 550,000 Israelis aged 18 to 22 will be voting for the first time this month, Israel’s Channel 12 reported.
In a recent poll commissioned by the channel, 74 percent of first-time voters described their policy views as right or center-right — an even higher share than the broadly right-leaning public at large.
The trend stands in contrast to many Western democracies where young people are among the most left-leaning voters — with some motivated by outrage over Israel’s actions in Gaza.
However, the right-wing turn of Israeli Jewish young people has been building for about two decades, pollster and analyst Dahlia Scheindlin said.
“Older people ... remember the hope of reaching full, comprehensive peace agreements with the Palestinians,” Scheindlin told reporters.
“Anybody who’s an 18-year-old now, his or her entire political consciousness is under [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu, it’s a very ultra-nationalist environment,” she said.
At a gathering of young activists for the center-left Democrats party in Tel Aviv last month, 18-year-old Gili said she felt society had turned its back on peace.
“I think especially young people, when they see something so huge happening, something that hurts so deeply and affects everyone, like what happened on October 7 [2023], then the first tendency is fear, to be afraid, and not to believe that peace is possible,” she told reporters. “It’s really logical that everyone kind of became more and more right-wing, and more and more extreme.”
Hamas’ attack in 2023 resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agency France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures.
In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive that has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the health ministry there.
Gili and her friends at the rally said they supported the Democrats’ vision of a political agreement with the Palestinians.
“Conflict management is not a solution and I don’t think the current situation can go on,” said Yuval, an 18-year-old from kibbutz Tel Yitzhak in central Israel. “Certainly not if we want to raise our children here, if we want to believe we have a real future for ourselves.”

SOUTH KOREA
Ceiling collapse hurts 38
At least 38 people sustained minor injuries after parts of a plaster ceiling collapsed at a supermarket in Daegu City, fire officials said yesterday. The Daegu Fire Department said that 66 other people evacuated the facility following the collapse, which was reported at 10:16am. Nine people received treatment at hospitals. While it was possible the injury toll could rise, emergency personnel at the scene said it was highly unlikely that anyone had sustained serious injuries, according to fire department official Yoon Jong-mi. A photo from the scene showed emergency rescuers searching through debris following the collapse on the second floor of the four-story building. It was not immediately clear what caused the collapse.
Photo: AFP
PANAMA
Quake collapses buildings
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake on Friday rocked the Central American nation, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least two people, with no deaths reported. The shallow tremor was felt across the nation, the National Civil Protection System said. Rene Garcia, the head of emergency operations, told reporters that so far there were no reports of fatalities. In Panama City, about 200km from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from skyscrapers. “I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged,” Salomon Andion, 46, told reporters after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. “Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking.” A video on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently, but remaining upright as vehicles traveled across it. The two injuries were reported by people trapped in different collapsed structures — one near a church in Veraguas, the other in a collapsed hotel in Cocle, Garcia said. The US Geological Survey said the quake struck at 12:56pm local time with an epicenter 10km from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera Province. “We are facing a major disaster,” President Jose Raul Mulino said. “It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school,” Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle Province told reporters.

UK bans Protestant march in N Ireland in a Catholic area
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

Britain’s Northern Ireland secretary on Friday banned a contentious Protestant parade through a mostly Irish nationalist and Catholic district after a nearly two-week standoff.
The Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body regulating contentious processions, had authorized 35 Orangemen to march silently along the mostly Irish nationalist enclave of Garvaghy Road in Portadown, without bands or supporters from 8am on Sept. 27.
However, thousands blocked the procession, halting the first parade, which had been allowed along the route in almost three decades.
Photo: AFP
The Orangemen have since remained at nearby Drumcree Church, demanding to complete the march, while residents maintained their protest.
“I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions,” the minister, Chris Bryant, said in a statement.
In the interest of public safety, Bryant said circumstances under which the procession was given the go ahead had now “changed considerably.”
“As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined,” he said, adding that “no one wants a return to the past.”
The procession last went along Garvaghy Road in Portadown, 40km southwest of Belfast, in 1997.
It was barred the following year, soon after a peace accord largely ended three decades of conflict over British rule in Northern Ireland.
Police Service of Northern Ireland Chief Constable Jon Boutcher welcomed the decision.
Boutcher said he wrote to Bryant on Friday asking him to review an earlier decision by the province’s Parades Commission.
Boutcher said he outlined his assessment “that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted.”
Any operation to allow the march to go ahead would have carried an “unacceptable” risk of serious injury and disorder, and would have had “catastrophic long-term consequences,” he said.

Several injured after attack on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.
"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.
Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.
At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."
Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Coalition vows to respond
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively."
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack."
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable."
He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, confirming that an American citizen was killed in the strikes.
"These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately."
What do we know about the Riyadh attack?
A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.
The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."
Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."
What did the Houthis say?
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.
However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.
In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."
When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."
Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week
Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.
Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.
Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.
The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.
The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s government on Friday announced new fuel tax cuts and extended subsidies aimed at lowering fuel prices, just over two weeks before a closely contested presidential runoff.
Fuel prices are a particularly sensitive issue for voters, who on Oct. 25 are to decide whether to elect Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, or grant Lula a fourth term.
Flavio Bolsonaro received about 2 million more votes than Lula in the first round on Sunday last week.
Photo: AFP
A new decree eliminates federal taxes on the import and sale of gasoline for 30 days, with the possibility of an extension. The measure was effective from Friday, the same day previous measures that lowered taxes expired. It extends a tax exemption and increases a subsidy for ethanol.
The government also said it would provide an additional subsidy to importers of diesel, who will receive 1.40 reais (US$0.28) per liter for 30 days.
That amount is in addition to the 2.12 reais per liter subsidy already in effect.
“The aim is to ensure that imports remain economically viable at a critical time for fuel supply,” the government’s secretariat for social communication said, adding that the measures were in line with the strategy adopted by the government since the start of the Iran war.
The fiscal impact of the measures would be offset by the revenues from the federal government’s oil assets, it added.
Crude oil prices shot up shortly after Israel and the US began their war with Iran in late February, largely because the fighting halted most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway where roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the conflict.
“The international situation has deteriorated since the measures announced in September,” the Brazilian government said, adding that international diesel and gasoline refining margins had risen to more than double their pre-war levels.

A birthday of Taiwanese’s choosing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

Yesterday, flags fluttered and fireworks lit up the sky to celebrate the 115th Double Ten National Day of the Republic of China (ROC) — but when will Taiwanese be able to celebrate a national day of their own choosing?
On Oct. 10, 1911, the Wuchang Uprising set the Xinhai Revolution in motion, leading to the fall of the Qing Dynasty and the founding of the ROC on Jan. 1 the following year.
When the first shots rang out in Wuchang (武昌), Taiwan was still under Japanese colonial rule. After Japan’s defeat in 1945, the ROC government came to Taiwan to govern. Taiwanese had hoped for postwar stability, but instead faced political corruption, social unrest and the 228 Incident in 1947, the violent suppression of an anti-government uprising.
After losing the Chinese Civil War in 1949, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government retreated to Taiwan, bringing with it the authoritarian politics of China’s civil war.
Taiwan remained under martial law for 38 long years, from May 20, 1949, to July 15, 1987. During this period, known as the White Terror era, countless people were arrested, imprisoned or even killed because of their speech, beliefs and political views. How can this history possibly be glossed over with the phrase “years of hardship?”
Taiwan’s democracy was not a favor bestowed upon it by its rulers, but something Taiwanese fought for at a great cost.
Martial law was lifted in 1987, and Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996. Taiwanese could finally elect their own head of state and bring about peaceful transfers of power through the ballot box. This democratic Taiwan has long since outgrown the political character of the ROC as it was established in China.
Even so, Taiwan continues to face pressure from China when participating in international events under the name ROC, with restrictions imposed even on the name it can use. Why can the democratic achievements of Taiwanese not be proudly presented to the world under the name Taiwan?
Double Ten National Day fireworks light up the sky every year, yet they cannot illuminate Taiwan’s own national birthday. How many more years must Taiwanese celebrate a Chinese revolution from more than a century ago before they can, on a national day of their own choosing, raise their heads high and proudly proclaim to the world, “We are Taiwan.”?
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.

Health minister defends drug harm reduction programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

Drug harm reduction programs do not encourage drug use or ask social workers to give out drugs, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said yesterday amid accusations that Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) had advocated giving out illicit drugs and needles at community centers.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀), a spokeswoman for Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) re-election campaign, on Friday said that “community centers are where people dance and exercise,” but they will be turned into places where social workers give out drugs and create addicts.
Earlier, Chiang’s campaign accused Shen, the Democratic Progressive Party’s Taipei mayoral candidate, of advocating the distribution of drugs and clean needles at community centers.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
Shen later said that his comments merely mentioned a program that has already been implemented elsewhere in Taiwan.
The Taipei-based National Union of Professional Social Worker Associations, Taiwan on Friday called on Lee to publicly apologize for her comments.
“Social workers are not drug providers,” the association said in a statement. “Please stop misleading the public about professional social work.”
Lee’s remarks falsely linked the professional role of social workers and drug harm reduction policies, which can easily lead to public misunderstanding and distrust of frontline social workers, it said.
“The social work profession has long been dedicated to substance addiction prevention and treatment, psychosocial support, family relationship restoration, community resource linkage and social reintegration services,” it said, adding that describing social work as providing drugs and creating addicts is inconsistent with the professional duties of personnel in the work.
In international public health, harm reduction programs minimize health and social risks associated with drug use, including disease transmission, overdoses, family dysfunction and social exclusion, the association said.
“Drug harm reduction does not mean encouraging drug use, nor does it mean providing drugs indiscriminately,” it said, adding that public figures should avoid spreading false information that undermines the social work profession and the people they serve.
“I must emphasize again that harm reduction programs do not encourage drug use and programs do not ask social workers to give out drugs,” Shih said yesterday. “I must solemnly state: Do not let unnecessary [political] mud-slinging distort or disrupt the programs.”
Harm reduction programs include syringe provision, methadone maintenance treatment, infection screening and social reintegration, work that relies on the collaboration of many professionals, he said.
The programs have yielded significant results, he added.
People should stop interfering with the work of frontline professional workers, Shih said.
Lee yesterday said that she agrees with the association that effective anti-drug policies should be grounded in scientific evidence, cross-disciplinary collaboration and a comprehensive social support system.
She said she firmly opposes a model in which community centers provide drugs and clean needles to drug users.
Social workers are not drug providers, she said, adding that their professional roles and responsibilities should not be undermined, and community safety should not be jeopardized.
Addiction prevention and harm reduction should follow the practice of providing methadone substitution therapy through medical institutions, where people must take the medication on-site under direct medical supervision and are not allowed to leave with it, Lee said.
The roles and responsibilities of medical professionals, social workers, drug abuse prevention centers and other specialists should also be clearly defined, she said, adding that cross-disciplinary collaboration and a clear division of responsibilities are essential to minimize the harm drugs cause to people and society.

Taiwan is to receive 500 Stinger missiles and 178 launchers from the US by the end of the year, the first batch under a planned two-stage acquisition totaling 2,621 missiles and 763 launchers, a defense official said yesterday on condition of anonymity.
The portable missiles would play a vital role in the nation’s air defense capabilities, the source said.
The army plans to deploy 2,235 missiles and 657 launchers to defend Taiwan proper and outlying islands, they said, citing military documents.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
The navy is allotted 295 missiles and 85 launchers to arm the Marine Corps and some surface vessels that lack air defense firepower, they said.
An additional 91 missiles and 21 launchers would be issued to the military police assigned to the defense of Taipei and the surrounding region, the source added.
The US has separately delivered a batch of Stinger missiles as part of a defense aid package, the source said, adding that those weapons have been spotted in the hands of military police over the past two years.
Military police have test fired Stinger systems, and used them at drills involving Taipei MRT stations and Wanban Bridge (萬板大橋).
In August, marines fielded a four-ship formation of M109 assault boats armed with Stinger air defense systems and Javelin guided anti-tank missiles in an asymmetric warfare coastal defense drill.
The Stinger missile is battle-tested with a proven record of performance in the Soviet-Afghan War and Russia’s ongoing war with Ukraine.
The Stinger is a fire-and-forget weapon that primarily targets aircraft. Weighing 15.7kg, the system can be carried by a lone infantry soldier to engage aerial targets up to 8,000m away, assuming ideal conditions. Practical range is more typically limited to 4,800m.
The most modern iteration of the Stinger missiles uses a dual-spectrum infrared and ultraviolet seeker module to defeat flares deployed by aircraft as a countermeasure against heat-seeking missiles.
