Lai calls for ‘guardian mountain chain’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:28 UTC
01:41:28 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday said Taiwan needed many industries across its economy to become a “chain of guardian mountains” to broaden the foundation of the nation’s economic strength.
Leading companies expanding overseas should help their supply chains establish deeper roots in Taiwan, Lai said in his Double Ten National Day address.
“We cannot rely on just one guardian mountain; we must ensure that all sectors join together to form a chain of guardian mountains,” Lai said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
His statement appeared to refer to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, the world’s largest contract chipmaker and a pillar of Taiwan’s economy. The US, Japan and other countries have encouraged it to build factories abroad to bolster supply security and reduce reliance on Taiwan.
Lai outlined government measures to support that development, highlighting Taiwan’s strong economic performance while warning of challenges from tariffs, energy issues and competition from Chinese supply chains.
Taiwan’s economy grew 14.15 percent in the first half of the year, he said.
Full-year growth could exceed 11 percent, which would be the highest in 39 years, while per capita GDP was projected to reach US$45,332, almost double its 2016 level.
The TAIEX has reached 49,000 points, making it the fourth-largest stock market by market capitalization, Lai said.
Taiwan also placed fourth the Institute for Management Development’s World Competitiveness Ranking this year, the country’s best performance to date, he said.
To sustain Taiwan’s competitiveness, the Executive Yuan is accelerating the development of strategic industries and emerging technologies, Lai said, highlighting the government’s “Five Trusted Industry Sectors” — semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), defense, security and surveillance, and next-generation communications — alongside the three core technologies targeted by its 10 new AI infrastructure initiatives: silicon photonics, quantum computing and robotics.
Technological advances should also benefit traditional industries, he added.
Other priorities include critical minerals, biotechnology and healthcare, an Asian asset management hub, public infrastructure and urban renewal, cultural and creative industries, and developing tourism into a trillion-NT-dollar industry.
A NT$100 billion (US$3.14 billion) program for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises would support their financing, workforce training, digital transformation, net zero upgrades and access to international distribution channels, Lai said.
To address labor and talent shortages, the government would maintain Taiwanese workers as the primary workforce and supplement them with foreign workers, he said.
Amendments to the Act for the Recruitment and Employment of Foreign Professionals (外國專業人才延攬及僱用法) would also expand opportunities for foreign professionals to come to and remain in Taiwan, and for foreign students to stay after graduation, he added.
On energy, the government would pursue stable electricity supply, energy security and a net zero transition through renewable generation, storage, conservation and grid upgrades, Lai said.
It would also assess different energy options based on scientific evidence, legal procedures and safety standards, he added.
Lai outlined plans to toughen penalties for drug-impaired driving, saying that the government will step up drug enforcement, strengthen rehabilitation and education, trace drugs to their source, and introduce rapid saliva tests at roadside checks to identify drug-impaired drivers.
Meanwhile, the Executive Yuan’s anti-fraud command center has become a permanent body, coordinating efforts to disrupt scams, from online advertising to the movement of money, he said.
As for the declining birthrate, the government from next year plans to introduce a NT$5,000 monthly allowance for every child from birth until they reach 18, Lai said.
The allowance would be accompanied by expanded childcare services, more family-friendly workplaces and housing assistance, he said.
The Long-term Care 3.0 plan launched this year aims to bring medical and community services together so that older people can receive care in familiar surroundings, while easing the pressure on family caregivers, he added.
On housing, the government will continue its program supporting 1 million renter households by expanding supply and providing rental assistance, Lai said.
A larger proportion of social housing would be reserved for newlyweds and families with young children, and the government would raise the amount they can borrow under the Preferential Housing Loans for the Youth 3.0 program, he said.
The president also pledged to advance gender equality, saying no one should be excluded because of gender, ethnicity, background or identity.

Eritrea urges UN to intervene in standoff with Ethiopia

Unknown Publisher

Eritrea urges UN to intervene in standoff with Ethiopia
The neighbouring countries blame one another for starting war amid heightened tensions and fears of a wider conflict.
Eritrea has asked the United Nations to take “deterrent measures” after what it called Ethiopia’s “declaration of war” in the conflict over the Tigray region.
Eritrea’s request comes a day after Addis Ababa, in a letter to the Security Council, accused Asmara of launching an “all-out invasion”, saying Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s Tigray.
In a separate letter to the council on Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh said the claims of an Eritrean incursion were part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression and urged the UN to intervene, invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows measures from sanctions to military action.
The neighbouring countries have accused each other of starting a war over Tigray, where Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing rebels.
An alliance of seven armed groups launched attacks against federal Ethiopian forces in the northern region last month, as they attempt to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
Eritrean forces have since reportedly intruded into Ethiopian territory, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
The Ethiopian army pushed TPLF rebels back this week and seized the region’s capital, Mekelle. It also said it launched drone strikes against Eritrean troops in the region.
“Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea … and take the requisite deterrent measures,” Eritrea’s Saleh said in the letter on Saturday.
He said Ethiopia’s action would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos on Friday accused Eritrea of “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
Timothewos invoked Ethiopia’s right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, but he did not specify what measures the country was taking.
Faisal Roble, a Horn of Africa specialist, believes both sides are “preparing for the last phase of an open conflict”.
“There is really no doubt that both of them are inching towards an open conflict,” he told Al Jazeera from the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
“Whatever they write to the United Nations, it is just posturing and making sure that they have some sort of international support on their side,” the analyst added.
‘Deceitful attempts’
In his letter, Saleh called Ethiopia’s actions “deceitful attempts to rationalise its brazen acts of war”, claiming that they were “hollow in substance”.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Friday of pursuing aggression against Eritrea through its demands for sovereign access to the Red Sea. Writing on X, he did not explicitly confirm or deny the reported troop crossings.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, and they fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000.
Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab.
TPLF fighters battled Ethiopian government forces, then backed by Eritrea, in a devastating 2020-2022 war.

Manchester City will face the full fury of Anfield on Sunday when the Premier League leaders confront old rivals Liverpool in their first game since being found guilty of breaking financial rules.
City can expect a hostile reception from Liverpool fans after an independent commission found they arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than US$1.2 billion between 2009 and 2018.
The financial breaches occurred during a period in which City won three Premier League titles and numerous other trophies, with Liverpool struggling to break the Etihad Stadium outfit’s silverware monopoly.
Photo: AFP
City have appealed the verdict and manager Enzo Maresca was confident on Friday that they will overturn the original ruling.
The Premier League season is in stasis awaiting a ruling on the appeal and possible sanction.
“I think the worst thing probably is the uncertainty, that no one knows what’s going to happen,” Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said on Friday.
A severe points penalty leading to relegation or even expulsion from the English top flight are possibilities, and there is speculation City could be stripped of titles.
“I think they have to be stripped of the titles. Otherwise you send the wrong message to anyone in the future,” John Gibbons of Liverpool podcast The Anfield Wrap said in an interview. “There can’t be any trust now, certainly not if there’s not an admission of guilt. For me, I don’t see how Manchester City continue in the league.”
Over the past 12 years, Liverpool have finished second to City on three occasions.
Only one of those, during the 2013-2014 season, was during the period under scrutiny.
City’s rivals believe the wrongdoing in that period built the foundations for a golden era under Pep Guardiola, who stepped down at the end of last season.
Twice Jurgen Klopp’s Reds missed out on the title despite amassing over 90 points.
Those title battles turned meetings between City and Liverpool into English soccer’s marquee event and the eyes of the world will be on Anfield again come Sunday.
“It just shows how remarkable that team that Jurgen Klopp built was and what they were up against,” Gibbons said. “They were obviously going against another side who it has been shown weren’t playing by the same rules as everyone else.”
Even in happier times, City have rarely enjoyed their trips to Anfield.
Last season’s 2-1 victory was City’s first win there in front of a crowd since 2003, with their other win coming amid COVID-19 restrictions in 2021.
City return to Anfield sitting atop of the Premier League after a flawless start to Maresca’s reign, featuring seven successive wins in all competitions.
Months after the charges against the club were announced in February 2023, City went on to win the treble, clinching the club’s first Champions League crown, as well as the Premier League and FA Cup.
The question is whether Maresca’s men can tap into that mentality once more, rather than wilting under the intense scrutiny.
Liverpool supporters have often created a hostile atmosphere for City’s visits since they emerged as title contenders following the takeover by their Abu Dhabi-based owners in 2008.
This weekend’s showdown is likely to set a new standard for venom directed at City’s players and fans.
“It’s going to be massively hostile,” said Dom Farrell, author of Glory Days for the Waifs and Strays, which chronicled City’s rise from the third tier to European champions. “If they were to win against Liverpool and then beat an off-form Paris Saint-Germain you really get a siege mentality going.”
“But there’s also a decent chance they get turned over and then it just starts to feel you’re in this sort of dead zone waiting for the verdict,” he added.

KMT’s Cheng Li-wun on the ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:21 UTC
01:41:21 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Kaohsiung mayoral candidate, Legislator Ko Chih-en (柯志恩), said in an interview that if the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) loses the election, it would only have its choice of candidate to blame, and would not be due to the record of Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁).
Chen issued a simple reminder: “A vote for Ko means supporting KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文).”
To prevent Chen’s high approval ratings from translating into an electoral asset for the DPP’s mayoral candidate, Legislator Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆), the KMT has been pursuing a strategy in which Ko praises Chen while taking jabs at Lai.
Remarkably, Ko’s line could be copied word for word in describing the Changhua County commissioner race as well: If the KMT loses, it could not be blamed on incumbent Wang Huei-mei (王惠美), but rather on Cheng’s hand-picked candidate to succeed her, Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政). Indeed, a vote for Wei in Changhua is to offer one’s support to Cheng.
Wang has repeatedly emphasized that the best way she can support the campaign and her party is to do her job well and work hard to fulfill her duties. That said, her record in office in Changhua is hardly comparable to that of Chen’s in Kaohsiung.
According to the Chinese-language magazine Global Views Monthly’s 2026 poll on public satisfaction with the performance of city mayors and county commissioners, Chen ranked first among the six special municipalities; Wang was last among central Taiwan’s five regions.
Wei has continued to play the respect card when it comes to Wang, undoubtedly hoping to piggy back off of her record. However, the county election ballot would ultimately bear Wei’s name and image, not Wang’s. Campaigning must return to the fundamentals and accept that the candidate’s qualities and efforts will determine the outcome.
KMT candidates running for township or city mayor, or county councilor positions across Changhua had hoped that the party’s county commissioner candidate, like a mother hen leading her chicks, would push the campaign forward and generate collective media exposure. Instead, it seems that the chicks have been left to lift the hen, with the candidates working to raise Wei’s profile while crossing their fingers that their own campaigns do not suffer too badly for it. It is a telling sign that campaign billboards featuring Wei alongside these candidates are virtually nowhere to be seen across Changhua County.
Since Cheng took over as KMT chairwoman, the Changhua county commissioner nomination has been one of the few cases she has taken a personal hand in. There is good reason to equate a vote for Wei with support for Cheng. One could go a step further and say that a vote for Wei also means support for Hsiao Ching-tien (蕭景田), the KMT’s Changhua County chapter director. It was Hsiao who recommended Wei to Cheng.
Hsiao had been convicted in a case involving the murder of a police officer, had alleged connections to the criminal underworld and was detained as part of the 1984 crackdown on gangs, known as Operation Clean Sweep. Now working behind the scenes within KMT ranks, he has become a defendant for the second time in a vote-buying case.
Looking back at the process that produced Wei’s nomination, Cheng, who has become something of an electoral liability, insisted on the party doing things her way. She forcibly placed Wang in the difficult position of serving as head of Wei’s campaign headquarters. With no promise of reward and certain to be blamed in the event of failure, Wang can only do her best to keep her distance. If Wei is defeated in next month’s elections, we can be sure that it is not Wang who is to blame.
Chen Yung-chang is a freelance writer based in Taipei.

Iran nuclear chief accuses IAEA of yielding to US and Israeli Pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:35:40 UTC
01:35:40 KST

Iran nuclear chief accuses IAEA of yielding to US and Israeli Pressure
TEHRAN — Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI), has criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its 'submission to pressure from the United States and Israel,' saying the UN nuclear watchdog has failed to uphold its responsibility to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and ensure equal access to the technology for all nations.
Speaking on Saturday, Eslami said the agency’s approach to Iran had departed from its legal and professional obligations under the influence of Washington and the Israeli regime. He argued that discriminatory approaches to nuclear issues, particularly the treatment of nuclear weapons and peaceful nuclear activities, had weakened international law and eroded confidence in the international system.
Referring to President Masoud Pezeshkian’s remark that “the bomb is in Israel, while the inspectors are in Iran,” Eslami said the statement highlighted a 'fundamental contradiction' in the international handling of nuclear issues: Iran’s peaceful nuclear program remains under international scrutiny, while Israel’s nuclear arsenal is not subject to comparable safeguards and inspections.
Eslami argued that such double standards, alongside 'unlawful conduct by powerful states,' had undermined the principles of the UN Charter and contributed to the erosion of international legal norms. He said the credibility of international institutions depended on their ability to apply established rules consistently, without political discrimination or pressure from influential countries.
Unilateralism and the Erosion of International Law
The AEOI chief also criticized the post-Second World War international legal order, saying unilateral policies and excessive demands by the United States had weakened the institutions and arrangements established to promote international cooperation.
According to Eslami, Washington has withdrawn from international organizations and cooperative frameworks when their decisions or rules have conflicted with its interests, while seeking to preserve a global order shaped around US preferences. He said such an approach had impaired multilateral mechanisms and made it more difficult to uphold international law on an equal basis.
Peaceful Nuclear Energy as a Universal Right
Eslami stressed that the peaceful use of nuclear energy is not the exclusive privilege of a limited group of countries, but an entitlement that should be available to all nations in accordance with international law and relevant safeguards.
He said the IAEA was established to encourage and facilitate the peaceful application of nuclear technology and to help countries benefit from its scientific, medical, agricultural, industrial and energy-related uses. In his view, the agency has failed for years to fulfil this mandate fairly in its dealings with Iran, instead adopting an approach that has impeded the country’s nuclear development under US and Israeli pressure.
Despite a 'sustained maximum-pressure campaign,' Eslami said Iran had continued to cooperate with the agency’s regulatory framework while advancing its nuclear capabilities.
He maintained that the country’s progress in nuclear science and technology demonstrated its determination to develop the peaceful applications of the field despite external pressure and restrictions.
Eslami also highlighted Iran’s advances in nuclear technology, saying the country produces and regularly distributes more than 72 radiopharmaceutical products, which are exported to 19 countries. He added that another 20 radiopharmaceuticals are at the research and development phase, and that Iran has joined the ranks of the world’s leading countries in producing certain alpha-emitting radiopharmaceuticals.
Eslami’s remarks come amid longstanding disputes over Iran’s nuclear program, the scope and implementation of international safeguards, and the role of the IAEA in addressing so-called nuclear proliferation concerns. Tehran has consistently maintained that its nuclear activities are peaceful and that access to nuclear technology for civilian purposes should be governed by international rules rather than political pressure.
Iran has also repeatedly called for a consistent approach to nuclear issues, arguing that the international non-proliferation system can retain its credibility only if its principles are applied without double standards.

‘We could have saved more lives’: Red Cross chief admits failures in Gaza hostage crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:33:28 UTC
01:33:28 KST

Three years after the October 7 Hamas massacre, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has acknowledged that greater pressure earlier in negotiations to free Israeli hostages held in Gaza might have saved more lives.
In an interview with The New York Times published Saturday, Mirjana Spoljaric said she personally believed that stronger pressure during the initial stages of negotiations could have helped secure the hostages' release sooner.
"I personally believe there was room to apply pressure earlier in the negotiations," she said, adding: "We could have saved more lives."
Asked directly whether Red Cross representatives had been allowed to visit the hostages held by Hamas, Spoljaric shook her head, indicating that they had not. She argued that arranging visits was considerably more complicated than facilitating the hostages' return.
Spoljaric emphasized that Hamas should have released the hostages unconditionally on the first day of the war, but said the organization had to operate within the realities of the conflict.
"We had to work with the tools available to us," she said, describing hostage-taking as among the most complicated and, in some respects, cruel situations humanitarian organizations confront.
She explained that Red Cross personnel themselves encounter hostage situations more frequently than the organization would wish, reinforcing the importance of negotiating swift releases. The objective, she said, must always be to bring the hostages home.
Spoljaric also disclosed details of her diplomatic efforts during the war, including meetings with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior Hamas officials.
She said she traveled to Qatar twice to meet Hamas leaders, including Ismail Haniyeh, who was later killed, and also held a face-to-face meeting with Netanyahu.
The discussions were difficult, she said, stressing that confidentiality was essential to maintaining the organization's ability to negotiate with opposing parties.
Spoljaric noted that the longer hostage negotiations continued, the more complicated they became, making early intervention especially important.
Red Cross also denied access to Palestinian prisoners
The interview also addressed Israel's refusal to allow the Red Cross access to Palestinian security prisoners held in Israeli facilities.
Spoljaric said the ICRC had enjoyed access to detainees held by Israel for decades before October 7, arranging tens of thousands of family visits over the years.
Securing access to detention facilities during wartime, however, was exceptionally difficult, she explained.
According to Spoljaric, parties to a conflict frequently suspend such visits on security grounds. She argued that the justification did not change the importance of ensuring humanitarian access.
The ICRC is an independent international humanitarian organization headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. It is not a United Nations agency and operates worldwide, including in conflict zones, as a neutral intermediary.
Throughout the war, the organization faced criticism in Israel over what was perceived as insufficient sensitivity toward Israeli civilians and hostages held by Hamas.
Israeli officials have generally regarded the Red Cross as less confrontational toward Israel than organizations such as UNRWA, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and the UN human rights office, but have nevertheless criticized aspects of its conduct.
The ICRC has traditionally placed considerable emphasis on access to detainees and prisoners, including Palestinians held in Israeli facilities. Israel's refusal to permit visits to security prisoners, including Hamas terrorists involved in the October 7 attacks, was therefore seen by the organization as a significant obstacle to fulfilling its humanitarian mandate.
Spoljaric's remarks mark a rare public acknowledgment that the international organization's efforts during the hostage crisis may have fallen short, even as she defended the confidential negotiations and neutral approach that underpin its work.

Gathering at Embankment, hundreds of thousands of people marched towards Downing Street, where the prime minister's office is located, to call for an end to the genocide and a full arms embargo on Israel.

AI generated

South Yorkshire Police in northern England said it responded to reports at around 1.30pm (8.30pm in Singapore) of a man entering the enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near the city of Doncaster.
“The tiger subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury,” the force said in a statement.
“Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the vest efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” it added.
Police said earlier the tiger remained in the enclosure following the incident and that there was no wider risk to the public. All visitors had been evacuated.
The wildlife park confirmed that a “serious incident” had taken place at its tiger enclosure, triggering the closure of the attraction.
Yorkshire Ambulance Service said it had sent two ambulances by road and an air ambulance to the scene.
The park’s “Land of the Tigers” feature has a 300m raised walkway.
From the walkway, visitors can view the park’s Amur tigers in their enclosure which includes woodland, grassland and a waterfall pool.
There are estimated to be only around 500 of the endangered subspecies left in the wild.
The park is due to remain closed on Oct 11. AFP

Multiple people wounded in suspected Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport
Many people were wounded in a blast at Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, according to two eyewitnesses and two people briefed on the matter, and travellers were evacuated from parts of the facility.
One of the eyewitnesses reported seeing an explosion and then seeing multiple people lying injured on the ground inside the airport. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport.
"Dozens of people were injured, most of them Saudi nationals. At least five of the injured - all Saudi nationals - are in intensive care," a source at a hospital told AFP, saying some patients were transported by helicopter.
A medical source in the city told AFP that "ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," and that "we were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh", with many in critical condition.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority later confirmed the attack, saying that the Riyadh airport "was targeted in an attack on Saturday afternoon, October 10, 2026, amid continued attacks targeting the kingdom's civil aviation facilities."
"The attack left several people injured, with the number still being assessed," the statement added.
Western embassies have warned their citizens to avoid the airport, with Spain's embassy, in a message on X, alerting nationals to a "new attack" by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on the airport.
A diplomatic source separately told AFP that the Houthis had hit the airport with a missile around 1200 GMT.
Canada's embassy said only that unspecified "ongoing military activity" was affecting Riyadh's international airport, while Germany's mission alluded only to "the current situation".
France's embassy on Friday urged French nationals to take "utmost care" in Saudi Arabia because of "strikes in recent days by the Houthis". It also warned French citizens not to record images of zones that were hit, nor share any online.

Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways earlier cancelled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday.
Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.
Organisers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security.
The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier this month.

From burning Sardis to bombing Tehran: What Rubio got wrong about Persia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:25:59 UTC
01:25:59 KST

From burning Sardis to bombing Tehran: What Rubio got wrong about Persia
Tehran Times speaks with Touraj Daryaee, historian of ancient Iran and editor of encyclopaedia Iranica
TEHRAN – U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s October 7 speech in Athens invoked ancient Greece as the foundation of Western civilization, linking the Persian invasion under Xerxes in 480 BCE to a broader call for Western ambition, national sovereignty and renewed American power. Speaking at the historic Pnyx, Rubio also criticized Iran’s leadership, contrasting his portrayal of Western heroism with what he described as Iran’s “cult of death.”
In this interview with the Tehran Times, Touraj Daryaee, historian of ancient Iran and editor of Encyclopaedia Iranica, challenges Rubio’s historical narrative and examines its political implications.
The following is the text of the interview:
 You noted that the Athenians helped burn Sardis, an important Achaemenid administrative center, in 489 BCE, before Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BCE. How does this episode change our understanding of the history Rubio presents?
 
I think the entire premise of Secretary Rubio’s speech is false. This was not a battle between East and West, but rather a conflict between a world empire spanning three continents and a number of Greek city-states on the other side of the sea. From this perspective, the entire premise is wrong.
 
However, the Athenians and their allies did come in 489 BCE and burn the center of the Lydian satrapy of the Persian Empire. They set it on fire, looted it, and completely destroyed it, along with the Temple of Cybele. An empire obviously does not sit still in response to such an attack; it has to take revenge. The burning of the Acropolis in 480 BCE was, in effect, retaliation for what had happened nine years earlier.
 
Rubio cites figures such as Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar and Hernán Cortés as symbols of ambition and expanding power. What does this reveal about his definition of Western civilization?
Empires do what they do when they have the power to do so. Of course, the nature of empires differs. In antiquity, we see figures who sought to conquer the world, such as Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.
I think Hernán Cortés was a different kind of figure. He belongs to the early modern period, when Europeans systematically set out to plunder the American, African and Asian continents, enrich themselves, enslave people to provide free labor, and build a capitalist economy. Their economy advanced beyond those of other continents partly because their natural resources had been taken.
This was different from the campaigns of Alexander or Julius Caesar, which sought to bring glory to Greece and Rome.
Rubio delivered his speech at the Pnyx, where ancient Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly. Why did he choose this historic site, and what message does it convey?
Rubio smartly chose this location because the United States is engaged in a war with Iran. By going to Greece, he can effectively say, “Look, the Iranians were doing the same thing 2,500 years ago,” as if nothing has changed. He is trying to use history as an ideological tactic against Iran and, more broadly, against those on the other side of the current conflict.
It is a perfect spot if you want to invoke history, but I think he is doing so in an awkward way. In Iran, we do not go to Persepolis and say, “Alexander burned Persepolis, and that is why the Americans want to do the same.”
Rubio traces Western civilization from ancient Greece and Rome through Christianity and Europe to the United States. How accurate is this narrative, and what does it overlook about cultural exchanges between Persia, Greece and other ancient civilizations?
Mr. Rubio is really reaching for the stars here. The idea that the United States, represented by Mr. Rubio, whose family comes from Cuba, is an inheritor of Western civilization is not entirely accurate.
In fact, the idea that the West’s heritage is directly connected to Greece is a relatively recent phenomenon, dating back only two or three centuries. A bridge was constructed between antiquity and the modern age, bypassing much of what happened in the medieval world and overlooking important historical developments. This is, indeed, a fallacy.
Greece and Iran, by contrast, have had extensive contact with one another. They have borrowed from each other and share many similarities in their traditions, from antiquity to the present day. The United States and Germany, by comparison, are far removed from what Greece was and is.
He opens with the Achaemenid invasion of Athens and later criticizes Iran’s current leadership. Is this a deliberate link between ancient Persia and modern Iran, or would that interpretation go beyond his speech?
Yes, absolutely. Secretary Rubio is trying to link the past to the present, however false that connection may be. He is essentially saying, “Look at what is happening in our dealings with Iran, and what we are doing against Iran. This is what you had to face in 480 BCE.”
The fallacy here is that the United States has military bases throughout the Middle East. It is the United States and Israel that have bombed Iran. Iranians have not gone to Europe or the United States to wage war against Europeans or Americans.
You have highlighted Western interventions in the East over the past two centuries. Which historical events best illustrate the gap between the West’s image as a defender of freedom and its record of foreign intervention?
I think Rubio had several things in mind. One was to argue that the West should not apologize for its past. However, while talking about Greece as a great civilization, he did not address the experiences of people around the world over the past two or three centuries: people whose countries have been attacked, whose communities have been bombed and looted, and whose populations have been enslaved.
These actions helped build Western nations, particularly the United States, into what they are today. To ignore this history is quite dishonest.
The U.S. Secretary of State delivered this speech amid the war involving the United States and Iran. How should this context shape our reading of his references to ancient Persia and Western civilization?
The context is that the United States and the West have been in conflict with Iran, a power that acted as a superpower in Asia and the East, for what Rubio presents as an enduring historical struggle spanning millennia.
This is how he has framed the issue to make his argument more persuasive. He is doing so in Athens, beside the Acropolis, to drive home his point.
Rubio used ancient history to frame his vision of Western civilization and American power. Is he seeking to establish a distinct political doctrine of his own and lay the groundwork for a potential 2028 presidential campaign?
I think his speech generally went over well with a European audience concerned about immigration and changes in the demographic and religious composition of both Europe and the United States.
His central message is that Western civilization is a noble civilization that made the West a superpower. He presents it as an enduring, unchanging civilization with a history stretching back thousands of years.
What he does not describe is what this civilization has done to the rest of the world over the past two or three centuries in order to reach its current position.
No one is against Western civilization, but we should always remain mindful of the atrocities that have also been committed. You cannot vindicate yourself before history simply by standing beside an ancient monument such as the Acropolis to make your point.

Visiting Abraham’s ‘birth chamber’ in southern Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:23:22 UTC
01:23:22 KST

The Torah portion of Noah, which we will read this Shabbat, concludes with a powerful verse: “And Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, and they went out together from Ur of the Chaldees to go to the land of Canaan.”
Jewish travelers don’t simply read what the Torah says; we want to see where it happened. There are places where the Bible stops being a story and becomes the soil beneath our feet.
We read a passage, board a plane, drive a road, and find ourselves wondering what Abraham’s path actually looked like. In these moments, the earth acquires a narrative, and that narrative begins to feel almost tangible.
Traveling to the 'City of the Prophets'
The biblical “Ur of the Chaldees” (Ur Kasdim) is modern-day Urfa, located in southeastern Turkey, 80 km from the Euphrates River, and less than two hours by air from Israel. The Turkish government renamed it Sanlıurfa in 1984, but in Kurdish, it is still known simply as “the City of the Prophets.” The local university bears the name Harran, a designation that immediately resonates with anyone familiar with Abraham’s journey.
A trip to Urfa is a spiritual and religious experience, not merely a geographical one. It doesn’t offer the shallow excitement of a typical tourist site where you snap a photo and move on. Instead, it leaves an almost physical impact, difficult to put into words.
But before the biblical narrative even enters the picture, Urfa enfolds you in its unique atmosphere. It is a city of pale stone, fierce sun, narrow lanes, and markets thick with the smell of grilled meat and sharp pepper. The local döner kebab, heavily flavored with the region’s distinctive smoky chili, Urfa biber, hangs in the air like an announcement of place.
In the center of the city stands a hill crowned with the ruins of an ancient fortress. Locals point to the remaining stone columns and call them “Nimrod’s Throne,” attributing them to the mighty king from Genesis.
Yet the sacred site nestled just below the hill draws Jewish travelers. A small, dark, humble cave is revered as the birthplace of Abraham. According to historical tradition, a synagogue stood above or near this site some 1,700 years ago, adding an intriguing ancient layer to the local heritage. The cave is also sacred to Christians, associated with Mary.
As you descend into the cave, something immediately shifts. The light dims, the stone walls close in, and the bustling world above recedes. Colored carpets cover the floor as you move deeper into the shadows.
No grand hall or imposing architecture greets you here; the cave is small, low, and cramped, leaving you with the distinct sensation that the entire weight of the city rests impossibly far above your head.
A natural spring flows directly from the rock wall. Today, the water runs through modern faucets and collects in large stone basins. The steady, rhythmic drip is almost hypnotic, an ancient whisper that could have sounded exactly this way thousands of years ago.
It’s difficult to remain indifferent in such a space. I’m standing where the founder of faith itself was born, a man whose influence would span millennia and cross the boundaries of religions and peoples. In this darkness, it’s impossible not to contemplate how far his footprints would reach.
Centuries ago, a Byzantine Christian church stood near these waters, reportedly built over an even older place of worship. When the Ottoman Empire ruled here, the “Mosque of Abraham” (the Rizvaniye Mosque) was erected along the complex in 1736 and is still standing today.
The site has become one of the most revered places in the region, comparable in its spiritual pull to the mosque above the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, where Abraham is buried. Muslim pilgrims and visitors arrive from around the world, but Jews and Christians are warmly welcomed too. (I visited there before the Turkish ruler’s antisemitism became apparent).
Abraham’s Pool
Beside the mosque lies Abraham’s Pool (Balıklıgöl), where thousands of carp circle endlessly in the still water like a living legend.
In his commentary, Rashi briefly cites the Midrash Rabbah, noting that Abraham’s father, Terah, was a dealer in idolatrous statues. One day, while still a child, Abraham smashed his father’s idols. Furious, Terah lodged a complaint against his own son with King Nimrod.
The midrash expands on this, describing a fierce theological debate between the young boy and the tyrant king. “If fire is divinity,” Abraham asks, “perhaps water is stronger? And if water, perhaps the clouds that carry it?”
The argument continues until the king loses his patience and orders Abraham cast into a fiery furnace. The midrash notes that Abraham was miraculously saved, but leaves the details mysterious.
Local tradition fills in the blanks with a happy ending: the moment Abraham hit the furnace, the fire miraculously turned into cool water, and the burning coals became fish. This is how Abraham’s Pool was created, and why the carp inside are considered sacred. Fishing here is strictly forbidden, and don’t even think of utilizing it for your gefilte fish.
Today, visitors purchase small packets of food from local vendors for a few lira to feed the fish. Watching hundreds of carp glinting in the sun while children point excitedly, it is fascinating to see the direct line connecting an ancient rabbinic midrash to a modern Turkish pool where the fish swim as if they are part of the story itself.
Şanlıurfa has another world-class attraction: the Urfa Man statue (Balıklıgöl Statue). Discovered during excavations near the pool, this limestone carving dates back roughly 13,000 years to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic period. Displayed in the city’s archaeological museum, it is widely considered the oldest known life-sized, naturalistic sculpture of a human being. (Apparently, the young Abram missed this one!).
Old travelers’ books occasionally mention a “House of Job” in Urfa. Job begins: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.” Because biblical Uz is frequently associated with Mesopotamia, local traditions placed his story here.
While finding the exact “house” remains elusive, the city’s historic Saladin Ayyubi Mosque stands on a site deeply tied to these ancient legends. In Urfa, it is often impossible to know where stone ends, and story begins.
Urfa’s lost Jews
For 2,500 years, a vibrant Jewish community thrived in Urfa. Five hundred years ago, a thousand Jews lived here – likely the descendants of exiles from Judah who arrived after the destruction of the First Temple.
In the Urfali synagogues, they prayed in Hebrew inflected with a distinct local accent. Their liturgical melodies absorbed the sounds of the streets around them, blending traditional prayers with Turkish musical structures and intricate maqam patterns. During Saturday morning prayers, they sang “Nishmat Kol Hai” to traditional Turkish tunes.
They lived in a Jewish quarter characterized by white stone houses squeezed along narrow lanes, where families could converse across rooftops and children easily jumped from house to house.
The Great Synagogue stood opposite what is now the historic Hayrullah Mosque. By the 19th century, the community was prominent enough to establish a yeshiva under the spiritual guidance of Hakham Abdallah Somekh, the revered rosh yeshiva of Baghdad.
By the end of the 19th century, the situation had changed. The Ottoman authorities began massacring the local Armenian population. While the violence was not explicitly directed at the Jewish community, the terrifying atmosphere prompted many of Urfa’s Jews to flee.
They went toward the Land of Israel, retracing the exact route taken by Abraham millennia earlier. Many families stopped in Aleppo, Syria, stayed for generations, and produced some of Aleppo’s most renowned rabbinic scholars. But the majority eventually completed the journey to Jerusalem and Tiberias, establishing tight-knit communities to preserve their unique Urfali traditions.
In doing so, a historical circle closed: the very city from which Abraham once departed to seek the Promised Land would, thousands of years later, send forth its own Jewish children to that exact same destination.
Today, you can still find physical traces of this community in Israel. In Jerusalem, the Urfalim Synagogue stands at 19 Bezalel Street. Until recently, the congregation still prayed from custom siddurim that followed the unique Urfa rite, though they have since transitioned to the standard Edot HaMizrach liturgy.
Another historic Urfali synagogue still stands in Rishon Lezion, founded at the turn of the 20th century by proud Urfali pioneers who built their new lives working in Baron Rothschild’s historic vineyards.
This may be one of the most moving aspects of tracing a vanished community: discovering that it hasn’t truly vanished. It’s simply changed address.
The journey continues
When we leave Urfa, it’s hard to shake the feeling that the story hasn’t really ended. The stones remain. The fish continue their circles. But the story travels with you. Am Israel Chai.
Anyone who has ever left home knows that feeling. Whether moving to another city or making aliyah, departure is always an act of faith. You know what you’re leaving. You don’t truly know what you’ll find.
I have visited many Jewish heritage sites around the world, yet few have left such a profound impression on me as the cave where tradition says Abraham, our forefather, was born. In my view, its significance as a Jewish tourist site surpasses even that of the Arch of Titus in Rome.
In Urfa, the ancient command “lech lecha” (go forth) sounds less like a biblical verse and more like a personal invitation to journey.
The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

Hiking the Holyland: Dodim Cave, the Ein Gedi most visitors never see
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:23:17 UTC
01:23:17 KST

Ein Gedi is not a secret. It’s one of the most visited nature reserves in the country, and after years of closures, it’s filling up again.
Just before Sukkot, the Parks Authority reopened the lower Nahal David trail to David Waterfall, the last major piece of a long restoration. The tour buses, school groups, and families lined up for ice cream are back, and almost all of them head for the same place: Nahal David and its waterfalls.
Most of them never learn that Ein Gedi reaches far beyond that one canyon. Above the crowds are quieter trails, climbing into the cliffs toward springs, ancient ruins, and pools that see only a handful of hikers a day.
The most beautiful of these is Dodim Cave.
On our last visit there, we pulled up to the gate just before 8 a.m., before it had even opened. Below us, the Dead Sea lay flat and blue in the morning haze. We had been to Dodim Cave years earlier. But this time we were approaching it from a different trail, because the way we used to get there was closed.
A reserve that keeps changing
Ein Gedi has had a hard few years. In August 2023, a deadly rockslide struck the Nahal David trail, and the Parks Authority closed it for months. Then, in May 2025, a sudden flood tore through the David and Arugot streams, washing away trails, stairs, and bridges. Since then, the reserve has reopened piece by piece: first Nahal Arugot, then the route to Ein Gedi Spring, and now the lower Nahal David trail.
The old path to Dodim Cave used to break off from Nahal David and climb from there. When we went, that route was closed. Thankfully, there is another way in, from a trail near Nahal Arugot on the other side of the reserve.
The Parks Authority describes this trail as suitable only for experienced hikers. We were warned that the two-kilometer climb would take at least three hours. So we came prepared to suffer.
But it wasn’t difficult at all. The trail climbed steadily through open desert, with the Dead Sea spread out below, and in less than 20 minutes we reached Ein Gedi Spring. It was uphill, and it was hot, but for any reasonably fit hiker, it’s a short and very manageable walk.
From spring to cave
Ein Gedi Spring is a small patch of green and shade in an otherwise bare landscape, with a shallow, pretty pool. It’s also the only place along the route where you’re officially allowed to picnic.
A little farther on, we began to hear water rushing beneath us. We followed the ridge, caught a glimpse down into the canyon, and then the first waterfall appeared. It poured over the white cliffs as if out of nowhere, water from white desert rock. We climbed down a few metal rungs, stopped for a dip in a deep pool, and kept going. One last set of rungs, and there it was.
At Dodim Cave, the waterfall crashed with real force into a shallow pool. Moss and hanging plants grew thick over the gray rock. Behind the falling water was the cave itself, dark and cool and misty, with clear water at its floor. Part of the pool sat in shade and part in the sun. It felt like a pirate’s cove somehow dropped into the Judean Desert.
We stood under the waterfall until we were completely soaked, then climbed up into the cave to explore. Afterward we spread a blanket on a dry ledge beside the falls to enjoy the view.
The name Dodim means “beloved” or “lovers.” It comes straight out of the Song of Songs, where the beloved is compared to “a cluster of henna in the vineyards of Ein Gedi.” Even 3,000 years ago, this oasis was shorthand for something rare and lovely.
The history here is older than the poetry. Just beyond Ein Gedi Spring are the ruins of a Chalcolithic temple, built more than 5,000 years ago on a ledge overlooking the Dead Sea. Its builders likely chose the spot for its view and its water.
Later came David, hiding from King Saul “on the rocks of the wild goats” at Ein Gedi, the ibex’s ancestors presumably watching from the cliffs. Later still, a Jewish town thrived below these springs, famous for its date palms and its precious balsam perfume. The town’s ancient synagogue floor still bears an inscription cursing anyone who reveals “the secret of the town” to outsiders. No one knows for certain what the secret was, but many scholars believe it was how the perfume was made.
Sitting at those falls, it was easy to understand why people kept coming back to this place, and why they wanted to keep it to themselves.
The Ein Gedi beyond Ein Gedi
Now that Nahal David is open again, the parking lot will be full on any good morning. Hundreds of people a day will visit Ein Gedi, see David Waterfall, and drive home feeling they’ve seen the place.
But they’ll miss the best part. Some of Israel’s most famous parks still hold corners that almost no one reaches, and they’re usually only a short climb from the crowds.
Location: Ein Gedi Nature Reserve, off Route 90 on the Dead Sea. About an hour and 20 minutes from Jerusalem. Start from the small trailhead parking area on the road toward Nahal Arugot, but pay or register at the Nahal Arugot entrance first, even if you have a parks card.
The route: Follow the black trail markers and signs toward Ein Gedi Spring, then to Dodim Cave, and return the same way. You’ll get a map at the entrance, and rangers can point out the route. It’s about 3.5 km. Round trip.
Difficulty: Moderate. There is a short, steady climb and a few metal handholds near the cave. Despite the official warnings, it’s well within reach of any normal hiker and of kids who like to hike.
Best season: Fall through spring. In summer, start at opening time.
What to bring: Good shoes, a bathing suit, plenty of drinking water, and sun protection. Picnicking is allowed only at Ein Gedi Spring. No dogs.
Before you go: Ein Gedi has reopened in stages since the 2025 flood, and trail access can change quickly, especially after rain. Check the Parks Authority website for current openings and hours.
The writer is the founder of Hiking the Holyland. Follow her hikes on Instagram @hikingtheholyland. This is the third in a series of columns exploring the lesser-known corners of Israel’s nature reserves and national parks.

Archaeologists discover lost temple to war god near abandoned Roman military fort in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:23:16 UTC
01:23:16 KST

A temple dedicated to the Roman war god Mars was unearthed during excavations in Germany’s Taunus forest, the Hessian State Office for Monument Preservation announced in September.
The excavation team, led by archaeologist Dr. Kai Mückenberger and Excavation Director Manuel Pieper MA, uncovered the temple during its third excavation season at the site.
It is located near Kapersburg, one of the best-preserved Roman forts along the Upper German-Raetian Limes in Hesse. A Roman auxiliary unit, the Numerus Nidensium, was stationed there for about 150 years before abandoning the site during the Limesfall.
Alongside the temple’s remains, archaeologists found inscribed two votive stones, a statuette of the goddess Victoria, and additional statue fragments, at the site.
The discoveries provide additional insight into the presence of religion at the edge of the Roman empire.
Researchers from the University of Frankfurt, led by by Prof. Dr. Markus Scholz, are analyzing the votive stones in attempt to parse their meaning. Scholz has previously helped translate a votive stone found in 2025, which is now displayed at the Wehrturm Museum in Rosbach vor der Höhe.
Evidence of later settlement found
The area of the temple also yielded an antique fibula (a clothing brooch) and fragments of handmade pottery. According to archaeologists, this marks the first archaeological evidence that the site was used after the Roman military left the site.
Both the fibula and the pottery have been linked to the Alemanni, a confederation of Germanic peoples who first appeared east of the Upper Rhine river during the third century CE before expanding outward.
The excavation has also shed light on the settlement, also known as the vicus, before it was abandoned. Extensive remains of craft activity, including a forge, were discovered.
Further, the site’s layers suggest the Romans have leveled the site as part of restructuring the settlement, later replacing it with residential buildings. Traces of Roman roads and the remains of terracing have allowed researchers to estimate the settlement’s layout and dimensions.
Incredible level of preservation
Mückenberger explained that the level of preservation is unlike anything else found in Hesse.
“Here we have layers of preservation that are unparalleled in Hesse, precisely because no agriculture has taken place here,” Mückenberger said. “The forest has preserved everything over the last centuries, maintaining it for us to such an extent that we find layers that are otherwise always gone.”
Mückenberger added that excavations at the settlement are not yet finished, hoping excavations continue in the coming year with students from the University of Frankfurt.

WWII air-raid shelter buried beneath German playground rediscovered during construction work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:23:06 UTC
01:23:06 KST

A forgotten World War II air-raid shelter was recently rediscovered ahead of residential construction in Quedlinburg, in west Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.
The underground trench-like shelter, whose discovery was announced in late July by Saxony-Anhalt’s Heritage Management and Archaeology State Office (LDA), is located overlooking the legendary Bode Gorge.
Shelters of this kind, known also as Deckungsgraben, were built deep underground with protective layers of earth atop it. However, unlike regular air-raid bunkers, they offered no protection against direct hits.
After beginning construction at the site, workers noticed the concrete roof of the shelter emerging from the earth, measuring about 2.5 meters wide.
Also unearthed are two branching “arms” of differing lengths used as entrances and exits. All-together, the bunker covers an area of approximately 20 by 14 meters.
Layout of the shelter
It was built in sections using unreinforced rammed concrete, without steel reinforcement.
Clear impressions of formwork boards can be seen on the interior walls of the shelter. On the outside of the vault, the concrete was neatly smoothed and given a protective coating.
Five openings in the roof, measuring 0.25 by 0.25 meters, were intended to ensure a supply of fresh air from above, while the interior could be sealed off by two double door lock installations.
During the time of the German Democratic Republic (GDR), the shelter was partially back-filled through the ventilation shafts, before a playground was built over it and the structure below forgotten.
Iron clips from electrical cables and a fuse box were recovered from within the remains of the structure. No furniture remains were discovered within the space.
Blind-ending section in the northeast can be interpreted, by comparison with similar structures, as a possible location for an emergency latrine.
“The air-raid shelter serves as a sobering reminder of how precious peaceful times are and how important it is to preserve them,” LDA said.
Europe’s summer heatwave reveals sunken Nazi relics in receding Danube River
Separately in August, Nazi-era relics were revealed along the Danube River as water levels fell following the summer's prolonged heatwaves and drought.
Near the Serbian port of Prahovo, the Danube’s receding water levels have revealed dozens of German battleships sunken during World War II.
At least 20 warships can be seen emerging from the Danube, according to CBS News, adding that they are believed to have belonged to Nazi Germany’s Black Sea fleet, sunken by the German’s during their retreat from Romania near the end of the war.
Additionally, the remains of two Nazi soldiers were found along the banks of the now-receded Danube in Budapest with their dog-tags intact, alongside a World War II motorcycle. The two were buried in the Budaörs German Soldiers Cemetery outside of Budapest.
The motorcycle, believed to be a DKW NZ 350-1, was discovered near Batthyány Square.
Several German Tellermine 35 anti-tank mines were also found, Volksbund said in its statement, as well as a Kuban Shield, a Nazi military decoration awarded to Wehrmacht forces who fought at the Kuban bridgehead in 1943.

Israeli medics face ICC complaint over torture of Palestinian detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:22:53 UTC
01:22:53 KST

The Hind Rajab Foundation has filed a complaint with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Israeli medical officials over torture and mistreatment of Palestinian detainees at the Sde Teiman military detention facility.
Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth reported on Saturday that the Brussels-based rights group submitted the complaint to the ICC prosecutor under Article 15 of the Rome Statute.
The complaint targets the Israeli Medical Association, Health Ministry officials and medical personnel over their involvement in abuses at the facility in southern Israel.
The foundation said the practices amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Allegations of systematic mistreatment
Since October 2023, the Sde Teiman military base in Israel’s southern Negev desert has been used to hold thousands of Palestinians from Gaza, most of them civilians, including men, women, children, older people, journalists and health and humanitarian workers.
The foundation said that detainees were classified as "unlawful combatants," a designation it described as a means of denying them basic legal protections and holding them without charge or trial.
The complaint said Israel's Health Ministry established a medical facility at Sde Teiman shortly after October 7, 2023.
According to the foundation, medical personnel were required to sign documents placing them under military police authority rather than the army's Medical Corps.
The complaint seeks investigations into officials from Israel's health and defence ministries, medical personnel, hospital administrators and the Israeli Medical Association.
Those named include former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, association chairman Zion Hagay, director general Leah Wapner and ethics board chairman Yosef Walfisch.
Detainees restrained during medical treatment
The foundation said a Health Ministry directive issued on December 19, 2023, required medical personnel to treat detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded.
According to the complaint, the directive also permitted forced medical treatment without adequate safeguards.
Medical staff were allegedly instructed not to disclose their names and to sign medical records using only their professional titles.
The foundation argued that these practices obscured individual responsibility and hindered documentation of injuries.
Amputations, surgeries without adequate pain relief
The foundation cited accounts from Israeli medical workers and former Palestinian detainees describing abuses at Sde Teiman.
According to the complaint, a doctor wrote to Israeli authorities in April 2024 that two detainees had undergone leg amputations within one week because of injuries caused by shackling.
The doctor reportedly described shackling as routine at the facility.
The foundation also cited medical workers who told the Associated Press they had witnessed surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
One account described an elderly detainee screaming and shaking during leg surgery.
Other workers reported detainees being blindfolded, forced to wear diapers and restrained by all four limbs to hospital beds.
The foundation said at least 29 detainees had died at Sde Teiman by November 2025 because of physical violence, medical neglect or both.
Medical association accused of complicity
The complaint accused the Israeli Medical Association of helping legitimise torture and mistreatment at the facility.
The foundation said the association responded to allegations of medical complicity with general reminders about professional ethics rather than sufficient investigative action.
It also said findings from an internal Health Ministry ethical assessment following a visit to Sde Teiman were not publicly released.
"Instead of investigating the allegations, leaders of the association publicly defended the medical care provided at Sde Teiman," the foundation said.
Established in February 2024 and based in Brussels, the Hind Rajab Foundation has pursued legal cases in several countries against Israeli officials and military personnel over violations in Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel's genoc’de in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures.

The US military will live-stream the upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Oct 8, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” Leo, the first pope from the United States, said in a social media post, without mentioning the Pentagon plan.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he added in the message posted on the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.
The livestream plan, championed by Hegseth, has drawn opposition from lawmakers, including from President Donald Trump’s Republicans, religious leaders and international observers.
Trump himself has said he has not yet decided whether to allow the live feed, while Vice-President J.D. Vance, who is a Catholic, expressed scepticism over whether the Pentagon would proceed with livestreaming the scheduled Dec 3 execution.
Vance also said he would not watch the livestream if it went ahead.
The execution plan comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following a botched lethal injection of a Tennessee woman last week. REUTERS

The National Hurricane Center said Isaias had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, with sustained winds of about 35 miles (55 km) per hour. The system was expected to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley before dissipating Sunday.
Forecasters warned of 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) of rain across parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia, with localized totals reaching 15 inches (38 cm).
Power outages affected about 872,000 customers nationwide, including more than 434,000 in Florida and around 317,000 in Alabama, according to PowerOutage.us.

The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights has urged India to immediately release people "arbitrarily detained" in protests against misconduct by electoral authorities.
"We are concerned by reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today's large-scale demonstrations in Delhi," the office said in a statement on Saturday.
"All those arbitrarily detained must be immediately and unconditionally released."
Earlier, Indian police detained the head of the satirical "cockroach" online movement as well as thousands of protesters trying to take part in a major demonstration in New Delhi against the country's election commissioner.
The protest is the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision by the Election Commission of India (ECI) that purges 130 million people, mostly Muslims, from the voter roll.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital, according to a statement from the group.
"They're being denied access to their lawyers and cut off from all contact with others," it said, adding the trio had been taken to "an undisclosed location".
The CJP also said that thousands more protesters were detained in New Delhi as they attempted to march to the main Jantar Mantar protest site, defying a massive security clampdown.
"More than 15,000 protesters have been detained," Ajinkya Shinde, a CJP leader, said at a news conference in Delhi.
"We will be back; let them fill up all the jails," Shinde said.
Dozens of protesters shouted anti-government slogans as they were taken away in police vehicles, reporters witnessed.
Calls for the ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar to step down have intensified in recent weeks as opposition parties and critics said his commission's voter-roll revision could disenfranchise millions of constituents and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Ahead of the protest, authorities in the capital deployed thousands of police, closed dozens of metro stations, cancelled more than 200 trains and temporarily shut down mobile internet around the protest site.
The demonstrations are widely seen as a reprise of the "cockroach" movement's mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal.
This time, protesters are demanding Kumar's resignation and a halt to the voter revision exercise.
The accusations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office.
Opposition parties have long alleged that legitimate voters are being struck off lists in India.
The issue flared up last month when the Indian Express newspaper reported that key decisions linked to the revision were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.
The Hindu newspaper reported that more than 5,000 protesters had been detained.
Media outlets, including The Scroll and Newslaundry, said their journalists had also been detained briefly.

The demonstration, billed as the "National March for Palestine," was part of a Global Day of Action organized by pro-Palestinian groups staging coordinated protests around the world.
Demonstrators waved Palestinian flags, wore red and green clothing and carried placards reading "Stop Arming Israel," "Sanctions on Israel Now," "Free Palestine," "End the Genocide in Gaza," "Ceasefire Now" and "Get Israel Out of British Politics."
One of the most prominent displays was a giant banner calling for the release of Barghouti, a senior Fatah figure serving five consecutive life sentences and an additional 40 years in an Israeli prison for terrorist attacks that killed five Israelis and wounded numerous others.
Footage circulating on social media showed protesters unfurling the large banner during the march. Another participant was seen carrying a portrait of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in February during Operation Roaring Lion.
Barghouti, a prominent figure in the Palestinian national movement, has been described by some Western supporters as a Palestinian equivalent of Nelson Mandela. However, an Israel Prison Service report previously obtained by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth described him as a dangerous prisoner who continues to promote efforts to unite Hamas and Fatah under his leadership while conveying violent messages from prison.
According to previous reports, Hamas demanded Barghouti's release during recent hostage negotiations, but Israel rejected the request.
A separate pro-Israel counterdemonstration was held in London, where participants carried signs calling on authorities to take action against antisemitism, including one urging police to "Start policing hatred of Jews."
Similar anti-Israel demonstrations took place in Berlin and the southern Italian city of Naples.
At the Berlin protest, demonstrators displayed a banner titled "The Cities of Palestine Before Colonialism," featuring a map of Israel in which Hebrew city names had been crossed out and replaced with Arabic names.
Among the examples was Jerusalem, whose Hebrew name was removed and replaced with "Al-Quds," the city's Arabic name.
The demonstrations formed part of the wider international protest campaign against Israel, with rallies taking place just days after commemorations marking three years since the October 7 massacre.

Rights group files ICC complaint against Israeli medical officials over torture of Palestinian detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:12:35 UTC
01:12:35 KST

Zein Khalil and Mohammad Sio
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
The Hind Rajab Foundation filed a complaint with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Israeli medical officials over torture and mistreatment of Palestinian detainees, Israeli media reported Saturday.
The complaint targets the Israeli Medical Association, Health Ministry officials and medical personnel over abuses at the Sde Teiman military detention facility in southern Israel.
According to the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, the Brussels-based rights group submitted the complaint to the ICC prosecutor under Article 15 of the Rome Statute.
The foundation said that Israeli medical personnel and officials were involved in practices amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Allegations of systematic mistreatment
Since October 2023, the Sde Teiman military base in Israel’s southern Negev desert has been used to hold thousands of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, most of them civilians, including men, women, children, older people, journalists and health and humanitarian workers.
The foundation said that detainees were classified as "unlawful combatants," a designation it described as a means of denying them basic legal protections and holding them without charge or trial.
The complaint said Israel's Health Ministry established a medical facility at Sde Teiman shortly after Oct. 7, 2023.
According to the foundation, medical personnel were required to sign documents placing them under military police authority rather than the army's Medical Corps.
The complaint seeks investigations into officials from Israel's health and defense ministries, medical personnel, hospital administrators and the Israeli Medical Association.
Those named include former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, association chairman Zion Hagay, director general Leah Wapner and ethics board chairman Yosef Walfisch.
Detainees restrained during medical treatment
The foundation said a Health Ministry directive issued on Dec. 19, 2023, required medical personnel to treat detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded.
According to the complaint, the directive also permitted forced medical treatment without adequate safeguards.
Medical staff were allegedly instructed not to disclose their names and to sign medical records using only their professional titles.
The foundation argued that these practices obscured individual responsibility and hindered documentation of injuries.
Amputations, surgeries without adequate pain relief
The foundation cited accounts from Israeli medical workers and former Palestinian detainees describing abuses at Sde Teiman.
According to the complaint, a doctor wrote to Israeli authorities in April 2024 that two detainees had undergone leg amputations within one week because of injuries caused by shackling.
The doctor reportedly described shackling as routine at the facility.
The foundation also cited medical workers who told the Associated Press they had witnessed surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
One account described an elderly detainee screaming and shaking during leg surgery.
Other workers reported detainees being blindfolded, forced to wear diapers and restrained by all four limbs to hospital beds.
The foundation said at least 29 detainees had died at Sde Teiman by November 2025 because of physical violence, medical neglect or both.
Medical association accused of complicity
The complaint accused the Israeli Medical Association of helping legitimize torture and mistreatment at the facility.
The foundation said the association responded to allegations of medical complicity with general reminders about professional ethics rather than sufficient investigative action.
It also said findings from an internal Health Ministry ethical assessment following a visit to Sde Teiman were not publicly released.
"Instead of investigating the allegations, leaders of the association publicly defended the medical care provided at Sde Teiman," the foundation said.
Established in February 2024 and based in Brussels, the Hind Rajab Foundation has pursued legal cases in several countries against Israeli officials and military personnel over alleged violations in Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures.
