Belief in supernatural evil is linked to blaming the system for poverty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:00:30 UTC
23:00:30 KST

People who believe in supernatural evil are more likely to blame society for poverty, while those who believe in a supportive deity are less likely to do so. These findings come from a recent survey of South Korean adults published in the Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion. The research reveals how specific theological ideas intersect with political ideology to shape public views on social inequality.
Sociologists use the term stratification beliefs to describe how people explain why some individuals are wealthy and others are impoverished. In this field of study, explanations for poverty are generally divided into two main categories. Individualistic beliefs place the blame on the poor themselves, citing a lack of effort, talent, or financial discipline. Structuralist beliefs fault the broader economic and social systems, pointing to issues like discrimination, low wages, or underfunded schools.
How a person explains poverty often predicts their support for welfare programs and redistributive economic policies. Past research has examined how religion influences these views, but most studies have focused simply on whether a person belongs to a specific denomination. Researchers often categorize people as Catholic, Protestant, or Buddhist without examining the specific nature of their personal faith.
To address this gap, sociologists Jong Hyun Jung and Muhan Chen of Sungkyunkwan University, along with Harris Hyun-soo Kim of Ewha Womans University, designed a study focused on specific supernatural beliefs. They wanted to understand how belief in a supportive divine presence compares to a belief in supernatural evil when it comes to predicting attitudes toward poverty. The team also sought to test these relationships outside of a Western context.
They chose South Korea for its unique blend of religious traditions, where Buddhism, Protestantism, and Catholicism coexist alongside a large population of people with no religious affiliation. Supernatural belief in South Korea is also moderate compared to heavily Christian nations like the United States. This environment provided a distinct cultural backdrop to see if previous theories about religion and economics hold true in a different setting.
The researchers analyzed data from an online survey of 1,632 South Korean adults conducted in August 2024. The participant pool was recruited to match the national population in terms of age, gender, and geographic region. Because the survey included questions about a person’s relationship with God, the researchers excluded respondents who stated they completely disbelieved in a deity.
The survey asked participants to rate their agreement with statements measuring two distinct theological concepts. Belief in divine support was measured by asking if respondents felt they had a warm relationship with God and if God was responsive to their personal needs. Belief in supernatural evil was measured by asking participants if they believed in the existence of demons, hell, and the devil.
Participants then rated the importance of various causes of poverty. To measure individualistic views, the survey asked about factors like personal irresponsibility and a lack of thrift. To gauge structuralist views, respondents evaluated the role of low wages, prejudice, and a failure of private industry to provide enough good jobs. The researchers also asked participants to rate their own political orientation on a scale from very liberal to very conservative.
When the researchers analyzed the data, they found that neither religious belief was associated with individualistic explanations for poverty. People who reported a warm relationship with God were no more likely to blame poor individuals for their circumstances than those with weaker divine beliefs. The same held true for those who firmly believed in demons and hell.
The authors suggest that this lack of association might stem from the charitable aspects of religious involvement. Believing in a supportive deity might increase a person’s sense of compassion for others. This humanitarian impulse could prevent believers from harshly judging those who fall below the poverty line, even if their faith encourages self-reliance in other areas of life.
A different pattern emerged when the researchers looked at structuralist explanations for poverty. Belief in divine support was negatively associated with blaming systemic and economic issues. In other words, individuals who felt closely supported by God were less likely to view poor schools or low wages as the primary drivers of poverty.
This result aligns with an academic concept known as the insurance effect. Some sociologists argue that religion provides psychological comfort and a sense of security that functions much like a social safety net. People who rely on a divine figure for support during hard times might feel less need for government intervention, prompting them to discount systemic explanations for economic hardship.
Conversely, belief in supernatural evil was positively associated with structuralist views. Respondents who expressed a strong belief in the devil, hell, and demons were more likely to blame society and economic systems for poverty. The researchers interpret this through the lens of a spiritual warfare worldview, which sees the universe as a battleground between good and evil.
In this worldview, adversarial supernatural forces are thought to be actively working to harm humanity. Believers might view oppressive social structures, rampant discrimination, or failing schools as manifestations of these dark forces. As a result, they may attribute the suffering of the poor to these external, corrupt systems rather than pointing the finger at the individuals experiencing the hardship.
The research team also looked at how political orientation interacted with these supernatural beliefs. In general, conservative respondents were much less likely to endorse structuralist explanations for poverty than liberal respondents. This aligns with a wide body of existing political science research.
However, a strong belief in supernatural evil modified this trend among political conservatives. For respondents who leaned conservative, higher levels of belief in demons and hell were linked to a sharp increase in structuralist views of poverty. In fact, conservatives with the strongest belief in supernatural evil were nearly identical to liberals in their tendency to blame the system for poverty. Belief in supernatural evil did not have this effect on liberal respondents, who generally favored structuralist explanations regardless of their religious views.
The researchers note several caveats to consider when interpreting these results. The survey captured a single snapshot in time, meaning the data cannot prove a specific directional relationship between the variables. It is entirely possible that a person’s preexisting views on poverty and inequality shape how they interpret their religious faith, rather than the other way around.
Cultural differences also provide important context for these results. Research in psychology indicates that people in East Asian societies often lean toward environmental and situational explanations for human behavior, whereas Westerners frequently favor individualistic explanations. This cultural baseline in South Korea might suppress any potential link between religious beliefs and individualistic views on poverty, a dynamic that could look entirely different in the United States or Europe.
Additionally, the concepts of God and evil carry different meanings across varying religious traditions. A devout Buddhist and a practicing Protestant might interpret survey questions about supernatural forces in entirely different ways. Future research will need to untangle how specific doctrinal teachings within different faiths interact with public opinions on wealth and inequality.
The study, “Belief in Supernatural Agents and Lay Explanations About the Causes of Poverty,” was authored by Jong Hyun Jung, Muhan Chen, and Harris Hyun-soo Kim.

Ukrainian Forces down some 4,700 aerial targets, over 48,000 drones in Sept
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:58:40 EEST
22:58:40 KST

In September 2026, the Ukrainian military destroyed more than 4,700 aerial targets and neutralized more than 48,000 tactical-level drones, the press service of the Ukrainian Air Force said on its Telegram channel on Saturday.
In particular, 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided air-to-surface missiles, six Iskander-K cruise missiles, and eight Zircon anti-ship missiles were destroyed during the month.
In addition, 86 S8000 BanderoL missiles, 2,722 Shahed-131/136 attack UAVs, 1,935 Shahed-238 attack UAVs, 1,009 reconnaissance drones, and 719 Lancet UAVs were destroyed.
"During September 2026, the Defense Forces destroyed more than 4,700 aerial targets and, in addition, neutralized more than 48,000 tactical-level UAVs," the press service said.
The Air Force also reported that its aviation units carried out more than 1,600 sorties in August. Of these, approximately 1,300 involved fighter aircraft providing air cover, while more than 250 were missions involving fire strikes and air support for ground forces.

Italy-Serbia: Belgrade Celebrates the 100th Anniversary of the ICE Agency
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:54:36 CEST
22:54:36 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Serbia, Luca Gori, attended the event organized at Palazzo Italia in Belgrade to mark the centennial of ICE—Italian Trade Agency (ITA). The event celebrated the Agency’s 100 years of activity in promoting Italian businesses and supporting their presence in international markets. In addition to the Ambassador and the Director of the ICE Office in Belgrade, Maria Lucia Martorelli, the evening was also attended by representatives from institutions, the Italian and Serbian business communities, as well as the Agency’s partners in Serbia.
                                    
During the event, the role played by ICE—from 1926 to the present—in supporting the internationalization of the Italian production system and in fostering Italy’s economic and commercial relations with other countries was highlighted. The celebration in Belgrade also served as an opportunity to highlight the strength of economic ties between Italy and Serbia. In 2025, trade between the two countries exceeded 5 billion euros, and in the first half of 2026, it totaled approximately 3 billion euros—a 32% increase compared to the first half of 2025.
                                    
“Reaching the 100-year milestone means celebrating a century of serving ‘Made in Italy’ around the world. Along this journey, ICE has successfully evolved and modernized to effectively respond to global challenges and the digital transformation, remaining a key point of reference under the auspices of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MAECI),” stated Maria Lucia Martorelli, Director of the ICE Office in Belgrade. “The Belgrade Office,” she continued, “which has been present in Serbia since 1997, serves as a strategic bridge in the Balkans, resolutely supporting Italian companies seeking to grow and establish themselves in this extraordinarily dynamic market.”
   “Over the past 100 years, ICE has supported the growth and internationalization of Italian companies, making a decisive contribution to promoting ‘Made in Italy’ around the world,” stated Luca Gori, Ambassador to Serbia. “Here in Serbia,” he added, “ICE’s contribution is an essential component of the ‘Sistema Italia’ initiative, all the more so at a time when we are working together to prepare for Expo Belgrade 2027.”

'Neither wanted to hang up': Putin-Trump diesel deal call draws ire of Ukraine, allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:53:31 UTC
22:53:31 KST

A conversation on Friday between President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump was "very substantive and friendly", and neither leader wanted to be the first to end the call, Russian news agency Interfax quoted a Kremlin aide as saying.
During the call, the presidents agreed that Russia would supply diesel to the US and global markets to lower fuel prices, prompting an unexpected temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian fuel that has dismayed Ukraine.
The Kremlin said most of the conversation focused on efforts to resolve the war in Ukraine. Putin also downplayed the likelihood of three-way peace talks resuming soon.
Interfax cited Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov on Saturday as saying the conversation lasted an hour and a half.
"Neither wanted to be the first to hang up," he said. "They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time."
Zelenskyy
Kiev is relying on US support in negotiations to end the war.
After news of the call broke, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the diesel deal in unusually blunt terms, calling it a "weak decision" and "an investment in a war that must be ended."
The West imposed sanctions, including restrictions on Russian energy imports, after the Russia-Ukraine war in February 2022. 
On Friday, negotiators from the US, Ukraine and European countries held talks in Miami aimed at reaching agreement on a unified peace proposal in the coming weeks that could be presented to Russia, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
UK
The UK government vowed to maintain pressure on Russia following a recently announced diesel deal.
"The UK’s position could not be clearer. We will continue working closely with international partners to ensure Ukraine has the military and financial support it needs to defend itself. We will also maintain pressure on Russia," a UK government spokesperson said in a written statement.
The spokesperson noted that London would maintain pressure through the "toughest sanctions regime" it has ever imposed by increasing the cost of "Putin’s aggression" and supporting efforts to secure peace.
Sweden
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson voiced regret.
"We regret the US agreement with Russia to supply diesel, as energy revenues are a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression," Kristersson wrote on X.
He reiterated Sweden's ongoing position to stand with Ukraine "for as long as it takes," and called for more pressure to be put on Russia and more support to be provided to Ukraine.
Germany
Germany said it would continue to push for new EU sanctions against Russia despite Moscow's agreement with Washington to release diesel to ease a fuel crunch.
"The German government sticks to its measures sanctioning Russia and is working jointly with its European partners on new sanctions," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.

When streets become a workplace: Gaza workers convert tents into offices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:50:05 UTC
22:50:05 KST

When streets become a workplace: Gaza workers convert tents into offices
Gaza doctors, lawyers, and teachers have converted tents into offices to maintain a livelihood.
Khan Younis, Gaza – Dr Mohammed al-Khalidi, a specialist in prosthetics and orthotics, sits in a modest tent in al-Mawasi, southern Gaza. It has been his place of work since his clinic on al-Bahr Street in Rafah was destroyed by Israeli bombing in April 2024. His second and third clinics in Khan Younis’s Old City, southern Gaza, were subsequently destroyed by Israel in May 2025.
After this triple heartbreaking setback, al-Khalidi salvaged whatever medical equipment he could find and moved into his new office, a tent, where he has received patients for the past two years.
This transitory space reflects a new reality in Gaza since Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave began in October 2023. Offices, clinics and shops have been wiped out in waves of Israeli air raids over the past three years, leaving professionals to conduct their work from tents or on the road.
This phenomenon emerged in December 2023 following the displacement of Khan Younis residents to a narrow strip of coastal land between their hometown and Deir el-Balah.
After a ceasefire, repeatedly broken by Israel, was announced for the enclave in October 2025, more of these tent offices, surgeries and shops emerged across Gaza as professionals sought to continue their practices.
Challenges
Working within these canvas confines presents multiple challenges for al-Khalidi. There is limited space, unreliable electricity, and the intense heat and loud noises to deal with.
The setting bears little resemblance to his previous practice in a bricks-and-mortar office, but he still feels this arrangement is better than suspending services altogether.
There is a massive need for prosthetics in Gaza, where between 5,000 and 6,000 people have undergone amputations between October 2023 and October 2025.
“Working from a temporary space is nothing like working in a fully equipped clinic, but for me, it is better than stopping the service altogether,” al-Khalidi told Al Jazeera.
“Patients who need prosthetic limbs or orthotic devices cannot always wait until conditions return to normal. Some have lost a limb during the war, while others need follow-up care or adjustments to devices they rely on in their daily lives.”
More than four-in-five buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since Israel’s genocidal war began in 2023, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS), creating a real estate crisis.
The lack of office space has seen rental prices reach unaffordable levels for most Gaza professionals. But resilience, necessity, and duty have encouraged Palestinians to find solutions to this situation. Tents are now where lawyers meet clients, doctors treat patients, and traders sell their wares.
Repeated displacement
After Omar al-Tawashi, a civil engineer and construction auditor, saw his office destroyed in an Israeli air strike in August 2024, he began work from his home in July 2025. But that too met the same fate, so he shifted operations to a tent in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, to continue his work.
“My move to a tent was not a professional choice. It was a direct result of the destruction of the place where I used to work, compounded by the rental crisis, which made finding an alternative office extremely difficult,” he said.
“In some cases, rents have risen to more than 10 times their pre-war levels, making a new office beyond my means”.
The tent is not a suitable environment for his engineering work, but there is no alternative for al-Tawashi.
“There is heat, cold and noise, and none of the privacy needed when discussing projects or reviewing technical files,” Omar said. “But stopping work would mean losing my source of income”.
In the crowded market in Nuseirat camp, central Gaza, accountant Mahmoud Shaheen receives clients inside a small tent amid the sound of neighbouring vendors and passers-by.
Shaheen was once responsible for a Gaza-based company’s accounts, but the office was destroyed in an Israeli air strike in November 2025.
“Moving to a tent was not so much a professional choice as a response to a reality imposed by the war,” he told Al Jazeera.
With the start of the new school year in Gaza last month, tents have been pitched across the country as substitutes for schools destroyed in Israeli air raids or converted into refuges for the displaced.
School starts
Teacher Palestine Hussein has been forced to adapt to this new reality. She previously taught English at an educational centre in Bureij in central Gaza, which she had spent years building.
It was destroyed in seconds when an Israeli air raid destroyed the educational facility, so she now teaches children from a tent at al-Balata, a camp for displaced Palestinians in Nuseirat.
There is a lack of seats for the students, ventilation, or protection from the noise and heat. But despite these challenges, Hussein is determined to provide children in the camp with some form of education.
“Although the tent may appear to be a temporary place, to me it represents an attempt to hold on to what remains of my profession and rebuild my dream from scratch, even with the most basic resources,” Hussein told Al Jazeera.
New reality
Trader Khalil al-Tahrawi saw his clothing store in Nuseirat destroyed by Israeli bombing in October 2023. After salvaging surviving merchandise from his destroyed shop, he displayed his goods – mostly men’s T-shirts and jeans – at a small tent in the Nuseirat market.
He pays $350 a month in rent for the small patch of pavement to sell the clothing, which he removes every night to protect them from thieves.
“This routine makes the work even more difficult and consumes my time and energy,” al-Tahrawi told Al Jazeera.
Repeated power cuts, unreliable internet and shortages of equipment have complicated efforts by Gaza’s business community to rebuild during this period of a relative decrease in bombing.
Customers, too, are changing their consumption patterns, heading to certain towns or camps for a particular good or service. Often what they find are prices more inflated than during Israel’s siege on Gaza before Israel’s genocidal war.
One customer, Mohammed Zweid, a 24-year-old IT worker, looks through a market in Nuseirat. “Accessing professionals in tents and temporary spaces is better than having no service at all,” he told Al Jazeera. “The transformation has changed not only where services are provided, but also how they are experienced.”

“An 11-year-old boy was killed as a result of an enemy attack in the Nikopol district,” Hanzha said. “The Russians dropped a munition from a drone in the Pokrovska community. Two more children were wounded – a 12-year-old boy and a 10-year-old girl.”

The Nikopol district, located across the Dnipro River from the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, faces daily Russian artillery shelling, loitering munition attacks, and tactical drone drops targeting civilian areas and municipal infrastructure.
Daylight drone and ballistic barrages across central Ukraine
The fatal drone drop in the Pokrovska community formed part of a wave of Russian strikes targeting non-combatants and civilian settlements across central and eastern Ukraine on Saturday.
In Kyiv, Russian forces conducted a daylight ballistic missile strike on the northern Obolonskyi district, hitting a restaurant building, sparking a major blaze, and scattering missile debris across an adjacent residential courtyard.

‘4-year-olds sleeping in the woods’: police expose suspected child-begging ring in northern Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:48:15 UTC
22:48:15 KST

Israeli police detained more than 40 people near Nazareth in a major crackdown on a suspected begging network that brought Palestinian women and children into Israel, including mothers who allegedly spent entire days soliciting money at busy intersections while holding infants in extreme heat.
The operation, carried out Friday by Northern District Police and Border Police officers, targeted apartments and makeshift shelters in wooded areas near the northern Israeli city. Among those found were children as young as four and five who police believe had been sent to intersections to collect money for adult organizers.
"We saw difficult and heartbreaking scenes," Inspector Tal Krispin, an officer with the Nazareth Police municipal policing unit, told ynet. "I questioned 21-year-old mothers who stood at intersections around Nazareth with babies less than a year old, begging all day in extreme heat of more than 40 degrees."
According to Krispin, some women could collect as much as 3,000 shekels in a single day. "They deliberately bring babies to attract attention and sympathy from drivers," he said, describing findings from police questioning.
Investigators believe most of the women came from the Jenin area of the northern West Bank, while others traveled from Nablus. Police suspect Israeli and Palestinian intermediaries arranged their entry into Israel and distributed them among busy intersections in Nazareth, Wadi Ara and Ahihud.
The alleged operation also involved young children who approached vehicles stopped at traffic lights, knocked on windows and asked motorists for money. Police believe the children were expected to hand over their daily collections to the adults who had sent them out to beg.
Many of the children were found living in wooded areas or temporary encampments near the intersections, according to police. Investigators are examining the roles of the adults suspected of organizing their activities and collecting the money.
The operation resulted in the detention of more than 40 people suspected of being in Israel illegally. Adult suspects were taken for questioning at the Nazareth police station, and a court extended the detention of several of them. Police said some women had previously been arrested multiple times but returned to Israel to continue begging.
Children below the age of criminal responsibility were transferred to Palestinian Authority representatives following coordination with the Israeli military. Adults being returned to Palestinian-controlled territory were taken to checkpoints, Krispin said.
The crackdown follows years of complaints about women and children approaching cars at major intersections across northern Israel. Around Nazareth, where tens of thousands of motorists travel through busy junctions, the practice has become a familiar sight, with young children moving between vehicles and mothers carrying infants approaching drivers for donations.
Beyond concerns about the suspected exploitation of children, local officials have warned that their presence on heavily traveled roads poses safety risks for both the children and motorists.
Shlomit Shichor-Reichman, head of the Jezreel Valley Regional Council, welcomed the police operation after what she described as dozens of requests for enforcement.
"After dozens of appeals I submitted on the issue, it is good to finally see decisive action to restore law and order at our intersections and throughout our region," she said, praising the Northern District Police and Brig. Gen. Ran Ofir.
Shichor-Reichman also described the presence of people staying in Israel illegally at major intersections as a security concern, warning that it could create opportunities for nationalist violence. She urged authorities to focus not only on those begging but also on the suspected organizers arranging their entry into Israel.
"Beyond the appalling exploitation of children, the presence of people staying in Israel illegally at major intersections constitutes a serious violation of sovereignty," she said.
She called on police to continue pursuing the intermediaries allegedly operating the network, saying enforcement should target those responsible for organizing the activities rather than end with the detention and removal of women and children found at the intersections.

Yemen says advancing against Houthis around key Bab al-Mandab strait
Yemen said Saturday that forces were advancing against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a week after the country's Saudi-backed government announced that it was initiating a counter-offensive to take back territory seized by the pro-Iran group during last month's lightning offensive. In Riyadh, diplomatic sources reported a missile attack on the civilian airport, with at least five Saudi nationals wounded being treated in intensive care.
Yemeni military sources said on Saturday their forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait but have not yet secured control of the waterway, after the government launched an operation to capture lost territory.
The Saudi-backed government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the pro-Iran group seized Yemen's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area but they claimed to have repelled the assault.
"Saudi-led forces attempted to advance from the Ras al-Ara area in Lahj governorate towards the area south of Bab al-Mandab," Hizam al-Asad, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, told AFP.
"However, our forces repelled them outside the Bab al-Mandab zone, inflicting heavy losses in personnel and equipment and forcing the survivors to retreat.
"Our forces maintain control over Bab al-Mandab, Mayun Island, and the remaining areas along the country's western coast," he said.
Sources from the military of Yemen's internationally recognised government also said Mayun Island – located in the heart of the strait – remained in Houthi hands as fighting continued.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.
Clashes in western Yemen, specifically around the strait, had killed at least 63 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP on Saturday.
Thirty-five members of government forces had been killed, while 28 Houthis had died, the sources said.

London Halal Forum kicks off, spotlighting global halal economy opportunities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:44:17 UTC
22:44:17 KST

Aysu Bicer
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
The London Halal Forum has kicked off on Saturday, bringing together entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and industry leaders to explore opportunities across a growing range of sectors.
The forum is organized by Halal360, a joint initiative of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce and Development and the Halal Products Development Company (HPDC), with Anadolu serving as its global communications partner.
Under the theme Halal Tayyib for Humanity, the forum will examine the halal economy’s expansion beyond certification and food products into investment, tourism, technology, supply chains, branding and international trade.
In his opening speech, Hassan Khalawi, Secretary-General of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture, said London offers an ideal environment for the halal industry to grow through creativity and international connectivity.
“We need the creativity and we need the connectivity, and this is what we can build and find easily here in London,” Khalawi said.
He stressed that the halal economy is moving beyond its traditional focus on food to encompass a wider range of Muslim lifestyle sectors, including media, technology and Islamic art.
At the forum’s second edition, held just 11 months after the inaugural event, organizers introduced three concepts focusing on halal lifestyle, halal technologies and Islamic art.
Khalawi said the aim is to take these initiatives beyond London and develop them in markets worldwide, highlighting plans for a halal reception in Paris and the upcoming ASEAN Halal Forum in Bangkok.
“What is next is to take that from here to the rest of the world,” he said, underlining the importance of international partnerships in expanding the industry.
Khalawi thanked the forum's partners and sponsors for helping "create creative halal concepts everywhere" as the intitiative expands globally. He noted that with the global Muslim population projected to reach between 25% to 30% by 2050, it is vital from a business perspective to understand the importance to "cover all lifestyle sectors."
'Halal has become more than a religious requirement'
For his part, Fahad bin Suliman Alnuhait, CEO of HPDC, said halal has become more than a religious requirement, emerging as a global benchmark for quality, safety and trust.
He said Saudi Arabia is seeking to transform its position from one of the world’s largest halal import markets into a producer and exporter under its Vision 2030 economic diversification strategy.
Alnuhait highlighted HPDC’s role in supporting this transformation through investments, industrial development and international cooperation.
Over its first three years, the company made more than six investments, enabled six factories and helped bring three international company headquarters to Saudi Arabia, he added.
The company also supported the creation of more than 3,000 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, while delivering 75 advisory projects and undertaking 10 international government projects to support halal strategy development across Organization of Islamic Cooperation member states, he explained.
Alnuhait said the London Halal Forum provides an important platform for connecting markets, producers and consumers, strengthening the halal value chain and creating new business opportunities.
“It's a bridge,” he said, describing the forum’s role in connecting European and UK markets with global opportunities.
Following the opening speeches, plaques were presented to sponsors. Anadolu Deputy Director General for Administrative and Financial Affairs Oguz Enis Peru received the plaque on behalf of Anadolu.

Global Islamic finance leaders to gather in London for annual AlBaraka Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:43:25 UTC
22:43:25 KST

Aysu Bicer
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Global financial and business leaders, policymakers and industry experts will gather in London on Oct. 13-14 for the 5th Annual AlBaraka Summit to discuss the role of Islamic finance in economic development.
The two-day event, held under the theme Ethics in Action: Rebuilding Foundations and Advancing the Global Impact of the Islamic Economy, will take place at JW Marriott Grosvenor House.
Anadolu will serve as the summit's global communications partner.
The gathering will bring together government ministers, scholars and representatives from Muslim-majority and non-Muslim-majority markets to explore ethical investment, financial inclusion, innovation and sustainable economic growth.
Discussions will focus on translating Islamic economic principles, including justice, accountability, risk-sharing and social responsibility, into practical outcomes across financial markets, regulation, technology and economic development.
The agenda will cover Islamic banking and capital markets, policy and regulation, social finance, Takaful, Waqf and Zakat, digitalization and entrepreneurship.
Participants will also examine the role of international financial centers in advancing the Islamic economy, the organizers said.
'Putting ethics into action'
"The Islamic economy has always been about more than financial products. Its foundations connect economic activity with justice, accountability and responsibility to society," Yousef Hassan Khalawi, secretary-general of the AlBaraka Forum for Islamic Economy, said in a statement.
"The challenge before us is to ensure those principles are not simply discussed, but put into action," he added.
Khalawi said London's position as a major international financial center made it an important venue for discussions on the future of Islamic finance.
"London provides an important setting for that conversation, connecting Islamic finance with one of the world's leading international financial centers," he said.
A panel of Islamic banking chief executives on the first day will examine policy, regulation and the sector’s global direction, including the evolution of regulatory frameworks, the role of ethics in public policy and priorities for the industry’s next phase.
The summit aims to explore how Islamic finance can strengthen its contribution to economic development by connecting financial activity with ethical principles and broader social responsibilities.

Trump, Zelensky clash over diesel deal as Russian strikes on Ukraine kill 21, including children
US President Donald Trump on Saturday told reporters that Ukraine should "get a new president", adding that his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries. This comes after Washington moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel and as Moscow's strikes on Ukraine, including the city of Zaporizhzhia, killed at least 21 people.
US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky traded barbs Saturday after Washington moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel and Moscow's continued strikes on Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including four children.
Trump, whose party faces dim prospects in next month's midterm elections partly over soaring US fuel prices, announced Friday that he had called Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin and agreed to allow Moscow to release large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Read moreTrump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
Ukraine and its European allies expressed dismay at the move, with Zelensky telling reporters Friday it was a "weak decision".
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas meanwhile said on Saturday that lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would only help fuel the Kremlin's war on Ukraine.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote online.
Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump told reporters that Zelensky had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries.
Trump said the strikes risk worsening global fuel shortages caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said of the strikes, before adding that Ukraine should "get a new president".
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
Deadly Ukraine bombardment
Moscow has intensified its deadly bombardment of Ukraine in recent months, sending civilian casualties soaring, while US-led efforts to broker an end to the more than four-and-a-half-year conflict remain deadlocked.
Early Saturday, a Russian glide bomb attack on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed 20 people, including three children, according to Ukraine's state rescue service.
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelensky said in a post on X.
An AFP correspondent at the scene saw rescuers pulling people from the rubble.
"We saw people under the rubble – a woman, her husband and a child," one rescuer, Daniil Pishkin, told AFP.
He added that he saw two people rescued from the wreckage but "unfortunately there was a little girl who died".
A resident of one of the buildings that was hit, who identified herself as Iryna, 69, said she just had time to seek refuge in the bathroom after receiving an air raid warning.
Her two neighbours were killed, she said.
"They were 75 years old. They were simply thrown out there, onto the street. They didn't make it to the hospital," she told AFP.
A Russian drone attack on Ukraine's central Dnipropetrovsk region killed an 11-year-old boy, the region's governor said.
Russian strikes meanwhile triggered large-scale power outages in the capital Kyiv, Ukraine's DTEK energy provider said, as the city's mayor reported a strike on a restaurant.
AFP reporters heard booms over Kyiv earlier in the day.
The Russian defence ministry said it had hit a "data centre" used by Ukraine's military.
Trump's talk with Putin
The announcement on Friday of the diesel deal came as US, Ukrainian and European officials were meeting in Miami, in a renewed diplomatic push to end the war.
Ukraine's delegation was headed home on Saturday, an aide to Zelensky said.
Trump, who has repeatedly touted his credentials as a peacemaker, has long sought to broker a deal since taking office last January.
US envoy Steve Witkoff posted to X after the meeting that the "constructive discussions" tackled "potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace".
Witkoff said the meeting included "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO".
The Kremlin said Saturday that Trump had conveyed his ideas about how to de-escalate the war to Putin during a phone call on Friday.
Putin received the proposals "with understanding", the Kremlin said, without elaborating on what the proposals were or the Russian president's response.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

As the detentions mounted, opposition leaders accused the government of suppressing dissent. BJP defended the police action and the SIR process, accusing the protesters of attempting to create unrest.
NEW DELHI: Delhi witnessed an extraordinary security clampdown on October 10 as police moved to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar. What began with barricades, transport restrictions and preventive detentions escalated into a day of mass arrests, street demonstrations, reported clashes and a fierce political confrontation over the right to protest.Delhi Police detained (and later released barring CJP leaders) more than 7,000 people across the national capital. Those detained included CJP leaders, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal, former Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, student activists, lawyers and other opposition leaders. Two police personnel were reported injured in incidents involving stone-pelting.As the detentions mounted, opposition leaders accused the government of suppressing dissent. BJP defended the police action and the SIR process, accusing the protesters of attempting to create unrest.CJP later announced to continue the agitation as it vowed to march again to Jantar Mantar on Sunday.Here is how the day unfolded for protesters, from the security measures before sunrise to the political confrontation that followed.
Early morning: Delhi tightens security, detentions begin
Delhi Police denied permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar, citing procedural lapses and law-and-order concerns. Authorities planned to deploy around 35,000 police and paramilitary personnel, with barricades, checkpoints, metro restrictions and mobile internet curbs in parts of central Delhi. Services to and from New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin stations were expected to be particularly affected.Police personnel wearing body cameras and drones were deployed for surveillance.Police also detained 30–40 people with criminal records as a preventive measure. At least 600 people had been detained across Delhi by 9am.
Morning: CJP leaders and Dhruv Rathee detained
CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained inside an aircraft shortly after it landed in Delhi from Mumbai. CJP called the action pre-planned and demanded their immediate release.YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was also detained from his Gurugram residence. CJP accused the government of targeting young people who questioned its actions.CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh and content creator Kavya Karnatac were also reported detained. CJP later alleged that Ratna Singh was being held inside a car surrounded by around 35 police personnel and the deputy commissioner of police. Police also placed several Congress workers and members of other political parties under house arrest ahead of the demonstration.Meanwhile, BJP president Nitin Nabin accused Rahul Gandhi and CJP associates of attempting to destabilise the country for political gains, alleging that their actions were driven by foreign forces.
Late morning: Students, lawyers and activists detained
More than 400 SFI members, other student activists and lawyers marching from the Supreme Court towards Jantar Mantar were detained. SFI and Left party workers staged protests at INA and near the BJP headquarters as the protest crackdown continued.Former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan was also reported detained.Student leader Neha Bora, CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya, and activist Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among those detained near INA market while heading towards the protest. Bora had led a march from Jor Bagh towards Dilli Haat-INA.CJP named Ajinkya Shinde to lead the protest in a pre-recorded video. Following the announcement, Ajinkya urged protesters to turn any location where police stopped them into their “Jantar Mantar”.Congress MP Shashi Tharoor described the situation as an “undeclared Emer-GenZ”. He criticised the heavy security deployment, train cancellations, metro closures and restrictions on movement.
Afternoon: Kejriwal and Mamata detained
Former Delhi CM Arvind Kejriwal, former Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee were detained while heading to join the protest. Mamata said they had been taken around in a prisoner van for two hours. She announced a sit-in at Dwarka North police station and said she would join the INDIA march on Monday.Congress leaders Mallikarjun Kharge and Priyanka Gandhi criticised the crackdown ahead of the planned protest. Kharge accused the Modi government of suppressing dissent, saying it had turned the “mother of democracy” into a "muzzled democracy”. Meanwhile, Priyanka alleged that the government had curtailed constitutional rights.Police officials reported stones being pelted at a bus carrying detained protesters in Jhandewalan. Two police personnel, including a Pink Force member, were reported injured. Another officer was injured in alleged stone-pelting near Baba Kharak Singh Marg in Connaught Place, where police said a scuffle broke out as they tried to disperse protesters.By late afternoon, the reported detention count had risen from at least 600 in the morning to around 1,000 by afternoon.
BJP defends SIR, criticises opposition
BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra accused Rahul Gandhi of attempting to drag the President into a street protest. The party defended the police action, describing it as a victory for democracy over “mob rule”. Nabin had earlier accused the protesters of trying to destabilise the country.
Court intervention and challenges to restrictions
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant communicated to authorities that lawyers detained while peacefully protesting outside the Supreme Court should be released. The intervention followed an urgent letter from the Supreme Court Bar Association, which said several advocates had been taken to the Yamuna Sports Complex.CPM general secretary MA Baby filed a petition in the Supreme Court challenging restrictions imposed ahead of the protest, including curbs on metro services and mobile internet connectivity. TMC spokesperson Saket Gokhale also wrote to the Delhi high court’s acting chief justice, seeking suo motu intervention over the transport restrictions.
Evening: Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi sharpen attack
Rahul Gandhi targeted PM Modi, Amit Shah, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, CEC Gyanesh Kumar and national security adviser Ajit Doval. He accused them of attacking the Constitution and vowed to continue the fight to defend democratic rights. Mamata Banerjee said she would remain in Delhi and join the INDIA march on Monday, in protest against the treatment of young people and other protesters.
Meanwhile, an open letter signed by 124 former IAS and IFS officers strongly defended the Election Commission and the SIR process, adding to the debate over the electoral-roll revision.
CJP vows to return to Jantar Mantar
CJP in a press conference announced to march to Jantar Mantar again on Sunday.
It said they will "not back down until demands are met" after mass detentions and alleged the Modi government feared that a united opposition could threaten its hold on power.

Slovakia Rejects Global Pledge on Returning Ukrainian Children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:36:00 UTC
22:36:00 KST

Slovakia was the only EU member state that refused to sign an international declaration committing to the return of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred to Russia, drawing severe condemnation from domestic opposition lawmakers.
According to Rapporteur, the “Toronto Pledge,” adopted on Sept. 29 during the multilateral Pathways to Peace conference, was endorsed by the EU and 26 of its 27 member states. Bratislava’s absence from the roster of signatories went largely unnoticed until the Slovak liberal opposition party Freedom and Solidarity (SaS) publicly disclosed the boycott on Friday, Oct. 9.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
SaS denounced the decision by Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico’s left-nationalist government as an “international disgrace” and an act of political “collaboration with the Kremlin.”
“Whom did this decision serve? Certainly not Ukrainian children, nor Slovakia. Once again, they are helping a man who is subject to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court,” the SaS leadership said in an official statement, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Fico’s pro-Moscow alignment
The decision to break European solidarity on child abductions follows a consistent pattern of foreign policy recalibration by Fico since returning to office in late 2023.
Under Fico’s leadership, Bratislava halted state-funded military aid shipments to the Armed Forces of Ukraine, repeatedly obstructed EU sanctions packages aimed at Russia’s fossil fuel sector, and called for the resumption of standard commercial and diplomatic ties with Moscow.
Finland Approves 35th Military Aid Package for Ukraine
In May, Fico became one of the few European heads of government to travel to Moscow to attend official Victory Day commemorations alongside Putin.
Opposition legislators and human rights advocates emphasized that by refusing to sign the declaration, Slovakia aligned itself against universal humanitarian principles. The International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Putin and Russian Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in March 2023, charging them with the war crime of unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied regions of Ukraine to Russia.
Slovak civil society organizations echoed the opposition’s criticism, warning that isolating the country from European human rights initiatives damages Bratislava’s credibility within both the EU and NATO.
International accountability
Slovakia’s refusal to sign the Toronto Pledge comes as international partners expand legal mechanisms to hold perpetrators of child deportations accountable.
In Washington, US President Donald Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18.
The statute formally established the forcible deportation, unlawful transfer, and unjust detention of Ukrainian children as statutory grounds for mandatory US sanctions, including asset freezes and travel bans against Russian state agencies, regional guardianship boards, and logistics intermediaries.
Maksym Maksymov, head of the Ukrainian presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA, observed that codifying child deportation penalties into binding law ensures that forced removals are treated with the same legal gravity as military offenses.
Ukrainian officials have documented the unlawful transfer of nearly 20,000 Ukrainian children to Russia and Belarus, where minors are subjected to forced naturalization, ideological indoctrination, and illegal adoptions by Russian families.
International human rights monitors have repeatedly warned that Russia’s institutionalized deportation apparatus seeks to systematically erase the national and cultural identity of displaced Ukrainian youth.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,420 Troops, 50 Artillery Systems in One Day

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,420 Troops, 50 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,420 troops, four tanks, and 50 artillery systems over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest figures bring Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,550,910.
Russian forces also lost six armored combat vehicles during the latest reporting period, raising cumulative losses to 12,406 tanks and 25,515 armored vehicles. Another 50 artillery systems were added to the tally, bringing the overall estimate to 51,000, while two multiple-launch rocket systems and six air defense systems brought those totals to 2,201 and 1,699, respectively.
Ukraine also reported 1,591 operational-tactical UAVs lost over the past day, pushing the cumulative total to 556,926. Another nine unmanned ground systems were recorded as lost, raising that category to 2,917.
Russia’s estimated aviation losses remained unchanged at 443 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while cruise missile losses stayed at 5,126. Naval losses also remained unchanged at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 534 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost, bringing the cumulative figure to 160,946, while two additional pieces of special equipment raised that total to 4,812.
Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 218 times across the front during the latest reporting period. Ukrainian forces repelled 22 Russian attacks in the Pokrovsk sector, 18 in the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, and 16 in the Kostiantynivka sector.
Russian forces also carried out 88 airstrikes, dropping 282 guided aerial bombs, and deployed 9,389 attack drones during the reporting period, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.
Earlier, independent researchers confirmed that a Ukrainian missile strike on Russian military command centers in temporarily occupied Donetsk on August 26 killed 20 Russian officers, including seven colonels and six lieutenant colonels.

Russia Kills Three Ukrainian Children Hours After Trump Hands Putin a Multimillion-Ton Diesel Lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:34:04 UTC
22:34:04 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Kills Three Ukrainian Children Hours After Trump Hands Putin a Multimillion-Ton Diesel Lifeline
As Washington moves to reopen the door to Russian energy exports, Moscow continues its deadly assault on Ukraine, striking residential buildings and launching waves of drones across the country.
Russian forces killed at least seven civilians, including three children, in an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on October 10—just hours after US President Donald Trump announced a major agreement with Vladimir Putin involving millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zaporizhzhia regional authorities on October 10, Russian strikes hit residential buildings across the city. A direct hit caused part of a five-story apartment building to collapse, leaving residents trapped beneath the rubble.
Three children were among the seven people killed, while at least 10 others were injured, including another child. Two victims remained in critical condition as rescuers continued searching for survivors.
The deadly assault came less than a day after Trump described his conversation with Putin as “highly successful” and announced a deal on Russian diesel exports despite US sanctions intended to restrict Moscow’s war revenues.
The attack was part of a broader Russian aerial assault involving 160 drones, including 110 jet-powered drones. According to Ukraine’s Air Force on October 10, Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 117 drones, including 82 jet-powered aircraft.
Russian strikes were recorded at 14 locations, while falling debris was reported at another 10. Air defenses were also activated around Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk in western Ukraine. At least seven people were confirmed killed in Zaporizhzhia, while a final nationwide death toll had not yet been established.
On October 9, Trump announced that Putin had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons afterward, and potentially an additional 3 million tons.
The announced shipments would total more than 4.8 million metric tons. The US Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports for six months, allowing additional shipments to international markets.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the agreement, warning that easing sanctions would strengthen Russia rather than bring an end to the war.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” Zelenskyy wrote, arguing that renewed Russian petroleum exports would help prolong Moscow’s military campaign.

Drones Strike Major Russian Oil Terminal in Rostov-on-Don, Sparking Large Fire
Drones struck a major oil-loading terminal in the southern Russian city of Rostov-on-Don overnight on October 10, triggering a large fire at a facility used to export petroleum products and supply fuel to Russian forces.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Exilenova+ on October 10, the attack targeted the oil-loading terminal associated with the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP), previously known as Yug Rusi. The facility is located in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district.
Exilenova+ published eyewitness footage showing large flames and thick smoke rising from the area following a series of explosions.
Rostov regional governor Yury Slyusar confirmed a drone attack on the region and reported a fire in the city. He also said a railway bridge had been damaged, forcing train traffic to stop in both directions.
The terminal handles petroleum shipments for export and is reportedly involved in supplying fuel to Russian military forces. Its designed annual handling capacity is approximately 2.5 million metric tons.
The full extent of the damage and its potential impact on terminal operations remains unclear. The facility was previously targeted in a drone strike on July 9, 2026.
The refinery has an annual processing capacity of approximately 4.2 million metric tons and produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and other petroleum products.
The strike came a day after Ukrainian drones targeted the Lukoil-Ukhtaneftepererabotka refinery in Russia’s Komi Republic, approximately 1,700 kilometers from the Ukrainian border. The facility processes around 4.2 million tons of crude oil annually and supplies fuel to several Russian regions, with some products exported through Baltic ports.

Former Sharp CEO loses court case against Foxconn Technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:32:25 UTC
22:32:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Former Sharp Corporation CEO Tai Jeng-wu (戴正吳) lost his NT$600 million (US$18.76 million) court case against Foxconn Technology, reports said Saturday.
Tai argued he was not properly compensated for his role in turning Sharp around after the 2016 takeover of the Japanese company by Foxconn. He said he signed an incentive contract with Foxconn’s then-Chair Terry Gou (郭台銘) which would give him 3% of Foxconn shares if he succeeded in his job at Sharp.
Tai managed to make the company profitable again and have it relisted on the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s first section in 15 months, but alleged he did not receive the promised sum from Foxconn.
Following several rounds of unsuccessful negotiations between Tai and Foxconn, the New Taipei District Court ruled against the former Sharp CEO, Mirror Daily reported Saturday. Foxconn argued that the promise of 3% had only been signed by Gou and never been approved by a board meeting or by the company’s wages committee. Gou’s attorneys said the document only showed a general proposal, but did not amount to a binding decision for Foxconn.
The New Taipei District Court agreed with the arguments by Foxconn and Gou, according to Mirror Daily. The court also ruled that incentive decisions could not be made by Gou alone as company chair, with the incentive contract only counting as a proposal. Since Foxconn and Tai never reached an agreement on a formula for the incentive payment, the proposal to give 3% of the stock to Tai was not binding, the court ruled.

Report: Iran rebuilds missile and drone factories, replenishes arsenal despite US-Israeli strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:31:10 UTC
22:31:10 KST

Iran has managed to preserve its missile and drone production facilities despite months of U.S. and Israeli airstrikes, allowing it to replenish its weapons stockpiles, Bloomberg reported Saturday, citing officials familiar with Western intelligence assessments. Western officials who spoke on condition of anonymity said Tehran retains the ability to manufacture weapons and rebuild its arsenal.
One official said Iran remains "well-stocked" with ballistic missiles and certain anti-ship weapons and can rapidly produce additional missiles. The official also said Russia has been supplying missiles to Iran, consistent with intelligence assessments reported in June. Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
The findings suggest that Iran has retained significant weapons production capabilities even as U.S. President Donald Trump refrains from launching further strikes ahead of November's midterm elections. The assessment contradicts repeated claims by Trump and senior administration officials that eight months of airstrikes have destroyed Iran's ability to threaten American military bases in the region and U.S. allies.
Earlier this year, Trump declared that Iran's military had been "totally destroyed." In a September 30 speech, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the United States had destroyed Iran's "military industrial capacity" and "their entire defense base." The latest findings raise the prospect that Tehran could further rebuild its missile forces if Trump follows through on his pledge, announced on social media Thursday, not to attack Iran before the November elections.
Meanwhile, Iran has intensified attacks on commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz. According to the British Navy, at least 10 vessels have been struck over the past week. Responding to Bloomberg's report, a White House spokeswoman rejected its findings.
"President Trump completely obliterated Iran's nuclear facilities during Operation Midnight Hammer," she said. "Then, during Operation Epic Fury, he successfully destroyed the conventional shield Iran sought to build around its nuclear program, including its ballistic missiles, production facilities and navy."
The report comes as Washington continues to weigh renewed military action against Iran despite Trump's public commitment to avoid further strikes before the elections. The New York Times reported Thursday that the U.S. military was preparing for the possibility of another large-scale offensive against Iran, with Pentagon planners developing options for an intensive military operation lasting approximately three days.
Despite extensive preparations and escalating Iranian attacks on oil tankers, Trump has remained reluctant to resume large-scale hostilities. In recent months, he has rejected five separate proposals for major military operations against Iran or the Houthis in Yemen, according to the report.
Trump has nevertheless once again instructed military officials to prepare strike options. Last Friday, senior administration officials discussed the plans during a meeting at Camp David led by Vice President JD Vance. The discussions centered on a short but powerful operation lasting approximately three days, targeting Iran's missile and drone capabilities, significant portions of which have been restored by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps since the opening stages of the war. Other potential targets under consideration include energy facilities, Revolutionary Guard headquarters and command centers.
'We are prepared for negotiations and do not fear them'
The future of the confrontation with Iran remains deeply uncertain. Negotiations between Tehran and Washington have produced no breakthrough, clashes over the Strait of Hormuz continue, and an agreement over Iran's nuclear program appears increasingly distant.
Iranian forces continue to issue threats and assert their military capabilities, while U.S. officials maintain that their operations have achieved major results. The approaching elections in both Israel and the United States have also raised questions in Tehran about how domestic political considerations could influence future military decisions.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Thursday that indirect negotiations with Washington were continuing and that Tehran was considering the American response to its proposed diplomatic framework. "The negotiation process is continuing, and messages are being exchanged through mediators," Araghchi said. "We presented our proposal for a seven-day plan and heard the American position regarding it. We are now reviewing that position, and I believe we will provide our response in the coming days."
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei also said in recent days that Tehran had clarified its conditions for ending the war on all fronts and restoring security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. He confirmed that messages were being exchanged between Iran and the United States through intermediaries. Despite those statements, Trump has already rejected the seven-day proposal Iran presented in September.
According to reports, the plan called for a weeklong suspension of hostile activities throughout the region, including Lebanon, the release of $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports and an end to the American blockade of Iranian ports. It also included guarantees concerning respect for Iranian sovereignty, commitments related to a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington, and an end to threats against Iran.
Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz on the seventh day if its conditions were met. Tehran has continued to insist on those demands despite Washington's rejection. Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani reiterated the country's position last week. "We are prepared for negotiations and do not fear them," she said. "We will defend our country, whether through war or through negotiations."
Iran also appears to be developing longer-term plans for the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to international shipping routes. Tehran has been holding discussions with Oman, which lies on the opposite side of the strait, concerning its future management.
Last week, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman said the two countries had agreed on the locations of safe shipping passages and reached an understanding on how to present the arrangements to the relevant international organization. That process, he said, would move forward soon.
Iranian state-aligned media have continued reporting incidents involving vessels accused of violating Tehran's maritime regulations in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials insist that the waterway remains under the complete control of their forces and that the current restrictions will continue until Tehran's demands are met. Washington disputes those claims. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that Iran had "completely lost" control of the strait.
Alongside the dispute over Hormuz, Iran's nuclear program has returned to the center of diplomatic discussions. On Wednesday, a senior source told the Saudi-owned Al Arabiya television network that control of the waterway was no longer Washington's main priority.
"Hormuz is no longer a priority for Washington after Iran lost control of it," the source said. "Progress in negotiations depends on Iran's response to Trump's demands regarding its nuclear capabilities. Washington is demanding that Iran acknowledge that it will not continue developing those capabilities."
On September 28, a senior U.S. official told Al Jazeera that there would be no agreement without addressing Iran's nuclear program. The official said Trump was prepared to ease sanctions on Iran and release frozen Iranian assets in exchange for progress on the nuclear issue.
Tehran, however, has shown little willingness to compromise on what it describes as its right to enrich uranium. Last week, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would never surrender that right and that Washington's position on the nuclear program directly contradicted Tehran's demands.
Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, reiterated that position Thursday. "We will not give up our right to enrichment, nor will we hand over our uranium," he said. "Nuclear negotiations were not on the agenda, and the American statements stem from desperation."
Iran threatens to expand attacks beyond Hormuz
As diplomatic contacts continue, Iranian military officials have maintained an increasingly confrontational tone, warning that further American attacks could trigger a broader escalation. Over the weekend, the Revolutionary Guards warned that their operations against vessels accused of violating Iranian regulations would no longer be confined to the Strait of Hormuz.
"From now on, action against violating vessels will not be limited to the Strait of Hormuz," the Revolutionary Guards said. "Any vessel traveling along an unauthorized route, anywhere in the region, will be punished."
Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi issued a similar warning last week, saying Iranian naval forces were prepared to respond decisively to what Tehran considers hostile actions or unauthorized maritime movements. "The naval forces are prepared to respond decisively to any miscalculation by the enemy and to the passage of vessels without authorization," he said.
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohabbi has also warned in recent weeks that another attack on Iran would prompt a fundamental change in Tehran's military strategy. "If another attack takes place, our defensive strategy will change, including expanding the geographical scope of the confrontation, using new equipment and weapons, and selecting different targets," he said. "Iran possesses strategic capabilities and targets that have not yet been used, but they will be activated if necessary."
Although such warnings form part of Iran's continuing propaganda campaign, several Western reports published in recent days suggest Tehran retains substantial military capabilities despite the sustained bombing campaign. Last week, satellite imagery reportedly revealed significant renewed activity at Min-Zadai, a nuclear weapons development complex northeast of Tehran that Israel previously exposed and attacked during Operation Roaring Lion.
The reported activity has added to concerns over how much of Iran's military and strategic infrastructure has survived the war and how quickly damaged facilities can be restored.
At the same time, Iran's political leadership has been urging national unity and domestic stability while acknowledging the mounting challenges facing the country. Years of sanctions, the economic consequences of the war and persistent social pressures have left Iran confronting serious internal difficulties. Differences also remain within the Iranian leadership and political establishment over the possibility of reaching an agreement with the United States.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged those challenges last week, calling for practical solutions and closer cooperation across government institutions and society. "In light of the challenges posed by the war and sanctions, solving the country's problems requires practical plans, cooperation and coordination among all government bodies and sectors of society," he said. "We must work to address economic and social problems while preserving national unity and avoiding confrontation."

Israel’s Center-Right is looking for a choice, not just an alternative - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:30:44 UTC
22:30:44 KST

For an Israeli voter somewhere on the Center-Right of the political map, the next election presents an extraordinarily difficult choice.
October 7 was not merely another intelligence failure or operational setback. Those who held the highest positions of authority when the catastrophe occurred, especially Benjamin Netanyahu, must bear responsibility for what happened on their watch.
A democracy cannot demand accountability from its institutions and then exempt its political leadership from the same principle.
And yet, when one looks at the alternatives, the decision becomes considerably more complicated.
The candidates who are presented as potential replacements for Netanyahu are not outsiders who were sitting on the sidelines. They held senior positions in the political and security establishment in the years leading up to October 7.
Gadi Eisenkot was IDF chief of staff from 2015 to 2019. He helped shape the IDF’s command structure and appointed senior officers who remained influential in the military establishment in the years that followed.
Naftali Bennett served as defense minister and prime minister.
Avigdor Liberman served for years in senior ministerial positions, including as defense minister.
These three want-to-be prime ministers are not outsiders, people who are disconnected from the system that ultimately failed. Are they really offering us a fundamentally different government or merely a different collection of insiders?
The political debate often makes it appear that there is an enormous ideological gulf between Netanyahu and the leading figures of the opposition. But when one looks beyond the personalities and political branding, the differences are not always so dramatic.
On many of the fundamental questions facing Israel, the Center-Right and much of the opposition are closer than the political rhetoric would suggest. Increasingly, the principal argument again being offered voters is “We are not Bibi.”
Israel needs more than a change of personnel. It needs a change in the way the political system operates.
The country is confronting an extraordinary collection of problems simultaneously.
The war against Hamas has not disappeared. The Iranian threat has not disappeared. Israel faces an increasingly difficult international diplomatic environment.
At home, the country must resolve the increasingly urgent question of haredi military service. It must address the housing crisis and the crushing cost of living. It must strengthen the economy while maintaining the massive defense expenditures required by the new security reality. It must develop and implement a unified policy regarding the future of Judea and Samaria. It must reinvent its educational system to meet the technology and other demands of the 21st century.
We must create a proactive, effective, and unified public relations team to combat the widespread hatred of Israel.
Israel's judicial reform
And, of course, Israel needs judicial reform. But it needs reform that is broadly accepted across the political spectrum and designed around the needs of most Israelis, not legislation crafted to satisfy the most ideological voices on either side.
The objective of any judicial reform should not be to weaken the judiciary or to empower it at the expense of elected government. It should be to establish a broad cross-party process that creates a sustainable balance between the branches of government, protects individual rights, preserves democratic accountability, and ensures that elected governments can actually govern.
All of these issues really point to the fact that what Israel desperately needs today is not simply a government of the blocs; it needs a unity government of the consensus. A government that will think country first. A government that will be accountable to its citizens, including the thousands upon thousands of reservists who dropped everything on October 7, put aside petty ideological differences, and fought side by side against our enemies, with the singular goal of winning so we could all continue living in our beautiful, holy land.
A unity government does not mean that every issue must be decided down the middle. It means building a Zionist governing coalition around the broad majority of Israelis who want a secure, prosperous, democratic, and Jewish state. No Itamar Ben-Gvir. No Yair Golan. No anti-Zionists, whether Jewish or Arab. Israel is exhausted by politics dominated by the extremes.
That does not mean that all Israelis who hold strongly ideological positions should be silenced or excluded from public debate. They have every right to participate in Israeli democracy. But policies should be built around the broad center of Israeli society, not around the factions most effective at creating division.
Some will argue that calling for a unity government means allowing those responsible for October 7 to escape accountability. It does not.
Israel should investigate October 7 thoroughly. October 7 revealed that Israel’s political and security establishment suffered from profound systemic failures. Changing the name on the Prime Minister’s Office door is not sufficient. We need to examine the assumptions that dominated the defense establishment. We need to examine how intelligence was interpreted. We need to examine the relationship between political leaders and the military. We need to examine how dissenting assessments were treated. And we need to ask why so many people across the political and security spectrum failed to anticipate the scale of the threat.
Perhaps the most important lesson Israel can draw from the catastrophe of October 7 is that no individual, party, or political camp possesses a monopoly on wisdom or blame.
The next government should therefore be judged not simply by whether it is Netanyahu’s government or an anti-Netanyahu government. It should be judged by whether Israel’s political leaders can put aside their egos and work together for the good of the country. We need the best and brightest of our country running our ministries; no more political hacks without experience and expertise.
Israel does not need another government whose principal achievement is defeating the other side. It needs a government of leaders humble enough to understand that the country is more important than any one of them.
Bibi, Gadi, Naftali, Avigdor, you have all done so much for our country. Now is the time to do the right thing and come together for the benefit of the State of Israel.
Put aside your political differences and work together to form a unity government.
The writer, a resident of Beit Shemesh, is the managing partner of Dekel Capital Management.
