Tehran tourism needs coordinated policies, not more infrastructure: council member
TEHRAN – Tehran’s main tourism challenge is not a shortage of infrastructure but fragmented policymaking and limited public awareness of the capital’s existing attractions, a city council member said.
Seyyed Ahmad Alavi, head of the Tehran City Council’s Tourism and Cultural Heritage Committee, said better coordination among municipal bodies and stronger promotion of the city’s historical, recreational and tourism facilities were essential to expanding domestic tourism.
Alavi said responsibility for tourism and leisure facilities had been divided among several municipal organizations, resulting in separate decision-making processes and a lack of integrated planning.
He said the council had pursued the establishment of a municipal tourism company to address the problem, a proposal that was eventually approved after years of discussion.
Under the previous arrangement, different organizations oversaw various aspects of tourism and recreation, including amusement parks, cultural facilities and urban beautification projects. A unified structure could help coordinate their activities and make better use of existing assets, Alavi said.
He also highlighted a significant increase in the budget allocated to tourism tours and sightseeing buses, adding that further funding could be considered if the proposed tourism company presented viable plans that could be incorporated into the municipal budget.
Reviving neglected recreational facilities has been another priority, he said. The Basij amusement park, which had remained closed for about six years despite previous investment, was among the facilities targeted for reopening. The amusement park at the Abbasabad cultural and recreational complex had also been completed during the current council’s term, while plans were being developed for six additional amusement parks.
Alavi said the city was also expanding sightseeing bus services and establishing dedicated routes connecting historical landmarks and sites associated with Tehran’s cultural identity.
These services could help residents discover attractions they might otherwise overlook, he added.
He acknowledged that reorganizing the sector was complicated by competing interests among municipal bodies. Nevertheless, he said the council aimed to improve coordination, public access and promotion of existing attractions rather than focusing solely on building new infrastructure.
The broader objective, he said, is to enable more residents to benefit from Tehran’s historical, cultural and recreational resources.

The period cycle: What happens in your body beyond the five days of bleeding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:20:01 UTC
22:20:01 KST

The days leading up to a period can be just as challenging as the bleeding itself.
“Chill! It’s just periods. You’ll feel better in a couple of days.”But do women really get better in three to five days or are they caught in a recurring loop of exhaustion, mood swings and hormonal shifts that returns month after month from their first period till end.From hormonal fluctuations and ovulation to fatigue, bloating and premenstrual symptoms, the menstrual cycle is a month-long process that extends far beyond the days of bleeding. Yet, what happens inside the body between periods remains poorly understood by many women.For some, menstruation brings severe cramps, exhaustion and an overwhelming need to be left alone. Others struggle with bloating, back pain, irritability or difficulty concentrating at work. And for many, the days leading up to a period can be just as challenging as the bleeding itself.“I feel like somebody is constantly stabbing me with a sword, not even a knife, in my stomach,” says Sasha Singh, describing her experience of menstruation.“Emotionally, I am so annoyed that eye rolls become the only friend that day. The Luteal phase is the worst for me, an indication of days ahead,” she added.For Shivanghi, the physical discomfort comes with an emotional toll.
“I feel like I need to punch whoever is talking to me and cry all the time. Physically its like my insides are getting drained and sawed repeatedly. I feel the first day and the day before that are the most painful.”Their experiences highlight how differently women can experience the menstrual cycle, both physically and emotionally. They also raise a larger question: What happens inside the body when there is no bleeding?The menstrual cycle is not confined to the three to seven days of menstrual bleeding. It is a continuous process involving hormonal fluctuations and changes in the ovaries and uterus, as the body prepares for a possible pregnancy.These changes can influence much more than the uterine lining. They may affect energy levels, sleep, appetite, skin, digestion and mood throughout the month.While some women notice distinct changes from one phase to another, others experience few symptoms beyond their period.
What your body goes through during the entire cycle.
What is menstruation?
Menstruation is the shedding of the uterine lining through the vagina when pregnancy has not occurred. The bleeding contains blood and tissue from the lining of the uterus, also called the endometrium.Periods generally last between three and seven days, although the duration and amount of bleeding vary. Menstruation usually begins during puberty, most commonly between the ages of 11 and 14, though it can start earlier or later. It continues through the reproductive years until menopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55.The menstrual cycle, however, covers the entire interval from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.A cycle is often described as lasting 28 days, but this is only an average. Many adults have cycles that fall within a range of approximately 21 to 35 days, and cycle length can vary with age and individual circumstances.The cycle is regulated by hormones that coordinate activity between the brain, the ovaries and the uterus. Its four commonly described phases are menstruation, the follicular phase, ovulation and the luteal phase.Importantly, these phases are not four completely separate stages. The follicular phase begins on the first day of menstruation and continues until ovulation, meaning the first two phases overlap.
The four phases: What happens inside the body?
MenstruationThe menstrual cycle begins on the first day of menstrual bleeding. When pregnancy has not occurred, the levels of hormones that support the uterine lining fall, prompting the lining to shed.The uterus contracts to help expel this tissue, which can cause cramps in the lower abdomen and sometimes pain in the lower back. Some women also experience bloating, headaches, fatigue, breast discomfort or changes in mood.According to Priyanka, the first two days can be particularly difficult. “During my period, I usually feel physically tired, bloated and uncomfortable, with severe cramps and lower back pain. Emotionally, I tend to feel more irritable, sensitive and overwhelmed than usual. The most challenging phase for me is the few days leading up to my period the Luteal phase, when PMS symptoms like mood swings, fatigue and bloating are at their peak. The first two days of my period can also be difficult,” she added.Hormone levels, particularly those of oestrogen and progesterone, are relatively low at the beginning of the cycle. But this does not mean that the body's reproductive processes have stopped. As menstruation begins, hormones are already signalling the ovaries to start developing follicles for the next stage.For most women, some discomfort during menstruation can be managed with appropriate measures. However, severe pain that interferes with daily activities should not automatically be dismissed as a normal part of having periods.The follicular phaseThis phase starts on the first day of menstruation and continues until ovulation.During this time, the pituitary gland releases follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which stimulates the development of follicles in the ovaries. Each follicle contains an immature egg, and usually one becomes dominant and continues to mature.As the follicle develops, it produces increasing amounts of oestrogen. This hormone helps rebuild and thicken the uterine lining after menstruation.The changes are taking place even after the bleeding stops, although they may not produce obvious symptoms.Some women report feeling more energetic or focused during the days after their period. Others do not notice any clear difference. These experiences can vary from one person to another and even from one cycle to the next.Vijaya notices significant changes in her energy and concentration around her cycle. “Oh yes!! It changes drastically. Energy drops, concentration is hindered. Sleep becomes overpowering, as if body is on energy saver mode.”However, it is important not to assume that every change in energy or mood is caused by menstrual hormones. Sleep, stress, nutrition, underlying health conditions and other factors can also influence how someone feels.The follicular phase illustrates why the menstrual cycle is more than a monthly episode of bleeding. While the body prepares an egg for possible release, the uterine lining is also being rebuilt.OvulationAs the dominant follicle matures, rising oestrogen levels help trigger a surge in luteinising hormone (LH). This surge causes ovulation, when the ovary releases a mature egg.Ovulation is often described as occurring around day 14 of a 28-day cycle, but its timing varies. It does not necessarily happen on the same day for everyone, or even in every cycle for the same person.After its release, the egg enters the fallopian tube, where it may be fertilised by sperm. The egg usually remains capable of fertilisation for approximately 12 to 24 hours. However, pregnancy can occur from sex in the days leading up to ovulation because sperm can survive in the reproductive tract for several days.Some women notice changes around ovulation, while some experience mild pain on one side of the lower abdomen. Others may notice no obvious physical changes.There is also considerable variation in whether women report changes in mood, energy or sexual desire around this time. These experiences should not be treated as universal signs of ovulation.Understanding ovulation is important not only for those trying to conceive but also for anyone seeking to understand the timing of their cycle. Calendar estimates and period-tracking apps can help identify patterns, but they cannot always predict the exact day of ovulation.
The changes are taking place even after the bleeding stops.
The luteal phaseAfter ovulation, the follicle that released the egg transforms into a structure called the corpus luteum. It produces progesterone, along with some oestrogen, to help maintain the uterine lining in preparation for a possible pregnancy.If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum breaks down. Progesterone and oestrogen levels fall, triggering changes that eventually lead to the shedding of the uterine lining and the start of the next period.For some women, this phase brings premenstrual symptoms, commonly known as PMS. These may include bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, fatigue, irritability, changes in appetite and difficulty sleeping.Shivanghi further claims that the emotional changes can be difficult to explain. “Getting irritated all the time and crying for no reason. It feels like everyone is being rude and they all hate me.” Sneha, meanwhile, says irritability is the main change she notices.Premenstrual symptoms vary considerably. Some women experience mild changes that do not disrupt their routines, while others experience symptoms that affect work, relationships, studies and everyday activities.In more severe cases, symptoms may be associated with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition that can cause significant emotional and physical distress.Women experiencing severe or persistent symptoms should discuss them with a healthcare professional rather than assuming they must simply endure them.
The effects of the menstrual cycle can extend beyond reproductive organs.
Why do hormones affect mood, energy, sleep & appetite
The effects of the menstrual cycle can extend beyond reproductive organs. Changes in oestrogen and progesterone may influence several bodily functions, although the extent of these effects differs between individuals.According to Dr Asha Susawat, senior obstetrician and gynaecologist at Cocoon Hospital, Jaipur, hormonal fluctuations can influence how women feel throughout the cycle.“While the hormonal fluctuations will be much more impactful than just your bleeding pattern, their importance will vary from woman to woman. For some, high levels of oestrogen before ovulation make them feel more energetic. Others will not perceive any significant differences. Following the occurrence of ovulation, the progesterone hormone increases the temperature levels in the body and may affect the sleep pattern. As the woman starts to bleed, some may feel sleepy, irritable, nervous, food craving, among other symptoms such as breakout, bloating, constipation, or diarrhoea. Nevertheless, not all the factors are felt by everyone and need more diagnoses.”
These accounts demonstrate the importance of recognising individual patterns.
Dr Rhythm Bhalla, senior consultant in obstetrics and gynaecology at Cocoon Hospital, Chandigarh, similarly notes that symptoms can begin before the next period arrives.“The physical effects of menstrual cycle on women may start long before the upcoming period. Variations in levels of oestrogen and progesterone affect moods, sleep, eating and energy levels. However, there is no standard experience in this regard since some women feel better before ovulation whereas some start experiencing fatigue, poor sleep, cravings and irritability prior to the onset of the period. Women may start experiencing acne and bloating, while digestive problems may turn into constipation or diarrhoea before the period starts. There may be minor symptoms but serious problems should not be overlooked.”
More than mood swings: The body's changing rhythms
Some women experience irritability, anxiety, sadness or emotional sensitivity in the days before their period. Others notice little change, or find that their mood varies for reasons unrelated to their cycle.Priyanka says she becomes more irritable and anxious before menstruation and sometimes struggles to concentrate. Shivanghi describes feeling upset and easily irritated, while Vijaya reports a noticeable decline in concentration and energy.Some women notice acne or changes in skin oiliness around their period. Others experience food cravings, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea.These symptoms may be associated with hormonal fluctuations, but their causes can be complex. Persistent acne, unexplained hair loss, increased facial hair or substantial changes in weight should not automatically be attributed to the menstrual cycle.The same applies to digestive symptoms. Occasional bloating or changes in bowel habits may occur around menstruation, but persistent or severe abdominal pain, ongoing digestive problems or symptoms that disrupt daily life warrant medical attention.
The information gap: What women know about their cycles
Despite menstruation being a regular part of life for millions of women, understanding of the complete menstrual cycle remains uneven.Many learn the basics at school or at home but receive little information about ovulation, hormonal fluctuations and the physical and emotional changes that can occur throughout the menstrual cycle.When asked whether they knew that hormonal changes continue throughout the month, even when they are not bleeding, the responses revealed varying levels of awareness.Vijaya said, “Yes. The whole cycle is in process and goes beyond just shedding blood. There is constant hormonal fluctuations which ultimately affects the energy and motivation throughout the lifetime.”Prisha Patnaik responded, “Yes, I think 4 phases?” while Shivanghi said, “I have a broad idea, like the luteal, follicular phases and all. Not really informed about the details.”Their responses point to a distinction between knowing that the menstrual cycle involves hormonal changes and understanding how these changes unfold across its different phases.For many, school provides only the basics, leaving them to turn to family members, friends or online resources for more information. Others have to seek answers on their own.Vijaya said, “I didn't learn about periods at home, it was only until I got them did I have the conversation. In school it was only what textbook had to offer, they didn't even teach about pads etc.”Priyanka said, “I learnt the basics at school, but very little about hormonal changes and their impact on our bodies. One common misconception I've encountered is that periods are just about bleeding, when they actually affect our physical and emotional well-being throughout the month.”Sneha said, “I don’t have much to say about how periods were discussed at school. I got most of my information at home and from Google, which I explored out of curiosity.”These experiences underline the need for menstrual-health education that goes beyond explaining bleeding.Girls and boys need age-appropriate information about the menstrual cycle, reproductive health, common symptoms and when medical attention may be necessary.The gap is not just in what women are taught, but also in how menstruation is discussed. For Sasha, her first lessons about periods at school offered little insight into the subject.Years later, she encountered another misconception in the workplace, where her mood was sometimes attributed to menstruation.“When I worked in an all-boys work desk, I was often asked if I was on periods if I was not in a cheerful mood. Bad mood can be a product of multiple things, not just periods,” she added.
Menstruation is something to hide rather than a normal biological process.
Menstruation, stigma and restrictions
In many parts of India, menstruation remains a subject surrounded by stigma and silence. Some women continue to face restrictions on entering kitchens, touching utensils, participating in religious activities or discussing periods openly.Pari (name changed), from Assam, describes the restrictions followed in her household."On the three days of my period, I sit and sleep on the floor. I eat on a separate plate as I am not allowed to enter the kitchen or touch any utensil or other furniture. I do not touch any male member be it my father, brother or husband. These customs have been followed for a very long time in my household and me, my mother and sister have applied the same in our lives."Her account reflects how cultural practices can shape women's experiences of menstruation beyond the physical symptoms themselves.Yash Sonkar points to the gaps in menstrual-health education, saying, “Menstruation isn’t even properly explained in our school curriculum… teachers skip the chapters at times.”For Trisha, the problem goes beyond inadequate education to the stigma surrounding menstruation. One of the most persistent misconceptions she has encountered, she says, is that periods make women “impure”.Vijaya's experience reflects how deeply such beliefs can become embedded in everyday life. “As for misconceptions, it's hard to think of one that I might not have been forced on. Days on which I can cut my nails, touching the pickle, touching gods or even mentioning it in front of a male entity,” she says, recalling the restrictions associated with menstruation.These beliefs can persist through seemingly ordinary practices, from discouraging women from entering places of worship to treating menstruation as something that must be kept out of sight.Even the habit of wrapping sanitary napkins discreetly or avoiding conversations about periods can reinforce the idea that menstruation is something to hide rather than a normal biological process.
Stress, thyroid disorders & PCOS: What else affects the cycle
The menstrual cycle is regulated by a complex interaction between the brain, the ovaries and the uterus. Several factors can interfere with this process, affecting ovulation, the timing of periods and the amount of bleeding.Dr Susawat explains that stress can affect the hormones involved in ovulation, potentially delaying periods or causing them to be missed. Thyroid disorders can influence cycle length and bleeding patterns, while PCOS may interfere with regular ovulation and lead to irregular or absent periods.Age is another factor. Cycles may be irregular during the years after menstruation first begins and may change again during perimenopause, the transition towards menopause. Hormonal contraception can also alter bleeding patterns, depending on the method used.Dr Bhalla said that the cycle depends on several systems working together. “Periods are the result of interaction between the brain, the ovaries and the uterus; there are many things that might interfere in this interaction. Stress, combined with big changes in weight or poor eating habits, may lead to ovulation delay,” Bhalla said.“Thyroid issues may cause changes in bleeding amount and frequency. In PCOS, ovulation may be less frequent and make periods irregular. The menstrual problems can occur during the period of adolescence before the beginning of menopause. As hormonal contraceptives have an impact on the level of reproductive hormones and uterine lining in some form, so the bleeding can be less, spotting or absence of periods can occur,” she added.This means that a change in the menstrual cycle does not necessarily indicate a serious health problem, but persistent changes should not be ignored.A healthcare professional may consider factors such as stress, medication, pregnancy, thyroid function and PCOS when assessing irregular periods.
When should you consult a gynaecologist?
Although changes in mood, energy and physical comfort may occur throughout the menstrual cycle, not every symptom should be attributed to hormones.According to Dr Susawat, excessive bleeding between periods, bleeding after sexual intercourse, persistent pelvic pain or pain during intercourse should be evaluated. Unusual vaginal discharge accompanied by an odour, irritation or fever also warrants medical attention.She highlights that women should seek an assessment if their menstrual pattern changes significantly or if they miss periods for three months. If pregnancy is possible, a missed period may be a reason to take a pregnancy test.Dr Bhalla similarly advises that frequent bleeding between cycles, bleeding after intercourse, persistent pelvic pain and unusual discharge accompanied by itching, a bad odour or fever should not be ignored.“This can be explained through the normal process of a woman. Abnormal bleeding that occurs frequently in between cycles, or bleeding following sexual intercourse, or constant pain in the pelvis area or during sexual intercourse should be dealt with appropriately. Unusual vaginal discharge accompanied by signs such as itching, bad odor and fever should be attended to. Irregular periods which result in absence of menstruation for over three months should also be considered and an examination carried out. This should be done as early as possible if pregnancy is one of the probable causes. Severe pelvic pain in addition to bleeding, missing periods and fainting should be handled as a matter of urgency. Excessive vaginal bleeding accompanied by weakness, dizziness and difficulty breathing should also be handled urgently,” she said.Other warning signs include bleeding that lasts longer than seven days, very heavy bleeding, severe or worsening menstrual pain and symptoms that interfere with work, studies or daily activities.Heavy bleeding can lead to iron deficiency anaemia, particularly when it occurs repeatedly. Severe menstrual pain may also be associated with conditions such as endometriosis or adenomyosis, while irregular cycles may warrant assessment for PCOS, thyroid disorders or other underlying causes.Severe pelvic pain accompanied by a missed period, bleeding or faintness requires urgent medical assessment, particularly when pregnancy is possible.The key is to recognise the difference between a symptom that occurs occasionally and one that is persistent, severe or unusual for the individual.The World Health Organisation (WHO) recognises menstrual health as more than a matter of managing bleeding. It includes access to accurate information, affordable menstrual products, safe sanitation facilities, appropriate healthcare and the ability to participate in everyday life without stigma.The WHO has also highlighted the limited availability of high-quality scientific research on menstruation. Better research and education can help improve care, support health policies and challenge myths surrounding the menstrual cycle.The organisation estimates that around 500 million people who menstruate worldwide lack access to the full range of menstrual-health materials, facilities and services. It has also cited emerging national data indicating that around 39% of schools provide menstrual-health education.These gaps matter because a lack of information can prevent women from recognising symptoms that require medical attention. It can also make it harder for them to discuss menstrual difficulties without embarrassment or fear of being dismissed.
Beyond the five days
For many women, menstruation is the most visible part of a process that continues throughout the month. While the uterus sheds its lining, the ovaries begin developing follicles. As oestrogen rises, the uterine lining rebuilds.Ovulation follows, and progesterone helps prepare the uterus for a possible pregnancy. If pregnancy does not occur, hormone levels fall and the cycle begins again.The physical and emotional effects of these changes are not identical for everyone. Some women experience significant discomfort before and during menstruation, while others notice little variation.Understanding the menstrual cycle means recognising that periods are not simply five days of bleeding. They are one stage in a continuous process shaped by hormones, health, age and individual circumstances.Better menstrual-health education can help women understand their bodies, challenge stigma and recognise when symptoms deserve medical attention.
It can also encourage families, schools and workplaces to treat menstruation as a normal health issue rather than a subject of embarrassment.The more women understand what happens between periods, the better equipped they are to recognise their own patterns, ask informed questions and seek medical care when something feels wrong.Greater awareness among men is equally important. When partners understand the physical and emotional changes women may experience throughout the cycle, they can offer greater empathy, support and understanding instead of dismissing symptoms or attributing every change in mood to menstruation.

Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Neither Putin nor Trump wanted to hang up first, Kremlin aide says after 'very friendly' call

During the call, the presidents agreed that Russia would supply diesel to the US and global markets to lower fuel prices, prompting an unexpected temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian fuel that has dismayed Ukraine.

The West imposed sanctions, including restrictions on Russian energy imports, after Moscow launched the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022. Efforts to end the fighting have so far stalled, partly over Russia’s demand for four Ukrainian regions it does not fully control.

USS Abraham Lincoln Returns to USA With Markers Indicating Destroyed Iranian Targets: 103 Drones, 34 Ships, and 10 Submarines

The U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned to the United States after a nearly 11-month deployment, during which its strike group participated in combat operations against Iran and destroyed dozens of ships, drones, and missiles.
This was reported by The War Zone, whose journalists analyzed photographs of the aircraft carrier after the conclusion of its combat deployment.
Markings in the form of silhouettes of destroyed targets have appeared on the ship’s superstructure. Journalists counted 103 markings for attack drones and 34 markings for ships and boats. The images of the drones resemble the Shahed-136, but may also represent other types of Iranian drones.
According to official data announced on October 7 by U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hagseth, during Operation Epic Fury, the carrier strike group shot down 77 attack drones, sank 64 Iranian vessels, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
These results cover the period from the start of Operation Epic Fury on February 28 until the carrier strike group’s departure from the region on August 22, 2026.
During this period, the group’s aircraft flew 3,693 combat sorties and expended approximately 621 metric tons of air-to-ground munitions. Escort ships also launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles at ground targets.
Specific markings on carrier-based fighter jets indicate the destruction of Iranian submarines. In particular, a corresponding image was recorded on an F/A-18F Super Hornet from the 41st Strike Fighter Squadron (VFA-41). In total, this squadron deployed 421 missiles and aerial bombs during combat operations.
At the same time, the number of marks on the aircraft carrier does not match official statistics.
On its superstructure, there were 26 more drone marks than indicated in the award document, but 30 fewer ship marks. The reasons for the discrepancies have not yet been explained.
The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned to San Diego on October 8 after more than 320 days of deployment. As part of the operation against Iran, its strike group received the Presidential Unit Citation for combat merit.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on August 22, the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group left the Middle East after completing its combat deployment and moved into the area of responsibility of the U.S. 7th Fleet.
The extended deployment was accompanied by logistical challenges due to the threat of Iranian strikes on ports in the region.

Vegan powerlifter says diet change solved his health problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Vegan powerlifter says diet change solved his health problems
Powerlifter Gert Koovit says switching to a vegan diet nine years ago solved his joint pain and health problems, adding his recovery has improved significantly.
Koovit, who grew up with six brothers and a sister, all fed on good countryside fare, said his wife suggested make the change. He now eats 180–240 grams of protein a day, but plant-derived, something which is viable nowadays without getting boared.
"There were six boys and one girl of us. We usually went through eight liters of milk a day, and everything else that goes with it," he said.
"I'm fully vegan, but that doesn't mean I only eat onions and potatoes. AS I'm a powerlifter, I need to be heavy. There's a very wide choice of vegan food. My daily protein intake is between 180 and 240 grams. On top of that comes about three times as much in carbohydrates — oatmeal, rice, potato and the rest. For me it's very important to get a lot of energy from food and for my weight number to be high," Koovit said.
His wife had been vegan for longer. "I reached a point in my sport where my joints started hurting and I felt I'd taken my body so far that if I pushed a little more, health problems would start. That was nine years ago. My wife then very cleverly suggested I try vegan products. When I get stuck with something, my dear wife comes up with a solution — without her I probably wouldn't be here," Koovit explained.
Pretty much every foodstuff has a vegan alternative, he noted. "In my case, it was that after four days of eating vegan food, I realized there was no way back, as I felt so good. For an athlete, the best thing is that the recovery becomes faster."
Koovit recalled that at the time he was living in London, and in the club where he trained he was one of the smallest men. "I was a little squirt there. As things started going so well for me, and I started setting Estonian records and winning medals, burly men who I'd been afraid even to talk to at first started asking me what I was doing to do so well. One after another they started trying vegan food too."
Meat dishes tend to be highly acidic and can cause inflammation in the body, he says. "When heavy training is added to that, more and more inflammation builds up in the body. Eventually the body can't cope with it anymore — that's why more and more athletes in the sports world have been finding vegan food," went on.
"Eating vegan food is very contagious, because you feel good and get the feeling that you'd like to try more. After eating, you don't get a heavy feeling. In sporting terms, that's the charm of it — since I can eat more often, I feed my muscles and cells more often. There are more nutrients, and through that recovery is faster too," Koovit said. "Protein can be obtained from vegan food in concentrated form."
The annual Veganmess food festival takes place in Tallinn this weekend.

Putin’s Vile Chess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:12:00 UTC
22:12:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has “played” the Game of Kings, or chess, against Ukraine and the West for years, but badly. But his attempt to conquer Ukraine has been disastrous.
Putin misread the board, opened in 2022 with a “blitzkrieg gambit,” expecting Kyiv to fall quickly, then overextended his “pieces” and lost the initiative.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He underestimated his opponent – notably Ukrainian courage, resilience, and technological innovation – and miscalculated Western cohesion. He then shifted into a horrific war of attrition, sacrificing 1.5 million men, spending $770 million a day, and squandering $680 billion since 2022, in return for minuscule territorial gains.
Now, Putin has decided to conduct saturation bombing attacks on Ukrainian women and children in Kyiv and other cities to bring the country to its knees. This is another blunder, like a “poisoned-pawn” mistake in chess, when a player gobbles up easily captured pieces but totally undermines his position and costs himself the game.
Russia’s war against Ukraine is fought on two chessboards. One involves missiles, drones, soldiers, and oil refineries. The other is a diplomatic chessboard involving Putin, US President Donald Trump, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Europe.
Putin has started to pound Ukrainian civilians, power, transport, and water facilities before winter to create a humanitarian disaster that will spill over into Europe. But his brutality backfires and upsets Americans and Europeans. It also exposes the stupidity of pursuing peace deals with Putin or falling for anything he says, including his thinly disguised “bribery” attempt to sell a Russian oil company to a group of Trump’s friends. It’s blood money. It’s also insulting.
Russian Ballistic Strike on Kyiv Injures 6 in Restaurant
In return for killing innocents intentionally, Russia should be booted from the UN and Trump must disinvite Putin from attending the G20 conference in December, then unleash the sledgehammer sanctions just given to him by Congress.
Fortunately, Kyiv and Ukrainians are tough. Blowing up and burning data centers provide striking visuals on Russian television, but Kyiv’s internet system, battle-tested for ages, is too decentralized to be shut down easily.
The same is true when it comes to keeping the power on. Ukrainians have learned to be good at repairing and replacing everything since the war started in 2022, and they are also psychologically resolute. Life in the capital continues. Concerts, fashion shows, baby showers happen as drones attack constantly. Schools operate in subways. Parliament now meets underground because of bombing attacks.
Says a close friend of mine in Kyiv: “There are long lineups at banks, grocery stores, and everything takes ten times longer to do. My friend’s due date is in two weeks, and she’s busy planning for her new baby, but buying formula and diapers is more difficult. But she’ll find a way. If the only choice is to give up to Russia, I don’t choose it, nor does anyone else. We stock up on what we need and use the shelters. It will get worse, and everyone’s preparing. We understand. It will be fine. I will be fine.”
In recent days, Zelensky issued an “SOS” to Ukrainians, confirming that Putin will ruthlessly escalate this autumn: “We know from intelligence and some people around Putin that at the beginning of September Putin said, ‘No rules now.’ The Russians couldn’t occupy us. So now they are doing massive attacks and massive killings. And of course, they want to go after our bridges and, from what we understand, after our data centers, internet, cell network, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to run away from their cities, and we need to do everything to save our people and cities.”
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s deep strikes have wrecked 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity, dramatically reducing the cash flow it needs to wage war. And the more war crimes Putin commits, the more pushbacks.
After Putin’s latest threat against civilians, Germany immediately announced another €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in military assistance, including long-range weapons, drones and satellite capabilities, and that German and Ukrainian companies are deepening defense-industrial cooperation.
Then on Oct. 4, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz even flew into Kyiv during a bombing attack to show support for Ukraine. “I traveled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks. If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us. And I will tell President Zelensky today: ‘You can continue to count on our help,’” Merz said.
Meanwhile, midterms approach in the US on Nov. 5, and Trump’s questionable, tepid, and foolish respect for Putin will do him in because the American public is simply not buying it, any more than they agree that his Iran war is a good idea. His popularity is at an all-time low due to corrupt practices, economic pain, and the Iran war. Russia is considered a scourge, not a potential G20 ally.
A major survey this week by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 86% of Americans blame Putin for the conflict. A YouGov poll found that 61% of Americans believe Russia started the war and only 6% blame Ukraine. Some 74% of Americans believe Putin’s invasion was unjustified and support weapons for Ukraine and lethal economic sanctions against Russia. And last month, Congress overwhelmingly approved a sledgehammer sanctions bill that Trump signed. In response, Putin snubbed this “leverage” by launching a bombing holocaust against civilians. Trump cannot ignore this.
Putin’s declaration that he will be murdering women and children, and destroying cities, is his “poison pawn” that undermines any credibility he may have had. Peace talks are pointless; only more weapons and sanctions are needed.
Obviously, Putin has never wanted peace and has been stringing Trump along. His threat to women and children in Ukraine is sufficient justification for Trump to use his sledgehammer sanctions, which are capable of strangling Russia’s cash flow and stopping his war. Trump must also remove all restrictions on Ukraine’s use of ATACMS, provide Patriots, and help fund Ukrainian defense production. Then Europe must release to Ukraine the $200 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets it holds in order to help it pay for weapons, defense, and repairs.
Putin must be defeated. Checkmate. He is not civilized, nor is his regime. He never wanted peace; he will never leave Ukraine alone; he wants Europe; he spreads war globally, and when it’s over, the West must provide Ukraine with arms and credible security guarantees backed by troops.
Putin hides with his family and cohorts in bunkers, as did Hitler in the end, and issues a declaration to slaughter innocents, which has gone too far. He has defeated himself and ended up in “zugzwang”, a situation in chess where every move worsens his military or economic position, including doing nothing.
Putin must go. He belongs in a gulag or on trial at The Hague or worse. This must end.

====================================================================================================

Bulgarian medical invention helps in cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:10:38 UTC
22:10:38 KST

News
Every tenth Bulgarian woman is diagnosed with breast cancer, which is increasingly affecting younger women, says Prof. Svilеn Maslyankov
Bulgarian medical invention helps in cancer surgery
The inventors are a team of engineers from the town of Gorna Oryahovitsa
Saturday 10 October 2026 14:25
Saturday, 10 October 2026, 14:25
PHOTO Zdravka Maslyankova
Font size
A team of engineers from the town of Gorna Oryahovitsa in northern Bulgaria has invented the first portable gamma spectrometer detector in Bulgaria to be used in oncology, particularly in breast cancer surgery.
“Every tenth Bulgarian woman is diagnosed with this serious disease, which is increasingly affecting younger women,” said Professor Svilеn Maslyankov, an oncological surgeon at Sofia's Alexandrovska Hospital. He has already operated on four women with breast carcinoma using a prototype of the medical invention.
“The use of this device in cancer surgery helps preserve patients’ quality of life and prevents postoperative complications,” Professor Maslyankov said.
The inventors from Gorna Oryahovitsa spent a year and a half developing the portable gamma spectrometer, working in consultation with a nuclear physicist and oncologist Professor Svilеn Maslyankov. There are international equivalents of the device, but according to its inventors, the Bulgarian version is more sensitive and accurate in cancer diagnosis.
“The purpose of the device is to detect tumour cells and, at the surgeon’s discretion, remove the affected soft tissue. Thanks to the sensor we developed, our device has greater sensitivity than the equivalent device against which Professor Maslyankov compared it in clinical conditions,” explained the inventor, engineer Mihail Chenkov.
Mihail Chenkov (left) and oncology professor Dr. Svilen Maslyankov
PHOTO Zdravka Maslyankova
The gamma spectrometer has a built-in temperature sensor, which is of great importance to surgeons:
“This temperature sensor provides information, and every 100 milliseconds the device automatically adjusts itself. A change of just one degree in the ambient temperature produces a 3% measurement error. Another innovation is the articulated arm, which bends at an angle of around 30 degrees. This allows the surgeon to access more difficult-to-reach areas in order to carry out the diagnostic procedure.”
The device is used for so-called sentinel lymph node mapping in breast cancer and other types of cancer.
“The day before surgery, a radionuclide is injected into the breast area where the tumour is suspected to be located. Its molecules accumulate in what is known as the sentinel lymph node. If there is no cancerous spread, only this lymph node is removed, rather than the entire lymphatic bundle, as is currently done. The precision of the procedure eliminates subsequent complications and significantly improves patients’ quality of life,” Professor Maslyankov explained.
“Breast cancer prevention in Bulgaria faces serious problems,” Professor Svilеn Maslyankov said:
“Some 6-8% of breast cancer cases are genetically determined. There are no programmes to identify and prevent them. There is no established screening programme. Mammography is performed after the age of 45 and is voluntary. A screening programme requires resources, but it would mean that patients could be diagnosed at a much earlier stage.”
Breast cancer is increasingly affecting younger women. Professor Maslyankov said that last year he diagnosed a 23-year-old woman with the disease, while several months ago he operated on a 28-year-old woman with breast carcinoma.
The invention developed by the engineers from Gorna Oryahovitsa, a portable gamma spectrometer that can assist in cancer surgery for breast cancer, melanomas and various other oncological diseases, is now awaiting certification. The process is expected to take at least a year before the device can be placed on the market. Its development was supported by a grant under the EU Operational Programme “Competitiveness”.

Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:10:02 UTC
22:10:02 KST

Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
RAMALLAH, Oct 10 - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed legislative elections due next month until September 11, 2027, and called a presidential poll for the same date, blaming Israel and the security situation in the Palestinian territories for the delay.
Abbas' decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections", the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
In a post on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, pointing to the last Palestinian election having been held two decades ago, rejected Abbas' remarks as "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability."
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead next month. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-2006, after which Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
Abbas has governed by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.
The Palestinian Authority held municipal elections in April in the West Bank and in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, the only city in the enclave to participate. The vote was the first election held in Gaza since 2006.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections this November.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
The decree called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to vote.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
Israel typically bans the Palestinian Authority from holding elections in East Jerusalem, territory it captured in the 1967 war and later annexed in a move most countries do not recognize.
The decision to postpone followed consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process.
PLEDGE TO HOLD VOTE AFTER TWO DECADES
Two Palestinian officials told Reuters on Thursday that leaders of Abbas' Fatah movement and rival Hamas had agreed at a meeting in Cairo on Wednesday to postpone the elections.
An August poll by the West Bank-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) showed declining support for both Hamas and Fatah, which many Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank blame for their continuing political divisions.
The delay comes just weeks after Abbas reaffirmed the November election timetable in his September 24 address to the UN General Assembly, as he sought to advance internationally backed reforms.
Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to hold presidential and legislative elections as part of France's recognition of a Palestinian state in September 2025.
France's foreign ministry said on Thursday that holding the elections was essential, and it welcomed the launch of an EU election observation mission. REUTERS

‘Anachronism’: Rubio’s civilisational rhetoric prompts pushback from Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:09:09 UTC
22:09:09 KST

‘Anachronism’: Rubio’s civilisational rhetoric prompts pushback from Iran
Rubio says threats faced by Western civilisation today are ‘every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity’.
Tehran, Iran – A speech by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoking memories of ancient Persia has been met with coldness or disdain across the Iranian political spectrum amid Washington’s ongoing war on Iran.
With the Acropolis in Athens as a backdrop, Rubio presented the United States, founded in the 18th century, as the inheritor of ancient Western civilisation running from Greece to Rome.
During the speech, he argued that modern-day Western countries have lost their confidence, weakened their industries and militaries, and need renewed ambition and power in the future.
Referencing the ancient Greco-Persian Wars, he used the Persian destruction of Athens in 480 BC under King Xerxes I as an example of Western civilisation surviving an external enemy.
“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines and razed the Acropolis to the ground,” Rubio said. He subsequently hailed the return of the Athenians and the construction of the Parthenon under Pericles.
The top US diplomat also directed his rhetoric against Iran’s current leaders, who have been in power since a 1979 Islamic revolution, calling them “fanatics” who run a “death cult” that wields martyrdom as a tool to achieve their political objectives.
“The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity,” Rubio claimed. He boasted that the choice of President Donald Trump’s administration was the “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.
The US and Iran have been at war since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. While fighting between the two sides has subsided, the US has continued a naval blockade on Iran while shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, and parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf both responded by invoking the Roman Emperor Valerian, who was captured alive by Persian King Shapur I’s forces in battle in 260 AD.
“Anyone who brings history into this must be prepared for its repetition,” Rezaei said.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused Rubio of flattening Greek, Roman, Christian and modern history.
It also accused the secretary of state of incorporating an “America First” narrative to legitimise a military escalation against Iran after a relative decrease in fighting since June when a now-defunct memorandum of understanding was agreed.
“It appears that the US has concluded it is better to justify its policy of coercion and force to the world under the beautiful neon lights of ‘philosophy of history’, instead of naked bullying that uses the language of cowboys,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said in a statement. He added that Rubio was resorting to “anachronism”, rehashing long buried historical events for modern-day legitimacy.
After the 2020 assassination of Qassem Soleimani, a commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Trump threatened to hit 52 Iranian sites “very hard”, including places “important to Iran & the Iranian culture”.
Since February, the US has been criticised for damaging Iranian historical and cultural sites during its bombing of Iran.
Culture Minister Reza Salehi-Amiri urged Western politicians to speak about Iran with a “language of respect” since “it is not an enemy created in a political speech but a living civilisation, a great nation and a lasting reality in world history” that dates back millennia.
Iranian historian Touraj Daryaei told local media on Friday that while Rubio’s account of the sack of Athens was true, he omitted an important fact cited by Greek historian Herodotus and others – a major motivation for the Persian attack was retaliation.
In 498 BC, Athens’ forces burned Sardis, a provincial Persian capital in western Anatolia. For Iranians who feel they were subject to an unprovoked attack by the US and Israel, this event could have modern-day relevance.
Shima, a 26-year-old resident of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that she did not appreciate Rubio’s attempt to use conflicts 2,500 years ago to muster support for the ongoing war with Iran.
“They want to continue the war, and they will say whatever they think will work in the moment,” she said.
During his January 2025 Senate confirmation hearing, Rubio had referred to Iranians as “the people of an ancient civilisation and culture with tremendous pride and advances who take great pride in their Persian heritage and identity”.
“I don’t know of any nation on Earth in which there’s a bigger difference between the people and those who govern them,” he said at the time. “In no way are the clerics who run the country representative of the people and its history and contributions it’s made to humanity.”
But the US war on Iran, its naval blockade of southern Iranian ports and isolating sanctions have not had the worst impact on Iran’s government and leaders but on Iranians themselves and have failed to change the behaviour of the government.
Trump’s comments on the potential “death of a civilisation” in Iran in case of a military escalation have instilled more pessimism among Iranians about the goals of the US war, which was initially cited as an attempt to free the people from their government.
Most Iranians reacted negatively to Rubio’s latest speech although some members of the diaspora or others opposed to the Islamic Republic argued that the US secretary of state is against Iranian authorities, not an entire ancient civilisation.
Iranian state media were quick to slam Rubio for his remarks with the hardline Vatan-e Emrouz newspaper on Saturday publishing a front page image of Rubio in ancient Roman military attire and holding a shield and sword.
“Ancient war” read the headline. The newspaper claimed that Rubio was trying to “create historical-ideological backing for the US war against Iran”.
Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, DC, told Al Jazeera he believes Rubio’s aim was to define a common enemy for the US and Europe to rebuild their relations around.
“He decided that Iran, rather than Islam, which was previously viewed as the civilisational enemy, should play that role to bind the West together,” he said. “It also reflects US frustration that Europe has not played a major role in the war and seeks to paper over deep divisions between the US and Europe on Russia and Ukraine.”
Rubio delivered his speech as Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to sell diesel fuel to the US and global markets despite sanctions on Russia. The US president said the agreement would lower diesel prices, which have risen to record levels due to the Iran war. Nasr said Trump’s announcement and Rubio’s speech together could be a message by the administration that Iran and not Russia is the enemy the West should be focused on.
“I think whether this rhetoric would alienate Iranians was no more a concern than President [George W] Bush’s Islamophobia was a concern alienating Muslims,” Nasr told Al Jazeera. “However, it makes clear that Washington sees no difference between Iranians and Iran as a civilisation and the Islamic Republic.”

Polish far-right politician Grzegorz Braun called for the restoration of the Nord Stream pipelines and Poland’s participation in the Russian-German energy project, saying he hoped to declare: “I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning.”
Braun, a member of the European Parliament who leads the Confederation of the Polish Crown Party, appeared alongside politicians from Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) at a conference in Lubmin on Wednesday, TVN24 reported.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A former Polish lawmaker, Braun was excluded from a sitting of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, in December 2023.
Lubmin, in the northeastern German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, is where the Nord Stream pipelines come ashore after crossing the Baltic Sea from Russia.
“Nord Stream 1, and probably Nord Stream 2 as well, will be restarted. Russian gas will flow west, because without it Europe will go bankrupt,” Braun said.
He argued that Warsaw should seek a stake in the project instead of opposing it.
“Poland should participate, not boycott. Poland should be the initiator,” he said, proposing that the country become a shareholder in Nord Stream.
Polish minister calls Braun’s position ‘treason’

Ukraine Strikes Samara Oil Blending Hub for Second Time
Polish Energy Minister Miłosz Motyka condemned Braun’s position.
“Grzegorz Braun backed the anti-Polish Nord Stream. Shame and treason,” Motyka wrote.
The minister said supporting the pipeline contradicted Poland’s national interests and amounted to backing Russian President Vladimir Putin’s Russia.
Poland has repeatedly warned that dependence on Russian energy allows Moscow to finance its war and use gas supplies as political leverage against European states.
AfD pushes for return of Russian gas
Braun appeared in Lubmin alongside AfD lawmaker Steffen Kotré. The German party has called for sanctions on Russian energy to be lifted and for gas imports from Russia to resume.
AfD leaders are already preparing talks with Putin’s economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev about restoring Russian gas supplies to Germany. The prospective meeting could take place in 2027.
Germany’s federal government opposes reopening Nord Stream and says the country has secured alternative energy supplies.
Nord Stream 1 stopped operating in 2022, while Nord Stream 2 never entered commercial service. Germany halted its certification on Feb. 22, 2022, two days before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Three of the pipelines’ four lines were subsequently damaged in underwater explosions in September 2022.
Any restart would face major legal and political obstacles. The pipelines remain under US and EU sanctions, and reopening them would require approval from the German government.
US and Russia discuss possible pipeline deal
Braun’s comments came as top US and Russian officials explored the possibility of bringing an American investor into Nord Stream, Reuters reported, citing five people familiar with the discussions.
The talks involved US envoy Jared Kushner and Dmitriev, although the extent of their discussions about the pipelines remains unclear.
A White House official said there had been “no Nord Stream discussions recently,” while another US official described a deal as unlikely in the medium term.
Poland and the Baltic states remain firmly opposed to restoring Russian energy supplies through the pipelines, viewing them as a threat to European security and a potential source of revenue for Moscow’s war against Ukraine.

How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:00:58 UTC
22:00:58 KST

When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.
Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England.
But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story.
Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset.
The businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt.
As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs.
And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge.
Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.
The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50.
Bekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room.
He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head.
Hugh Thomas, a food writer from Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.”
Some, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs.
Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomed a cage of endangered red squirrels. But there, too, lay a problem.
The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds.
Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.”
While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds.
People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.
Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”
The worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”. The local authority declared an emergency that evening.
Villagers have also set up a petition against the spraying of pesticides on the Newt’s farmland.
The model and actor Gabriella Wilde, who also lives locally, said: “I was surprised and a little disappointed to learn that they are using such harmful chemicals in their farming operations. That is certainly not the image they project to their guests and local fans. Is it really necessary, especially given how many local farms are making great strides in moving away from old school harmful practices, and towards more nature friendly farming?”
Farmers have been suspicious that new boreholes drilled by the hotel have dried up sections of the River Brue, the stream that Bruton is named after. The cider-maker Oliver Dowding, the nextdoor neighbour of the hotel, has entered negotiations with the Newt via the Environment Agency over his section of the river, which runs through his land. He said, ironically, that the newts which used to live on his land had disappeared.
Though the Newt boasts that its food is “locally produced”, its farms do not have organic certification. John Sykes, who lives nearby, pointed to the severely trimmed hedges around the estate as well as the sterile lawns.
“Look, there are no berries for the birds here. And what bothers me is the land immediately adjacent to our village used to be an organic farm, now they’ve bought it, and it isn’t any more. They are continuing to buy farmland, and I don’t know when they will stop. I don’t want to live somewhere that’s just one man’s estate,” Sykes said.
A spokesperson for the Newt in Somerset said: “Fundamental to our philosophy is a love of gardens, respect for the land and a determination to share that passion with a broad audience. To ensure best practice, we employ experts across our operations, including agronomists, horticulturists, arborists, conservationists, educationalists, beekeepers, nutritionists, livestock and wildlife specialists, alongside our hospitality teams.
“We are equally committed to our local community, maintaining close relationships with local organisations and proudly employing more than 650 people, who are either from or live within the local area.”

If she really was raped, why didn’t she speak up earlier? Why did she get drunk? Why was she wearing such a short skirt? Why did she walk home by herself?
God, it’s exhausting, isn’t it? Every time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without fail. People accuse the woman of asking for it. They question her motives; they scrutinize her looks; they attack her character. And without fail, she is punished for speaking up.
It happened to Christine Blasey Ford when she accused Brett Kavanaugh, then a supreme court nominee, of assaulting her when they were both teenagers in the 1980s. Ford and her family reportedly had to flee their home because of threats and harassment.
According to her lawyers, her email was hacked and she was impersonated online. Her entire life was turned upside down. Meanwhile, Kavanaugh was praised by Donald Trump and now has a lifetime appointment on the supreme court.
It happened with E Jean Carroll, who accused Trump of sexually assaulting her back in 1996. Trump said Carroll was not his “type” and “totally lying”. His lawyer asked Carroll why she didn’t scream during the alleged attack and why she didn’t go to the police at the time. Carroll’s life was upended and the Trump administration opened a criminal investigation into her.
Now we’re seeing the cycle repeat with the woman known as Jane Doe in the Cornell gang-rape case. According to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, Doe is receiving threats from people who have discovered her identity and is terrified for her safety. Nobody ended up dead on that particular occasion, but Doe’s character is systematically being assassinated. “What attracts women to those parties – late at night, like Jane Doe – to walk alone to a fraternity house and take her chances?” Caitlin Flanagan tut-tutted in the Free Press. “What she’s really looking for is a man. She has a whole video online talking about her cankles. And she possibly enjoyed being admired. This is how women make these mistakes.”
It should go without saying that being raped is not a “mistake”. It should go without saying that a woman should be able to go to a party and have a drink and walk home at night and wear whatever she likes without it being an invitation for men to rape her. And yet it seems that women have to keep saying all this over and over again.
