Does voting by mail make for better choices? A 2020 election study suggests it might
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:00:22 UTC
22:00:22 KST

Casting a ballot from home might do more than offer convenience; it could also help citizens select leaders who genuinely reflect their personal political beliefs. A study published in Political Behavior indicates that Americans who voted by mail during the 2020 presidential election were more likely to vote for the candidate who best aligned with their stated views than those who cast ballots in person. The findings suggest that having the flexibility to review ballot choices at home may improve the quality of democratic decision-making.
What does it mean to vote correctly? In political science, the term does not mean choosing the objectively best leader or backing the winning candidate. Instead, it refers to whether a citizen votes for the candidate who best matches their own expressed preferences on policy issues, partisan identity, and assessments of character. When a voter picks a candidate who is a weaker match for their own stated preferences than another candidate on the ballot, researchers call that an incorrect vote.
The research was conducted by Jennifer Wolak, a professor of political science at Michigan State University, and Carey E. Stapleton, a lecturer in the Department of Analytics and Computational Social Science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. They examined how different voting environments shape these electoral decisions.
At a traditional polling place, citizens often wait in line and then typically spend three to four minutes completing a lengthy ballot. The authors argue that because many voters are reluctant to hold up others waiting behind them, they rely largely on memory to recall where each contender stands across multiple offices.
Mail-in ballots, by contrast, can be completed at a kitchen table, and voters report taking about two days on average to fill them out. The authors propose that this extra time lets people look up unfamiliar candidates, read through ballot measures, or talk over choices with family members, which may help them make more considered choices.
“With the pandemic, a lot of people voted by mail for the first time,” lead author Wolak told PsyPost. “Filling out your ballot at home is often a different experience than casting your ballot at a polling place. You can take your time when filling out your ballot at home, without worrying about holding up the line or being late to your next appointment.”
“When you are uncertain about how to vote or unfamiliar with a certain electoral race or ballot question, you can do additional research prior to casting your official ballot,” she explained. “Our suspicion was that under these conditions, people might be better able to identify which candidates are aligned with their political goals.”
Research on political knowledge highlights how access to information shapes voter decision-making. For example, a 2019 study suggested that the ability to look things up online may partly stand in for political knowledge stored in memory, particularly among younger Americans who grew up with the internet. Having the ability to look up candidates while filling out a ballot at home may help offset gaps in memory.
At the same time, convenience voting can introduce its own complications. In a 2011 study of California’s 2008 presidential primary, researchers found that precincts with more mail voting gave more votes to candidates who had already dropped out, since mail voters often decided before late-breaking campaign developments. That finding suggests voting from home carries potential drawbacks as well as benefits.
Researchers have also noted that people who take advantage of flexible voting options often differ from those who vote at a polling place. Specifically, a 2020 study suggested that individuals who already possess high political knowledge are more likely to seek out convenience voting methods in the first place. In the 2020 election, mail voters tended to be older, more educated, more liberal, and more knowledgeable, making it necessary to separate the method of voting from these personal traits.
To evaluate whether mail balloting helps voters make better choices, the authors analyzed data from the 2020 American National Election Studies. This extensive survey asked participants about their issue preferences, partisan loyalty, and opinions about candidate traits. The authors combined these responses with official state voter records, which allowed them to verify the exact method each participant used to cast their ballot.
To determine whether someone voted correctly, the researchers used a widely used measure developed by political scientists Richard Lau and David Redlawsk. It scores how well each presidential candidate matched a respondent’s own answers on partisanship, policy issues, evaluations of the incumbent’s performance, perceptions of the candidates’ traits, and ties to social groups associated with each party. A participant who chose the candidate with the higher score was coded as voting correctly.
The authors first tested this relationship using a statistical model of 4,728 voters while holding several background factors constant. The model accounted for political interest, strength of party affiliation, political knowledge, education, ideology, age, gender, race, and ethnicity. The authors also included a measure of in-person early voting to see if voting before Election Day carried similar benefits.
The results indicated that casting a ballot by mail was associated with an estimated 2.6 percentage point increase in the probability of voting correctly. In baseline terms, roughly 90 percent of in-person voters selected the candidate aligned with their preferences, compared to nearly 93 percent of mail voters, a gap roughly equivalent to the boost associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in political knowledge. In contrast, the difference in correct voting between in-person early voters and Election Day voters was not statistically significant, suggesting that the advantage was tied to voting at home rather than to voting early.
To ensure that this pattern was not simply the result of differences in who chooses to vote by mail, the authors used statistical matching procedures. One method, known as coarsened exact matching, paired mail voters with in-person voters who fell into the same broad ranges on key traits. Across three versions, which matched on political factors such as interest and knowledge, on demographics, or on both, voting by mail remained associated with an estimated gain of roughly 2.1 to 4.7 percentage points in correct voting, with sample sizes ranging from 523 to 4,907.
The authors also applied entropy balancing, an analytical technique that reweights the data so that mail voters and in-person voters look alike on many characteristics without discarding participants. Balancing on the same factors used in the earlier models produced an estimated 2.7 percentage point gain among 4,728 voters, and adding measures such as concern about the election outcome, belief in one’s ability to influence politics, ideological consistency, and past voting produced a 1.7-point gain among 4,658 voters. In an expanded model of 4,634 voters that also balanced on state-level factors, such as campaign competitiveness and the ease of voting by mail, the estimated boost was 5.0 percentage points.
The authors then evaluated how state election laws influenced these outcomes across 4,658 voters using a mediation analysis. In 2020, states took very different approaches to mail voting: nine states and the District of Columbia mailed ballots directly to all registered voters, while other states required specific excuses or notarized documents to cast an absentee ballot. Voters living in states that mailed ballots automatically had a 92 percent predicted probability of voting by mail, compared to only 38 percent in states without universal ballot distribution.
The mediation analysis suggested that state policies making mail-in ballots easier to obtain were indirectly linked to more correct voting by encouraging more residents to vote by mail. This indirect pathway was associated with an estimated increase of about 1.3 to 1.6 percentage points in correct presidential votes. However, the overall difference in correct voting between states with easier and harder access to mail ballots was close to zero, because the indirect boost was offset by a small direct association in the opposite direction that was not statistically significant.
The authors conducted additional analyses to see if the link between mail voting and correct voting existed outside the unusual conditions of the 2020 pandemic. By examining a panel of participants surveyed in both 2016 and 2020, they found that voters who switched from in-person voting in 2016 to mail-in voting in 2020 were more likely to vote correctly in 2020. An analysis of respondents from the 2016 election who were re-surveyed in 2020 indicated that voting by mail was associated with roughly a 5 percentage point gain in correct voting after balancing for demographic and political traits.
“A lot of the discussion around encouraging vote-by-mail has been about increasing participation,” Wolak noted. “Most research has found that introducing vote-by-mail can boost voter turnout, especially among some of the groups who are the least likely to vote.”
“Our work shows an even wider set of civic rewards for vote-by-mail,” she added. “Giving people the opportunity to complete their ballot at home not only increases their likelihood of participating, but it also can increase the odds that they choose the candidates that best match up to their political preferences.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study relied on survey and voting records rather than an experiment where people were randomly assigned to vote by mail or in person, the authors cannot establish direct cause and effect. Although the statistical models accounted for education, political knowledge, and numerous other traits, unmeasured personal factors might still influence both the decision to vote by mail and candidate choice.
Another factor to consider is the modest size of the observed effect, which ranged between two and five percentage points across the various models. In presidential elections, voters already encounter an abundance of news coverage and campaign advertising, which helps roughly 80 to 90 percent of citizens vote correctly regardless of how they cast their ballots. As a result, the room for measurable improvement in presidential contests is relatively small.
“We estimate that compared to those who vote in-person, people who vote by mail are about two percentage points more likely to select the presidential candidate that best lines up with their political preferences,” Wolak pointed out. “It’s a small effect, but we would expect the improvements in the quality of voter decision-making to be even greater in down-ballot races where people have less knowledge about the candidates.”
The authors also emphasized that their research focused on the presidential race because reliable survey measures comparing voter preferences to candidate positions are rarely available for congressional or gubernatorial contenders. In lower-profile contests where campaigns receive less attention, voters typically have far less information stored in memory. Future studies could investigate whether having a ballot at home leads to even larger gains in these less publicized races, where having extra time to look up candidates online might matter most.
The study, “The Effects of Voting by Mail on Correct Voting,” was authored by Jennifer Wolak and Carey E. Stapleton.

Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine returned 16 citizens from the temporarily occupied territories through the "Novi Yarylovychi" checkpoint. Among them were people who needed medical assistance.
Another 16 Ukrainians were successfully returned from the temporarily occupied territories to the territory of Ukraine under its control. This was reported by Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, UНN reports.
Details
The return of 16 Ukrainians from the temporarily occupied territories is 16 different stories, circumstances, and paths to safety. For some, the journey home became an opportunity to finally receive medical care; for others, a chance to reunite with their loved ones. Each such return requires an individual approach, careful preparation, and coordination among many people
He noted that this evacuation took place through the "Novi Yarylovychi" checkpoint.
Lubinets said that one of the women had remained alone in the occupied territory for a long time. Due to her health condition and limited mobility, she could not make the journey home on her own. Her return required arranging special transportation, medical assistance, and a safe route. At the same time, preparations for her departure had to avoid attracting the attention of the occupation authorities and exposing the woman to additional danger.
Another story concerns a family for whom time proved decisive: in temporarily occupied Luhansk region, a married couple had long been unable to leave because of the wife's serious health condition. In April this year, the woman suffered a massive stroke and required constant care. Her husband—an elderly person with a disability and a liquidator of the Chornobyl nuclear power plant accident—also required treatment and could no longer care for his wife on his own

In August–September, 41 Ukrainian citizens returned from the occupied territories through the "Mokrany - Domanove" checkpoint in Volyn.

The Palestinian struggle needs a unified nation-building project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Three years into the genocide against our people in Gaza, the Palestinian question can no longer be reduced only to ending the war or rebuilding what has been destroyed. The deeper question is whether this moment will restore the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and national independence, or enable the liquidation of the Palestinian cause through the fragmentation and occupation of the land while its people are without political rights.
These two trajectories are unfolding simultaneously. Alongside Gaza’s unprecedented destruction, settlement expansion, annexation, and ethnic cleansing, settler violence continues across the West Bank, steadily eroding the territorial and political foundations of an independent Palestinian state.
At the same time, international recognition of Palestinian self-determination has expanded, as has support for ending the occupation and establishing a Palestinian state. The unity of Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is increasingly affirmed as a political principle. But the problem is not a lack of opportunity, but the danger that on-the-ground changes will outpace the Palestinian capacity to turn international shifts into political leverage. This is particularly serious as the Palestinian leadership remains in a state of waiting and lacks initiative.
The danger is already visible in the emerging governance arrangements for Gaza. The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), established under President Trump’s Board of Peace, is a technocratic body tasked with civilian administration and reconstruction. It operates within an international structure headed by the Board’s High Representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov. Whatever its immediate practical role, such an arrangement risks turning Gaza into a separately administered territory unless it is anchored within a unified Palestinian national and governmental framework.
This is the strategic danger: Gaza could become a separate humanitarian and reconstruction file, the West Bank could be increasingly fragmented through settlement and annexation, and political division could further erode the national framework capable of protecting the unity of the Palestinian people and their land.
These are not separate risks, but form a single interrelated process: separating land from politics, politics from national representation, and representation from the capacity to act. If allowed to consolidate, liquidation can take place without ever being formally declared.
Yet, international recognition, global solidarity, and readiness to support reconstruction create a political window that should not be wasted.
A consensus government is the national bridge
This is why an interim consensus government should become the center of gravity of the next phase. It would not replace the PLO or elections, or become another formula for factional power-sharing, but it can function as a legitimate Palestinian governmental address to the outside world and the practical instrument for preventing Gaza from becoming politically separated from the West Bank.
Its purpose should be clear: one governmental and financial framework for Gaza and the West Bank, unified public institutions and services, a national reconstruction plan, protection of Palestinian fiscal and institutional capacity, and coordination of Arab and international assistance through a Palestinian national channel.
The tasks of such a consensus government would include overseeing two vital matters of national sovereignty: the reconstruction of Gaza and, above all, creating the conditions for credible elections and the reform of the PLO as a more representative political institution that comprises all Palestinians, including the diaspora.
If elections have to be postponed because conditions do not permit them, that should not produce a political vacuum. On the contrary, a time-bound consensus government becomes even more necessary to prevent the vacuum from being filled by separate arrangements imposed on Gaza, such as the U.S.-imposed NCAG.
The mandate of this government must therefore be temporary, operational, and measurable, with clear benchmarks, public reporting, and effective oversight. The government should be judged by what it delivers, not by political appointments. Its purpose is to restore national capacity and prepare the ground for renewed legitimacy – not to create a new political order.
Rebuilding the relationship between Palestinians inside and outside the homeland, and mobilizing diaspora expertise and capital, could provide important political and economic leverage. A national diaspora fund, alongside more independent Arab and Islamic partnerships, deserves consideration as a means of supporting recovery while reducing dependence on externally imposed priorities.
Three years into the genocide, Palestinians face not two abstract alternatives but two unfolding trajectories: one that fragments Palestinian land, representation, and the capacity to act; and another that reconnects them within a national framework capable of using the international shift to advance Palestinian rights.
The struggle ahead is therefore not only over Gaza or the future of the Palestinian Authority, but over whether Palestine remains the cause of a people for national self-determination.
The window will not remain open indefinitely. The longer it takes to rebuild unified national capacity, the more room there will be for facts on the ground to determine the future.
After three years of genocide, it is not enough to prevent the worst outcome. The task is to open a different path: from managing division to unifying institutions, from managing catastrophe to rebuilding, and from waiting for others to act to restoring the Palestinian initiative.

Ethiopian forces regain control of border city after reported Eritrean incursion

Ethiopian forces regain control of border city after reported Eritrean incursion
Oct 10 - Ethiopian government forces and their militia allies entered Adigrat, near the border with Horn of Africa neighbour Eritrea, on Saturday, three residents said, days after Eritrean troops were pushed back from the strategic city.
The incursion by Eritrean troops, which Eritrea has denied and Reuters could not independently verify, has raised fears of a return to all-out war along Ethiopia's northern border where the two nations have clashed before. Conflicts elsewhere in the region and tensions across the Red Sea have further raised the stakes.
Three Adigrat residents told Reuters they had seen the Ethiopian army and an allied militia in the city on Saturday morning, with one of the residents saying they saw soldiers on patrol along with military vehicles.
Reuters could not confirm whether the army was in control of Adigrat, which is located 30 km (19 miles) from the border with Eritrea. Ethiopia's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and city officials were not reachable on Saturday.
Ethiopia said in a letter to members of the UN Security Council this week that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km (37 miles) inside Tigray in recent days, warning that the presence of foreign forces left it with no option but to defend itself.
Eritrea has said reports of an Eritrean incursion are false and part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression.
Explosions were reported near Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday as the US-based conflict monitor ACLED said Ethiopia used drone strikes against Eritrean forces, who then withdrew from positions near the city.
The explosions continued on Friday, according to an Adigrat resident, who told Reuters they had heard repeated explosions overnight and into the morning several kilometres outside town.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s spokesperson and Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
ETHIOPIAN SEA ACCESS A FLASH POINT
Yemane said on Friday that Eritrea had shown restraint, accusing landlocked Ethiopia of declaring a war of aggression against his country by stating in 2023 it would acquire sovereign access to the sea.
Ethiopia had access to a coastline for decades until Eritrea gained independence from Addis Ababa in 1993. Ethiopia argues that restoring sea access is an existential issue but has said it would be restored through peace and dialogue.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of backing the rebel alliance that has been battling government troops since September 23 in its northern regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Eritrea has denied doing so.
After years of war, Eritrea and Ethiopia made peace in a 2018 agreement that earned Ethiopia's Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize. Eritrea fought in support of Ethiopia’s federal government during a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray, but relations soured again toward the end of that conflict.
The fighting that broke out last month has been the biggest escalation of violence since the Tigray war, in which hundreds of thousands died. REUTERS

India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders detained; New Delhi in lockdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:50:34 UTC
21:50:34 KST

India arrests 2,000, including ‘Cockroach’ leaders, in New Delhi crackdown
Police lock down New Delhi to foil protest demanding resignation of the country’s election chief.
Police in India’s capital, New Delhi, have detained more than 2,000 protesters, opposition politicians, journalists, lawyers and the founders of the “Cockroach” youth movement in a bid to quash a rally demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city on Saturday, while mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district as authorities moved to stop a demonstration organised by the satirically-named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other youth groups.
Dozens of metro stations and markets were also shut.
The Hindhu newspaper, citing New Delhi police sources, said nearly 2,500 protesters were detained across the capital. The Reuters news agency, meanwhile, citing a Ministry of Home Affairs official, put the figure at about 2,000.
Some 600 people were also arrested in the city of Mumbai, India’s financial hub, over the protests, according to the ANI news agency.
The protesters were demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a revision of voter lists they say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Protesters accuse the BJP of using the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists to sway results, and opposition parties say the revisions affected several recent state elections the party won, casting a shadow over polls in the world’s largest democracy.
Kumar has not commented, but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.
The CJP had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central New Delhi. But on Saturday, the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.
Security forces also set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points across the city of 20 million people, boarded buses searching for protesters, and inspected vehicles.
Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes.
CJP leaders detained
Police detained the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, as well as his associates, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, in an aeroplane upon arrival in New Delhi from Mumbai.
Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.”
In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke was seen addressing the flight’s passengers.
“It was nice to know you all. We can see where the nation is heading,” he said. “This is dictatorship, where Delhi police has entered in the flight and trying to arrest us.”
Delhi police also detained other CJP members: YouTuber and Modi critic Dhruv Rathee; Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist); Dipankar Bhattacharya, the general secretary of the party; and Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court.
Some opposition lawmakers, as well as former chief ministers – Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala – were also detained, television channels showed.
Despite the detentions of the founders of the youth movement, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”.
Shranaya, a state committee member of the left-wing Students’ Federation of India (SFI), who goes by her first name, told Al Jazeera that the SFI’s office in New Delhi had been under surveillance for hours, but members inside had managed to escape and protest.
“This is dictatorship, live and in front of us, just to protect a bureaucrat who steals elections for the BJP on Modi’s behest. They are murdering democracy in the daylight in the Indian capital,” she said.
“This government is unaware of the power of the people, and that is our upper hand. We do not have weapons, but we have zeal. We will be again on the streets, and we will keep returning,” she added. “We are students. We are unemployed. We are ‘cockroaches’ – and we will return.”
She then climbed a barricade but was dragged away by police and taken away in a bus.
Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.
Challenge to Modi
The protests represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi and intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar’s revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.
The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation.
BJP spokesman Sambit Patra dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements” and said that “their flop show has been completely demolished”.
“What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance,” he told reporters.
The opposition Congress party’s president, Mallikarjun Kharge, slammed Modi’s government after the detentions.
“Modi government has turned the ‘Mother of Democracy’ into a ‘Muzzled Democracy’!” he posted on X. “Detentions, arrests, jails, lathis [batons] and pellets cannot deter the people of India. Since the days of our freedom struggle, the youth have been at the forefront of shaping the nation’s destiny.”
Global condemnation
The United Nations Human Rights Office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
“We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” UN Human Rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement.
He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
Amnesty International warned that the detentions signal the Indian government’s desperate attempts to “suppress critical voices”, while the Committee to Protect Journalists urged Indian police to “respect journalists”.
The Indian mission to the UN in Geneva, however, called the global concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution. “As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order,” the statement added.
The unrest comes before a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.
Sanjay Kapoor, editor of Hard News Magazine and a political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is “very strange” to see Modi’s government “so panic-driven and fearful of what the protesters might do”.
“The truth is that the BJP and the centre have been very, very scared of how it will all play out,” he said.
Kapoor noted that most people coming to the protests do not want Modi’s BJP to continue to govern.
“Modi’s government has begun to lose a lot of credibility at the moment,” he said. “BJP is afraid that the ground has shifted dramatically against them and they would find it very difficult to come back to power.”

Nearly 50,000 women, girls killed or wounded by Israel in Gaza

Breadcrumb
Nearly 50,000 women, girls killed or severely wounded by Israel in Gaza since 2023
Nearly 50,000 women and girls have been killed or severely wounded in Gaza since October 2023, UN Women revealed in a report on Friday.
The agency said the majority of recorded casualties occurred in the first two years of the war, noting that violence, demolitions and killings have continued despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.
Data complied by the group further revealed that at least 277 women and girls have been killed since the truce came into effect.
"More than 38,000 killed and 11,700 left with injuries so severe that they now live with lifelong disabilities," Sofia Calltorp, UN Women's chief of humanitarian action, commented.
She said that almost a million women and girls have also been forced out of their homes and remain displaced, living in makeshift tents or the unsafe ruins of their homes.
Caltrop also said that the number of female-headed households has doubled, meaning one in four households in Gaza are now headed by women, who carry the burden of securing a livelihood and providing food.
The figures come as Israel continues to heavily restrict aid into Gaza and funding cuts for aid organisations have also had a marked impact on women, making them even more vulnerable.
According to data from UN Women, aid organisations have reported an increase in gender-based violence as a result of the dire humanitarian situation, while poverty and mental health distress has also been on the rise since 2025. At least 13 organisations also reported an uptick in child marriages recorded.
The organisation has demanded a full and proper ceasefire, and for international law to be respected. It also urged for accountability to be taken for violations committed in the enclave.
Several rights organisations have sounded the alarm over restrictions on emergency supplies in Gaza, noting that access to food, clean water, hygiene items and vital services remain severely limited.

Pillay&#8217;s defiance, Sharif&#8217;s disgrace: The prize, the praise, and the politics of prostration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:44:31 UTC
21:44:31 KST

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has exposed two political universes: a South Africa that defies imperial power and Israeli impunity, and a nuclear-armed Pakistan whose prime minister has elevated subservience into an instrument of statecraft.
History occasionally delivers a political verdict so devastating that satire becomes redundant. The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has produced precisely such a spectacle. On one side stands Navi Pillay, the formidable South African jurist who confronted apartheid and exposed Israel’s conduct in Gaza as genocide. On the other stands Shehbaz Sharif, prime minister of nuclear-armed Pakistan, who has repeatedly championed Donald Trump for the same distinction, apparently convinced that a president presiding over devastating wars deserves humanity’s highest honour for peace-making. One confronted Pharaoh. The other volunteered to polish his throne.
The contrast exposes something more damning than diplomatic embarrassment: Sharif’s spectacular deficit of political dignity.
South Africa, without nuclear weapons, has confronted Israel and its Western protectors through international law. Sharif, governing a nuclear-armed nation with one of the world’s largest militaries, cannot apparently distinguish a defender of international justice from its most powerful antagonist. South Africa confronts empire; Sharif competes for its affection.
South Africa’s defiance deserves extraordinary admiration because it challenges the imperial order’s central hypocrisy: international law binds Western adversaries while Western allies enjoy institutionalized impunity. Its historic genocide case against Israel shattered the presumption that Palestinian suffering must remain beyond judicial scrutiny whenever accountability inconveniences Washington.
Guterres in Islamabad: Genocide, cowardice, and the cage of Imran Khan
Pillay’s leadership of the UN commission concluding that Israel committed genocide in Gaza embodies this magnificent tradition of principled resistance.
A nation that defeated apartheid has become a formidable challenger of Zionist domination and Israeli impunity. Where Western governments manufacture euphemisms to sanitise atrocities, South Africa demands accountability.
Sharif, meanwhile, has perfected a more contemptible diplomatic philosophy: never confront power when you can flatter it, never defend principle when you can exchange it for patronage. His renewed campaign for Trump’s Nobel ambitions comes amid Gaza’s devastation, American-Israeli aggression against Iran, and Washington’s vindictive
assault upon international judicial institutions.
The slaughter at Minab, where a 28th February American air strike killed scores of Iranian schoolchildren, remains among the war’s most horrifying atrocities. Yet Sharif continues campaigning for Trump’s glorification.
For grieving Iranian families, his enthusiasm must appear positively obscene: a neighbouring Muslim nation’s leader lobbying to honour the president responsible for unleashing the war that devastated their lives.
And what qualifies Trump for this sanctification? His administration has armed and shielded Israel amid Gaza’s destruction, prosecuted a catastrophic war against Iran, threatened sovereign nations, and sanctioned international judicial officials. His presidency exemplifies imperial aggression stripped of diplomatic cosmetics: military violence marketed as peace, coercion presented as negotiation, and impunity defended as strategic necessity. His Nobel ambitions mock the prize’s professed principles, although its history of rewarding dubious peacemakers makes such ambitions less surprising.
Sharif’s justification is Trump’s supposed salvation of South Asia from nuclear catastrophe. How convenient that a ceasefire between two sovereign states should become Washington’s personal miracle, with Sharif volunteering as its principal evangelist. Even granting American diplomacy some credit, preventing one war cannot absolve responsibility for prosecuting others. Otherwise, the Nobel becomes an imperial rewards program in which powerful men collect humanitarian honours while their military campaigns accumulate civilian corpses.
The contrast with Pillay makes the absurdity complete. The Nobel Committee, exceptionally, recognises someone who actually embodies the prize’s professed ideals: a jurist who strengthened institutions capable of prosecuting humanity’s gravest crimes. Washington punishes those institutions. Sharif campaigns to celebrate the president responsible.
The contradiction could scarcely be more damning: one leader defends international justice, another undermines it, and Sharif insists that the latter deserves a peace prize.
READ: Pakistan’s Mecca Pact: The guns Gaza never got
Sharif personifies the culture of political subordination within sections of Pakistan’s ruling establishment, where foreign patronage masquerades as statecraft. The generals monopolise strategic authority; Sharif supplies the civilian genuflection. Yet his obsequiousness remains his own choice, not an unavoidable diplomatic necessity.
Pakistan’s participation in Trump’s Board of Peace compounds the disgrace. Sharif calls it engagement, but influence requires independence and the willingness to dissent. Without these, participation risks becoming complicity in the management of the ongoing mass murder of Palestinians.
Diplomacy requires negotiating with power, not worshipping it. Pragmatism protects national interests; sycophancy sacrifices dignity for personal favour. Sharif has made the latter his political signature. The Nobel decision has exposed a devastating contrast. Pillay’s South Africa demonstrates that moral authority requires neither nuclear weapons nor Washington’s permission. Sharif demonstrates that commanding a nuclear-armed nation cannot compensate for the absence of political independence.
Navi Pillay confronted Pharaoh and received the Nobel Peace Prize. Shehbaz Sharif bowed before Pharaoh and received only the spectacle of his own humiliation. One defended the dignity of the oppressed. The other squandered the dignity of a nation for an imperial patron’s applause.

Ceasefire ‘in name only’

NATO ‘Theory of Victory’ plan not directed against Russia — chairman of military committee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:40:40 UTC
21:40:40 KST

ROME, October 10. /TASS/. NATO’s new "Theory of Victory" plan is intended to ensure that "war never begins," Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chairman of the NATO Military Committee, assured said in an interview with La Repubblica newspaper, responding to a question about criticism that the plan was a "provocation against Russia."
"The word ‘victory’ in this context means, first and foremost, just one thing: war will never begin because those who threaten us are convinced not to start it. That is precisely why we must demonstrate that our collective deterrence system is reliable and suited to current conditions," he said.
"Defense planning is not a provocation; it is the duty of any responsible military organization. [It is based] on the principle that deterrence is effective only when the adversary knows that an attack has no chance of success," Dragone explained. In his view, the best victory is one that does not have to be fought for.
NATO's military command has drawn up a new defense plan for the alliance's eastern flank, focusing on drones and artificial intelligence. Dubbed the "Theory of Victory," it will be presented to NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich on October 12. The plan aims to clarify responses to a "possible invasion of NATO territory" and emphasizes countering hybrid threats and deterrence through combat readiness.
Russia’s leadership has repeatedly rejected speculation that the country may attack NATO states by 2030. Russian President Vladimir Putin said last year that Moscow was ready to "formalize an agreement on mutual non-aggression with Western countries in order to address existing concerns in this regard." Later, at a TASS-organized meeting with the heads of leading global news agencies, the Russian leader stressed that claims of Moscow allegedly preparing to attack Europe were not merely nonsense, but a provocation and disinformation aimed at deceiving their own populations.

Russia Looks to China Transit as Ukrainian Drone Attacks Paralyze Southern Ports

Russia Looks to China Transit as Ukrainian Drone Attacks Paralyze Southern Ports
Russian grain exporters are exploring new supply routes through China to send grain to global markets, as operations at Azov and Black Sea ports remain disrupted following Ukrainian drone strikes, The Moscow Times reported on October 9.
Speaking at the Golden Autumn 2026 exhibition in Moscow, Russian Grain Association (RGA) executive director Ksenia Bolomatova confirmed that the organization is working on transit options via China.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s total export potential is expected to fall from a planned 59 million tons to 39 million tons out of a total harvest of approximately 140 million tons, leaving an estimated 20 million tons of grain without buyers.
Baltic ports allow Russia to supply customers in the Middle East, Türkiye, and North Africa, but reaching Asian markets such as Indonesia from those locations is difficult due to high logistics costs.
To address these bottlenecks, Russia is expanding transshipment capacity in its Far East region, where more than ten terminals have experience handling grain shipments. Additional facilities are being connected, and established operators are building infrastructure to increase storage capacity, according to The Moscow Times.
The delivery problems emerged after operations stopped at Azov Sea ports and Black Sea terminals were paralyzed by Ukrainian drone strikes.
Vladimir Petrichenko, head of the analytical firm ProZerno, estimated that 20 million tons of grain could be left without buyers.
The head of SovEcon, Andrey Sizov, stated, “The harsh reality is that there are simply no export routes that could replace the Black Sea.” Over-supply has already cut grain prices in southern Russia roughly in half, dropping them to 4,000 to 5,000 rubles per ton. ProZerno estimates that carryover stocks could reach 34.8 million tons by the end of the year.
Over the course of a week from July 6 to July 12, 2026, Ukrainian unmanned systems carried out a systematic campaign in the Sea of Azov, striking 90 Russian vessels—including tankers, tugboats, ferries, and cargo ships—before reaching a total of 105 vessels targeted within eight days.
In response to the continuous drone attacks, Russia temporarily suspended navigation through the Don–Azov Canal and stopped processing applications for passage through the Kerch Strait to protect its fleet.
The operation targeted river-sea class tankers and support ships used to deliver fuel to Crimea, transfer crude oil into the Black Sea, and sustain Russian military logistics along the occupied coastline.

Palestinian Authority President Abbas postpones November legislative elections until late 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:35:17 UTC
21:35:17 KST

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree on Saturday canceling legislative elections scheduled for November 28, 2026, and setting presidential and legislative elections for September 11, 2027, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
The new decree calls on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip to participate in "free and direct elections to elect the Palestinian president and members of the Palestinian Legislative Council simultaneously, in accordance with the law," WAFA said.
His decree also cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections," the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
This follows consultations among Palestinian factions, political forces, and the Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). Serious doubts had emerged that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead next month. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The Executive Committee reached a consensus, deciding that Israeli measures in the West Bank and Gaza posed a significant obstacle to holding elections at the previously scheduled date, WAFA explained, adding that the postponement is to allow for the establishment of "suitable political, security and field conditions for free, fair and inclusive elections."
WAFA cited Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence, restrictions on freedom of movement, and the withholding of Palestinian revenues.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions," the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction, and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilization forces and police.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
PA vice president reportedly informed France of election postponement
Two Palestinian officials told Reuters on Thursday that leaders of Abbas' Fatah movement and rival Hamas had agreed at a meeting in Cairo on Wednesday to postpone the elections.
The WAFA report follows Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al Sheikh informing France of election postponements, citing worsening conditions across the Palestinian territories, according to a Thursday-dated letter addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot seen by Reuters.
"The assessment concluded that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for November 28, 2026, was based, have not materialized," the letter said. "Holding them (the legislative elections) under the current circumstances faces fundamental obstacles affecting their inclusiveness, freedom of participation, and the integrity of the electoral process."
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar calls Abbas a 'corrupt dictator'
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar responded to the report in an X/Twitter post later on Saturday, describing Abbas as a "corrupt dictator."
"His attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability," wrote Sa'ar. "Just like the other lies about 'reforms' that were never implemented - ending payments to terrorists and their families, and stopping incitement in the Palestinian education system. For over twenty years, Abbas has been selling the same thing: lies."

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the casualties and destruction on his official Telegram channel, stating that firefighters and emergency crews deployed to contain a blaze at the damaged restaurant and administer emergency aid to the victims.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“In the Obolonskyi district, there was a hit on a restaurant building. At another address in Obolon, missile debris fell in the courtyard of a residential building,” Klitschko said.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) confirmed that missile fragments landed in an open area adjacent to residential housing in the district, noting that specialized emergency brigades and law enforcement teams were dispatched to verify whether any casualties had occurred.
The ballistic barrage followed repeated waves of turbojet-powered strike drones earlier in the day that damaged regional power distribution nodes, shut down the capital’s metro system, and disrupted municipal water supplies.
Ukrainian air defense units intercepted a portion of the incoming ballistic missiles over the metropolitan area, but falling wreckage and kinetic impacts damaged civilian structures.
Belarus Summons Ukraine Envoy Over Alleged Bryansk Drone Strike
Later, Klitschko reported that the number of victims had risen to 6. Five of the injured were hospitalized. One person was treated at the scene.
Zelensky links ballistic strike to oil sanctions relief
Speaking following the attack, President Volodymyr Zelensky linked the daylight ballistic assault directly to recent Western commercial accommodations permitting Russian petroleum exports.
The president warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets generates fresh financial resources that are immediately funneled into expanding the Kremlin’s arsenal of ballistic weapons and high-speed loitering munitions.
“What it means to permit Russia to sell petroleum products was heard best in Kyiv today, when after numerous deployments of jet-powered Shaheds against energy facilities, a ballistic attack also began,” Zelensky stated.
“A portion of the missiles was downed. This demonstrates once again what Russia’s true intentions are. They count on continuing the war, terrorizing ordinary people, and destroying infrastructure.”
Zelensky stressed that international sanctions enforcement remains the only viable mechanism to limit the Kremlin’s capacity to sustain long-range bombardments.
“Every additional billion dollars they are able to earn from exports will be spent on precisely this: searching for and importing critical components, equipment for arms manufacturing, reinforcing Shaheds, producing missiles, and recruiting additional mercenaries for the front line,” Zelensky said.
“Yesterday, unfortunately, there were entirely different signals for Russia – signals that continuing attacks is supposedly permissible. This must be corrected. Strong signals are needed from the United States, Europe, and other partners.”
Bilateral consultations with Macron under fire
During the ballistic bombardment, Zelensky held an urgent telephone consultation with French President Emmanuel Macron to coordinate defense assistance and diplomatic responses to sanctions easing.
Zelensky expressed gratitude to Paris for continuous solidarity, emphasizing that the intensifying combination of ballistic missiles and turbine-powered drones necessitates expedited deliveries of modern air defense complexes and interceptors.
“It was precisely during today’s Russian ballistic attack against Kyiv that we spoke with the President of France,” Zelensky said.
“The need for additional air defense packages for Ukraine is obvious, and we are working with all partners for corresponding decisions. Unfortunately, a distinct threat of further missile strikes persists these days. It is vital to increase pressure on Russia in response, and joint bold steps must follow.”
Zelensky reported that discussions with Macron focused heavily on joint countermeasures to reverse the dilution of energy sanctions against Moscow.
“We discussed the challenges stemming from the easing of sanctions against petroleum products,” Zelensky added.
“The Russians must feel that their potential to prolong the war will no longer exist. We are coordinating substantively and preparing upcoming meetings.”
Compounding infrastructure crisis in the capital
The ballistic strikes capped a day of intense aerial bombardment that strained municipal services and civilian infrastructure across Kyiv.
Earlier on Saturday morning, Russian drone strikes damaged a major energy installation in Kyiv region, precipitating voltage drops that paralyzed all three lines of the Kyiv metro network, halted municipal electric surface transport across multiple districts, and forced energy operators to introduce emergency blackouts in Pivdenna Borshchahivka.
The grid instability also knocked offline regional water pumping stations, leaving taps dry across large parts of the capital.
Concurrently, falling drone debris struck an eight-story commercial office building and a 25-story residential tower in the Solomianskyi district, alongside fragments landing in Podilskyi district.

China, EU reaffirm stable, balanced ties as key trading partners: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:33:48 CST
21:33:48 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China and the European Union (EU) have reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining stable and balanced trade ties as key trading partners after a meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, an official with China's commerce ministry said Saturday.
Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic jointly chaired the second meeting of the consultation mechanism from Thursday to Friday in Beijing.
The two sides confirmed that they would address trade and economic differences and each other's concerns in a balanced manner within the framework of World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, explore ways to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation, and promote balanced growth and further development in China-EU trade.
Both sides agreed the consultation mechanism had been operating smoothly and efficiently, and that "the successful convening of its second meeting marked a new beginning rather than an end," said the official.
The outcomes agreed upon at the meeting demonstrated that China and the EU had both the willingness and the wisdom to manage and properly resolve differences through dialogue and consultation, effectively preventing tensions from escalating, the official said.
The two sides held intensive consultations in a spirit of mutual respect, equality and mutual benefit, discussing in depth ways to address each other's concerns on an equal footing, expand two-way market access and promote dynamic balance in China-EU trade, covering topics including medical devices, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, inverters, and agri-food products.
According to the official, the two sides agreed to explore the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods within the framework of WTO rules, and hold a technical dialogue on the EU's Foreign Subsidies Regulation.
In-depth discussions were also held on trade in electric and hybrid vehicles, which helped prevent further escalation, effectively safeguarded the actual export interests of Chinese companies and supported the stable development of China-EU trade in hybrid vehicles.
Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to addressing each other's concerns regarding export controls. The EU side will continue to work toward making progress in resolving key licensing cases involving China in the dual-use sector, said the official.
They agreed that China and the EU have significant potential for cooperation in new energy, artificial intelligence, trade in services, the digital economy, and green and low-carbon development, and that they could further explore new opportunities and expand areas of cooperation.
China will continue to welcome EU companies investing and doing business in China and to improve its business environment, said the official.
China also expects the EU to provide Chinese companies with a fair, transparent and predictable business environment, effectively protect their legitimate rights and interests, and strengthen their confidence and expectations regarding investment and business operations in the EU.
Looking ahead, the two sides will step up efforts on key trade and economic issues of mutual concern and work together to implement the outcomes and agreements reached at the meeting, said the official.
They also agreed to hold the third meeting of the mechanism in March 2027. In the meantime, they will maintain close communication at all levels, including through a ministerial-level video conference next January.
It was agreed that stable and healthy China-EU economic and trade relations serve their shared interests and also inject certainty and positive momentum into global economic growth and the stability of industrial and supply chains, said the official. ■

Verstappen wins F1 Singapore Sprint after Russell crashes out of lead
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:33:16 CST
21:33:16 KST

By F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SINGAPORE, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed his first Formula 1 victory in Singapore on Saturday, winning a rain-hit Sprint race that saw Mercedes' George Russell crash out of the lead and McLaren teammates Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri collide on the final lap.
Verstappen, who started from pole position, finished ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli taking fourth after benefiting from the late McLaren collision.
The victory marked Verstappen's first win of any kind at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, previously the only venue on the current Formula 1 calendar where the four-time world champion had never won.
Singapore's first-ever Sprint race was also its first Formula 1 contest held in daylight, but a torrential downpour shortly before the start forced a delay, echoing the disruption caused by heavy rain at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
After two formation laps, the 20-lap race began from a standing start on a track that remained wet in places, particularly along the main straight, despite some sections having already dried.
Russell made the better getaway from second on the grid, sweeping past Verstappen to take the lead, while Hamilton surged from sixth to third.
However, Russell's advantage lasted barely a lap. The Mercedes driver lost control exiting the final corner and spun into the barriers along the pit straight, damaging the right-rear of his car and bringing out the safety car.
"Sorry," Russell told his team over the radio.
The incident compounded a difficult weekend for the Briton, who is already set to start Sunday's Grand Prix from the back of the grid after incurring penalties for exceeding his allocation of power unit components.
Russell's retirement handed the lead back to Verstappen, with Hamilton and Leclerc second and third.
The opening laps descended into further chaos as Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez collided near the back of the field, eliminating both drivers.
Isack Hadjar also retired after reporting an engine braking problem, while Franco Colapinto stopped on track. Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas were among the other casualties, and Arvid Lindblad came under investigation for driving in the wrong direction while recovering from a spin.
With Russell's damaged Mercedes and debris being cleared from the circuit, the remaining cars were briefly directed through the pit lane before racing resumed at the end of lap six.
Verstappen controlled the restart and gradually established himself at the front, and with Hamilton unable to mount a serious challenge, the Dutchman eased to victory.
"The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something that we need to improve on because if you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over, if nothing crazy happens," said Verstappen, who had battled back to win last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia after having initially lost the lead at the start.
"Not ideal, but we got a bit lucky with what happened with George out of the last corner.
"And after that, you just want to keep it calm and under control, because you know that you can't pass around here, especially around here in these conditions with the intermediate.
"I'm happy to win here in the Sprint, but I also know that I want to win tomorrow [in the grand prix], not today."
Although a dry racing line began to emerge as the race progressed, drivers remained on intermediate tyres, with the limited number of laps remaining making a switch to slicks increasingly unattractive.
Overtaking opportunities were also scarce on Singapore's narrow street circuit, and with only eight championship points available to the winner, drivers had little incentive to risk damage ahead of qualifying for Sunday's main race.
By lap 16, Alex Albon had also retired, leaving just 14 cars running and making it the most attrition-hit Sprint race in Formula 1 history.
The closing stages appeared set to pass without further incident until Norris attempted to overtake teammate Piastri on the inside during the final lap.
The two McLarens made contact and spun, with Piastri forced to retire and Norris recovering to finish eighth, taking the final championship point.
Norris apologized to his team over the radio.
"Thought I was fully alongside, ran out of space," the Briton said.
The collision allowed championship leader Antonelli to finish fourth and collect five points, two more than he would have earned in sixth.
Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson finished fifth, ahead of Haas driver Ollie Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, with Norris completing the points-paying positions.
The qualifying session for Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix takes place later on Saturday. ■

Book on history of vehicle license plates in Iran unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:30:54 UTC
21:30:54 KST

Book on history of vehicle license plates in Iran unveiled
TEHRAN – A book tracing the history of vehicle license plates in Iran, from the arrival of automobiles to the introduction of the country’s national registration system, was unveiled on Saturday at the Mostazafan Foundation’s headquarters in Tehran.
Titled Nomreh Aval (First Number), the book was prepared through a joint initiative involving the Applied Research Center of Iran’s Traffic Police, the Historical Car Museum of Iran and the Dafineh Museum Institute, which is operated by the Mostazafan Foundation.
Hamidreza Soleimani, managing director of the Foundation’s Museum Institute, said the publication was the culmination of at least 12 years of research by the institute and its research team.
“The technology that entered Iran also changed our social contracts,” Soleimani said, explaining how the introduction of automobiles and traffic regulations reshaped public behavior. Street signs, for example, now guide how vehicles should move and interact on roads, he noted.
He described the book as the first comprehensive reference on the history of vehicle license plates in Iran, saying it could serve researchers and automobile enthusiasts.
Soleimani also highlighted the research potential of the Historical Car Museum of Iran, which houses 320 historic vehicles, each with its own story and historical significance.
The book examines the evolution of vehicle registration plates in Iran, beginning with the arrival of automobiles and the establishment of the first numbering systems, and continuing through the introduction and adoption of national license plates.
According to its publishers, the work draws on historical research, documentary evidence and reliable sources, particularly archival materials held by Iran’s classic car museum. It brings together information that, in many cases, had not previously been compiled in a single publication, aiming to provide a documented account of how vehicle plates developed over time.
Reza Sakhaei, head of the Applied Research Center of the Law Enforcement Command’s Traffic Police, said vehicle license plates might initially appear to be a simple administrative matter, but they also reflect aspects of Iran’s modern history.
He added that vehicle registration and identification systems now serve purposes beyond their original function.
Sakhaei also discussed plans to develop smart glasses for traffic police officers, saying the technology could help officers monitor vehicles and drivers. The proposed device would incorporate a camera similar to those worn on police uniforms, with additional functions allowing users to move menus to the palm of their hand, he said.
Sakhaei described the newly unveiled book as a contribution to preserving Iran’s historical identity and collective memory.
Ainollah Jahani, the book’s technical supervisor, said the research had also brought to light unusual old vehicles, some of which could be used for museum displays and, in certain cases, might still be operational.
The publication adds to the research potential of Iran’s historic automobile collections, documenting how a practical system of vehicle identification evolved alongside the country’s transportation infrastructure and changing social practices.

Estonia's central bank adds stone barrier after multiple vehicle strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Estonia's central bank adds stone barrier after multiple vehicle strikes
After multiple instances of the building being hit by vehicles, the Bank of Estonia has installed street-side rock barriers.
The Bank of Estonia (Eesti Pank) is located on Kentmanni and Estonia pst. in central Tallinn, and has seen around 20 instances in as many years of drivers, generally those driving under the influence of alcohol, hit its exterior wall.
Part of the issue is the central bank's building lies adjacent to a left turn, if coming from Freedom Square (Vabaduse väljak) and its traffic lights, around 150 meters away. Vehicles have been known to speed along this stretch of Estonia pst. and run out of road at the turn, hitting the bank building.
"For the past 20 years, drivers speeding across Freedom Square have rammed the bank building's wall around twenty times. There have been accidents on the curve by Eesti Pank where a drunk driver has driven into the bank's wall. To prevent this, a stone barrier has now been brought there, " the bank said.
The Saaremaa-quarried dolomite blocks will prevent stray vehicles hitting the bank itself. The blockes are irregular shapes and will be "greened" by the next summer.
The bank's management also recalled the April 2007 "Bronze Soldier Night" riots, though the building remained adequately protected during those incidents.
Much of the bank's real estate is state owned, noted Rait Roosve, adviser to the Bank of Estonina board.
"We have quite a lot — or let's say, an unbelievably large amount of property in the Eesti Pank quarter, and that property doesn't belong to us, it belongs to the Republic of Estonia, or to put it more precisely, to the people of Estonia, and we have an obligation to guard and protect it at the maximum level," he said
Since the area is public urban space, the Bank of Estonia says it cannot cannot and does not want to build a wall there. At the same time, the row of blocks being installed must ensure the safety of ordinary traffic and stop cars and small trucks.
It is not, however, a national defense structure, ;the stones will not be sufficient to defend the building from armored vehicles such as tanks, for instance..
"This is Estonian national stone, limestone, specifically dolomite, and these have been brought from Kaarma on Saaremaa. It will certainly slow a tank, but considering the mass of these dolomite blocks and the mass of a tank, purely physically or mechanically the victory is certainly on the tank's side. But it also won't allow a tank to ram straight into our wall," Roosve continued.
The project, carried out in cooperation with Tallinn city government, will be completed by the end of next week. Grasses planted by the stones should conceal them come next summer, making the area in front of the bank on Kentmanni tänav greener, planners say.

Bulgaria’s Diesel Export Decision Draws Criticism After Trump-Putin Supply Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:19:03 UTC
21:19:03 KST

US President Donald Trump’s agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to the United States and global markets has intensified criticism of Bulgaria’s decision to lift restrictions on petroleum product exports, with GERB leader Boyko Borissov warning that Bulgarian consumers and businesses could bear the costs.
Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons  of diesel to the United States and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons immediately afterward. He said the agreement had been reached during a discussion with Putin.
Borissov criticized the Bulgarian government led by Prime Minister Rumen Radev for allowing petroleum product exports to resume. On Facebook, the GERB leader recalled that on September 23, 2026, the National Assembly repealed a decision adopted on October 31, 2025, that had temporarily restricted exports and intra-community supplies of petroleum products, mainly diesel and aviation fuel. The new decision took effect on September 29, 2026.
Borissov said he had previously warned that lifting the restrictions was a serious mistake that could generate substantial profits for certain traders at the expense of consumers.
“While other countries are doing their best to provide fuels for their own economies, we are allowing them to leave the country,” Borissov wrote on Facebook.
He argued that the interests of a small number of traders should not take precedence over those of Bulgarian farmers, carriers, businesses and entrepreneurs, adding that the state should protect the national interest rather than increase the wealth of a few individuals.
The debate has also prompted comments from President Iliana Yotova and Nikolai Denkov, chairman of the parliamentary group of We Continue the Change (PP).
Yotova said the agreement between Washington and Moscow should be considered within the broader set of problems arising from the war in Ukraine, adding that its specific terms needed to be examined before its potential effects could be assessed.
The president expressed hope that the agreement could bring down diesel prices, while emphasizing that fuel shortages were creating difficulties across Europe and the world.
“You know that gas storage facilities are also a little more than half full. Deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz are difficult. Next year, the transition period with deliveries from Russia” expires, Iotova said.
She also described the meeting between Radev and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s chief of staff as useful in the context of the Ukrainian official’s subsequent visit to the United States, where concrete steps toward peace negotiations are expected. Yotova said the presidential administration had not received a request for a meeting with the Ukrainian official.
According to the president, Bulgaria was expressing its position on ending the conflict in Ukraine and the need for peace negotiations at every level. She said she was placing hopes in the US talks involving representatives of European countries and institutions.
Asked whether there were suspicions about the origin of the drones that struck two ships in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, Yotova said she could not draw conclusions without evidence. She recalled that the Advisory Council for National Security had explicitly stated that Bulgaria would make every effort to gather evidence before taking specific decisions and that the government would inform the public.
Denkov, meanwhile, argued that Trump’s agreement with Putin was driven by domestic political considerations, as rising fuel prices in the United States could hurt the president ahead of the November elections.
Speaking on Nova TV, the PP parliamentary group chairman compared the agreement to the 1939 pact between Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and Nazi leader Adolf Hitler to divide Poland, which he said had been followed two years later by a full-scale war.
“My concern is that Putin is currently trying to make a deal, to take Eastern Europe - Ukraine, the Baltic republics, Moldova and perhaps south to Bulgaria, Romania, and this would be a prerequisite for tragic events,” Denkov said.
He warned that agreements lacking principles and promoting the right of force could have lasting consequences, drawing parallels with the First and Second World Wars.
Denkov also criticized the Radev government for permitting fuel exports at a time of shortages, contrasting its approach with Borisov’s calls to protect the national economy.
According to an American official cited by Axios and the Ukrainian news agency UNIAN, Trump decided to reach the diesel agreement with Russia after Zelensky rejected six US demands to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The official said Zelensky had misjudged the situation by continuing the strikes, arguing that they had undermined the confidence he had built with Trump over the previous six months.
The source said Zelensky had offered to halt attacks on Russian refineries if Moscow also stopped striking Ukrainian power plants, but Trump rejected the proposal.
According to the official, Trump wanted Ukraine to stop the refinery attacks unilaterally because they contributed to higher fuel prices in the United States. The official also said Trump did not regard Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries as equivalent to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s electricity grid.
The agreement announced by Trump has drawn sharp criticism from Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the United States as “weak friends,” arguing that the deal amounted to support for the continuation of the war and warning that the “gift” to Putin would be repaid with more terror.

Waiting times will be around 12-15 minutes on the red and green lines and more than 15 on the blue line.

Lockheed Martin Develops New PAC-3 Edge Interceptor to Counter Hypersonic Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:18:22 UTC
21:18:22 KST

The American company Lockheed Martin has developed a new PAC-3 Edge interceptor missile for the Patriot air defense system, designed to counter hypersonic and advanced missile threats.
This was announced on the company’s website on October 9.
The PAC-3 Edge was developed as part of the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor program, based on combat-proven technologies from the PAC-3 MSE interceptor, as well as new solutions designed to improve target interception effectiveness.
The new interceptor features an upgraded seeker head, a multi-pulse solid-propellant rocket motor manufactured by Northrop Grumman, and an enhanced guidance system.
According to the developer, these solutions are designed to provide better interception performance at long ranges and high altitudes.
“The PAC-3 Edge interceptor utilizes combat-proven PAC-3 MSE technology, delivering even greater maneuverability, power, and speed to ensure that the Army’s layered defense architecture remains the most advanced in the world,” said Tim Cahill, president of the missile systems division Lockheed Martin.
One of the key elements of the PAC-3 Edge will be a new homing seeker currently under development at Lockheed Martin’s Strigo Product Center.
The company notes that it has invested $250 million in this center to implement new homing technologies designed to improve the accuracy and maneuverability of the interceptors.
Testing of the PAC-3 Edge is scheduled to begin in 2027. The interceptor is expected to be ready for deployment by 2031.
The new interceptor missile is designed to integrate with the U.S. Army’s existing and future integrated air and missile defense systems, including the IBCS combat command system, the M903 launcher, containerized launchers, and HIMARS Flex.
As a reminder, in July, Lockheed Martin unveiled the low-cost PAC-3 ACE interceptor missile for the Patriot air defense system. It features simplified components, including the engine and homing seeker.
In August, a Lockheed Martin executive stated that the missile’s first flight test would take place in 18 months, and production would begin in ‘a few years.’
