High cognitive ability in women predicts workplace victimization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:00:43 UTC
20:00:43 KST

Women who score high on cognitive ability tests face unique social penalties in the workplace, including heightened hostility and a lack of support from their colleagues. Men with similarly high cognitive scores do not experience these same social consequences, and in some cases, they actually receive better treatment from their peers. These observations come from a recent paper published in the Journal of Applied Psychology.
In the workplace, gender continues to shape how people are evaluated and treated by their peers. According to social role theory, society holds unwritten rules about how men and women should behave. Women are traditionally expected to exhibit communal traits. Communality involves being helpful, kind, and attentive to the needs of others. Men are typically expected to display agentic traits. Agency involves being decisive, independent, competitive, and highly capable.
When individuals violate these unwritten expectations, they often face social disapproval. Past research has established that women who show dominance, by acting forcefully or aggressively, frequently face professional penalties. Yet newer studies have suggested that displaying competence, such as high intelligence, might benefit women when they are evaluated for leadership roles.
A team of researchers led by Nitya Chawla at the University of Minnesota wanted to know if this benefit extended to daily interactions with team members. They suspected that displaying high cognitive ability might actually backfire for women in everyday team settings. Cognitive ability generally refers to a person’s capacity to learn, reason, solve problems, and comprehend complex ideas.
To investigate this, Chawla and her colleagues relied on a psychological concept known as the implied communality deficit. This concept suggests that when women display high competence, their peers unconsciously assume they lack communal traits. In other words, peers might assume a highly intelligent woman is not just less warm, but actively cold or hostile. The research team suspected this dynamic would lead to fewer instances of colleagues helping out and more instances of colleagues actively victimizing the highly competent woman.
To test these ideas, the researchers conducted two distinct investigations. The first study tracked 432 undergraduate business students at a public university in the United States. The students were divided into small teams to complete a semester-long consulting project for local organizations.
About four weeks into the semester, the students took the Wonderlic test, a standard assessment used to measure general mental ability. Seven weeks later, the participants evaluated their teammates, rating the extent to which each peer exhibited hostility or anger. A few weeks after that, the students reported how often they received help from their teammates and how often they experienced subtle forms of victimization, such as teammates withholding information.
The results showed a distinct difference in how cognitive ability affected social dynamics for men and women. For women, higher cognitive ability was linked to higher ratings of interpersonal hostility from their teammates. Because these women were perceived as more hostile, they subsequently reported experiencing more victimization.
These same women also received less help from their peers. Teammates were less likely to assist them with tasks or offer emotional support. For the men in the study, higher cognitive scores did not predict any increase in perceived hostility or changes in the amount of help or victimization they received.
For their second study, the researchers moved from a university setting to a corporate environment. They recruited 394 full-time employees working in small teams at a financial company in China. The company requires all job candidates to take a cognitive ability test during the hiring process, which provided the researchers with objective intelligence scores for each participant.
The employees completed an initial survey where they rated each of their team members on both interpersonal hostility and communality. About three weeks later, the employees completed a second survey reporting how often they were victimized by their team members and how much help they received. By separating the surveys by several weeks, the researchers aimed to capture how initial perceptions translated into workplace behaviors over time.
The findings mirrored the results of the student study while providing additional detail. Women with higher cognitive ability scores were once again viewed as more hostile by their colleagues. They were also rated as less communal than their peers.
These negative perceptions predicted worse treatment for the women. They faced more victimization and received less task-related and personal help from their colleagues. The highly competent women essentially experienced a double bind, being viewed as lacking warmth while simultaneously projecting hostility.
The men in the corporate sample experienced a completely different reality. For them, higher cognitive ability was linked to lower ratings of hostility from their peers. Because they were seen as less hostile, these men experienced less victimization and actually received more help from their teammates.
While the findings present a consistent pattern across two different cultures, the studies relied on moderate sample sizes. Additionally, the university students and the corporate employees represent highly specific environments where cognitive ability is already heavily screened. In the general population, the range of intelligence scores would be much wider, which could alter the strength of these associations.
The researchers also measured victimization and help through self-reported surveys. While peer perceptions were gathered from the teammates themselves, the actual experiences of mistreatment or support were filtered through the perspective of the individual. Future studies could use independent observations to verify how often highly competent women are actually targeted or ignored in group settings.
Finally, these findings do not account for racial or cultural intersections within a single environment. Stereotypes regarding competence and warmth differ across racial groups. Future research could explore whether women of different backgrounds experience this competence penalty differently within the same workplace.
The study, “Understanding the Intersection of Gender and Cognitive Ability on Interpersonal Outcomes: A Multistudy Investigation,” was authored by Nitya Chawla, Trevor M. Spoelma, Seo-Hyun Kwon, Allison S. Gabriel, Aleksander P. J. Ellis, and Wen Wu.

Marshall Aerospace sold to private equity investor
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:00:12 BST
20:00:12 KST

Marshall Aerospace, the British military maintenance and special mission conversion specialist with roots going back to 1909, has been bought by the private equity investor AURELIUS, according to the company.
The acquisition completed on 8 October and separates Marshall Aerospace from the wider Marshall Group, leaving it as an independent mid-tier British aerospace and defence company.
Bob Baxter, the chief executive of Marshall Aerospace, said: “This change of ownership is an important new chapter for Marshall Aerospace as an independent mid-tier British aerospace and defence company.
“In AURELIUS, we have found an owner that recognises the strength of our capabilities and the importance of the work we are delivering for our customers. Just as importantly, they have the expertise and resources to back our next phase of growth and capitalise on emerging opportunities as the defence industry continues to transform.”
The company works in military maintenance, repair and overhaul, applied aerospace engineering and advanced manufacturing, supporting operators from the Royal Norwegian Air Force to the US Marine Corps and acting as a supplier to Boeing, Lockheed Martin and Thales.
Marshall holds a multi-year agreement covering entry into service and sustainment for twelve C-130J aircraft bought by the Turkish Ministry of National Defence, and a fourteen-year contract from Thales to produce sonar modules for the Royal Navy.
The C-130 is the aircraft the company is best known for, having supported the Hercules since 1966 and earned a series of world-first accreditations and permissions on the type. Its design organisation approvals let it plan, integrate and certify complete programmes, from avionics upgrades to bespoke special mission conversions.
AURELIUS describes itself as a global private equity investor with an operational approach, and says the combination gives Marshall a platform for its next phase of growth and opportunities to contribute to defence programmes important to Britain and its allies.
Marshall Aerospace had earlier planned to move its operations from Cambridge Airport to a new facility at Cranfield under a relocation announced several years ago.

Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

Nvidia GPUs are the most sought-after processors in AI, and they're in such demand that the chipmaker's stock climbed to yet another record this week, lifting its market cap close to $6 trillion.
Customers can now shop around for access to the chips at the giant clouds from Amazon, Microsoft and Google, as well as at so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave. They can also go to various online marketplaces or even buy the costly hardware directly.
For Nvidia, it all adds up to unrelenting growth, as management anticipates $108 billion in revenue for the October quarter, which would mark an 89% year-over-year jump.
But the paradox of choice can be a headache for companies needing computing power yesterday.
While cloud infrastructure providers have ranked at the top of Nvidia's customer list for several years, the business is diversifying. Five clients accounted for at least 10% of Nvidia's accounts receivable in July quarter, up from three in January, according to a filing.
Industry research firm SemiAnalysis counted 323 Nvidia GPU providers as of September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier.
"You're going to see a whole new crop of really, really exciting neoclouds with hundreds of billions of dollars backlog together," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at a Goldman Sachs tech conference in San Francisco last month.
Here's a rundown of the various options for accessing GPUs, and why each might make sense:
Hyperscalers
Many big companies spend tens of millions of dollars per year on a smorgasbord of cloud services from Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Since the 2022 launch of ChatGPT, companies have increasingly turned to the hyperscalers for GPUs so they can run generative AI workloads.
The top cloud providers come with a reputation advantage. If a software company relies on Amazon and Microsoft for GPUs and other capabilities, it won't need to panic about prospective customers questioning its suppliers.
"When you're talking to enterprises, your subprocessor had better be Azure," said Bindu Reddy, CEO of AI assistant startup Abacus, referring to Microsoft's cloud infrastructure.
In the past year, leading AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI have committed to spending over $500 billion between Amazon and Microsoft, which controlled 59% of the cloud infrastructure market in 2025, according to industry researcher Gartner.
"Hyperscalers are in a good position to show trust to the enterprises because of their 10-plus years of full-stack capabilities," said Gartner analyst Hardeep Singh. But hyperscalers don't always have as many GPUs as enterprises require, he said.
Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, told analysts in July that the retailer and cloud pioneer won't be able to serve all the demand it foresees this year.
"I believe this dynamic will also be true in 2027," he said.
Flagship neoclouds
If the hyperscalers were adequate, neoclouds wouldn't be proliferating.
Modal, a startup operating virtual sandboxes where AI agents work independent of main IT environments, went from running on the hyperscalers to signing up with the major neoclouds, and now it uses 25 of them, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson.
"You can get a few hundred GPUs or maybe a thousand, but at our scale, we needed way more GPUs," he said.
The hyperscalers themselves are also chasing the neoclouds. Google and Microsoft have started tapping CoreWeave, even as they all compete with one another.
"Some of the hyperscalers have approached us about taking care of customers they're worried about because they don't have the ability to service those customers when they need it," said Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer of Nebius, a Netherlands-based neocloud with operations in the U.S.
Video generation startup Reactor uses GPUs through Nebius and hyperscalers, said CEO Alberto Taiuti. The location of data centers matters, he said, because Reactor wants user-created videos to show up right away. Nebius delivers the specific GPUs Reactor needs, solid customer service and sufficient hardware and software, at a good price, Taiuti said.
The most visible neoclouds can require some upfront payment, and chips might not come online for months, because providers raise funding based on contracts and set up the data center equipment, Bernhardsson said.
It would be difficult for CoreWeave to turn over 10,000 GPUs to a new customer with one day's notice, said Chen Goldberg, an executive vice president. CoreWeave's near-term capacity remains essentially sold out, CEO Mike Intrator said on the company's August earnings call.
Baby neoclouds
If companies want GPUs immediately, they might have to go beyond the name brands. Some neoclouds aren't household names because they target specific countries, which can be viable in certain cases.
"Capacity right now is tight, and your relationships with your suppliers is actually one of the most closely guarded secrets for companies like ours," said Zhen Lu, CEO of Runpod.
Specialist neoclouds can offer more flexibility than the larger GPU clouds, which often require upfront payments and long-term commitments. Some sell so-called bare-metal GPUs, which give customers more control but also require them to manage more of the technical work themselves.
Companies using these smaller neoclouds share the same concerns: When can they get the GPUs, and at what price? Sunny Smith, co-founder and technology chief at Massed Compute, said customers are often willing to commit to capacity when they expect prices to rise.
Bring your own
Oracle, one of the world's largest cloud providers, is letting clients bring in their own GPUs. The software maker has more debt than Amazon or Microsoft, and its credit rating is lower so it has less flexibility to go on a GPU spending spree. But it's happy to operate the technology.
"As we're generally able to preserve and improve margins in the case of things like bring-your-own-hardware, the ROIC for those types of structures will be even higher," Oracle CFO Hilary Maxson told analysts on a June earnings call, using the acronym for return on invested capital.
Oracle hasn't disclosed the names of companies that choose this path. John DiFucci, a Guggenheim Securities analyst who recommends buying Oracle shares, said it would make sense for Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia, the top two producers of GPUs, to bring their own to Oracle.
Instead of buying thousands of GPUs, early-stage startups with limited capital can borrow them for hours at a time for less through clouds. And for companies with heavy-duty computing needs, Oracle's new route might be more attractive than building whole data centers. OpenAI committed to spending over $300 billion with Oracle over five years, but it hasn't mentioned anything about bringing in GPUs.
OpenAI declined to comment.
The method might make sense for companies that have the capital to purchase AI chips but don't have enough power, data center space or skilled labor. Like its hyperscaler peers, Oracle works hard to secure all three in healthy quantities.
Tactical deals
Another emerging option is to cut large deals with firms that have truckloads of GPUs for rent.
SpaceX arranged to turn over excess capacity in separate deals with hyperscaler Google and open-source startup Reflection.
In April, SpaceX agreed to provide Cursor with GPUs and then bought the AI coding startup outright for $60 billion. And in May, SpaceX landed a deal to rent GPUs to Anthropic for $1.25 billion each month through mid-2029. That's more than what most startups can afford.
For SpaceX, though, the numbers work out nicely.
"The current economics have translated into a less than one-year payback on our new capital deployments for compute," Bret Johnsen, the company's finance chief, told analysts in August.
It's not only SpaceX. In July CNBC reported that Meta was working to form a cloud unit that could sell AI computing power.
Going old school
Meanwhile, companies continue to install GPU-filled servers in on-premises data centers the old-school way as CEOs work to balance capability with cost control.
Revenue nearly doubled in the enterprise and small and medium business parts of hardware maker Lenovo's Infrastructure Solutions Group during the June quarter. "We're seeing more and more enterprises now starting to say, 'How do I bring AI into my four walls?'" said Vlad Rozanovich, a senior vice president.
The hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes.
Collaboration software maker Dropbox relies on GPUs in its data centers, CEO Ashraf Alkarmi said.
"If we want to do a lot more, I think our supply chain connections will still be beneficial and a structural advantage," he said.
Everpure, which sells data center storage hardware and software, has acquired its own GPUs, to run open-weight AI models for the company's software engineers, said CEO Charlie Giancarlo.
"In a very dynamic pricing environment, it's always good to have multiple sources that you can go to," he said.

Indonesia’s raging wildfires endanger orangutans, scorch forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Wildfires raging across parts of Indonesia’s Borneo island are threatening endangered orangutans, forcing rescuers to evacuate animals found injured, stranded or struggling to survive amid thick smoke and scorched forests.
Among dozens of orangutans rescued from fires across Sumatra and Borneo in recent months was a female Bornean orangutan known as Novita.
Rescuers found her clinging to a nearly leafless tree as dense smoke engulfed the charred landscape of the Katune forest in Central Kalimantan province, said Jamartin Sihite, chairman of the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation.
“The palms of her hands and the soles of her feet suffered burns that were likely sustained when Novita crossed a burned area while trying to reach a tree,” Sihite told The Associated Press in an interview. He said Novita, estimated to be 3 to 4 years old, was tranquilized, given oxygen and intravenous fluids, and taken to the rehabilitation center in Nyaru Menteng.
Once her burns have healed, Novita will be evaluated to determine whether she can climb and survive in her natural environment, Sihite said.
“We have previously released orangutans missing several fingers, and they were still able to survive in the forest, so we remain hopeful that Novita can eventually return to the wild.”
Forest and land fires in Indonesia have worsened this year as El Niño intensifies a prolonged dry season, affecting not only the Indonesian part of Borneo but also some regions of Sumatra. Water shortages in affected areas have hampered firefighting efforts, while Japan has provided firefighting assistance on the island.
A male orangutan named Sampurna, believed to be around 20 years old, was found struggling to breathe by residents early last month on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan’s Ketapang district, an area affected by wildfires. He died hours after being rescued, Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry said.
More than 270 wild animals in Kalimantan had been rescued, rehabilitated or guided to safer habitats as of Saturday, the ministry said.
Government data showed that more than 202,000 hectares (499,000 acres) of land burned between January and July. The independent Nusantara Atlas project, which monitors fires using satellite imagery, estimated that nearly 896,000 hectares (2.2 million acres) had burned by the end of August.
Toxic haze and smoke have also caused a health crisis in neighboring countries. The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) away. In Malaysia, authorities declared an emergency last week in Sarawak, on the Malaysian part of Borneo.
Novita’s case highlights the impact of forest and peatland fires on wildlife as well as people, said Andi Muhammad Kadhafi, head of the Central Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency, a government body.
“Wildfires do not only affect humans but can also threaten wildlife and their habitats,” he said. “Fire prevention, habitat protection, monitoring and rapid response need to go hand in hand.”

Are Firing Squad Executions Seeing a Revival in the U.S.?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Lethal injection has long been the prevailing method for carrying out the death penalty in the U.S. But supply-chain issues and a series of high-profile botched executions are increasingly causing officials around the country to weigh alternative options—including one that, until recently, had been all but entirely left in the past.
Following the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week—the second botched execution in the state this year using lethal injection—several Tennessee lawmakers have publicly called for the state to turn to other methods.
“If we’re having this much trouble with this particular means of execution, we need to take it off the table and go to something that’s far more reliable and predictable,” Tennessee Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson said while speaking on a local radio show on Monday. Republican Rep. Tim Burchett, who represents Tennessee's second congressional district in the House, similarly told local station WVLT last Friday that Tennessee should abandon lethal injection in favor of other methods that have “very little room for mistakes.” Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton told The Associated Press in an interview published on Monday that “I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.”
Among the potential alternatives named by both Johnson and Burchett was execution by firing squad. The method has been used exceedingly rarely in the U.S.: between 1976 and 2024, just three people were put to death by firing squad in the country, all of them in Utah.
But the Tennessee lawmakers aren’t the only ones who have recently suggested reviving the practice—and some state officials and President Donald Trump have already made moves to do just that.
Trump on Monday approved the U.S. Army’s first execution of a soldier via firing squad since World War II, greenlighting the use of the method to put to death Nidal Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people in a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, following a recommendation by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hasan’s execution is scheduled to take place on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood and, Hegseth has announced, to be livestreamed.
The approval comes months after Trump authorized the use of firing squads in federal executions in April.
Both South Carolina and Idaho have also taken steps in recent months to either enable the use of firing squad executions or to carry them out.
Last year, in the wake of a failed 2024 execution attempt using lethal injection in the state, South Carolina put three people to death by firing squad—doubling the number of such executions that had been carried out in the entire U.S. over the prior half-century.
Idaho, meanwhile, enacted a law earlier this year that established the firing squad as the state’s primary method for carrying out the death penalty. That move, too, followed a high-profile botched execution via lethal injection in the state in 2024.
How does a firing squad execution work?
The specific procedure for execution by firing squad varies across different states, but the general method remains the same, according to Austin Sarat, a professor of law and political science at Amherst College and the author of Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death Penalty,.
He explains that traditionally, a person is strapped to a chair, a hood is placed over their head and a target is put on their heart, to highlight where the shooters should aim.
Then, between three and five people with high-powered rifles will fire at the target. In some states, one rifle will be loaded with a blank bullet, so that the shooters do not know who fired the fatal shots. “When the signal is given, they shoot into the heart of the condemned,” Sarat says.
Which states allow execution by firing squad?
Firing squad executions are currently permitted in just five states: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah.
Idaho, under its recently enacted law, is the only state that uses the firing squad as its default method.
The other states have designated execution by firing squad to be used as a fallback method if they are unable to carry out the death penalty by lethal injection, or as one of several methods that can be chosen by either corrections officials or inmates themselves to perform an execution.
Utah in 2015 designated the firing squad as the alternative method to turn to if the state cannot, for instance, obtain the necessary drugs to perform an execution by lethal injection. Oklahoma permitted firing squads in 2011 as a method of last resort.
Mississippi in 2022 gave discretion to corrections officials to choose among four methods, including the firing squad.
And in South Carolina, the firing squad has since 2021 been one of multiple methods that death row inmates can choose for their means of execution, along with electrocution and lethal injection. If they do not choose a method, electrocution is used.
Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit organization that provides analysis and research on capital punishment, tells TIME that at least one inmate appears to have opted for the firing squad in the state last year due to a lack of information provided regarding what other forms of capital punishment entail.
“Prisoners who asked for information about the other two methods of execution, namely the electric chair and lethal injection, were not given complete answers to understand how those methods would be used, and so at least in one of those cases, the prisoners felt like the firing squad was the only method of execution they knew enough about to choose,” Maher says.
Lethal injection issues prompt a search for solutions
Oklahoma became the first state to authorize lethal injection in 1977, as it sought more humane methods for capital punishment. From the late 1970s on, lethal injection was performed in Oklahoma and, later, other states using a three-drug protocol, explains Richard Levy, an anesthesiologist at Columbia University: one drug, sodium thiopental, to induce unconsciousness; a second paralytic drug to stop breathing; and potassium chloride to stop the heart from beating.
In 2011, the company which manufactured sodium thiopental, Hospira, stopped manufacturing the drug, leaving states to revise their protocols for lethal injection.
“Each state basically has adopted some variation on the theme,” Levy says in reference to the original three-drug protocol. He explains that the majority of states have since “gone to a single-drug approach,” a method he describes as “flawed and problematic.”
Many states use a single dose of pentobarbital, which depresses the central nervous system. Levy explains that compared to thiopentol, pentobarbital doesn’t as effectively induce unconsciousness, “and probably doesn't reliably stop one from breathing.” Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital in her failed execution attempt before she was hospitalized; she complained that her arms were burning as the pentobarbital was administered, after several needles were unsuccessfully used to access a vein.
Following the botched attempt, her lawyers believed she was brain dead on Monday, before she woke up on Tuesday. As of Thursday, Pike was “up and walking,” according to her lawyer.
States have also struggled to obtain lethal injection drugs as a result of pharmaceutical companies’ opposition to supplying their products for executions. As a result, many states have substituted different drugs or opted for alternative execution methods.
In South Carolina for instance, the state was unable to carry out executions for more than a decade after struggling to obtain lethal injection drugs, until 2021, when the state authorized firing squads and made electrocution its default method.
In 2023, the governor’s office revealed that it had reached out to more than 1,300 contacts for execution drugs before finally obtaining pentobarbital. The state then resumed executions by lethal injection, but in March of 2025, a death row inmate chose to be executed by firing squad over fears of prolonged suffering related to lethal injection, becoming the first person to be executed by a firing squad in the state’s history.
Republican Utah state Rep. Paul Ray, who sponsored the bill that reinstated firing squads in his state, cited difficulty obtaining the necessary drugs as a reason for the move when speaking with The Los Angeles Times in 2015. “We found out last year that there we had no ability to purchase more drugs. So looking down the road, we had to come up with a backup plan,” Ray told the outlet. “We decided to make it automatic to go to the firing squad.”
Federal officials have given voice to similar reasoning. Before Trump authorized the use of firing squads for federal executions, the Department of Justice released a report in April which said that switching to “manners of execution that are currently provided for by the law of certain states … will help ensure the Department is prepared to carry out lawful executions even if a specific drug is unavailable.” The report also acknowledged “supply chain challenges that limit the availability of lethal injection drugs.”
As those issues have complicated efforts to carry out lethal injection executions in recent years, botched attempts like the one in Pike’s case have also contributed to officials’ decisions to shift toward alternative methods.
Lethal injection, by far the most common method of the death penalty in the U.S, also comes with the highest rate of botched attempts, according to research performed by Sarat, the Amherst college professor. In one comprehensive study that examined executions between 1890 and 2010, Sarat found that just over 7% of executions by lethal injection were botched. In a subsequent study looking at executions performed between 2010 and 2020, he found that the rate was over 8%.
“It is certain. It is quick. And it brings justice for the victims and their families in a more expeditious manner than other types,” said Idaho state Rep. Bruce Skaug, who sponsored the bill that established the firing squad as the state’s default method.
Historically, in the scant instances when firing squad executions have been carried out in the U.S, they’ve rarely—if ever—been botched, according to Sarat’s study. Out of 34 executions by firing squad between 1890 and 2010, he found, not one went significantly awry.
In one of the three firing squad executions performed in South Carolina last year, though, an autopsy report concluded that the firing squad missed the heart of the victim, indicating that he did not immediately die and may have endured suffering.
Sarat argues that firing squads, though involved in far fewer botched executions, remain a “brutal” form of capital punishment that “was abandoned because it didn't meet the evolving standards of decency of the society.”
“Since the end of the 19th century, the United States has been on a quest to find a method of execution that would be safe, reliable, and humane. The firing squad has never played a big role in that story,” Sarat tells TIME. “It hasn't played a big role in that story because it is a brutal way to kill someone, and its brutality is very obvious.”
Other forms of capital punishment have also received consideration in recent years in the search for potential alternatives to lethal injection. The DOJ’s report from April directed federal prisons to expand their methods of execution to include, along with firing squads, gas asphyxiation and electrocution. Alabama in 2024 became the first state to execute a death row inmate using nitrogen gas, and four other states have adopted the practice since. In 2025, 19 bills in 14 states were introduced to alter or augment execution methods, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Despite the moves to revive largely bygone execution methods or implement new ones, however, Sarat emphasizes that capital punishment is overall trending down.
The death penalty is currently outlawed in 23 states, while 10 others have not carried out an execution in the last decade, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. An additional four states have not had an execution in the last five years.
“The United States is on the road to abolition … The death penalty is dying,” Sarat says. “I don't think that either what Trump has done about the firing squad or Christa Pike's failed execution, in and of itself, is going to make a huge dent in America's death penalty.”

Under the Gun: Understanding America’s Defense Spending Paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

On May 9, 1915, more than 11,000 British troops were killed or wounded in a single day during an ill-fated assault on an entrenched German position in Aubers, France. The reason for the disaster: a shortage of artillery shells to support the assault, particularly the high-explosive shells best suited for trench warfare. The resulting “Shell Crisis of 1915,” led to a major reorganization of the British government’s defense production system. It still wasn’t enough to prevent the fall of Prime Minister H.H. Asquith a year later.
The shell crisis of World War I reminds us just how hard it is to prepare for long wars. “In almost every war there comes a point when it's clear that the peacetime defense industry, even if it had been ramping up, is inadequate for the demands of war,” says Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Colonel who is now a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
More than a century later, the world, and warfare, have changed. But even in a world of fighter jets, nuclear weapons, satellite communications, drones, and AI, ammunition still matters. The decline of the British Empire was followed by the rise of the United States as Earth’s military superpower, the Cold War's onset and end, and numerous conflicts throughout the Middle East. Now, America faces an arms shortage of its own. Even given the historical precedent, the current U.S. predicament is stunning.
The United States spends more on defense than the next seven countries combined, including rivals China and Russia. And yet, the U.S. military finds itself concerned about running short of key munitions in a war with a country, Iran, that could generously be described as a “middle” power.
In August, Reuters reported that the United States had used up “virtually all” of its long-range precision weapons during five months of fighting with Iran. The U.S. also reportedly used more than two-thirds of its supplies of Patriot interceptors in the Middle East, and the global Patriot shortage has in turn left Ukrainian cities dangerously vulnerable to Russian strikes.
President Donald Trump has angrily insisted that the U.S. has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition.” However, the Pentagon’s own accounting tells a different story. An inspector general’s report in September admitted that the war had revealed “strategic inventory shortfalls.” Warnings from his senior military commanders about the state of U.S. stockpiles were reportedly one major reason why Trump has refrained from a return to full-scale combat against Iran.
If that’s what a few months of combat with Iran does to U.S. stockpiles, it’s hard to be optimistic about a potential war with China. A CSIS report warns that the U.S. would likely run out of some types of long-range missiles after just a week of combat in a war over Taiwan.
All of this begs the question: How is it possible that the most expensive military in the history of the world doesn’t have enough ammunition to fight a war?
American ammunitions
The origin of the current munitions miseries is often traced back to a particular night in 1993, when Deputy Secretary of Defense William Perry invited defense industry executives to a secret dinner at the Pentagon, which came to be known as the “Last Supper.” Perry warned the executives that Cold War-era defense budgets were no longer sustainable and predicted that many of them would likely go out of business.
Perry’s prediction proved correct. Between 1988 and 1997, defense budgets fell by around 30% and about a dozen major U.S. defense contractors consolidated into four. Much of those budget cuts were taken out of funding for new weapons as the military drew down on Cold War-era stocks.
But the issue wasn’t just money. In the decade following the 9/11 attacks, U.S. defense spending more than doubled, though even amid growing tensions with China and Russia, it’s still less than half of 1980s budgets. But even with budgets creeping up toward a trillion dollars, dividing up the pie is harder than you’d think. Operations costs, maintenance, and spending on military personnel—including pay and retirement benefits—consume a significant portion of the U.S. defense budget. When it comes to what’s left, new high-budget platforms—aircraft, ships, planes—were often prioritized over munitions supplies.
“For many years, in internal defense budget deliberations, to find savings to meet the overall target, munitions were often the ‘bill payer,’” says William LaPlante, who served as Under Secretary of Defense for acquisition and sustainment in the Biden Administration.
The decisions were made easier by the fact that the wars being fought against insurgent groups in Iraq and Afghanistan didn’t require the same amount of missiles, shells, and air defense interceptors needed for a war against a nation-state military.
All that changed with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, sparking a war featuring the kind of artillery use not seen in Europe since the days of the Battle of Aubers, as well as missile barrages on Ukrainian cities requiring a massive number of interceptors. All of a sudden, munitions were in high demand. After years of declines in America’s defense industrial base and manufacturing capabilities, increasing production of artillery shells as well as more advanced missiles and interceptors has been a frustratingly slow process.
What happened to the economic principle that supply rises to meet high demand? Defense companies have been reluctant to build out production capacity for new wars when the demand may disappear in a year or two. Indeed, it may even behoove some defense companies to stick to a high-demand, low-supply, high-margin business model. The impact for Americans, though, is that the cost to taxpayers stays high, even as the military struggles to keep up with the resource demands of modern combat.
Blaming and buzzwords
Trump, for his part, has blamed Biden’s decision to supply Ukraine for the current shortages in the war with Iran. This is misleading: the vast majority of the weapons systems sent to supply Ukraine’s land war are of little use in the war in Iran. A notable exception is advanced air interceptors like Patriots, which are at a premium in both conflicts.
Both conflicts have made clear that the economics of using multimillion-dollar interceptors to knock down cheap cruise missiles and drones—akin to “throwing Ferraris at frisbees,” as Rep. Ted Lieu memorably put it—are brutally expensive for the defending side.
These days, the buzzwords for defense planners, as well as the crop of Silicon Valley-linked defense startups that have emerged in this post-Last Supper era, are systems that are “attritable,” meaning cheap and replaceable, and “modular,” meaning they can be easily adapted for future wars. Plans for the defense of Taiwan, for instance, involve building swarms of cheap and most likely AI-controlled drones to create a “hellscape” for Chinese invaders. But given how fast battlefield technology and tactics are advancing, even those plans may soon be obsolete. 
“The whole system has to be shaken up because the move, counter-move cycle in modern warfare is eye-wateringly short, and we are not prepared,” says Mackenzie Eaglen, a defense analyst and senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. 
In response, the Pentagon has announced a series of steps to speed up weapons acquisition by centralizing buying authority and cutting red tape. Though some of the plans have received pushback from Congress over the new powers being claimed by the department and concerns that it will incentivize companies to deliver inferior products quickly, it’s notable that virtually nobody is standing up to defend the old system—and changing this system will likely be a significant challenge in its own right.
Too few shells, or too many wars?
Analysts often use the phrase “turning an aircraft carrier” to describe the challenge of reforming the bureaucratic behemoth that is the Pentagon and defense industry for a new age of warfare. The metaphor became literal earlier this year when the USS Ford was diverted from the Mediterranean to Venezuela and then back to the Middle East again as the administration jumped from one conflict to another. The ship would spend a record 326 days at sea—a mission that included food shortages, sewage leaks, and a nearly disastrous fire.
The logistical challenges of deploying the US Navy’s limited number of aircraft carriers, as well as concerns about munitions stockpiles, are reminders that even the world’s most powerful military is constrained by scarce resources, particularly given the growing number of wars it has been fighting lately.
The Pentagon has prioritized the production of 14 critical munitions in its spending priorities, but it’s still going to have to compete with big-ticket priorities, including Trump’s dreams for a $1.2 trillion “golden dome” missile defense system, a new focus on space-based weapons, and nuclear modernization. Even with a proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, it’s going to be difficult to do all those things while fighting one, if not more, ongoing military conflict—as well as preparing for a potentially much larger one to come.
What if the problem is less how the U.S. prepares for wars than the wars themselves? “Restrainers” on both the left and right argue that the munitions crisis should prompt a rethinking of whether the U.S. should get involved in as many armed conflicts as it does and whether it can credibly commit to defending allies in a potential superpower conflict with China.
Money can buy you a lot of firepower, but it doesn’t exempt you from the need to make real choices about priorities.

This Is Not a War for Ukrainian Territory, It Is a War Against the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

For some time now, we have regularly seen reports of more territory retaken by Ukraine, as well as large numbers of occupying troops being taken prisoner. Liberated villages and prisoners of war are, of course, good news, but unfortunately they do not change the overall situation.
Every square kilometer retaken and restored to Ukraine’s territorial integrity is undoubtedly a positive development. But it is important to remember that this is not a war over territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The full-scale war that has been ongoing since 2022 is not a war over Ukrainian territory, but a war being fought on Ukrainian territory. The Kremlin needs territorial gains to justify its policy and present them as evidence that it is achieving its stated objectives. But in reality, the goal is to bring Ukraine under political subordination.
Such subordination does not necessarily mean full occupation, nor does it have to happen within a short period of time. Putin has consistently pursued what he outlined in Munich in 2007 and Bucharest in 2008. The objective is to rebuild a sphere of influence across the territory of the former Soviet Union, whose collapse the Russian dictator considers one of the greatest tragedies of the 20th century.
The means to the end
The Kremlin is pursuing its objectives consistently and, unlike the West, is not constrained by democratic processes, which simply makes such a policy easier to implement. Russia has a wide range of means at its disposal – from political influence, disinformation, sabotage and economic pressure to drones and missiles, or the air terror experienced by residents of Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.
US Envoys Pressure Kyiv on Refinery Strikes
Turning Ukraine’s capital into a place that is increasingly difficult to live in, violating the airspace of NATO countries and Moldova, and undermining confidence in the functioning of military alliances are all tools aimed at spreading fear, weakening unity and polarizing societies in countries that Moscow considers adversaries, or even enemies.
The warnings coming from intelligence agencies of NATO countries about an expected escalation by Russia and the possibility of sabotage on a larger scale than before are perhaps the clearest evidence of this.
Russia’s goals and the United States
Will Russia succeed in achieving its objectives? Much depends on the determination of the West and Ukraine. One of the key factors is US policy towards Russia, Belarus and Ukraine.
Unfortunately, for some time now we have seen considerable inconsistency. On the one hand, there have been announcements of permanent US troop bases in Poland, the maintenance of a military presence in Lithuania, and Trump’s signature on sanctions introduced by the late Lindsey Graham. On the other hand, we still do not know whether these sanctions will actually be used against Russia.
Washington has eased some sanctions, including those affecting Belarusian potash fertilizers. The talks between Witkoff, Kushner and Putin also make it difficult to remain optimistic, without even mentioning the reported idea of reopening the Nord Stream pipelines. Not to mention the absurdity of blaming Ukraine for the ongoing fuel crisis.
How this should be interpreted remains an open question. Some conclusions can nevertheless be drawn. The US military presence in NATO’s eastern-flank countries constitutes a red line being drawn for Russia by Washington. At the same time, the United States does not rule out economic cooperation, including in areas such as fuel or Belarusian potash fertilizers.
Maintaining only very limited support for Ukraine, meanwhile, could be interpreted by the Kremlin as a green light to continue its actions in Ukraine. Russia has no genuine desire for peace talks, and Washington is aware of this. It is also aware of the problems Ukraine may face during the coming winter.
In a sense, this can be seen as a carrot-and-stick approach: the US military presence in Eastern Europe will be maintained, while there is also an incentive to pursue common business interests. The United States may be seeking to de-escalate the situation in order to maintain peace and stability in European NATO countries.
That would, however, be naïve. Russia operates according to a completely different logic, one that goes beyond what Europe or the United States would consider rational. The clearest evidence of this is the very fact that Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Strength through resilience and partnerships
The fact that this is a war being fought on Ukrainian territory, rather than a war over Ukrainian territory, means that it is also a conflict involving the West – and particularly NATO and EU countries on the eastern flank. This is where we are seeing the greatest number of hostile acts of sabotage and other forms of hybrid activity.
Bringing Ukraine into a state of subordination or reducing it to a severely weakened condition is one objective. Weakening, or even dismantling, Western alliances is another.
A conventional war in Europe currently appears highly unlikely. But it is important to remember that war itself is an extension of politics and a tool for pursuing political objectives.
There is little doubt that Russia will continue to pursue its objectives with the same consistency it has demonstrated so far. Tanks and missiles are means to an end, just as sabotage, disinformation, economic influence and acts of subversion are.
Countering this requires genuine unity within NATO and the EU, which remains evident, as well as continued support for Ukraine. That support depends both on its Western partners and on the foreign policy pursued by Kyiv. In this respect, it would also be worthwhile to avoid conflicts with partners that have so far proved reliable.
Only decisive and unambiguous action can create the conditions for an adequate response to Russia and help prevent further escalation.

Our cells keep a record of every workout—and that memory persists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:48:07 UTC
19:48:07 KST

Have you ever taken months off training—maybe due to an injury, a new baby or crushing work deadlines – and come back convinced you were starting from zero?
Research from our team has some good news: At the cellular level, you probably weren’t.
We found that muscle and liver cells store memories fromevery training session in ways that may help improve endurance, control blood sugar levels and even slow weight regain after inactivity.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Use it or lose it? Maybe not
For most of the past century, long before fad diets and fancy workout trends took off, exercise was considered one of the most effective lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, several cancers and early death for people of all ages. But people typically understood exercise as something whose beneficial effects fade away over time: You use it or lose it.
When you stop training, your maximum oxygen uptake, muscle gains and insulin sensitivity drift back to where they started, often within weeks. Physical activity guidelines are built on this fact, which is why they emphasize consistency above all else.
Consistency, however, is a luxury that roughly 3 in 4 American adults aren’t able to enjoy. People can experience injuries, illness, pregnancy or jobs that limit their time for or ability to exercise. If adaptation really resets, every time you step into the gym would be as if you’ve never been there before. But that scenario doesn’t match what coaches and returning athletes typically describe: In practice, people who have trained before can get fit again faster than those who haven’t undergone similar training.
In recent years, however, scientists have started challenging the concept of “use it or lose it.” New research hints that your cells might keep a record of your training history so all of your gains are not completely lost.
More than muscle
We are exercise physiologists who study how cells remember exercise. Our lab and others have shown that the body is able to store a form of exercise memory across different organs.
To study how this exercise memory works, our team of researchers use an ON-OFF-ON exercise training protocol in mice, which involves an initial four- to eight-week training period, followed by detraining—a period of no exercise—and a second training bout. This method allows us to examine how cells form a memory of exercise, maintain a record of exercise through detraining, and recall memories of prior training when exposed again to exercise.
Using this strategy, our team found that skeletal muscle memory accelerates muscle growth. Compared to mice with no training history, mice who retrained grew bigger muscles, and the individual muscle fibers inside those muscles grew too. Larger muscle fibers meant that the working cells were themselves getting bigger, rather than the surrounding tissue.
Looking more closely at these muscle cells, we found that retrained muscle is better at matching energy production to demand– meaning, the muscles were better at drawing from energy stores when it’s needed most – and this ability persists without further exercise. This memory held even when the mice ate a high-fat diet, suggesting that prior training can still offer benefits even when diet is working against those gains.
Muscle isn’t the only body part that learns from exercise. Working muscle needs fuel, and the liver supplies it during and after training sessions.
My colleagues and I found that liver cells also store exercise memory and uses it to feed muscle more efficiently. In both mice and people who trained, stopped, then trained again, their livers released higher levels of a family of enzymes called carboxylesterases. These enzymes chop up lipids circulating in the blood, delivering fat in a form that muscle can take up and burn as it grows.
A record that outlives you
Recorded cellular memories of exercise may even be passed down to future generations.
In mice, we found that three to four weeks of maternal and paternal endurance exercise can have a lasting effect on their offspring. Compared to offspring born to sedentary parents, parental exercise granted protection against poor blood sugar levels and excess weight gain for an entire year after birth.
Researchers have hypothesized numerous ways that prenatal exercise may affect offspring. For example, maternal exercise might allow offspring to spend more time developing in the womb or lead parents to producer higher quality milk.
But there remains much to be discovered on how parents influence the health of their children and whether their lifestyle could provide a fitness advantage across generations.
Every cell remembers
Biology has traditionally granted memory to a short list of cells. Neurons store memory in the connections between them. Immune cells store memory so they can recognize pathogens faster and more strongly the next time they encounter them.
Researchers previously considered all other cells to be memoryless; a cell responds to a signal, then returns to baseline without keeping a record of that interaction. But that assumption is now coming apart.
Skin stem cells can keep a record of inflammation, allowing them to heal a new wound faster months later. Human fat cells keep a record of obesity that persists even after substantial weight loss, which may account for why you gain weight faster when switching back to a high-calorie diet—the so-called yo-yo effect.
We propose that every cell in the body remembers exercise, regardless of how little or how much someone trains. The question is how long these records are stored and whether researchers could prolong or expand each cell’s storage capacity. Better understanding of how cells learn and remember exercise, where they store memories and how those memories are preserved could help improve exercise guidelines for those who cannot exercise for prolonged or consistent periods of time.
To be clear, none of these findings are evidence for skipping the gym; nothing in our data suggests the effects of past training can substitute for present training. But there is hope that the work you put into getting in shape isn’t completely lost over time.
Somewhere, deep in your cells, there is a record waiting to be replayed the next time you lace up your running shoes, pick up a pair of dumbbells or want to fulfill a New Year’s resolution.

This time, they are demanding ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar resign from his post.

Three years after Oct. 7, police dog Jerry is still fighting his own battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:46:14 UTC
19:46:14 KST

After nearly a year of operational service, during which he took part in dozens of complex and covert missions against terrorist organizations and dangerous crime families, Jerry, a Belgian Malinois police dog, accompanied officers from the Border Police's Tactical Brigade into the fierce fighting at Re'im on October 7, 2023.
According to his handlers, Jerry emerged from the battle with symptoms resembling post-traumatic stress, making him the only police dog in the unit known to have developed such a condition following the massacre. After two years of rehabilitation at the Tactical Brigade's base, he was transferred to a special police kennel for dogs retired from operational service, where his health has gradually improved.
Now five years old, Jerry was brought to Israel from the Czech Republic and joined the Tactical Brigade, considered one of the Border Police's elite units, responsible for responding to terrorist threats and serious criminal activity.
The brigade operates 22 working dogs. Some specialize in detecting drugs, cash, explosives and weapons, while others carry out tactical assignments, including clearing buildings and open areas of hostile suspects. Jerry belonged to the second group.
"On October 7, the brigade was called up by its commander at the time, Chief Superintendent Yaron Dahan," said Chief Sergeant Major Zvi Blumenberg, commander of the Tactical Brigade's canine unit.
"The officers were deployed to different fronts around the Gaza border communities, while the tactical dog handlers and their specially trained dogs were sent to Re'im. For hours, they carried out meticulous searches to clear houses, all while coming under intense fire from dozens of terrorists."
After the officers identified a building occupied by armed terrorists, Jerry was sent inside to search it.
"During the search, an RPG was fired toward the area where Jerry was operating," Blumenberg said. "That left him in a condition where he could no longer function."
Jerry had arrived at the unit when he was just one year old and completed four months of professional training before becoming a fully operational tactical police dog.
"He participated in dozens of operations against criminal and terrorist threats and was considered one of the best and most promising dogs in the unit," Blumenberg recalled. "We expected him to have a brilliant future. During operations, he saved our officers' lives more than once by being the first to enter buildings and putting his own life at risk."
But the incident at Re'im changed everything. "Within minutes of the RPG fire, Jerry stopped being the dog we knew," Blumenberg said. "The handler responsible for him realized something was wrong. Suddenly, Jerry seemed completely disconnected from what was happening around him, from the intense battle itself. If he had remained in action, he would have endangered both himself and his team."
Blumenberg explained that a tactical dog that loses its ability to respond to commands can become a serious operational liability.
"When a dog loses control, it can become dangerous. If the handler fails to recognize that and sends it into a building, the dog may not understand what it is being asked to do. The team would then have to enter a building that had not been properly searched or cleared to rescue it, putting both the officers and the dog at risk."
Fortunately, Jerry's handler recognized the problem immediately. "He understood that Jerry was experiencing a breakdown, withdrew him from the operation and brought him to one of the unit's designated vehicles for treatment," Blumenberg said.
The officers continued fighting in Re'im while the canine team evacuated Jerry to the brigade's home base. Initially, his handlers hoped that a few days of rest would be enough for him to recover. Instead, his condition deteriorated. "We conducted training exercises at the base and discovered that Jerry could no longer function, not even during training," Blumenberg said.
"He stopped eating, lost his appetite and became apathetic. We consulted the police veterinarian, who began a series of comprehensive examinations. The conclusion was that Jerry was suffering from stress and anxiety following the intense fighting."
The unit had never encountered anything like it. "We had never experienced a disaster like October 7, and we had never encountered a dog suffering from post-traumatic symptoms," Blumenberg said. "Once we understood his condition, we continued looking after him with dedication and love at our base until he was transferred to the special kennel."
For Blumenberg, Jerry's suffering is especially painful because of the dog's years of service. "We treat him the way we would treat a heroic soldier who was wounded in a difficult battle and needs medical care," he said. "It makes me sad to see a heroic dog struggling with post-traumatic stress."
He will never return to operational duty
The special police kennel was established about a year ago at a police facility that previously housed the police training academy. It currently accommodates 10 dogs that have retired from operational service. The oldest is 12 years old, while the youngest is just three, having been removed from active duty because of a medical condition.
Chief Sergeant Major Zaher Daher, who manages the Israel Police's canine retirement kennel and also serves as a dog evaluator in the police Animal Division, has overseen Jerry's treatment and rehabilitation over the past year. "Jerry is the only police dog suffering from post-traumatic stress," Daher said. "He fought in Re'im on October 7. Afterward, he became severely malnourished and nearly died because he had lost so much weight."
Jerry's psychological distress was reflected in his behavior. "He was afraid of everything. Every noise startled him, and he even bit two handlers. That was his way of coping with the trauma he had experienced. He had lost his confidence."
Since arriving at the kennel, Jerry has received individual attention and a carefully managed rehabilitation program, including more time outdoors. "I take care of him as though he were my own child," Daher said. "He needs a lot of warmth and affection."
"The goal is to give him the emotional and psychological support he needs. I monitor his condition regularly, and every Sunday we weigh him."
The changes, Daher said, have been encouraging. "I feel we've managed to rehabilitate him. He has gained a significant amount of weight, he's more relaxed, he interacts with more people and he looks much better physically."
Still, the effects of the trauma have not disappeared. "Because of his post-traumatic symptoms, he can go into a panic and bite people," Daher explained. "My team takes him for walks off-leash when there are no people or vehicles nearby. We also drive him to wooded areas so he can relax. We give him as much warmth and affection as possible."
Jerry also undergoes blood tests every two weeks. "There is no chance he will ever return to operational work," Daher said. "As far as I'm concerned, he's a disabled war veteran. He's the only dog in my kennel dealing with post-traumatic stress."
Chief Inspector Dr. Uri Arieli, the Israel Police's chief veterinarian, has been responsible for Jerry's medical treatment over the past year. When Arieli first examined the dog, his physical condition was alarming. "Jerry came to me in very poor physical condition, having lost about 25% of his body weight and suffering from low protein levels," he said.
"He also had an intestinal disease, which may have been caused or aggravated by stress. It is very plausible that different illnesses could emerge or worsen following a traumatic event."
Arieli emphasized, however, that he does not make behavioral diagnoses in dogs and therefore cannot independently confirm the handlers' assessment that Jerry suffers from post-traumatic stress. "I do not diagnose dogs behaviorally, so I cannot comment on the handlers' diagnosis regarding post-traumatic stress," he said.
Jerry currently receives medication every morning and evening to manage his intestinal illness. "We are gradually reducing the dosage," Arieli said. "His condition is improving, he's gaining weight and he appears much more energetic."
Jerry is also fed a specially formulated medical diet, making him the only police dog receiving that particular nutritional treatment. Although his handlers and veterinarians agree that his operational career is over, that has not diminished the commitment to his care.
"Even though he will never return to being an operational working dog, we continue to provide him with the best possible treatment," Arieli said. "From our professional perspective, he deserves the highest standard of care even when we know he will never return to active duty. It's a matter of values."
For Jerry, that commitment means a permanent home at the police kennel, surrounded by the people responsible for his recovery. "Jerry is expected to remain at our kennel for the rest of his life," Arieli said, "receiving all the care and conditions that the police provide for animals that have served the force."

Amelia Earhart mystery draws new search to remote Pacific island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

A team of U.S.-based marine archaeologists has set sail for a remote island in the western Pacific in hopes of uncovering new evidence in one of the 20th century’s most enduring mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.
Supported by Purdue University, which has long been associated with Earhart and her legacy, the team aims to determine whether an object detected beneath the waters of the island’s lagoon in satellite imagery six years ago is the wreckage of her twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E aircraft.
If confirmed, the discovery would lend decisive support to a longstanding theory that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and died as castaways, hundreds of miles from their intended refueling stop.
The expedition departed Los Angeles earlier this month and was expected to reach Nikumaroro on Tuesday, Oct. 13, local time. The uninhabited island lies in the remote Phoenix Islands, part of the Pacific nation of Kiribati.
“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, who is leading the effort in conjunction with Purdue, said in press materials for the mission.
Purdue general counsel and expedition member Steve Schultz, who was in Fiji conducting advance work for the expedition last week, said in an interview: “This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century.”
The mission has its skeptics. Chief among them is rival Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of TIGHAR, short for The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, and author of the 2024 book “One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy.”
Gillespie has led a dozen expeditions of his own to the atoll over three decades and is the leading proponent of the Nikumaroro castaway theory. But he predicted the Pettigrew-Purdue team would find no airplane wreckage or anything else of consequence left on the island.
The Purdue team credits Gillespie with laying the foundation for the theory it hopes to prove. It also cites a compelling body of evidence he has amassed over the years, including human artifacts recovered on the island, such as a 1930s-era glass cosmetic jar for freckle cream and remnants of a jackknife like one Earhart carried on the plane.
Gillespie’s investigation also encompassed modern forensic analysis of records documenting measurements of skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s; logs of radio transmission bearings from distress calls picked up by wireless operators in the days immediately after Earhart vanished; and a photograph taken of the island’s shoreline months later showing an object that Gillespie said appears to be the Electra’s landing gear.
In a Reuters interview last week, Gillespie said he believes the plane has since been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed largely intact and carried into the sea, where it sank and broke apart in the surf.
Two previous attempts to locate the plane’s wreckage in the surrounding ocean, including a 2019 operation conducted by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, known for discovering the wreck of the Titanic, proved fruitless, Gillespie said.
A plane-shaped sonar image from elsewhere on the seafloor turned out to be a pile of rocks.
“I’d love to find that airplane. It ain’t gonna happen,” Gillespie said.
Pettigrew and his team are betting otherwise. To them, the multibranched shape first noticed in a 2020 satellite image resembles an aircraft fuselage and wings. They assert that the object, or part of it, has since been spotted in earlier aerial images of the island’s lagoon dating to 1938.
Gillespie said he is certain the object in question was actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like evergreen native to the region, that washed into the lagoon.
“You can see the root ball. You can see the branches,” Gillespie said in the interview. “It’s a tree. People see what they want to see.”
The official U.S. government view has long been that the Electra ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its intended destination, Howland Island, another small island about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
Earhart was last seen taking off in her Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea, en route to Gardner, about 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) to the east, during a multistage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world.
Definitive radio contact with the plane was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported that “gas is running low,” followed by her final known transmission giving her geographical line of position.
The disappearance prompted the largest U.S. government search ever undertaken for a missing aircraft, including a flyover of Gardner, but no trace of the Electra or its crew was found at the time.
The $900,000 Purdue mission, consisting of 17 people, plans to remain on Nikumaroro for five days before making the six-day return boat trip to the Kiribati capital, Tarawa, according to Schultz.
Purdue, based in West Lafayette, Indiana, would ultimately seek to bring back any pieces of the Lockheed Electra that might be recovered.
Earhart was essentially a visiting faculty member at Purdue for two years, serving as a women’s career counselor and adviser to the school’s aeronautics department. A Purdue research grant paid for development of the Electra, which she called her “flying laboratory.”
Purdue lawyer Schultz said that if the plane were found, no artifacts would be removed from it on this trip. Any effort to extract the aircraft wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government, he said.

Swiss food firms bet on protein ingredients as demand for meat alternatives slows

Swiss food firms bet on protein ingredients as demand for meat alternatives slows
The hype around veggie burgers and soya yoghurt has faded in Switzerland. As a result, start-ups focused on plant-based nutrition are shifting their attention to the B2B market, selling protein ingredients rather than finished products.
Meat alternatives are finding it harder to win over consumers. According to Coop’s latest Plant-Based Food Report, sales of meat substitutes fell in 2025 compared with the previous year. After several years of strong growth from 2019 onwards, the market slowed in 2024 and slipped slightly in 2025.
The impact is already being felt. This summer, for example, the Bern-based start-up Outlawz, known for its vegan bacon bits made from bean and wheat protein, filed for insolvency. Despite the downturn, some Swiss companies still see opportunities in the plant-based protein market.
More
The Swiss have to eat less meat by 2050. Here’s how.
The key is business-to-business (B2B): selling products to other companies rather than directly to consumers, known as business-to-consumer (B2C).
Fabas is one company operating in this area. Founded in 2021, it initially launched as a consumer-facing brand, selling products such as hummus, veggie burgers and falafel. Since 2025, however, the company has shifted its focus to developing functional plant-based ingredients for food manufacturers.
Bean protein in ice cream and yoghurt
“We realised that the main challenge often lies with the plant-based ingredients,” co-founder Katharina Pälchen told the AWP news agency. “Ice cream and yoghurt manufacturers need ingredients that can be easily integrated into existing production processes and help them create plant-based products that appeal to consumers.”
More
Dutch cities are banning meat advertising – will Switzerland follow?
Fabas now supplies liquid legume protein extracts that can be processed in much the same way as cow’s milk. “Our ingredients are particularly attractive to manufacturers looking to develop new plant-based products without having to completely overhaul their production processes,” says Pälchen.
One of its customers is the Appenzell-based ice cream maker Sigrist, which uses the extracts to produce vegan ice cream.
Breakfast cereals made from brewers’ grains
The Appenzell-based start-up Upgrain is pursuing a similar approach. Working with the Locher brewery, it turns the spent grain left over from the brewing process into proteins, fibres and flakes. These can then be used in a range of products, including baked goods, breakfast cereals, snacks, drinks and meat alternatives.
+ Swiss court bans animal names for vegan meat substitutes
“We want to establish spent grain protein as a mainstream ingredient in the food industry,” says co-founder William Pyndt Beiskjær. One of the company’s partners is Coop.
Planted expands its business-to-business operations
Meat substitute maker Planted is also stepping up its focus on the business-to-business market. “B2B is a strategic growth area for Planted, and one we plan to expand further in the years ahead,” says co-founder Pascal Bieri.
Alongside its consumer products, including chicken alternatives, the Kemptthal-based company plans to supply structured pea-protein cuts to meat processors and convenience food manufacturers. These products can then be processed locally by customers.
Egg substitutes for more stable supply chains
Companies also see opportunities in the growing market for egg alternatives. Illnau-based start-up Eggfield is using aquafaba, the liquid left over from cooking pulses, to replicate many of the functional properties of eggs, “without compromising on quality or ease of processing”.
More
For example, the ingredient can be whipped in much the same way as egg whites, making it suitable for products such as baked goods, desserts and pasta.
The product was originally developed in 2019 for use at Leibacher Biber-Manufaktur. Looking for a natural, functional alternative to eggs for its vegan Biber biscuits, co-founder Silvan Leibacher wanted a solution that did not rely on a long list of additives.
Today, he supplies the egg substitute to food manufacturers and catering businesses, including Hiltl.
“Bird flu has highlighted just how vulnerable the egg supply chain can be,” says Leibacher. As a result, food manufacturers are increasingly looking to reduce their reliance on any single ingredient. Plant-based alternatives can help diversify supply chains and improve resilience.

The association also called for immediate access to legal assistance and the release of those against whom there were no lawful grounds for detention. It further sought an examination of the reported use of force and appropriate action in accordance with the law.The letter enclosed an SCBA resolution expressing “grave concern” over the reported detention of advocates participating in peaceful protests in the Supreme Court area.“The Supreme Court Bar Association resolves to request the Chief Justice of India to intervene urgently and take up the matter with the concerned authorities,” the resolution stated. Detentions in Delhi amid CJP protestThe incident unfolded amid a sweeping security crackdown in Delhi ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed demonstration at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, several Opposition leaders, activists, journalists and other protesters were also detained as police attempted to prevent demonstrators from reaching Jantar Mantar.
More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the capital, with 45 metro stations closed, traffic diversions imposed and extensive barricading put in place. The CJP had called the demonstration over allegations of voter-list manipulation during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and changes relating to Form 6, used for voter registration.
