US buys Avon Protection half mask for special forces
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:37:33 BST
19:37:33 KST

The United States has ordered the MITR respiratory system from the British manufacturer Avon Protection for its special operations forces, according to the company.
The order from the Department of War covers the MITR-M1 half mask and the MITR-PG1 powered goggle, together with particulate and riot filters and integrated helmet and communication accessories.
Avon’s argument for the system is that a full-face respirator is more protection than a tactical operator needs most of the time, and slower to put on when they do. The MITR arrangement protects eyes, nose and mouth separately, letting users scale up during fast-moving missions.
The half mask carries NIOSH certification and a flush-fitting curved profile that preserves weapon sighting, with voice amplification for communications, and it clips directly to a helmet through a mount kit so it can be donned without taking the helmet off. The goggle constantly purges air, resists fogging and works with combat helmets and night vision systems.
Both filters give NIOSH P100 protection, removing more than 99.97 per cent of harmful airborne particulates, with the riot filter adding an activated carbon layer for riot agent vapour.
Steve Elwell, president of Avon Protection, said: “This award culminates nearly four years of working collaboratively with end-users developing a solution that meets their mission requirements. Securing the U.S. DoW as another customer for the MITR System demonstrates continued focus on protecting the health of personnel, both in the short-term and the long-term.
“For tactical operators, MITR is not just about protection during today’s mission, it is about reducing lifetime exposure to hazardous particulates that can contribute to long-term health issues and helping ensure those who serve remain healthy long after their careers end. This award represents an important step in bringing this capability to a wider community of users.”
The United States is the second Five Eyes nation to take the MITR-M1, following Canada in May.
Avon Protection is part of Avon Technologies, and its chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear protection products are in use by more than four million people worldwide. The company is based in Melksham in Wiltshire, with the MITR announcement datelined from its facility in Cadillac, Michigan.

Turkey bans social media for kids under 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:37:22 UTC
19:37:22 KST

The government of Turkey on Saturday formally banned access to social media platform for children under the age of 15.
The law was published today following the Turkish Parliament's adoption of the bill last April. The ban will come into force on Nov. 1.
Social media platforms will have to "take the necessary technical and administrative measures, including age verification," to implement the new rules, the law states. The age verification system would work with a government-issued "token", according to the law's Article 7.
Advertisement
The law also includes provisions for minors over 15, stating that platforms cannot offer them services that could have "an addictive effect."
Turkey has often implemented tough restrictions on social media services, frequently banning individual accounts from media outlets or activists, and at times banning access to entire platforms. Ankara banned Instagram for a week in 2024 amid claims the Meta-owned platform censored users mourning Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh.
Last week Turkey blocked a news website and its social media accounts over what a court deemed to be "LGBT propaganda," sparking outrage from human rights and media freedom groups.
A 2025 report from the U.S.-based think tank Freedom House described Turkey's internet as "not free."
Turkey joins a growing group of states, including Australia and Indonesia, that are introducing or exploring tougher age restrictions on social media access.
In September the European Union presented a legal proposal to restrict children's access to social media and video-sharing platforms until they turn 15, following months of intense pressure from EU leaders on the issue.
Austria, Denmark, France, Greece and Spain are all pushing ahead with national laws to restrict kids' access to social media. The United Kingdom is also expected to introduce a ban next year.
Canada has also presented a bill to restrict access to social media platforms for children under 16.

QinetiQ and Serco join Canadian air training bid
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:34:46 BST
19:34:46 KST

Two British defence services companies have joined a consortium bidding for Canada’s programme to modernise its air weapons ranges, alongside two Indigenous enterprises and a Canadian engineering firm, according to QinetiQ.
Team StrīQ brings together QinetiQ Group Canada, Serco Canada, Des Nedhe Group Defence, Cold Lake First Nations Defence and Arcfield Canada to pursue the Range Advancement Generation Next and Airspace Revitalization programme, known as Ragnar.
The work would expand the military training ranges at Cold Lake and Bagotville and build expertise at Goose Bay, connecting live aircraft, synthetic systems, threat environments, telemetry, secure networks and training centres into one system.
Corrie Dale, managing director of QinetiQ Canada, said: “Ensuring Canada’s next-generation aircraft and systems are matched by a next-generation training environment is the principal driver behind Team StrīQ’s proposal. QinetiQ has a long-term partnering agreement with the UK Ministry of Defence to ensure mission-critical capability is safe, interoperable and operationally ready. We look forward to bringing state-of-the-art expertise developed over many years to support Canada’s ambitions.”
Natasha McLean, managing director of Serco Canada, said: “We’re excited to be part of Team StriQ and build on our 30-year partnership with Canada’s Armed Forces. Our proven expertise in next-generation live and virtual training can ensure the Royal Canadian Air Force can test, train and exploit operational capabilities today and for years to come, all while boosting Canada’s defence industry and economy.”
The Cold Lake Air Weapons Range sits within Cold Lake First Nations traditional lands, and Chief Kelsey Jacko said the community is committed to supporting its protection while helping advance the programme, bringing Indigenous-led business solutions and regional knowledge to the team.
Grant Oliver, president of DNG Defence, said: “Ragnar is one of the most important defence investments Saskatchewan and Alberta will see in a generation. DNG Defence and Cold Lake First Nations are committed to making sure it builds lasting Indigenous businesses, careers and prosperity across western Canada, while giving the RCAF the world-class training range it needs to better protect our borders and support our allies.”
Luc Sabourin, vice president at Arcfield Canada, said the company’s platform agnostic capabilities would help sustain advanced systems and support long-term readiness.
The team is supported by D-TA Systems, Inzpire, the University of Alberta, the Northern Alberta Institute of Technology and Raymond EMC, and says its approach remains subject to Canadian government acquisition decisions and procurement processes.
The Long Term Partnering Agreement cited by Ms Dale is the arrangement under which QinetiQ runs much of the test and evaluation estate for the Ministry of Defence. Inzpire, among the supporting companies, is another British training specialist.

The new owner of the Telegraph is preparing to make significant job cuts to its newsroom, just months after stating it would invest in the title to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.
Axel Springer, the German media company overseen by its billionaire chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to be examining proposals that would make between 50 and 100 journalists redundant.
A source familiar with the plans said a forthcoming consultation was likely to propose cutting a “significant proportion” of editorial staff, possibly before Christmas.
They said such proposals called into question Axel Springer’s promise to “back an investment programme in [the Telegraph Media Group] to grow and expand the business”.
A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group declined to comment. No redundancies have been announced to staff so far.
It would mark the first big intervention by Axel Springer since its £575m purchase of the Telegraph earlier this year. The sale ended three tortuous years for the Telegraph and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.
The proposed cuts have confused some Telegraph figures, who are struggling to understand how it aligns with Döpfner’s pledge to “bring that uncertainty to an end”.
At a recent Axel Springer leadership summit held in London, Döpfner is also said to have stated that the company could not cut its way to growth.
Axel Springer, which also owns Politico and the German titles Bild and Die Welt, recently brought in consultants to examine the financial health of the Telegraph titles, which include the Daily Telegraph, the Sunday Telegraph and its online news operation.
Döpfner has made no secret of his desire to boost the Telegraph’s US operation, with senior editors already deployed to the US to develop those plans.
However, consultants are understood to have drawn up potential cuts to the existing news operation at the 171-year-old titles.
Sources said consultants had also recommended that the Telegraph set up side projects to support its journalism, such as price comparison sites and healthcare. Some insiders were said to be baffled by some of the suggestions.
A source familiar with the proposals said they would anger Telegraph staff, who had hoped Axel Springer’s ownership would mark the arrival of “sunny uplands” after three years of being “starved of any form of investment, pay rises or management changes that could move us on”.
“The path to growth is not to cut jobs,” they said. “They’re still going to need to hire people in the States if they’re going to make any sort of push there, but staff haven’t been told where that money is going to come from.”
The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed that it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m.
However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.

====================================================================================================

EU budget: Ireland pitches €141bn cuts to appease the ‘frugals’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:22:30 UTC
19:22:30 KST

Ireland proposes cutting the next EU budget by 8%, with global cooperation and competitiveness taking the deepest cuts, while agriculture and cohesion funding is reduced by only 3%. It also includes a €55bn-a-year package of own resources. EU leaders will discuss the plan on 15-16 October.
Ireland, which currently holds the EU’s rotating presidency, has proposed trimming the bloc’s next long-term budget by €141bn in a bid to win over the Germany-led ‘frugal’ countries.
The so-called negotiating box will anchor the sensitive budget talks when EU leaders meet next week. It concentrates most of the reductions on the programmes for economic competitiveness and global cooperation.
“The negotiating box acts to bridge the many differences between the member states. It brings us closer to resolving the so-called budgetary trilemma,” said Thomas Byrne, Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs, who leads on the file.
Byrne said the proposal strikes a delicate balance between financing new priorities such as competitiveness and defence, protecting core policies like agriculture and cohesion, and reflecting the fiscal realities every member state faces.
Negotiating box
EU governments are entering the crunch stretch for finalising the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028-2034.
Dublin proposes cutting the overall volume to €1,622bn in 2025 prices, 8% below the Commission’s proposal and still 30% above the current MFF. In current prices, that comes to around €1,825bn.
The funding dedicated to cohesion, agriculture and fisheries, by far the largest item of expenditure, takes the smallest cut: 3%, to €914bn. The programme for economic competitiveness, research and defence is trimmed by 13% to €456bn.
As expected, EU administration also takes a heavy hit, down 8.8% to €95bn. Member states had called for the cut as many capitals face constraints in their own civil services.
Global Europe, which finances cooperation projects in third countries, is cut by 17% to €157bn. That is unlikely to dent the EU’s network of 145 delegations worldwide, which gives many small member states a global reach.
“I am confident that this revision to the overall volume and the rebalancing of priorities that it acts to address the preferences of Member States, and it will open the door to the next stage of negotiations,” Byrne said.
Own resources
The Irish presidency’s compromise text also includes a new package of own resources, EU-wide levies that would feed directly into Brussels’ coffers, estimated to raise €55bn a year.
The biggest change from the Commission’s initial proposal is that Dublin wants to raise the call rate for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tariff on carbon-intensive imports, from 75% to 90%.
The text also allows the Emissions Trading System (ETS) own resource to be phased in for member states supported by the Modernisation Fund, following strong opposition over the revenues capitals would have to give up.
The Commission’s proposals for a tobacco excise duty (TEDOR), a corporate resource for Europe (CORE) and an electronic waste levy are kept, along with the plan for the EU to retain 90% of customs duties.
The box leaves out the three own resources proposed by the European Parliament, which would tax digital services, online gambling and crypto assets, even though recent estimates put their yield at up to €32bn a year.
“We had three tests for new own resources. One, that they command unanimity. Two, that they can deliver substantial funds. And three, that they’d be ready, by the 1st of January, 2028,” Byrne continued.
“It wasn’t clear to us, either on the funds question, or that there could be deliverable on the 1st of January, 2028.”
Political context
The aim is a political agreement by the end of the year, before several key countries head to the polls in 2027. In France, a Eurosceptic candidate is currently the favourite to become the next President of the Republic.
Elections are already complicating the picture. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called snap elections for 29 November, in the middle of the negotiations. Regional victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany are expected to harden Berlin’s stance.
Germany leads a coalition of six ‘frugal’ countries that want the Commission’s proposal cut by “several hundred billions” and spending focused on emerging priorities such as defence and economic competitiveness.
By contrast, Italy’s Giorgia Meloni is leading a 17-strong front of southern and eastern member states, the ‘Friends of Cohesion’, which put protecting funding for farmers and the poorest regions first.
In June, the then Cypriot presidency of the EU Council proposed a €32.8bn reduction that concentrated the heftiest cuts on competitiveness and defence spending, drawing the ire of the frugal camp.
Ireland’s compromise tries to split the difference, with an 8% cut against Cyprus’s 2%. However, some frugal countries have already expressed their disappointment with the proposal.
"The new MFF negotiating box is unreasonable. The overall volume must come down significantly. The numbers that have been put on the table still present a wildly unaffordable increase, and we are therefore nowhere near an agreement," Jessica Rosencrantz, Sweden's Minister for EU Affairs, said on X.
EU ambassadors will discuss the Irish proposal on Sunday, before ministers take it up at the General Affairs Council on 13 October and leaders at the European Council on 15-16 October.

Greens must avoid ‘capture by extremists and racists’, says party MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:22:16 UTC
19:22:16 KST

A Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists” amid the continuing fallout from the “Zionism is racism” vote.
The party faces a political maelstrom over its policy decision last week to treat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, as any other form of racism, and to back a single Palestinian state over a two-state solution. The motion was passed at the annual party conference with just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.
Ellie Chowns, the party leader in the House of Commons, said the ability to pass such a “significant and damaging policy” in that way made it clear the party’s structures and policymaking processes were not working.
“I don’t think that policy, ‘Zionism is racism’, represents the large majority of Green party members, nor of people in the country,” Chowns told BBC’s Radio 4 Today Programme on Saturday.
“We don’t want to be in debates about the meaning of contested terms, we want to be united and focusing in contesting and criticising the horrific actions of the Israeli government,” said Chowns, who lost a co-leadership run against Zack Polanski in 2025.
The debate over whether the Greens’ decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly comes hours after the party’s leader for England and Wales was defeated by Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
Polanksi, who received just under 33% of the vote on Friday, insisted he intended to remain as Green leader, despite calls to stand down, including from the chair of the Jewish Greens. The party normally holds leadership elections every two years, meaning the next election would be in the summer of 2027.
Chowns said Polanksi’s “clear” lack of leadership over the Zionisim motion was “disappointing”, but that he had an opportunity to unite the party, having recognised the flaws in the motion.
Tensions were heightened between the UK and Israel after the Labour government imposed sanctions on illegal settlements in occupied Palestine, and Israel retaliated by trying to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Research carried out before the motion was passed found that Jewish people who vote for the Greens felt their attachment to Israel had weakened, even as the percentage of British Jews who identified as Zionist rose more broadly between 2022 and 2025.
When asked about extremism and racism within the party – not only in relation to the motion but comments made by the deputy leader, Mothin Ali, after the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 in which he called for an end to “white supremacist European settler colonialism” – Chowns stressed the importance of the party’s internal processes.
“I don’t know if there are extremists and racists in my party but I want to make sure that my party isn’t vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, I want to make sure my party’s policies represent the views of the majority of members of the Green party who absolutely are not that sort of person at all,” she said.
“Of course its legitimate to have difference of opinions including on many of the matters that this motion covers,” she added.
Polanski has been accused of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate and the vote at the conference to instead campaign in the byelection, and for giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.
In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.
On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, the chair of the Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”
However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.

Severe injuries at French student protests draw scrutiny to police tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:20:54 UTC
19:20:54 KST

Severe injuries at French student protests draw scrutiny to police tactics
Twenty-four investigations have been opened by French police watchdog IGPN into incidents linked to the ongoing high school protest movement, the interior ministry said. The police response has reignited calls to scrap rubber bullets and launcher-fired riot-control weapons, long denounced by rights groups and UN experts as dangerous and excessive.
Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said.
Read moreFrench students vow to keep up protests as UN voices 'concern' over violence
The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone metres away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A second officer then fired a tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face.
"(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said.
A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. According to the prosecutor’s office, the police officer said that he was seeking to protect himself and his colleagues after the student confronted police. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after the incident.
The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of student unrest over conditions in schools. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades.
The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other European countries and have been repeatedly criticised in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate.
It has also sparked anger among the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated discontent with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election.
Read moreFrench student protests fuel political clash ahead of 2027 presidential vote
Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback.
In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off – likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who paused the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case.
Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said.
Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors.
“France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims – we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research.
“It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said.
Watch moreFrench high school students react to education minister’s measures
Calls alls to ban 'less lethal' weapons
Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades.
Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche.
In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added.
A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye.
“He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said.
The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets.
The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden.
Read more‘Nothing will stop us’: French student protests show few signs of ending
Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security.
“We must withdraw the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party told Reuters. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police.
Thierry Clair, a police union representative, said that serious injuries such as Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions.
“How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.”
(FRANCE24 with Reuters)

Zelenskyy calls Trump-Putin diesel deal ‘not fair and not honest’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:20:16 UTC
19:20:16 KST

Kanyshai Butun
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that US President Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel was “not fair and not honest.”
In an interview with Axios, Zelenskyy said the deal “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin,” adding: “It looks absolutely terrible.”
Zelenskyy said he spoke with US envoy Steve Witkoff several days ago about efforts to reach a diplomatic breakthrough before winter and the US midterm elections.
"Steve proposed to meet in Florida. And of course I accepted to go there and speak about the possibilities of negotiations. The Americans said they have some ideas and we agreed to come to discuss," he said.
Zelenskyy said US envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner did not mention a potential diesel deal with Russia during their discussions. He said he understood that the envoys would convey messages from the Florida talks to Moscow and could then travel to Kyiv to pursue a peace agreement.
Zelenskyy said his negotiators in Florida informed him about an hour before Trump's announcment that Trump planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin and might announce a decision on sanctions, without providing further details.
"It's not honest, really, because we tried to build our relations in the best way," he said. "It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this."
Zelenskyy said he would have supported easing sanctions on Russian energy as part of an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure in both countries during winter.
"If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good," he said, adding that Trump would presumably have announced such a breakthrough if Putin had agreed to it.
"What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world," Zelenskyy said.
He compared the decision to the Anchorage summit between Trump and Putin last year, which reportedly ended with the US president agreeing to many of the Russian demands regarding the war in Ukraine without getting anything in return.”
Zelenskyy questioned whether granting Moscow a benefit without an apparent concession would complicate further diplomacy, but stopped short of saying Washington could no longer mediate between Kyiv and Moscow.
"We need the Americans to try to stop this war," he said.
Zelenskyy said he planned to speak with his negotiating team to get a full account of its discussions with Witkoff and Kushner. He also said he wanted to understand whether the diesel deal was linked to a planned visit by Trump’s envoys to Russia.
"If you allow them to export diesel, and you think before that you have to go to Russia to negotiate, it looks that you are buying this meeting," Zelenskyy said, while stressing that he did not know whether that was actually Trump's intention.
"Maybe I'm not right," Zelenskyy said. "But it looks this way. Otherwise, why do it?"
 
Putin-Trump phone call
Trump spoke with Putin over the phone on Friday and described the conversation as a “highly successful discussion.”
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the talks resulted in an agreement for Russia to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
He said another 500,000 tons would be supplied in November, followed by 1 million tons and an additional 3 million tons “within a short period,” depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.
Putin said Russian diesel supplies to US and global markets would benefit the world economy, adding that the two leaders discussed the global energy sector, prospects for resolving the Ukraine war, the situation in Iran, and bilateral relations.

Protest rights in India: When can police stop a protest or detain you?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:18:14 UTC
19:18:14 KST

AI generated image used for representative purpose
NEW DELHI: A protest is a constitutionally protected way to express dissent. However, the right to assemble peacefully does not mean that demonstrations can take place anywhere or without restrictions. Police and local authorities can regulate gatherings to maintain public order, protect public safety and prevent serious disruption. But they must act within the law, and the mere inconvenience caused by a protest does not automatically justify stopping it or taking participants into custody.So, do you need police permission before holding a protest? Can the police order a peaceful gathering to disperse or detain people who refuse to leave? And what can you do if you believe you have been arrested unlawfully? Here is what the law says about your right to protest and the limits on police powers.Police permission and the right to protest“There is no single, nationwide rule that every protest requires police permission,” said senior advocate Vivek Narayan Sharma. The requirements depend on local laws, the proposed venue and the circumstances. Authorities may require permission or impose conditions relating to the venue, timing, route and size of a gathering.The Constitution protects both freedom of expression and the right to assemble peacefully.
Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) guarantee these rights, while Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions on public assemblies in the interests of public order and the sovereignty and integrity of India.Sharma said the Supreme Court has recognised the state's responsibility to protect the right to peaceful assembly. As he put it, “the state must actively facilitate peaceful assembly, not merely tolerate it.”In Ramlila Maidan Incident v Union of India, the Supreme Court examined the state's obligations towards a gathering and the limits on police action. The judgment underscores an important distinction: authorities can regulate protests, but they must also respect the constitutional right to hold them.Vishal Gehrana, partner at Karanjawala & Co, said authorities must have a lawful basis for regulating demonstrations.“The authorities may regulate demonstrations to protect public order, public safety, traffic and the rights of others. Such regulation must, however, have a lawful basis and be justified by the circumstances. Preventive powers cannot be used arbitrarily or beyond the purpose for which the law confers them,” he said.
-
When authorities can restrict a demonstrationAuthorities may restrict a protest when there are specific safety concerns, a credible threat to public order or a serious obstruction to essential access. They may also impose restrictions when a valid prohibitory order is in force. However, such measures must be justified by the circumstances, rather than by disagreement with the protesters' views.One provision that authorities can invoke in urgent situations is Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which replaced Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It empowers an Executive Magistrate to issue orders to prevent situations involving danger, obstruction or a disturbance of public tranquillity.Such an order must be in writing and state the material facts justifying it. It ordinarily remains in force for up to two months, although the state government may extend it for a further period of up to six months, subject to the law. An affected person can also apply to have the order withdrawn or modified.Does the existence of such an order automatically make every restriction lawful? No. The reasons for issuing it, its scope and the manner in which it is enforced remain relevant.“An order covering an area or the public generally is not automatically unlawful; its factual basis, scope and operation must be examined,” Gehrana said.In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India, the Supreme Court held that Section 144 orders cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression and that restrictions must be justified, proportionate and open to judicial review.When police can disperse a gathering or take people into custodyPolice can order an assembly to disperse when the legal conditions for doing so are met. Section 148 of the BNSS deals with dispersing unlawful assemblies and certain other gatherings of five or more people that satisfy the statutory conditions concerning public peace.Sharma emphasised that the power to disperse an assembly does not amount to a blanket ban on peaceful protests.“Section 148 BNSS…is a dispersal power, not a blanket prohibition on peaceful protests,” he said.However, ordering a gathering to disperse and arresting its participants are distinct actions. Whether either is lawful depends on the circumstances and the legal grounds invoked. Simply being part of a crowd does not, by itself, establish grounds for arrest.Gehrana said the legality of a mass operation must be assessed individually, rather than on the assumption that the same grounds apply to everyone.“A mass detention is not automatically unlawful merely because several people are taken into custody at the same time. However, the scale of the operation cannot dispense with the requirement for a lawful basis for each person's deprivation of liberty,” he said.Preventive arrest vs preventive detentionPreventive arrest and preventive detention are often used interchangeably, but they refer to different legal powers.Preventive arrest is intended to stop a cognizable offence that police believe is about to be committed. Preventive detention, by contrast, involves detaining a person under a special law, such as the National Security Act, to prevent certain acts considered threatening to public order or national security.Section 170 of the BNSS allows police to arrest a person without a warrant to prevent the commission of a cognizable offence when the statutory conditions are met, including where the offence cannot otherwise be prevented. An arrest under this provision cannot ordinarily be made solely as a precaution: the police must have the required information and grounds for believing that the offence is likely to occur.Custody under Section 170 cannot exceed 24 hours unless further detention is authorised under another legal provision.These powers do not give police unrestricted authority to detain people attending a protest simply because the gathering is inconvenient or may cause disruption. The circumstances and the legal grounds for the action remain decisive.Sharma said preventive powers must be used only for the purposes for which the law grants them. Gehrana similarly stressed that the legality of an arrest depends on the facts, the power invoked and compliance with the applicable safeguards.“The legality of the action depends on the facts, the power invoked and compliance with the applicable safeguards,” Gehrana said.
-
Rights and safeguards after an arrestAn arrest does not strip a person of their basic legal rights. The Constitution and the BNSS provide safeguards that police must follow.An arrested person has the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest and to consult a lawyer of their choice. Article 22(1) of the Constitution protects these rights, while Section 47 of the BNSS requires the arrested person to be informed of the grounds of arrest and, where applicable, their right to bail.Police must also inform a relative, friend or another person nominated by the arrested individual about the arrest and where they are being held. Section 48 of the BNSS sets out this requirement, while Section 53 provides for a medical examination of the arrested person.Another important safeguard is the 24-hour rule. Under Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section 58 of the BNSS, an arrested person must generally be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time required for the journey. Further custody requires lawful authorisation.The law also provides specific safeguards for the arrest of women. Under Section 43(5) of the BNSS, a woman should generally not be arrested between sunset and sunrise, except in exceptional circumstances and subject to the prescribed procedure, including prior permission from a magistrate.
These protections apply even when police take several people into custody during a protest.“The arrested person must be informed of the relevant rights, and the Magistrate must verify compliance with the applicable requirements,” Gehrana said.
-
Legal remedies if you believe your detention was unlawfulIf you believe you have been unlawfully detained or arrested, you can approach the courts. The appropriate remedy will depend on the circumstances and the legal grounds for your detention.
Seek bail or challenge continued custody: Apply to the competent court for bail, where available, or challenge the legal basis for continued detention.
File a habeas corpus petition: Approach a high court under Article 226 of the Constitution or, where appropriate, the Supreme Court under Article 32 to challenge unlawful detention.
Seek compensation: In appropriate cases, a person whose fundamental rights have been violated may seek compensation. It is not automatic and depends on the facts, evidence and applicable law.
The right to protest peacefully is constitutionally protected, but it is subject to lawful and reasonable restrictions. Police can intervene when the law permits them to do so, but they must have valid legal grounds for their actions and comply with the safeguards protecting individual liberty.

Estonia condemns US sanctions on International Criminal Court
Estonia's Foreign Ministry has publicly condemned US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), joining a growing list of countries criticizing the move.
The ministry said the ICC is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and a key safeguard against impunity, and offered to discuss US concerns.
The U.S. announced sweeping sanctions on the ICC on Friday.
"Estonia regrets the decision by the US to impose sanctions against the ICC. The International Criminal Court is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and a vital safeguard against impunity. Estonia remains unwavering in its support for the ICC's independence, impartiality, and integrity," the Foreign Ministry said via social media on Saturday.
The ministry stressed that the ICC is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and an important safeguard against impunity.
"Estonia firmly supports the independence, impartiality and credibility of the International Criminal Court," the ministry said, confirming it was ready to communicate with the United States to discuss the concerns raised and find a solution.
Estonia regrets the decision by the US to impose sanctions against the ICC. The International Criminal Court is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and a vital safeguard against impunity. Estonia remains unwavering in its support for the ICC's independence, impartiality, and integrity. We are prepared to engage with the US to further discuss its concerns, in order to resolve this situation.
— Estonian MFA | #StandWithUkraine (@MFAestonia) October 10, 2026
Several other countries have hit out at the U.S. decision.
The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the U.K. issued a joint statement expressing support for the ICC and confirming their opposition to the US decision to impose sanctions on the court.
"If implemented, these would have a significant impact on the court's work, its dedicated staff and their families. We continue to stand united in support of the ICC and consider inclusive and constructive dialogue with non-member states important," the countries said.
Spain's Foreign Ministry also condemned the sanctions. "Spain deplores the decision by the United States Government to impose new sanctions against the International Criminal Court and reaffirms its unwavering support for the Court, which is at the forefront of the fight against impunity for the most serious international crimes," Spain's foreign ministry said.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said that, at Belgium's initiative, support for the ICC will be discussed with EU foreign ministers on Monday and at the upcoming European Council.
⚖️ I strongly condemn the new US sanctions against the International Criminal Court. Seeking to cripple the Court's work denies victims a path to justice and puts those responsible for the gravest crimes beyond its reach. At Belgium's initiative, support for the ICC will be discussed with my EU foreign affairs colleagues on Monday and at the forthcoming European Council. We will press for concrete protection. The Court's independence cannot depend on whom it investigates. Europe must act. Belgium is calling for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the Court and those who support its work. We must also defend our right to uphold international law without foreign sanctions dictating our choices. @BelgiumMFA @IntlCrimCourt
— Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 9, 2026
German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig said the U.S. move was "utterly staggering". "Historically, hardly any country has done more for international criminal law than the USA. For it was the United States that, after the Second World War, championed the cause of bringing the principal perpetrators of the Nazi regime to trial in Nuremberg – and thereby laid the foundations for international criminal law. It is utterly staggering that the US, of all countries, is now setting out to destroy this idea once and for all."
The European Commission expressed support for the ICC as well.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, expressed support for the actions of U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Netanyahu, who is on an ICC wanted list too, said that it was not a court but a political body.
The UN and several human rights organizations also condemned the sanctions.
The US has previously imposed sanctions on the court's prosecutors and judges.
The Trump administration announced sweeping sanctions on the ICC on Friday, targeting the institution itself rather than individual judges and officials, after previously sanctioning 17 ICC personnel. The U.S .says the court threatens American sovereignty, while the ICC has called the measures an assault on the rule of law; a six-month grace period allows member states to keep funding the court's operations in the meantime.
Founded in 2002, the ICC's purpose is to try war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. In March 2023 it issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin, over war crimes.

Amelia Earhart expedition heads to Pacific atoll hoping to find her plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:15:05 UTC
19:15:05 KST

Amelia Earhart expedition heads to Pacific atoll hoping to find her plane
- A Purdue-backed marine archaeology team has sailed to Nikumaroro island to check whether a submerged object there is Amelia Earhart’s missing Lockheed Electra, lost in 1937.
- Supporters say satellite, aerial and artefact evidence may prove Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on Nikumaroro and died as castaways, but sceptics say the object may just be a fallen pandanus tree.
- The five-day mission hopes to solve a major aviation mystery, but any recovery will need more permission from Kiribati, and past searches have found nothing.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – A team of marine archaeologists has set sail for a tiny island in the far western Pacific seeking to examine the latest tantalising clue to one of the 20th century’s great unsolved mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.
Backed by Purdue University, an institution long affiliated with Earhart and her legacy, the group aims to learn whether a submerged object detected by satellite imagery in the island’s lagoon six years ago is the wreckage of Earhart’s twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E airplane.
Such a finding would conclusively prove the hypothesis of some scholars that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and perished as castaways there, hundreds of kilometres from their intended refuelling stop.
After embarking from Los Angeles earlier in October, the group was expected to arrive on Oct 13 at Nikumaroro, an uninhabited speck of land in the remote Phoenix islands, part of the archipelago nation of the Kiribati Republic.
“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” said Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, who is leading the effort in conjunction with Purdue.
Purdue general counsel and expedition member Steve Schultz, who was in Fiji conducting advance work for the expedition last week, said in an interview: “This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century,”
The mission has its sceptics. Chief among them is rival Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of TIGHAR, short for The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, and author of the 2024 One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy.
Tree or plane?
Gillespie has led a dozen expeditions of his own to the atoll over three decades and is the leading proponent of the Nikumaroro castaway theory. But he predicted the Pettigrew-Purdue team would find no airplane wreckage or anything else of consequence left on the island.
The Purdue team credits Gillespie for laying the foundation of the theory they hope to prove. And they cite a compelling body of evidence that he has amassed over the years, including human artefacts recovered on the island, such as a 1930s-era glass cosmetic jar for freckle cream and remnants of a jackknife like the one Earhart carried on the plane.
Gillespie’s investigation also encompassed modern forensic analysis from records of measurements of skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s; logs of radio transmission bearings from distress calls picked up by wireless operators in the days immediately after Earhart vanished; and a photograph taken of the island’s shoreline months later showing an object that Gillespie said appears to be the Electra’s landing gear.
In an interview last week, Gillespie said he believes the plane has since been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it landed largely intact and was carried into the sea to sink and break apart in the surf.
Two previous attempts to locate the plane’s wreckage in the surrounding ocean, including a 2019 operation conducted by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, famed for his discovery of the wreck of the Titanic, proved fruitless, Gillespie said.
A plane-shaped sonar image from elsewhere on the sea floor turned out to be a pile of rocks.
“I’d love to find that airplane. It ain’t gonna happen,” Gillespie said.
Pettigrew and his team are betting otherwise. To them, the multi-branched shape first noticed in a 2020 satellite image resembles an aircraft fuselage and wings.
They assert that the object, or part of it, has since been spotted in earlier aerial images of the island’s lagoon dating as far back as 1938.
Gillespie said he is certain that the object in question is actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like evergreen native to the island region, that washed into the lagoon.
“You can see the root ball. You can see the branches,” Gillespie said in the interview. “It’s a tree. People see what they want to see.”
‘Gas is running low’
The official US government view has long been that the Electra ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its refuelling destination of Howland island, another dot of land about 640km north-west of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner island.
Earhart was last seen taking off in her Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea en route to Gardner, about 4,000km to the east, during a multi-stage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world.
Definitive radio contact with the plane was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported “gas is running low”, followed by her final known transmission giving her geographical line of position.
The disappearance spawned the largest US government search ever undertaken for a lost aircraft, including a flyover of Gardner, but no trace of the Electra or its crew was found at the time.
The US$900,000 (S$1.1 million) Purdue mission, consisting of 17 people, plans to remain on Nikumaroro for five days before making the six-day return boat trip to the Kiribati capital, Tarawa, according to Schultz.
Purdue, based in West Lafayette, Indiana, would ultimately seek to bring back any bits of the Lockheed Electra that might be recovered.
Earhart was essentially a visiting faculty member at Purdue for two years as a women’s career counselor and adviser to the school’s aeronautics department. A Purdue research grant paid for development of the Electra, which she called her “flying laboratory”.
Purdue lawyer Schultz said if the plane were found, no artefacts would be removed from it on this trip. Any effort to extract the aircraft wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government, he said. REUTERS

Breadcrumb
Turkey social media ban for under-15s to take effect in November
Turkey on Saturday formally declared a ban on the use of social media for under-15s, scheduled to come into effect on 1 November.
It has joined a growing number of countries legislating to protect children and teenagers from the harmful effects of online platforms.
The official state journal published the decision following the adoption of a law by parliament in April.
It stipulates that social media providers must "take the necessary technical and administrative measures, including age verification, to implement" protections for young people.
"No service likely to produce an addictive effect in children may be offered."
Countries including Australia have introduced restrictions on social media for children, and others such as Britain and France are pushing to do the same.
They aim to protect children from digital risks such as screen addiction, lack of sleep, bullying and eating disorders.
Rights groups have complained of restrictions on freedom of expression in Turkey targeting LGBTQ communities, the media and the political opposition. Numerous social media accounts have been blocked in recent weeks.

20 Russian Officers Killed Following Precise Ukrainian Missile Attack in Donetsk

Minister: We have been pressuring Silmet to cut Russian raw material reliance
Unknown

Minister: We have been pressuring Silmet to cut Russian raw material reliance
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna says an Estonian rare earth processing firm must set a deadline for ending its use of Russian raw materials, suggesting early next year as a target.
Tsahkna said Estonia has been pressuring the Sillamäe-based NPM Silmet and its owner Neo Group to find alternative suppliers, and that a deadline must now be set.
The European Commission on Friday selected Silmet 2.0 as one of 46 new strategic projects aimed at securing the EU's supply of critical raw materials; Estonia this week pushed to exclude a Russian supplier to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package.
Tsahkna said the project must come with a firm deadline for ending the company's reliance on Russian raw materials.
"We will work with the European Commission to set a clear deadline for NPM Silmet to stop using Russian raw materials," he told told "Aktuaalne kaamera," adding: "We cannot allow an industry critical to Europe's security to remain dependent on supplies from an aggressor state."
Asked what that deadline might be, Tsahkna said: "We're talking, I think, optimistically about the beginning of next year, next year, which is a pretty fast pace."
Tsahkna confirmed the Foreign Ministry and the government have been pressuring Silmet and Neo Group. "There has actually been pressure, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Estonian government have also been cooperating more broadly with both Silmet and Neo Group," he went on.
He said attempts had been made to find new supply sources, including in Brazil, but that so far it had not been possible to end the dependence on Russia. The supply chain runs through the Solikamsk plant, owned by the Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom.
Tsahkna said Estonia had requested an exemption for the Rosatom-linked supply chain. "We demanded that this supply chain not be interrupted and that Silmet not cease its activities and that the entire European technology industry not be put under attack through this," he said. He added that Estonia has also supported sanctioning Rosatom, but does not see appetite for it in Europe.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said the decision is not in line with Estonian values. Asked about this, Tsahkna said the two issues should be separated: pressure on Russia through sanctions, and standing up for Estonian industry.
"I've talked a lot with the Prime Minister about this issue, and we agree that these steps need to be taken, no matter how unpleasant it is," Tsahkna said.
Ukraine has already sanctioned the factory. Tsahkna said he would meet Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha on Monday.
Earlier this week, Estonia successfully pushed to exclude a Russian company supplying rare earth metals to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package.
Background:
The European Commission on Friday selected Silmet 2.0 as one of 46 new strategic projects aimed at securing the EU's supply of critical raw materials and reducing reliance on third countries. NPM Silmet processes rare earth metals at its Sillamäe plant for use in electronics, medicine, automotive, aviation and defense industries across the EU.
Earlier this week, Estonia pushed to exclude a Russian company supplying rare earth metals to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package, which is awaiting formal approval. Estonia's representation in Brussels confirmed the request, saying the company supplies NPM Silmet with materials of strategic importance to Europe, and that Estonia will reconsider adding the company and an individual associated with it to the sanctions list next year.
EU ambassadors agreed on October 7 to sanctions targeting 743 individuals and 826 companies linked to Russia's military-industrial complex. The package awaits final approval by member states' foreign ministers and is expected to take effect in the coming days.

The country lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast zone of seismic and volcanic activity where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Iran’s cycling continue downward slide in Nagoya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:10:03 UTC
19:10:03 KST

Iran’s cycling continue downward slide in Nagoya
TEHRAN - Iran’s cycling team continued their disappointing decline at the Nagoya Asian Games, failing to deliver any encouraging results. A review of the past five editions of the Asian Games highlights a steady deterioration in the country’s performance, raising serious questions about the development and future direction of the sport in Iran.
The 2006 Asian Games in Doha marked one of the most successful campaigns in Iran’s cycling history. The national team collected four medals, including three silver and one bronze. Mehdi Sohrabi claimed silver in the men’s road race, while Iranian cyclists also secured podium finishes in various road and track events.
Four years later, at the 2010 Guangzhou Asian Games, Iran’s medal tally declined. Hossein Askari won bronze in the individual road time trial, while Iranian riders secured two additional bronze medals in team track events, bringing the country’s total to three medals, ana.ir reported.
At the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon, Arvin Moazemi Goudarzi delivered another significant result by winning silver in the men’s road race. In a closely contested competition against some of Asia’s leading riders, he secured second place and kept Iran competitive in road cycling.
However, despite that silver medal, Iran’s overall performance across other disciplines was not strong enough to suggest sustained progress. In track cycling, mountain biking and other events, the country’s representatives struggled to establish themselves among Asia’s leading contenders.
Iran’s decline became more pronounced at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, where the cycling team failed to win a medal despite competing in road, track and mountain bike events.
Farzad Shokri and Faranak Partoazar finished fourth in mountain bike cross-country, while Mohammad Ganjkhanlou also placed fourth in the track omnium. Hossein Zanjanian finished fifth in the men’s downhill, and Iran’s road cyclists were unable to reach the podium.
After several editions in which Iranian cyclists had won medals, Jakarta marked a disappointing campaign, with fourth-place finishes representing the team’s best results.
At the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, Iran managed to return to the podium, but only once. Ali Labib finished fourth in both the men’s road race and the track omnium, narrowly missing out on medals in both events. Partoazar, however, won bronze in the women’s mountain bike cross-country, securing Iran’s only cycling medal of the Games.
Although the overall medal haul remained modest, the fourth-place finishes in Jakarta and Hangzhou suggested that some Iranian cyclists were still capable of competing closely with their Asian rivals.
At the Nagoya Asian Games, however, the results in road cycling offered little cause for optimism. Mandana Dehghan finished 13th in the women’s individual time trial and 14th in the women’s road race. In the men’s individual time trial, Nabi Mirbagheri placed eighth.
Mirbagheri, Iran’s sole representative in the track omnium, also endured a difficult campaign, finishing 12th.
Ali Labib, who represented Iran at the Olympic Games, was left out of the squad for Nagoya following disagreements, resulting in Iran forfeiting one of its allocated places.
A review of Iran’s performances across five Asian Games editions, from Doha to Nagoya, reveals a troubling downward trajectory. The country won four medals in 2006, three in 2010, and a silver medal in Incheon. Iran then finished without a medal in Jakarta before claiming just one bronze in Hangzhou. In Nagoya, the cyclists remained well off the pace for a podium finish.
The repeated failure to contend for medals, alongside finishes ranging from fourth to 14th place, raises serious questions about the direction of Iranian cycling and the effectiveness of its development programs.
Iranian cycling needs far more than simply sending athletes to the Asian Games to reverse this decline. Rasoul Asadi, president of the Iran Cycling Federation, must address the team’s deteriorating results and provide a transparent explanation for why a sport with a history of Asian Games success has been unable to maintain its former standing in recent years.

Swiss drivers warned as wildlife collisions increase in autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:09:57 UTC
19:09:57 KST

Swiss drivers warned as wildlife collisions increase in autumn
The risk of collisions with wildlife on Swiss roads rises sharply in autumn. According to figures from an insurer, Eastern Switzerland and the Espace Mittelland record a particularly high number of such accidents.
Over the past five years, insurer Mobiliar has recorded more than 10,500 wildlife collisions. Analysis of data from 2021 to 2025 shows that the number of accidents in the final quarter of the year was around 12% above average. A further peak was recorded in April.
+ Hunters in eastern Switzerland shoot 3,500 deer
Eastern Switzerland hard hit
According to Mobiliar, accident rates vary considerably across the country. The highest rate was recorded in canton Thurgau, with 2.05 claims per 1,000 insured vehicles. Canton Graubünden ranked second with 1.85 claims per 1,000 vehicles, followed by canton Jura with 1.75. The national average stood at 1.16 wildlife collisions per 1,000 vehicles.
More
Record number of fawns saved by Swiss drone volunteers
Roe deer and red deer were involved in the majority of collisions, accounting for around 7,350 claims. Accidents involving foxes (1,020), badgers (900) and wild boars (510) were less common. Collisions with larger animals tended to be the most costly. According to Mobiliar, a collision with a wild boar resulted in an average claim of around CHF3,000 ($3,615), while accidents involving roe deer and red deer cost about CHF2,700 on average.
There are several reasons why wildlife collisions become more common in autumn. As the days grow shorter, more commuters are on the roads in the twilight hours, when many animals are most active. Other contributing factors include the deer rut, which begins in October, the disruption caused by the hunting season and animals searching for food ahead of winter.
Mobiliar warns Swiss drivers
Mobiliar is urging drivers to take extra care, particularly on rural roads and near woodland. Motorists should slow down if they see a wildlife warning sign. If an animal appears on the road, they should brake firmly but in a controlled manner and dip their headlights. Swerving to avoid an animal is strongly discouraged, as it often leads to more serious accidents than the collision itself.
If a collision does occur, drivers should stop, switch on their hazard lights and make the scene safe. The police or the local gamekeeper should then be notified. Under no circumstances should injured animals be approached or touched. Any damage should also be reported to the insurer as soon as possible.
More
Are hunters an endangered species in Switzerland?
According to figures from the environment ministry, road traffic accidents are the second most common known cause of death among large wild animals in Switzerland, after hunting.

Ireland has proposed cutting the EU budget by €159 billion – Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:08:50 EEST
19:08:50 KST

Ireland has proposed cutting the EU budget by €159 billion – Politico
Kyiv • UNN
Ireland proposes reducing the EU budget for 2028–2034 by €159 billion. Spending on competitiveness and aid will be cut the most.
Ireland has proposed cutting the EU budget for 2028–2034 by €159 billion compared with the European Commission’s initial plan. The proposal envisages cutting spending on external aid, competitiveness and the bloc’s administrative needs. Politico reports, UNN writes.
Details
The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is leading the negotiations, has proposed cutting the bloc’s overall budget for the 2028–2034 period by approximately 8% to meet the demands of the Germany-led camp, which is calling for substantial cuts.
The Irish negotiating document, or negobox, provides for cuts of €122 billion in current prices compared with the previous negobox presented by the Cypriot presidency in June. This sets the stage for tense discussions among the 27 EU leaders at next week’s summit.
The bloc is divided between countries pursuing austerity and demanding cuts of several hundred billion euros from the proposed budget of nearly €2 trillion, and the opposing camp of southern and eastern states, known as the “Friends of Cohesion,” which oppose cuts.
As a concession to the “Friends of Cohesion,” Ireland shielded subsidies for farmers and regional payments from any cuts; these account for half of the overall budget and are politically sensitive issues.
Instead, most of the cuts fell on external aid, which was reduced by €38 billion; competitiveness, which was cut by €75 billion; and EU administrative costs, which were reduced by €10 billion.
Dublin also scrapped a rainy-day reserve fund, known as the “EU shock-absorption mechanism,” which allowed the European Commission to raise funds to address unforeseen emergencies during the seven-year budget cycle.
However, Ireland’s proposal is unlikely to satisfy the “frugal” countries, which had warned against disproportionate cuts to funding for new pan-European priorities such as competitiveness, defense and development.
Germany and its allies criticized the previous Cypriot presidency of the Council for cutting only €32 billion in the latest package of proposals in June.
The 27 EU ambassadors will respond to this package of proposals at a meeting on Sunday, where they will also prepare for the leaders’ discussion scheduled for Thursday.
Governments are rushing to reach a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year, before elections in France, Poland and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.

Performer from China's Zhejiang Wu Opera Research Center performs on stage during a cultural event celebrating the 60th anniversary of Lesotho's independence in Maseru, Lesotho, Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Silence Charumbira/Xinhua)
MASERU, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Performers from China's Zhejiang Wu Opera Research Center received a standing ovation in Maseru on Friday evening at a cultural event celebrating the 60th anniversary of Lesotho's independence.
Hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Lesotho, the gala was attended by Lesotho's Queen 'Masenate Mohato Seeiso, Deputy Prime Minister Nthomeng Majara, and Speaker of the National Assembly Tlohang Sekhamane, alongside cabinet ministers, senior diplomats, and legislators.
The troupe from Jinhua City, east China's Zhejiang Province, mesmerized the audience with a six-part repertoire blending singing, dance, martial arts, and acrobatics.
The showcase featured theatrical classics including "Lyu Bu Tries the Horse," set during the Three Kingdoms period (220-280), in which actors depicted a warrior taming the legendary steed Red Hare through tumbling and intricate stagecraft, and "Dang Ma," set in the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127), which staged an intense duel arising from a mistaken identity.
The program also presented a solo on the huihu, a traditional Chinese bowed string instrument, a string-puppet performance featuring the legendary demon queller Zhong Kui, and concluded with "Golden Monkey Celebrates Spring," starring the iconic Monkey King, Sun Wukong.
Chinese Ambassador to Lesotho Yang Xiaokun said that Wu Opera, with a history spanning over 400 years, offers a vibrant window into traditional Chinese performing arts.
Noting that 2026 marks the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges, Yang emphasized that cultural performances serve as vital bridges for interpersonal connections and lasting friendship between the two nations.
Lesotho's Minister of Gender, Youth, and Social Development Pitso Lesaoana expressed appreciation for China's long-standing support in capacity building, human resource development, and technical assistance.
"The relationship between our two countries is not simply between governments and institutions; it is increasingly strengthened through meaningful connections between our peoples," Lesaoana said, calling for deeper bilateral cultural engagement.
Sekhamane commended China's impressive economic development, stressing that people-to-people exchanges form the foundation of strong bilateral ties, while expressing hope for more platforms to enable Basotho artists to perform in China. ■

Epidemiological investigations showed that all 21 patients reported engaging in high-risk sexual behaviour during the incubation period, including having sex with male strangers or multiple partners, and having sex without a condom, the centre said.

UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:00:55 UTC
19:00:55 KST

The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.
The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.
The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.
“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.
In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.
“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.
Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”
He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.
Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030.
“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.
“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.”
Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”
Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.
Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.
In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology.
Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”
“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.
“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.
Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”
He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”
Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards.
“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.
