Autism in boys and girls looks genetically similar, but early and late diagnoses don’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:00:36 UTC
19:00:36 KST

Autism is diagnosed more frequently in boys, who also tend to receive their diagnosis earlier than girls. A new study published in Behavior Genetics suggests that the genetic signal for early-diagnosed autism carries links to educational and cognitive traits that cannot be explained by biological sex. Whether the stronger ties between late-diagnosed autism and conditions like depression reflect diagnosis timing or sex, however, could not yet be untangled.
Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder that typically appears in childhood. It is characterized by difficulties with verbal and nonverbal communication, challenges in social interactions, and the presence of repetitive behaviors or highly restricted interests. Historically, autism has been diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys than in girls.
Along with this difference in diagnosis rates, boys and girls often differ in when they are identified. A 2012 study demonstrated that males typically receive autism diagnoses at a younger age than females. Because girls are frequently diagnosed later in life, scientists have wondered if outward traits associated with biological sex might be masking or confusing the traits associated with the timing of a diagnosis.
Recently, a 2025 study provided evidence that early-diagnosed autism and late-diagnosed autism possess distinctly different underlying genetic profiles. The authors of that earlier study concluded that sex differences were unlikely to account for these diverging pathways. To directly test this claim and untangle these overlapping categories, a team of researchers conducted a new investigation.
“Because boys are typically diagnosed earlier, we wanted to know whether those early-versus-late differences were partly explained by sex differences,” lead author Sophie Breunig, a PhD candidate in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience and the Institute for Behavioral Genetics at the University of Colorado at Boulder, told PsyPost. “If certain interpersonal, cognitive, and behavioral traits are more typical of autism in females, that knowledge could eventually help clinicians recognize autism in girls sooner and get them support earlier.”
The research team set out to determine whether the unique genetic profile of late-diagnosed autism is simply a byproduct of the fact that late-diagnosed individuals are more likely to be female, or if the age of diagnosis points to a genuinely different genetic pathway. They utilized a statistical approach known as genomic structural equation modeling. This technique allows scientists to analyze large sets of genetic data to identify how different traits and conditions share underlying genetic risk factors.
The authors analyzed genome-wide association study data, which scans the complete set of DNA across many people to find tiny genetic variations associated with a particular condition. They used genetic summary statistics for autism divided into four categories: early-diagnosed, late-diagnosed, male, and female. In the contributing studies, early diagnosis generally meant before about age 6 to 9, depending on the cohort, while late diagnosis meant age 10 or older.
The sample sizes comprised individuals of European genetic ancestry, including an effective sample size (a statistical estimate of how much data each group contributes) of 33,608 for early-diagnosed autism and 21,775 for late-diagnosed autism. The sex-specific data included 15,025 male cases and 4,845 female cases, each compared against more than 19,000 controls.
To explore how these four categories relate to other areas of human health and behavior, the researchers compared them against 68 external traits. These traits included psychiatric conditions like depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), cognitive abilities like memory and general intelligence, and social outcomes like loneliness and family satisfaction. The researchers first tested which of these traits were linked differently to male versus female autism, and to early- versus late-diagnosed autism. They then used multiple regression models to check whether differences tied to diagnosis timing could be explained by sex, and vice versa.
“In this study, we measured genetic correlations, which range from −1 to 1 and describe how much the genetic influences on two traits overlap across large groups of people,” Breunig explained. “These are population-level patterns and therefore can’t be used to diagnose or predict anything about an individual person. Their value is in showing that people who share a diagnosis, such as autism, aren’t all the same. Paying attention to subgroups, like biological sex or whether they were diagnosed earlier or later in life, may eventually help clinicians know what to look for and how to tailor support.”
When looking at biological sex, the researchers found that the genetic profiles of male and female autism were highly similar, sharing a genetic correlation of 0.81. Out of the 68 external traits tested, only two showed distinctly different associations based on sex. Anorexia nervosa shared a stronger genetic overlap with female autism, while a tendency toward speeding in traffic was negatively associated with female autism but not male autism.
The finding that common genetic variants for autism are highly similar between sexes adds nuance to other recent research. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that the overall heritability of autism was higher in boys (about 87 percent) than in girls (about 76 percent). However, higher heritability in boys is a different question from whether the exact same genetic influences are involved, and that earlier study analyzed family-based registry data rather than common genetic variants across the broader population.
In contrast to the strong similarities between sexes, early- and late-diagnosed autism showed much less genetic overlap in the new study, with a genetic correlation of 0.42. Thirty-one of the tested external traits displayed diverging genetic associations depending on when the autism diagnosis occurred. Late-diagnosed autism was more strongly linked to an increased psychiatric burden, showing greater genetic overlap with major depressive disorder, PTSD, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
Late diagnosis was also linked to adverse social outcomes, such as higher levels of loneliness and lower satisfaction with friendships and family relationships. Early-diagnosed autism, on the other hand, showed stronger genetic links to education and certain cognitive tests, though in different directions. It shared more genetic overlap with higher educational attainment than late-diagnosed autism did, but it was also genetically linked to lower performance on a memory test and a symbol-matching task that measures processing speed. Both subtypes showed similar positive genetic overlap with general intelligence.
When the researchers adjusted for biological sex, the most distinctive associations of early-diagnosed autism held up and even grew stronger, including its links to the parts of educational attainment not explained by cognitive ability and to a symbol-matching task. This suggests the early-diagnosed profile is not simply a byproduct of the large number of boys diagnosed early. Similarly, when the models were adjusted to account for early diagnosis, the two female-specific links to anorexia and a lower tendency for speeding also remained robust. The same test could not be run for late-diagnosed autism, whose genetic signal was almost identical to that of male autism (a correlation of 0.99) and very similar to that of female autism (0.91).
“Because girls tend to be diagnosed later, we checked whether these early-versus-late differences were explained by sex differences,” Breunig noted. “For the early-diagnosed group, they weren’t and we can’t tell yet for the late-diagnosed group. The late-diagnosed genetic signal overlapped so much with both male and female autism that our analyses couldn’t separate them.”
The team also ran follow-up analyses grouping major depressive disorder, anxiety, and PTSD into a single general category representing internal emotional distress. They found that female autism and late-diagnosed autism both shared stronger genetic overlap with this distress factor, though the gap between female and male autism was slight and only just met the study’s statistical threshold, so it awaits confirmation.
When the researchers factored this general emotional distress into their models, the genetic link between late-diagnosed autism and adult ADHD dropped from 0.42 to near zero; early-diagnosed autism had shown almost no link to begin with. This indicates that the connection between autism and adult ADHD might actually be driven by general psychiatric distress rather than overlapping pathways specific to autism.
Accounting for this distress factor also shrank autism’s genetic overlap with ADHD far more for female autism (from 0.39 to 0.07) than for male autism (from 0.51 to 0.23). “The surprising part was that when we statistically removed that shared signal, we saw that in females, much more of the genetic overlap between autism and ADHD was explained by internalizing problems than in males,” Breunig said. “This suggests that the link between autism and ADHD in girls and women may operate through broader emotional distress.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. The study relied exclusively on genetic data from individuals of European ancestry. Because genetic frequencies and environmental interactions can vary across populations, these findings might not fully apply to people of other ancestral backgrounds. The researchers also note that “male” and “female” in this dataset refer to sex assigned at birth.
In addition, because late-diagnosed autism was so genetically similar to both male and female autism, the researchers could not test whether its stronger links to depression, PTSD, and other psychiatric conditions reflect diagnosis timing or sex. The authors advise treating claims that late-diagnosed autism carries its own distinct psychiatric overlap as tentative until larger studies are available.
“It is also worth noting that late-diagnosed autism is still autism,” Breunig pointed out. “While it was genetically not very related to earlier diagnosed autism, it was about as closely related to autism overall as early-diagnosed autism was. Some of its extra overlap with other conditions may reflect the challenges of diagnosing autism in adulthood, when other conditions can mask or mimic it.”
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to build on this framework. “We would like to repeat these analyses as larger datasets become available to fully separate the effects of sex and age at diagnosis,” Breunig added. “We also want to study other traits, like depression or ADHD, separately in males and females, since sex differences can be missed in large genomic studies where everyone is combined.”
The study, “Uncovering the Role of Biological Sex in the Divergent Genetic Profiles of Early and Late-Diagnosed Autism,” was authored by Sophie Breunig, Lukas Schaffer, Jeremy Lawrence, Alexander Sheppard, and Andrew Grotzinger.

Paternity Leave Is More Than a Perk. It Builds a Baby’s Brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

We often treat paternity leave like a company perk—something HR lists next to the gym stipend and the 401k match. The research says we are wrong about that categorization. Paternity leave should be part of routine medical care during this stage of life: interventions we already agree are worth investing in because the return on investment continues years later in a child’s brain.
The U.S. is one of the only wealthy nations on Earth with no federal guarantee of paid paternity leave. The data on the impact of those first months on a child’s brain suggest we have been treating a critical developmental window like a scheduling inconvenience.
Employers and employees basically agree on a need to strive for work-life balance. And while the gender equity argument is used to both advance and stymie conversations about paternity leave, it is more than a values fight. It turns out that paternity leave and a father’s engagement during infancy is associated with better cognitive, social, and emotional regulation outcomes for the child that can be measured.
In a review of existing fatherhood research, Sarah Schoppe-Sullivan, a researcher at the Ohio State University, highlighted better peer relationships, higher intelligence test scores, greater math and language readiness and development, and more secure attachment formation among children who experience positive and sustained father involvement compared to those who don’t. Though these trends are correlational, these father-involvement gains show up on report cards as early as preschool and can continue into adulthood.
One possible avenue through which these benefits pass from father to child is the quality of play. Canadian researcher Daniel Paquette observed that father’s play often includes excitement, surprise, awe, and temporary shock and disruption for children, and this kind of interaction is the foundation for crucial developmental skills like risk-taking, personal efficacy, and self-advocacy.
Children who have more consistent positive engagement with their fathers have better outcomes across some of the main child mental-health domains, including anxiety, depression, and behavioral problems. Paternity leave creates space for and helps develop active involvement like physical play, showing up to school events, and careful listening to a child, and these are connected to healthy child development. Secure attachment, more prosocial sibling interactions, and better social competence result in other benefits, like self-regulation. This is a hallmark indicator of school readiness and success, and here, too, father engagement pays dividends. What looks like fathers rough-housing, developmentally speaking, is training for children to build capacity for self-regulation, managing arousal, and controlling impulses and emotions in real time.
Early literacy and home-visiting programs like Head Start are widely celebrated for similar child development outcomes, but father engagement has additional social, developmental, and familial benefits including improved parenting relationships. Moreover, other countries have found success in persuading more fathers to take paid paternity leave after shifting to a “use-it-or-lose-it” policy, by which a portion of paid parental leave is reserved exclusively for fathers and is non-transferable to the mother. Compared to earlier trends dating back to the early 2000s, paid paternal leave uptake has steadily increased; in Iceland, just 15% of fathers took leave in 1998, while more than over 80% did in 2002. Spain recorded a 400% increase from 2000 to 2007. Also in 2007, after Germany replaced their flat-rate leave pay with an income-based benefit (i.e., 67% of net earnings) and reserved two “use-it-or-lose-it” months for fathers, uptake of parental leave increased from 3.5% in 2006 to 24.8% in 2021.
The U.S. is lagging far behind in this area. Where paternity leave does exist, it is often unpaid and unguaranteed, and mothers for instance, cannot transfer a portion of their allotted maternity leave to the father to allow him to take extra time off. This means that many fathers do not use this critical child development and family resource. Most new fathers are back at their desk within a week of their child’s birth, right as the research suggests their presence does some of its most consequential work.
We can increase the uptake of this resource with federal paid leave legislation, which will improve access to leave for all fathers. This would have the potential to lead to widespread positive cognitive, academic, and emotional development of children.
Employers need not wait on legislation. They can apply the “use-it-or-lose” approach at their companies in the best interest of their employees.
Fathers’ access to and use of paternity leave is not a question of available employment benefits. It is a developmental one, and we already know how to answer development questions. We don’t treat prenatal care as a “nice perk.” We should not be treating the first months of a father’s presence like that, either.

Allies Press Greece, Spain for Expiring Patriot Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

NATO and EU officials are lobbying Greece and Spain to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles nearing the end of their operational shelf life to Ukraine, The Telegraph reported.
Athens and Madrid hold some of Europe’s largest national inventories of Patriot PAC-2 interceptors, weapons that Ukrainian defense planners urgently require to protect urban population centers and energy infrastructure from Russian ballistic and cruise missile strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
President Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated that Ukrainian forces require between 300 and 360 Patriot interceptors to withstand anticipated winter bombardments.
According to military records cited by The Telegraph, Greece holds at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose certified 23-year operational lifespan is approaching expiration. While the exact quantity held in Spanish military depots remains classified, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed last month that Madrid would deliver five interceptors to Kyiv.
Allied defense coordinators argue that transferring aging munitions before they surpass statutory shelf limits represents a pragmatic solution for both donor nations and Ukraine.
Patriot interceptors carry manufacturer-guaranteed shelf lives during which performance is certified; once that operational window elapses, the missiles must undergo expensive and logistically intensive factory recertifications.
Medvedev Warns Against Travel to Europe, Claims It Is ‘Targeting Russians’
“We know that some countries have interceptor missiles that will expire soon,” EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas said during multilateral consultations in Ireland last month. “So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine.”
Global Patriot shortfalls and US-Iran conflict
The diplomatic initiative to unlock southern European stockpiles arrives as Western defense planners confront severe bottlenecks in interceptor manufacturing, compounded by ongoing military operations involving the United States in the Middle East.
Ukraine historically relies on a NATO-coordinated framework for roughly 95 percent of its Patriot interceptors, a mechanism under which European partner governments pool financial resources to purchase replacement missiles directly from American production lines.
However, heavy expenditure of surface-to-air missiles during the US conflict with Iran has precipitated a severe global inventory deficit.
US military stockpiles of Patriot missiles have fallen to fewer than 1,700 units, fueling doubts among European allies regarding the Pentagon’s willingness to release additional interceptors from strategic reserves while active combat operations in the Middle East continue.
With US supply lines backlogged by multi-year production lead times, Western defense coordinators have intensified efforts to identify existing surface-to-air missiles stored within European arsenals that can be deployed to Ukrainian batteries immediately without degrading the conventional defense readiness of donor nations.
Eastern flank reinforcement
The scramble to source interceptors for Ukraine coincides with expanding NATO deployments to protect the primary logistical conduits funneling Western military assistance across the Ukrainian border.
On Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Swedish government announced that Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense battery alongside approximately 100 military personnel to southeastern Poland in December.
The Swedish detachment, drawn from the Air Defence Regiment with support from the Blekinge Air Wing, will be stationed around Rzeszów, the principal transit hub through which international military aid and humanitarian cargo enter Ukraine.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson confirmed that the system – designated domestically as Air Defence System 103 – will operate under NATO Air Command as part of the alliance’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense network through the end of 2026, with planning underway to extend the mission into 2027.
The ground battery supplements Swedish JAS 39 Gripen multirole fighters that integrated into NATO air policing over Poland earlier in October.
The allied mission in Rzeszów aligns with broader moves by Warsaw to reinforce Poland’s eastern boundary, including the positioning of Polish Patriot units in the Lublin region to deter airspace incursions as Russian standoff strikes continue along the Ukrainian frontier.

Commentary: Public executions are the work of tyrants. Now, the U.S. is joining in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Public executions are the work of tyrants. Now, the U.S. is joining in
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Iran. Afghanistan. North Korea. Somalia. And now, the United States.
If Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is to be believed, America will soon gain the dubious distinction of joining the only four countries on the globe that carry out executions in public.
Hegseth said Thursday that he wanted the execution of convicted F.t Hood shooter, Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, to be available for public viewing.
“It was a radical Islamist attack ... so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be,” Hegseth said in an interview with far-right political activist Jack Posobiec. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it’s public. Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
The execution is scheduled to be live streamed Dec. 3 from the same military base where Hasan opened fire in 2009, killing 13 and wounding 32.
A gunman opened fire at the Fort Hood military base near Killeen, Texas on Wednesday, April 2, 2014.
The planned public display is, in a word, barbaric. It’s the archaic act of tyrannical monarchies, staged in the shadow of a looming tower or in the town square. The Taliban and ISIS were big on public executions. So was Nazi Germany. They were either fighting a war on their own soil or had just come out of one. It’s a poor excuse, but the U.S. military can’t even point to that as justification for the animalistic intention of broadcasting a state-sanctioned murder.
Should plans for the livestream of Hasan’s killing become a reality, our peers will be countries that the U.S. has long held up as the worst of the worst. Oppressive “shithole” countries, to use a Trump term, that wield intimidation and the threat of death to keep their people in line.
Iran carries out its hangings in public squares, typically using truck-mounted cranes as makeshift gallows. The Taliban exacts its death penalty in sports arenas. Amnesty International reports that North Korea forced local residents, students and workers to watch the 2008 execution of 13 women and two men as a deterrent. Their crime? Attempting to flee to China.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist and a Muslim, opened fire on dozens of his fellow soldiers as they were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He was reportedly angry about the U.S. involvement in the region and in Iraq. In court, prosecutors argued that he was radicalized online and motivated by an ideology that called for “jihad duty.”
His crimes were horrific, and he should be punished. Whether you believe in the death penalty or not (I do not), turning his execution into a morbid form of entertainment — or a warning to never do what he did — would mark a new low for this country.
And we are pretty low as it is. On Thursday, ICE agents in civilian clothing fired at least seven rounds, at 4 p.m. on a busy Manhattan street, into a car with a 5-year-old boy inside. They hit the driver, who survived, and by some act of god missed the child.
Federal immigration agents have shot at least 21 people, killing seven, since President Trump returned to office less than two years ago with the promise of cracking down on crime and making the country safer via mass deportations. The public execution of Hasan, who is a U.S. citizen, is being sold as part of that tough-on-crime initiative. Hegseth himself said the public killing is meant as a deterrent.
The idea that keeping a population safe requires removing the guardrails of civilized society is absurd, though despots throughout history would have us believe otherwise.
If Hasan’s death is televised, it will be the nation’s first government-sanctioned execution carried out in public since 1939. It will be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 and the first military death by firing squad, or “musketry,” since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
The Army had planned a very different type of execution for Hasan. ABC News reported that officials were preparing to use lethal injection if Trump authorized the execution of one of the four prisoners on the service’s death row.
Trump’s approval of Hasan’s execution last Friday came days after a botched lethal-injection execution in Tennessee. Christa Pike, who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder she committed as a teenager, survived despite being injected with two supposedly lethal doses. She is now said to be lucid and even walking.
Hasan, who is partially paralyzed and uses a wheelchair after being shot by officers who were responding to the Ft. Hood attack, will be put to death in a more dramatic fashion — and for everyone to see.
“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” Oklahoma City Archbishop Paul Coakley said in a statement Friday. “The word of God exhorts us: ‘do not repay anyone evil for evil’ (Romans 12:17).”
A few congressional Republicans even broke ranks with their party and criticized Hegseth’s plans for the livestream. Sen. John Curtis of Utah posted on X that “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite.”
There is no reason the U.S. should stoop to the barbarism of public executions. It’s ghoulish, inhumane and a marker of tyrannical rule. Do we really want to join Iran, Afghanistan, North Korea and Somalia in the global hall of shame?

USA Lifted Sanctions on Diesel Fuel Exports From Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:57:03 UTC
18:57:03 KST

The U.S. has lifted sanctions on diesel fuel exports from Russia following a statement by U.S. President Donald Trump announcing an agreement to export 4.8 million metric tons of fuel ‘on a short-term basis.’
This was revealed in an announcement by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
The document permits transactions related to the sale, delivery, unloading, and import of diesel fuel of Russian origin, which are otherwise prohibited under U.S. sanctions regimes. The authorization is valid until 12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time on April 7, 2027.
Donald Trump stated that he had reached an agreement with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin on the supply of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets. According to him, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons, another 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million metric tons immediately thereafter.
Russia is subsequently expected to supply another 3 million metric tons of diesel fuel on a tight schedule, subject to the capacity of its oil refineries.
“Thanks to our complete control over the Strait of Hormuz and this wonderful news regarding Russian energy resources, diesel fuel prices for Americans—and indeed for the whole world—will drop rapidly and significantly,” said U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has already stated in a comment to TASS that Russia is immediately beginning to lift restrictions on diesel fuel exports ahead of schedule.
According to a September report by the International Energy Agency (IEA), the global diesel market suffered significant supply losses due to the war with Iran, shipping restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz, and, to a lesser extent, strikes on Russian refineries.
In August, total net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Persian Gulf countries and Russia were approximately 215,000 metric tons per day lower than in February. This amounts to 6.7 million metric tons for a 31-day month. Other suppliers only partially offset these losses.
According to IEA data, the Persian Gulf countries accounted for a reduction of 156,000 metric tons per day in exports, while Russia accounted for 59,000 metric tons per day—representing approximately 73% and 27% of total losses, respectively. On a monthly basis, this amounts to 4.8 million and 1.8 million metric tons.
The shipments announced by Trump—300,000 metric tons, another 500,000 metric tons in November, 1 million metric tons thereafter, and subsequently another 3 million metric tons—represent only a small fraction of the losses caused by the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.
For example, 4.8 million metric tons is roughly equivalent to a one-month reduction in supplies from the Persian Gulf countries. The first 300,000 metric tons represents only 1.81 days’ worth of supply.

3 in 5 AI models fail terrorism safety tests: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:54:38 UTC
18:54:38 KST

Merve Berker
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Three in five artificial intelligence (AI) models have failed terrorism safety tests, with models stripped of safeguards consistently providing potentially dangerous information, according to research reported by CBC News on Friday.
The study, conducted by the UK-based nonprofit Tech Against Terrorism, evaluated more than 130 AI models using hundreds of requests resembling those a terrorist planning an attack might submit.
Researchers found that models modified through a process known as "abliteration," which removes safety safeguards, failed every test.
Meta's Llama 3.1 8B model scored 97 out of 100 on the organization's safety benchmark before modification, compared with approximately three afterward.
Researchers said the modified model provided detailed responses to requests involving attacks, terrorist financing and radicalization, while its original version refused such requests.
"Understandably, there's concern about loss of control, existential risk of AI," said Adam Hadley, founder and executive director of Tech Against Terrorism.
"The thing is actually, this has already happened because a lot of these open models have already been broken — it's just no one's noticed yet."
The organization found more than 29,000 repositories advertising uncensored or unprotected AI models on Hugging Face as of late last month.
Hugging Face said it regularly moderates content violating its policies but warned that some recommendations in the report could undermine open research.
Meta said its models undergo safety evaluations and that its policies prohibit harmful or illegal uses.
The report found no evidence of terrorist or extremist groups using the tested models, apart from one extremist chatbot identified by researchers.
Tech Against Terrorism recommended independent safety benchmarks, stronger protections against safeguard removal and restrictions on distributing modified models.
"This idea that we can't have safety and progress, I think, is false," Hadley said.

The Latvian Saeima has so far not supported amendments on permanent residence permits for Ukrainians
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:48:50 EEST
18:48:50 KST

The Latvian Saeima has so far not supported amendments on permanent residence permits for Ukrainians
Kyiv • UNN
A committee of the Latvian Saeima postponed consideration of amendments on simplified permanent residence permits for Ukrainians. A decision is expected after the Ministry of Finance issues its opinion.
The Saeima Committee on Defense, Internal Affairs and Corruption Prevention has so far not supported, at first reading, further advancement of amendments to the law on support for the civilian population of Ukraine in Latvia, which provide for a special procedure for obtaining a permanent residence permit in Latvia for Ukrainian citizens. Delfi reports, according to UNN.
The committee decided not to submit the bill for further consideration for now, as it is necessary to obtain an opinion from the Ministry of Finance on the possible impact of the proposed changes on the state budget. The committee is expected to return to consideration of the amendments next week
Under the bill, Ukrainian citizens who hold only Ukrainian citizenship and have obtained or currently have temporary protection in Latvia will be able to apply for a permanent residence permit under specially established conditions.
At the same time, the current regulations provide for refusing to grant a permanent residence permit to individuals who previously received temporary protection in Latvia.
The proposed amendments stipulate that the five-year period of residence may also include the period during which a person stayed in Latvia on the basis of a long-term visa or residence permit.
It is also planned to establish special requirements regarding the availability of sufficient funds for subsistence.
Men will also be required to provide confirmation from the competent Ukrainian authorities that they are exempt from conscription for military service in the event of mobilization.
The authors of the bill believe that the proposed changes will provide Ukrainians with greater legal certainty regarding their future status in Latvia.

On October 8, the period of temporary protection for Ukrainian refugees in Germany was extended until March 2028.

Memory for 100,000 killed by Nazis: Germany recognizes special responsibility to Ukraine and links it to support against Russia’s war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:48:21 UTC
18:48:21 KST

The German Bundestag has made a historic decision, officially recognizing Germany’s special responsibility to Ukraine for the crimes of Nazism. On 9 October, it adopted two resolutions ahead of the 85th anniversary of the Babyn Yar massacre and linked that responsibility to Germany’s current help for Ukraine amid Russian aggression, Oleksii Makeiev, Ukraine’s ambassador to Berlin, says.
Babyn Yar in Kyiv became one of Europe’s largest sites of the mass murder of Jews during the Holocaust, where more than 100,000 people were killed over two years of Nazi occupation. Germany now casts a debt from that war as a moral duty to help defend Kyiv against Russia today.
Both motions stress the importance of researching Nazi crimes in Ukraine and preserving the memory of their victims. One came from the governing CDU/CSU and SPD parties, the other from the opposition Greens, a rare alignment of coalition and opposition on a single theme.
“The situation is unique: two motions on this subject were approved at once, from the coalition and the opposition. By the usual parliamentary logic, that should not happen,” Makeiev says.
A debt turned into support for Kyiv
The coalition motion backs research and documentation of Nazi crimes in Ukraine and closer work among German, Ukrainian, and other European archives and memorial institutions. It also calls for countering antisemitism, racism, and historical revisionism, and for continued political, economic, financial, humanitarian, and military support for Ukraine.
Makeiev says he felt a sense of deja vu watching the debate from the visitors’ gallery.
“I was in that same gallery in the fall of 2022. I saw how German democratic parliamentary groups can demonstrate unity on what matters most. At that time, the Bundestag recognized the Holodomor of 1932–1933 as genocide,” he adds.
A clause on the deported children
A separate point of the resolution concerns Ukrainian children and teenagers who Russia has illegally taken from Ukraine. The document calls for efforts to return about 20,000 of them to their parents or relatives, folding the issue into Germany’s wider policy toward Ukraine.
The director of the Babyn Yar National Historical and Memorial Preserve, Rosa Tapanova, considers the Bundestag’s decision an important step toward re-examining the shared history of Ukraine and Germany and overcoming distortions of historical memory propagated for decades by the Soviet authorities and now being exploited by Russia.
“The Bundestag’s decision marked an important step toward Germany’s recognition of its historical responsibility toward Ukraine," she says.
The Bundestag’s decision and the participation of German representatives in commemorative events underscore the importance of continued Ukrainian-German dialogue. For the Babyn Yar National Historical and Memorial Preserve, this work encompasses historical research, the documentation of testimonies, educational and memorial projects, and international cooperation.

Swiss consumers keep spending despite rising prices
Despite rising prices, consumer spending habits remain unchanged in Switzerland.
In September, the PostFinance consumption indicator, based on card payments made by its 2.4 million customers, rose by 0.9% compared with the same period in 2025. The increase was 0.8% in August, 1.1% in July and 1.8% in June.
More
Why Switzerland has such low interest rates
“Consumer spending in Switzerland continues to grow, although at a slightly slower pace than over the summer,” analysts at PostFinance said in a recent report.
With the holiday season now over, spending on travel and social activities has fallen back, as reflected in a fall in restaurant visits both in Switzerland and abroad. By contrast, consumers spent significantly more on cosmetics and beauty treatments.
More
Why Switzerland’s fuel stockpiles are for Swiss use only
“Overall, consumer spending remains resilient despite the added pressure on household budgets from the recent rise in inflation,” PostFinance analysts concluded.

Beijing announces jobs initiative amid AI impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:47:30 UTC
18:47:30 KST

In China's latest effort to adapt its workforce to rapid technological changes, a senior official on Saturday announced an initiative to promote employment in response to artificial intelligence development.
Li Zhong, vice minister of human resources and social security, said China would actively address the impact of AI and other emerging technologies on employment, promoting the responsible development of technology and bolstering quality employment.
Adapting to AI-driven changes has become an increasingly prominent part of China's employment policy. Several official documents issued this year have outlined measures to harness technological advances while supporting employment.
The 2026 government work report vowed to take more effective measures to facilitate employment and entrepreneurship through better adaptation to the development of AI technologies.
A five-year plan on implementing the employment-first strategy also identified promoting employment amid AI advances as a key task, calling for creating jobs through AI applications and tapping the potential in traditional sectors.
AI is already reshaping China's economy and transforming its labour market, with demand growing for workers equipped with specialised technical skills.
According to Maimai, a networking and recruitment platform, the number of new AI-related job postings in the new economy on the platform rose about 789 percent, year on year, from January to July. 
Online job-seeking platform Zhaopin also said in a report that demand was particularly strong for AI engineers, including those working in automotive manufacturing and intelligent driving.
China's core AI industry has exceeded 1.2 trillion yuan in scale, with more than 6,200 enterprises operating in the sector. AI adoption rate across key industries has surpassed 80 percent.
Beyond AI, China is also seeking to generate employment opportunities by developing emerging and future industries.
During the past five years, China introduced 72 new occupations, including AI trainers and carbon emissions managers, incorporating them into the country's official occupational classification system. Since the beginning of 2026, authorities have announced another 11 new occupations.
Wu Liduo, an official of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security, said the ministry would establish a regular mechanism for identifying new occupations, focusing on emerging fields such as AI, the digital economy, green and low-carbon development, and modern services.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the ministry plans to formulate or revise more than 200 national occupational standards, Wu said. (Xinhua)

76 people detained in Poland following attacks at educational institutions
Kyiv • UNN
Polish police inspected nearly 50,000 educational institutions following attacks and a possible attack. A total of 231 incidents were recorded.
Large-scale police operations are ongoing in Poland following attacks at schools in Ostrołęka and Leszczydół-Nowiny, as well as the prevention of a potential attack in Sierpc. As of Saturday morning, law enforcement officers had inspected nearly 50,000 educational institutions and detained 76 people. Polsat News reports this, writes UNN.
Details
On Saturday morning, police published a statement about the operation launched following attacks at schools in Ostrołęka and near Wyszków, as well as the prevention of a potential attack in Sierpc.
Across Poland, measures aimed at ensuring the safety of children, young people, and all employees of educational institutions are ongoing.
As of 6:00 a.m., 231 incidents had been recorded, in connection with which law enforcement officers are taking action due to a reasonable suspicion that an offense has been committed.
Nearly 50,000 institutions have now been inspected and 76 people detained.
Police officers are working not only to establish the circumstances of the aforementioned incidents, but also continue to monitor the internet around the clock and respond to every report
Attacks at schools in Ostrołęka and Leszczydół-Nowiny
On Thursday, at a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny (Masovian Voivodeship), a 15-year-old teenager attacked three people, including a 37-year-old employee of the institution. The woman died.
The day before, at Vocational School Complex No. 4 in Ostrołęka, a 19-year-old man attacked nine people with a knife, including five students and two teachers. He also had a backpack containing a homemade explosive device.
Police also prevented a potential attack at a school in Sierpc. The detained 17-year-old teenager, who had threatened that he would "do something bad," was charged and remanded in custody for two months.

Suspect killed after 13 kindergarteners taken hostage, beaten in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:45:14 UTC
18:45:14 KST

Suspect killed after 13 kindergarteners taken hostage, beaten in Brazil
Man spreads flammable liquid in a room with 13 children while holding a lighter as police try to negotiate.
Brazil police rescue 13 children taken hostage at kindergarten
Brazilian police have rescued 13 children who had been taken hostage at a kindergarten in the southern city of Curitiba after killing the suspect, who threatened to set fire to the building, according to officials.
At least one of the children was wounded in Friday’s incident, the commander of the military police special forces unit in Parana state, Alexandre Lopes Dias, told reporters without elaborating on who or what injured the child.
Parana police spokesperson Leticia Martins told journalists outside the kindergarten that the suspect jumped the gate on Friday, broke into a classroom and held 13 children hostage.
He then spread a flammable substance in the room and held a lighter in his hand. He was carrying a knife and also what was initially believed to be a firearm, but later was found to be fake.
“Our negotiating teams were in place but saw no alternative but to neutralise him,” said Martins, who did not specify whether the suspect had expressed a specific reason for his actions.
The incident took place in the neighbourhood of Sao Braz in Curitiba, a city of 1.8 million residents located 400km (250 miles) south of Sao Paulo.
Lopes Dias told reporters the suspect was identified as a man who suffered from schizophrenia, but he did not reveal the man’s identity or how he was killed.
“During the entire negotiation, he stayed with all the children around him and one on his lap,” the police official said.
Children beaten
Talks lasted up to three hours. The children became agitated, and the attacker started hitting them, Lopes Dias told reporters.
“Once we realised that the kids were becoming increasingly upset and that the attacker started assaulting them physically, we opted for a tactical intervention to avoid a greater problem,” he explained.
Local media showed footage of tearful parents outside the school waiting for information as the negotiations between the suspect and police were ongoing. Minutes after what local media described as flash bangs, officers emerged carrying some of the children outside.
“We entered the classroom using a very tactical approach with little risk for the children,” Lopes Dias added.
Curitiba Mayor Eduardo Pimentel wrote on Instagram: “The 13 children are alive and safe! After anguishing and tense moments, this is the news we were all waiting for.”
Brazil in recent years has experienced multiple attacks on schools. In April 2023, a man killed four children with an axe at a day care in Blumenau, also in southern Brazil.
Curitiba City Hall said in a statement that the children and school staffers would receive psychological support.

Rosatom Says it Wins Tribunal Ruling in Finnish Nuclear Plant Dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:45:05 UTC
18:45:05 KST

Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom said on Saturday that an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal had ruled in its favour in a long-running dispute with Finnish utility Fennovoima over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project.
Rosatom said the tribunal found that Fennovoima had unlawfully terminated the contract for the construction of the planned plant in northern Finland in 2022.
The parties have been locked in legal disputes since Fennovoima scrapped the 7 billion euro ($7.8 billion) project in May 2022, citing significant delays and political risks shortly after Russia launched its conflict in Ukraine.
Rosatom said the tribunal found that the project was making good progress when it was terminated.
"Today's victory is important, but not final. We will continue to prove that we are right regarding the Finnish project in courts of various instances," Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said in a statement.
Fennovoima did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The contract to build the 1.2 gigawatt plant was signed in 2013 with Fennovoima, a consortium in which Finnish stakeholders including Fortum, Outokumpu and SSAB originally controlled two thirds through a joint venture, and the Russian side held one third.
After the project's termination, Fennovoima wound down its operations and is primarily engaged in legal proceedings.

Bulgarian Health Fund Finds More Than €1 Million in Pharmacy Irregularities
Bulgaria’s National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) has identified violations involving more than €1 million in funds received without legal grounds during coordinated inspections of 21 pharmacies across 12 regions, the fund announced.
The inspections were carried out jointly by the NHIF, the State Agency for National Security (SANS), the Economic Police at the Ministry of Interior, and the Ministry of Health. The irregularities involved dispensed medicines for which the national drug number did not match the product code, known as the Global Trade Item Number (GTIN).
Following the findings, the NHIF has requested additional technical information from Information Services AD (IS) for 2025.
Measures are also being coordinated with IS, the Bulgarian Pharmaceutical Union, and marketing authorization holders to introduce real-time checks and prevent similar cases in the future.
The NHIF said it would continue strengthening its oversight and take the necessary steps to ensure that public funds are spent properly and in accordance with the law.

- The EU said China agreed to “moderate” hybrid vehicle exports, which could cut shipments by more than half over four years, easing pressure on European carmakers.
- The talks also covered electric vehicles and rare earth supplies, with both sides pledging more work on shared trade issues and another meeting set for March.
AI generated
BEIJING – China and the European Union can avoid “escalation” in various contentious disputes, Beijing said on Oct 10, as worries of a damaging trade war simmer.
Discussions earlier in October in Beijing between Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and EU counterpart Maros Sefcovic were “successful” and marked “a new starting point”, China’s commerce ministry said in an online statement.
“The outcomes and consensus reached by both sides fully demonstrate that China and the EU have both the willingness and the wisdom to manage and properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation, and to effectively avoid escalation of frictions,” it said.
Sefcovic said on Oct 9 after the conclusion of two-day talks that Beijing had agreed to “moderate” exports of hybrid vehicles to the 27-nation bloc, where local carmakers are increasingly feeling pressure from Chinese competitors.
The EU trade chief told reporters that the deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export (of hybrids) by more than a half”, based on projections over a four-year period.
Shipments of vehicles to the EU are among the most controversial in China’s mounting trade surplus with the bloc that now reaches around €1 billion (S$1.43 billion) every day.
Many in Europe accuse China of unfair trade practices, including supporting firms with huge subsidies, price dumping and currency manipulation.
Exacerbating the issue is a persistent demand slump in China’s domestic economy, prompting manufacturers to seek alternative markets abroad.
A joint statement published on Oct 9 said the two sides had “reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles in a (World Trade Organisation) compliant manner”, describing the discussions as “intensive”.
Beijing’s commerce ministry said on Oct 10 that the talks included “in-depth discussions on trade in electric vehicles and hybrid vehicles, avoiding escalation of the situation and effectively safeguarding the practical export interests of Chinese enterprises”.
The talks also saw China commit to continue the supply of vital items including rare earth minerals to the EU – a topic closely followed since Beijing’s introduction of export licence requirements in 2025.
“Both sides will continue to step up work on important economic and trade issues of common concern,” Beijing’s commerce ministry said, adding that the next such meeting will be held in March. AFP

Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
October 10, 2026
Taiwan plans to boost defense spending to deter war, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday, as China steps up military pressure to assert its claim over the self-governed island.
Lai's government has allocated a record NT$1.1 trillion ($34.5 billion) for defense spending in 2027, equivalent to more than 3% of GDP.
Taiwan's 23 million people face the threat of a Chinese attack. Beijing claims the island as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring it under its control.
"Our aim in increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, but to deter war," President Lai Ching-te said in a speech marking Taiwan's National Day.
Successive governments have increased military spending as Taiwan strengthens its defenses against a potential Chinese invasion and seeks to demonstrate to the United States its commitment to defending itself.
Lai says China must respect Taiwanese people's right to exist
"We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others," Lai said in his annual address outside the Presidential Office in Taipei, attended by thousands of people, including foreign diplomats.
He warned that peace could not be taken for granted, accusing China of using military and grey-zone activities to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.
Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China but stressed that Beijing must respect "the right of the people of Taiwan to exist."
Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan remains unchanged under President Donald Trump, although some of his remarks have raised concerns in Taipei.
US arms deal in focus as Taiwan awaits Trump's approval
Trump raised concerns in May when he suggested that US arms sales to Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, following their meeting in Beijing.
Taiwan is awaiting Trump's approval of $14 billion in weapons sales, including the US-made Patriot air defense system.
At a high-profile summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in September, trade and artificial intelligence dominated the agenda. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was discussed only behind closed doors.
Ahead of Lai's speech, Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital.
Facing China's much larger military, which continues to expand its arsenal with advanced weapons, including stealth fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a vast array of missiles, Taiwan is increasing defence spending and modernising its armed forces.
Washington remains Taipei's most important security backer
China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lai's speech. Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls Lai a "separatist" and has rejected his offers of talks.
Democratically governed Taiwan faces growing military and political pressure from China, which claims the island as its territory despite strong objections from the government in Taipei.
The United States welcomed Lai's commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A senior US administration official said that, referring to China, "a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions."
The United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, but Washington is Taipei's most important security backer.
Saturday's celebrations marked the 115th anniversary of the 1911 revolution that toppled China's Qing dynasty and paved the way for the founding of the Republic of China.
The dispute between China and Taiwan dates back to the Chinese civil war, when nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek fled to the island in 1949 after his forces were defeated by Mao Zedong's communists.

New compromise EU budget maintains Ukraine support, but trims help for EU integration

New compromise EU budget maintains Ukraine support, but trims help for EU integration
BRUSSELS, Belgium — A new compromise proposal for the EU's 2028-2034 budget published Oct. 10 has been forced to cut costs, including for EU candidate countries, but support for Ukraine emerges relatively unscathed.
The bloc operates on a seven-year budget cycle, and countries hope to finalize the next budget by the end of 2026, before France, Poland, Italy, and many more countries hold elections in 2027.
The budget is also important for Ukraine, both because it supports countries working to integrate into the bloc and because the EU is Kyiv's leading financial backer.
The latest proposal includes dedicated Ukraine support of 88.87 billion euros ($99.55 billion).
The amount is unchanged from the last attempt at compromise, published in June, but remains below the 100 billion euros ($112 billion) initially proposed by the European Commission.
"Our commitment to Ukraine is central to our overall ambitions," reads the proposal put forth by the Irish Council Presidency of the EU, which leads negotiations on the budget.
But the budget requires unanimity of the 27 EU countries in order to pass, and several countries, often described as 'the frugals', have pushed for wide-ranging cuts.
read also
That has led to a reduction in the size of the "Global Europe" pot, which finances the EU's development budget, humanitarian aid, and support for countries working to integrate with the EU — including Ukraine.
The latest proposal has reduced the Global Europe pot by just over 20 billion euros ($22.4 billion), from 169.5 billion euros ($189.9 billion) down to 149 billion euros ($167 billion).
Within that, support earmarked for EU candidate countries has fallen by almost four billion euros ($4.5 billion), down from 36.5 billion ($40.9 billion) to 32.6 billion ($36.5 billion) — just over 10%.
Realistically, Ukraine is not the most at risk of suffering from that 10% cut, with the proposal stating that "additional funding for Ukraine may be prioritized from the Enlargement and Europe and Global pillars."
Rather, the two big financial questions for Ukraine remain outside the scope of these budget negotiations.
Ukraine anticipates a $42 billion hole in its 2027 budget, even after accounting for support from the EU's 90 billion euro ($100.9 billion) loan.
Given that the loan is unable to single-handedly cover two years of support for wartime Ukraine, it is unclear how the EU will continue to find new money to help Kyiv if the war rages well beyond 2028.
In a briefing with journalists on the future of enlargement, a senior EU official said of the long-term funding of Ukraine due to the war, "there is a massive uncertainty, no one is pussyfooting about that."

Russia’s demographic crisis — not just due to war
Hello! Welcome to your weekly guide to the Russian economy, written by demographer Salavat Abylkalikov, a fellow at the University of Regensburg, and brought to you by The Bell. This week we dig deep into Russia’s demographic crisis — a challenge decades in the making that is much bigger than just the Ukraine war.
The demographic crisis is back
Russia is facing a worse demographic crisis than at any point in the post-Soviet era. Both the birth rate and the absolute number of births are in decline. The war in Ukraine has intensified the crisis, but is not a root cause: there are longer-standing trends behind the deteriorating situation. Vladimir Putin has spent 20 years claiming Russia’s demographics are his top priority. But the country has only just started hitting the kind of spending levels of other developed nations, and now the military is the top priority for the budget.

National Children’s Day marked at MAHAK with a focus on childhood alongside treatment
TEHRAN - MAHAK Pediatric Cancer Treatment and Research Center (MPCTRC) marked National Children’s Day with a series of cultural, artistic and recreational activities designed to provide children undergoing cancer treatment and their families with opportunities for play, interaction and joyful experiences alongside their treatment journey.
The program was organized with consideration for the children’s medical conditions and in accordance with the health and safety requirements of the hospital environment. Through music, cultural and artistic activities, and age-appropriate entertainment, the event created a setting different from the routine of medical treatment and provided children with opportunities to engage in activities suited to their age and circumstances.
Spending extended periods in a medical environment and undergoing lengthy treatment can affect some of the everyday experiences of childhood. Providing opportunities for play, social interaction and recreation can therefore help children continue to experience aspects of childhood in ways appropriate to their individual conditions, even while receiving treatment.
At MAHAK, attention to children’s emotional and social needs is considered alongside their medical needs. Opportunities for play, interaction with others and participation in activities that celebrate childhood while taking into account their individual circumstances are part of supporting children’s quality of life throughout the treatment process.
The National Children’s Day program reflected this approach by bringing moments of celebration and interaction into the hospital environment. It offered children and their families an opportunity to step away, for a time, from the routine of treatment and experience activities centered on childhood and participation.
Alongside providing specialized pediatric cancer treatment, MAHAK supports children and their families by addressing different dimensions of their well-being throughout the treatment journey. This approach encompasses not only medical care, but also attention to the psychological, social and emotional needs of children and their families.
The celebration of National Children’s Day at MAHAK was held in line with this broader supportive approach, reaffirming the importance of preserving opportunities for childhood, joy and connection while children continue their journey through cancer treatment.

The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone meters away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A second officer then fired a tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face.
"(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said.
A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. The prosecutor's office said in a statement that the student had confronted the police and the officers tried to push him back. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after the incident.
The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of student unrest over conditions in schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades.
Calls for police to stop using rubber bullets, grenade launchers
The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other European countries and have been repeatedly criticized in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate.
It has also sparked anger among the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated discontent with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election.
Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback.
In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off - likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who paused the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case.
Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said.
Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors.
“France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims - we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research.
“It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said.
Calls to ban 'less lethal' weapons
Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades. Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche.
In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added.
A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye.
“He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said.
The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets.
The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden.
Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security.
“We must withdraw the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party told Reuters. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police.
Thierry Clair, a police union representative, said that serious injuries such as Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions.
“How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.”

Harris remains undecided about 2028 presidential campaign

For now, she has continued to frame her political activities around the November 2026 midterms, in which Democrats hope to regain control of the House and Senate and secure additional governorships.

Latvia’s Pro-Ukraine Landslide Hides a Weakness Putin Could Exploit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

Latvia has just held what its own public broadcaster called “a bit of an embarrassing” election. This bashfulness from Latvia’s National Public Service Broadcaster, LSM, was because only 51.8% of eligible voters turned out, the lowest result since Latvia’s first parliamentary election in the modern era in 1993.
Yet those who did turn out handed Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs and his United List 35.3% of the vote and 42 of the 100 seats in the Saeima, Latvia’s parliament – the strongest result achieved by a single political force since Latvia regained independence.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Latvia has emerged from the election with an unusually strong government and an unusually disengaged electorate.
For most European democracies, that would primarily be a political problem. For Latvia, it is also a security problem.
Latvia is a NATO frontline state of just 1.8 million people, bordering both Russia and Belarus. Its grand strategy can be reduced to one overriding objective: make Latvia impossible to isolate.
Internationalize survival
Latvia cannot deter Russia through mass. It has to do it through connections. That means embedding NATO troops on Latvian soil, keeping the United States and Canada strategically invested in the Baltic region, and integrating more closely with Poland and the Nordic states.
It means spending close to 5% of GDP on defense, building fortifications along the eastern frontier, investing in drones and air defense, and reducing Russian economic and informational leverage.
Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
Above all, it means supporting Ukraine. For Riga, Ukraine is both an ally and a forward school of national defense. The Ukrainian battlefield provides lessons in drones, electronic warfare, air defense and Russian tactics that Latvia hopes never to have to learn for itself.
Kulbergs has received a powerful mandate to continue this Atlanticist course. A likely coalition with the National Alliance and New Unity would control 59 seats. Support for Ukraine and NATO remains firmly anchored at the center of the Latvian government.
But Latvia’s defense strategy also depends on something NATO cannot provide: a cohesive and politically engaged society.
                                                                                                                                                                         Barely half Latvia’s electorate voted, raising uncomfortable questions for a national defence strategy built partly around participation and social cohesion. (Photo: PAP/Abaca)                             
The internal front line
Latvia follows an all-of-society approach to defense. Its National Security Concept is explicit that “the existence of the State of Latvia depends on a responsible attitude of all inhabitants of Latvia towards the State and its security.” It links national resilience to the readiness of society as a whole, while defining internal security as resting on a “cohesive civil society” whose citizens participate actively and are prepared to contribute to the defense of the state in a crisis.
Defense Minister Raivis Melnis put it clearly just over a week before the election: “The real first thing is resilience, which is people and country resilience.”
Then almost half of Latvia’s electorate stayed at home. Low turnout does not mean half the country would refuse to defend Latvia. But it does expose weakness in some of the social foundations on which Latvia itself says national resilience depends.
President Edgars Rinkēvičs has already drawn attention to the danger. “Disappointment and indifference are dangerous to the democratic foundations and future of our country,” he said after the result.
Participation was particularly weak in parts of Latgale, Latvia’s easternmost and most heavily Russian-speaking region. Turnout in Daugavpils, where Russian is dominant in everyday life, was just 46.55%. This takes us to the most sensitive part of Latvia’s security dilemma.
Russian-speaking does not mean pro-Russian
Almost a quarter of Latvia’s population is ethnically Russian, while Russian is spoken at home by a much larger share. That demographic legacy of the Soviet period has long made Latvia different from Lithuania and has placed questions of language, history and identity close to the center of national politics.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the temptation has been to view this population primarily through the lens of security.
The evidence is considerably more complicated. Former Latvian integration minister Nils Muižnieks said: “I do not think that we can talk about a fifth column in Latvia.”
Research among Russian-speaking Latvians also suggests that straightforward support for Moscow is a minority position. One major study found 55% supporting neither Russia nor Ukraine. Researcher Mārtiņš Kaprāns argues that this “neutrality cannot be reduced to apathy or ignorance.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Latvia’s parliament has emerged with a stronger governing majority, but record-low turnout raises questions about political engagement beyond its walls. (Photo by Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)                             
The bigger problem appears to be alienation. Parts of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population have become detached from the country’s mainstream political and media environment. Some distrust Riga.
Some dislike policies reducing the public role of the Russian language. Some have become politically homeless following the collapse of Harmony, the party that once dominated Russian-speaking politics.
This election suggests that the two responses to that alienation are abstention and protest voting. Latvia First and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, both considerably softer towards Moscow than the governing parties, will together control 32 seats.
That does not turn their voters into Kremlin loyalists. But from the perspective of national resilience, alienation is important.
The next stage of Latvian security
Russia does not need Latvia’s Russian speakers to become a fifth column. A population that distrusts state institutions, withdraws from politics or feels that the Latvian state belongs to somebody else already creates a seam Moscow can exploit.
Latvia therefore faces a difficult balancing act. It has good reason to restrict Russian influence, dismantle the remnants of Soviet political power and protect Latvian as the language of the state. At the same time, successful resilience ultimately requires Russian-speaking citizens to feel that they have ownership of that state too.
Latvia has spent years hardening its borders, strengthening its military and embedding itself so deeply inside NATO that Moscow could never confront it alone.
Kulbergs’s landslide gives him an unusually strong mandate to continue that work. The embarrassing part of this election is the reminder that Latvia’s next line of defense has to be built from citizens who believe strongly enough in the Latvian state to participate in it.

Türkiye bans social media platforms from serving children under 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:32:44 UTC
18:32:44 KST

Türkiye's Official Gazette has published on Saturday a new regulation on verifying the ages of social media users, barring platforms from providing services to children under 15.
Under the regulation, drafted by the Cybersecurity Presidency, age verification will be carried out through the e-Devlet government portal.
Social media service providers will not be allowed to serve children under 15. Accounts belonging to users who have turned 15 will be subject to child-specific services that take into account the child's best interests and their physical, mental, psychological, social and emotional development.
The regulation requires platforms to apply strict privacy settings by default on children's accounts, set them to private, and disable live broadcasts and personalised advertising on them.
Platforms must also ensure children can only receive messages from accounts they follow, and hide their followers and following lists from other users.
They are also required to provide parental control tools that allow parents to manage their children's account settings, set usage time limits and approve paid transactions.
The regulation is due to take effect on November 1. Age verification for existing accounts must be completed by March 31, 2027, and accounts found to belong to users under 15 will be closed.
