A year after the ‘ceasefire’, Gaza’s healthcare is still collapsing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:30:14 UTC
18:30:14 KST

A year after the ‘ceasefire’, Gaza’s healthcare is still collapsing
Continuing attacks, restrictions on medical aid and delayed evacuations are still killing Palestinians.
When the “ceasefire” was announced on October 10 last year, we knew how much needed repairing. For the first time in a long while, we thought we might have the breathing space to do it.
We thought medicines and equipment could arrive more regularly. Hospitals and clinics could begin to be restored. Patients could leave Gaza for treatment. Emergency medical teams could come from overseas to support Gaza’s exhausted health workers. We could finally look beyond the next crisis and plan how to care for people over the coming months and years.
None of that happened.
Three years into the genocide, there is barely a moment to catch our breath. We’re being asked to do far more than Gaza’s devastated health system can sustain, while regular deliveries of medical supplies and equipment are still restricted and medical evacuations stalled.
People are still arriving at our clinics with traumatic injuries because Israel’s bombardment continues. More than 1,470 people have been killed since the “ceasefire” started. Even reaching a health centre can now put patients at risk. As the security situation has deteriorated, services supported by Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) have had to be suspended in parts of Gaza. Last month, a 65-year-old patient was killed by Israeli military quadcopter fire while seeking treatment at a MAP-supported health centre in Jabalia.
While treating new arrivals with new injuries, we are trying to look after patients whose treatment may take months or years.
Those who have lost limbs need rehabilitation, prosthetics and more surgery, but Israeli authorities heavily restrict the needed supplies. Children who survived acute malnutrition now live with anaemia and stunting, which need treatment, while people with diabetes and high blood pressure struggle to get their medicines. Cancer patients can’t get the radiotherapy they need, and people with kidney failure can’t count on regular dialysis.
Last month, a colleague of mine at MAP in Gaza lost her aunt, Iktimal. In February, Iktimal sensed something was wrong and had a biopsy, but the lab, like so many across Gaza, didn’t have the supplies to test the sample on time. It was more than a month before she learned she had cervical cancer, a disease that is usually curable when found early.
She had surgery in April, but her recovery was slow and painful, and she went on to develop kidney complications that needed specialist treatment unavailable in Gaza. Her family applied for a medical evacuation, but the process was slow, unclear, and bureaucratic. By the time Israeli authorities approved it, her condition was critical. She travelled to Egypt hoping she would finally get the care she needed, but two weeks later, she died.
Iktimal’s case is not unique. According to the World Health Organization, more than 15,000 people in Gaza are still waiting for medical evacuation; if delayed too long, many of these patients could be lost to a preventable death.
We had another tragic case a month ago: A newborn with a serious heart condition died at Assahaba Medical Complex, a hospital MAP supports. The baby needed emergency surgery that isn’t available in Gaza. The doctors knew what was needed but had no way to provide it.
Sometimes we struggle to provide treatment because even basic medical supplies are running short. Hospitals are also short on IV fluids, anaesthetics and surgical supplies. Even oxygen is in short supply.
Staff in many hospitals have to carry cylinders to a central station for refilling. Across Gaza, more than 500 patients rely on oxygen, some of them around the clock: People with cancer, pulmonary fibrosis and heart conditions, and babies and children in intensive care.
In August, the Palestinian Ministry of Health warned that 22 of Gaza’s 34 oxygen stations had stopped working, and only four of 30 machines used to fill oxygen cylinders were still running.
The stations that still function could fail soon. Israeli authorities continue to block the spare parts needed to repair them, classifying them as “dual-use” items. For similar reasons, Gaza has no working MRI machine, and only one or two CT scanners serve about two million people.
Doctors are sometimes left to make decisions without the scans, tests or medicines they would normally rely on.
A cancer that could have been caught early becomes harder to treat. An injury that could have healed with rehabilitation becomes a permanent disability. A child who needed proper food and treatment can be left with chronic malnutrition, stunting and developmental difficulties that may last a lifetime.
We were told the “ceasefire” would give people in Gaza time to heal and rebuild. It hasn’t. The restrictions that stood between Iktimal and her diagnosis, her treatment and her evacuation are still in place, and her story is one of thousands across Gaza in the past year.
Every delay has a cost. Every week a medicine is held back, a scan can’t be done, a patient is refused exit, someone’s condition passes the point where it can be treated.
Iktimal ran out of time. Right now, thousands of people in Gaza are running out of time, too.

Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed.
Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant. With this resolution, researchers can now see that these filaments are not continuous as they had previously appeared. Instead, they’re shaped more like beads on a string, made up of pearl-like knots of gas of relatively uniform size.
These “cosmic pearls” are, in fact, enormous. According to the study published in The Astrophysical Journal, each bead measures about four light-days in diameter. “The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare,” Ilaria Caiazzo, a coauthor of the study, said in a press release. “The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them.”
How exactly the pearls formed is not yet entirely clear, though it’s assumed they are concentrations of material ejected during the explosion. What’s strange, however, is their regularity. In the aftermath of a supernova, astronomers expected to find much more oddly shaped accumulations, but the knots are similar in size and appear aligned along the filaments. This peculiar order is a new feature that could help researchers gain a deeper understanding of stellar death.
The Pa 30 nebula is also particularly unusual because the central star isn’t exactly dead. Instead, it’s considered a “zombie star.” Typically, a thermonuclear supernova is the violent death of a star, which is completely destroyed in the explosion. But in rare cases, part of the star may survive, and scientists do not yet fully understand how or why this happens. The unusual structures of Pa 30 could help astronomers reconstruct more precisely how these kinds of detonations occur and how zombie stars can live on afterward.
All of this has been discovered because scientists seem to have a bit of a crush on Pa 30. Few astronomical structures connect modern observation so directly with human accounts from more than eight centuries ago. The nebula matches the records left by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1181, who described the appearance of a new star in the sky that remained visible for several months. At the time, it was impossible to know that they were witnessing the aftermath of a massive stellar explosion. Centuries later, scientists linked that event to the supernova that gave rise to Pa 30.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

“They created obstacles, but we stood firm and the way forward opened up,” Pezeshkian said, adding that sanctions could be overcome if the country pursued shared goals and a common resolve while improving productivity.
He stressed that Iran needed to make better use of its resources, including water and soil, and improve agricultural efficiency. Falling behind other countries in these areas was unacceptable, he said.
Pezeshkian called on managers to identify the country’s existing capabilities, draw on the expertise of scientists and specialists, and learn from successful international experiences to address shortcomings and promote development.
He said the first step was to acknowledge that the current situation was not satisfactory and then examine how other countries had achieved better results.

‘No divisions, no borders’, French astronaut says of seeing Earth from space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:23:47 UTC
18:23:47 KST

‘No divisions, no borders’, French astronaut says of seeing Earth from space
COLOGNE, Germany – French astronaut Sophie Adenot went through “all human emotions, from the most joyful to the hardest” during her eight months in space, she said back on solid ground on Oct 10 in Germany.
Adenot splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on Oct 8 off the coast of California in the Dragon capsule that carried Crew-12, having returned to Earth from a mission on the International Space Station.
She spent a total of 235 days in space, breaking the record for the longest uninterrupted orbital stay by a European astronaut.
At 400km away from Earth, Adenot could see there are “no divisions, no borders” but “just a precious planet that we all share”, she said on the tarmac of the European Space Agency (ESA) training centre in Cologne, occasionally in tears.
The 44-year-old astronaut looked visibly weakened on her arrival in Germany and was assisted by two ESA physicians.
In space, the body adapts to the absence of gravity, which leads to bone loss, muscle wasting, cardiovascular deconditioning and even visual problems.
Adenot must now begin an intensive recovery programme of about three weeks to regain her pre-flight condition.
“It’s a cocktail of astonishing emotions. It’s incredible. It’s great to be back on Earth, but it also comes with its share of challenges, especially physiological ones,” she told reporters.
She also described the “difficult” moment of the splashdown on Oct 9, when the capsule bringing back the four astronauts on her team had to endure “a lot of waves for 25 minutes”.
“And when the commandos pulled me out of the capsule, the first thing I said to them was, ‘Send me back to space, please!’ It was much easier up there,” she said.
During the mission, Adenot became the first French female astronaut to venture outside the space station for a spacewalk. In all, she undertook three spacewalks on Aug 18 and 25, and Sept 1. AFP

Palestine welcomes Navi Pillay’s 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:23:37 UTC
18:23:37 KST

Palestine on Friday welcomed South African jurist Navi Pillay’s being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, saying the honor recognizes her efforts to defend international law and document Israeli crimes, Anadolu reports.
The Foreign Ministry said Pillay’s win represented an elevation of “the voice of truth and the voice of the oppressed,” and recognized her efforts to advance peace and international law.
It said Pillay devoted her career to upholding law and justice and defending the rights of oppressed people in South Africa and around the world, including Palestinians.
The ministry praised her leadership of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, which she chaired from 2021 to 2025.
It said the commission helped document genocide, sexual violence, attacks on children and other Israeli violations.
The ministry said the prize was also recognition for defenders of international law and justice and encouragement for efforts to hold perpetrators of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity accountable.
It added that Pillay has consistently defended the universality of law and equality among people, including Palestinians, and said the award underscored that “there can be no lasting peace without justice and equality for all.”
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that it awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to the 85-year-old jurist “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”
“This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law,” it said, highlighting her work in international courts and as UN high commissioner for human rights.
Pillay, born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, under apartheid, began her legal career challenging racial discrimination and defending opponents of the apartheid system.
She served as UN high commissioner for human rights, as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. She has also served as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice.
The UN commission she chaired concluded in a 2025 report that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, a finding rejected by Israel.
The Nobel Peace Prize will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

Economic Watch: AI-enabled spending fuels China's holiday economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:21:32 CST
18:21:32 KST

SHANGHAI, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Shoppers crowded into stores across China to try the latest artificial intelligence (AI) gadgets during the week-long National Day holiday, as smart devices continue to transition from the showroom to the mass market.
At Z·Pilot, an AI experience store in Shanghai, China's financial hub, a furry AI pet robot drew a steady stream of browsers during the holiday. When the robot was presented with a toy carrot, its digital eyes lit up in a "feeding" expression; a gentle touch revealed a warm surface, close to lifelike.
"Companionship products are doing well," a staff member said. The fast-selling AI pets offer voice and tactile interaction along with long-term memory, gradually adapting their personality to their owners over time -- delivering the feel of a pet without the upkeep.
AI glasses attracted similar interest. "When traveling abroad, if you don't know how to say something in the local language, you can just translate it directly," a staff member said while demonstrating a pair of the glasses. Beyond real-time translation, the hot-selling devices offer navigation, teleprompting, photo and video capture, letting users leave their phones in their pockets.
At a JD.com mall in Shanghai's Qibao area, 3D printers became a magnet for families, with parents and children building model boats and cars on the spot. Many parents said they were buying the printers to bring home what their children had learned in school, turning the devices into hands-on toys for kids to design and print their own models.
Ms. Qi, who brought her child to a robotics store in the city, said she wanted the child to engage with the technology early. "Let children explore hands-on and get a feel for how AI will shape the way they live, learn and work," she said.
The trend is not unique to Shanghai. In Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province, a tech-mall branded as Wensan was a popular spot for locals and tourists to check out the latest gadgets during the break. Serving as a micro tech supermarket, it brought together more than 700 smart products, ranging from AI companion robots and AI glasses to smart rings and exoskeletons, catering to consumers across all age groups.
In Beijing, a robotics and AI experience brand under Shoucheng Holdings now operates eight stores in the city. Its outlets offered more than 200 robot and AI hardware products, and drew long queues of consumers during the holiday. A representative for the brand said in-store feedback pointed to particularly strong performance in companion-style AI products, entertainment-oriented smart devices and interactive robotics.
Retailers say the momentum is measurable. According to data released this week by Chinese retail giant Suning.com, foot traffic at its flagship stores rose 50 percent year-on-year from Oct. 1 to 7, while sales of AI-equipped home appliances climbed more than 40 percent. Smartwatches, AI glasses and action cameras all posted solid gains.
The surge sits inside a broader AI boom built on a wave of homegrown models. Tools such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Doubao have become everyday fixtures for millions of Chinese users.
On the industry side, the numbers are equally telling: China's AI enterprises surpassed 6,000 last year, with the core AI industry posting strong year-on-year growth.
China had more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, per an industry research report.
Policy support has further deepened the integration of AI and consumption. In June, eight government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, issued guidance to boost AI-enabled consumption, calling for more AI-powered products and expanded AI-driven services.
A subsequent action plan on smart home consumption extended this push, letting localities set their own subsidy categories and standards under the 2026 trade-in policy, including support for whole-house smart home purchases.
"Consumer uptake of AI products is accelerating from a phase of novelty toward mass adoption," said Fan Chunyan, vice president of Suning.com. "Demand for smart devices, immersive experiences and ongoing services will continue to rise." ■

China to launch initiative to boost employment amid AI advances
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:20:43 CST
18:20:43 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on promoting high-quality development in employment and social security during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Fan)
BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- In China's latest effort to adapt its workforce to rapid technological changes, a senior official on Saturday announced an initiative to promote employment in response to artificial intelligence (AI) development.
Li Zhong, vice minister of human resources and social security, said at a press conference that China would actively address the impact of AI and other emerging technologies on employment, promoting the responsible development of technology and bolstering quality employment.
Adapting to AI-driven changes has become an increasingly prominent part of China's employment policy. Several official documents issued this year have outlined measures to harness technological advances while supporting employment.
The 2026 government work report vowed to take more effective measures to facilitate employment and entrepreneurship through better adaptation to the development of AI technologies.
A five-year plan on implementing the employment-first strategy also identified promoting employment amid AI advances as a key task, calling for creating jobs through AI applications and tapping the potential in traditional sectors.
AI is already reshaping China's economy and transforming its labor market, with demand growing for workers equipped with specialized technical skills.
According to Maimai, a networking and recruitment platform, the number of new AI-related job postings in the new economy on the platform rose 789.47 percent year on year from January to July. Online job-seeking platform Zhaopin also said in a report that demand was particularly strong for AI engineers, including those working in automotive manufacturing and intelligent driving.
China's core AI industry has exceeded 1.2 trillion yuan (about 178.23 billion U.S. dollars) in scale, with more than 6,200 enterprises operating in the sector. AI adoption rate across key industries has surpassed 80 percent.
Beyond AI, China is also seeking to generate employment opportunities by developing emerging and future industries.
During the past five years, China introduced 72 new occupations, including AI trainers and carbon emissions managers, incorporating them into the country's official occupational classification system. Since the beginning of 2026, authorities have announced another 11 new occupations.
Wu Liduo, an official of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security, said Saturday the ministry would establish a regular mechanism for identifying new occupations, focusing on emerging fields such as AI, the digital economy, green and low-carbon development, and modern services.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the ministry plans to formulate or revise more than 200 national occupational standards, Wu said.
Amid the changes brought by technological advances, China's overall employment situation has remained stable.
The country created 10.52 million new urban jobs in the first nine months of 2026, achieving 87.7 percent of its annual target, according to figures released at Saturday's press conference. The surveyed urban unemployment rate averaged 5.2 percent in the first eight months of the year. ■

Finland records first snowfall with up to 20 cm in Puolanka
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:18:41 EEST
18:18:41 KST

Finland has recorded its first snowfall of the autumn season, with snow reaching depths of 20 centimetres in parts of the country on Saturday, 10 October. The Finnish Meteorological Institute confirmed snow cover across Kainuu, Koillismaa, Lapland and North Savo, marking the arrival of winter conditions in northern and eastern Finland.
Snow began falling in Kainuu on Friday and continued overnight, leaving several areas covered by Saturday morning. The heaviest accumulation occurred in Puolanka, where measurements reached approximately 20 centimetres.
Other weather stations reported snow depths ranging from two to six centimetres.
Finland officially records the first snow of autumn when a weather station measures a continuous layer of at least one centimetre on the ground during its morning observation.
During daylight saving time, the measurement takes place at 9 am, while the winter observation takes place at 8 am.
Although snow began falling on Friday, the measurements taken on Saturday morning established the season's first snowfall under the institute's official definition.
The arrival of snow follows Finland's seasonal weather pattern, although the timing differs between regions. Central Finland generally experiences its first snowfall around the middle of October.
In Lapland, where winter lasts approximately seven months, snow generally arrives earlier than in southern Finland.
The Finnish Meteorological Institute distinguishes between the first recorded snowfall and permanent snow cover, which refers to the longest uninterrupted period during winter when at least one centimetre of snow remains on the ground.
The ground still retains heat from autumn, which contributes to snow melting. Nevertheless, the snow cover had shown little reduction by Saturday morning.
Forecasters expect little additional snowfall during the remainder of the weekend as the existing precipitation areas move eastwards.
A low-pressure system approaching from the southwest will instead bring rain to southern Finland from Saturday evening into the night.
In the Helsinki metropolitan area, Saturday will remain largely cloudy, with temperatures between five and ten degrees Celsius. The Baltic Sea continues to moderate temperatures along the southern coast.
Light drizzle is expected during the day, followed by more substantial rainfall as the low-pressure system approaches.
Sunday will bring similar conditions to the capital region, with clouds and intermittent drizzle.
Parts of central Finland might experience a mixture of rain and sleet overnight into Sunday morning, although forecasters do not expect any resulting snow to remain on the ground.
While southern and central Finland face cloudy conditions, parts of Lapland are expected to receive periods of sunshine on Saturday.

“I will give everything I know, leave my impressions and let them understand the reality,” Avi Gil said in the interview. “The past few weeks have set me on a different path and signaled to me that I need to come out and tell the truth.”
Gil, 54, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary from July 2021 to May 2024, told Israel’s Channel 12 that a stenographer in the Prime Minister’s Office approached him in January 2024 and said she had been instructed by Netanyahu’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6.40 am (0340GMT) local time to 6.29 am (0329 GMT).
“She told me, ‘I’m not allowed to change it. The computer shows and says 6:40 to 6:44,’” said Gil, accusing the head of Netanyahu’s office of manipulating telephone records.
“Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them,” he added.
Gil said he immediately documented the stenographer’s account in a handwritten note to the attorney general and recommended that any future commission of inquiry obtain the original recordings rather than rely solely on transcripts, according to the newspaper.
“This is changing a transcript, changing the truth,” he said. “Factually, there was an instruction to change the time of a call.”
Gil also said Israeli security officials had repeatedly recommended targeted military operations in the Gaza Strip before Oct. 7, but the political leadership rejected that course.
“There were recommendations from time to time to carry out targeted operations in Gaza. Those recommendations were not accepted,” he said.

Bar told Netanyahu, “I am giving you a warning of war today. I cannot give you an exact day and hour, but this is the warning,” according to the warning previously reported by Yedioth Ahronoth.
Gil stressed that the warning was not specifically about an impending attack from Gaza.
“Was there a specific, focused warning from Gaza? Absolutely not,” he said.
Gil also rejected claims that the intelligence available during the preceding night would normally have required Netanyahu to be awakened immediately, saying the information repeatedly described the situation as “routine” and did not indicate immediate urgency.
He also said he could not confirm reports that Netanyahu had received warnings from Egypt or the United Arab Emirates before Oct. 7, noting that he was not in the office on dates linked to the reported Emirati contact.

"Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers," police said, according to the report.
"Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement."
Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment, the report added.
The police website lists unsolved homicides, accepts public tips, and offers a $20,000 reward for information leading to an arrest.
Authorities encouraged the public to continue submitting legitimate information through the platform.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A US official disputed that the American envoys issued an explicit threat, but confirmed that Witkoff and Kushner conveyed that Washington expected reciprocity from Kyiv given US deliveries of ammunition and intelligence, warning that Ukrainian actions should not harm American consumers.
“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the US official told Axios. “[President Volodymyr] Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the goodwill that he has built with Trump over the last six months.”
According to Axios, the talks in Miami centered on finalizing post-war security guarantees that the US, Europe, and NATO would provide to Ukraine as part of a settlement framework to end the conflict, alongside prospective territorial compromise proposals.
Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
Witkoff and Kushner presented a post-war reconstruction and security package, with discussions addressing Ukraine’s accession path to the EU, post-war relations with NATO, and a durable European security architecture.
Trump’s diesel pivot
The diplomatic rift deepened after Zelensky rejected US demands for a unilateral halt to deep strikes on Russian petrochemical assets.
Ukrainian officials had proposed a mutual energy armistice, conveying to Trump, Witkoff, and Kushner that Kyiv would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow concurrently halted missile and drone bombardments against Ukraine’s electricity grid and heating plants.
However, Trump insisted on an unconditional, unilateral suspension of strikes on Russian refining facilities, arguing that the operations contributed directly to domestic fuel inflation ahead of winter.
The US president did not view strikes on Russian commercial refineries as equivalent to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure, the US official told Axios.
“President Trump decided to strike the diesel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen US requests to stop attacking Russian refineries,” the official stated.
In an interview with Axios following the White House announcement, Zelensky described the agreement as an unexpected and “unfair” development, characterizing the sanctions waiver as an unjustified concession to Putin.
The US official maintained that the administration seeks to engage Moscow in diplomatic negotiations, asserting that while Putin continues to strike Ukrainian territory, Washington assesses the Kremlin remains open to discussions on concluding the war if an acceptable framework is presented.
Refining deficits and operational defiance
The friction over refinery targeting unfolds as Ukrainian officials reaffirm that Kyiv will not abandon asymmetric deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times on Saturday that Ukraine intends to press ahead with drone strikes on refineries, stating plainly: “We will burn [Russian] refineries.”
Energy market analysts have expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s physical capacity to fulfill the export volumes announced by Trump, citing extensive operational damage across the Russian refining sector.
Independent market tracking by intelligence firm Kpler indicates that Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of installed capacity due to emergency maintenance and equipment deficits caused by Ukrainian drone waves.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel monthly by sea, but maritime shipments collapsed throughout 2026 as successive strikes idled primary distillation and cracking units across European Russia and Siberia. Constrained refining output prompted the Kremlin to enact an export ban on domestic diesel in July to stave off domestic fuel deficits.
Trump’s announcement claimed Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling to 3 million tons depending on refinery operations.
Following the announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was enacted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which aimed to expand statutory sanctions across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.

A man named Hitler Mussolini wins a mayoral race in Peru
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:05:49 UTC
18:05:49 KST

A politician bearing the names of two of history's most notorious dictators has emerged victorious in a local election in Peru, securing a mayoral post with just 229 votes.
Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores, 45, won the race in Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to the BBC. He defeated his closest rival by just 25 votes, securing 229 ballots in the local election.
The candidate, representing the center-left Ahora Nación party, finished ahead of his opponent from the right-wing Renovación Popular Perú party.
Figures published by Peru's electoral authorities indicate that slightly more than 700 people participated in the vote, with Flores receiving approximately 34% of ballots cast.
Although he will represent a community of fewer than 1,000 residents, his unusual name has turned an otherwise obscure local election into a story attracting international attention.
Flores was born in Queropalca, located in the central Peruvian region of Huánuco, approximately 360 kilometers (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his official candidate profile.
His first two names immediately evoke Adolf Hitler, the dictator of Nazi Germany, and Benito Mussolini, the fascist ruler of Italy.
Peruvian news outlet Peru21 described the unusual combination as a striking feature of the election, noting the historical significance of the two names. Yet Flores is hardly the first politician in Peru to attract attention for sharing a name with an infamous historical figure. In 2018, a man named Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez won the mayoral election in Yúngar, another district in the Peruvian Andes.
His campaign drew widespread attention not only because of his name, but also because his opponent was reportedly called Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde, whose names recalled Soviet revolutionary Vladimir Lenin.
Alba Sánchez embraced the unusual circumstances, reportedly campaigning under the slogan: "I'm the good Hitler."
Similar headlines emerged in Africa in 2020, when Adolf Hitler Uunona won a local election in Namibia. The southern African country was once a German colony, and German-influenced given names, including Adolf, have remained in use among parts of the population.
Now, six years later, another candidate with a name associated with Europe's darkest chapter has found himself in the international spotlight, this time after winning a small municipal election in the mountains of Peru.

Raul Eamets: Estonia is haunted by an overblown debt‑burden specter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Raul Eamets: Estonia is haunted by an overblown debt‑burden specter
We forget two factors when talking about the growth of the debt burden — factors that affect the whole picture: economic growth and price growth, writes Raul Eamets.
The state budget has reached the Riigikogu, and discussions will show in what form it will ultimately be adopted. Nothing will come easily, because a minority government no longer has a voting steamroller.
Those who say (for example, the Fiscal Council) that the savings are temporary and short‑term, achieved mainly by pushing certain expenses into the future, are right. No structural changes have been made.
This is understandable, because elections are at the door, and no one will stop the indexation of social benefits or cut education costs before elections. Instead, cosmetic, symbolic‑value topics are addressed.
For example, Prime Minister Kristen Michal claimed that the salary increase for senior state officials will not come in the amount prescribed by the formula (law). In real life, this means that in 2023 the coefficient determining salary growth was reduced for some officials. The lowered coefficient was initially supposed to apply until 2028, but now it has been decided to extend it until 2031. The financial impact is symbolic; as a message, it is an important step to gain a bit of support. Simply put, pure political technology.
One negative aspect of the entire budget and budget strategy, constantly emphasized by critics, is the rapid growth of the debt burden and the interest costs that must be paid starting in 2030.
If our public‑sector debt burden is roughly 26 percent of GDP, then according to current plans and forecasts it will grow to 38.6 percent of GDP by 2030. Interest payments will grow from €205 million to €650 million. To solve the situation even somewhat, the budget should be brought into balance as quickly as possible.
One must agree that paying current expenses — especially those indexed to price increases — with borrowed money is not very wise. Current expenses should be covered by current revenues. That seems logical. If investments are needed — expenses that will bring revenue back in the future — then borrowing is practically unavoidable.
It must be kept in mind that investment is not only pouring money into concrete or railways, but also investing in human capital. Whether it is for increasing birth rates, improving healthcare, or improving education. All these expenses bring greater returns in the future, whether in the form of more taxpayers or healthier and smarter workers.
But let's return to those three claims and look at each separately. The first is simple. What happens if the debt burden grows to 39 percent of GDP by 2030? The honest answer is: nothing happens. We will certainly still be among the last three in the EU in terms of debt burden, perhaps among the last four, but that does not change the big picture.
According to the EU's founding principles, a 60‑percent debt‑to‑GDP ratio is acceptable; the EU average is 90 percent. Finland's national debt is moving toward that 90 percent, and Finland can borrow on financial markets at very normal interest rates. Scare tactics claiming that "no one will lend to us then" simply do not work in real life.
The second claim — that interest costs in four years will be as large as current spending on science and higher education combined — does not hold for a very simple reason. Carrying current costs into the future requires accounting for price increases; inflation reduces the value of money in the future.
A cost of €650 million will be worth €589 million in four years if we assume a modest 2.5‑percent price increase. Considering what is happening in the world, one can assume that the impact of the oil crisis on prices will be longer and deeper, meaning that a 3‑percent annual inflation rate could easily be used. In that case, the value of €650 million in four years would be €578 million.
Now the other side of the equation. Our higher‑education costs will certainly not be €650 million in four years. If we assume that higher‑education costs grow by roughly five percent annually, then in four years they will be €790 million. Compare the two numbers: 578 and 790 are not exactly in the same magnitude. A five‑percent annual growth rate is more than modest; looking back in time, the growth number could be much, much higher.
The third claim — that we must achieve a balanced budget at any cost, and only then will happiness arrive — also does not withstand much criticism. We forget two factors when talking about the growth of the debt burden: economic growth and price growth.
Everyone wants economic growth, and price growth — at least to some extent — is unavoidable. Has anyone ever thought why the EU has a three‑percent deficit rule, a 60‑percent debt limit, and a two‑percent inflation target?
If we put these numbers into a formula and calculate how the debt burden changes in a year when the economy grows three percent, inflation is two percent, and the budget deficit is three percent, we get a surprising result. Under these conditions, the debt burden does not grow in a year — it stays the same.
If we continue the thought experiment, the current average EU debt burden of 90 percent of GDP would decrease by 0.8 percentage points in a year if we use a forecasted three‑percent inflation rate, a 3.3‑percent consolidated budget deficit, and assume 1.5‑percent economic growth. These are indicators that could characterize the euro‑area economy in 2026. All this happens while the budget is 3.3 percent in deficit, not balanced. For the debt burden not to grow under certain conditions, the budget does not need to be balanced.
Of course, no one knows what our economic growth, inflation, or actual borrowing needs will be in four years. It is impossible to predict because global uncertainty is too great. Therefore, all kinds of model calculations are made, which in turn rely on various assumptions.
Economic forecasting has become mathematics. All the more important is to talk about nominal and real indicators, about how inflation reduces the purchasing power of money in the future, and how economic growth changes ratios relative to GDP. Life is a bit more complicated than simply waving around numbers whose magnitudes are incomprehensible to ordinary people anyway. The specter in the room is much smaller than it is being painted. About the size of a matchbox.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

32-Element CRPA Antenna, Likely Manufactured in Alabuga, Was Found in Downed Geran-4 Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:03:34 UTC
18:03:34 KST

A 32-element CRPA antenna, likely manufactured at a plant in Alabuzha, Russia, was found in a Russian Geran-4 strike drone shot down in Ukraine.
This was reported by The Insider, citing an analysis of photos and videos of the downed drones.
The new antenna looks very similar to products made by the Chinese company Harxon, but shows signs of local production.
The rough finish of the metal casing and the factory marking ALB stamped directly onto it point to the possibility that production was localized in Russia.
The Russians are likely gradually transitioning to at least screwdriver-style assembly of such circuit boards in Tatarstan.
They first purchase test batches on marketplaces, and then order large production runs or license their manufacture.
Last year, it was revealed that the main supplier of multi-element antennas to Alabuga was the Chinese company Harxon. After this information was made public, the company fell under international sanctions, and its representatives announced the dismissal of employees who had been in contact with Russia.
As a reminder, it first came to light in July that Ukraine had seized a 32-element CRPA antenna that was mounted on a Russian weapon system.
This is effectively two antennas, each with 16 elements, assembled into a single unit. The first 16 elements operate in the L1 band, like the Kometa, while the other 16 operate in the L2 band. The L1 band operates at a base frequency of approximately 1,575 MHz and is the primary channel for civilian and military satellite navigation.
CRPA antennas, which support only the L1 band, are the most compact and inexpensive, which is why they are widely installed on drones and missiles. The L2 band operates at a lower frequency of approximately 1,227 MHz and is designed for transmitting secure and encrypted signals.
A CRPA antenna (Controlled Radiation Pattern Antenna) is a specialized navigation module designed to protect GPS/GLONASS satellite signals from electronic jamming. It consists of several separate antenna elements and a digital processor that analyze the surrounding space.
The number of elements in the antenna directly determines its resistance to interference. Each additional element allows the system to block yet another separate source of jamming.

Waffling at the UN: OpenAI, Anthropic and selling Artificial Intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:02:27 UTC
18:02:27 KST

They are a trying lot, spruiking their overvalued, loss-making firms, sowing discord and fear, and then seeking state collaboration that will serve to implicate all the parties concerned should things sour. And what will the rest of us get? Hardly the promised land. But the United Nations, for the first time in history, became a centre stage for the propagandists from Artificial Intelligence firms during the September deliberations, diplomats hanging off the banal declarations from such figures as Sam Altman, the CEO from OpenAI, and Dario Amodei, his equivalent from Anthropic.
In his September 23 address to the UN Security Council, no less, Altman slipped into that familiar messianic tone about choices to be made, largely because these choices are being made for the rest of humanity by his ilk. “We have a choice in front of us. AI can either be more like a new Renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new Industrial Revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Why the binary proposition? And why the need for the choice in the first place?
Altman is irritatingly condescending, suggesting that “people are much more capable than they imagine themselves to be, but have been held back by limited technology that was meant to empower but instead distracts and often steals attention.” Examples are not forthcoming, but the monotonous tone is set: AI, like the son of the good Lord, is a gift to humankind. “It is about giving people more agency in an ever more complex world: more ability to learn, to create, discover, build, participate.”
This is drivel, since AI, even as this is being penned, is imposing disabilities on learning by turning the process into one of lazy, numbing consumption, negating creativity by stealing it from creative human sources, not so much discovering as synthesising what has been scraped and not so much building as demolishing and removing the human subject from participation. The agenda is distinctly anti-human.
Altman, however, had hit his stride, saying that, “AI should be built for the people, not simply to turn the crank of the machines faster for their own sake. Some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies.” This bleat is no doubt directed at the effusive warnings of technology researcher Jacob Coxon, who had worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic and found his Damascene conversion. “They are racing straight toward self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said last month on resigning from Anthropic. “The people building AI genuinely believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Perilous surrender: The Pentagon falls for artificial intelligence
These catastrophic forecasts are boons for Altman and the AI fraternity. The greater the risk of a gloomy end, the greater the need to be a leading force in preventing that terminus from being reached. “It doesn’t matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10%, or 1%, or 12%, or .1%. None of these levels are remotely acceptable.” He suggests that “we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we will be able to keep under human control.” Risibly, Altman goes on to also warn that such systems could become the preserve of the elite – “too much power in too few hands. No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else.” Which is exactly what he was doing at the UN Security Council, showing what concentrated power looks like.
What, then, to do? Altman posits three principles, none particularly profound. The first is to retain a human element at the centre of AI, a delightful proposition from the CEO of a company working to remove the human from the equation, exemplified by the hack of Australia’s Medicare system by an OpenAI agent in June that subverted privacy protections. The second is the corollary of the first: “the benefits of scientific progress and economic growth must be by people and for people.” Tools are not to replace human agency. The third entails a word that really ought to be banished to the lexical mausoleum. Such “technology must empower people individually.” The term “empower” is only ever used by those who ration power to begin with.
Unperturbed, Altman has an advertiser’s pitch. He is selling a product. Governments are to be involved. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through the democratic processes, and by governments accountable to the people that they serve.”
He suggests international cooperation and “a mechanism for complementary national and international frontier AI standards. These would measure capabilities, assess risks, determine the adequacy of safeguards “and preserve meaningful human oversight as systems become more autonomous.” Common standards would enable states to compare evidence and verify compliance. A regime to report incidents expeditiously and learn from them rapidly would be vital. Secure channels among governments and what Altman calls “critical infrastructure operators” and “technical experts” (that’s the pitch for his company) would “share emerging vulnerabilities and new threats.”
Amodei’s address was even more blatant in self-advertising, including the virtues of the Claude large language model. “Just today, Anthropic announced the Claude-led discovery of a new molecular machine,” he boasted. This could lead to “a new gene editing mechanism that could have applications in gene therapy.” But risks abounded. AI models might be misused by, for instance, bioterrorists in creating biological weapons. Another risk was the “loss of control, model capabilities accelerating beyond developers’ ability to control them.” As with Altman, a similar theme emerged: all of humanity needed to be concerned, including governments representing it. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole.” Then comes his pitch: Anthropic was better placed than any to be the knight in shining armour, given its “best track record in the industry for preventing these risks, both operationally and in our research.” Through testing was taking place for all models regarding dangers and risks. Safeguards were installed in “our most capable models, and we publish our work in these areas.” The company was also without peer in its transparency practices.
READ: Denial as a way of life: Netanyahu on Egyptian warnings about 7th October
This was the prelude for another three-step suggestion. For starters, much like a “food inspector” (these people are truly imaginative), external evaluators should be embedded across AI companies. Second, industrial standards should be set, thereby modulating “the pace of progress.” The final point entails global cooperation across governments “to set international standards.” Specifically for the Security Council, Amodei suggested initial narrow agreements “that every member can support such as a ban on using AI to make biological weapons or permitting your AI technologies to be used to make biological weapons.” (Why the fascination with those weapons?) Evaluation and verification systems should be established to “have visibility into frontier model capability”. And “common global standards for testing AI models for loss of control risks and misuse risks, and a notification system for AI incidents that are significant for global security.” Lecture concluded.
UN officials are certainly in a muddle about how to approach what is both a poisoned chalice and rich cornucopia of opportunity. Volker Türk, the top UN human rights bureaucrat, seems besotted and dismayed all at once. He also seems all too trusting, noting with approval the meaningless, voluntary accord signed by US President Donald Trump and the heads of six AI companies on September 29 regarding safeguards, self-regulation and assessing risk.
In what must be a momentous occasion, the president actually used the term “morally binding”, neither word having ever had any truck in his vocabulary. At least Türk acknowledges the need for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in the development of the technology, warning against a creeping, unnoticed dystopia. A good start in that regard would be a consensus on banishing machines from the realm of decision making on whether human life is allowed to continue or expire. That sounds like tender hearted naivete, given that human agents are already deferring their responsibilities and ethical compass to AI machines. What Altman and Amodei are doing with brio is playing out their ongoing and proposed crimes against humanity in plain sight.

Russian strikes kill 8 in Ukraine as Trump’s diesel deal backfires

Russian strikes killed at least eight people, including three children, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday, as President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel drew sharp criticism from Kyiv over concerns that the shipments would help finance Moscow’s war.
At least 16 people were wounded when Russian aerial bombs struck residential buildings in the southeastern region, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the regional defense council, said.
The attack came amid an intensifying Russian bombardment that has killed more than 55 people across Ukraine over the past four days, according to Ukrainian officials.
The two countries remain largely deadlocked along the front line more than 4.5 years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, while their forces continue to wage a long-range aerial war.
The latest casualties underscored the mounting pressure on Ukraine as it struggles to defend its territory against increasingly deadly Russian attacks.
They also came a day after Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to the United States and global markets, marking a significant shift in Washington’s approach to Moscow as fuel prices rise ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the deal, warning that allowing Russia to expand its petroleum exports would provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its military campaign.
“Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in the war, which must be ended, not prolonged,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Friday.
He warned that Moscow would repay the agreement with further attacks and what he described as “terror and perfidy,” arguing that the arrangement would encourage Russia to continue its offensive while undermining Washington’s efforts to end the conflict.
In a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelenskyy described the agreement as “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners.”
The Ukrainian leader was particularly angered that Trump announced the deal while his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war. Zelenskyy said the proposed fuel arrangement had not been raised during those talks.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
In an interview with the U.S. news outlet Axios, Zelenskyy also described the agreement as “not fair and not honest,” warning that any relaxation of restrictions on Russian energy exports would weaken pressure on the Kremlin.
Trump defended the deal, saying the United States needed additional supplies to help ease prices.
“We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it,” he said.
Trump announced the agreement on his Truth Social platform Friday after a phone call with Putin that had been expected to focus on a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump said the Russian leader had agreed to arrange substantial diesel shipments, beginning with more than 300,000 metric tons immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward. A further 3 million tons could arrive within a relatively short period, he said, depending on supply conditions.
The Kremlin confirmed that Russia was prepared to supply oil and petroleum products to international markets.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak separately announced the immediate lifting of Moscow’s ban on diesel exports, according to the state news agency TASS. Novak outlined a schedule of 300,000 tons in October, 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December, contingent on repairs to refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks.
Russia produced about 7 million tons of diesel per month last year, but its production capacity has since fallen by roughly half, according to the figures cited in reports on the agreement.
The initial 300,000-ton shipment would represent only a small share of global diesel demand and is unlikely to significantly reduce prices on its own. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, that volume would theoretically cover just over 14 hours of U.S. consumption of diesel and other distillate fuels.
The agreement nevertheless represents a notable reversal in Washington’s approach to Russia. Last month, Trump signed legislation granting his administration broad powers to impose additional sanctions on Moscow, including measures targeting the energy exports that help fund its war against Ukraine.
Following the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary exemption from sanctions allowing the sale, supply, unloading and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The move comes as the Trump administration faces competing pressures to contain fuel costs at home while maintaining leverage over Russia. Rising energy prices have become a growing political concern ahead of the November midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
Fuel costs have surged worldwide amid the U.S. war with Iran and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passage for global oil supplies. Some Republicans have also blamed the conflict with Iran for the rise in prices.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that they contribute to fuel shortages and higher costs. He has urged Kyiv to halt the strikes, which target infrastructure that helps sustain Russia’s energy exports and war effort.
In his latest social media post, Trump said the diesel agreement, combined with what he described as Washington’s “TOTAL CONTROL” of the Strait of Hormuz, would drive prices sharply lower.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” he wrote.
Despite his criticism of the diesel agreement, Zelenskyy reiterated Ukraine’s willingness to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow agreed to end its strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“We are proposing precisely such an agreement to America and believe that the strength of the United States is sufficient to achieve such a compromise,” he wrote.
The proposal reflects Kyiv’s push for reciprocal restrictions on attacks against energy facilities, which have become central targets in the war.
Russian strikes have repeatedly damaged Ukraine’s infrastructure, while Ukrainian forces have targeted Russian refineries in an effort to disrupt fuel production and the revenues supporting Moscow’s military campaign.
Zelenskyy warned that easing sanctions or allowing Russia to expand its energy sales would signal weakness and encourage the Kremlin to take Washington less seriously.

Alleged abuse victims at British military school in Germany tell of agonising fight for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:00:53 UTC
18:00:53 KST

Anne and Jane* were 10 years old when a member of staff connected with their British military school in Bünde, Germany is alleged to have singled them out and sexually abused them.
Now in their 50s, the women say he coerced them into keeping silent, and for decades they had only discussed their experiences with one another. “He said if we ever told anybody, then our fathers would lose their jobs and they would be kicked out of the army,” Jane said. “Being two young 10-year-old girls who basically followed their fathers around the world, their jobs were our lives.”
But five years ago, with her father retired from military service, Anne found out the man was still alive and decided to come forward to report the alleged abuse. She said she did so in the hope that she and Jane would finally see justice.
More than 40 years later, they are affected by what they allege happened to them.
“He was my first sexual encounter at the age of 10,” Jane said. “I struggled with relationships at an early age … I’ve never ever been able to be in a loving relationship.”
Similarly, Anne said that from a young age “there was a spiral of self-destruction” and she had been left traumatised. As a school governor, she said smells from her childhood brought back memories of the alleged abuse. “I remember walking through the school corridor, and I just felt sick,” she said.
But despite their efforts to bring their alleged abuser to justice, a joint investigation by the Guardian and openDemocracy has found that he cannot be prosecuted, because although he was a British citizen, employed by the British army, incomplete records of his employment have repeatedly halted investigations into the allegations.
Nato rules state that countries with armed forces abroad can apply their laws to people who fall under their jurisdiction, including serving members of the military and civilian employees. But the absence of the man’s employment contract, along with no proof that he paid tax to the British crown, meant the police could not prove he was employed on a Ministry of Defence (MoD) London contract rather than a locally employed contract.
The women say the MoD refuses to take responsibility for the abuse they allege they suffered while under its care.
_____
Anne and Jane believe their alleged abuser deliberately targeted them because they were isolated from other children at the school.
“I was shy, very, very shy and introverted, and also struggled with all the moving,” Anne said. “I was in quite a bad place anyway by the time I got to Germany.”
She said it initially felt “so exciting to be singled out by this incredibly charismatic man. Everyone sort of swooned in his presence, adults and children alike.”
She added: “When he did turn his gaze very singly on me, I absolutely fell for it.”
The man’s interactions with the girls became sexual, they said, with much of the alleged abuse taking place in his office.
“Once we’d get into that room, he’d lock the door from the inside,” Jane said, “and then it went very, very dark very quickly.”
Jane can still remember the number plate of his car, reciting it effortlessly. “My stomach used to sink when I saw that car,” she said, “because I knew he was in there and I knew what the day was going to entail for both of us.”
The alleged abuse, which took place in the 1980s, began to affect the girls straight away. Anne said she “went into a state of terror” at the time.
“I was having night terrors, I was sleepwalking, I believed someone was outside looking into my bedroom. I hated getting changed at night, I’d go to bed in my clothes.”
_________
Anne and Jane kept in contact for a few years after they left the school, writing letters to each other in which they would reference the alleged abuse – and which Anne still has.
But later they lost touch. It was only when they were in their 50s that they reconnected on Facebook, after Anne had come forward in 2018 to disclose what had happened as part of the Truth Project, run by the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse in England and Wales.
As part of her disclosure, Anne said she would be willing for the police to be notified, and the case was passed to the Royal Military Police (RMP).
The force told her that it would only be able to proceed with the case if it was able to track down Jane to corroborate her story.
Around the time the pair connected online, detectives also found Jane, after the police knocked on her parents’ door and told them that the RMP needed to speak to her as an “important witness” in a case – leading her to disclose to her parents for the first time what had happened to her.
With the RMP now able to investigate, Anne believed her alleged abuser would be brought to justice.
“I thought they could arrest him and make him go to court and go to prison,” she said.
Her hopes were shattered when the RMP said it was unable to progress the case because they did not have jurisdiction.
She was told that her alleged abuser could not be prosecuted in the UK because they could not find evidence that he had paid tax to HMRC, meaning that the case would have to be prosecuted in Germany – where the statute of limitations had expired.
The women were also told the RMP had been unable to find any evidence of his tax contributions in Germany.
Although the RMP was passed some evidence of his employment at the school, including staff lists, witness accounts and photographs, a lack of more formal evidence about his employment or tax status stalled all progress in their case.
After the women complained about the outcome, they received a written apology from a senior officer, who said: “The handling of your case fell below the professional standards you had every right to expect.”
The MoD’s then newly formed Defence Serious Crime Unit (DSCU) launched a second investigation, but it reached the same conclusion. Army records for the school from the time had been destroyed, and without evidence of his employment contract, which may have indicated his tax status, they were told there was no way forward.
Jane said it felt like “another door slamming in your face” when the second investigation ended.
__________________
While Anne and Jane want justice for themselves, they are also telling their story in the hope that it may resonate with others and expose the jurisdiction issues that have denied them resolution.
Emma Norton, a lawyer from the Centre for Military Justice, said: “To be told after so long, and after having taken the incredibly brave step of reporting the abuse, that nothing now can be done because they appear to have fallen into a ‘jurisdictional gap’ is devastating.”
She added: “Given the number of overseas military schools, there is a serious risk that this gap is likely to affect other victims too.”
Jess Phillips, a former safeguarding minister, said the case “exposes a cultural issue within the MoD”.
“The MoD needs to treat these two women as people who have been wrongfully treated while under their care,” she said. “We do not have to continue the cultural failing of the past – we can make the future better.”
Jane said: “The MoD had a duty of care to us. They were our caregivers.”
She added: “We need somebody to stand up and say: ‘We failed you.’”
While they are losing hope that their alleged abuser may be prosecuted, they are still fighting for an acknowledgment of, and accountability for, the alleged childhood abuse they say they suffered and that has affected their whole lives.
“We should not have had to go through that,” Anne said. “I want public accountability.”
But she feels increasingly pessimistic that anyone will be held responsible for what she and Jane experienced. “Hope feels like a very stupid act right now for me,” she added.
A spokesperson for the Defence Serious Crime Command, which the DSCU is part of, said: “Every child has the right to be safe at school, and our thoughts remain with the victims.
“We deeply regret that the initial handling of the case fell below the standards we expect and have formally apologised to the victims. A new investigation launched earlier this year concluded the Defence Serious Crime Command does not have jurisdiction to pursue charges.
“We have taken a number of steps to strengthen investigative practices across defence and remain committed to ensuring every case is fully and thoroughly investigated to deliver justice for victims.”

Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why | Kitty Sayers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:00:53 UTC
18:00:53 KST

Young British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up in France as a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets.
“To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past.
The lycée protests in the past week have displayed the organisation and bravery of the French students. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost his hand to a police grenade during a blockade. More than 6,000 people have been arrested, many of them under 18. Hundreds of schools across France are either blockaded or closed. These teenagers know the risks and commit to turning up anyway, day after day. I can’t imagine that happening in Britain, so what makes the French so different?
First, there’s the history. France’s republic was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it. French pupils learn that protest, uprising and rioting are the origin story of their freedoms, so these methods are championed in promoting change. We grew up in school with the idea that if you don’t like something, you have the power to change it. The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education. The French Revolution appears in the curriculum twice, for pupils aged 12 and then again at 16; the student protests of 1968 are taught at age 14 and again at 17. Debating is encouraged in schools from as early as collège, or at about 11 years old. Young people are expected to have an opinion and not be afraid to defend it.
Even I, at 11, started to feel patriotic during our moral and civic education classes, despite not having a French passport. Protesting is taught as a legally framed fundamental right and a civic responsibility. Of course, with lycéens not yet being old enough to vote, protest is the next best thing.
In the final year of lycée, pupils study Rousseau’s Du Contrat Social (The Social Contract), which argues that citizens should only surrender their unrestricted natural liberty in exchange for civil and moral freedoms. You give up your individual interests for the volonté générale (general will) – put simply, you pay heavy taxes and in return you expect the country to work. That bargain is how the French understand their relationship with the state. When the government raises the retirement age, lets electricity bills soar or cuts school budgets, that is seen as a breach of the social contract. Protest is the automatic response.
Britons, on the other hand, are subjects of the UK and are characterised more by an American-style individualism and a desire to live and let live. There is less collective spirit. Britain has an extraordinary history of protest, spanning Peterloo, the Chartists, the suffragettes and the poll tax riots, but there is arguably a different cultural relationship to these events. They can be remembered as stand-alone episodes and interruptions to the national story rather than as the story itself. The Thatcher era also did permanent damage to unions, contributing to the British public being a grumbling but compliant one, lacking in organising power.
Because these values are ingrained across French society, and in every generation, the student protesters are emboldened by the firefighters, nurses, lawyers and teachers who have joined them in solidarity. Across social media, you can see these moments of support and unity. A viral video of the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, protecting students from the police is a striking example of this. It’s difficult to imagine British teenagers taking to the streets, because they would be alone.
Parents have joined their children in protesting, and have called on other parents to do the same for the planned general strike on 17 October. (This is also a response to the police brutality witnessed in the past week.) Many parents were themselves lycée students and marched against education reforms and cuts. The anti-Macroniste parents (of whom there are many) don’t treat their children as delinquents, but as citizens exercising their rights.
That does not mean every French parent supports every protest, or that French society is wholly united behind its students. While the French state technically encourages protest through the curriculum, the force and violence with which it has met its students says otherwise. And there is resentment of the protests among some students, particularly those who come from conservative households and believe that the blockades are a leftwing plot.
Students in France are not necessarily more political than their British counterparts – young British people are active, but tend to take part in established and larger movements such as Extinction Rebellion or the Gaza protests rather than initiate protests themselves. The biggest difference lies in the French willingness to take to the streets, suddenly and en-masse. Unlike in the UK, the state is something the French are taught to engage with as citizens, and to challenge when necessary. If anything, the lycéens are just being good students.
- Kitty Sayers is a master’s student in journalism
