‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:00:53 UTC
18:00:53 KST

On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.
“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”
The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.
“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”
The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.
Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.
Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.
“We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”
The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.
Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.
In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.
Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.
“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”
The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.
Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.
“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.
Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.
Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.
Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”.
She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”

The everyday foods that make Switzerland unique
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The everyday foods that make Switzerland unique
Switzerland is known for fondue, raclette and chocolate, but they tell only part of the story about the nation's culinary identity. This is defined just as much by everyday favourites like a hard-boiled egg sprinkled with Aromat or a bottle of Rivella.
Switzerland loves seasonings, perhaps even more than its neighbours. In many traditional cafes and restaurants, salt and pepper can be found on tables next to Aromat, a blend of spices and flavour enhancers, and Maggi, a liquid condiment with hints of stock and a flavour reminiscent of the herb lovage.
Aromat is not confined to kitchens and restaurants. On hikes and at picnics, it’s not unusual to see someone produce the familiar yellow shaker from their backpack and sprinkle a hard-boiled egg at the top of a mountain.
Over time, these well-known Swiss seasonings have found their way into Swiss dishes – much to the surprise of foreigners. Adding a few drops of Maggi to a risotto is perfectly normal in some households, a practice that would spark protests on the other side of the Alps.
For many Swiss, Aromat is more than a seasoning. When reports surfaced earlier this year about the possibility of Aromat being boughtExternal link by an American group, many people reacted as though a piece of the country’s national heritage were under threat. Their reaction speaks volumes about the place Aromat occupies in everyday life in Switzerland.
A fizzy drink from the cheese dairy
The Alpine nation’s relationship with milk is well established. Raclette, fondue, and Gruyère and Emmental cheese are known around the world.
But the Swiss don’t just turn milk into cheese. Sometimes their passion for dairy products takes on more unexpected forms. Since the 1950s, they have also been using it to make fizzy drinks.
Made from whey – the liquid left over after producing cheese – Rivella has become one of the country’s most popular soft drinks. This simple by-product of the dairy industry has culminated in the creation of a national drinkExternal link.
Rivella’s success also owes much to the image it has cultivated over the decades. For generations of Swiss people, the soft drink is tied to memories of orienteering, school camps, hikes and sporting competitions. After hours of exertion, a chilled bottle can seem remarkably refreshing.
But love for the whey drink is not universal. Despite numerous attempts, Rivella has never managed to replicate its success abroad. One of the few exceptions is the Netherlands. It may be a coincidence, but cheese-loving nations are perhaps more receptive to the idea of turning whey into a soft drink.
Beer on toast
A whey-based soda might seem like an unusual idea. But turning brewer’s yeast into a spread is perhaps even more so. Switzerland is not alone, however. The British have Marmite, the Australians Vegemite, and the Swiss have Le Parfait and CenovisExternal link.
Like Rivella, these products originated from a “circular economy” approach. In both cases, the aim was to make use of by-products from the brewing industry. Rich in protein and B vitamins, brewer’s yeast and fermentation residues emerged at the start of the 20th century as an attractive resource at a time when food supplies were a major concern for authorities and industry.
There was also a social dimension to the project. The spreads were intended to provide a nutritious and affordable foodstuff capable of supplementing or replacing more expensive products, particularly meat, but at a lower cost. Created in 1931 in a brewery in canton Aargau, Cenovis embodies this ambition even in its name, derived from Latin roots evoking food and strength.
Over time, however, the nutritional story has given way to an emotional one. Le Parfait has become a familiar sight on Swiss dining tables. Cenovis, on the other hand, belongs to a more particular category: food you either love or hate. For its fans, it evokes childhood memories, breakfasts and a certain sense of comfort. For its detractors, a single slice of toast spread with Cenovis is often enough to confirm they will never join the club.
When dessert makes an appearance
Perhaps the final major characteristic of the Swiss palate is its fondness for sweet-and-savoury combinations. Admittedly, Switzerland did not invent these. They can be found in many cuisines around the world, from China to the Middle East. But few European countries seem to have integrated them so naturally into everyday life.
Mixing sweet and savoury belongs to a certain Swiss tradition. In the Fribourg region, for example, cuchaule [a saffron-infused brioche bread] is served with Bénichon mustard, a preparation whose sweetness is sometimes more reminiscent of jam than mustard. Pear bread, found in several Swiss Alpine regions, is also an example of this long-standing habit of blurring culinary boundaries.
Swiss preferences do not stop there. Hawaiian pizza has for years been one of the country’s most popular varieties. In a nation that readily combines sweet and savoury, the idea of adding a few pineapple chunks to a pizza probably seems less revolutionary than elsewhere.
This familiarity with sweet-and-savoury combinations is not universally shared. In canteens and dining halls, many German-speaking Swiss happily mix Apfelmus [apple sauce] with macaroni or cornettes pasta and minced meat. Meanwhile, people from French-speaking Switzerland and canton Ticino often eat the same dishes with the same apple purée, but generally save the apple purée for dessert.
Riz Casimir, a curry dish that combines meat, cream and tropical fruit, is perhaps the most iconic example of this tradition. Long a fixture on Swiss restaurant and canteen menus, it often inspires bewilderment abroad. In 2023, it even landed on TasteAtlas’s list of the world’s worst-rated dishes, an honour its fans could happily have done without.
None of these customs is uniquely Swiss. But their coexistence in such a small country creates a surprisingly distinctive culinary landscape, one whose originality many locals only fully appreciate when they leave the country.
Edited by Pauline Turuban / Translated from French, sub-edited by Alexandra MV Andrist/sb

How This Tiny Startup Built the World’s Safest Bike Helmet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

For decades, researchers judged cycling helmets on how well they protected against direct impacts. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) still does, even though research shows the danger isn't just how hard your head hits the ground, but how violently it twists. That rotational movement can make the brain twist and stretch inside the skull, increasing the risk of concussion and other brain injuries.
Not waiting for the CPSC to catch up, the cycling industry got to work. Multidirectional Impact Protection System, or MIPS, hit the market in 2007 and is now a common feature on premium helmets. At the same time, Virginia Tech turned helmet safety into something of a competition for manufacturers. In 2018, it launched helmet STAR ratings (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk), testing beyond the legal minimum and measuring both linear and rotational impacts.
Only four of the first 30 helmets earned five stars, but by 2025, 167 of 272 achieved five stars, and Virginia Tech had to tighten its grading. That only drove competition and improved helmet technology. Suddenly, hitting the number one spot was good for business and brains.
Sitting comfortably ahead of the competition, with a 4.61 score (10.1 or lower earns a five-star rating; lower is better), is the Pikio Si Oblik road cycling helmet, featuring a new safety system called Oblik. Inspired by the headbanging, concussion-proof woodpecker, this new design has wiped the floor with the competition. For context, Pikio's 4.61 score is 2.21 points lower than the previous best Canyon Deflectr’s 6.82. That’s about 32 percent lower, a massive shift when many of the highest-rated helmets score only between 7 and 10 points.
How has this relatively obscure Vancouver startup gotten it right the first time? As founder Daniel Abram explains, it “comes from 18 years researching impact protection and helmet design.” After studying mechanical engineering, he moved into helmet research at Simon Fraser University, where he helped develop BrainShield, a system designed to reduce rotational forces during impacts. He later founded helmet technology company BiaGuard, before MIPS paid around $1 million for the patents and intellectual property in 2022.
Most bike helmets use a thin plastic shell over expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam, which crushes on impact to absorb energy before it reaches your skull. Oblik takes that familiar foam structure and breaks it into independently mounted sections rather than one continuous block.
Each section attaches to the base EPS layer with flexible connection points, allowing them to move separately or detach if the helmet takes a serious impact. Combined with dual-density foam that absorbs direct impact, the movement helps to minimize the twisting force transmitted to the head. Abram explained how, “Rather than compressing material in one direction, the system is able to deform, deflect, and detach depending on the impact's intensity, location, and direction, helping manage both linear and rotational impact energy.”
Other helmet technologies approach the problem very differently. The now-ubiquitous MIPS remains the dominant commercial system, using a low-friction layer that can move 10 to 15 millimeters during the first 5 to 10 milliseconds of an impact. MIPS Spherical uses two nested liners that rotate relative to each other, while 6D’s Omni-Directional Suspension (ODS) suspends one liner inside another. WaveCel uses an engineered cellular structure that flexes, crumples, and glides under angled impacts.
Pikio's closest rival, the Release Layer System (RLS), featured on Canyon’s Deflectr and the third-placed, 3D-printed Hexr Miden RLS, tackles rotation from the outside, using external shell panels floating on tiny polycarbonate ball bearings that can roll and detach, redirecting rotational energy before it reaches the head.
Lab testing is one thing, but real-world data is something else. If your Pikio helmet is called into serious action, you will need to replace it—as with most EPS foam designs—but the company is offering a 30 percent discount on a replacement if it can get its hands on your damaged helmet.
“So far we’ve had four helmets returned and replaced,” Abram says. “Each has proven invaluable, not least because they’ve done their job and kept riders safe.”
At $379, the Pikio is a premium choice—a cool $219 more expensive than the second-best STAR-tested Canyon Deflectr RLS. Much of the cost stems from a vastly more complicated manufacturing process. Abram says a standard cycling helmet has around eight to 10 parts, but the Pikio Si uses around 80 individual components. The separate foam sections, intricately engineered flexible connection points, and dual-density construction all add to the cost.
It’s a small price to pay if it saves your life, but how does it fare day to day? I’ve been riding with the Si Oblik for the past month and have been impressed by how few compromises there have been in the pursuit of protection.
At 279 grams (in medium size), it's respectably light, though not class-leading, and the dial-to-fit cradle hugs my head neatly without pinch points. It’s a little bulky for a road lid, but is extremely comfortable; the 17 air vents keep my head refreshingly cool, and nobody has laughed at me for wearing it (yet). I would have preferred Pikio to use a magnetic Fidlock fastening under the chin as they’re brilliant, but it is a minor complaint—which Abram quickly quashed: “Fidlock weighs around 13 grams; a buckle is just four grams.”
It’s a great helmet loaded with unique, deliberately safety-first tech. Abram was keen to point out he is not interested in what he called “crown-like cycle helmet” aesthetics, and that “form always follows function.” The Pikio lacks a little of the cool factor you’ll find with a POC or Giro helmet, but it’s certainly not ugly.
For a company most cyclists have never heard of, taking the top spot at Virginia Tech is an extraordinary result. The harder part may be persuading people to trust an unknown name with something as consequential as head protection. MIPS faced a similar problem before turning an independent safety technology into something licensed across much of the helmet industry, and Oblik could conceivably follow the same path.
Whether Pikio becomes a major helmet brand—a second design is due early in the new year—a technology supplier, or both remains to be seen. But for now, it has given the cycling industry a new number to chase.

Reading performance of Bertolt Brecht's "The Caucasian Chalk Circle" in Tehran

Reading performance of Bertolt Brecht's "The Caucasian Chalk Circle" in Tehran
TEHRAN - The Nofel Loshato Theater in Tehran will host the reading performance of the play "The Caucasian Chalk Circle" by the German modernist playwright Bertolt Brecht on Saturday night, October 10.
Directed by Morteza Sabahi, the play will be read by Abbas Sherizadeh, Alireza Sharif, Hossein Mousavi, Hashem Issalou, Zeinab Mohiabadi, Parisa Davoudi, Bahar Same'eh, Masoud Mahmoudi, Farshad Asadi, Delaram Shakeri, Paeiz Ghorbani, Alireza Motamed, Arian Nayeb-ol-Sadr, Sahar Kilani, Farhaneh Kalantari, Pegah Asharizadeh, and Fardin Kasehpour, Mehr reported.
An example of Brecht's epic theater, the play is a parable about a peasant girl who rescues a baby and becomes a better mother than the baby's wealthy biological parents.
The play was written in 1944 while Brecht was living in the United States. It was translated into English by Brecht's friend and admirer Eric Bentley. After Bentley failed to have it programmed at the University of Minnesota, where he taught, it was premiered by his student, Henry Goodman, in a student production at Carleton College, Northfield, Minnesota, in 1948.
"The Caucasian Chalk Circle" is one of Brecht's most celebrated works and one of the most regularly performed German plays.
It reworks Brecht's earlier short story "Der Augsburger Kreidekreis." Both derive from the 14th-century Chinese play "The Chalk Circle" by Li Xingdao.
Brecht, in his typical anti-realist style, uses the device of a "play within a play". The "frame" play is set in the Soviet Union around the end of the Second World War. It shows a dispute between two communes, the Collective Fruit Farm Galinsk fruit-growing commune and the Collective Goat Farmers, over who is to own and manage an area of farmland after the Germans have retreated from a village and left it abandoned.
A parable has been organised by one group, an old folk tale, to be played out to cast light on the dispute.
The Singer, Arkadi Tcheidse, arrives with his band of musicians, then tells the peasants the parable, which forms the main narrative and intertwines throughout much of the play. The Singer often takes on the thoughts of characters, enhances the more dramatic scenes with stronger narration than simple dialogue, and is responsible for most scene and time changes. Often the role is accompanied by several "musicians" that help the Singer keep the play running smoothly.
At the end, he states that the land should go to those who will use it most productively, the fruit growers, and not those who had previous ownership.

When a Threat Alone Moves a Superpower&#8217;s Bombers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:55:34 UTC
17:55:34 KST

On Sunday, Oct. 4, every American B-1 bomber at RAF Fairford lifted off and flew home. Twelve aircraft, the backbone of the only forward bomber base available to Washington in Europe, left within hours. No ceremony marked the departure. U.S. European Command confirmed only that “all U.S. bombers that were deployed to R.A.F. Fairford are redeploying to their home stations in the United States.” The reason traced back eight days to a Sunday morning when five British men were arrested near the base’s perimeter, three white vans were found suspicious enough to trigger a bomb-disposal response, and 85 homes were evacuated.
Iran did not fire a shot. It did not need to.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC on Sept. 30 that “there are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation.” He would not elaborate, saying he would “say more in due course.” Iran’s response was immediate and furious. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi mocked Burnham directly on X, paraphrasing him sarcastically: “PM Burnham says the UK Government ‘can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part’ in the RAF Fairford incident.” Iran’s embassy in London went further, saying it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” linking Tehran to the five suspects, who were released on bail without charge.
The episode was not without precedent. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard had named Fairford directly in July, declaring that any British base used to strike Iranian territory would be considered “a legitimate target.”
President Trump, asked on the South Lawn whether the bombers had been moved in response to a threat, did not equivocate. “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident,” he said. “There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we keep them there? So, we moved them around a little bit, not very far.” He added, pointedly, “We actually know the people who made the threat.” Vice President JD Vance offered a more clinical gloss, saying the aircraft had been redeployed “out of an abundance of caution, trying to protect our guys.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the underlying incident “a very serious situation” that “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor,” though he separately sought to frame the bomber withdrawal itself as routine, telling reporters the Pentagon is “constantly reallocating resources where they need to be.”
That framing has not held up well in Washington’s own commentary.
Critics, writing in outlets not reflexively hostile to this administration, have called the episode something closer to a retreat than a routine rotation.
One described the pattern bluntly: “I don’t care whether you do the attack or not, but threatening an intensive attack and then backing down projects enormous weakness.” A Newsweek analysis titled “The Hidden Irony of the Fairford B-1 Retreat” noted that the base was one of only a few European airfields suited to heavy bombers, and that Trump himself had earlier complained, when Britain briefly withheld access, of American aircraft “flying many extra hours.” The irony, as that piece put it, is that a Pentagon trying to shrink its European footprint has just demonstrated why that footprint mattered.
The operational consequences are real, whatever the political framing. Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum, put it plainly: “The U.S. has lost a crucial launching pad, not a core strike capability.” Christoph Bergs, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera that the withdrawal “reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat.” The arithmetic explains why. RAF Fairford sits roughly 2,500 miles from Iran’s western border. Diego Garcia, the remote atoll in the Indian Ocean that now becomes the likelier alternative, is about 2,300 miles from Iran’s eastern border, broadly comparable in distance but requiring aircraft to cross the width of the country to reach western targets. Continental U.S. bases sit roughly 6,500 miles out. Every one of those miles has to be covered twice, out and back, by aircraft that either carry extra fuel or depend on a chain of aerial tankers that must themselves be protected, fueled, and scheduled. More distance means fewer sorties per week, more crew fatigue, and a tanker fleet stretched thinner across a wider arc.
Gulf bases closer to Iran would shorten that chain considerably, but they carry a different cost: hosting nations that have already absorbed Iranian retaliation during this war are wary of being treated as co-belligerents for a campaign they did not choose.
Into that gap steps the Navy. The USS Theodore Roosevelt left San Diego on Sept. 27, bound for the region to help build what officials describe as a three-carrier presence alongside the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, the largest Gulf buildup since the 2003 Iraq invasion. Carriers offer flexibility bombers forward-based in Europe cannot. They also offer Iran a single, enormously valuable target to study, track and, conceivably, threaten in turn.
What Fairford demonstrated, in the end, is not that American power has weakened. It is that the premium on convenience—the quiet advantage of a short flight to target—has become expensive in a new way. A non-state plot, never charged, never fully explained, forced a superpower’s bombers off NATO soil in a single day.
Whether that was a one-time scare or the opening move in a longer contest over where American airpower can safely sit will depend less on Tehran’s next statement than on what the Pentagon decides convenience is now worth.

India detains ‘Cockroach’ leaders amid voter list protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:50:00 UTC
17:50:00 KST

Indian authorities mounted a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi on Saturday, detaining thousands of protesters as the country’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement sought to escalate a nationwide campaign against a contentious revision of voter lists.
The dispute has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of the capital.
Officers chased away some protesters and detained many others, with several dragged away and bundled into police vehicles before being taken to temporary detention centers.
Several leaders of the “Cockroach” movement were also detained before reaching the venue, severely disrupting the planned demonstration before it could begin.
The security operation extended well beyond the protest site, with police setting up checkpoints on roads leading into the capital.
Officers stopped buses, cars and other vehicles and searched them for demonstrators as authorities moved to prevent protesters from gathering in the city.
Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet access and movement in parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.
The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi.
The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the “Cockroach” movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi’s education minister to resign in July.
Movement leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of Saturday’s protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai.
A video shared by the “Cockroach Janta Party” on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
“The preplanned interception by Delhi police aims to cripple the leadership of today’s peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site,” the movement said in a statement.
Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.
“We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn’t we fight for our rights?” said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?”
The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
“Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out,” opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.
The protests center on the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters.
Protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the revision, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Saturday’s planned demonstration followed days of protests in the capital, where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign. Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police.
Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi’s party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while BJP supporters have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
For the “Cockroach” movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi’s home state, will test the party’s standing.

stefan sagmeister and ekn transform global data into colorful sneakers and boots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:49:48 UTC
17:49:48 KST

stefan sagmeister and ekn transform global data into colorful sneakers and boots
the designer collaborates with ekn footwear on a data-driven sneaker and leather boot for his upcoming paris exhibition.
STEFAN SAGMEISTER AND EKN TURN DATA INTO WEARABLE DESIGN
Stefan Sagmeister is taking his data visualizations somewhere they rarely go: onto people’s feet. In collaboration with Frankfurt-based ekn footwear, the Austrian graphic designer has developed a sneaker and a boot that translate statistics on renewable electricity and street homelessness into wearable objects. The two designs accompany his exhibition Finally, Something Good., opening at La Gaîté Lyrique in Paris on October 15, 2026. Rather than simply reproducing existing artworks on footwear, the project brings together graphic design and traditional shoemaking. ‘It was about seeing what happens when Stefan’s way of thinking meets our way of making things,’ ekn founder Noel Klein-Reesink tells designboom in an exclusive interview.
For Sagmeister, the attraction lies in reaching an audience beyond the exhibition space. ‘A painting in a gallery or museum is seen by people who decided to come in and look. A shoe is seen on the street by people who decided nothing of the sort,’ he explains to designboom. The collaboration extends his ongoing exploration of long-term social progress through visualized data, previously presented across historic paintings, installations and everyday objects. Klein-Reesink sees a natural connection between this approach and footwear design. ‘What has always interested us about his work is the way he turns complex information into something immediate and visual,’ he says. Here, the artwork no longer has to wait for visitors. It can catch their attention on the way to the supermarket.
RENEWABLE ENERGY AND HOMELESSNESS SHAPE TWO SHOE DESIGNS
The first model, Bring It On, is a colorful suede sneaker visualizing worldwide renewable electricity generation between 1965 and 2022, including hydro, wind, solar and other renewable sources. The rising figures become a graphic composition across the shoe’s upper, while the complete dataset appears on the footbed. ‘With Bring It On, the shapes and colours became part of the overall design of the sneaker, while the complete information sits on the footbed,’ explains Klein-Reesink from ekn. For Sagmeister, the subject carries particular significance. ‘While everybody is talking about AI, I find the improvement in renewable electricity generation more consequential,’ he tells designboom, pointing to the possibilities that cheaper renewable energy could unlock, from vertical farming to desalination and carbon capture.
The second design, Like a Complete Unknown, takes a more uncomfortable subject and gives it the form of a cream-colored leather boot. Its embroidered graphics visualize reported street homelessness across six countries, drawing on the OECD Affordable Housing Database. The figures range from 76 people living on the street or in public spaces per 100,000 inhabitants in the United States to 46 in Germany, 16 in the United Kingdom, eight in France, five in Mexico and two in Japan. ‘For Like a Complete Unknown, the graphic is embroidered directly onto the leather,’ Klein-Reesink explains. Sagmeister is equally direct about the limitations of the comparison: ‘The numbers are not perfect.’ Different national definitions and collection methods mean that the figures cannot be treated as an exact measure of relative homelessness. Yet the designer argues that imperfect statistics can still open discussions that might otherwise remain abstract.
EKN BRINGS SAGMEISTER’S GRAPHICS TO FOOTWEAR
Turning the graphics into functional footwear required more than choosing where to place a colorful motif. Both designs build on existing ekn silhouettes, adapting the original visualizations to the curves, panels and construction of each model. The sneaker uses chrome-free tanned suede, while the boot combines chrome-free tanned smooth leather with embroidered graphics. According to Klein-Reesink, the process involved repeated exchanges with embroidery specialists and manufacturing partners in Portugal. ‘It was a very practical process. You make a sample, look at the actual shoe, change a detail and try again,’ he explains. The challenge was to preserve Sagmeister’s visual language without forgetting the rather essential requirement that the finished objects should still work as shoes.
The collaboration also raises a question that neither partner appears interested in avoiding: what does it mean to sell a luxury-priced boot addressing homelessness? ‘There is something awkward about a 350 euro boot that carries homelessness data, and I don’t think a donation makes that go away,’ Sagmeister acknowledges. The boot retails for €350, while the sneaker costs €300. Ten percent of each sale will support organizations connected to the respective subjects: €35 from each boot goes to the Coalition for the Homeless in New York, and €30 from each sneaker to Future Cleantech Architects in Germany. As Klein-Reesink explains, ‘ten percent of the retail price goes to organisations working in the respective fields.’ The donations do not resolve the tension between the products and their messages, but they form part of an attempt to connect the visualized information with action beyond the objects themselves.
EKN FOOTWEAR EMBRACES MADE-TO-ORDER PRODUCTION
Both models are handmade at a footwear workshop in Portugal and will be produced through a limited pre-order system rather than manufactured in advance. Orders will be accepted from October 14 to November 15, 2026, with delivery scheduled for January 2027. Available in EU sizes 36 to 46, the shoes will enter production according to actual demand, an approach intended to reduce unsold stock. ‘The main advantage is very simple: after the pre-order period, we know how many pairs people actually want,’ Klein-Reesink explains. For the founder, who established ekn in 2015, the system reflects a broader philosophy of responsible manufacturing. ‘Sustainability is not only about choosing a better material,’ he adds, emphasizing the importance of production methods, durability and quantities.
Ultimately, the project returns to a relatively simple proposition: information becomes more accessible when it enters everyday life. Sagmeister’s exhibition Finally, Something Good. examines the distance between public perceptions of the world and measurable developments over time, using visual culture to question the often overwhelmingly negative narratives of contemporary life. These two shoes carry that investigation onto the street, where a graphic might initially attract attention for its colors or unusual composition before revealing what it represents. ‘For us, good design also means making something properly and making it to last,’ Klein-Reesink says. Whether wearers end up discussing renewable energy, homelessness or simply their new shoes remains open. For Sagmeister, the exchange itself is what matters: ‘That conversation is the piece.’

designer: Stefan Sagmeister | @stefansagmeister
partner: ekn footwear | @eknfootwear
exhibition dates: October 15, 2026 – April 18, 2027
pre-order: October 14 – November 15, 2026

The IDF order activated during the flydubai hijack attempt and its extreme measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:48:03 UTC
17:48:03 KST

Ten days after the attempted hijacking and crash of a flydubai passenger aircraft, details have emerged about an IDF directive known as "World Trade," which governs the military's response to suspected hijackings of civilian aircraft.
Under the directive, Israeli fighter jets can be scrambled to confront hijackers or terrorists and prevent an aviation incident from escalating into a wider catastrophe, including attacks on strategic installations or additional casualties beyond those aboard the aircraft. In an extreme scenario, the procedure allows fighter jets to shoot down the passenger plane. Alternatively, they can escort it to a secure landing at an airport.
The decision to shoot down a civilian aircraft would be exceptionally rare and could be made only following consultations with senior defense officials acting under the direction of Israel's political leadership.
Such a measure is intended to prevent an even greater disaster, including mass casualties on the ground in addition to those aboard the aircraft, or an attack on strategic infrastructure that could cause severe damage to national security.
During the initial moments of the flydubai incident, the circumstances remained unclear, and the IDF prepared for the possibility that the aircraft was being hijacked.
Shortly after the military received an alert about the situation aboard the plane, two Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled to escort it while officials assessed the developing incident and considered their response.
The scramble was carried out under procedures the IDF regularly practices for scenarios involving civilian aircraft approaching Israel that deviate from their designated flight paths, fail to respond to radio communications, transmit distress signals or become the target of a hijacking attempt.
When necessary, fighter jets are dispatched to identify and escort the aircraft, while authorities simultaneously consider whether to close Israeli airspace. The Israeli Air Force maintains continuous readiness to respond to a wide range of aerial threats and prevent unauthorized incursions into the country's airspace. Its units operate around the clock, monitoring the skies, identifying irregularities and detecting potential threats while maintaining the ability to scramble aircraft at short notice.
This readiness relies on a continuously updated aerial picture, forces on standby and regular exercises simulating different emergencies. The objective is to identify unusual incidents as early as possible, make rapid decisions and respond according to how the situation develops.
One of the scenarios regularly rehearsed by the Air Force involves civilian aircraft approaching Israel.
Under the dedicated directive, the military can respond to situations in which an unusual incident may develop into an airborne terrorist attack, including a hijacking or an attempt to deliberately crash an aircraft with its passengers aboard.
The procedure can be activated under a variety of circumstances, including an aircraft deviating from its planned route, failing to respond to radio calls, transmitting a distress signal, experiencing a technical malfunction or facing a medical emergency requiring an urgent landing.
Once activated, measures are taken to protect Israeli airspace. In some cases, these may include closing the country's airspace entirely to prevent a potentially more serious incident.
The Air Force regularly rehearses its response, focusing on reducing reaction times and ensuring it can move quickly from detecting an irregularity to understanding the situation and implementing the appropriate measures.
The IDF emphasizes that activating the directive does not necessarily indicate a suspected security incident. In some cases, the procedure may be triggered by a technical malfunction, communications failure, deviation from the planned flight path or human error by the aircraft's crew. Each unusual incident is investigated and handled until the concern has been resolved and authorities have established a clear picture of what happened.

Burgas Chamber of Commerce and Industry analyses Bulgaria’s business environment

2026-10-10

Article
Burgas Chamber of Commerce and Industry analyses Bulgaria’s business environment
Saturday 10 October 2026 10:25
Saturday, 10 October 2026, 10:25
PHOTO Archive
Font size
Predictable regulations, a skilled workforce and sound infrastructure are among the factors increasingly shaping where international companies choose to invest. This is one of the key findings of a special analysis by the Burgas Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) examining Bulgaria’s advantages as a business destination.
The analysis also notes that wages in Bulgaria are rising while the working-age population is shrinking, leaving companies across a range of sectors struggling to find suitably qualified employees.
According to the report, productivity, access to financing, the administrative environment and, above all, the predictability of regulations, including tax rules, are becoming increasingly important. Uncertainty in these areas has prompted some companies to scale back or relocate their operations outside Bulgaria.
One example cited is Japanese company Sumitomo Electric Bordnetze SE (SEBN SE), which has closed its plant in Mezdra in northwestern Bulgaria and announced steps to reduce its operations in Karnobat, in the southeast of the country. The reasons include high production costs and a substantial increase in labour costs. Some of its production has been transferred to Moldova and Romania.
The Sumitomo Electric Bordnetze SE plant in Karnobat
PHOTO SEBN BG
The BCCI analysis also cites other similar cases, including Bosch’s planned closure of its engineering centre in Sofia by mid-2027, affecting around 670 employees; the shutdown of MD Elektronik’s plant in Vratsa, resulting in the loss of approximately 550 jobs; and Unilever’s relocation of production from the Bulgarian town of Debelets to Romania, Greece and Turkey.
The report also examines the Finance Ministry’s proposal to introduce a one-off additional tax on profits in 2027 across six sectors: banking, insurance, telecommunications, large supermarket chains, currency exchange bureaux and payday lending companies.
The Burgas Chamber stresses that, for businesses, the issue extends beyond the level of taxation to encompass the predictability of tax policy and confidence in the long-term stability of the rules. It also warns that changes to banks’ capital positions could affect lending conditions for businesses.
The analysis further cites a survey conducted by the German-Bulgarian Chamber of Industry and Commerce among 83 companies. According to the findings, 70% of respondents plan to maintain or increase their investments in Bulgaria, while 77% are not considering relocating their operations.

The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) will issue a gold collector coin dedicated to St John (Ivan) of Rila, the heavenly patron saint of Bulgaria, on 12 October, the bank has announced. The coin, part of the Bulgarian Iconography series, has a face value of €100 and will be sold at an issue price of €1,508.
In the Bulgarian Orthodox tradition, Saint John of Rila the Wonderworker is revered as the spiritual father, guide and heavenly protector of the Bulgarian people. He was born around 876 in the village of Skrino, in the Osogovo Mountains. It is believed that he received his education and embraced the monastic life at the Monastery of St Demetrius, below Ruen Peak. He later left the monastery and withdrew into solitude, dedicating himself to fasting and prayer.
As a hermit, St John lived in several remote places before reaching the Rila Mountains, where he settled for the remainder of his life. There he founded the Rila Monastery, a sacred sanctuary and enduring stronghold of Orthodox faith and Bulgarian identity to this day.
The year 2026 marks the 1,150th anniversary of the saint's birth and the 1,080th anniversary of his blessed repose.

US Tests Ukrainian Counter-Drone Technology in Key Defense Initiative
Ukrainian electronic warfare systems built by Phantom Defense have been tested in the United States as part of Gauntlet II, a key stage of the American Drone Dominance program, according to Militarnyi.
During the trials, the company deployed a complete anti-drone defense network combining electronic countermeasure systems, the Streamhunter video interception system, and a command and control (C2) framework used for target detection, classification, action execution, and outcome verification.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Phantom Defense reported that its combat-proven systems have detected over 11,000 enemy drones during deployment in integrated defense systems, with video footage officially confirming more than 7,000 successful neutralizations.
The equipment presented included the Specter PRO, a dome-type and directional electronic warfare system created to safeguard company strongpoints, brigade headquarters, and critical infrastructure facilities.
The trial also featured the Specter L, Specter X, and Specter XL, which form a series of compact electronic warfare tools optimized for complex and extreme environments. These mobile units are used by front-line teams to shield military personnel and vehicles operating close to the combat line, Militarnyi reported.
During the event, Phantom Defense used its Streamhunter technology to intercept live video feeds broadcast from participating unmanned aerial vehicles. The integrated C2 platform oversaw situational awareness, shared target data, and coordinated all active countermeasures.
The company confirmed to journalists that every radio-controlled aircraft permitted in this testing phase was affected by its jammers, stating, “Not a single radio-controlled platform passed the test without being affected by our systems. Depending on the scenario, the impact hit the control channel, the video link, or other parts of the radio signal.”
Testing took place under strict radio frequency regulations that differed from actual operational conditions in Ukraine, though specific performance metrics regarding individual drone manufacturers remain confidential, as reported by Militarnyi.
Beyond jamming duties, Phantom Defense simulated real battlefield conditions to measure how active electronic warfare alters unmanned flight performance. Following the successful trial, American organizers invited the Ukrainian firm to participate in upcoming events and future testing phases within the Drone Dominance initiative.
Earlier, at the Eurosatory 2026 defense exhibition in Paris, Ukrainian defense company Phantom Defense showcased an integrated counter-drone ecosystem that combined detection sensors, electronic warfare tools, kinetic interceptors, and a command-and-control platform.
Operating under a "Detect–Defeat" framework, the system processed data from radars, ELINT sensors, and video feeds to track threats, assist operators, and record engagement outcomes.
The presentation featured the Specter electronic warfare suite, Blade and Balaban interceptor drones, Karakurt net launchers, the Streamhunter video interception system, and the Skydarix AESA radar. According to the company, these technologies were combat-tested in Ukraine to protect urban infrastructure, successfully neutralizing over 7,000 enemy drones.

Isaias weakens after making landfall in US Gulf Coast as hurricane
More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama have been left without power as Isaias downs trees, power lines.
Hurricane Isaias has crashed into the United States Gulf Coast before losing speed and turning into a post-tropical storm as it moved over southern Alabama, threatening flash flooding and strong winds farther inland.
The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Saturday that Isaias is about 89km (55 miles) south-southwest of Montgomery, with maximum sustained winds of 100 kilometres per hour (65 miles per hour).
When it made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), the agency said.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways.
While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended their emergency response on Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama were also flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines.
Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could reach 0.91-1.52 metres (3-5ft) from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Florida’s Aucilla River, according to the hurricane centre.
The storm grounded most Friday flights at several airports, including all flights in and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport.
‘Under control’
Asked about hurricane preparations, President Donald Trump told reporters outside the White House, “We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” adding that it was “under control”.
Florida’s National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, with search-and-rescue teams ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.
“Emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X, as residents were urged to take shelter and watch out for hurricane conditions.
Another tropical storm, Rachel, was also expected to bring strong winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.
And Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrelled towards Mexico’s coast early on Saturday.
The NHC said Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 225km/h (140mph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along the coast of Jalisco and in parts of Michoacan, Colima, and Nayarit.
Forecasters warned of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Faster front-line delivery with new Testing and Evaluation programme
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
09:30:01 BST
17:30:01 KST

Faster front-line delivery with new Testing and Evaluation programme
MOD and QinetiQ launch Project Safari, a joint programme opening up access to UK test and evaluation facilities for SMEs.
- MOD and QinetiQ revolutionising access to Test and Evaluation facilities for SMEs, delivering new tech into service faster
- SAFARI will remove barriers to UK sites, helping new capabilities move from development to deployment quicker
- Supports SDR commitment to support SMEs with additional £2.5 billion every year by 2028
Technologies such as hypersonic missiles, directed energy weapons and autonomous systems will be assessed, refined and delivered quicker than ever before, following a joint Ministry of Defence (MOD) and QinetiQ programme transforming how defence capabilities are tested and evaluated at the pace of modern warfare.
Project Safari will revolutionise access to the UK’s sovereign Test and Evaluation (T&E) facilities for Small and Medium Enterprises, creating an agile environment to prove and deliver new technologies into service faster.
For too long, companies – especially those that are SMEs or new to working in defence – have faced barriers that have prevented them getting their ideas and technology tested in real life scenarios, such as outdated bureaucracy to gain multiple levels of approvals.
This programme will remove barriers to UK sites, providing a single front-door for SMEs to access facilities and improving the approval processes for trial activity. That smoother route for innovative firms into the sector will help support jobs and investment in their local economies, powering growth in every postcode.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP, said:
  We know that limited access to test and evaluation facilities have been holding back smaller businesses and new entrants from working with defence.
By working hand-in-hand with QinetiQ, we are unlocking British innovation by developing, testing and delivering military capabilities for the UK and our allies at speed.
Group CEO QinetiQ, Steve Wadey, said:
  Turning ideas into trusted frontline capability faster than our adversaries is what delivers military advantage and we’ve got to go faster to stay ahead. Project Safari will transform how the UK approves new technologies, creating a world-leading test and evaluation enterprise that helps government, industry and regulators work together to accelerate the delivery of military capability at the pace demanded by modern warfare.
Project Safari will bring together government, industry, regulators and technology innovators to support the UK’s warfighting readiness and streamline how companies access specialist facilities and expertise, modernise the infrastructure so it’s fit for a fast-moving digital environment and reduce unnecessary barriers to accelerate decision making.
During a visit to MOD Hebrides, the UK’s largest weapons test range, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP, signed an agreement with QinetiQ for the first design stage of a multimillion-pound investment to develop the site to enable the testing of hypersonic missiles and other advanced technologies.
The minister was joined by QinetiQ CEO, Steve Wadey to host a roundtable with SME representatives, including Greenjets and Cambridge Aerospace, to listen to the experiences of SMEs accessing T&E services and the barriers they can face.
Luke Pollard MP also met one of the UK companies competing in Project Brakestop, MGI Engineering. An Oxfordshire-based SME, they are developing low-cost long-range weapons for Ukraine.
Project Safari is a practical demonstration of the ambitions set out in the Strategic Defence Review, which committed defence to increasing its spend with SMEs by £2.5 billion a year by summer 2028.
The announcement builds on the work of the Defence Investment Plan, backed by £298 billion of funding in UK defence over the next four years. The plan will drive sustained investment across British industry – including SMEs – ensuring the UK’s defence sector remains a cornerstone of the country’s economic renewal.

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Pakistan received 10.9 billion U.S. dollars in workers' remittances during the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27, up 14.74 percent year on year, the State Bank of Pakistan said Friday.
Remittances stood at 3.6 billion dollars in September, up 12.7 percent from 3.2 billion dollars in the same month last year, but down 1.9 percent from August, according to the central bank.
Saudi Arabia remained the largest source of remittances in September, with inflows reaching 899.13 million dollars, up 19.73 percent year on year. Remittances from the United Arab Emirates rose 10 percent to 748.53 million dollars.
Inflows from Britain increased 13.3 percent year on year to 515.15 million dollars, while those from the United States rose 13.7 percent to 305.87 million dollars.
Remittances from European Union countries totaled 447.71 million dollars, down 9.7 percent from August, the data showed.
Workers' remittances are a key source of foreign exchange for Pakistan, helping support its external account and household incomes. ■

====================================================================================================

FIA admits human error affects Singapore GP sprint qualifying
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:26:30 CST
17:26:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Formula One's governing body, the FIA, has admitted that human error in race control caused some drivers to have less engine power than others during Friday's sprint qualifying session for the Singapore Grand Prix.
The problem occurred after a red flag in the opening session (SQ1), caused by Sergio Perez damaging the front wing of his Cadillac, and affected drivers differently depending on their position on the track and the timing of their flying laps.
The FIA said overtake mode, which allows drivers to use additional electrical energy, was automatically disabled during the stoppage but was not immediately reactivated when the session resumed.
Officials subsequently enabled the mode for 27 seconds before switching it off again, leaving some drivers with a power advantage over their rivals.
"During the first period of sprint qualifying there was a human error in race control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1," the FIA said in a statement.
"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap."
The governing body said the second and third sessions of sprint qualifying were unaffected.
Williams driver Carlos Sainz, who was slowest of all and eliminated in SQ1, criticized the inconsistency and questioned why the FIA had not intervened to ensure equal conditions for all competitors.
"Half the cars did the lap with half a second quicker engine than the others," Sainz said.
"There was another software issue and we were on the bad end of it, and for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, again didn't decide to do sporting equity."
Sainz acknowledged that his own performance had been poor and that brake problems had also compromised his session, adding that he did not believe he would have progressed even without the power deployment issue.
Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll were also among those affected and eliminated in SQ1. Stroll's teammate Fernando Alonso encountered the problem but advanced to SQ2, eventually qualifying 15th.
Mercedes driver George Russell was told over team radio during the session that the reduced power was caused by an FIA settings issue, while several other drivers complained of unexpectedly limited energy deployment.
The incident came just a week after a separate software malfunction disrupted the initial starting procedure for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, prompting further questions about the reliability of the systems governing Formula 1's new generation of cars.
Friday's qualifying was also affected by an unrelated timing system glitch that prevented some lap times from being recorded correctly at the end of SQ1.
The problem briefly delayed the start of SQ2 while officials verified the results and established the correct running order.
The FIA said the power deployment error was separate from the timing malfunction, and there was no indication that either problem had directly changed which drivers were eliminated from the opening session. ■

U.S. reports record measles cases in decades
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:26:29 CST
17:26:29 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The United States has reported over 4,000 confirmed measles cases this year, topping the highest annual total since 1991, according to data released Friday by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
As of Thursday, a total of 4,080 measles cases had been confirmed in the United States in 2026, with 4,062 reported from 47 U.S. jurisdictions and 18 from international visitors. The total has already surpassed the 2,289 cases reported last year.
As many as 414 patients or about 10 percent of the total have been hospitalized, while 1,716 infected people aged 5 to 19 accounted for 42 percent or the largest share of all cases.
The CDC data showed that 95 percent of patients were unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.
Pennsylvania has recently seen a sharp rise in measles cases. The state's health department reported Friday that 1,136 cases had been confirmed so far, including 219 patients hospitalized and five dead, the largest state-level measles outbreak in more than three decades, said Pennsylvanian health officials.
The CDC recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as the best protection against measles. The agency said that when more than 95 percent of people in a community are vaccinated, community immunity, also known as herd immunity, helps protect more people from the disease. ■

MANILA, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Mount Kanlaon Volcano in the central Philippines erupted just over noon Saturday, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology said.
According to the institute, a "moderately explosive eruption" occurred at Mount Kanlaon Volcano in Negros Island at 12:46 p.m. local time Saturday. The eruption lasted for about two minutes.
The institute said the event generated a plume that rose 5 km to 6 km above the crater. The ashfall is expected to drift north and northeast.
Alert Level 2 is maintained over Mount Kanlaon volcano, with Level 5 the highest in scale.
The Philippine archipelago straddles the Pacific "Ring of Fire" and is prone to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. ■

====================================================================================================

Trump Administration Sanctions International Criminal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:26:00 UTC
17:26:00 KST

Trump Administration Sanctions International Criminal Court
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of the tribunal’s former judges received the Nobel Peace Prize, Deutsche Welle reported.
The move follows months of increasingly open U.S. efforts to weaken the court, in what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described as a “sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court.”
The United States and Israel have strongly opposed ICC arrest warrants issued against senior Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Washington has also objected since 2020, during the final part of Trump’s first term, to investigations into military operations in Afghanistan. Those inquiries have shifted priority away from alleged U.S. wrongdoing and toward the Taliban, although U.S. actions may still be included.
“President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said in a statement.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” the secretary of state added.
The ICC condemned the measures, saying they sought to obstruct an independent international tribunal backed by more than half of the United Nations’ member states.
“The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said. Akane is already subject to U.S. sanctions.
Based in The Hague, the Netherlands, the International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal. It is the only permanent international court with theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.
Established in 2002, the ICC operates under the Rome Statute. A total of 125 countries have signed and ratified the treaty, becoming full members. Several major powers, including China, India, Russia, the United States and Israel, do not recognize the court’s jurisdiction.
However, the ICC can consider cases brought by member states against individuals from countries that have not accepted its authority. This has led to high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Netanyahu, following complaints brought by Ukrainians and Palestinians, respectively.
During Trump’s second term, the U.S. administration has intensified its criticism of the court, with Rubio frequently leading the campaign. In an opinion article published by The Wall Street Journal in mid-July, he argued that the United States had never accepted the authority of an international tribunal to supersede its own legal system.
“America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution,” Rubio wrote.
He warned that U.S. “soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders” could be “dragged before an international court” and judged by “from random countries across the globe.”
On July 25, Venezuela’s new administration announced plans to leave the Rome Statute and the ICC. The announcement followed the U.S. abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January.
The U.S. State Department welcomed the decision, praising “the new Venezuelan government's partnership on American-led efforts to dismantle the corrupt and worthless ICC” and urging “all members of the ICC to withdraw from the Rome Statute.”
Several days later, Chad’s military junta also announced that it would withdraw from the court. The authorities said the decision followed a request from Washington, which was urging other African countries to follow suit.
The sexual misconduct scandal involving ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, also gave Washington further grounds to criticize the institution.
In August, the United States imposed sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese judge, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court. The launch of the sanctions had initially been expected around the time of the United Nations General Assembly.
Speculation had grown in recent months that Washington would eventually target the ICC as an institution rather than limiting sanctions to individual officials.
Last month, widespread reports suggested Trump might announce the measures during his address at the U.N. headquarters in New York. Unnamed sources in the United States and in The Hague said preparations for the sanctions were underway.
Trump ultimately delivered a sharp attack on the ICC in his September 22 speech, calling it an “evil” organization, but did not announce new sanctions at the time.

Cambodia celebrates traditional Pchum Ben festival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:25:50 CST
17:25:50 KST

A woman prepares offerings during the Pchum Ben festival in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Oct. 10, 2026. Cambodia on Saturday started to observe its traditional three-day Pchum Ben holiday, also known as Ancestor's Day, running from Oct. 10 to 12. (Photo by Sovannara/Xinhua)
PHNOM PENH, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia on Saturday started to observe its traditional three-day Pchum Ben holiday, also known as Ancestor's Day, running from Oct. 10 to 12.
Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said that Pchum Ben is a deeply rooted tradition celebrated annually since ancient times.
"As we observe this traditional festival, I wish all families and loved ones a safe journey to your hometowns to reunite with your families," he shared in a social media message. "May this occasion bring you good health, lasting happiness, and success in every endeavor."
As part of the holiday rush, hundreds of thousands of workers and residents leave Phnom Penh to visit their families.
The prime minister said that to support travelers, the Phnom Penh Capital Administration arranged 600 free public buses to help ease financial pressure and ensure safe holiday transit.
Pchum Ben is the second-largest celebration in Cambodia following the Lunar New Year. During this occasion, Cambodians engage in alms-giving and merit-making to honor relatives and ancestors who have passed away.
Buddhist devotees travel to local pagodas to present offerings to monks, believing these acts transfer spiritual merit to their deceased loved ones, who in turn bestow good luck upon the living.
According to the Ministry of Cult and Religion, Buddhist devotees make up roughly 95 percent of the nation's population. ■
People offer steamed rice to honor their ancestors during the Pchum Ben festival in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Oct. 10, 2026. Cambodia on Saturday started to observe its traditional three-day Pchum Ben holiday, also known as Ancestor's Day, running from Oct. 10 to 12. (Photo by Sovannara/Xinhua)
