Cuneiform tablets from Hittite King unearthed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:40:41 UTC
15:40:41 KST

Recent excavations at ancient Samuha uncovered a major finding illuminating Hittite state records.
A total of 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments dating to the reign of Hittite King Tudhaliya II have been unearthed during excavations at Kayalıpınar in the central Turkish province of Sivas, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced.
Ersoy announced on social media that recent excavations at ancient Samuha uncovered a major finding illuminating Hittite state records.
“In the 2026 excavations, we unearthed 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments dating to the reign of King Tudhaliya II at ancient Samuha. Together with those found in the previous season, the number has reached 184,” Ersoy said. “Thus, the royal archive at Kayalıpınar has taken its place in history as the most extensive Hittite-language archive discovered in the 21st century. These documents, written in Hittite and Hurrian, directly convey to the present day information about state administration, military developments, religious beliefs and the experiences of the royal family approximately 3,400 years ago.”
Ersoy said the tablets contain evidence of a high-fever epidemic that spread from city to city and particularly affected children and infants. The records include the health condition of an infant princess who fell ill, her subsequent death and the funeral ritual held for her.
Another letter sent to the king by Hittite generals in western Anatolia reveals that they requested soldiers, horses and chariots in the face of an enemy threat, warning that the army could be destroyed if reinforcements failed to arrive, Ersoy said.
Tablets documenting the routes and observations of bird diviners also provide previously unknown information about Hittite divination practices, he added.
“This unique archive opens a new door in many fields, from Hittite history and religious practices to the development of language and the culture of scribes,” Ersoy said.
Excavations at Kayalıpınar have been conducted since 2021 by a team led by Çiğdem Maner, an associate professor at Koç University’s Department of Archaeology and History of Art.
The 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments discovered at the same site in 2025 are also believed to belong to the royal archive. With the 131 new finds from 2026, the archive now contains 184 tablets and fragments.
According to the excavation team, the royal archive uncovered at Kayalıpınar is the most extensive Hittite-language archive discovered in the 21st century. The archive contains texts covering divination, omens, letters, rituals and prayers. Among the most striking documents are those describing a high-fever epidemic that spread from one city to another.
The disease appears to have been particularly deadly for children and infants. The tablets show that the health of young princes and princesses, as well as children of high-ranking Hittite officials, was monitored through divination inquiries.
The texts also reflect the anxiety the epidemic caused within the Hittite royal family. One document records great concern over the health of an infant princess who was still being breastfed, with attempts made to determine her future through divination. Another tablet records the princess’s death and the funeral ritual performed for her.
Military threats
Documents from the royal archive also shed light on the military threats faced by the Hittite state.
In a letter sent by Hittite generals in western Anatolia to the Hittite king at Samuha, the generals report that the Hittite territory was surrounded by enemies. They requested soldiers, horses and chariots to defeat the attackers.
The letter warned that without immediate support, the situation would deteriorate and risk destroying the Hittite army. The generals made it clear to the king that if reinforcements were not sent, they would not take responsibility for the outcome.
One tablet records, in diary form, observations made by bird diviners who traveled beyond Samuha to different regions.
The documents outline the diviners’ routes, the cities they visited and the birds they observed. Additionally, these cuneiform texts reveal new details on how the Hittites performed, evaluated, and interpreted bird divination.

Feature: The ferryman of life for eternal peace
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:40:36 CST
15:40:36 KST

Lu Guijun, a doctor at the Department of Pain Medicine, examines a patient at a hospice ward of Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital in Beijing, China, Sept. 28, 2026. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- In the morning, after being dressed in a white shroud, Lu Guijun was laid gently in a coffin surrounded by lilies and chrysanthemums. Relatives and friends came to say their goodbyes, one by one.
When the ritual ended, he sat up, climbed out, and hugged his wife and two children, unable to hold back his tears. It was a rehearsal funeral.
"I wanted to experience death once," he said. "So I can help my patients face the end of life."
Lu is a doctor at the Department of Pain Medicine of Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital.
When he was working at a hospital in north China's Hebei Province in previous years, he found that while the physical pain of patients with terminal cancer could be relieved, they were still tormented by regret and unfulfilled wishes as they neared the end of life.
In 1998, he started to explore hospice care on his own. At that time, few doctors in China specialized in this field.
Hospice care, which provides comprehensive support for the terminally ill, aims to manage pain, improve quality of life, and ensure a decent, peaceful passing through multidisciplinary care.
According to China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), the country will expand rehabilitation services and hospice care.
In 2019, Lu joined Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital and established a hospice team, which comprises doctors, nurses, social workers, psychological counselors, and volunteers.
For most people in China, talking about death with patients is considered taboo. But in hospice wards, it is an open topic.
"Patients here are all informed about their condition, with nothing hidden from them, and they also know they will soon leave this world," Lu said, noting that the hospice team will help them fulfill their wishes, such as cooking a meal for the family, displaying personal art masterpieces, and recording their voice.
In the hospice wards of Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, a large oil painting hangs on the wall. In the painting, a golden river meanders across the cosmic background. Lu introduced the work titled "The Long River of Life."
"The painting is filled with patients' names. Some were written by patients themselves, and some were written by relatives after the patients had died," Lu said peacefully.
Sometimes he saw relatives of deceased patients come back and gaze at the painting.
Although Lu talks about death calmly, he used to experience the panic of facing it.
In 2016, his second sister was diagnosed with liver cancer. Lu took her to many famous hospitals across China, looking for a cure. But a colleague finally told him the truth: there was no treatment left that could save her.
"At that time, I felt conflicted. As a doctor, I should accept the reality. However, as a brother, I wanted her to live longer," Lu recalled. "Whenever someone asked about my sister's condition, I could say nothing and just shed tears in silence."
After going through despair, he came to accept the reality.
In her final months, Lu and other family members stayed by her side. Each of them said what they wanted to say.
"I didn't hide her diagnosis from her or the family and always told her not to worry," Lu said. "Because our mom, dad, siblings, and her husband and children were all standing with her."
Eight months after being diagnosed, Lu's sister passed away at 46.
"From the evaluation system of hospice care, she died without regrets," Lu said. "Having experienced my sister's death, I realized that our hospice team members need to put ourselves into different perspectives."
Every Monday afternoon, Lu conducts hospice care grand rounds with his hospice team. They often review recent cases, discuss what could be improved in hospice care, and sometimes even rehearse funerals: one member lies in bed as the dead patient, while others play relatives or strangers.
"The purpose of the grand rounds sessions is to let our team experience death from a first-person perspective," Lu said. "If we do not put ourselves in patients' or their relatives' shoes, we cannot empathize with them." He added that it is a form of education about life and death for team members.
Among them is Pan Minglu, an anthropology student at Renmin University of China, who has volunteered with Lu's team for three years.
When she saw a patient pass away in the ward, she was not afraid and helped make funeral arrangements together with her team members and the patient's relatives.
"It is in hospice wards that I realized death is a natural end of the life process," she said. "Here, we can make death a foreseeable ending, which means we can see it coming and prepare for it." She explained that the horror of death for people lies in its uncertainty.
Pan is not the only university student touched by Lu's work.
In his spare time, Lu also teaches courses on life and death at universities such as Tsinghua University and Peking University Health Science Center.
Rather than giving lectures, he leads students in designing their own funeral plans and takes them to visit a funeral home.
Over time, Lu saw the students stop tensing up at the mention of death. Now they openly discuss hospice care, living wills, and body donation.
"Death is a part of life, and nothing special. The more we avoid it, the more we fear it. Only by facing death head-on can we understand it," he said. ■
Lu Guijun and his hospice team carry out the hospice care grand rounds at a conference room of Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital in Beijing, China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua)

Entering its fourth season, Türk Telekom’s “Accessible Theater” initiative continues to make arts and culture more inclusive for visually and hearing-impaired audiences, in collaboration with the Istanbul State Theater and Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM).
Launched in 2024, the project opened its new season on Oct. 9 with “Eternal Peace,” written by Juan Mayorga and translated by Canan Şahin. It will continue on Oct. 11 with “Oh, What a Wonderful Country,” a children’s play written by Şermin Yaşar.
The project makes theater performances accessible through audio description, stage tours and surtitles. 
The initiative has already reached over 1,000 visually and hearing-impaired theatergoers, and Türk Telekom plans to expand its impact even further this season.
Before performances, visually impaired theatergoers can take special stage tours, allowing them to familiarize themselves with the sets and costumes by touch. During performances, audio descriptions convey visual details such as the setting, characters and silent actions between the dialogue. For hearing-impaired audience members, surtitles provide the dialogue on screen in real time.
“Eternal Peace” explores concepts of good and evil and questions the choices between following orders and doing what is morally right, as well as whether neutrality and lasting peace are possible.
“Oh, What a Wonderful Country,” based on the question “Why does school exist?” examines school life from a child’s perspective, focusing on rules, responsibilities and living together.
Arif Sancaktaroğlu, Türk Telekom’s deputy general manager for communications, TV and digital platforms, said the company uses technology with a focus on people and social benefit.
“We will continue to develop projects that reach different segments of society, bring the power of culture and the arts to wider audiences,” Sancaktaroğlu said.

An Italian restaurant that respects its masters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:39:51 UTC
15:39:51 KST

A new Italian restaurant has opened in Istanbul: Lucente. But what first caught my attention was not its menu, but the approach taken to create it. The team learned pasta-making from a family that has been producing fresh pasta for three generations, pizza from a pizzaiolo trained in the tradition of Gabriele Bonci, gelato from one of Rome’s respected artisans, and coffee from an Italian barista. Because cooking the cuisine of another country involves far more than reproducing a handful of good recipes. Sometimes, it means first becoming a student at the feet of a master.
We have a peculiar confidence when it comes to Italian cuisine. After making a few decent pasta dishes, finding what we believe to be the right tomatoes and spending some time in front of a pizza oven, we can easily convince ourselves that we have mastered it. Our beloved country is full of chefs running Italian restaurant kitchens without ever having set foot in Italy. Yet, in my view, Italian cuisine is one of the world’s great culinary traditions most frequently underestimated.
Perhaps its apparent simplicity has something to do with it. A good carbonara requires only a handful of ingredients. A plate of ravioli has little room for theatrical presentation. And a Margherita pizza has very few ingredients behind which to hide. But simplicity and ease are not the same thing.
In fact, quite the opposite is often true. The fewer the ingredients, the fewer places there are to conceal a mistake. From the composition and thickness of pasta dough to the way a sauce clings to it and the precise point of doneness; from the flour and hydration of pizza dough to its fermentation and those crucial few minutes in the oven, dozens of seemingly minor decisions shape the final result. The mastery of Italian cuisine lies less in grand displays of technique than in these small decisions that may appear insignificant to an outsider.
This is precisely what impressed me most about Lucente, which has opened in Gümüşsuyu. Rather than placing the entire responsibility for developing the kitchen on the shoulders of a single chef, gastronomic consultant Elvan Uysal Bottoni brought specialists from different disciplines of Italian gastronomy to Istanbul to work directly with the restaurant’s team.
The master invited to teach fresh pasta was Antonio “Tony” Gamberoni. The story of Rome’s Bottega Gamberoni dates back to 1964. Heads of state, bureaucrats, celebrities and devoted food enthusiasts have all been among the regular customers of Tony’s pasta. Today, the third generation of the Gamberoni family continues the tradition of fresh egg pasta. A glance at Lucente’s menu makes the significance of this training immediately apparent: Fettuccine with butter and Parmesan, porcini mushroom gnocchi, ricotta-filled ravioli, spaghetti with bottarga, cavatelli with pesto, lasagna and mafaldine with meat ragù.
This is a repertoire that does not regard pasta merely as a carbohydrate vehicle for sauce. Gnocchi demands one kind of understanding of dough; filled ravioli requires another. The texture of cavatelli and the relationship fettuccine develops with its sauce are entirely different matters. One of the simplest dishes on the menu, Pasta Doppio Burro di Tony, seems to me a particularly eloquent expression of this philosophy: Fettuccine, butter and Parmesan. Nothing more.
And this is where Italian cuisine reveals its unforgiving side. In a dish built around just three components, there is nowhere to hide if the pasta is not good enough. The texture of the dough, the precision of the cut, the degree of cooking, the way the butter envelops the pasta, the emulsion it forms with the cheese — everything is exposed. You can learn a recipe from the internet. But you cannot learn the touch of a master’s hand from a screen. I believe what Tony Gamberoni has truly passed on to Lucente is not so much a fettuccine recipe as this tacit knowledge, acquired through the hands.
Alessandro Ruver, who came to teach pizza-making, represents another lineage of craftsmanship. A pizzaiolo who spent years working alongside Gabriele Bonci, one of the leading figures in contemporary Roman pizza, Ruver brings expertise in high-hydration doughs, long fermentation and an extraordinary attention to the dough itself. The menu includes options such as Margherita with stracciatella, pizzas topped with ragù or mushrooms and Quattro Formaggi alla Turca, which opens a small door to Turkish cheeses. The latter is particularly interesting. In selecting ingredients, Elvan chose outstanding local alternatives whenever Italian ingredients of the desired quality were unavailable. Replacing an ordinary ricotta with fresh lor cheese delivered daily from Ayvalık, for example, illustrates the philosophy rather well.
Gelato training was entrusted to Marco Radicioni, founder of Otaleg in Rome. And I think Lucente’s decision here speaks volumes. There are not twenty varieties on the gelato menu. There are just three: Pistachio, olive oil and vanilla. I like that. After all, Radicioni’s approach centers on allowing the raw ingredient to express itself with the greatest possible clarity. I am already curious about the seasonal gelato flavors that will follow.
For coffee, the restaurant worked with award-winning barista Gianni Olimpo. I consider this detail every bit as important as the pasta. Because, for me, espresso is inseparable from the experience of dining at an Italian restaurant. A panna cotta or tiramisu arrives at the table, followed by a poorly extracted espresso made with excessively roasted beans, and suddenly an otherwise beautifully composed meal ends on a disappointing final note.
Looking at the menu as a whole, I also see that Lucente is not afraid of the classics. Creating a menu like this is, in fact, a risk. Because a classic dish can sometimes be even more unforgiving than a creative one. Perhaps this is where Lucente’s respect for its masters acquires its deepest meaning. The team has not attempted to reinvent Italian cuisine. First, they wanted to learn to speak its language properly.
Elvan Uysal Bottoni brought the right masters to Istanbul and orchestrated this transfer of knowledge. Tony Gamberoni taught the feel of pasta-making; Alessandro Ruver, the behavior of dough; Marco Radicioni, the integrity of ingredients in gelato; and Gianni Olimpo, the finer points of coffee. Now the responsibility for bringing all that knowledge together rests with Aykut Doğanok and his team.
And to me, that is what makes Lucente worthy of praise at this stage. Not a declaration that every dish it serves is flawless, but the seriousness with which it has approached the creation of its 
kitchen.

Antalya takes underwater ‘X-ray’ to assess marine damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:39:34 UTC
15:39:34 KST

Authorities lower an underwater scanning device into the sea off Antalya to assess local marine life and evaluate coastal biodiversity.
Alarm raised by footage exposing a barren seabed off the Mediterranean province of Antalya has pushed local authorities to launch a full survey beneath its famous turquoise waters to map what little marine life remains.
The work is part of the Blue Mediterranean Initiative, launched by the Antalya Governor’s Office at the beginning of the year to protect the sea and coastline and help restore damaged marine habitats. Surveys are underway in Kemer and Kaş, while authorities plan to examine underwater life in Belek, in the Serik district, in the coming period.
Antalya Governor Hulusi Şahin told state-run Anadolu Agency the project would track underwater life, identify and map biodiversity and determine how years of damage could be repaired. Divers, biologists and other teams are working in the field with support from public institutions. The study is expected to take three years and could continue longer.
“We watched the camera footage. There is almost no life under the sea; it resembles a desert,” Şahin said, describing the condition of the underwater environment. He said the initiative aims to bring damaged marine life and biodiversity back to their former state.
Prompted by initial survey footage, officials banned fishing around Kemer’s Üç Adalar so divers and biologists could safely examine the area’s marine biodiversity. Şahin noted local authorities partnered with the Istanbul-based Marine Life Conservation Association to replicate their Tavşan Island protection model in Antalya, starting with the fishing ban.
In Kaş, teams from the Mediterranean Fisheries Research, Production and Training Institute are working to protect seagrass meadows and develop artificial reefs. Planned work includes ecological restoration, mapping and regular monitoring of seagrass, alongside the placement of artificial reefs to create new breeding grounds for marine life.
Akdeniz University’s Underwater Research Institute is also working in Kaş. Şahin said researchers were growing seagrass as seedlings before planting them and using thinning methods in areas where the plants grow densely.
Şahin said the projects were intended to help marine ecosystems recover without undermining fishing or harming local livelihoods. He pointed to the global pandemic, when people stayed away from the sea for several months, as an example of how quickly marine environments can recover when human pressure eases.
Restored biodiversity could also create new opportunities for diving and other forms of tourism, potentially generating new sources of income, Şahin said. Preparations for the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), which Antalya will host, have also given the initiative added momentum.

Türkiye opens 15 smoking cessation clinics for adolescents

Türkiye has opened 15 smoking cessation clinics for adolescents aged 12 to 18 across nine provinces, offering age-appropriate counseling and treatment to help young people quit tobacco use.
The clinics, launched in June 2026, are located in Ankara, Ağrı, Antalya, Bursa, Çanakkale, Çorum, Kahramanmaraş, Kırşehir and Kütahya, the Health Ministry said.
The ministry warned that adolescence is a particularly vulnerable period for nicotine addiction due to peer influence, social media, indirect tobacco promotion and access to newer nicotine products.
Nicotine use during childhood and adolescence can adversely affect brain development, with potentially lasting consequences for attention, learning, memory and impulse control. Early tobacco use may also increase the risk of alcohol and other substance use later in life.
The clinics will offer tailored counseling and treatment for adolescents, involving families and collaborating with child psychiatrists, psychologists, and social workers as needed.
The ministry has also prepared clinical guidelines for doctors working at the facilities. It plans to expand the network nationwide to strengthen early intervention, prevent nicotine addiction from becoming chronic and reduce tobacco-related health risks.

The United States has temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel after President Donald Trump announced a supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, drawing criticism from Ukraine that the move would help Moscow prolong the war.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a license on Oct. 9 authorizing the sale, delivery and import of Russian diesel, including shipments to the United States, until April 7, 2027.
Trump said on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons to U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons immediately afterward.
A further 3 million tons would follow, depending on the condition of Russian refineries, he said.
Trump predicted the supplies would bring down diesel prices, saying relief for American farmers, ranchers and truckers was a priority.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow would immediately begin lifting its own diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule.
He told TASS that exports could reach 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December, potentially rising to nearly 3 million tons a month later.
Putin separately confirmed Russia’s readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to U.S. and global markets, saying the shipments would benefit the world economy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized the agreement, arguing that easing sanctions without a clear and lasting agreement to reduce hostilities would give Russia more resources to continue fighting.
“Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he wrote on social media.
Zelensky said Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries were a response to attacks on its energy infrastructure. Kiev was ready to halt those strikes if Moscow stopped targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, he said, urging Washington to broker a reciprocal agreement.
Asked about Zelensky’s criticism before departing the White House, Trump said the United States remained a strong partner of Ukraine. He also thanked Putin for the diesel agreement.

A year of 'ceasefire' in Gaza, Israel killed over 1,450 Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:37:27 UTC
15:37:27 KST

One year ago, US President Donald Trump declared the war in Gaza over. Twelve months on, Palestinians are still being killed, Israeli troops are still occupying huge areas of the enclave, and families are still queueing for hours for a single meal.
Here is where the October 10, 2025 ceasefire stands.
Israel got its captives, and Gaza got no peace
Three days after the deal was announced, the Palestinian resistance group Hamas released the 20 remaining living captives, delivering the first and most immediate demand of the agreement.
Gaza has also stayed silent for a full year. Not a single rocket has been fired from the Palestinian side since the truce took effect. Palestine has held to the terms it could meet on the ground, while Israel has kept up near-daily strikes and violated the ceasefire with little consequence.
The US military set up a command post with allies near the border to monitor the truce. A year on, the monitoring has produced no accountability, and no one has stopped Israel from attacking.
A 'ceasefire' that kills nearly every day
Israel said it has scaled back its attacks. The Palestinians under its bombs would struggle to recognise the claim.
Israeli strikes have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the truce began, according to Gaza's health ministry, whose figures the United Nations considers accurate. That is a death toll of a war, recorded during what was supposed to be peace.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, locked in a tight election race, is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Yet he has vowed to kill everyone involved in the October 7 attack.
On the anniversary he boasted that 4,000 of 6,000 Hamas members had been killed. His war has killed more than 73,600 Palestinians since October 2023, in a brutal war that rights groups and UN officials have described as genocidal.
A leader who campaigns on killing, and who is accused of war crimes, is not committed to a ceasefire.
Occupying 70 percent of the Palestinian enclave
Under the terms of the truce, Israeli forces were allowed to remain in 53 percent of Gaza. A year later, official accounts show they control about 70 percent.
That means the occupier has not withdrawn. It has advanced beyond the lines it agreed to, swallowing more of a territory already reduced to rubble.
Almost every building in Gaza was damaged or destroyed by Israel's near-constant bombardment, and the people who lived in them have nowhere to return to.
Disarmament pretext
The deal's second phase promised a political transition away from Hamas. Technocrat Ali Shaath was named to head the new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, and Hamas said in July it was dissolving its governing body and handing over administration.
Hamas still runs security through civilian police in the limited areas of Gaza not under Israeli occupation. The resistance group announced it would give up its weapons and, according to Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza Peace Board's high representative, agreed to transfer civilian and security authority to a UN-recognised transitional administration. But it has not yet disarmed.
The handover depends on that administration being able to function, and it cannot do so while Israel bars Palestinian technocrats from entering Gaza and the promised international security forces have yet to deploy.
With no functioning body to receive its weapons, Hamas's armed wing has refused to disarm until the next phase of the Gaza ceasefire is implemented. Netanyahu rejects this and demands verifiable decommissioning of all weapons, down to individual guns, before Israel withdraws.
Whatever the failings of the transition, Israel has used them as a pretext. It has refused to reciprocate with any withdrawal, turning a phased deal into a one-sided demand and holding territory hostage to conditions it keeps raising.
Reconstruction: big promises, no money
Trump created a "Board of Peace" and recruited former British prime minister Tony Blair and Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov as key figures. In January, he promised $10 billion in US funding to a board he controls, and Gulf allies pledged more.
No money is known to have reached Gaza reconstruction. In September, the board proposed a $2.45 billion recovery plan, to span six months. For now it remains a slide in a presentation, while two million people live among ruins.
The human cost: hunger that never left
Behind the diplomacy are people like Niyaha al-Masri, a 35-year-old mother of eight in Khan Yunis. Every day she spends six hours or more queueing at a community kitchen, because without it her family would have "nothing at all". Her husband was wounded in both legs by an air strike. The family of 10 lives in a tent and eats one meal a day.
In August 2025, the UN-backed IPC declared famine in Gaza. The UN lifted the declaration in December after two months of improved supplies.
The World Food Programme’s Shaun Hughes says the situation is still "extremely serious", with 1.4 million of Gaza's roughly 2.1 million people acutely food insecure and 200,000 of them one step below famine.
Nutrition is failing, too. Medecins du Monde found that 93 percent of pregnant or breastfeeding women showed symptoms of anaemia, and only 17 percent had a varied enough diet. Hughes warned that repeated acute malnutrition in children is something people "just don't recover from".
Masri's children dream of fruit and spend their days gathering scraps of nylon and cardboard to patch their tent. "I swear to God, this isn't normal," she said.
A ceasefire in name only
The truce did what Israel wanted: its captives came home and its border fell quiet. For Palestinians, it has brought continued killing, shrinking land, hunger and an empty promise of rebuilding.
A year on, Israel has yet to withdraw from Gaza, and no one has been held to account for breaking the terms it signed.

Türkiye’s seismic research vessel Oruç Reis has reached waters off Kyrenia as surveys continue for a planned natural gas pipeline linking Türkiye and Turkish Cyprus, with operations targeted to begin in 2028.
The project envisages two pipelines along a 101-kilometer route from Anamur in the southern province of Mersin to Teknecik, east of Kyrenia. The route includes 97 kilometers beneath the Mediterranean and four kilometers on land.
Oruç Reis is mapping seabed conditions along the proposed route.
The current survey program runs through Oct. 25, while engineering studies are expected to be completed by the end of the year.
Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz and Turkish Cypriot Prime Minister Ünal Üstel signed a memorandum of understanding for the project on July 10.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said at the signing that the system would be designed to transport gas in both directions.
Alongside supplying Turkish Cyprus, it could eventually carry gas from future discoveries in the Eastern Mediterranean to Türkiye and onward to Europe.
The gas supplied from Türkiye would initially be used for electricity generation.
Bayraktar said the project would help meet growing demand and reduce reliance on imported petroleum products.
The surveys come as Greece prepares to resume work on a separate electricity interconnector linking Crete and Greek Cyprus, with a later extension to Israel.
Türkiye says surveys and cable-laying in areas where it asserts continental shelf rights require prior coordination with Ankara.
Athens has rejected seeking Turkish permission for the work.

Türkiye sets rules for under-15 social media ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:33:44 UTC
15:33:44 KST

Türkiye has published regulations barring social media platforms from serving children under 15 and requiring users to verify their age through the e-Devlet government portal.
The rules, prepared by the Cyber Security Directorate and published in the Official Gazette on Oct. 10, take effect on Nov. 1.
Platforms must complete age verification for existing accounts by March 31, 2027.
Registration requests from children under 15 will be rejected, while existing accounts found to belong to users below that age will be closed.
Verification will use a digital token generated through e-Devlet and uploaded to the platform.
The token will indicate whether users meet the 15 and 18 age thresholds without containing names or other identifying information.
Accounts belonging to users aged 15 to 17 must remain private, with no option to make them public.
Platforms will be prohibited from offering livestreaming or displaying personalized advertisements on these accounts. Infinite-scrolling feeds will also be banned.
Teenagers will only be able to receive messages from accounts they follow. Their follower and following lists will be hidden from other users.
Platforms must also provide parental controls allowing parents to manage account settings, monitor and limit screen time, and approve purchases and other paid transactions.

Speaking to reporters after leaving the meeting, Otyakmaz said Mustafa Temel Bozbağ, Zafer Bahadır Saraç, Bilal Arslan and Murat Şahin had resigned alongside him.
“We felt there was no point in continuing. When differences of opinion emerged, we decided to resign,” he said.
Otyakmaz wished the remaining board members success, adding that discussions about Montella’s future were still underway when the five left the meeting.
The TFF also appointed alternate board members İbrahim Özbay and Metin Akyüz to replace two members who had resigned previously.
Serdar Yıldız was named general secretary, replacing Abdullah Ayaz, who had submitted his resignation.
Ahmet Erzurumlu, the federation’s registration director, was appointed deputy general secretary.

Hind Rajab Foundation asks ICC to investigate Israeli doctors over alleged Sde Teiman torture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:28:59 UTC
15:28:59 KST

The Hind Rajab Foundation accused Israeli medical personnel and senior health officials of complicity in the alleged torture, abuse, and deaths of Palestinian detainees at the Sde Teiman detention facility, announcing on Thursday that it had submitted a request to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague to investigate their involvement.
The request names medical professionals, hospital administrators, senior Health Ministry and Defense Ministry officials, and leaders of the Israel Medical Association (IMA) in connection with alleged abuses at the facility since October 7, 2023.
Among those the Hind Rajab Foundation is seeking to have investigated are former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, IMA chairman Prof. Zion Hagai, IMA director-general attorney Leah Wapner, and Dr. Yosef Walfisch, chairman of the IMA's Ethics Bureau.
According to the foundation, the alleged acts could constitute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and even genocide.
The submission was filed under Article 15 of the Rome Statute, which allows organizations and individuals to provide the ICC prosecutor with information about alleged crimes and request that it be examined. The submission is not an indictment, nor does it constitute a decision by the court to open an investigation into any of the individuals named.
Allegations of medical abuse at Sde Teiman
The timing of the move is not coincidental. From October 7 to 10, the World Medical Association (WMA) is holding its General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, with representatives of the IMA also participating.
Hagay chairs the WMA's Socio-Medical Affairs Committee, while Wapner serves on its advisory committees.
At the center of the submission is the field hospital established at the Sde Teiman detention facility following the October 7 attacks.
According to the Hind Rajab Foundation, the Health Ministry was responsible for establishing and operating the hospital, while the medical personnel working there were placed under the authority of the Military Police.
The organization refers to guidelines it claims were issued by the Health Ministry in December 2023, including provisions for treating detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded, prohibiting medical personnel from identifying themselves by name, restricting transfers to civilian hospitals, and allowing involuntary medical treatment.
The foundation also relies on previously published testimony, including an Associated Press report in which medical personnel described surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
It also cites a letter written in April 2024 by a doctor who worked at Sde Teiman, warning that two detainees had undergone leg amputations following injuries caused by prolonged shackling.
A separate section of the submission is devoted to the Israel Medical Association.
The Hind Rajab Foundation accuses the association's leadership of providing what it describes as professional and ethical backing for conditions at the detention facility.
It cites a letter published in April 2024 in the American Journal of Bioethics by Hagay, Walfisch, and Malka Boro of the IMA, in which they maintained that detainees at Sde Teiman were receiving appropriate medical care.
The authors noted that Walfisch had visited the facility as part of a delegation of medical ethics experts and acknowledged that isolated violations of ethical rules might occur. However, they maintained that, to the best of their knowledge, the doctors were fulfilling their professional obligations.
The foundation's director-general, Dyab Abou Jahjah, criticized the participation of Israeli representatives in the Rotterdam conference.
According to Abou Jahjah, the WMA must explain why it continues to host an organization that he claims provided institutional backing for torture.
Israeli Medical Association faces international pressure
In early July, the IMA announced that more than 5,000 doctors from 46 countries had signed a petition opposing efforts to remove it from the WMA.
In its statement, the association argued that the campaign represented an attempt to bring politics into medicine and that the accusations against it included false or disputed claims.
The IMA has previously opposed calls for its suspension, arguing that disagreements over government policy should not affect cooperation between medical professionals.
At the WMA's meeting in Portugal last year, the Israeli association also succeeded in blocking an attempt to suspend its membership.
However, the Hind Rajab Foundation has made clear that its submission to The Hague is only the beginning of a broader initiative.
In its statement, the organization warned that it was preparing individual case files against Israeli doctors and medical professionals who also hold foreign citizenship, with the intention of filing complaints against them with prosecuting authorities in their countries of citizenship.
Through this initiative, the foundation seeks to expand its legal activities targeting Israeli military personnel to include members of the healthcare system, in an effort to subject them to criminal proceedings outside Israel.

====================================================================================================

Premature birth may cause lifelong kidney damage, Israeli researchers find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:28:51 UTC
15:28:51 KST

Imagine starting life with a permanent biological deficit that you won’t discover until decades later. For the 15 million babies (one in 10 births) born each year prematurely, this is the hidden reality of kidney health. Until now, scientists knew that early arrival doubled the lifetime risk of chronic kidney disease, but the underlying biological culprit remained a mystery.
Prematurity is defined as a live birth before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Thanks to improvements in treatment and research in this field, the rate of live premature births has increased dramatically within the past decades. But preemies can suffer from an increased rate of adult diseases, when organs such as the kidney have not developed well in the uterus.
A groundbreaking joint study by researchers at Hadassah-University Medical Center in Jerusalem’s Ein Kerem and at Monash University in Melbourne has finally uncovered the cellular mechanism behind the shortfall – and, crucially, pinpointed the narrow therapeutic window where intervention might protect these vulnerable organs for life. The signs precede the diagnosis by many years.
Dr. Morris Nechama of Hadassah’s pediatric nephrology unit and the Faculty of Medicine of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem led the study, together with Athar Amleh, a doctoral student from the Palestinian Authority carrying out her doctoral research at Hadassah, whose scholarship was funded by the Yad Hanadiv Foundation.
Amleh designed and carried out the experiments and is the first author of the paper. Dr. Oded Volovelsky, director of Hadassah’s pediatric nephrology, and Prof. Alexander Combes of the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute in Melbourne, Australia worked with them.
The new study just published in iScience, under the title “Preterm birth disrupts nephron progenitor cell dynamics predisposing to renal disease,” provides the authoritative answer of why the kidneys of premature babies remain vulnerable for life.
Using an advanced mouse model, the research team has identified the exact cellular disruption caused by premature birth that limits the development of kidney filtration units – opening up a specific, limited period during which action must be taken for future preventative treatments.
A healthy human relies on roughly one million microscopic filtration units built entirely before or around birth, which never regenerate. The study reveals for the first time how premature birth short-circuits this delicate developmental window, leaving millions of adults going through life with a lower kidney reserve that they never knew they were missing.
The cellular mechanism leaves the kidney with too few filtration units and the short window of time in which intervention may be possible. The findings could make possible a technique to protect the kidneys of babies born prematurely, the researchers said.
“We have known for years that children born prematurely reach adulthood with more vulnerable kidneys, but we didn’t know exactly what went wrong and when. Here, we saw it happen in real time: nephron progenitor cells enter distress within the first hours after birth, and their timing is disrupted. They try to compensate later, but the window has already closed,” Nechama said:
Health effects from premature birth
In an American study of 15-year-olds who had been born prematurely, about half already had high blood pressure, protein in the urine, or smaller-than-normal kidneys. Thus, many people go through life with kidneys that started out with less reserve, without knowing it, until something begins to go wrong.
A healthy kidney consists of about a million tiny filtration units called nephrons in each normal human kidney. The creation of human nephrons ends by the 35th week of gestation, but this number varies greatly between different individuals. They don’t regenerate after birth. Some babies are born with more and some with fewer, Volovelsky explained in an interview with The Jerusalem Post; a person born with fewer nephrons carries a smaller kidney reserve throughout life.
Preterm birth is increasingly recognized not merely as an acute neonatal event but as a lifelong determinant of renal health. But the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving this developmental programming have remained elusive, often confounded in clinical settings by two or more medical conditions that occur at the same time in a person – such as sepsis, medications that harm the kidneys, or having received steroids after birth.
The human nephron, the basic functional unit of the kidney, is a structure that produces urine in the process of removing waste and excess substances from the blood. At present, little can be done clinically to increase the number of nephrons.
Epidemiological studies have already shown that children and adults born prematurely suffer more often from high blood pressure, protein in the urine, and reduced kidney function. Until now, it was not clear why.
“Our research, using a mouse model of premature birth, provides the answer. The researchers examined the progenitor cells that give rise to nephrons and found that the sudden, early transition from the womb to the outside world disrupts the delicate timing of their development and maturation. The cells enter a state of stress and lose the opportunity for repair. We believe the findings are relevant to human babies as well,” Volovelsky added.
“Immediately after premature birth, the progenitor cells enter a state of cellular stress, triggering an emergency molecular response known as the unfolded protein response. At the same time, the genes responsible for differentiation into mature nephrons are suppressed. In other words, the cells focus on survival instead of building.”
A day later, they try to compensate for the delay with a faster wave of division and differentiation, but the compensation comes too late.
“One surprising finding of our study is that in the preterm animals, the period of nephron building lasts about 24 hours longer than usual, yet this extension does not fill the gap. The result is a permanent nephron deficit, clearly measured about a month after birth and already accompanied by signs of declining kidney function,” Volovelsky noted.
In a later examination, at an age equivalent to adulthood, the kidneys of these mice showed signs of chronic damage: the glomeruli (filtration bodies) had enlarged to compensate for their small number, protein appeared in the urine, and markers of kidney tubular damage accumulated. In other words, damage caused in the first days of life keeps unfolding for decades.
“We accompany children born prematurely in the clinic and see the result years later, sometimes only in adolescence. This study indicates that the first few days after birth are not only a period of survival but also a period in which the kidney’s reserve for life is set. It’s a perspective that can change what we monitor and how we monitor these children. Preemies should be monitored for kidney disease as they get older.”
An additional finding is a difference between the genders. “The impairment in nephron number and kidney function was significant in males but not in females, consistent with previous evidence that male fetuses are more susceptible to adverse perinatal conditions, and it may help in assessing risk in the future,” the pediatric nephrologist stated.
Identifying the stress response in progenitor cells as the point of failure suggests a possible intervention window in the first few days after premature birth. If this stress response can be curbed in time, it may be possible to preserve some of the nephrons that are lost today.
The researchers emphasize that this is an early stage; the study identifies the mechanism and the timing, but a treatment that prevents the damage has not yet been tested, and that is the goal of their next study.
Nechama and Volovelsky said their research could eventually revolutionize the care of kidney disease. The notion that nephron numbers can be restored with timely intervention in experimental models gives hope to the important struggle to find a cure for kidney diseases.
The study grew out of an Israeli-Australian collaboration supported by AUSiMED, an Australian charity that promotes joint medical research between the two countries.
The collaboration continued without interruption throughout the war, with the lab work in Jerusalem and the bioinformatic analysis in Melbourne advancing in parallel, in daily coordination across the time difference and the security situation. For the teams, it was also proof that international medical research can keep working under the most difficult conditions, they said.

US President Donald Trump told reporters that hurricane preparation were "under control," adding that "We are watching it very closely."
The hurricane has produced high winds, downed power lines, and caused travel delays, including the closure of all roads through Houston county, Alabama.
"Widespread damage and power outages are likely as this system passes through the state. All actions to protect property should have already been completed for the southern half of Alabama and should be completed across the northern half by 10 pm," Alabama's EMA warned.
Additionally, the Florida division of the EMA extended a tornado watch for parts of North Florida until Saturday morning.
National Hurrican Center warns of potential for flooding
The post-tropical cyclone, crossing over southern Alabama after making landfall earlier near Destin, Florida is about 55 miles (89 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), the agency added.
The center warned of possible storm surges, urban and river flooding and flash floods across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.
Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland through Saturday even after it becomes post-tropical, the NHC said.
Isaias is expected to cross Alabama and go into the Tennessee Valley over the weekend, the NHC said.

Post-tropical cyclone Isaias is about 55 miles (88.5 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), NHC said.
Continued weakening is expected, but Isaias will continue to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the agency added.

Fund bill sets out repayment terms for affected investors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:28:26 UTC
15:28:26 KST

About 350,000 investors in funds under liquidation could recover their net principal through advance payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras under a bill before parliament, ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) parliamentary group leader Abdullah Güler said.
Güler put the number of affected investors at roughly 455,000, explaining that inflation compensation would be calculated separately at the final settlement.
“Think of it as an advance payment,” he said.
Under the proposal, investors whose net investment is below 1 million liras could receive that amount, while those with larger investments could receive an advance capped at 1 million liras. Payments would depend on available assets and verified entitlements.
If available cash is insufficient, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) could prioritize investors with the smallest balances or set a common minimum advance.
Where fund assets fall short of the value of investors’ holdings, repayment calculations would use actual cash invested and withdrawn, adjusted for inflation through the liquidation date.
The adjustment would reflect the average change in the consumer price and domestic producer price indices, with withdrawals deducted from the earliest investments first.
Further payments would follow as assets are sold and money recovered.
Güler said no public funds would be used.
The bill also addresses responsibility for losses caused by unlawful transfers of fund assets.
The portfolio management company that founded or managed the fund would bear primary liability. If recovery from the company proved impossible, other individuals and entities found responsible by the SPK could be held personally liable.
Leaving office would not remove responsibility for transactions and decisions made during their tenure.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) would collect recovered money in separate accounts for each fund.
Where appointed as trustee, it could sell seized assets before the conclusion of court proceedings.
Investors found by the SPK to have participated in market abuse or acted with those responsible would be excluded from repayments.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek told daily Sabah that investigators had identified more than 187 billion liras in allegedly unlawful gains made by 141 individuals and 73 companies through Tera, Pusula and Hedef funds.
He said their details had been sent to the TMSF, which had begun issuing repayment notices.
The nine-article bill, submitted on Oct. 9, covers funds ordered into liquidation by the SPK on Sept. 17 whose liquidation remains unfinished when the legislation takes effect.
Güler said the proposal was scheduled for consideration by parliament’s Plan and Budget Commission the following week, before proceeding to the General Assembly.

Professor Rıfat Atun has become the first Turkish academic to hold a deanship at Harvard University.
The Turkish Cypriot academic took office on Aug. 1 as dean for education and innovation at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
His responsibilities cover the school’s degree and non-degree programs, including efforts to introduce artificial intelligence and other technologies into teaching.
He previously served as vice dean for non-degree education and innovation.
Atun also holds the Julio Frenk Professorship of Public Health Leadership and is a professor of global health systems. His research focuses on health system performance, financing, reform and the adoption of new technologies.
He has advised the World Health Organization, the World Bank and G20 presidencies on health policy and reform, and previously chaired the Stop TB Partnership’s coordinating board.
Atun has published more than 500 papers, according to his Harvard profile. It lists him among Clarivate’s highly cited researchers for 2020–2025 and Stanford–Elsevier’s most influential scientists for 2021–2025.

`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:26:13 UTC
15:26:13 KST

At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.

One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.

Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration has resumed processing citizenship applications that were suspended because of errors in the country’s Central Criminal Register.
The ministry announced the decision in a press release after the National Police concluded that the errors had only a very limited impact on the register.
Immigration authorities have also been instructed to restart affected cases involving permanent residence permits and family reunification, according to an update from the Danish Immigration Service.
The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.
The errors became public in early September when National Police Commissioner Lasse Boje informed politicians at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, that some criminal records had been deleted incorrectly.

If problems are identified, police will work with the relevant authorities to determine how those cases should be handled.
The errors also disrupted the issuance of child protection certificates, which are background checks used to identify certain criminal convictions relevant to working with children.
Applications for these certificates were temporarily suspended while police reviewed the affected records.
The National Police reopened applications September 18.
During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.

Prosecutors challenged that decision, but the Eastern High Court reached the same conclusion Friday.
The investigation remains ongoing, and no decision has been made on whether the officers will face trial.

Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.
Business groups warn 200 DKK cruise passenger tax could drive tourists away
Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.
Dansk Industri (DI), the Confederation of Danish Industry, and Dansk Erhverv, a business organization representing companies across several sectors, are responding to the government’s proposal to introduce the tax from 2028.
“A cruise tax at this level will hit both the major cities and rural districts,” said Lars Bertolt Winther, head of tourism, culture and experiences at DI, in a press release.
Jesper Kronborg, industry director for transport at Dansk Erhverv, also criticized the proposal.
“In Dansk Erhverv’s view, it is a bad proposal, or at least a proposal that requires a very thorough analysis,” he said in a press release.
The government expects the tax to generate an additional 300 million DKK in annual revenue from 2028.
The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.
Figures from Statistics Denmark show that 1.1 million cruise passengers visited Denmark in 2025. The number of cruise ships calling at Danish ports increased by 16% compared with the previous year.
Copenhagen, Aarhus, Skagen and Rønne on the island of Bornholm are the country’s main cruise destinations. Together, they account for more than 98% of cruise passengers.
DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.
“Following the introduction of a high passenger tax, bookings dropped significantly, especially to the smaller ports, and the tax was subsequently lowered to limit the damaging effects,” Winther said.
“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.
According to the industry organization Danske Havne, which represents Danish ports, Iceland now charges 85 DKK per cruise passenger, while Greenland charges 50 DKK.
Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.
Drop in exports to the US drags down Danish exports
Danish exports fell by 3.3 percent in August, driven in part by a decline in goods exports to the United States, according to Statistics Denmark.
Total exports of goods and services amounted to 194 billion DKK in August, down 3.3 percent from July. Goods exports fell by 6.2 percent, while services exports rose by 0.7 percent.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, described the overall decline as “worryingly large”.
“But it is part of the story that a large part of the decline is concentrated around the US, where we also see fluctuations from month to month,” he wrote in a comment.
Exports of goods and services to both the US and the United Kingdom fell in August. Total exports to the US amounted to 31.7 billion DKK, down 2.8 billion DKK from July.
Goods exports to the US fell by 3.3 billion DKK, while services exports rose slightly.
Kristensen said fluctuations in the prices of products such as medicines sold by Danish companies in the US could partly explain the decline. He therefore cautioned against drawing too negative a conclusion from the latest figures alone.
The August decline followed an increase in exports in July. Overall, Danish exports of goods and services rose by nearly 19 billion DKK, or more than 10 percent, between August 2025 and August 2026.
According to Kristensen, Danish exports have so far held up despite geopolitical unrest, higher energy prices and rising interest rates.
Still, the August figures are bad news for the Danish economy when viewed in isolation.
“However, it will take several months of this development before we become worried,” Kristensen wrote.
Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”
After gaining access, the hacker said they created two computer programs to retrieve CPR information and store it outside the system.
The person’s identity has not been made public, and their account has not been independently confirmed.
The hacker told Politiken they had no plans to sell or publish the personal identification numbers and were “really shocked” by the security weaknesses they encountered.
To describe the situation, the hacker compared it to someone leaving dangerous material unattended.
“Someone leaves a suitcase with 10 kilos of plutonium unattended at a train station. Then a homeless person steals it,” the hacker said.
“Yes, of course you shouldn’t steal other people’s suitcases. But you also shouldn’t leave nuclear material at a train station.”
The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.
Politiken conducted its interview with the hacker in English through an encrypted communication service.
Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.
University of Copenhagen to merge and reorganize faculties from 2028
The University of Copenhagen is changing how its academic departments are organized, with several faculties set to merge or split over the next three years.
The university announced that its Faculty of Theology and Faculty of Humanities will merge into a single Faculty of Humanities and Theology on January 1, 2028.
The Faculty of Law and Faculty of Social Sciences will also combine into a Faculty of Law and Social Sciences on the same date.
Further changes will follow on January 1, 2029.
The Faculty of Health Sciences will be divided into two faculties: Clinical and Public Health Sciences, and Health Sciences. The new divisions will focus on clinical and preclinical subjects, respectively.
The Faculty of Science will also split into two. One will cover traditional natural sciences, while the other will focus on biological, environmental and geosciences.
Despite the restructuring, the university will retain six faculties.
A faculty is a major academic division responsible for particular subjects and degree programs.
The university said most students would not be affected because the content and structure of their degree programs would remain unchanged.
Rector David Dreyer Lassen said the changes were necessary because the university’s faculties had developed differently in size and complexity over the past 15 years.
“When the differences become very large, it challenges our balance, leadership power, and cohesion,” he said.
The University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479 with four faculties: theology, law, medicine and philosophy.
Its faculty structure has changed several times since then.
Today, theology students can pursue studies leading toward the priesthood, while humanities programs include history, English, education and rhetoric.

Denmark had a record 1,175,187 state pensioners in August, according to figures from the Jobindsats statistical database reviewed by pension company Velliv.
