World Insights: Okinawa murder case exposes price of Japan's U.S. security dependence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:49:43 CST
14:49:43 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- The Okinawa prefectural assembly has adopted a protest resolution and an opinion statement over a U.S. Marine's suspected robbery-murder of a local woman in the southern Japanese prefecture, demanding that the U.S. take effective measures to prevent similar incidents and calling for a fundamental review of the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA).
Analysts said the case had once again exposed the consequences of Japan's long-standing security dependence on the United States and the unequal nature of their bilateral relationship. Meanwhile, Japan's continued military buildup in Okinawa is adding to security concerns among local residents, who have long borne the burden of hosting U.S. military bases.
CRIME REIGNITES PUBLIC ANGER
The suspect, identified as Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed in Okinawa, allegedly killed Anna Yagi, a 39-year-old local woman, and stole her wallet and other belongings at a hotel in the prefectural capital of Naha in the early hours of Oct. 3.
Okinawa police arrested him on Oct. 4. Japanese media, citing police sources, reported that surveillance footage showed a person whose physical characteristics matched those of Ballard. He has denied the allegations, responding "I don't know" to police questioning, according to the reports.
Following the arrest, the U.S. side expressed condolences to the victim's family and said it would cooperate with the Japanese investigation, but did not issue an apology.
The killing and the U.S. response have fueled anger among local residents. On Oct. 4, more than 100 people gathered in Naha to protest. One female demonstrator said she was constantly afraid that she or her daughter could become the next victim.
Anger has also spread across social media, with comments accusing the Japanese government of weakness and excessive deference to Washington, while some users likened Japan's position to that of a colony.
NIGHTMARE LINGERS IN OKINAWA
The anger in Okinawa is rooted in a long history of wartime trauma and the burden of hosting U.S. military bases.
Japan forcibly annexed the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1879 and established Okinawa Prefecture. During the final stages of World War II, Okinawa became a major battlefield as Japan sought to delay the U.S. advance toward its mainland, resulting in heavy civilian casualties. After the war, the islands came under U.S. administration.
Although the United States returned administrative control of Okinawa to Japan in 1972, the prefecture has continued to bear a disproportionate share of the U.S. military presence. Okinawa accounts for only about 0.6 percent of Japan's land area, yet it hosts approximately 70 percent of all exclusive-use U.S. military facilities and installations in Japan. Crime, noise and pollution associated with the bases have long troubled local communities.
According to Okinawa Prefecture statistics, U.S. military personnel and their family members committed 6,409 criminal offenses from 1972 through 2025. Cases involving U.S. military-related personnel have shown an upward trend in recent years.
Analysts say the recurrence of crimes involving U.S. military personnel is closely linked to the special legal status granted to U.S. forces under the Japan-U.S. SOFA, signed in 1960.
Under the agreement, the United States has the primary right to exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed by U.S. military personnel while on duty, while Japan has the primary jurisdiction over crimes occurring off duty.
However, if a U.S. service member is accused of a crime over which Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect manages to return to a U.S. military base before being arrested by local authorities, custody legally remains with the United States until the person is formally indicted by Japanese prosecutors.
In practice, this arrangement can complicate Japanese investigations and the transfer of suspects to Japanese custody. Critics argue that the special treatment afforded to U.S. personnel undermines accountability and public confidence in the justice system.
The issue has remained contentious since a 1995 case in which three U.S. servicemen brutally raped an Okinawan schoolgirl, triggering widespread protests and calls for a revision of the agreement. Yet its fundamental provisions have remained unchanged.
Analysts point out that Japan's reluctance to pursue substantive revisions reflects its dependence on the United States for security. An editorial in Japan's Mainichi Shimbun criticized the government's hesitation over fundamental measures, including revising the SOFA, saying it exposed Tokyo's underlying fear of antagonizing Washington, its key security ally.
MILITARY BUILDUP ADDS TO CONCERNS
Beyond the burden of U.S. bases, Okinawa residents are facing new risks as Japan accelerates its military buildup, analysts say.
In recent years, Japan has stepped up its military expansion and designated Okinawa as a "forward base for combat readiness" amid shifts in U.S. security strategy and Washington's growing expectations that Tokyo assume a greater military role.
The government of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who took office in October 2025, has been particularly active in promoting military expansion. During a visit to Ishigaki and Yonaguni islands in Okinawa Prefecture in November 2025, Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi said plans to deploy a medium-range surface-to-air missile unit on Yonaguni Island were proceeding as scheduled.
In June this year, Japan's Akahata newspaper reported that the Defense Ministry planned to expand the number of beds at the Japan Self-Defense Forces' Naha Hospital and establish a medical evacuation system to transport casualties from outlying islands in Okinawa to mainland Japan.
Koja Genta, who was recently elected Okinawa governor with support from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, has also said he is willing to adapt prefecture-managed airports, ports and other infrastructure to better support the government's military deployments "in times of emergency."
Local media and left-wing figures in Japan have criticized the government's approach, arguing that its pledges to ease Okinawa's burden and revitalize the local economy have not translated into meaningful relief. Instead, they say, the military presence is being reinforced, further entrenching Okinawa's role on the front line of Japan's defense buildup.
Tomoko Tamura, chairperson of the Japanese Communist Party, criticized the government for pushing ahead with military expansion while disregarding Okinawa's history of devastating wartime suffering, warning that the prefecture could once again become a battlefield.
Hiromori Maedomari, a professor at Okinawa International University, has also argued in an article that strengthening military deployments in Okinawa in the name of responding to a so-called emergency threatens local livelihoods and the regional economy, warning that Japan's continued reliance on military means could lead the country toward war.
For Okinawa, the latest killing is therefore more than an isolated criminal case. It has renewed questions about the unequal security arrangement with the United States, the Japanese government's ability to protect local residents, and the risks of turning the prefecture into an increasingly militarized frontier. ■

Lai casts Taiwan as a beacon of democracy in National Day address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:44:11 UTC
14:44:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Saturday outlined his vision for Taiwan as an example of democracy, resilience, and shared prosperity in a world facing conflict and authoritarianism in his National Day address.
Marking 30 years since Taiwan’s first direct presidential election, Lai recalled how voters went to the polls despite missile threats in 1996, fulfilling a long-standing aspiration for its people to determine their own future. Over the past three decades, Taiwan has undergone democratic transformation, experienced changes of ruling parties, and faced numerous challenges, Lai said.
Against this backdrop, Lai framed his vision for Taiwan around the themes of a city on a hill, salt of the earth, and light of the world. The imagery reflects democratic foundations, a commitment to freedom and peace, and its role in the international community.
He outlined plans to improve living standards and expand social welfare. He also called for individuals across the political spectrum to work toward a shared future for the country.
Lai said the government would work to ensure that economic growth translates into better living standards for the public. One priority is addressing Taiwan’s declining birthrate, with a growth allowance for children and young people aged 18 and under set to be introduced next year.
Housing affordability is another priority. Lai said the government plans to increase the supply of social housing through direct construction, rent subsidies, and additional units secured through urban renewal and floor-area incentives.
Turning to national security, Lai said Taiwan seeks peaceful relations with other countries while maintaining the defense capabilities needed to deter aggression. He cited China’s continued military and gray-zone activities around the nation, which he said were aimed at changing the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.
Lai pledged to continue defense reforms and strengthen domestic defense industries. He also highlighted the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience initiative, which brings together government agencies and civil society to maintain essential services such as energy, communications, finance, food supplies, and healthcare during a crisis.
Beyond security, Lai highlighted innovation, economic cooperation, and social inclusion as pillars for Taiwan’s international role. He cited the country’s development from traditional industries to advanced semiconductor manufacturing as evidence that an economy with limited natural resources can become an important contributor to global prosperity.
To sustain that progress, the government is accelerating development in 13 key strategic industries, including semiconductors and quantum computing. The initiative extends beyond technology to cover critical minerals, biotechnology and healthcare, urban renewal, cultural and creative industries, and tourism.
A separate development and revitalization program aims to help small- and medium-sized enterprises and microbusinesses improve their competitiveness. Support includes financing, workforce training, digital transformation, net-zero upgrades, and access to international markets.
Lai stressed the benefits of technological development should extend beyond major technology companies. He called for closer ties between advanced and traditional industries, with large corporations helping domestic suppliers expand alongside their international operations.
Economic growth must also improve household finances, Lai said. He cited 11 consecutive annual increases in the minimum wage and five pay raises for military personnel, civil servants, and public school teachers over the past decade. He also pointed to salary adjustments for professional and supervisory positions this year.
With local elections approaching, Lai called for political competition to coexist with a shared commitment to the nation’s future. He acknowledged that political parties and voters hold differing views, but said disagreements should not divide society or undermine respect for democratic institutions.
Concluding his address, Lai called on Taiwan to remain open to the world and continue sharing the benefits of its development. He said the country should draw on the strength of its people and industries to contribute to global progress while upholding freedom, equality, and innovation.

US hosts ‘productive’ trilateral talks to end Russia-Ukraine war

Russia kills 20 in Ukraine as US hosts ‘productive’ talks to end war
US says it held talks with European and Ukrainian officials to ensure lasting peace before winter approaches.
Twenty people, including three children, have been killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, the day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv.
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House.
A six-year-old girl was among those killed when one attack reduced part of an apartment block to rubble, according to the Reuters news agency.
Russia hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday, said a senior official in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin.
It was the third mass casualty attack on Ukraine this week. Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian attacks on Wednesday and Thursday.
“There are more and more daytime attacks taking place across Ukraine,” said Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv. “For example, a glide bomb hit a bus stop earlier in the week, killing 30 people and in Kyiv recently, more and more jet-powered drones are striking targets during the daytime.”
One video showed “a man standing in front of a school and running from a building when he heard the jet approaching, surviving only by a few seconds”, she added.
Our reporter said it all underscores just how dangerous things have become for civilians in Ukraine.
Zaporizhzhia, with a pre-war population of over 700,000, has been a regular target of Russian bombardment, with attacks intensifying in the past few months.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Saturday that lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would help fuel the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia and Europe won’t,” she wrote online.
Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the US conflict with Iran.
Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.
Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine’s power grid.
US, Ukraine, EU meeting
The attacks come after US, Ukrainian and European officials met in the US to discuss a proposal for ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
A delegation of Ukrainian officials who visited Miami, Florida, was heading home on Saturday, Dmytro Lytvyn, an aide to Zelenskyy, told AFP.
US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Friday that “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace”.
Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO”.
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict”, Witkoff said.
He also noted the “productive” talks discussed “Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession”.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday the conflict had reached a dangerous “stalemate”, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
“The other way that stalemates end is through escalation,” Rubio told reporters, warning that the conflict could spread to neighbouring NATO countries.

Palestine welcomes Navi Pillay’s 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown

Abdelraouf Arnaout and Mohammad Sio
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Palestine on Friday welcomed South African jurist Navi Pillay’s being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, saying the honor recognizes her efforts to defend international law and document Israeli crimes.
The Foreign Ministry said Pillay’s win represented an elevation of “the voice of truth and the voice of the oppressed,” and recognized her efforts to advance peace and international law.
It said Pillay devoted her career to upholding law and justice and defending the rights of oppressed people in South Africa and around the world, including Palestinians.
The ministry praised her leadership of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, which she chaired from 2021 to 2025.
It said the commission helped document genocide, sexual violence, attacks on children and other Israeli violations.
The ministry said the prize was also recognition for defenders of international law and justice and encouragement for efforts to hold perpetrators of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity accountable.
It added that Pillay has consistently defended the universality of law and equality among people, including Palestinians, and said the award underscored that “there can be no lasting peace without justice and equality for all.”
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that it awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to the 85-year-old jurist “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”
“This year's laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law,” it said, highlighting her work in international courts and as UN high commissioner for human rights.
Pillay, born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, under apartheid, began her legal career challenging racial discrimination and defending opponents of the apartheid system.
She served as UN high commissioner for human rights, as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. She has also served as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice.
The UN commission she chaired concluded in a 2025 report that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, a finding rejected by Israel.
The Nobel Peace Prize will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

The UN on Friday condemned a sharp escalation in attacks on civilians in Ukraine, reporting that more than 100 people were killed and at least 429 injured over the past week as Russian strikes hit residential areas, passenger buses and critical infrastructure.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, told the UN Security Council that attacks by the Russian Federation had reached “a new horrifying level” since the council’s briefing Sept. 23.
“We strongly condemn all attacks against civilians,” said Khiari.
He said the pattern of escalating attacks had contributed to a "significant increase" in civilian casualties this year, with every month recording more casualties than the corresponding month in each of the previous three years.
Beyond the immediate loss of life, he warned that repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure were disrupting life for millions.
The official also expressed concern about reported attacks on telecommunications networks, retail businesses, food suppliers and logistics companies.
“All attacks on energy infrastructure and on population centers must cease immediately,” said Khiari, stressing the urgency of protecting vulnerable civilians before winter sets in.
Black Sea attacks threaten shipping
Khiari also expressed concern about civilian deaths and injuries resulting from intensified attacks by Ukrainian forces inside Russia.
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded reports of 3,890 civilian casualties in Russia between January and September, including 496 deaths and 3,394 injuries, said Khiari.
“All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately,” he added.
Khiari warned that the consequences of the war were increasingly extending beyond Ukraine and Russia, threatening regional security and international trade.
"Particularly worrisome, in the Black Sea, attacks on civilian vessels have multiplied and expanded in geographic scope," he said.
He welcomed diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and securing safe civilian navigation in the Black Sea, urging both to negotiate credible and sustainable arrangements.
Khiari warned that attacks on ports, transport networks, grain facilities and other agricultural infrastructure were contributing to rising global food prices.
He urged Russia and Ukraine to halt the escalating attacks on civilians and pursue renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
“The current cycle of escalating attacks against civilians must end now before the civilian toll reaches new, devastating levels,” he said.
Diplomacy and dialogue must prevail and be given a genuine chance to succeed, he noted.
“It is time to end this war,” Khiari added.

'Crashout', 'Ragebait' or 'Peak': Want to know which word is favoured by Germany's youth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:30:23 UTC
14:30:23 KST

The three frontrunners 'Crashout', 'Ragebait' and 'Peak' are in the running to become Germany's youth word of the year 2026, with anglicisms particularly trendy. The winning term will be announced this Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair.
For weeks, young Germans have been able to vote on which word best reflects their generation. The favourites are "Crashout", "Ragebait" and "Peak". Together, they attracted votes in the mid six-figure range. The poll was open to 11- to 20-year-olds.
On Saturday, Langenscheidt, the publishing house behind the vote, will announce this year's winning term at the Frankfurt Book Fair. These are the favourites.
Crashout
If you "crashout", you've lost control. "Completely losing your composure, freaking out or emotionally exploding," is how the Langenscheidt jury defines the term, which has already made it into the top three.
The twist: it does not always mean that someone is genuinely overreacting. The word can also be used ironically, especially when an emotional outburst is triggered by something trivial.
Ragebait
This term refers to digital posts on social media: content deliberately designed to provoke a reaction. "With provocative takes, blatant false claims or completely wild opinions, people try to stir up anger," explains the Langenscheidt jury.
For responses are the currency on platforms such as Instagram or TikTok. Reactions bring clicks, comments, shares and reach. The more outrage there is, the more often a post is shown: the algorithm boosts it.
Peak
This originally English word can in fact be translated literally in German: it is about peak values, highlights and summits. "If something is peak, it is the best of the best – the absolute high point, maximum quality or simply 10/10," is how the Langenscheidt jury puts it.
The other most voted words of 2026:
Altogether, 43 percent of all votes cast went to the top three terms, according to an analysis by the publisher. Since 2008 it has been choosing the Youth Word of the Year.
For Langenscheidt's spokesperson there was a surprise. The popular 67 (Six Seven), which comes with a hand gesture, only made it into the top ten and not into the three most popular terms. It is less about a fixed meaning than about belonging. The trend went viral thanks to TikTok, basketball memes and above all the song "Doot Doot (6 7)" by US rapper Skirlla.
"We were actually sure that 67 would end up in the top three," said the publishing house's spokesperson. "Once again, it shows how unpredictable and fast youth language evolves." The fact that many of the words are Anglicisms, on the other hand, came as little surprise to the publisher – that was already the case back in 2023.
Another absolute classic, "Digga", was among the submissions once more, but the term has never yet taken first place.
In addition, the line "Du bist gut genug" ('You are good enough') from a song by KitschKrieg, Shirin David and Blumengarten made it into the top ten. The short sentence went viral on TikTok and other platforms and has also delighted audiences abroad. According to the Langenscheidt jury, there are now countless memes, remixes and parodies of it.
Another term, "Gute Käse", does not have a literal meaning but roughly stands for "really good" and "solid", and ranks among the ten most popular expressions. "Macker" can mean boyfriend, crush, mate or simply a guy, depending on the context. "Schere" comes from gaming and is used in the sense of "Sorry, my bad".
Yet another language made it into the top ten: the Turkish version of the word "super". The term became widely known through a viral video of an ultramarathon runner who, when asked "How are you?" after his race, simply replied "Süper".
"Mehrzweckeier" ruled out by jury
The jury also excluded a term this year that had been submitted many times: "Mehrzweckeier". The expression first appeared at a demonstration against the reintroduction of conscription. The placard originally carried the slogan "Merz leck Eier", which was confiscated by the police. The protester then faced an investigation for slander and defamation.
Afterwards, a campaign on Reddit called on people to submit the altered term "Mehrzweckeier" as a candidate for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year. The jury vetoed it "because the term stems from a campaign and at the same time is based on a personal insult", as the reasoning puts it. It therefore meets two key exclusion criteria, the jury said.
Gammelfleischparty: The very first Youth Word of the Year
In 2008, "Gammelfleischparty" was chosen as the very first Youth Word of the Year. It refers to an over-30s party and is a cynical comment on how young people see older generations.
As the years went by, terms such as "hartzen", "swag" and the acronym "Yolo" ('you only live once') were voted winners.
More votes than ever before
Thanks not least to social media and Susanne Daubner reading out the shortlist on the main German news programme Tagesschau, the vote on the Youth Word of the Year has attracted huge attention.

Flydubai co-pilot drifted towards 'extremism and terrorism' while studying at RMIT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:29:30 UTC
14:29:30 KST

In brief
- Omani national Hammam al-Hammami become acquainted with individuals from a group called "My Centre", run by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza".
- The co-pilot attacked captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month.
The Omani Flydubai co-pilot who was accused of trying to crash a plane into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport last month was radicalised at an Australian mosque while studying in Melbourne in 2017, according to the United Arab Emirates attorney general.
Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, 29, allegedly attempted to hijack flight FZ1073 with 182 people onboard travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September before passengers and crew intervened.
A statement by UAE attorney general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi shared on UAE government social media said al-Hammami's radicalisation happened when was a student at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT). During mosque visits, al-Hammami became acquainted with individuals associated with a centre known as "My Centre".
The statement said al-Hammami had revealed the centre was managed by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza" and allegedly received support from an association linked to the Muslim Brotherhood.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The co-pilot "drew inspiration" from the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in the United States and had also used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to "familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport", , according to the statement.
Al-Hammami, who joined Flydubai in January, had previously worked for several airlines in different countries, the UAE's investigation had found.
The statement did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing, and contained the most detailed account yet from prosecutors about what they believe to have happened. Flydubai was not immediately available for comment.
Bloodied and beaten
The aircraft was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe, typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies.
Bloodied and beaten, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, alerting passengers and crew to the assault.
The incident caused the airliner to plunge 4900 metres in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia.
Al-Hammami was transferred to the UAE, Flydubai's home country.
Investigators examined Flydubai's recruiting procedures and found al-Hammami had met all professional and security requirements, including holding a pilot's licence and providing a certificate of good conduct.
"However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," al-Shamsi added.
He said the 29-year-old had worked for airlines in different countries including Oman Air before joining Flydubai in January 2026.
The investigation found there were signs of al-Hammami drifting towards "extremism and terrorism" as early as 2017, while he was studying in Australia.
Royal Air Maroc has said that he underwent three months of training there in 2025 but that his application to work for the airline afterwards was rejected.
Al-Shamsi said al-Hammami had told investigators he had prepared psychologically and physically for the attack by viewing material promoting terrorism and taking boxing lessons.
Saudi Arabia has launched a separate safety investigation into flight FZ1073, sources had told Reuters.

Israel’s economy prospers despite years of war, but prices worry voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:28:33 UTC
14:28:33 KST

Israel’s economy prospers despite years of war, but prices worry voters
Tech is driving the economy, and investments are flowing in. But food costs are rising and debt is growing, making the economy a concern for many voters.
After three years of Israel’s multi-front war in the Middle East, it would be no surprise if this month’s Knesset elections were taking place against the backdrop of an economy in dire straits.
Instead, Israel’s economy is – by many measures – flourishing.
After slowing sharply in the initial aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel has rebounded to become one of the fastest-growing advanced economies in recent years.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025, picking up from a 1 percent expansion in 2024, and 3.2 percent in the first half of this year, according to government figures.
The Bank of Israel has forecast 4 percent growth for the whole of 2026 and 5.5 percent growth in 2027 – projections that far exceed the outlooks for major economies such as the United States, United Kingdom, France, Canada, and Japan.
Over the past three years, the shekel has strengthened against the US dollar, hitting a three-decade high in May, and Israel’s stock market has surged, with the benchmark TA-125 up more than 110 percent.
Meanwhile, unemployment stands at 2.8 percent, while inflation is modest at 1.5 percent.
Against this relatively rosy economic backdrop, campaigning for the October 27 election has been dominated by national security, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, and retired general Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar, each claiming to be most qualified to keep Israelis safe.
Driving Israel’s striking economic resilience has been a booming tech sector largely insulated from its conflicts spanning Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran and Yemen.
Despite being on a war footing since October 2023, Israel has attracted record levels of investment in tech, the driver of about one-fifth of economic activity, amid the frenetic global rollout of artificial intelligence (AI).
Total direct foreign investment hit a record $26.2bn last year, up 78 percent from 2024, led by US tech giants Alphabet and Palo Alto Networks’ record-breaking acquisitions of Israeli cybersecurity firms Wiz and CyberArk, respectively.
Foreign capital has continued to flood into the country this year, with inflows reaching a quarterly record of $14.1bn in the January-March period, according to government figures.
Along with prospering from the global AI boom, Israel’s tech scene has benefitted from its close ties to the local defence sector, which has ramped up orders from hundreds of startups supplying everything from radar systems to communications platforms and anti-drone technology.
While Israel’s economy has bounced back in part due to robust employment and wage growth, its resilience is primarily an “export-driven story that reflects strong global technology demand, particularly in areas where Israel – and multinational firms operating from Israel – is globally competitive, such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence,” said Keren Uziyel, a senior analyst for the Middle East and Africa at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU).
“Interest in Israel’s technology goods and services is driving high levels of FDI and venture capital fundraising, and boosting the capital markets, which in turn is having significant wealth effects and boosting government revenue,” Uziyel told Al Jazeera.
But Israel’s military campaigns have come at an enormous cost to the public purse.
In March, the Bank of Israel estimated that Israel’s war costs to date had reached approximately 350 billion shekels ($114.6bn) – a figure not including the then recently-launched Iran war.
Military expenditures are on track to rise substantially in the coming years as Israeli leaders double down on “national security”.
Netanyahu, whose right-wing coalition has cast security as “the foundation of everything else”, has pushed to raise the annual defence budget to 183 billion shekels ($60bn), equivalent to roughly 9 percent of GDP.
If passed, the budget would raise military spending by two and a half times what it was before October 7.
Outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid has backed an expanded defence budget, but has clashed with Netanyahu about how to fund it.
Economic concerns
Though security has dominated the run-up to the election, opinion polling suggests that Israelis also view the economy as a key concern.
In an opinion poll released by the Israel Democracy Institute last month, 38 percent of Jewish Israelis and 46 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up about 20 percent of the population – chose the economy and the cost of living as the most important or second-most important election issue.
Israel’s high cost of living, in particular, has long been a source of public discontent.
Israel has for years ranked among the most expensive countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a dynamic economists attribute to the country’s limited trade relations with its neighbours and cumbersome regulations.
Though Israel’s overall rate of inflation has been modest, food prices have risen at a faster pace, increasing 8 percent between the start of 2024 and mid-2026, according to consumer advocacy group Lobby 99.
“People are worried about the economy but not so much about the macroeconomic situation, more so on their personal perspectives, especially cost of living,” Ayal Kimhi, vice president of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research in Tel Aviv, told Al Jazeera.
“However, the security situation dominates the public discourse for obvious reasons, so I do not think the economy will play a major role in the vote,” Kimhi said.
“Some parties do not even bother presenting a vision or an agenda,” he added.
“Other parties do not differ much about economic issues.”
While Israel’s headline economic figures are impressive, they come with caveats attached.
Economists note that while Israel’s economy has grown much faster than its peers, GDP has been boosted in part by the country’s usually high population growth, which has averaged nearly 2 percent over the past decade.
Israel’s growth trajectory has also taken a hit despite the expansion, with the Bank of Israel estimating an accumulated loss of output through the end of 2025 equivalent to 8.6 percent of annual GDP.
Joseph Zeira, a professor of economics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said the country’s economic performance has “not been great at all” considering that growth has consistently lagged the pre-conflict trend since late 2023.
“Actual living standards depend on the area,” Zeira told Al Jazeera, adding that Israelis are grappling with “higher prices, or rather lower real wages and incomes”, and deteriorating public services.
“The only improvement is some decline in housing prices due to a vast wave of construction in recent years,” he said.
Government debt
The long-term health of Israel’s public finances is another concern.
While Israel’s debt-to-GDP ratio of about 68 is far below that of peers such as the US, the UK, France, and Italy, the gap between government revenue and spending has grown rapidly over the past three years.
In its latest annual report, the Bank of Israel said it was “essential” for the government to “restore orderly budgetary processes” and implement “credible measures” to reduce the public debt.
Other long-term challenges include boosting labour participation among ultra-Orthodox Jewish men – whose refusal to do military service has become a major election issue – and Arab women (among Palestinian citizens of Israel), both of whom are employed at much lower rates than the general population.
“The cost of the military campaigns and mobilisation has severely strained public finances,” Omer Moav, a professor of economics at the University of Warwick and at Reichman University, told Al Jazeera.
“Deficits and national debt have expanded significantly, making current spending trajectories unsustainable without fiscal consolidation,” Moav said.
“The next government is facing a huge challenge.”
Regardless of who prevails in the election, economists say, Israel’s economic prospects will in large part hinge on whether conflict in the region escalates or subsides.
“We expect growth to reach around 4 percent in 2026 and to exceed this level in 2027,” said Uziyel, the EIU analyst.
“However, significant downside risks to growth remain should conflicts in Gaza, Iran, or on the Lebanon front resume.”
“The outlook depends greatly on the security situation,” said Kimhi of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research.
“If we are able to put an end to the war and reduce military spending, the future could be bright.”

‘Cockroach’ party rally: young Indians return to streets as Delhi braces for large protest

Unknown Publisher

05:26:42 UTC
14:26:42 KST

Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.
Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.
The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.
Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.
On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”
Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.
Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.
Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge.
In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.
Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.
In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.
Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.
Buses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.
Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.
After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”
Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”
Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.
“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”
The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.
The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.
Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.
This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.
Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.
By Saturday evening, young people continued to gather in central Delhi neighbourhoods as the police continued pick up protesters en masse. Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.
“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.
“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”

The EU and China have reached an agreement on limiting imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:17:14 EEST
14:17:14 KST

The EU and China have reached an agreement on limiting imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles
Kyiv • UNN
The EU and China have reached a common understanding on limiting the export of Chinese hybrids to Europe. They also agreed to reduce tariffs and simplify the export of rare-earth materials.
China and the European Union have reached an agreement that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the EU by more than half, European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said on Friday after talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU’s rapidly growing trade deficit with China. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to Šefčovič, the "common understanding" reached will make it possible to "curb" exports of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU. This will reduce imports by several million vehicles over four years. Following the two-day talks, he did not provide details on the mechanism for implementing the agreement.
Against the backdrop of this news, shares in European automakers, which have steadily fallen over the past two years due to U.S. tariffs and the rapid growth of Chinese exports, rose overall.
The agreement was preceded by three months of talks between Šefčovič and Chinese officials, including Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. They marked another stage in the years-long disputes between Beijing and Brussels over the rapid growth of Chinese exports, particularly automobiles.
EU leaders will discuss the results of the talks at the beginning of a summit in Brussels next Thursday. They must determine whether this agreement marks the beginning of a rebalancing of the EU’s trade deficit with China, which has grown to more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion) per day.
The chair of the European Parliament’s Committee on International Trade said the hybrid agreement should be extended to other sectors and that the EU should also apply trade-defense measures more effectively.
According to Šefčovič, the parties also reached agreements on reducing China’s import tariffs on certain goods from the EU with a total value of about €4 billion, including auto parts, olive oil and footwear. In addition, they agreed to simplify China’s procedure for issuing export licenses for rare-earth elements and permanent magnets.

Ex-justice chancellor: Orthodox church has slim chance in European court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:13:00 UTC
14:13:00 KST

Ex-justice chancellor: Orthodox church has slim chance in European court
Ex-justice chancellor Allar Jõks says the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church and Pühtitsa Convent have little chance in European court after filing a complaint prematurely.
The Estonian Christian Orthodox Church (EKÕK) and Pühtitsa Convent have challenged amendments to Estonia's Churches and Congregations Act that require them to sever ties with the Russian Orthodox Church by December 28.
Jõks said the rules for bringing a case before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) are very strict: applicants must first exhaust all domestic legal remedies and show that their rights have actually been violated.
"The ECtHR does not assess laws in the abstract to determine whether they comply with the European Convention on Human Rights, much less issue advance rulings on how they should be applied," he explained.
As both the EKÕK and Pühtitsa Convent still have until late December to make the changes required by law, Jõks said it's too soon to conclusively determine whether either one's rights have been violated and, if so, whether they have exhausted all domestic legal remedies before turning to the European court.
Estonian court system skipped
The Interior Ministry cannot assess any changes until after the December 28 deadline. If it finds them insufficient, it can ask a district court to order the religious organizations' dissolution.
Even if dissolution proceedings begin, however, Jõks said the church would still have access to judicial review and the right to appeal, meaning the dispute could therefore pass through three levels of Estonia's court system.
If questions arise over the constitutionality of the Churches and Congregations Act, he continued, the case could also trigger a constitutional review, potentially leading to a different outcome from the Supreme Court's June 8 ruling upholding the legislation.
Jõks said the EKÕK and Pühtitsa Convent's premature complaint to the ECtHR thus appears to signal distrust of the Estonian judicial system.
"Anyone who agrees with that line of thinking should try testing the judicial system on the other side of the Narva River," he said, referring to Russia.
Six months to cut ties with Moscow
The Ministry of the Interior has given the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church, which remains affiliated with the Moscow Patriarchate, six months to appoint a new metropolitan and sever its ties with the Russian Orthodox Church.
Its previous leader, Metropolitan Eugene (legal name Valeri Reshetnikov), was ordered to leave Estonia in February 2024 after authorities refused to extend the Russian citizen's residence permit on national security grounds.
In its rejection, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) cited Reshetnikov's activities and public statements as a representative of the Moscow Patriarchate in Estonia.
The Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS) likewise said both he and Patriarch Kirill, the religious leader of the Russian Orthodox Church, had consistently supported Russia's war against Ukraine and helped advance the Kremlin's security policy in Estonia.
Formerly known as the Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate (MPEÕK), the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church (EKÕK) is separate from the Estonian Apostolic Orthodox Church (EAÕK), the legal continuation of the Estonian Orthodox Church (EÕK) under the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople.

Taiwan president says defence spending boost aims to ‘deter war’
China condemns Lai’s speech, saying it ‘disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public’.
Taiwan President William Lai Ching-te says the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom” in a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office in Taipei.
Lai made the remarks on Saturday in front of thousands of people, including foreign guests and diplomats. Fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over Taipei before his speech.
“We are open to exchanges but will not accept subordination,” he said. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office condemned Lai’s speech, saying it “disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives”.
It said Lai “stubbornly clung to ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist thinking” and exaggerated the “threat from the mainland”.
“There is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is part of China – this is the true status quo in the Taiwan Strait,” it said.
Taiwan’s future “can and must be decided jointly by all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in Taiwan”, it also said.
Pressure from China
The holiday marks the 115th anniversary of a 1911 uprising that toppled China’s last imperial dynasty and led to the founding of the Republic of China.
Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory, has never renounced the use of force to take it and calls Lai a “separatist”.
Beijing has rebuffed his offers of talks.
Lai said China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait”.
Grey-zone tactics are actions that stop short of open war. “Peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” he added.
Lai’s government has set aside a record 1.1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($34.5bn) for defence in 2027, more than 3 percent of its gross domestic product.
China held war games around the island shortly after Lai’s first National Day speech in 2024 but not last year. Its last drills near Taiwan were in late December after news of an $11bn arms deal with the United States, the largest ever US weapons package for the island.
Lai said he welcomed talks between the US and China but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist”.
He urged democracies in the Asia Pacific to join forces to preserve peace and stability in the region.
Lai also said China has exerted pressure to try to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait and the island’s “resolve” is not just about its own survival in the face of “authoritarian expansion”. It’s also about whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules, he added.
According to Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence, 21 Chinese military aircraft and seven navy ships were operating around Taiwan in a 24-hour period ending at 6am on Saturday (22:00 GMT on Friday). Thirteen of the aircraft crossed the median line in the Taiwan Strait, which once served as an unofficial barrier between the two sides, and entered the island’s air defence identification zone.
Eswatini King Mswati III and Indiana Lieutenant Governor Micah Beckwith were among the foreign guests who offered their congratulations in Taiwan, Lai’s office said. Eswatini is Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in Africa. A Japanese parliamentary delegation also visited the island and joined the National Day celebrations.
The US switched its official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago but remains Taiwan’s most important security backer.
Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump.
In May, after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, Trump suggested arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, which set off alarm across the world.
Taiwan is now waiting for Trump to sign off on $14bn worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system.
The dispute dates back to China’s civil war, when the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after defeat by Mao Zedong’s communists.
The Republic of China remains the island’s formal name.

When will El Niño peak and end? A full timeline of the weather phenomenon taking the world by storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:02:03 UTC
14:02:03 KST

A ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is still intensifying in the Pacific. When will we see the weather phenomenon peak – and when will it come to an end?
2026 will go down in history for what could become the largest El Niño in living memory, as the world scrambles to prepare for an onslaught of extreme weather.
The natural weather phenomenon (Spanish for ‘the boy’) occurs irregularly – roughly every two to seven years – when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. Experts first started warning that a strong El Niño could form at the beginning of this year, supported by large amounts of heat in the subsurface ocean and the expected weakening of low-level trade winds.
In the first week of June, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed that El Niño conditions were officially underway. Towards the end of summer, experts warned that the “unprecedented” El Niño could become the largest event since the 19th century – gaining the nickname of a ‘Godzilla’ or ‘Super’ El Niño.
Is El Niño getting stronger – and what are the impacts?
According to the WMO, sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October, November and December.
Sea-surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region at the heart of El Niño, are measured by the widely used Niño 3.4 index. This increased markedly from an average +1.6 °C above normal in June 2026 to +2.5 °C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the seasonal average Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly is forecast to reach approximately +3.7°C. This would be the highest since observations began and is stronger than the previous record of +2.6°C in November 2015-January 2016.
Previous El Niño events have contributed towards record-breaking heat, fuelling long-standing droughts, flash floods and deadly wildfires across the globe.
El Niño’s weather impacts are mainly felt in the tropics, but Europe can experience milder, wetter winters. An El Niño peak can also weaken the polar vortex, increasing the likelihood of a cold snap.
South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.
Extreme weather overseas will still have a knock-on effect for Europe. The IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands has been working in areas that are directly impacted by El Niño and warn that many staple foods that Europe imports could be at risk.
For example, in Nicaragua, crops such as maize and beans may fail in already fragile areas, leading to food insecurity and income loss in the country. A lack of rain and low flows in rivers also mean that irrigated crops in Colombia, Northeast Brazil and India will face severe restrictions or will need to rely more on groundwater, potentially causing overexploitation in the area – and export shortages.
A timeline of El Niño: When will it peak and end?
The WMO’s latest statement says that El Niño is forecast to peak in December, and will continue into next year.
“El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” warns WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 per cent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”
The almost-certain figure isn’t from one climate model. The WMO has coordinated ocean buoy, satellite and radiosonde data from 13 national and international centres to make the prediction.
El Niño isn’t expected to end until spring 2027, but its impacts will likely stretch further. It’s why experts warn that next year could become the hottest on record.
El Niño clashes with climate change
Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.
Human-caused global warming from the burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. It is this that paved the way for Europe’s scorching summer, long-standing drought and deadly wildfires.
Nowadays, El Niño’s impacts are compounded by an already warming world – one that has a much stronger influence on the extreme weather we’re witnessing. 2025, for example, was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally-forming cool drag of El Niño’s counterpart, La Niña.
Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño events too, by making them 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era.
“El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok in October.
“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”

Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

Often, the greatest dishes are made from very few ingredients and with pretty standard techniques, and this tart is one of them. It’s based on an old Frédy Girardet recipe that, despite his reputation as one of the all-time greats, calls only for a simple application of process to deliver a knockout result (which is one reason I put it in my latest book). A pastry case is spread with sugar and cream, then dotted with butter and sprinkled with cinnamon. The pastry is not blind baked, but filled and baked in a very hot oven. That sounds wrong, but it is not: a fierce heat is needed to bake the pastry under its filling and to meld the cream, sugar and butter. A pinch of flour is mixed with the sugar and, as it all boils up, that smidgen of flour holds everything together as it bubbles and reduces until it takes on the appearance of condensed milk while the pastry cooks and toasts at the edges. I still use Girardet’s quantities because, unsurprisingly, they work perfectly. Merci, chef.
Tarte Vaudoise a la creme
Prep 10 min
Cook 1 hr + cooling
Serves 4-6
For the pastry
140g plain flour, plus extra for dusting
5g baking powder
1 pinch salt
1 generous pinch caster sugar
60g unsalted butter, at room temperature and cut into small pieces
50ml cold whole milk
For the filling
100g caster sugar
1 generous pinch plain flour
250ml double cream
50g cold unsalted butter, diced
A little ground cinnamon (freshly ground is worth the faff)
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. To make the pastry, sift the flour into a large bowl, then mix in the baking powder, salt and sugar. Add the butter, then work it in with your fingertips until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs.
Pour in the milk and mix with as light a hand as possible to bring the dough into a ball. Don’t rest the pastry, because that will activate the baking powder too soon and the pastry will puff up through the filling while it cooks. Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface into a circle big enough to line a 25cm tart tin, then lay it in the tin and prick the pastry all over with a fork.
For the filling, mix the sugar and flour, then spread it in an even layer over the base of the pastry case. Pour in the cream, then scatter over the diced butter and a light sprinkling of ground cinnamon. Bake for about 25 minutes, until the edges of the pastry are a good biscuit colour and the cream has bubbled up and looks thick and almost about to split.
Remove from the oven and transfer the tin to a rack to cool completely. To serve, carefully remove the tart from its tin and cut into slices.
- Henry Harris is chef/co-owner of Bouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go to guardianbookshop.com
