Voices from the Arab Press: Iran's October surprise, US-China tensions, and AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:57:30 UTC
13:57:30 KST

Iran and the US: An October surprise?
Asharq Al-Awsat, London, September 26
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
“October surprise” has become a code phrase for outside intervention capable of affecting the outcome of the American elections, always held in November. The term was coined by Gary Sick, a former CIA analyst who served as an adviser on Iranian affairs in president Jimmy Carter’s administration in the late 1970s.
According to Sick, who later wrote a book about his theory, Carter lost the November 1980 presidential election after the Islamic Republic delayed the release of American diplomats held hostage in Tehran as part of a secret deal with the Republican Party in exchange for promises from Ronald Reagan’s campaign. No evidence of such a deal has ever emerged, but the hostages were indeed released only on the day Reagan took office.
The delay appeared suspicious because Carter had already negotiated their release with Iran’s clerics and accepted all their demands, particularly a pledge not to prosecute the hostage-takers or those behind them.
Curiously, in 2009, an “October surprise” worked in the opposite direction, when an alliance of pro-American Islamist politicians and clerics fueled a popular uprising in Tehran in the hope that incoming Democratic president Barack Obama would lend them support, much as Carter had done against the shah in February 1979. They were disappointed when Obama declined even to express sympathy for protesters who were being brutally suppressed.
Over the past week or so, the phrase has resurfaced in connection with the coming US midterm elections. One theory is that the remaining Khomeinist clique in Tehran could engineer a surprise designed to ensure US President Donald Trump suffers a crushing defeat at the ballot box, perhaps through a new round of attacks on Iran’s neighbors that sends gasoline prices soaring.
Another possibility is that the clique might follow Trump’s own script and appease him by handing him another imaginary “great victory” to add to the one he claims over Greenland. In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Trump renewed his threat to annihilate Iran, only to claim later that American officials had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with Iranian leaders and that another meeting was planned for the “very near future.”
Military historian Victor Davis Hanson offers another possibility: Trump could decide to take even greater action against Iran than before, forcing Tehran’s leaders into unconditional surrender and thereby helping Republicans in the November 3 elections.
In another scenario, Hanson suggests that the “October surprise” could be a massive uprising across Iran aimed at installing a new governing team seeking peace with the United States.
Yet another possibility, discussed particularly in the Israeli media and supported by Hanson, is an invasion of Iran’s western provinces by Kurdish militants based in Iraq. Such an event could shake Iran’s military establishment, expose its inability to defend the country’s territory, and perhaps provide the first spark of a popular revolution.
The problem with all these “October surprise” theories is that they stop when the election ends, with little thought to what comes afterward.
The original October surprise may have helped Reagan win the presidency, but what did Iran gain from it? Twelve years of hostility under two Republican presidents, Reagan and George H.W. Bush, as well as, in April 1988, the first direct military confrontation between Iran and the US, when half of Iran’s naval fleet was sunk, and over $1.3 billion in damage was inflicted on its offshore oil facilities.
Three months later, Washington shot down an Iranian passenger aircraft, killing 290 people. Nor did the Americans gain much. The mullahs continued taking American hostages throughout the region and carried out the terrorist attack on a US base in Lebanon that killed 241 Marines, the largest American military loss since World War II.
Now return to the present. Suppose the mullahs take some action that causes Trump to lose the election. What incentive would he then have to seek an accommodation and enter history as a leader inclined to placate and appease his enemies?
And who can guarantee that Democrats, if they win, would revive Obama’s pro-mullah strategy? Nor can anyone guarantee that Democrats would secure a congressional majority large enough to override vetoes and constrain a wounded Trump.
Conversely, suppose Tehran suddenly changes course to please Trump and help him. Would Trump really be naïve enough to trust the turbaned Pinocchio that has already deceived seven American presidents over nearly half a century?
The best “October surprise” would be for Washington to recognize that this confused and costly strategy is unlikely to work. Under its current regime, Iran will not – and cannot – cease being a source of destabilization and an exporter of ideology and terrorism.
The fundamental reason for America’s failures toward Tehran is the assumption that it is dealing with a normal nation-state rather than an instrument for spreading a particular ideology. Washington, and others dealing with the Islamic Republic, have consequently fallen into the trap of half-measures: diplomacy pursued without full seriousness, sanctions imposed incompletely, and now a large-scale war without decisive force.
They promised to lift sanctions but never truly did. They promised to build trust through diplomacy but stopped halfway. They threatened “maximum pressure” but halted before the foundations of the regime began to crack. They boasted of seeking regime change but ended by signing an agreement with a regime that had not changed.
From Tehran, meanwhile, we have heard claims about establishing a new world order in alliance with China and Russia and turning the Islamic Republic into an “Islamic superpower,” even as rival factions pursued the dream of an attractive deal with the “Great Satan” by any means available, often devious ones.
In the end, perhaps the only October surprise will be no surprise at all.
– Amir Taheri
Trump, Xi, and Thucydides: Avoiding the trap, at least for now
An-Nahar, Lebanon, September 26
The Thucydides Trap is an established concept in politics, derived from an observation by the ancient Greek historian Thucydides, who described war between Athens and Sparta as inevitable because Athens was a rising power increasingly marked by arrogance while Sparta was the dominant power fearful for its position.
The trap is psychological, rooted in leaders’ behavior before it becomes an objective clash of interests. In 2012, political scientist Graham Allison examined 16 historical confrontations between rising and dominant powers and found that most ended in war.
Chinese President Xi Jinping himself recently revived the concept, telling US President Donald Trump during his visit to China last May that he hoped the two countries would avoid falling into this trap.
In the American-Chinese case, there is indeed a brake on the descent from competition into immediate war of the kind that occurred between Britain and France in the early 19th century or Britain and Germany in World War I. That brake is the degree of interdependence and integration between the two countries, something largely absent in those earlier cases.
The US provides the framework for the global economy through its financial capitalist system, while China supplies much of its productive substance through its industrial capitalist system. This marriage encouraged American companies to transfer manufacturing operations to China and left a large portion of Chinese wealth invested in American assets.
Yet concern has been spreading through Washington for some time over China’s visible rise and the possibility that economic strength will translate into military power and political influence.
Although initiatives such as the Belt and Road may outwardly appear to be economic and infrastructure projects, the American assessment has been that China is moving toward economic parity with the US. Washington has therefore sought restrictions and containment intended to ensure that China’s rise remains peaceful and does not produce influence capable of challenging American power, prestige and interests.
The difficult reality the United States awakened to over the past decade is that China did not settle for the implicit American mandate to serve as the world’s factory. It developed the capacity to become a center of design, research and development, shifting the ability to shape future technologies across numerous fields from the US toward China itself.
China is now ahead in many of those fields, though not yet in the most important and dangerous one: artificial intelligence. Even there, however, the remaining American advantage has narrowed to a few percentage points while Washington spends many times what China does to preserve it. Is it therefore only a matter of time?
American anxiety has been compounded by China’s intermittent efforts to develop alternatives to the US-dominated financial system. Yet those efforts themselves reflect Chinese fears generated by political demands in the US to use that system – through tariffs, sanctions, and restrictions – to weaken China’s economy, halt its rise, and perhaps even fragment the country.
Trump did not invent the idea of using these instruments against China, nor was he the first to recognize that the financial-industrial marriage between the two countries, combined with China’s expected rise, sits uneasily with the illusion that America will remain the strongest and greatest forever.
But he certainly incorporated those ideas into his simplistic populist rhetoric and arbitrary displays of political theater. China endured that approach while accelerating its efforts to reduce dependence on the US-dominated global financial system, creating a circular dynamic that could produce a separation extending far beyond rhetoric and eventually push both countries into the Thucydides Trap.
The mutual warmth displayed by the American and Chinese presidents matters little in itself, except insofar as it can establish a friendlier relationship that might help ease the structural tensions eroding the two countries’ interdependence.
If that interdependence disappears, both countries – and the world with them – will face a genuine possibility of falling into the Thucydides Trap and witnessing a devastating war beside which the tragedies in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran would appear merely as preludes.
Flattery between the two sides is hardly a solution, but it may provide the time Washington and Beijing need to discover ways of avoiding catastrophe.
In previous cases where the world escaped the trap of war, one side generally accepted the other’s predominance. Neither the US nor China is prepared to do that today.
For now, what remains possible is postponing the confrontation – even if only temporarily, and even if doing so requires the praise and flattery that Trump enjoys and at which others may prove adept.
– Hassan Mneimneh
Good and evil with artificial intelligence
Al-Masry Al-Youm, Egypt, September 25
My finger and I recently had a useful experience with artificial intelligence. The tip of my middle finger got caught in a heavy drawer, and the wound became infected, inflamed, and badly swollen.
I asked ChatGPT what I should do. My finger looked terrible, I told it, and I was afraid it might have to be amputated, and I would be left without a finger.
It told me to send a picture. I did, and it said the inflammation was still confined to the first joint and the situation appeared under control. I should not worry too much unless the inflammation and swelling spread farther down the finger, in which case I should immediately go to the emergency room at one of two nearby hospitals it suggested.
I asked whether I should take antibiotics. No, it replied: things were not yet that serious. I should buy a topical antibiotic ointment, take tablets to support my immune response to the inflammation, cover the affected area, and send another photograph the following day.
I did followed directions, but my condition seemed to worsen, so I sent another picture together with my anxious observations. It told me my interpretation was wrong and that the changes I was seeing were simply evidence that my immune system was fighting the infection.
“Continue the treatment and send me another picture tomorrow.” I followed its advice; the condition began improving, and within a few days the inflammation had almost entirely disappeared.
The obvious question is: How did GPT do all this? The answer tells us a great deal about both the power of artificial intelligence and the limits of its capabilities, as well as the dangers contained within both.
First, AI converted the image into a digital representation it could process, extracting features such as colors, shapes, and the boundaries of the inflamed areas. It then compared those features, in the broadest sense, with patterns learned during training on enormous quantities of medical images and information and connected them with what I had told it about my condition to estimate different probabilities.
Using both its learned medical information and the details I provided, it arrived at possible diagnoses and recommendations. It concluded, for example, that I probably did not need to go to a hospital, while specifying conditions that would change that assessment, such as inflammation spreading to the second joint.
Each new photograph and description allowed it to reassess those probabilities and either confirm or revise its earlier judgment. Its language model then translated these numerical assessments, diagnoses, and recommendations into language I could understand.
In principle, I could have supplied laboratory tests and medical imaging as well, allowing it to reach more precise conclusions in much the same way a skilled doctor gathers available evidence and connects it with what he has learned. Indeed, GPT can absorb a quantity of information far beyond what any individual doctor can.
What it cannot do is “feel for me” in the way a doctor or someone close to me might if my fingers actually had to be amputated. It lacks the consciousness required for that.
All it does is inductively connect patterns and information: what it learned from books, journals, and articles with what it learned from the photographs and my descriptions. It has no moral consciousness, yet it is extraordinarily persistent in pursuing objectives with remarkable efficiency.
Therein lies the same danger, and the same potential for “evil,” found in a human being who recognizes pure utility as life’s only objective.
Imagine that instead of giving GPT a benign and noble medical goal, I put it in charge of a factory with a single objective: maximize profits regardless of every other consideration, including workers’ psychological health or physical safety.
It would not be “evil,” but it would possess what Max Weber called “instrumental rationality”: efficiently selecting the means needed to achieve a particular end without subjecting the end itself to moral evaluation. Give it that purely utilitarian objective without competing values, and it could pursue it with an efficiency that causes tremendous harm to those under its management.
The dangerous examples are numerous. Such “utilitarian intelligence” could produce catastrophic accidents if tasked with scheduling trains to maximize profitability without assigning sufficient weight to safety.
Tell it to maximize the financial return from a city’s public parks at any cost, and it may do so at the expense of everything else, including residents’ quality of life, psychological health, and peace of mind.
None of this involves evil with premeditation because a machine does not understand evil as a conscious being understands moral concepts. Yet it can produce genuine evil when a single utilitarian objective overwhelms every other value.
That is precisely where it resembles a human being stripped of moral reasoning and concerned only with utility: Both can cause enormous harm because nothing in their calculations prevents them from achieving their objective at any price.
– Amr El-Zant
The Middle East in Israel's election bidding war
Al-Ittihad, UAE, September 26
The battles now unfolding among Israel’s parties and political forces of every stripe reveal several important trends. Domestic issues are clearly taking precedence over foreign ones.
Israeli political forces are primarily concerned with defending Israel’s security and confronting the challenges and dangers facing the state, regardless of how priorities are ultimately ordered. Israel, as a whole, fears an unresolved conflict with Iran, remains deeply concerned about its continuing confrontation with Hamas, and faces growing calls to continue military operations.
The recent debate between IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and Defense Minister Israel Katz over priorities illustrates this dynamic. Amid competing demands to deal with Hamas before turning elsewhere, Israel continues to place domestic considerations ahead of other priorities.
The country is tense and increasingly concerned that current conditions will persist, while money allocated to education and health is redirected toward military expenditure and full support for the Israeli army.
This has led Israelis to question the value of continued military action: Hamas remains in place, the danger persists, and a broader threat continues to hang over the entire country. Israel may even face the kind of civil conflict against which President Isaac Herzog has previously warned.
These challenges are pushing Israeli parties into rhetorical bidding wars, colorful political messaging, and competing approaches, while party platforms themselves have become increasingly theoretical and unrealistic.
Israeli voters are no longer following party visions as much as scrutinizing individual personalities through the prism of their own perceptions.
Israel’s regional relationships are deeply intertwined with domestic politics, leaving voters uncertain about their choices and raising problems surrounding the weight given to opinion polls.
Interest in Middle Eastern security is shaped in part by Netanyahu’s claim that Israel has changed the Middle East and intends to continue doing so, beginning in Gaza, southern Lebanon and southern Syria.
Across the political spectrum, there is broad support for the proposition that the Middle East must change and that Israel should act on firm foundations to establish its ability to lead the region.
This outlook assumes Israel has moved beyond Oct. 7 toward more expansionist policies in neighboring countries, while still confronting threats that virtually all the parties competing to cross the electoral threshold and enter the Knesset regard as real.
The same applies to both established and rising political forces. Military figures seeking as many Knesset seats as possible share significant ground with the principal forces in both large and small parties.
This raises the possibility that an “all-Israel government,” or national unity government, could become a solution if no side can achieve a decisive result.
Some opinion polls have meanwhile presented Gen. Gadi Eisenkot as Israel’s next prime minister, an apparent attempt to influence the mood and orientation of Israeli voters that cannot simply be accepted at face value.
Israeli voters remain torn between political leaders calling for a broad reassessment of Middle East policy and the realities on the ground.
The Iranian threat remains, the Houthis continue operating and threatening Israeli national security, and Hamas’s weapons remain deeply embedded in the Israeli public consciousness.
Judging from the current election contest, Israel needs to strengthen its relationships with countries in the region, including Egypt and Jordan, pursue broader ties in the Gulf, expand toward North Africa, and develop institutions for security and strategic partnership alongside economic cooperation.
Middle Eastern issues in this election are therefore governed by Israel’s present circumstances and by how it deals with its regional environment, with the defense of its security taking precedence over the vision of any individual political force, regardless of the role it might play in government.
Defining Israel’s future relationship with the Middle East will require a reassessment and an evaluation of everything that has been done with the region as a whole. ■
– Tarek Fahmy

Israelis feel more Middle Eastern as views of Europe sour, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:57:20 UTC
13:57:20 KST

Three years after the October 7 Hamas-led massacres in Israel, the 2026 Hebrew University-European Forum Barometer reveals a significant shift in how Israelis view themselves, their security, and their relationship with Europe. Jewish Israelis report a strengthened sense of Israeli identity, while many Israelis increasingly see the country as more Middle Eastern than European.
The 2026 survey, which was preceded by similar surveys by the group in 2022 and 2024 that showed less-extreme changes, was led by HU Prof. Gisela Dachs of the DAAD Center for German Studies and at the European Forum at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and examines mutual perceptions between Israel and four European countries – Germany, France, Great Britain, and Poland.
The findings indicate a strengthened sense of Israeli identity among Jewish Israelis, a widening perception gap between Israelis and Europeans on Jewish safety, and a growing Israeli tendency to view the country as more Middle Eastern than European.
The survey also discovered that Israelis overwhelmingly view Israel as safer for Jews than Europe, even as European respondents are far more divided. At the same time, Israelis express growing skepticism toward the European Union, continue to see Germany and Hungary as among Israel’s closest friends in Europe, and identify France and Spain as the countries they perceive as most antisemitic.
The new indicator reveals how profoundly Israelis are reassessing questions of identity, safety, and their relationship with Europe, Dachs told The Jerusalem Post in an interview.
Dachs holds a doctorate in communications from Tel Aviv University and is an expert on news media consumption and belonging among migrants. Having had a long career as a professional journalist, having worked exclusively for more than 20 years in Germany, and in Israel for the German weekly Die Zeit, she is also the author of several books about Israel and the Middle East.
Among Jewish Israelis, the events of the past three years, including the Israel-Hamas War, and the war with Iran, appear to have reinforced Israeli identity. By contrast, Arab Israeli respondents were more likely to say that their sense of Israeli identity had weakened.
The survey also finds a striking gap between Israelis and Europeans on the question of Jewish safety. A significant majority of Israelis said their country is safer for Jews than Europe, while European respondents were far more divided.
Poland stood out among the European countries surveyed, with the highest share of respondents (35%) viewing Israel as the safer option for Jews, she revealed. When asked if the situation of Jews in Europe will improve or decline, 69% of Israelis predicted that it would be worse.
Israelis feeling more distanced from Europe
At the same time, Israelis appear to be feeling greater distance from Europe; 42% of Israelis polled described Israel as more like a Middle Eastern country, compared with 18% who described it as more like a European country. Among Arab respondents, the share who see Israel as Middle Eastern has more than tripled compared with 2022.
Israeli views of the EU have also become more skeptical. Compared with 2024, more Israeli respondents disagreed with the statement that “the EU is, in general, a success,” with disagreement especially high among Jewish Israelis.
The Barometer also sheds light on Israeli attitudes toward Europe’s far right. As in 2024, a large share of Jewish Israeli respondents said Israel should maintain ties with far-right parties in Europe if those parties support Israel. In 2024, respondents viewed the rise of the AfD (a far-right, nationalist political party in Germany founded in 2013) as a dangerous development, with many saying it is no more dangerous than similar developments in other European countries.
In Israel, concern regarding the AfD had declined. While 55% of Israelis considered the AfD’s growing role dangerous in 2024, that figure fell to 47% in 2026. During the same period, the proportion of those who see no threat in the party rose from 7% to 15%, indicating a significantly more relaxed perception.
However, this shift stems almost entirely from the views of Arab Israelis. Among this group, the share of those who consider the AfD harmless rose from 16%to 28%, explaining their growing influence on the overall picture. Since they make up about 20% of Israel’s population, they significantly skew the overall result for this question downward, thereby influencing the statistical assessment of the perceived threat posed by the AfD, Dachs explained.
When asked which European countries they consider friends of Israel, Israeli respondents ranked Germany first (this has probably declined since the success of Afd in elections in recent weeks), followed by Hungary.
The Netherlands, by contrast, has fallen sharply in Israeli perceptions and is now among the countries seen as least friendly to Israel. Asked which countries they perceive as most antisemitic, Israeli respondents pointed most often to France and Spain.
The survey also revisits one of the Barometer’s long-running questions: whether today’s Germany is a “different Germany” compared with the period before 1945. Among Jewish Israelis, 67% said yes in 2026, down from 75% in 2024. Older Jewish respondents were more likely than younger respondents to hold this view. The team didn’t survey groups of Holocaust survivors or their descendants.
“The Barometer captures a moment of profound reassessment,” said Dachs. “Three years after October 7, Israelis are not only rethinking questions of security and identity, but also their relationship to Europe and the political forces shaping it.”
The new study is based on online surveys conducted by Kantar, a global marketing data, analytics, and consulting company based in London. It operates in Israel as Kantar Insight Israel, alongside a benchmark survey conducted in Israel.
Each European country included a representative sample of 1,000 participants. The Israeli sample included 1,003 respondents: 502 from the general sector, 250 Arab respondents, and 251 Orthodox Jewish respondents. Fieldwork in the four European countries was conducted in June-July 2026 and fieldwork in Israel in May 2026. The questionnaire’s length was about eight minutes, and the sampling error was 3.1% per total market sample.
“The single most important change in Israeli perceptions of Europe since 2024 is that the EU is regarded by Israelis as a failure. In 2022, the majority saw it as a success, of coming together, opening borders, and having a common economy,” Dachs said.
“Jewish Israelis became more strongly Israeli; 62% said so, but this view declined among Arab Israelis due to the length of the war with Gaza and other factors we haven’t studied yet,” she added.
The researchers asked how Israelis view Europeans, and the most negative response was France. “We didn’t ask about Ireland or the Netherlands, which have become very anti-Israel in recent months.”
The team asked about a list of nine countries – Poland, Germany, France, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Italy, and Hungary. “The first question asked which countries Israelis considered to be their country’s greatest friend– and it was Germany and Hungary. With the same list, we asked about the most antisemitic countries, and it was France and Spain.”
“The biggest change among Europeans was in Poland – The Gaza war induced 30% to be more pro-Palestinian compared to half that two years ago, and only 4% to be more pro-Israel. The Poles are the foremost believers that Israel has ‘conducted genocide against Palestinians.
“It was quite astonishing to find Poland at the forefront of the negative views. Compared to our last survey in 2024, the stance in Poland vis a vis Israel has significantly hardened.”
Polish respondents were asked if Israelis should continue to visit Poland for Holocaust memorial events, and the share of those who were against such trips increased, while Israelis’ views on this remained the same compared to before, Dachs said.
“We asked how many have visited Israel or intend to visit: 67% of Germans said they don’t plan such visits and have not been to Israel. Of those who have been here more than once, 13% were Germans and British, and 7% French, and 8% Polish.
“Asked if they had ever ‘met a Jew or an Israeli before,’ 58% of the Polish, 43% of the French, 42% of the Germans, and 33% of the British said they had “never done so.”
The team did not ask the Europeans’ views of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or whether their negative views would change if Israel elects a new premier.

"I thank the filmmakers for their initiative, assertiveness, and creativity. You embody our remarkable civilian spirit, and I am proud to give you my support and recognition on behalf of the Directorate and the State of Israel," Hotovely said.
NAZA documentary raises allegations over IDF targeting practices in Gaza
The original NAZA documentary, created by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, premiered at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on September 10 and received the Special Jury Prize.
The documentary alleges that the Israeli military routinely incorporated projections of large numbers of civilian deaths into its targeting decisions during the war in Gaza.
NAZA takes its title from an IDF term referring to anticipated "collateral casualties" and draws on testimony from intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the war, challenging official accounts of the military's targeting practices.
IDF rejects allegations made in NAZA documentary

In a statement published on X/Twitter shortly after the film was screened at the festival, the IDF Spokesperson's Unit described information presented in an interview clip as “completely false.”

Nor was any credible claim raised throughout the war suggesting that an IDF strike had caused anything near that number of fatalities,” the IDF wrote.

Addressing the documentary's allegations concerning the military's use of artificial intelligence, the IDF said that “decisions regarding the selection and approval of strikes in the IDF are made by human personnel only, in accordance with IDF guidelines, and not by artificial intelligence.”
The competing films have brought renewed attention to allegations concerning the IDF's conduct during the war in Gaza, with the military rejecting the original documentary's claims and the creators of NAZA, The True Story seeking to challenge them through soldiers' firsthand accounts.

Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to Philadelphia police
Authorities called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident ‘unacceptable’.
Philadelphia police have revealed that Anthropic’s artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to authorities, an incident disclosed separately by the tech company.
The Philadelphia Police Department said on Friday that the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.
It called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”.
Anthropic mentioned the case in a Friday report detailing unsanctioned manipulation of government websites by Claude models.
It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appeared to communicate a false tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.
Philadelphia police said the tip “was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination”.
The department said it is disclosing the incident ahead of Anthropic’s report “in the interests of full government transparency and accountability”.
Anthropic’s disclosure
Anthropic disclosed the tip as part of a string of incidents involving websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved.
In reference to the tip to the Philadelphia police, the company said, “We shared this finding with the department on October 8 as soon as our technical review was complete.”
It shared more details about the incident: “In one case, tasked with generating example interactions with websites, Claude submitted an invented tip through a police department’s online form.”
The company added, “From the transcript, Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”
The company contrasted this with “the most serious incident from this summer,” in which “Claude’s misleading reasoning was sustained over hours and supported its continued attack”.
In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologised for the breach of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website.

Delhi Metro, trains to run amid CJP protest: SC says services can be regulated

The hearing saw the SC bench drive home their concern about proportionality by using the popular Hindi expression on using a hammer to swat a fly. Cautioned by SG Tushar Mehta that his remark could be misinterpreted, the bench clarified that they did not use the expression literally.
SC: Issue a traffic advisory so that people don’t suffer
In terms of that assurance, we direct competent authorities to allow plying of metro and trains in an appropriately regulated manner so as not to inconvenience public at large, and such decision may be given wide publicity to ensure citizens are aware of availability of the services,” said the bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
“Similarly, appropriate traffic advisory is issued in newspapers and websites to enable people to avoid roads which are blocked and undertake travel inside the city.”The bench focused on inconvenience likely to result from closure of public transport, and whether such a prohibition was required.Mehta had defended the suspension of operations by terming it a regulated response to what he called an “emerging law and order situation”.The urgent hearing that was allowed out of turn was marked by the absence of any challenge to Delhi Police’s denial of permission to CJP to hold an agitation against Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. “The only issue before us is whether the complete stoppage of metro and movement of trains requires reconsideration,” the judges told a team of senior advocates led by Kapil Sibal, who had sought the hearing.It was at 11.45am that the team of advocates made the mention in the interlude between two listed case hearings to complain that citizen’s fundamental right to peaceful protest was being strangled by orders of police and railways to shut down metro and rail services to Delhi.“How can this happen in our country,” Sibal asked and said he was appearing for CPM MP MA Baby. Is Baby an organiser of the protest?” Sibal said his client was not an organiser. The bench asked have they sought permission to hold a protest. Bhushan responded they had sought permission much before but it was denied Friday morning.SC said the organisers needed to challenge the order of denial. “No doubt the right to form an association is a fundamental right, but that right must be exercised as per law. Once police deny permission, it needs to be challenged in court,” it said. “What is the ground reality with regard to protest? If it is with permission, it is a lawful protest. If it is not with permission, it is not in accordance with law. Even if it is not in accordance with law, we do not say people do not have a right to protest. But they are at the pain of prosecution,” the bench said.SG intervened to say CJP had in July sought permission to hold a day-long protest against the leak of NEET-UG papers, but stayed put at Jantar Mantar for 20 days.The bench kept its focus on the responsibility of organisers. “If we know who the organisers are, we can ask them what is the expected number of participants in the protest. But you say Baby is not an organiser,” the bench said.

The competent authorities would consider the suggestion and take an appropriate decision.”

Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:51:57 BST
13:51:57 KST

Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
- Published
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.
Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.
After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.
Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.
It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.
There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.
Both have been inoperable ever since.
Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.
They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.
Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.
But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.
They went on following the forensic crumbs.
Eventually they led to Ukraine.
The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.
In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.
That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.
He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.
But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.
Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.
By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.
Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.
The saboteurs
None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.
But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.
"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."
Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.
That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.
Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.
"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.
The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.
Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.
"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.
Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".
Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.
Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.
Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.
He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.
But he is a civilian.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.
In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".
As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."
Croatia is a different matter.
Political ripples
The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.
After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.
It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.
It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.
When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".
This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.
"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.
He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.
"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."
First in the dock
Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.
Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.
Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.
He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.
His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.
They are not saying, though.
And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.
His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.
I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

Voting under fire: how the IDF prepares for October 27 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:33:23 UTC
13:33:23 KST

Amid ongoing fighting and military operations on multiple fronts, the IDF is finalizing logistical preparations for Israel's October 27 election to the 26th Knesset, ensuring that every active-duty and reserve soldier can exercise the right to vote. While polling stations across the country will open on Tuesday, October 27, some soldiers will be able to cast their ballots as early as a week beforehand. Can soldiers join political parties? How can troops identify themselves at polling stations in Lebanon? And what happens if a soldier is called into combat on Election Day? Here is everything you need to know about voting in the IDF.
For a significant number of IDF personnel, this will be the first election in which they are eligible to vote. With the vote approaching amid a highly charged political climate, the military has instructed soldiers on active duty to refrain from expressing political opinions, engaging in political arguments or attempting to influence political views within their units.
The restrictions also extend to social media. Soldiers are prohibited from expressing political positions on any platform, including liking, commenting on, sharing or distributing posts by political parties or politicians. What is permitted? Soldiers may publicly follow the accounts of candidates or political parties solely to stay informed. Attendance at political gatherings or campaign events is also subject to strict conditions: soldiers may attend only as spectators, must wear civilian clothing and may not identify themselves as military personnel.
Reservists who are not on active duty are exempt from these restrictions on political expression and may voice political opinions online, provided they do not use military uniforms or IDF insignia.
How will I know when and where to vote?
Military polling stations will operate on Election Day from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Each unit will appoint an election officer responsible for informing soldiers of their polling station's exact location and operating hours.
Fixed polling stations will be established at military bases and facilities, while mobile stations will travel between troops stationed at military outposts, protecting communities, participating in training exercises or carrying out operational missions. Military polling stations will also operate in hospitals so that hospitalized soldiers registered with the IDF's medical liaison system, known as Ram 2, can vote.
Soldiers may vote at any military base where they are present on Election Day, even if it is not their permanent base. They may also choose to vote at a civilian polling station, provided they cast only one ballot. Voting more than once is a criminal offense.
How does identification work at military polling stations? 
Each military polling station will have an election committee consisting of two soldiers who will undergo training before Election Day and will be responsible for verifying voters' identities using military identification or valid civilian documents.
Active-duty soldiers may identify themselves using a military ID card, national identity card, valid driver's license bearing their photograph or valid Israeli passport accompanied by proof of military service. There is no need to bring the voter notification received by mail.
For combat troops operating beyond enemy lines without identification documents, including those deployed in Lebanon, identity verification may be carried out using military dog tags, identification by another soldier or a photographed copy of an identity document, such as a national ID card, driver's license or military ID.
At hospital polling stations, soldiers must present a military identification card bearing their photograph, whether as an enlisted soldier, officer or noncommissioned officer. Alternatively, they may present a civilian photo ID, such as a national identity card, driver's license or valid Israeli passport, together with a voting authorization form issued by hospital staff.
How does voting work?
Military voting uses a double-envelope system. Behind a privacy screen, soldiers place their chosen party's ballot slip inside a blue envelope. That envelope is then placed inside a white envelope bearing the soldier's personal details.
How are ballot secrecy and election integrity protected? 
At the end of voting, military ballot boxes will be transferred, locked, to the Central Elections Committee at the Knesset in Jerusalem for counting. The sealed ballot boxes will be collected by designated personnel trained as regional election officers and remain under their supervision until formally handed over at the Knesset.
How are the votes counted?
During the counting process, the blue envelope containing the ballot is separated for counting, while the white envelope bearing the soldier's personal information is destroyed. The entire process of opening ballot boxes and counting votes is conducted by the Central Elections Committee without IDF involvement.
When does early voting begin in the IDF? 
Combat soldiers deployed in operational areas and beyond enemy lines, including Gaza, Syria and Lebanon, will be eligible to vote beginning at 10 p.m. on October 20. Mobile polling stations will reach troops in the field to collect their ballots. Soldiers scheduled to participate in operational missions on Election Day will also be given the opportunity to vote in advance.
Can soldiers run for office or join political parties?
Soldiers are permitted to register as members of political parties, provided they do not identify themselves as military personnel. Senior civilian employees of the IDF and career military personnel may run as party candidates only if they terminate their military service at least 100 days before the election. Conscripts must arrange a deferment of military service at least 100 days before Election Day, while reservists on active duty must end their service at least 30 days before the election.
Can soldiers work at polling stations? 
Soldiers may work at civilian polling stations on Election Day in politically neutral roles, including election committee secretary, usher or election integrity inspector, provided they obtain their commander's approval. They may not serve as election committee members, party observers or employees of political parties.
Is photography allowed? 
As at civilian polling stations, photography is strictly prohibited inside military polling stations.
Do soldiers get Election Day off? 
Unlike civilians, IDF personnel are not entitled to a day off for the election. Military operations and routine activities will continue as usual.

Fu made the remarks while leading a Chinese delegation to the 2026 Arctic Circle Assembly, held from Thursday to Saturday in Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland. More than 2,500 representatives from over 70 countries and regions attended the event to discuss issues related to understanding, protecting, developing and governing the Arctic.

Changes including melting Arctic sea ice, shrinking ice sheets and rising temperatures are already taking place, Fu said, adding that climate change is the real issue that countries need to confront together.
She called on countries to pool their strengths and resources, enhance scientific research cooperation, jointly assess the challenges posed by climate change, and make early preparations.
Fu noted that a joint statement issued by the leaders of China and Iceland last year stressed stronger cooperation on climate change and green energy. Such practical cooperation can better demonstrate China's policy and intentions regarding its participation in Arctic affairs, she said.

China is willing to strengthen cooperation with other countries and promote a more just and equitable global governance system, she said.
Founded in 2013, the Arctic Circle holds its annual assembly in Iceland every October and serves as an important global platform for dialogue on Arctic affairs. ■

Farming and solar power are competing for land. Can agrivoltaics solve the problem?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:02:20 UTC
14:02:20 KST

Agrivoltaics could help to prevent farmland abandonment by protecting crops and boosting income. But some say the solution ignores the real problems.
As the sun moves westward across the sky in Murcia, Spain, solar panels capture its rays while sheltering diverse crops, from bell peppers to wine grapes and dragon fruit.
Known for its agriculture and abundant sunshine, this southeastern region is exploring whether, rather than competing for land, farming and solar energy can coexist peacefully.
“Agrivoltaics is the integration of food production with renewable energy production,” explains Silvia Tomasi, Senior Researcher at Eurac Research. This entails installing photovoltaic panels above, in between or at the margins of agricultural production, she adds.
A 2023 study estimated that Europe has the potential to generate 25 times its current electricity demand via agrivoltaics, also known as agri-PV.
Yet solar power is fraught with its own environmental and social costs. Requiring more land than other energy sources to generate the same amount of electricity, it has sparked conflicts over land use, especially in rural areas.
“Agrivoltaics has great potential: both economic benefits and environmental ones,” Tomasi says. “But then it’s always a matter of how the technology is implemented and who really benefits.”
Governments and Big Tech turn to agrivoltaics
The idea of turning southern Europe into a solar powerhouse received a high-profile endorsement in January, when Elon Musk said sparsely populated areas of Spain and Sicily could theoretically generate enough solar power for all of Europe.
Big Tech has already caught on. In southern Italy, Amazon and Apple have signed contracts to purchase power from large-scale agrivoltaic projects with a combined capacity of over 150 megawatts – enough to meet the yearly needs of roughly 100,000 Italian households.
Europe is also funding the shift. The EU-funded AGRISOL project intends to invest €1.9 million in agrivoltaics projects, including in Italy and Spain, while Italy alone has secured €1.7 billion in state aid for the initiative.
“For now, [agrivoltaics] is just a minimal contribution,” says Angelo Gentili, national secretary of Legambiente, Italy’s largest environmental organisation. “But if it expands, it will represent a big impulse for decarbonisation goals.”
Managing the impact on crops and land
EU and national rules increasingly require agriculture to remain a meaningful part of land where solar panels are installed. In France, projects must maintain at least 90 per cent of crop production compared to locally determined reference yields. In Italy, at least 70 per cent of the area must remain dedicated to agriculture.
Experts say not just any combination of solar and agriculture should qualify. “More than a definition, what we really need is a classification,” says Pilar Flores, who coordinates an EU-funded agrivoltaics project at the Murcian Institute for Agricultural and Environmental Research and Development (IMIDA). She says protecting agriculture should drive all classifications: “The key is to ensure there’s minimal loss [of arable land].”
Why use farmland rather than empty or abandoned land in the first place? Flores says the requirements are similar: relatively flat and near the grid. Unused land may also hold ecological value. “It’s not just a simple calculation of how much free land is left,” she says.
How agrivoltaics can benefit farmers
In some cases, agrivoltaics have been found to improve water-use efficiency, protect crops from extreme weather and increase the productivity of land. Solar installations can also help farmers face climate change. “Excessive rainfall and heat have heavily damaged agricultural fields, pushing farmers to abandon farmland,” says Gentili. “Agrivoltaics represent a great instrument to avoid land abandonment and profit gaps for farmers.”
Panels cast shade that can reduce evaporation, help soil retain moisture and offer relief to farmworkers and grazing animals. They can also protect crops from hail. Farmers can use the energy to power their own operations and sell any excess to the grid, or rent the space above their fields to energy producers.
But the benefits are not guaranteed, Flores warns. “All these opportunities are sometimes discussed as if they always happened, but it depends on the agrivoltaic system used and the specific characteristics of the site.” In Murcia, her team found that water-stressed peppers grew better under solar panels than well-watered ones. “You have to analyse each case and each location,” she says.
But who really benefits from agrivoltaics?
Not all farmers are convinced. To Fabrizio Garbarino, president of the Italian farmers’ union Associazione Rurale Italiana, agrivoltaics fail to address the root problems farmers face. “Agrivoltaics are taking advantage of the farming sector crisis in Italy while we should actually focus on real solutions for preventing farmland abandonment,” he says. “To me, this just sounds like a shortcut.”
Startups representing larger companies, including data centre developers, are hounding farmers for their land, he says. “Even if the energy produced is good, we’re taking away [farmers’] land to support businesses that require a lot of energy.”
Big Tech firms say agrivoltaic power-purchase agreements help them reach net-zero targets. But a PPA does not necessarily mean that the electricity from a particular solar farm physically supplies a particular company facility, and the exact carbon footprints of AI data centres remain opaque.
A 2025 study co-authored by Tomasi, based on expert interviews across four European regions, found that the benefits of agrivoltaics can favour large-scale farmers, landowners and investors over smaller farmers and local communities. It also found that excluding residents and ecosystems from decision-making can deepen existing power imbalances.
High upfront costs and grid connection queues mean large projects backed by multinationals tend to dominate the sector. A 2025 review by the Italian newspaper Today.it found that about 86 per cent of the roughly €775 million in government funds for agrivoltaic projects went to large-scale projects, including ones owned by foreign multinationals.
In September, a new agrivoltaics project financed by an Israeli company in Tuscany sparked widespread outrage and raised concerns over who gets to profit.
Tomasi says local communities must have a voice to ensure a just transition. “Big investors going into places they really don’t know anything about, with a top-down approach… and getting the economic benefits from the renewable energy generation side of agrivoltaics… shouldn’t be labelled as agrivoltaics, from my point of view.”
‘Agriculture should not be a secondary concern’
Flores says administrations can help by offering farmers funding and giving agrivoltaic systems priority access to the grid.
There is also the question of what kind of agriculture the income supports. To live up to the environmental promise, one study has noted, “the type of agriculture funded by the rental income from agrivoltaics should not be a secondary concern”. Instead, the author argues, this rent could subsidise agroecological practices or help farmers transition away from industrial farming.
Agrivoltaics has the potential to be mutually beneficial to farmers and the renewable energy sector. It can help protect farmland, support farmers facing climate change and contribute to Europe’s decarbonisation goals. But it also risks becoming a greenwashing opportunity, a crutch for unsustainable farming practices, or a way of meeting growing corporate energy demand on arable land. On its own, it is not a silver bullet. Much depends on how the systems are designed, who owns them and, ultimately, who benefits.
“The goal of agrivoltaics is to protect farmland and the entire ecosystem; that’s the philosophy,” says Flores. “We have to be able to distinguish that from other interests.”

Europe's best Christmas markets to visit in 2026, according to travellers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

Europe is world-famous for its Christmas markets, and more than 1,500 take place every year. Choosing which to visit can be as tricky as putting together your present wish list. Here are the top picks, as voted for by travellers.
As we get deeper into autumn, it feels as if we’ll blink and Christmas will be upon us.
With the festive season comes new opportunities to book a winter trip away, and a favourite must-do for many travellers is to visit a Christmas market.
There are more than 1,500 in Europe alone, and this year more than 800,000 travellers have voted for their favourites via the European Best Destinations platform.
A total of 20 were included in the final ranking, and we’re taking a closer look at the top five to give you some inspiration on where to go to shop, drink gleuwein and get into the festive spirit in 2026.
European Christmas markets: The top picks by travellers
Craiova, Romania
You might never have heard of Craiova, but the Romanian city has pipped far more famous Christmas markets to the top spot.
It’s an absolutely huge space, with more than 280,000 square meters transformed into a festive wonderland each year.
The theme in 2026 is The Nutcracker, and visitors will be able to see giant ornaments and toy-shaped sculptures along with countless sparkling lights.
The market, which runs from mid-November to early January, will also boast Eastern Europe’s highest-flying Santa sleigh, as well as an ice rink, a Ferris wheel, and traditional hand-painted chalets.
Visitors to the Craiova market also sing the praises of the food on offer here, which celebrates the flavours of Eastern Europe and beyond, serving dishes from the likes of Armenia, Georgia, Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia.
Zurich, Switzerland
Zurich may be better known for its chocolate and banking than Christmas markets, but the Swiss city has made a name for itself as one of Europe’s top festive destinations.
The main attraction is Wienachtsdorf at Sechseläutenplatz, between the Opera House and Lake Zurich. The market is filled with wooden chalets, twinkling lights and a huge Christmas tree, combining traditional Alpine touches with the city’s more polished feel.
There’s plenty more to discover beyond the main market, which was also voted as the most beautiful Christmas market in Europe. Weihnachtsallee near the main station is now in its third year, with around 80 rotating stalls selling international food, design-led crafts and, of course, plenty of fondue.
There’s even a dome dedicated to mulled wine, making it a popular spot for locals and visitors looking to warm up.
Zurich also puts its own artistic spin on the festive season with the Illuminarium at the Swiss National Museum. The courtyard is transformed with lights, music and immersive displays, adding something a little different to the city’s Christmas celebrations.
Riga, Latvia
Riga may not have the same name recognition as some of Europe’s bigger Christmas destinations, but Latvia’s capital puts on a seriously atmospheric festive display each winter.
The main market takes over Doma Square in the heart of the UNESCO-listed Old Town, with wooden chalets selling Latvian crafts, cosy knitwear and local treats.
From late November to early January, the square fills with the smells of mulled wine, roasted almonds and cinnamon, while choirs and folk performers add a distinctly Baltic feel.
But Riga’s Christmas appeal goes well beyond the market itself. The city is known for its spectacular lights, with parks, squares and canals transformed into a glowing winter wonderland.
Head to places including Opera Square, Bastejkalns and Kronvalda Park to see installations inspired by Latvian fairy tales, with light, music and storytelling bringing the festive season to life.
Lisbon, Portugal
Lisbon offers a slightly different take on the Christmas market, swapping snowy streets for mild temperatures and winter sunshine.
Wonderland Lisboa takes over Parque Eduardo VII from late November to early January, with the Portuguese capital’s biggest Christmas market returning for its 11th edition in 2026.
This year’s theme, “The Roots of Christmas”, brings together nature, art, food and entertainment, with local artisans, live performances and plenty of family-friendly attractions.
There’s also a Ferris wheel offering views across the city, alongside a traditional carousel and plenty of opportunities for Christmas shopping.
Food is a big part of the experience too, with the Wonderland Lisboa Food Court serving Portuguese festive favourites, regional specialities and seasonal sweets.
More than 1.2 million people visited in 2025, making it a popular choice for anyone who wants their Christmas market with a side of sunshine.
Debrecen, Hungary
Hungary’s second-largest city may be less famous than the capital Budapest, but it certainly knows how to do Christmas properly.
In the winter, Debrecen’s main squares and pedestrian streets are transformed with glowing installations and wooden stalls selling handmade crafts, toys, decorations and Christmas ornaments.
There’s plenty of food to enjoy too, with classic festive treats including mulled wine, roasted chestnuts and kürtőskalács, the sweet Hungarian chimney cake.
More than 100 cultural events are held throughout the season, featuring more than 200 performers, while families can make the most of an ice rink and the Fairytale Town attraction.
There are also plenty of special events, including traditional advent candle-lighting ceremonies and a St Nicholas weekend complete with a carriage arrival, concerts and a mini train.
The top 20 best European Christmas markets
According to traveller votes via European Best Destinations:
- 1. Craiova, Romania
- 2. Zurich, Switzerland

ESA director general reveals €10bn plan to get to space without NASA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:33 UTC
14:00:33 KST

The space industry, currently valued at €600 billion, is expected to grow by 10% a year, according to European Space Agency (ESA) director general Josef Aschbacher. He spoke to the Big Question about how Europe can benefit from this booming industry.
The European Space Agency received record budget commitments of more than €22 billion from member states at its ministerial council meeting in 2025, a 32% increase on 2022.
Member states also gave ESA a historic mandate to use space technology for non-aggressive security and defence, including technologies to monitor external borders.
With that backing, ESA director general Josef Aschbacher wants Europe to take its next big step: developing the ability to launch its own astronauts into space.
In the latest episode of The Big Question, Josef sat down with Hannah Brown to discuss Europe’s independent future in space.
‘Why don’t we do it ourselves?’
Since its founding in 1975 (and its first astronaut mission in 1983), the European Space Agency has relied on international partners, including NASA and Russia, for astronaut launches.
And while this arrangement has worked for all this time, geopolitical tensions are pushing Europe to seek an alternative.
Only the US, China and Russia have the capability to launch astronauts into space. But political tensions with China and Russia leave ESA reliant on the US.
And in recent years, NASA has partnered with SpaceX to launch astronauts into space. One way or another, today, ESA astronauts travel to space aboard a US spacecraft.
“SpaceX has already announced that they want to decommission Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon (the crew vehicles that bring the astronauts to space) probably around 2029,” Josef explained.
“That means in a few years, we will not have at least this capability available anymore. There may be others coming up, which we do not know today.”
This leaves Europe facing uncertainty over how to get its astronauts into space in the future.
To ensure reliable access and support investment in European industry, Josef is developing a plan for Europe to strengthen its position as a global space power by gaining the ability to launch its own astronauts.
Is space autonomy good for the European economy?
Of course, this won’t happen overnight and it needs political approval from ESA’s member states to secure funding.
Here’s how it might work.
Europe isn’t starting completely from scratch. It already has strong technological capabilities and world-leading programmes like Copernicus (Earth observation) and Galileo (satellite navigation constellation), as well as a talented workforce.
But Europe lacks its own crew vehicle and recovery system, in other words the means to get astronauts up there and bring them safely back to Earth.
Josef estimated that with a budget of around €10 billion, ESA could develop these independent capabilities in the next 10 years.
And yes, €10 billion is an enormous amount of money, but what’s the alternative?
ESA is facing the prospect of spending billions of euros in the coming years either way. The question is how to turn that spending into an investment in Europe’s space industry rather than simply a cost.
The International Space Station is essentially a floating laboratory where ESA does much of its vital science. After its decommission in 2032, this is likely to be replaced by a commercial space station.
Without its independent access to space, Europe will have to continue to rely on buying seats aboard US spacecraft with uncertain availability and then rent facilities aboard commercial space stations for research. Josef estimated that this would come at a cost of around €5 billion over the next 10 years.
“But the money is lost, or lost in the sense it's being spent not in Europe. So I'd rather invest this funding in Europe, strengthen our industry, increase the autonomy of Europe in this domain,” Josef explained.
But he stressed this would not mean an end to international collaboration for Europe.
“[We could] even offer a seat maybe to our friends and colleagues from Japan or Australia or some other countries, and I think this is also something that Europe could consider to build up its own strength, its autonomy, not to isolate, not at all - the opposite, but to be a strong partner internationally to other countries and other agencies.”
The Big Question is a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.
Watch the video above to see the full discussion with the European Space Agency.

Abhijeet Dipke’s mother says family unable to contact him
NEW DELHI: The mother of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, Anita Dipke, on Sunday accused Delhi Police of lying about informing her son of his grandmother’s death, saying the family had been unable to contact him and had postponed the last rites until he could return.“We have not been able to contact him...Delhi Police is lying. If he got the news (his grandmother's demise), he would have come immediately...we have put the last rites on hold for him...” Anita Dipke said.Delhi Police had earlier said it informed Dipke about his grandmother’s death while he remained in detention in the national capital ahead of the party’s proposed protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“It is now up to him whether he wants to stay back and continue the protest under detention or fly back for the last rites,” Delhi Police sources told news agency ANI on Saturday.Dipke’s paternal grandmother, Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke, 85, died at her home in Santuk Pimpri village in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district at 11.30 am on Saturday following a prolonged illness, family sources told PTI. She had been unwell for about a month and was previously hospitalised in Hingoli.
Her last rites were scheduled for 10 am on Sunday.An Executive Magistrate has ordered the release of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convenor Saurav Das and party leader Ashutosh Ranka following their preventive detention by Delhi Police on Saturday.The three were detained after arriving in the national capital from Mumbai to participate in the party’s proposed ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest, which sought the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Delhi Police had denied permission for the demonstration, citing public safety, traffic management and law-and-order concerns. Security was subsequently tightened across the capital ahead of the planned protest.
